body:
[Lemma lem:Metzler largest eigenvalue of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] Suppose that $M$ is a $d\times d$ Metzler matrix. Let $r$ denote the largest eigenvalue of $M$. Let $r'$ denote the maximum over $\varnothing\ne I\subsetneq[d]$ of the largest eigenvalue of the (Metzler) matrix $M^I$. Then $r'\le r$.
\begin{proof}
    This lemma, but for specifically non-negative matrices rather than general Metzler matrices, is Proposition 4 in [Gantmacher_1959]. To extend to Metzler matrices $M$, let $N:=M+\alpha I_d$ for some $\alpha\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ no smaller in absolute value than all diagonal entries of $M$, so that $N$ is non-negative. Then the largest eigenvalue of $N$ is $r+\alpha$. Moreover, for each $\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[d]$ the largest eigenvalue of $N^I$ is $\alpha$ plus the largest eigenvalue of $M^I$. It follows that the maximum over $I$ of the largest eigenvalue of $N^I$ is $r'+\alpha$. Since the lemma holds for non-negative matrices we have $r'+\alpha\le r+\alpha$; the lemma in full generality follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:Metzler largest eigenvalue of arXiv:2507.09421

DRAFT independently checked special-case derivation (w359 KEEP). For centered isotropic X=Exp(1)-1 observed through independent Gaussian noise of variance t>0, let Y=X+sqrt(t)G with independent G~N(0,1), nu_t=Law(Y), T_t f(y)=E[f(X)|Y=y], and D_rho(g)=integral |gprime|^2 d rho. Test f_a(x)=exp(a x), 0<a<1/2. A positive-tail calculation gives liminf as a increases to 1/2 of D_nu_t(T_t f_a)/D_mu(f_a)>=exp(-t/4). Hence any all-function coefficient q(t) must be at least exp(-t/4). At t=1 the explicit a=49/100 test has ratio greater than 7/10, using only the tail y>=5 in the untranslated observation coordinates. The exact Gaussian affine coefficient 1/4 at t=1 cannot hold for this law. This does not refute existence of some q<1.

[Lemma 84 (First Picard multiplier products) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Put $\alpha_V=1/2-\betasum-\kappa$ and let $V\in C_T\cC^{\alpha_V}$ be spatially localized.  If $G\in C_TH^\lambda\cap L_T^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma}$ with $\lambda\ge0$, $0<\sigma<\alpha_V$, and
\[
  r<\min\{\alpha_V,\lambda\},
\]
then
\begin{align}
  \norm{VG}_{C_TH^r}
  +\norm{VG}_{L_T^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma}}
  \lesssim
  \norm{V}_{C_T\cC^{\alpha_V}}
  \paren{\norm{G}_{C_TH^\lambda}+\norm{G}_{L_T^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma}}}.
\end{align}
The same conclusion holds when $G$ is another localized $\cC^{\alpha_V}$ function, with any $r<\alpha_V$.  Consequently every term in $\mathscr U_{\W}^\rho \mathscr U_{\K}^\rho$ containing at least one first Picard factor belongs to
\[
  L_T^1H^{s_2-1}\cap L_T^1B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma-1},
\]
with an explicit factor $T$ and the corresponding bilinear Lipschitz bounds.

body: [Lem touching-loops of arXiv:2604.14122, 'The scaling limit of random walk and\\ the intrinsic metric on planar critical percolation'] There exists a coupling such that almost surely $(\Lambda_n,d^{{\mathrm {path}}}_n,\pi_n) \to (\Lambda,d^{{\mathrm {path}}},\pi)$ in GHf and the following holds. Suppose that $(\Lambda_n,d^{{\mathrm {path}}}_n,\pi_n)$ and $(\Lambda,d^{{\mathrm {path}}},\pi)$ are isometrically embedded into a common metric space $(W,d_W)$ such that the sequence converges under the $\Delta_{\Haus}+\Delta_f$ metric in~(equation eq:ghf of the paper). Let $\gamma,\gamma'$ be two different $\CLE_6$ loops that touch at a prime end $z\in\Lambda$ that is outside the loops $\gamma,\gamma'$. Let $\gamma_n,\gamma'_n$ be percolation interface loops converging to $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ respectively. Then there exists $n_0$ such that for all $n\geq n_0$, the loops $\gamma_n$ and $\gamma'_n$ touch (i.e., come within distance $1$ of each other) at a point $z_n$ such that $z_n\rightarrow z$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ in $d_W$ (and hence also $\pi_n(z_n) \to \pi(z)$ in $\mathbf R^2$). The analogous statement holds for a loop $\gamma$ that touches itself at a point $z$, and for a loop $\gamma$ that touches the boundary $\partial [0,1]^2$.

body: Every elliptic curve over Q is modular: its L-function coincides with that of a weight-2 newform of level equal to the curve's conductor. Proved by Wiles and Taylor-Wiles for semistable curves (1995) - enough, with Ribet's level-lowering and Frey's construction, to yield Fermat's Last Theorem - and completed for all curves by Breuil-Conrad-Diamond-Taylor (2001). It is the GL_2 case of the Langlands program's bridge between arithmetic and automorphic forms.
title: Modularity Theorem

[Proposition lim-TtoInf of arXiv:2504.18739, 'discrete analogues of second-order Riesz transforms'] For a compactly supported function $f:\mathbb{Z}^d\to \mathbb{R}$, the limit in~(equation limitcP_A of the paper) exists and 
\[
    \mathcal{P}_A(f)(n)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}^d}\mathcal{K}_A(n,m)f(m),
\]
where 
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{K}_A(n,m)= \int_0^\infty \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}H_s(x)\nabla \left(\frac{P_s(x-m)}{H_s(x)}\right)\cdot A(x,s)\nabla \left(\frac{P_s(x-n)}{H_s(x)}\right)\,dx ds.    
\end{align}

$Z_t = Z_u + (t-u)ae_i$ for some $i=1,2$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}$,
one has $\mathbb{A}_{u,v}(Z) = 0$.

[Lemma eq:shuff0 of arXiv:2411.06827, 'The Exponential Lie Series and a Chen--Strichartz Formula for L{\'e}vy Processes'] With the notation of the previous section, we obtain
$$
	\mathrm{Id}=\sum\limits_{w\in{\mathbb A}^\ast}w\otimes\overline w=\sum\limits_{w^0\in({\mathbb A}^0)^\ast}w^0\otimes\overline w^0.
$$
Further, the expression of the coproduct in the basis $(\overline{\mathbb A}^0)^\ast$ of ${\mathbb R} {\langle}\overline{\mathbb A}{\rangle}$ dualises to the expression of the product $\star$  as a shuffle product in the basis $({\mathbb A}^0)^\ast$ of ${\mathbb R} {\langle}{\mathbb A}{\rangle}$:
\begin{align}
	(a_1^0\cdots a_n^0) \star (a_{n+1}^0\cdots a_{n+m}^0)
	&=\sum\limits_{\sigma\in Sh(n,m)}a^0_{\sigma(1)}\cdots a^0_{\sigma(n+m)} \\
	&=:(a_1^0\cdots a_n^0){\,\llcorner\!\llcorner\!\!\!\lrcorner\,} (a_{n+1}^0 \cdots a_{n+m}^0),
\end{align}
for  $a_i^0\in{\mathbb A}^0$, and where $Sh(n,m)$ stands for the set of permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n+m\}=:[n+m]$ such that $\sigma^{-1}(1) < \cdots < \sigma^{-1}(n)$ and $\sigma^{-1}(n+1)< \cdots < \sigma^{-1}(n+m)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma eq:shuff0 of arXiv:2411.06827

body: Let A and B be n by n normal matrices (A A* = A* A, B B* = B* B) with eigenvalues alpha_1, ..., alpha_n and beta_1, ..., beta_n respectively. Then there exists a permutation pi of {1, ..., n} such that sum_{i=1}^n |alpha_i - beta_{pi(i)}|^2 <= ||A - B||_F^2. [Lemma 16 of arXiv:2608.26662, 'Boundary–Moment Universality and Curvature Corrections in Random Geometric Graphs on Riema'] Let \(W_n\) be nonnegative integer-valued random variables and put
$\lambda_n:=\E W_n$.
Suppose that \((\lambda_n)\) is uniformly bounded and that
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}
\bigl(
\mathcal L(W_n),
\operatorname{Po}(\lambda_n)
\bigr)
\le
C\eps_n.
\]
Then
\[
\Pp\{W_n=0\}
=
e^{-\lambda_n}
+
O(\eps_n).
\]

Moreover, suppose that
$a_n\downarrow0$,
$\eps_n=o(a_n)$,
and
$\lambda_n
=
\lambda_0+\lambda_1a_n+o(a_n)$.
Then
\[
\log\Pp\{W_n=0\}
=
-\lambda_0-\lambda_1a_n+o(a_n).
\]

The logarithmic conclusion is uniform on a parameter set \(K\) whenever
the total-variation bound, the upper bound on \(\lambda_n\), and the
expansion of \(\lambda_n\) are all uniform on \(K\).

[Definition def:godel-translation of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] We inductively define the \emph{G\"odel translation} $(\cdot)^G: \mathscr{L}_p \to \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$:
  \begin{align*}
    \bot^G &\coloneq \Box \bot, &
    p^G &\coloneq \Box p, \\
    (\psi_1 \land \psi_2)^G &\coloneq \psi_1^G \land \psi_2^G, &
    (\psi_1 \lor \psi_2)^G &\coloneq \psi_1^G \lor \psi_2^G, \\
    (\psi_1 \to \psi_2)^G &\coloneq \Box(\psi_1^G \to \psi_2^G).
  \end{align*}

[Thm 12 (Stationary coupling) of arXiv:2604.12853, 'Coupling Markov Chains \\with a Common Image Chain'] Consider stationary time-homogeneous Markov chains  $\Xoriginal$, $\Yoriginal$, and $\Zoriginal$ with time indexed by  $t\in\mathbb{Z}$.
    Suppose for maps $f: A \to C$ and $g: B \to C$ that \[(f(\Xoriginal_t))_{t \in \mathbb{Z}} \eqdist \Zoriginal \eqdist (g(\Yoriginal_t))_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}.\]
    Then there is a stationary Markov chain $(X_t,Y_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ such that $(X_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}} \eqdist \Xoriginal$, $(Y_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}} \eqdist \Yoriginal$, and $f(X_t) = g(Y_t)$ for all $t \in \mathbb{Z}$. Moreover, $(X_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and $(Y_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ may be taken to be conditionally independent given $(f(X_t))_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stationary coupling

In a finite graph with inherited positive edge weights, give each simple n-edge path starting at a probability proportional to its product weight, with terminal vertex free, and assume positive total weight C_n(G;a). Define C_m(H;v) as the total weight of simple m-edge paths from v in H, with C_0=1 for a retained vertex. At a realized k-edge prefix eta, delete all its visited vertices except its tip to get G_eta. For a forbidden vertex or edge set A excluding a, the conditional avoidance probability is zero if the prefix hit A, and otherwise C_(n-k)(G_eta minus A;tip)/C_(n-k)(G_eta;tip). The denominator is positive on every realized prefix; at k=n use the avoidance indicator. Replacing C_(n-k) by an all-length partition sum changes the model.
Finite graph, fixed length n, positive inherited weights, C_n(G;a)>0
Free endpoint; no prescribed chordal terminal point
Only realized prefixes are divided by; forbidden vertices exclude the start

[Lemm l:removing-completion of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] Let $(\Xi,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be as in (def:white-noise of the paper), and let $\mathcal{N}$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by all $\mathbb{P}$-null subsets in $\mathcal{F}$.
    Fix any sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}\subset \mathcal{F}$ and write $\overline{\mathcal{G}}\coloneqq \mathcal{G}\vee\mathcal{N}$.
    Let $S$ be a Polish space and let $Z:(\Xi,\overline{\mathcal{G}}) \to (S,\mathcal{B}(S))$ be a $\overline{\mathcal{G}}$-measurable $S$-valued random variable.
    Then there exists a $\mathcal{G}$-measurable $Y:(\Xi,\mathcal{G})\to (S,\mathcal{B}(S))$ such that $\mathbb{P}(Z=Y)=1$, where the event $\{Z=Y\} \in \overline{\mathcal{G}}$.
title: Lemm l:removing-completion of arXiv:2607.18194

body: [Lemma 11 of arXiv:2609.04139, 'The conformally invariant metric on CLE$_4$ II:\\ existence of geodesics'] Let $z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4$ be points on $\partial \BD$ ordered counterclockwise. Let $\{\eta_{12}, \eta_{34}\}$ be a bichordal SLE$_4$ in $\BD$ with link pattern $\{\{z_1, z_2\}, \{z_3, z_4\}\}$. Fix $\delta \in (0,1)$ and let $z_0 \in \partial \BD$ be such that $\dist(z_0, \{z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4\}) \geq \delta$. Then, there exists a constant $C =  C(\delta) > 0$, uniform over all such configurations, such that for all $\varepsilon > 0$, the probability that both $\eta_{12}$ and $\eta_{34}$ intersect $B_{\varepsilon}(z_0)$ is at most $C \varepsilon^4$. (For $\varepsilon$ bounded below, the estimate holds trivially after enlarging $C(\delta)$.) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 11 of arXiv:2609.04139

[Proposition prop:harmonic-grad of arXiv:2609.02987, 'Tail Likelihood Reinforcement Learning'] Under (as:tailrl-smooth,as:tailrl-finite,as:tailrl-bounded of the paper), for every $\theta\in U$ and every $T \ge 1$,
\begin{equation}
\nabla_\theta J^{(T)}_{\mathrm{TailRL{}}}(\theta;x)
=
\sum_{k=1}^{T} \frac{1}{k}\,\nabla_\theta\, \text{\emph{Best-of-}}k(\theta;x)
=
\int_0^1 \frac{1-\big(1-p_\theta(x,\tau)\big)^{T}}{p_\theta(x,\tau)}\,\nabla_\theta p_\theta(x,\tau)\,d\tau .

\end{equation}

[Theorem 13 (Power-sum convergence principle) of arXiv:2608.24616, '2608.24616'] Let $P(t)=(P_j(t))_{j\geq1}$, $t>0$, be random finitely supported
subprobability weight sequences, independent of iid random variables
$X,X_1,X_2,\ldots$.  Thus,
almost surely, $P_j(t)\geq0$, only finitely many entries are nonzero, and
$\sum_jP_j(t)\leq1$.  Suppose that
\[
  \E X=0,\qquad 0<\E|X|<\infty.
\]
Put
\[
  R_t=\sum_jP_j(t)X_j,
  \qquad m_t(s)=\E\sum_jP_j(t)^s\quad(s>0).
\]
Suppose that, for some $r\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t>0}m_t(r)<\infty,
  \qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}m_t(1)\ \hbox{exists},
  
\end{equation}
and that $R_t$ converges in distribution to a nondegenerate random
variable.  Then there are $p\in(1,2]$ and $c\in(0,1]$ such that
\begin{equation}
  m_t(p)\longrightarrow c.
  
\end{equation}
More precisely, with
\[
 X_+=\max(X,0),\qquad X_-=\max(-X,0),
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 a_+&=\sup\{q>0:\E X_+^q<\infty\},\\
 a_-&=\sup\{q>0:\E X_-^q<\infty\},\\
 a_X&=\min(a_+,a_-),
 \end{aligned}
\]
one may take any fixed $p\in(1,2)$ when $a_X=1$, $p=a_X$ when
$1<a_X<2$, and $p=2$ when $a_X\geq2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Power-sum convergence principle

body: For an invertible matrix A and a choice of induced operator norm ||.||, the condition number of A is kappa(A) = ||A|| * ||A^{-1}||. For the linear system A*x = b, kappa(A) governs the worst-case amplification of relative perturbations: if (A+dA)(x+dx) = b+db for small perturbations dA, db, then to first order the relative error of the computed solution satisfies ||dx||/||x|| is bounded, up to a constant, by kappa(A) * ( ||dA||/||A|| + ||db||/||b|| ). In the matrix 2-norm, kappa_2(A) = sigma_max(A) / sigma_min(A), the ratio of the largest to smallest singular values of A. Always kappa(A) >= 1; a matrix with large kappa(A) is called ill-conditioned, and one with kappa(A) close to 1 is well-conditioned.
title: Condition Number of a Linear System

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN label-deletion method;
UNCHECKED this exact active-field bound. The claim concerns the actual
source process at every finite time, including long times at fixed p.

Use the sparse critical synchronous particle-hole law on Z^d, d>=1,
P(eta=1)=P(eta=-1)=p, P(eta=0)=1-2p, 0<p<1/2. Let A_t count active
particles, H_t indicate unfilled holes, h_t=E A_t(0)=E H_t(0), and
r=p/(1-2p). For every site x and every nonnegative measurable function
F of the final active-count and hole fields,

    E[A_t(x) F(A_t-delta_x,H_t)] <= r E[F(A_t,H_t)].

The left function is evaluated only when A_t(x)>0. Consequently, with
falling factorials and every integer k>=1,

    E(A_t(x))_k <= r^(k-1) h_t,
    E A_t(x)^2 <= (1+r)h_t,
    P(A_t(x)>0) >= (1-r/2)h_t.

The last inequality remains valid when its right side is negative, and
is informative for sparse p. In particular surviving active particles
have uniformly controlled multiplicities relative to their density.

## 1. A law-equivalent marked-label construction

Give each possible initial +1 excess particle a label equal to its origin
y, an independent infinite nearest-neighbor walk, and independent continuous
tie priorities at each round. At a hole, settle the smallest-priority
arriving label. This chooses uniformly among arrivals; fresh priorities
make it a construction of exactly the source law. All random variables
are assigned even to origins that do not initially have a particle.

If label y is active at x after round t, it has never settled during
those rounds. Delete it by changing eta(y)=1 to 0, keeping all assigned
walks and priorities. All other trajectories and hole fillings through t
are unchanged. Prove this round by round: at any unfilled hole visited
by y, some other label was the priority winner, since y remains active;
deleting a loser leaves the winner unchanged. Visits to filled holes
have no effect. Away from its presence nothing changes. Thus the final
fields after deletion are exactly A_t-delta_x,H_t.

This argument must use an active, never-settled label. Deleting a settled
particle can change which holes fill and does not have this property.
It uses per-label walks, a law-equivalent construction, rather than
pretending deletion leaves fixed site-stack indices unchanged.

## 2. Change of initial-sign weight and summation

For a fixed origin y, the deletion map is injective on the full assigned
randomness; the original sign is recovered as +1. Its measure changes by
the factor (1-2p)/p, so the contribution from that active label is at most

    r E[1{eta(y)=0} 1{X_t^y=x} F(A_t,H_t)].

The image also obeys constraints making the restored label stay active,
but dropping these constraints only increases the expectation. When
eta(y)=0 its assigned walk is unused by the base process and independent
of both final fields. Hence this bound equals

    r p_t(x-y) E[1{eta(y)=0}F(A_t,H_t)].

Sum over origins y. Every active particle at x has exactly one origin,
and Tonelli applies to nonnegative contributions. Since sum_y p_t(x-y)=1,

    E[A_t(x)F(A_t-delta_x,H_t)]
      <=r E[F(A_t,H_t) sum_y p_t(x-y)1{eta(y)=0}]
      <=r E F(A_t,H_t).

No independence of the survival events is used. At fixed t only finitely
many origins can reach x, so the sum also has a finite-propagation version.

## 3. Factorial moments and occupancy

Take F(A,H)=(A(x))_(k-1). For k>=2 the inequality gives
E(A_t(x))_k<=r E(A_t(x))_(k-1), proving the first assertion by induction
from E A_t(x)=h_t. The k=2 case yields
E A_t(x)^2=E(A_t(x))_2+h_t<=(1+r)h_t.

For each nonnegative integer n,
n-1{n>0}<=(n)_2/2. Taking expectations gives
h_t-P(A_t(x)>0)<=r h_t/2 and the occupancy bound.

## Source and scope

Primary model: Bou-Rabee--Panagiotis, arXiv:2609.02820v1, Section 2,
Theorem 1.6's sparse law, and the one-particle per-label walk construction
used in Proposition 8.3. Source (47) supplies equal mean active and hole
density. No stochastic domination of the whole field is claimed here;
the displayed Campbell inequality and its moment consequences are what

[Theorem 88 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Assume that 

(i) $\sigma$ and $b$ are smooth
and $b$ is bounded;

(ii)  there is a nonnegative integer $k$ and
there are Borel functions $b_{i}(t,x)$,
$0\leq i\leq k$, 
such that $b =\sum_{i=0}^{k}b_{i} $,  and 
we are given properly tight $(d_{0},q_{i},p_{i})$,
$i\leq k$. Furthermore, for
$$
\hat{b}_{\rho}=\sup_{r\leq\rho}r
\sup_{C\in \bC_{r}}\sum_{i=0}^{k}
\dashnorm b_{i}\|_{L_{(q_{i},p_{i})}(C)},
$$  
and the constant $  N_{0}=N_{0}(d,\delta)$, which is the constant from   Corollary \ref{corollary 3.26.1},
 we have  
\begin{equation}
                    
N_{0}\hat{b}_{\rho_{b}}< \sfb_{0}   
\end{equation}
for some $\rho_{b}\in(0,\infty)$
(note strict inequality). 
Then
\begin{equation} 
                          
 \bar b_{ \rho_{b}}\leq \sfb_{0}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\left(

-\lambda_1^n(t,X_{t-})
+\lambda_2^n(t,X_{t-})

\right]

+
\mathbb E^{\mathbb P_1^n}\!\left[

H\!\left(
\eta_1^n(t,X_{t-},\cdot)\,\middle\|\,\eta_2^n(t,X_{t-},\cdot)

\right].

body:
[Lemma LEM:sol of arXiv:2512.23957, 'Concentration and fluctuations of sine-Gordon measure around topological multi-soliton man'] Let $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] When $x>\xi$,
\begin{align*}
2e^{-|x-\xi|} \le |m_{\xi }(x) -2\pi  | \le 4 e^{-|x-\xi|}, \quad 2 e^{-|x-\xi|}  \le |m_{\xi }^{-}(x)  | \le 4 e^{-|x-\xi|},
\end{align*}

\noindent
uniformly in all centers $\xi$ and all $x\in \mathbb{R}$.

\medskip  

\item[(ii)] When $x<\xi$,
\begin{align*}
2 e^{-|x-\xi|} \le |m_{\xi }(x)  | \le 4 e^{-|x-\xi|}, \quad 2 e^{-|x-\xi|}   \le |m_{\xi }^{-}(x)-2\pi  | \le 4 e^{-|x-\xi|},
\end{align*}

\noindent
uniformly in all centers $\xi$ and all $x\in \mathbb{R}$.

\medskip 

\item[(iii)] 
We have
\begin{align*}
|\partial_{\xi} m_{\xi}(x) |
+|\partial_{\xi}^2 m_{\xi}(x) | 
\le 4 e^{-|x-\xi|},  
\quad |\partial_{\xi} m_{\xi}^{-}(x) |
+|\partial_{\xi}^2 m_{\xi}^{-}(x)| 
\le 4 e^{-|x-\xi|},  
\end{align*} 

\noindent
uniformly in all centers $\xi$ and all $x\in \mathbb{R}$. The same holds with $\xi$-derivatives replaced by $x$-derivatives. 

\end{itemize}

\begin{proof}
The parts (i) and (ii) follow from direct computation using $m_{\xi}(x)=4\arctan (e^{x-\xi})$ and $m^{-}_{\xi}(x)=4\arctan(e^{-(x-\xi)})$.
The part (iii) follows from the fact that $\partial_{\xi}m_{\xi}(x)=-2\textup{sech}(x-\xi)$,
and $\partial_{\xi}^2  m_{\xi}(x) =2 \textup{tanh}(x-\xi) \textup{sech}(x-\xi)$ and direct computations.
These derivatives are highly localized profile around $\xi$ with an exponentially decaying tail.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma LEM:sol of arXiv:2512.23957

Let kappa,a0 be the positive constants in claim006v2. Set epsilon=eta>0,
38<lambda_1<38+kappa and lambda_2>38. Run ordinary bias-corrected Adam
on H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2), standard m0=v0=0, with

The second coordinate's scaled preconditioned curvature is exactly
 eta*lambda_2/(sqrt(vhat_2,t+1)+epsilon)=lambda_2>38 at every t.
The gradient is exactly aligned with the first coordinate, so the scaled
active curvature equals the first coordinate's scaled curvature and tends
to 38 by claim006v2. The scaled top sharpness tends to lambda_2>38 and
is at least lambda_2 from time 0. In particular it remains a positive
fixed distance above 38 while the active curvature tends to 38.

There is no requirement lambda_2>lambda_1: it is the PRECONDITIONED
eigenvalue that is top. In this family, lambda_2>38 is also necessary for
a strictly positive asymptotic top-sharpness gap. The full asymptotic
formula is eta S_t ->max(38,lambda_2), since the active first coordinate
has limit 38. lambda_2=38 gives zero limiting gap and lambda_2<38 makes
the active coordinate eventually top. The gradient-alignment condition
here is exact: g_2,t=0, not merely small. The initial condition is a
coordinate subspace, not an almost-sure generic two-dimensional start.

This completes the active-convergence step absent from Fong-Yang's
illustrative dormant-coordinate example (arXiv:2608.20638v2 p.7), only
on the near-threshold standard-initialization range proved in claim006.

gradient has no component in the supercritical top eigendirection.
If k_2<38, both weights are positive, and equivalently
 g_1^2/g_2^2=(d_1/d_2)*(38-k_2)/(k_1-38).
If k_2>38 equality is impossible for a nonzero gradient.

approximately aligned trajectories. Persistence for the exact dormant

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Renewal-type argument on the cluster process viewed from the local maximum: depth-h count as a branching-like functional of the concentric decomposition. Result: Writing the cluster as the field pinned at a local maximum, e^{-alpha h} E nu(f_h) is the expected number of points at depth h weighted by e^{-alpha h}; the concentric decomposition expresses the cluster as a random walk with a Bessel-like entropic repulsion plus independent fine fields, so f_h is a sum over scales k <= log(h) of contributions, each of order e^{alpha h} times the probability that the walk is at height h at scale k. A renewal theorem for the walk under entropic repulsion would give the limit; the walk is not a true random walk (steps depend on scale through the binding fields), which is where the existing tools stop. Existence of the limit is therefore reduced to a scale-inhomogeneous renewal theorem. Obstruction: Scale inhomogeneity of the concentric-decomposition walk defeats the standard renewal theorem.

[Thm restate of X and nu of arXiv:2607.19658, 'Hitting time mixing for random $k$-cycles'] Let $n_1,n_2,\ldots$,$k_1,k_2,\ldots$, and $t_1,t_2,\ldots$ be sequences of positive integers such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}n_N=\infty$.
\item $2\le k_N\le n_N$ for all $N\ge 1$, and $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{k_N}{n_N/(\log n_N)^4}=0$.
\item $|t_N-\frac{n_N\log n_N}{k_N}|\le \frac{n_N}{2k_N}\log\log\log n_N$ for all $N\ge 1$. 
\end{enumerate}
Define the measures $X_{t_N},\nu_{t_N}$ over $\mathfrak{S}_{n_N}$ the same way as in (sec: Intro of the paper). Then, we have 
$$\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}d_{TV}(X_{t_N},\nu_{t_N})\cdot(\log n_N)^{5/2}=0.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm restate of X and nu of arXiv:2607.19658

[Defi 32 of arXiv:2606.24887, '2606.24887'] A pair $(U,\patchi)$ consisting of a graph $U$ and a path $\patchi=(\chi_1,e_1,\chi_2,e_2,...,e_{n-1},\chi_n)$ with $\chi_1,...,\chi_n \in V(U)$ and $e_1,...,e_{n-1} \in E(U)$ is \textup{normal} if the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $V(U) = \{\chi_1,...,\chi_n\} = [s] $ where $s = |V(U)|$.
    \item The vertices of $U$ are visited by $\patchi $ in increasing order, i.e if $\chi_{i} \notin \{\chi_1,....,\chi_{i-1}\}$ then $\chi_i > \max_{j \le i-1} \chi_j$.
\end{enumerate}
 We set  $|\patchi| := n-1$ and call it the \textup{length of $\patchi$}. 
 For each $e \in E(U)$, we set $m_{e}(\patchi) := |\{ i \in [n-1] \colon e_i=e\}|$ the \textup{multiplicity} of $e$ in $\patchi$, i.e.\ the number of times the path $\patchi$ 
 traverses the edge $e$.
title: Definition 32 of arXiv:2606.24887

body:
[Definition 10 (Constrained dynamic) of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] Fix $H_-,H_+:D\mapsto \mathbb R$ with $H_-\le H_+$ pointwise,
let $\Omega_{H_\pm}$ be the set of tiling configurations in $\Omega_D$ such that  ${H_-}\le H_\eta\le {H_+}$ (we assume $\Omega_{H_\pm}\ne \emptyset$) and fix an initial
condition $\eta_0\in\Omega_{H_\pm}$. The Glauber dynamic
with \emph{floor constraint} $H_-$ and \emph{ceiling constraint}
$H_+$ is the Markov chain on $\Omega_{H_\pm}$ that is defined just like the original Glauber dynamic, except that any update that would violate the constraint $H_-\le H_{\eta_t}\le H_+$ is discarded.

Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have INDEPENDENT coordinates taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces, and let P be the product law on the product space. For a subset A and a point x define the convex distance d_T(x, A) = sup { inf_{y in A} sum_{i=1}^n alpha_i 1{x_i != y_i} : alpha in R^n, alpha_i >= 0, |alpha|_2 <= 1 }. Then for every measurable A, E[ exp( d_T(X, A)^2 / 4 ) ] <= 1 / P(A), and consequently P(A) P( d_T(X, A) >= t ) <= exp( - t^2 / 4 ) for every t > 0. COROLLARY for convex Lipschitz functions: if f : [0,1]^n -> R is CONVEX and 1-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm and the coordinates of X are independent with values in [0,1], then for every t > 0, P( |f(X) - M| >= t ) <= 4 exp( - t^2 / 4 ) where M is a median of f(X). The hypotheses are exactly: independence, a product structure, and for the corollary convexity together with a bounded range. Convexity cannot be dropped - the conclusion is false for general Lipschitz functions of bounded independent variables at this strength, which is why the bounded-differences (McDiarmid) inequality with its sum-of-squared-ranges denominator is the general-purpose tool and Talagrand's is the sharp one for convex functionals. The centring is at a MEDIAN; converting to the mean costs an absolute constant. [Talagrand (1995), Publ. IHES 81; see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 7.11 and Section 7.4]
X has independent coordinates and P is a product measure
for the corollary: f convex and 1-Lipschitz for the Euclidean norm, coordinates valued in [0,1]
the corollary centres at a MEDIAN, not the mean

[Prop 25 of arXiv:2608.28148, 'Flows and homotopies of Banach Lie algebroids'] Fix a Banach manifold $M$ and $k \in \N \cup \{\infty\}, k \geq 2$. We consider a $C^k$-map ${\g}\colon [0,1]\times [0,1] \to  M,$ such that
$$\g(\varepsilon,0)=\g(0,0) \text{ and }\g(\varepsilon,1)=\g(0,1), \text{ for all }\varepsilon\in [0,1]$$
There exists $\eta>0$ and a $C^k$-extension $\hat{\g} \colon [0,1] \times [-\eta, 1+\eta] \rightarrow M$ such that $\hat{\g}(\varepsilon,t)=\g_\varepsilon (0)$ for $t\in ]-\eta,-\frac{\eta}{2}]$ and $\hat{\g} (\varepsilon,t)=\g_\varepsilon (1)$ for all $t\in  [1+\frac{\eta}{2},1+\eta]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:Dist_d of arXiv:2604.16206, 'Extrapolation of max--stable random fields with Fr\'echet marginals'] Let $(X_1,X_2)$ be a simple max-stable random vector. Then it holds 
$$
\mathcal{E}_{H}(X_1,X_2)=\frac{d(X_1,X_2)}{4+d(X_1,X_2)}, \qquad  d(X_1,X_2)=4\frac{\mathcal{E}_{H}(X_1,X_2)}{1-\mathcal{E}_{H}(X_1,X_2)},
$$
where $\mathcal{E}_{H}$ is the excursion metric and $d$ is the Davis--Resnick distance introduced above.
title: Proposition prop:Dist_d of arXiv:2604.16206

body: In theoretical computer science, the busy beaver game aims to find a terminating program of a given size that either produces the most output possible, or runs for the longest number of steps. Since an endlessly looping program producing infinite output or running for infinite time is easily conceived, such programs are excluded from the game. Rather than traditional programming languages, the programs used in the game are n-state Turing machines, one of the first mathematical models of computation.
title: Busy beaver

body: A family F of functions on a metric space (X,d) is equicontinuous at x if for every eps > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(x,y) < delta implies |f(x) - f(y)| < eps for EVERY f in F simultaneously; uniformly equicontinuous if delta can be chosen independently of x. On a compact metric space, pointwise equicontinuity of the family implies uniform equicontinuity.
title: Equicontinuity

[Prop Main Proposition of arXiv:2411.07671, 'Long Time Behavior of General Markov Additive Processes'] Consider a MAP $((\xi,\Theta),\mathbb{P})$, such that Assumptions 1,2, and 3 are satisfied. Then, we have\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 \item $\xi_t$ drifts to $-\infty$ $\:\mathbb{P}_{0,\pi}$-a.s., if and only if
 $\Bar{g}_\infty < \infty$  and $\underline{g}_\infty = \infty$   $\:\mathbb{P}_{0,\pi}$-a.s.
 \item $\xi_t$ drifts to $+\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_{0,\pi}$-a.s., if and only if $\Bar{g}_\infty = \infty$  and $\underline{g}_\infty < \infty$  $\:\mathbb{P}_{0,\pi}$-a.s.
\item $\xi_t$ oscillates $\mathbb{P}_{0,\pi}$-a.s., if and only if $\Bar{g}_\infty = \infty$  and $\underline{g}_\infty = \infty$  $\:\mathbb{P}_{0,\pi}$-a.s.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, the axiom of choice, abbreviated AC or AoC, is an axiom of set theory. Informally put, the axiom of choice says that given any collection of non-empty sets, one can identify another set containing one element chosen from each set, even if the collection is infinite. Formally, the axiom establishes existence rather than a construction; it states that for every set I and every I-indexed family (S_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, there exists an I-indexed set (x_i)_{i in I} of elements of the union of the S_i such that x_i in S_i for every i in I. The axiom of choice was formulated in 1904 by Ernst Zermelo in order to formalize his proof of the well-ordering theorem.
title: In mathematics, the axiom of choice, abbreviated AC or AoC, is an axiom of set theory

[Lemma le:tightness_bdry_good_fl of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] There exists $\zeta>0$ such that the following is true. Fix $M,p > 0$, $r \in (0,1)$, and suppose $\delta < r$. Let $h$ be a GFF on $r\mathbf{D}$ with boundary values as in Section~(se:intersections_setup of the paper), and let $\theta_1,\theta_2$ be as in~(equation eq:angles_intersection of the paper). Let $w_1,w_2 \in B(0,r/4)$, and let $E_\delta$ denote the event that the following hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item Let $\eta_{w_1}^{\theta_1+\pi}$, $\eta_{w_1}^{\theta_1}$, $\eta_{w_2}^{\theta_2}$, $\eta_{w_2}^{\theta_2-\pi}$ be the flow lines with respective angles starting at $w_1$ (resp.\ $w_2$) and stopped upon exiting $B(0,3r/4)$. Then
\begin{itemize}
\item The right side of $\eta_{w_1}^{\theta_1}$ intersects the left side of $\eta_{w_2}^{\theta_2}$ with angle difference $\theta_1-\theta_2$, and they do not intersect in any other way.
\item $\eta_{w_1}^{\theta_1+\pi}$ does not intersect $\eta_{w_2}^{\theta_2}$, $\eta_{w_2}^{\theta_2-\pi}$; and $\eta_{w_2}^{\theta_2-\pi}$ does not intersect $\eta_{w_1}^{\theta_1+\pi}$, $\eta_{w_1}^{\theta_1}$.
\item Let $U$ be the region bounded between $\eta_{w_1}^{\theta_1}, \eta_{w_2}^{\theta_2}$, and sample the internal metric in $U$. There exist $x,y \in \eta^{\theta_1}_{w_1} \cap \eta^{\theta_2}_{w_2}$ such that if $U_{x,y} \subseteq U$ denotes the region between $x$ and $y$, then $\mathrm{diam}(U_{x,y}) \le \delta$ and
\[ D_\epsilon^{\partial U_{x,y}} \ge \delta^\zeta+\epsilon^{a_0} . \]
\end{itemize}
\item The event $G_{0,r}$ from the statement of Lemma~(le:good_scales_merging of the paper) occurs for $h$.
\end{itemize}
Then
\[ \mathbf{P}[E_\delta] = o^\infty(\delta) \]

body: In mathematics, the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem limits the number of sets in a family of sets for which every two sets have at least one element in common. Paul Erdős, Chao Ko, and Richard Rado proved the theorem in 1938, but did not publish it until 1961. It is part of the field of combinatorics, and one of the central results of extremal set theory.
title: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem

If it is common certainty at $\omega$ that Alice assigns probability $q_A$ to $E$ and Bob assigns probability $q_B$ to $E$, and local consistency holds at $\omega$, then $q_A = q_B$.

[Corollary 28 (Martingale projection) of arXiv:2604.22159, 'Adapted optimal transport between filtered Gaussian processes'] Let $L \in \mathscr{L}(N, d)$. Then $\hat{L} \in \mathscr{L}_{\mgle}(N, d)$ is optimal for
\[
\inf_{M \in \mathscr{L}_{\mgle}(N, d)} \dist_{\mathrm{AW}}(L, M)
\]
if and only if it has the form
\[
\hat{L}_{t,t} = \left( \frac{1}{N - t + 1} \sum_{s = t}^N L_{s,t}\right) Q_t
\]
where $Q = \diag(Q_1, \ldots, Q_N) \in \mathscr{O}(N, d)$.
title: Martingale projection

Own-work draft; F0124_C19 version 1; status: independently checked proof. For two-sided nearest-neighbor iid increments with 0<p<1, q=1-p, independent iid fair sign scenery and n>=1, define r(k)=+1 for k=0,1 mod4 and -1 otherwise. For a=0 or 1 let E_a be the EXTRA event that every scenery site z in [-n,n] equals either r(z+a) for all z or r(z+a+2) for all z. These two complete assignments have equal prior probability. Given E_a and ANY exterior word eta on 0<|t|<=n, if eta_-1=eta_1 then P(C0=+1|E_a,eta)=1/2. If eta_-1 differs from eta_1, P(C0=eta_1|E_0,eta)=p^2/(p^2+q^2), whereas the E_1 value is q^2/(p^2+q^2). Each site has one neighbor of each color, so its next observed color uniquely determines an increment. Within a phase pair the forward paths coincide in phase after their first step, as do the backward paths; every later likelihood factor cancels. The first paired weights are pq versus qp for equal neighbors, p^2 versus q^2 otherwise. Extra scenery conditioning is not an admissible remote color-tail modification. Even hypothetical perfect phase-pair forcing would give no gap for equal immediate neighbors or p=1/2. A separate mechanism is needed; no badness or novelty is asserted.

[Thm pitman of arXiv:2412.06701, 'Matsumoto-Yor processes on Jordan algebras'] The process $\lambda = \left( \lambda_t \ ; \ t \geq 0 \right)$ defined for $t \geq 0$ by
$$
   \lambda_t := b_t^{(\nu)} - 2 \inf_{0 \leq s \leq t} b_s^{(\nu)} \ ,
$$
is a Markov process, whose natural filtration is strictly contained in that of $b$, i.e. for all $t > 0$, ${\mathcal F}_t^\lambda \varsubsetneq {\mathcal F}_t^b$.

Furthermore, we have the conditional distribution
$$
   {\mathbb P}\left( b^{(\nu)} \in dx \ | \ {\mathcal F}_t^\lambda, \ \lambda_t = \lambda \right) 
   = \frac{\nu}{2\sinh(\nu \lambda)} \exp\left( \nu x \right) \mathds{1}_{\{ -\lambda \leq x \leq \lambda \}} dx \ .
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Pitman's Theorem \cite{pitman1975one}

[Thm 66 (The key estimate with general initial data in all dimensions) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Consider any (microscopic) sequence of measures $\nu_N$ on $I$ for which the associated (macroscopic) sequence of initial conditions $\mathfrak H^N(0,\bullet)$ as defined in \eqref{hn} is a good sequence in the sense of Definition \ref{goodseq}, converging weakly as measures on $\mathbb R^n$ to a measure $\mathfrak H_0$. Let $Q_N(t,\bullet; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})$ be as in \eqref{qfield}. Then, we have the limits:
     \begin{itemize}
        \item If $d=1$ and $N^{1/4p}   \varsigma_N\to   0$ then we have 
            $$\lim_{N \to \infty}\;  \Ex\big[ Q_N^f(t,\phi; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})\big] =\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(f)\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb R} \big((G_s * \mathfrak H_0)(a)\big)^2 \phi(a)\dr a\dr s.$$
     
         \item If $d=2$ and $(\log N)^{1/2p}   \varsigma_N\to   {\boldsymbol v}$ with $|\boldsymbol v|$ sufficiently small, then we have 
            $$\lim_{N \to \infty}\;  \Ex\big[ Q_N^f(t,\phi; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})\big] =\frac{\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(f)}{1- \frac12 \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}(  {\boldsymbol v})^2}\cdot 2\pi \cdot \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb R^2} \big((G_s * \mathfrak H_0)(a)\big)^2 \phi(a)\dr a\dr s.$$
         \item if $d\ge 3$ and if $  \varsigma_N\to   {\boldsymbol v}$ with $|\boldsymbol v|$ sufficiently small, then 
         $$\lim_{N \to \infty}\;  \Ex\big[ Q_N^f(t,\phi; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})\big]= \Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2(f;   {\boldsymbol v}) \cdot c_d\cdot \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb R^d} \big((G_s^{(  {\boldsymbol v})} * \mathfrak H_0)(a)\big)^2 \phi(a)\dr a\dr s,$$ where $\Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2( f,  {\boldsymbol v})$ is as in Proposition \ref{4.1c}.
     \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The key estimate with general initial data in all dimensions

[Proposition 117 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Fix $\eps>0$. There exists $\delta>0$ such that for each of the four types \emph{void-band-void}, \emph{void-band-saturated}, \emph{saturated-band-void}, \emph{saturated-band-saturated}, each $\hat{n} \in \big(\eps,\frac{1}{\eps}\big)$ and $\theta \in \big(\eps,\frac{1}{\eps}\big)$, each $\hat A_1'$, $\hat B_1'$
 satisfying
 \[
 \max\big(\hat B'_1- \hat A'_1- \theta \hat n,| \hat B'_1-\hat A'_1 -2\theta \hat n|\big) > \eps \qquad \textnormal{and} \qquad \max\big(|\hat A'_1|,|\hat B'_1|\big) < \frac{1}{\eps}
 \]
 and each interval $(\alpha,\beta)$ such that
 \[
 0 < \alpha - \hat A'_1 < \delta \qquad \textnormal{and} \qquad 0 < \hat B'_1 - \beta < \delta,
 \]
 we can find $\hat A'_2$ and $\hat B'_2$ such that the equilibrium measure $\widetilde \mu$ of Theorem~\ref{Proposition_ZW_equilibrium_measure} has the prescribed type and the band $(\alpha,\beta)$. Moreover, $\hat A'_2$ and $\hat B'_2$ can be chosen to depend smoothly on $\alpha,\beta, \hat A'_1, \hat B'_1, \hat n, \theta$.

 For the types \emph{void-band-void} and \emph{saturated-band-saturated}, if we additionally set $\alpha - \hat A'_1 = \hat B'_1 - \beta$, it is sufficient to require $|\hat B'_1-\hat A'_1 - 2\theta \hat n|\neq 0$ instead of $>\eps$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Diaconis asks which perfect matching to add to a connected d-regular graph with an even number n of vertices to obtain fastest mixing of nearest-neighbor random walk on the (d+1)-regular augmentation. The problem includes accurate convergence rates for a cycle with an added matching. A separate variation adds a weighted edge to a finite reversible chain and Metropolizes the result to preserve its stationary law, asking which edge best improves mixing or spectral gap. These variants must distinguish total-variation mixing time, ordinary gap, absolute gap, and any laziness convention. A single unadjusted edge changes degrees and generally changes stationary law. Bounded-degree random-matching cutoff is known (Hermon-Sly-Sousi); the present bounded literature check does not certify current openness of general deterministic optimization. This is an open-question record, not a theorem.

[Prop 4 (Joint Chain Rule) of arXiv:2607.28078, '2607.28078'] \cite[Proposition 5.102]{CAR}
For a given $T>0$, let $V:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[$\rm(1)$] For any $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the function $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\ni(t,x)\mapsto V(t,x,\mu)$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^{1,2}$, namely $\partial_tV$, $\partial_xV$ and $\partial^2_{xx}V$ are continuous in $(t,x,\mu)$.	
\item[$\rm(2)$] For any $(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d$, the function $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\ni\mu\mapsto V(t,x,\mu)$ is continuously L-differentiable and, for any $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, we can find a version of the mapping $\mathbb{R}^d\ni v\mapsto\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)$ such that the mapping $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\times\mathbb{R}^d\ni(t,x,\mu,v)\mapsto\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)$ is locally bounded and is continuous at any $(t,x,\mu,v)$ such that $v\in\textnormal{supp}(\mu)$.
\item[$\rm(3)$] For the version of $\partial_\mu V$ mentioned above and for any $(t,x,\mu)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the mapping $\mathbb{R}^d\ni v\mapsto\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is continuously differentiable and its derivative, denoted by $\mathbb{R}^d\ni v\mapsto\partial_v\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, is locally bounded and is jointly continuous in $(t,x,\mu,v)$ at any point $(t,x,\mu,v)$ such that $v\in\textnormal{supp}(\mu)$.
\end{enumerate}
Assume further that, for every compact subset $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, 
\[
\sup_{(t,x,\mu)\in[0,T]\times\mathcal{K}}\Big\{\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\big\|\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)\big\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^d}d\mu(v)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\big\|\partial_v\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)\big\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}}d\mu(v)\Big\}<\infty.
\]
Moreover, let $\{X(t)\}_{0\leq t\leq T}$ be an It\^o process of the form 
\[
dX(t)=b(t)dt+\sigma(t)dB(t),\,\,X(0)=X_0\in L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}),
\]
where $\{B(t)\}_{t\geq0}$ is an $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq0}$-Brownian motion with values in $\mathbb{R}^m$, $\{b(t)\}_{t\geq0}$ and $\{\sigma(t)\}_{t\geq0}$ are $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq0}$-progressively measurable processes with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$, respectively, and satisfy
\[
\mathbb{E}\Big\{\int_{0}^{T}\big(\|b(t)\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^d}+\|\sigma(t)\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}}\big)dt\Big\}<\infty.
\] 
Let $\{\xi(t)\}_{t\in[0,T]}$ be another $d$-dimensional It\^{o} process on the same filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq0},\mathbb{P})$ of the form $d\xi(t)=\eta(t)dt+\gamma(t)dB(t)$, $\xi(0)=\xi_0\in L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$, where the $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq0}$-progressively measurable processes $\{\eta(t)\}_{t\in[0,T]}$ and $\{\gamma(t)\}_{t\in[0,T]}$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$, respectively, satisfy
\[
\mathbb{P}\Big\{\int_{0}^{T}\big(\|\eta(t)\|_{\mathbb{R}^d}+\|\gamma(t)\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}}\big)dt<\infty\Big\}=1.
\]
Then, almost surely, for all $t\in[0,T]$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
V(t,\xi(t),\mathcal{L}_{X(t)})&=V(0,\xi_0,\mathcal{L}_{X_0})+\int_{0}^{t}\partial_xV(r,\xi(r),\mathcal{L}_{X(r)})\cdot(\gamma(r)dB(r))\\
&+\int_{0}^{t}\big(\partial_tV(r,\xi(r),\mathcal{L}_{X(r)})+\partial_xV(r,\xi(r),\mathcal{L}_{X(r)})\cdot\eta(r)\big)dr\\				&+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\textnormal{tr}\big[\partial^2_{xx}V(r,\xi(r),\mathcal{L}_{X(r)})(\gamma\gamma^\top)(r)\big]dr\\
&+\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{\mathbb{E}}\big[\partial_\mu V(r,\xi(r),\mathcal{L}_{X(r)})(\tilde{X}(r))\cdot\tilde{b}(r)\big]dr\\
&+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{\mathbb{E}}\big[\textnormal{tr}\big(\partial_v\partial_\mu V(r,\xi(r),\mathcal{L}_{X(r)})(\tilde{X}(r))(\tilde{\sigma}\tilde{\sigma}^\top)(r)\big)\big]dr,
\end{aligned}	
\end{equation}
where the process $(\tilde{X}(t),\tilde{b}(t),\tilde{\sigma}(t))_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a copy of the process $(X(t),b(t),\sigm (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

If R is a Noetherian ring (every ideal finitely generated, equivalently the ascending chain condition on ideals), then the polynomial ring R[x] is Noetherian. By induction R[x_1, ..., x_n] is Noetherian; in particular every ideal in a polynomial ring over a field is finitely generated.

[Lemma lem:burning of arXiv:2605.19419, 'Tail exponents of the three-dimensional uniform spanning tree and Abelian sandpile'] Let $K\Subset\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ contain $0$ and all nearest neighbours of $0$. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an event of subsets of $K$ such that every $A\in\mathcal{A}$ contains at least one nearest neighbour of $0$. Then
\begin{equation}
\nu_{K}\bigl(W_{1,K}\in\mathcal{A}\bigr)
= g_{K}\,\nu_{K}^{(0)}\bigl(\mathfrak{T}_{K}\in\mathcal{A}\bigr),
\qquad
 g_{K}:=\frac{|R_{K^{\circ}}|}{|R_{K}|}=G_{K}(0,0),
\end{equation}
where $G_{K}$ is the inverse of the finite-volume toppling matrix.

For F in L^2(T), F = L^(-d) sum over xi of F^(xi) e^(2 pi i xi.x) in L^2, and integral over T of |F|^2 dx = L^(-d) sum over xi of |F^(xi)|^2. For F, G in L^1(T) the convolution (F * G)(x) = integral over T of F(y) G(x - y) dy has (F * G)^(xi) = F^(xi) G^(xi). For F, G in L^2(T), (F G)^(xi) = L^(-d) sum over eta of F^(eta) G^(xi - eta). At L = 1 these are the usual formulas with no factors.

[Proposition prop:6 of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Almost surely, for any fixed $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}\in \mathbb{C}$ and simultaneously for all $0<t<s$, the following hold.
      \begin{enumerate}
      \item There is a finite set of points $\mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})\subseteq \partial \mathcal{B}_t^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ such that every leftmost $D_h$-geodesic from $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}$ to a point on $\partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ passes via some $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$.
      \item  There is a unique $D_h$-geodesic from $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}$ to $x$ for each $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$.
      \item For $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$, let $I_x$ denote the set of $y\in \partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ for which the leftmost $D_h$-geodesic from $0$ to $y$ passes via $x$. Each $I_x$ for $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ is a connected arc of the Jordan curve $\partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ and $\partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ is a union of the arcs $I_x$ for $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$, with any two such arcs being disjoint.
      \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let A be a closed operator on a Banach space with resolvent set rho(A) and resolvent R(z) = (z I - A)^{-1}. Then: (i) the FIRST RESOLVENT IDENTITY R(z) - R(w) = (w - z) R(z) R(w) holds for z, w in rho(A), so resolvents at different points commute; (ii) rho(A) is OPEN and R is analytic on it, with the Neumann expansion R(z) = sum over k >= 0 of (w - z)^k R(w)^{k+1} valid whenever |z - w| is strictly less than 1 / ||R(w)||; (iii) consequently the distance from w to the spectrum is at least 1 / ||R(w)||, so the resolvent norm blows up at least like the reciprocal of the distance to the spectrum as z approaches it. For a BOUNDED A the series R(z) = sum over k >= 0 of A^k / z^{k+1} converges for |z| > the spectral radius.
A closed (so that the resolvent is bounded by the closed graph theorem) and the resolvent set nonempty.
The lower bound on the distance to the spectrum is an equality only for normal operators on Hilbert space;
for a non-normal operator the resolvent norm can be enormous far from the spectrum, which is the pseudospectrum phenomenon and the reason spectral information alone does not control transient behaviour.

body: In mathematics, the four color theorem, or the four-color map theorem, states that no more than four colors are required to color the regions of any map so that no two adjacent regions have the same color. Adjacent means that two regions share a common boundary of non-zero length. It was the first major theorem to be proved by use of a computer. Initially, this proof was not accepted by all mathematicians because the computer-assisted proof was infeasible for a human to check by hand. The proof has gained wide acceptance since then, although some reservations remain.

Own-work research draft; status proof (unaudited), independent review and priority assessment pending. Fix k>=2, D>=k+1, L>=0, M>=kappa>0, H>=0 and 0<lambda<=1. Let h extend C2 to a neighborhood of [0,1]^k with |grad h|<=L and kappa I<=D2h<=M I on the cube. Put F(x)=(x,h(x)), with any isometric embedding into R^D. Let p be a probability density with p>=lambda and Lip(p)<=H, and let mu=F#(p dx). For continuous scalar-input piecewise-affine generators with at most N pieces, including plateaux, the infimum W1 error from uniform noise is between c_lower N^(-beta) and c_upper N^(-beta) for every N>=1. Here beta=2/(2k-1), b=sqrt(1+L^2), omega_(k-1) is unit-ball volume in R^(k-1), A=5^k+8 omega_(k-1) sqrt((2L+3)/kappa), c_lower=(lambda/2)(2A)^(-beta), C0=b(sqrt(k-1)+sqrt(k))/2+bH/4+M/8, and c_upper=8C0+b sqrt(k). The new lower proof bounds every affine-line tube preimage by A r^(k-1/2) for 0<r<=1: near-vertical lines have diameter <=5r; other lines are sliced into two-sided height bands of kappa-strongly convex one-dimensional functions, whose total length is <=8 sqrt(epsilon/kappa). The upper half depends on the unaudited general C2 construction T1-003 v1. For exactly uniform surface probability on any such graph, the area density J=sqrt(1+|grad h|^2), V=integral J, p=J/V satisfies p>=1/b and Lip(p)<=M; take lambda=1/b and H=M. Thus the matching exponent covers a whole nonquadratic strongly convex graph class and its uniform-surface laws. This is not a theorem for every C2 image, a closed-manifold class, merely bounded varying densities without a common regularity bound, or deep generators.
All graph, curvature, density and generator assumptions in the statement. Matching upper depends on unaudited T1-003 v1. No independent audit or priority claim.

[Lemma lem: net_Tvectors of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] There exists an absolute constant $C>0$ such that the following holds. Let $n\ge 1$ and let $C\log n\le d\le n/2$. Let $0<\rho\le  \sqrt{n}/(B_\mathcal{T} d^{3/4})$. Let $i\in \{2, 3\}$. There exists a set $\mathcal{N}_i=\mathcal{N}_i'+\mathcal{N}_i''$, $\mathcal{N}_i''\subset \mbox{span} \{\1\}$, with the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $|\mathcal{N}_i|\le \exp(6n_{i}\log d)$.
        \item For every $u\in \mathcal{N}_i'$ one has $u_j^*\le 1/4+d^{-3/4}$ for all $j\ge n_{i}$.
        \item For every $x\in \mathcal{T}_i'$ there is $u\in \mathcal{N}_i'$ and $w\in \mathcal{N}_i''$ such that 
       \[\|x-u\|_\infty \le \frac{1}{ d^{3/4}}, \quad \quad \|w\|_\infty \le \frac{1}{ d^{3/4}}, 
        \quad\quad \mbox{ and }  \quad \quad {\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert\kern-0.25ex\left\vert x-u-w 
    \right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert\kern-0.25ex\right\vert} \le \frac{\sqrt{2n}}{ d^{3/4}}.
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem: net_Tvectors of arXiv:2604.10446

[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2608.21063, '\textbf{Non-bijective scaling limits and phase transitions of planar maps}'] Let $Z_{3/2}$ denote the $3/2$-stable random variable whose Laplace transform satisfies $\Ex{\exp(-\lambda Z_{3/2})} = \exp(\lambda^{3/2})$. Let $h$ denote its density function. With
$
	g_{\cM} = \left(\frac{16}{243}\right)^{1/3}
$ we have
\begin{align*}
\Pr{ \ed(\cV(\mM_n)) =  \ell} = \frac{1}{g_\cM n^{2/3}}\left(h\left(\frac{ n/3 - \ell}{g_\cM n^{2/3}}   \right) + o(1)\right)
\end{align*}
uniformly for all integers $\ell \ge 0$. Consequently, 
\begin{align*}
	\frac{n/3 - \ed(\cV(\mM_n))}{g_\cM n^{2/3}} \convd Z_{3/2}.
\end{align*}
Moreover, for any sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$ and any $0 < \delta < 1/3$ we have
\[
	 \Prb{\ed(\cV(\mM_n)) \le \epsilon n / \log(n)} = o(n^{-2/3})
\]
and
\[
	\Prb{\ed(\cV(\mM_n)) \le \delta n} = O(n^{-2/3} ).
\]

body:
[Corollary 2 (Modified Lyons--Sidorova conjecture) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous tree-reduced bounded-variation path, and let $v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0$. Then
\[
R\bigl(\log S(\gamma)\bigr)=\infty
\]
if and only if there is a based prefix $\beta$ of $\overline\gamma=\gamma-\gamma_0$ such that
\begin{equation}
\overline\gamma
 \sim_{\mathrm{rep}}
\beta*\lambda_v*\overleftarrow{\beta}.
\end{equation}
When $v=0$, the tree-reduced path is constant. When $v\neq0$, $S(\beta)$ is the gate from the identity to the unique minimum-displacement axis of left multiplication by $S(\gamma)$ in the signature tree. This prefix is unique up to waiting intervals and weak increasing reparametrisation. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Modified Lyons--Sidorova conjecture

[Theorem thm:geod_direction of arXiv:2605.22787, 'Invariant measures for half-space geometric LPP: classification and the one force--one sol'] Let $c \in [0,q^{-1})$. Then, on a single event of probability one, whenever $\gamma$ is any semi-infinite geodesic for $\operatorname{GLPP}_c$,  the limit
	\[
	\lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{\gamma(-k)\cdot \mathbf e_1}{\gamma(-k) \cdot \mathbf e_2}
	\]
	exists and lies in the set $[0,\xi_{\max}^c) \cup \{1\}$. Here, $\mathbf e_1 = (1,0)$ and $\mathbf e_2 = (0,1)$ are the standard basis vectors.  
	
	
	In particular, if $c \le 1$, then the set of allowable limits is $[0,1]$. If $c > 1$, then the set of allowable limits is  
	\[
	\biggl[0, \Bigl(\frac{1-qc}{c-q}\Bigr)^2\biggl) \cup \{1\}.
	\]
    Furthermore, for each $\xi$ in this set and for every lattice point $\mathbf x \in \mathbb{Z}^2_{\mathrm{HS}}$, there exists at least one semi-infinite geodesic from $\mathbf x$ in that direction. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:geod_direction of arXiv:2605.22787

body: [Theorem 5 of arXiv:2512.19063, 'Sharp Decoupling Inequalities for the Variances and Second Moments of Sums of Dependent Ra'] For any nonnegative dependent square-integrable variables $d_{1},...d_{n}$, and the mutually independent variables $z_{1},...,z_{n}$ such that $z_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{L}}}{{=}}d_{i}$ for all $i=1,...,n$, we have the following sharp inequality $\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{i}\right)^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{i}\right)^{2}.$

[Prop 7 of arXiv:2506.21087, 'Quasi-Stationary Distributions of Interacting Dynamical Systems and their approximation'] Assume \ref{condhmv} and $D$ has ${\cal C}^2$-boundary. Assume that $(\gamma_n)$ satisfies \eqref{hyp:pas}. Let $h>0$ and assume that $\zeta_h$ has a positive {${\cal C}^1$} density $g_h$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] Let $h>0$.  Then, $(\mu_n^h)$ is tight on ${\cal P}(\bar{D})$ and every weak limit of $(\mu_n^h)$ is a QSD $\mu^\star_h$ for $(K_{\mu,\partial}^{(h)})_{\mu \in {\cal P}(\bar{D})}$. Furthermore, $\mu^\star_h(\partial D)=0$. 
\item[(ii)] {Furthermore, if $(\zeta_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a Brownian motion and if
 \begin{align*}
    \sup_{(x,\mu)\in\MM\times{\cal P}(\MM)}\bigg[\frac{\delta b(x,\cdot)}{\delta m}(\mu,\cdot)\bigg]_{1}\vee\bigg[\frac{\delta\sigma(x,\cdot)}{\delta m}(\mu,\cdot)\bigg]_{1}<+\infty,
\end{align*}} such a sequence  $(\mu^\star_h)_{h>0}$ is tight on $D$ and every weak limit (when $h\rightarrow0$) is a QSD for the McKean-Vlasov diffusion $(Y_t)_{t\ge0}$, defined in \Cref{rq: model1} and killed at time $\tau:=\inf\{t\ge0, Y_t\in D^c\}$. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:collision-exact-sequence of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] The map
\[
 \partial_q:\mathcal C_q(A)\longrightarrow\mathbb R^m,
 \qquad
 \partial_q\!\left(\sum_u\gamma_ue_u\right)=\sum_u\gamma_u u,
\]
has image $L_q(A)$, contained in the coordinate-sum-zero subspace.  With
\[
 \mathcal N_q(A)=\ker\partial_q,
 \qquad \operatorname{cnul}_q(A)=\dim\mathcal N_q(A),
\]
there is an exact sequence
\begin{equation}
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal N_q(A)
 \longrightarrow\mathcal C_q(A)
 \xrightarrow{\partial_q}L_q(A)
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $\Delta_q(A)=M_{q,m}-|qA|$, then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\Delta_q(A)=r_q(A)+\operatorname{cnul}_q(A).}
\end{equation}
For $C=\Sigma_{\ell,c}A$,
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_q(C)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\min(q,\ell-1)}\Delta_{q-j}(A)
  +\sum_{j=\ell}^{q}M_{q-j,m},
\end{equation}

body:
[Prop gl-spectra-pres-sym-mon of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The symmetric monoidal global $\infty$-category ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}^\otimes$ is globally presentably symmetric monoidal.
    \begin{proof}
        For any compact Lie group $G$, the symmetric monoidal product on ${\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-gl}$ is equivalently given as the left derived functor of the left Quillen bifunctor from Corollary~(cor:smash-gl-left-Quillen of the paper), and hence preserves colimits in each variable. As we already know that ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}$ is globally presentable, it therefore only remains to show that the Beck--Chevalley map $\textbf{\textup{L}}\alpha_!(X\otimes \alpha^*Y)\to(\textbf{\textup{L}}\alpha_!X)\otimes Y$ is invertible for any $\alpha\colon G\to G'$ and $X\in{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-gl},Y\in{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G'$-gl}$. As both sides preserve ordinary colimits in both variable separately and since both ${\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-gl}$ and ${\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G'$-gl}$ are stable in the usual sense, we reduce to the case where $X$ and $Y$ are generators as in Proposition~(prop:gl-spectra-compact-generators of the paper), and hence in particular contained in the essential image of the symmetric monoidal left adjoint $\Sigma^\bullet_+$ from the previous construction. Using that Beck--Chevalley maps compose as in the proof of Proposition~(prop:equiv-sp-equiv-cc of the paper), the claim then follows from Corollary~(cor:S-gl-times-initial of the paper).
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop gl-spectra-pres-sym-mon of arXiv:2608.28504

|F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$}_1,\text{\boldmath $h$})-F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$}_2,\text{\boldmath $h$})|\le L\|\text{\boldmath $B$}_1-\text{\boldmath $B$}_2\|.

body:
[Theorem 30 (Critical ancestry amplification principle) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let \(r\ge1\).

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.8em]
\item Suppose \(\mathcal P\) is an exact critical \(r\)-packet and
\[
 s_N(B_{\nu,j})\sim \frac{a_{\nu,j}}N,
 \qquad a_{\nu,j}>0.
\]
Set
\begin{equation}
 \kappa(\mathcal P)
 :=\sum_{\nu=1}^m |c_\nu|\,\operatorname{Tr}|C_\nu|
       \prod_{j=1}^r a_{\nu,j}.
 
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 \mathcal P\models\operatorname{Crit}_r(\kappa(\mathcal P)).
\]

\item Let \(Y_L\) be uniformly bounded in \(\mathfrak W^{[r]}\).  Suppose
that, after fixed two-sided contractions, it has a principal exposure
\[
 Q_+Y_LQ_-=c_LU
 (B_{1,L}\otimes\cdots\otimes B_{r,L})V+R_L,
\]
where \(\inf_L|c_L|>0\), the \(B_{j,L}\) are window-critical with uniform
constants, and the remainders are uniformly bounded in
\(\mathfrak W^{[r-1]}\) when \(r\ge2\), or have uniformly bounded rank and
operator norm when \(r=1\).  Then there are constants
\(N_r,c_r,C_r>0\), independent of \(L\), such that
\begin{equation}
 s_N(Y_L)\ge c_r\phi_r(N)
 
\end{equation}
whenever
\[
 N_r\le N\le C_rL(\log(e+L))^{r-1}.
\]
Consequently no grade \(q<r\) can bound such a family uniformly on
arbitrarily long windows.
\end{enumerate}

\mathbb{S}^{n-k}_{+,\sqrt{2(n-k)}}\times \mathbb{R}^{k}.

body: [Defn def-end of arXiv:2506.18827, 'Random walk reflected off of infinity, with applications to uniform spanning forests and s'] Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of one-sided infinite paths $P : \mathbbm N_0 \to \mathcal V\mathcal G$ which are simple (i.e., they visit each vertex of $\mathcal V\mathcal G$ at most once). We define an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathcal P$ by $P\sim Q$ if and only if the following is true. For each finite set $A\subset \mathcal V\mathcal G$, there is exactly one connected component of $\mathcal V\mathcal G\setminus A$ which contains both infinitely many vertices of $P$ and infinitely many vertices of $Q$. An equivalence class $\omega$ under this equivalence relation is called an \textbf{end} of $\mathcal G$.
title: End of $\mcl G$

body: In mathematical analysis and in probability theory, a σ-algebra is part of the formalism for defining sets that can be measured. In calculus and analysis, for example, σ-algebras are used to define the concept of sets with area or volume. In probability theory, they are used to define events for which a probability can be defined. In this way, σ-algebras help to formalize the notion of size.

[Propdef conjstab of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Given a stability condition $\sigma=(Z,(\cC_{\phi})_\phi)$ on a triangulated category $\cC$, there is a corresponding stability condition on the opposite triangulated category $\cC^{\mathrm{op}}$, the \textbf{conjugate stability condition}, given by $\overline{\sigma}=(\overline{Z},(\cC_{-\phi})_\phi)$.
(Thus, the semistable objects of phase $\phi$ in $\cC^{\mathrm{op}}$ are the semistable objects of phase $-\phi$ in $\cC$.)

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.22470, 'A Logarithmic Fluctuation Hierarchy for Sequential Interacting Diffusions'] Under \hyperref[ass:A]{Assumption~A}, as \(N\to\infty\),
\begin{equation}
(Y^{N,n})_{n\ge0}
\LawConv
(Y^n)_{n\ge0}
\end{equation}
in \(E^{\mathbb N_0}\), equipped with the countable product topology.
The initial hierarchy \((Y_0^n)_{n\ge0}\) has a centered Gaussian law with
covariance
\begin{equation}
\mathbb E\!\left[
\langle Y_0^n,\varphi\rangle
\langle Y_0^k,\psi\rangle
\right]
=
\frac{(n+k)!}{n!\,k!}
\left[
\langle\bar\rho_0,\varphi\psi\rangle
-
\langle\bar\rho_0,\varphi\rangle
\langle\bar\rho_0,\psi\rangle
\right]
\end{equation}
for all \(n,k\ge0\) and \(\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\R^d)\).
For this initial hierarchy, the limiting family \((Y^n)_{n\ge0}\) is the
unique probabilistically strong solution in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:log-hierarchy-solution}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$

$\mathbb{D}_N\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} ((X_n,\varepsilon_n))_{n=1}^N$ and
$\mathbb{D}_N^0\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} ((X_n,0))_{n=1}^N$.  Then, for every
$f\in \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho);1)$ and every $\delta\in(0,1)$, if
\begin{equation}

    N

    \log\left(\frac{M_\varepsilon}{\delta}\right)
,

upon defining $

    \big\|
        \mathcal{E}(f|\mathbb{D}_N)
        -
        \mathcal{E}(f|\mathbb{D}_N^0)

$ we have
\begin{equation}

        \big|
        \le
        \varepsilon

body:
[Theorem thm:local-monotonicity of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Fix $\theta\in(0,1)$ and let $\alpha_{s,\theta}$ be defined by
\[
F_s(\alpha_{s,\theta})=\theta.
\]
Then, as $s\downarrow 0$,
\[
\alpha_{s,\theta}
=
\alpha_{0,\theta}
+
\frac12\,\alpha_{0,\theta}\bigl(\alpha_{0,\theta}-2\bigr)s^2
+o(s^2),
\qquad
\alpha_{0,\theta}=-\log(1-\theta).
\]
In particular, with
\[
\theta_c:=1-e^{-2},
\]
one has:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $\theta>\theta_c$, then $\alpha_{s,\theta}>\alpha_{0,\theta}$ for all sufficiently small $s>0$;
\item if $\theta<\theta_c$, then $\alpha_{s,\theta}<\alpha_{0,\theta}$ for all sufficiently small $s>0$.
\end{itemize}

Let $\psi(\cdot ;\zeta_e)$ be the principal eigenfunction of the eigenvalue problem (equation eq:Intro:EigenvalueProblem of the paper),  normalized so that $\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \psi(x;\zeta_e) dx=1$. Then for every $t>0$ and $f:[0,\infty)\to \mathbb{R}$,

    \]

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2608.23491, 'Stochastic Dynamics of Low Earth Orbit Near Full Capacity'] Let $Y$ be a unit-rate Poisson process and $\widetilde Y = Y - \mathrm{id}$. Let $a \in \bR$, $b \geq 0$, and let $w^N$ be a nondecreasing adapted process with $w^N(t) \leq W t$ on $[0, T]$. Then
\[
\E\Big[ \sup_{t \leq T} \big( N^{-a}\widetilde Y(N^{b} w^N(t)) \big)^2 \Big] \leq 4 W T\, N^{\,b - 2a}.
\]
In particular, if $2a > b$ then $\sup_{t \leq T} \big| N^{-a}\widetilde Y(N^{b} w^N(t)) \big| \probc 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $g \in L^2(\mathbb{R}, \gamma)$ have Hermite rank $d \ge 1$, and let $\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} |\rho(k)|^d < \infty$. For $t \in [0, 1]$, define the continuous-time empirical path $F_n(t) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} g(Y_k) + \frac{nt - \lfloor nt \rfloor}{\sqrt{n}} g(Y_{\lfloor nt \rfloor + 1})$. body: In 1933 Karol Borsuk conjectured that every bounded subset of n-dimensional Euclidean space can be partitioned into at most n+1 pieces, each of strictly smaller diameter than the original set. This is TRUE for n=1, 2, 3, and for all smooth convex bodies in every dimension. The conjecture is FALSE in general: Kahn and Kalai showed in 1993, adapting a counterexample of Frankl and Wilson, that partitioning into only n+1 smaller-diameter pieces fails for all sufficiently large n; the smallest dimension with an explicit known counterexample was later narrowed to 64 by Jenrich and Brouwer in 2014. The truth for intermediate dimensions, roughly 4 through 63, remains open.
title: Borsuk's conjecture

body:
[Lemma DtYts of arXiv:2608.21805, 'Logarithmic derivatives of variational and singular stochastic partial differential equati'] Under Assumptions (ass:LR of the paper), (ass:diff2 of the paper), and~(ass:SC of the paper), for $0 \leq s \leq t \leq T$, $r \in [0,T]$, and every $v \in H$, the Malliavin derivative of the $H$-valued random variable $Y(t,s)v$ is given fibrewise by
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{D}_r [Y(t,s)v] \;=\; \mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)\,v,
\end{equation}
both sides being elements of $L^2(\Omega; L_2(U,H))$ for a.e.\ $r$, and directionally
\[
  \mathcal{D}^a_r[Y(t,s)v] \;=\; \mathcal{Z}^{a}(t,s;r)v \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega; H), \qquad a \in U .
\]
Here $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)v$ is the unique doubly-fibrewise solution, in the sense of Theorem~(thm:Z-wellposed of the paper), of the linearised equation (equation eq:second-var of the paper) obtained by applying both sides to $v$ and to the direction $a$, with initial condition~(equation eq:Z-initial-cond of the paper) (reproduced from Definition~(def:second-var of the paper)):
\[
  \mathcal{Z}(\max(s,r),s;r)\,v \;=\;
  \begin{cases}
    0 & \text{if } r < s,\\
    \mathcal{B}'_u(r,X(r))(Y(r,s)v) & \text{if } s < r \leq t,\\
    \mathcal{B}'_u(s,X(s))\,v & \text{if } r = s \text{ in Regime A},\\
    0 & \text{if } r = s \text{ in Regime B}.
  \end{cases}
\]
For $r > t$, $\mathcal{D}_r [Y(t,s)v] = 0$ (by causality). The relation~(equation eq:DtYts-explicit of the paper) is to be read fibrewise in $v$ and, in the noise slot, as an identity in $L_2(U,H)$. For each fixed $v \in H$, both sides are well-defined elements of $L^2(\Omega; L_2(U,H))$ (the left-hand side as the Malliavin derivative of the $H$-valued random variable $Y(t,s)v$, the right-hand side by Theorem~(thm:Z-wellposed of the paper)). The shorthand notation ``$\mathcal{D}_r Y(t,s) = \mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)$'' refers to this fibrewise identity, not to an operator-norm equality in $L(H)$ which would require the strictly stronger operator-valued moment bounds discussed after Proposition~(prop:Y-moments of the paper).

In the particular case $s = 0$, the explicit representation is, fibrewise,
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{D}_r [Y(t,0)v] \;=\; \mathcal{Z}(t,0;r)\,v \qquad \text{for every } v \in H,
\end{equation}
an identity in $L_2(U, H)$ whose directional form reads $\mathcal{D}^a_r[Y(t,0)v] = \mathcal{Z}^{a}(t,0;r)v$ in $H$ for every $a \in U$.
This is the infinite-dimensional analogue of the ``second variation'' $D_t Y_T$ appearing in Lemma 5.4 of [mirafzali2025malliavin]; the present formulation differs from the finite-dimensional setting in being fibrewise rather than operator-valued, since the operator-norm interpretation requires structural input not provided by the abstract framework (cf.\ the discussion after Proposition~(prop:Y-moments of the paper) and Theorem~(thm:Z-wellposed of the paper)).

body: Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f: Omega -> R (or C) a measurable function. The essential supremum of |f| is ess sup |f| = inf{M >= 0 : mu(|f| > M) = 0}, with the infimum of the empty set taken to be infinity. The space L-infinity(mu) consists of equivalence classes, under equality mu-almost everywhere, of measurable functions f with ess sup |f| < infinity, normed by ||f||_infinity = ess sup |f|; with this norm L-infinity(mu) is a Banach space. [standard, e.g. Folland, Real Analysis]
title: Essential Supremum and the Space L-infinity(mu)

[Lemma lem:h-conc-entries of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$. Let $j\ge 1$ be an integer, and suppose $j$ is sufficiently large. Fix an integer $\tau \ge 0$, a real number $\nu\ge 0$, and $\overline{a} \in (\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0})^j$. Let $E^+$ be a constant-escape process on $[j]$ with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time $\tau$, end-of-step arrival rate $\nu$, and $\overline{\mathrm{arr}}_{[j]}^{E^+}(\tau) = \overline{a}$. Fix integers $t > \tau$ and $k \in [j]$, and let
\[
\mu = (t-\tau)\nu + \sum_{t'=0}^{t-\tau-1} p_{k-1}h_{k-1}^{\nu,\overline{a}}(t').
\]
Then with probability at least $1-j^{-3j}$,
\[
\Big|\bigcup_{t'=\tau+1}^t\big(\mathbf{s}_{k-1}^{E^+}(t') \cup \mathbf{arr}_k^{E^+}(t')\big)\Big| \le \max\Big\{j(\log j)^2, \Big(1+\frac{j}{\mu^{1/2}}\Big) \mu \Big\}.
\]

body:
Let S be a compact C^k hypersurface in R^n with k >= 2. Then there is delta > 0 such that on the tubular neighbourhood { x : dist(x, S) < delta } the nearest point of S to x is UNIQUE, the projection map is C^{k-1}, and the signed distance function d is C^k with gradient of unit length equal to the outward normal at the projected point. The largest such delta is governed by the REACH of S, which is bounded below by the reciprocal of the supremum of the principal curvatures and shrinks where the surface nearly self-touches. For a merely C^1 hypersurface the reach can be zero and the projection can fail to be unique arbitrarily close to the surface, so no tubular neighbourhood of uniform width need exist - the standard trap when a proof written for C^2 surfaces is applied to a C^1 one.
C^2 (or better) regularity and compactness;
the width of the neighbourhood depends on curvature bounds and is not uniform over all surfaces.
For a convex set the projection is globally unique and 1-Lipschitz with no curvature hypothesis, which is a different theorem, resting on convexity rather than smoothness.

[Theorem 17 (Sufficient condition for a classical Riemannian Bernoulli solution) of arXiv:2609.00571, '\textbf{Shape Optimization and Bernoulli Free Boundary Problems\\ for the Riemannian $p$-L'] Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold and let $K\Subset M$ be a
compact domain with sufficiently regular boundary. Assume that the
admissible class satisfies the compactness and regularity hypotheses
used in the existence theorem for the shape optimization problem.
Assume moreover that:

\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm (i)}]
\item the optimal domains satisfy the Riemannian contraction
      hypothesis {\rm (RC)} and the associated monotonicity result;

\item the successive construction admits a nested sequence
      \[
      \Omega_0\supsetneq\Omega_1\supsetneq\cdots
      \]
      with
      \[
      c_0>c_1>\cdots>c;
      \]

\item the boundary and state stability condition {\rm (SC)} holds;

\item the reference family satisfies {\rm (RA)}, and there exists a
      sequence $R_N$ such that
      \[
      q(R_N)>c,\qquad q(R_N)\to c,
      \]
      for which the first-crossing indices are defined;

\item the limiting boundary $\partial\Omega^\ast$ is sufficiently
      regular for the classical normal derivative to be defined.
\end{enumerate}

Then the successive construction has a limit $\Omega^\ast$ and a
state $u^\ast$ satisfying
\[
\begin{cases}
-\Delta_{p,g}u^\ast=0
&\text{in }\Omega^\ast\setminus K,\\
u^\ast=1
&\text{on }\partial K,\\
u^\ast=0
&\text{on }\partial\Omega^\ast,\\
-\partial_{\nu_g}u^\ast=c
&\text{on }\partial\Omega^\ast.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular, $(\Omega^\ast,u^\ast)$ is a classical solution of the
Riemannian exterior Bernoulli problem.

[Theorem theo:main-complete of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Assume that \(K\) and \(\Gamma\) satisfy Assumptions (assump:interaction-kernel of the paper) and (assump:plasticity-function of the paper).
	Consider the solution \((X_i^{N},w^N_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq N}\) to the system of SDEs (equation eq:multi-agent-discrete of the paper),
	starting from independent initial states and weights \((X^N_{i,0},w^N_{ij,0})_{1\leq i,j\leq N}\) satisfying
	Assumptions (assump:weights of the paper) and (assump:initial-data of the paper). Define the associated (random) extended empirical measure \(\mu^N_{[0,t]} \in \mathcal{P}_{2,2,\nu}(\mathcal{C}_t^d\times [0,1])\) and empirical probability-graphon \(q^N_{t} \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu \otimes \nu}(\mathbb{R}\times [0,1]^2)\) as follows:  
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\mu^{N,\xi}_{[0,t]} &= \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathds{1}_{I_i^N}(\xi) \delta_{X_{i,[0,t]}^N}, \quad &&\xi \in [0,1], \quad t \in [0,T], \\ 
			q^{N,\xi,\xi'}_{t} &= \sum_{i,j=1}^{N} \mathds{1}_{I_i^N\times I_j^N}(\xi,\xi') \delta_{Nw_{ij}^N(t)}, \quad &&(\xi,\xi') \in [0,1]^2, \quad t \in [0,T].
		\end{aligned}
	\]
    
	Then, there exist a subsequence \(N_k\to \infty\), a sequence of measure-preserving maps \(\varphi_k \in S_{[0,1]}\),
	a limiting initial probability-graphon \(q_0\in \mathcal{P}_{\nu\otimes\nu}([-W,W]\times [0,1]^2)\), and a limiting
	initial fibered probability measure \(\mu_0\in \mathcal{P}_{2,2,\nu}(\mathbb{R}^d\times [0,1])\) such that the following
	holds. 
	
	Set any initial states $(X_0(\xi))_{\xi\in [0,1]}$ distributed according to \((\mu_0^\xi)_{\xi\in [0,1]}\) and any family of Wiener processes $(W(\cdot,\xi))_{\xi\in [0,1]}$ and, by virtue of Proposition (prop:well-posedness-multi-agent-macroscopic-solved-weights of the paper), let \((X(\cdot,\xi),q_{\gamma}^{\xi,\xi'})_{\xi,\xi'\in[0,1]}\) be the unique strong solution to the continuum system of McKean-Vlasov SDEs
	(equation eq:multi-agent-macroscopic-SDE of the paper) whose initial datum $X_0$ and its initial probability-graphon is given by \(q_0\). Denote by \(\mu_{[0,T]}\in \mathcal{P}_{2,2,\nu}(\mathcal{C}_T^d \times [0,1])\) the fibered pathwise law of the solution \(X\), and define the probability-graphon
	\(q_t\in \mathcal{P}_{\nu \otimes \nu}(\mathbb{R} \times [0,1]^2)\) as: 
	\begin{equation} 
		q^{\xi,\xi'}_t= \int_{\mathcal{C}_t^d} \mathbb{E}[q^{\xi,\xi'}_{\gamma}(t)] \, d\mu^{\xi'}_{[0,t]}(\gamma), \quad (\xi,\xi') \in [0,1]^2, \quad t \in [0,T].
	\end{equation}
	Then, as \(k \to \infty\), we have the following convergence for the extended empirical measure:
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			d_{W_2,2}(\mathbb{E}\mu^{N_k,\varphi_{k}}_{[0,T]},\mu_{[0,T]}) &\to 0,  \\ 
			\mathbb{E} W_2(\mu^{N_k,\varphi_{k}}_{[0,T]},\mu_{[0,T]}) &\to 0,
		\end{aligned}
	\]
	and for the empirical probability-graphon:
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\sup_{t\in [0,T]}d_{\text{BL},\square}(\mathbb{E}q^{N_k,\varphi_{k}}_t,q_t) &\to 0, \\ 
			\sup_{t\in [0,T]}\mathbb{E}d_{\text{BL}}(q^{N_k,\varphi_{k}}_t,q_t) &\to 0.
		\end{aligned}
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Proposition 3.1 of arXiv:2608.08073, 'eIRWR: Enhanced Iterative Random Walk with Restart for Scalable Root Cause Analysis in Mic'] shows that basic IRWR is not a new graph model at all. The ablation in Section 4.3 confirms this equality numerically and shows that walking on the true transpose W ⊤(a genuinely “backward” matrix) is in fact catastrophic. The consequence for evaluation is that basic IRWR must be benchmarked against a restart-tuned PPR, not the default; once that is done, its advantage disappears.
