(1) Galois's criterion: a finite extension obtained by adjoining radicals lies in a Galois extension whose group has a chain of normal subgroups with cyclic quotients (adjoining a primitive root of unity gives an abelian extension; adjoining a k-th root of an element, in the presence of the k-th roots of unity, gives a cyclic Kummer extension); a group with such a chain is solvable, and subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are solvable, so the Galois group of a polynomial solvable by radicals is solvable. Conversely a solvable Galois group yields a radical tower, again by Kummer theory. (2) The Galois group of the general polynomial of degree n over Q(a_1, ..., a_n) is the full symmetric group S_n: the roots are algebraically independent and the coefficients are the elementary symmetric functions of them, so every permutation of the roots extends to an automorphism fixing the coefficient field. (3) S_n is not solvable for n >= 5: its only nontrivial proper normal subgroup is A_n, and A_n is simple and non-abelian for n >= 5 (every element of A_n is a product of 3-cycles, all 3-cycles are conjugate in A_n for n >= 5, and any nontrivial normal subgroup of A_n contains a 3-cycle). Hence the general quintic is not solvable by radicals. (4) For the explicit examples: x^5 - 4x + 2 is irreducible over Q by Eisenstein at p = 2; it has exactly three real roots (its derivative 5x^4 - 4 vanishes at two points and the values there have opposite signs), so complex conjugation acts as a transposition; irreducibility makes the group transitive of order divisible by 5, so it contains a 5-cycle; a 5-cycle and a transposition generate S_5. The same argument, with the reduction of x^5 - x - 1 modulo 2 and 5 to produce the needed cycle types, gives S_5 for x^5 - x - 1 (irreducible modulo 5 since it has no root and no quadratic factor there). For n <= 4, S_4 is solvable (S_4 > A_4 > V_4 > 1 with abelian quotients), which is why the cubic and quartic formulas exist.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:e6f2a04e4ac8507250bf39ca99bd4be01dc87b100ccb98a635efbbbcfd665292","revision_digest":"sha256:115d87a98ec962f9b30fe189acf038bc99ce62e12c2461843b01819a67bf4895","source_id":"rederived:urn:mb-agent:21720ba24e313383","source_revision":"standard-theorem-2026-09-03; stated and proved in outline by the author from Galois's criterion and the simplicity of A_n; references: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra, section 14.7 (Theorem 39 and Corollary 40); Stewart, Galois Theory, chapters 8 and 15; Artin, Galois Theory","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 58 (Universal critical endpoint and its sharp boundary) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Suppose \(H\) is infinite dimensional.  Then, for every \(K,T>0\),
\begin{equation}
 p_{\mathrm{univ}}(\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{cont}}(K,T);H)=1.
 
\end{equation}
The exponent-one upper bound is dimension free and is quantified by
\eqref{cc:eq-universal-weak-area-bound}.  It is sharp in all of the
following distinct senses.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.8em]
\item No \(\mathcal S_{p,\infty}\) with \(p<1\) contains all terminal
areas in \(\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{cont}}(K,T)\).
\item No finite critical Lorentz ideal \(\mathcal S_{1,\rho}\),
\(0<\rho<\infty\), is universal.
\item Given any deterministic positive sequence
\(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\), there is one
martingale in \(\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{cont}}(K,T)\) such that, almost surely,
\begin{equation}
 A_{0,T}\in\mathcal S^0_{1,\infty}(H),\qquad
 \sup_n\frac{n s_n(A_{0,T})}{\varepsilon_n}=\infty,
 \qquad
 A_{0,T}\notin\bigcup_{0<\rho<\infty}\mathcal S_{1,\rho}(H).
 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Thus there is no conflict between
\eqref{cc:eq-individual-little-weak} and universal sharpness: each fixed
martingale area has \(ns_n(A)\to0\), while dimension-varying Brownian
blocks make that convergence arbitrarily slow and destroy every fixed
finite Lorentz refinement.

[Theorem thm:markov of arXiv:2607.14266, 'The Swapping Mechanism for Interacting Diffusions: Framework, Comparison with Switching, a'] Under Assumptions~(ass:A1 of the paper)--(ass:A3 of the paper), $Z=(Z_t)_{t\ge 0}$ is a
		homogeneous Feller--Markov process on $\mathbb{R}^{2d}$. Its infinitesimal
		generator coincides on $C_b^2(\mathbb{R}^{2d})$ with
		\begin{equation}
			\mathcal{L} f(z)=\mathcal{L}_0 f(z)+\gamma(z)\bigl[f(\tau z)-f(z)\bigr],\qquad z=(x,y),
		\end{equation}
		where $\mathcal{L}_0$ is the decoupled jump--diffusion generator:
		\begin{align}
			\mathcal{L}_0 f(x,y) &=\langle\beta_1(x),\nabla_x f\rangle
			+\langle\beta_2(y),\nabla_y f\rangle
			+\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}\bigl(\alpha_1(x)\alpha_1(x)^\top\nabla_x^2 f\bigr)
			+\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}\bigl(\alpha_2(y)\alpha_2(y)^\top\nabla_y^2 f\bigr)
			\notag\\
			&\quad+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\!
			\bigl[f(z+\psi_i(z,u))-f(z)-\langle\nabla f(z),\psi_i(z,u)\rangle\bigr]
			\nu_i(\mathrm{d} u).
			
		\end{align}

Let Sigma and Gamma be finite alphabets with N=|Sigma|>=2 and k=|Gamma|>=1. Let P be any fixed probability distribution on Sigma, H=-sum_a P(a)*ln P(a) its Shannon entropy in nats, with0*ln0=0, and let phi:Sigma->Gamma be a uniformly random function, so the labels phi(a) are independent uniform samples. Write r(b)=sum_{a:phi(a)=b}P(a). Then P_phi(sum_{b in Gamma}min(1/k,r(b))>=H/(4*ln N))>=1-2^(k-H*exp(H/2)/(4*ln N)). This is the stated Golowich-Moitra C.1 bound with an explicitly corrected proof: the source light-set mass estimate is not valid unconditionally, but follows in the only regime where this probability lower bound is positive. This card is unaudited and does not claim a new concentration theorem.
N>=2 and k>=1; natural logarithms; fixed P independent of the uniform random map.
Uniform random function means fully independent output labels, not merely an arbitrary pairwise-independent hash family.
Source-proof repair is explicitly labeled and awaits independent review.

[Proposition 31 (Mesoscopic CLT for $\infty$-Ginibre ensemble) of arXiv:2506.11707, 'Fluctuations of two-dimensional determinantal processes associated with Berezin--Toeplitz '] Let $f \in C^1_0(\C)$ be a fixed function and let $g=f(\cdot \eta_N^{-1})$ where $\eta_N\le 1$ satisfies $N\eta_N^2 \to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$. 
Then $\Upsilon(g, P_N) \to  \Sigma^2_\C(f)/2$ as $N\to\infty$. 
In particular, if $\X_N$ denotes $\infty$-Ginibre point process, then as $N\to\infty$
\[
\X_N(g) -  N\int g \d \bgamma \,\Longrightarrow\, \sqrt{\Sigma^2_\C(f)}\, \mathcal{G}. 
\]
This generalizes \eqref{bulkCLT} on mesoscopic scales.

[Thm adaptation_of_stroock_varadhan of arXiv:2412.06701, 'Matsumoto-Yor processes on Jordan algebras'] Consider i.i.d. increments $p^n_1$, $p^n_2$, $\dots$ in $P \subset G$ with $p^n_j = \Prm\left( w_j^n \right)$. And set for $t \geq 0$
$$ \tilde{g}_t = p^n_1 \dots p^n_{\lfloor nt\rfloor} \ ,$$
which is a random walk on $G$. If $p^{(n)} = \Prm\left( w^{(n)} \right)$ has the same law as one of the increments, we assume 
\begin{itemize}
\item the following asymptotic behavior of the mean
$$
    \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} n {\mathbb E} \log_E w^{(n)} = m \in E \ ,
$$
\item the convergence in law
$$
    \sqrt{n} \log_E w^{(n)} \stackrel{{\mathcal L}}{\longrightarrow} X
$$
with $X$ having identity covariance,
\item with the moment ${\mathbb E} \| \sqrt{n} \log_E w^{(n)} \|^{2+\delta}$ remaining bounded, for a given $\delta>0$.
\end{itemize}
Then, for any finite time horizon $T>0$, $\tilde{g}$ converges in law in ${\mathcal D}( [0,T] , G)$ towards a diffusion with generator
$$
   2L(m) + 2 \sum_{i}^{\dim E} X_i^2 \ .
$$

PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. Let G be a countable connected graph of maximum degree Delta>=2 with iid finite nonnegative edge weights W. If for some theta>0, (Delta-1) E exp(-theta W)<1, then almost surely every vertex pair has a finite path attaining its passage-time infimum. Counting simple paths, exponential Markov bounds and Borel-Cantelli make all bounded-cost competitors have bounded lengths. In particular (Delta-1)P(W=0)<1 suffices, even without a positive lower bound or a finite mean. On Z^d this gives the known sufficient subrange P(W=0)<1/(2d-1), leaving the arbitrary-law question unresolved.

[Definition 3 (Petite set) of arXiv:2606.23222, 'A Route to Harris ergodicity for Non-Feller Markov Kernels'] A measurable set \(C\subset S\) is petite if there exist a probability
distribution \(a=(a_n)_{n\ge1}\) on \(\mathbb N^*=\{1,2,\ldots\}\) and a
non-zero measure \(\nu\) on \(S\) such that
\[
        \sum_{n\ge1} a_n P^n(x,\cdot)\ge \nu(\cdot),

\]
Equivalently, \(C\) is small for the averaged kernel
\[
        K_a=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nP^n .
\]

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2410.23509, 'Dynkin Games for L\'evy Processes'] Consider a L\'evy process $X$,
a discount rate $r>0$, and two continuous reward functions $G_1\leq G_2\colon\mathbb{cR}\to\mathbb{cR}$.
Assume that there exist two points 
 $x_I<x_S$
and two continuous non-decreasing functions: 
$Q_I$ s.t. $Q_I(x)=0$ for  $x_I\leq x$
and
$Q_S$ s.t. $Q_S(x)=0$ for $ x\leq x_S$
(named \emph{averaging functions});
and such that
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x Q_I(I)+\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x Q_S(S)=
\begin{cases}G_1(x),&\quad\text{when $x_S\leq x$,}\\
\\
G_2(x),&\quad\text{when $x\leq x_I$,}\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where $I$ and $S$ are defined in (equation eq:supinf of the paper).
Define the function
\begin{equation}
V(x)=
\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x Q_I(I)+ \operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x Q_S(S), \text{ for all $x\in\mathbb{cR}$.}\end{equation}
Then, if the condition
\begin{equation}G_1(x)\leq V(x)\leq G_2(x),\end{equation}
holds for all $x\in[x_I,x_S]$, the DG  of Definition (def:dg of the paper)
has value function $V(x)$ in (equation eq:ve of the paper), and optimal stopping rules given by
\begin{equation}\sigma^*=\inf\{t\geq 0\colon X_t\leq x_I\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tau^*=\inf\{t\geq 0\colon X_t\geq x_S\}.\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Integrator-authored exact restricted calculation or proof-obstruction analysis after primary-source comparison Result: In the limiting decorated Poisson process, restrict leader heights to [-t,H] and let F_s be the number of sites in one cluster within depth s. Conditional on Z, Campbell's formula gives expected truncated count Z(A)*exp(alpha*t)*integral_0^(t+H) exp(-alpha*s)*E[F_s] ds. If E[F_s] is asymptotic to c*exp(alpha*s), this is asymptotic to c*Z(A)*t*exp(alpha*t) when H=o(t), explaining the conjectured t factor. The conditional variance, when finite, is Z(A)*exp(alpha*t)*integral_0^(t+H) exp(-alpha*s)*E[F_s^2] ds. Its negligibility after division by t^2*exp(2*alpha*t), and control of high leaders and finite-N approximation, are additional requirements, not consequences of the first-moment formula. Check: The change of variables s=t+h transforms the leader intensity exp(-alpha*h)dh to exp(alpha*t)*exp(-alpha*s)ds. For bounded cluster truncations, both Poisson moment formulas follow directly from independent increments; monotone convergence gives the expectation identity with possibly infinite values. Let A = (a_ij) be a complex n x n matrix and for each i let R_i = sum_{j != i} |a_ij| be the i-th deleted absolute row sum and D_i = { z in C : |z - a_ii| <= R_i } the i-th Gershgorin disc. Then every eigenvalue of A lies in the union of the discs D_1, ..., D_n. Applying the theorem to the transpose, every eigenvalue also lies in the union of the column discs (radii the deleted column sums), so the spectrum lies in the intersection of the two unions. Refinement: if a union of k of the discs is disjoint from the union of the other n - k, then exactly k eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity) lie in the union of those k discs. Consequences: a strictly diagonally dominant matrix (|a_ii| > R_i for all i) is invertible, since 0 lies in no disc; a Hermitian strictly diagonally dominant matrix with positive diagonal is positive definite; and the discs can be shrunk by a diagonal similarity D^{-1} A D, which changes the radii to sum_{j != i} |a_ij| d_j / d_i.
A a square complex matrix; eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity in the refinement
the discs are closed; a point of the union may fail to be an eigenvalue (the theorem localises, it does not characterise)

[Theorem thm:stationary-phase of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Let $(G,\rho)$ be a stationary random rooted graph that is almost surely infinite, and let $(\sigma(v))_{v\in V}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables sampled independently of~$(G,\rho)$, with $\mathbb{E}[\sigma] = \mu$ and $\mathbb{E}[|\sigma(\rho)|/\deg(\rho)] < \infty$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
			\item If $\mu > 1$, then $\mathbb{P}(\sigma \textup{ stabilizes}) = 0$.
			\item If $\mu < 1$, then $\mathbb{P}(\sigma \textup{ stabilizes}) = 1$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The first factorial moments of the beta binomial distribution are
$$\widetilde{M}_1=\frac{na}{a+b}$$
$$\widetilde{M}_2=\frac{n(n-1)a(a+1)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}$$
$$\widetilde{M}_3=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)a(a+1)(a+2)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)(a+b+2)}$$
$$\widetilde{M}_4=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)a(a+1)(a+2)(a+3)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)(a+b+2)(a+b+3)}$$
and this allows computing $(E,V,\gamma,\kappa)$, with $E,V$ being as before, the skewness being 
$$\gamma=\frac{(2n+a+b)(b-a)}{a+b+2}\sqrt{\frac{a+b+1}{nab(n+a+b)}}$$
and with the formula of the kurtosis looking fairly bad.

body:
[Proposition 52 (No universal bound below the first moment) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $d\ge1$. Suppose there exist a constant $K>0$ and a nondecreasing functional
\[
\Psi:\ \{ \text{nonnegative integer-valued random variables} \}
\longrightarrow [0,\infty]
\]
with the following \emph{universality property}:

\smallskip

For every finitary coding $\varphi$, every i.i.d.\ input $X$, every local observable $f$, and every $n\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\E\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\big(c_i^{(n)}(X)\big)^2
\ \le\ K\,\|\delta f\|_2^2\, \Psi\big(r_\varphi^{(n)}(X)\big),
\]
where $r_\varphi^{(n)}$ denotes the truncated coding radius at the origin.

\smallskip

Then, for all $n$,
\[
\E\,\big|B_\infty\!\big(0,r^{(n)}_\varphi(X)\big)\big|
\ \le\ K\, \Psi\big(r_\varphi^{(n)}(X)\big),
\]
and letting $n\to\infty$,
\[
\E\,\big|B_\infty\!\big(0,r_\varphi(X)\big)\big|
\ \le\ K\, \liminf_{n\to\infty}\Psi\big(r_\varphi^{(n)}(X)\big).
\]

In particular, any universal squared-influence bound depending only on the random variable $r_\varphi$
must control at least the first moment of the coding volume; no strictly smaller such functional
can replace it.

body:
[Lem 4.3 of arXiv:2412.00708, 'Stochastic PDE approach to fluctuating interfaces'] Let $W(t,z,\underline{x})$  be the Gaussian white noise process (i.e.\ the time
integral of $\dot{W}$) on ${\mathbb{R}}\times {\mathbb{T}}^{d-1}$.
For $\varphi_1=\varphi_1(z)\in L^2({\mathbb{R}})$, define $W(t,\underline{x};\varphi_1)$ by 
$\int_{\mathbb{R}} W(t,z,\underline{x}) \varphi_1(z)dz$, or more precisely, for $\varphi_2=\varphi_2(\underline{x})$,
$$
W(t,\varphi_2;\varphi_1) := \langle W(t),\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2\rangle_{{\mathbb{R}}\times{\mathbb{T}}^{d-1}}.
$$
Then, $W(t,\underline{x};\varphi_1)$ is the Gaussian white noise process on
${\mathbb{T}}^{d-1}$ multiplied by $\|\varphi_1\|_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}$.

body:
Let $W$ be $n \times n$ with i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1/n)$ entries. Then $\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}} \to 2$ almost surely as $n \to \infty$; equivalently, for entries $\mathcal{N}(0,\alpha/n)$, $\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}} \to 2\sqrt{\alpha}$. Consequently $\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}} \le 1$ eventually almost surely when $\alpha<1/4$, and fails eventually almost surely when $\alpha>1/4$. At the critical value $\alpha=1/4$ neither holds: the edge fluctuation is of Tracy-Widom type, so $\mathbb{P}(\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le 1)$ converges to a limit strictly between $0$ and $1$, and the threshold is approached but not attained.
entries are i.i.d. centered Gaussian with variance 1/n (finite fourth moment is what the general theorem needs)
the matrix is square; for m x n with m/n -> y the limit is 1 + sqrt(y)

body: [Lem stablypositive of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a foliation on $\mathbb{T}^2$ which is horizontal with respect to coordinates $\mathbb{T}^2 \cong S^1_x \times S^1_y$ and has $\slope(\mathcal{G})>0$. Then $\mathcal{G}$ is isotopic, via an arbitrarily small $C^0$-isotopy, to a stably positive $C^0$-foliation.

body:
[Theorem thm:HOMFLY splitting of arXiv:2608.29986, 'Khovanov-Rozansky homology over $\F[U,V]$'] Let $K \subset S^3$ be a knot and let $\mathit{CH}_{\mathcal{R}_1}(K) = \mathit{CH}(K) \otimes_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}} [U,V]} \mathcal{R}_1$ be its Khovanov-Rozansky complex over $\mathcal{R}_1 = \frac{\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}} [U,V]}{(UV)}$. Then
\[\mathit{CH}_{\mathcal{R}_1}(K) \simeq S_1 \oplus \dots \oplus S_m \oplus L_1 \oplus \dots \oplus L_k\]
where $S_1, \dots, S_m$ are snake complexes and $L_1, \dots, L_k$ are local systems. Moreover, the direct summands are unique up to permutation. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary 16 of arXiv:2609.03946, 'The groups $\SL_2(\F_{13})$ and $\SL_2(\F_{19})$ are Galois over $\Q$'] For each $\ell\in\{13,19\}$ there is a continuous surjection
\[
 \rho_\ell\colon\GQ\twoheadrightarrow\SL_2(\Z_\ell)
\]
unramified outside a finite set of primes, whose reduction modulo $\ell$ cuts
out $M_\ell$, for which every complex conjugation lies in $\ker\rho_\ell$.
Consequently, the fixed field $M_{\ell,n}$ of
$\ker(\rho_\ell\bmod\ell^n)$ is totally real with
$\Gal(M_{\ell,n}/\Q)\cong\SL_2(\Z/\ell^n\Z)$, the fields satisfy
$M_{\ell,n}\subset M_{\ell,n+1}$, and all are unramified outside one fixed
finite set.

[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2512.05466, 'Stochastic Flows and Marked Stable Processes'] Let $\delta_1^* \ge 0$, $\delta_2^*\in \bR$, $z\ge r_0$, $b\ge 0$ and $Y$ be the ${\rm BESQ}(\delta^*_1\,|_z\, \delta_2^*)$ flow line starting at $(b,r_0)$ driven by $-\cW^*$ and killed on $(z,\infty)$.    Let $\delta_3\ge 0$ such that $\delta_3\ge 2-\delta_1^*$ and $\cS$ be the ${\rm BESQ}(2-\delta_2^*-\delta_3\,|_{-z}\,2-\delta_1^*-\delta_3)$ flow driven by $\cW$.  Consider the collection of processes defined by
 \[
\cS^{+}_{r,x}(a) :=\max(\cS_{r,x}(a+ Y_{-r})- Y_{-x},0), \qquad a\ge 0,\, r\le x\le -r_0
\]
and 
 \[
\cS^{-}_{r,x}(a) :=
\cS_{r,x}(a), \quad  -\zeta^*<r\le x\le -r_0,\,\quad 0\le a < Y_{-r}, 
\]

\noindent where $\zeta^*$ is the absorption time of $Y$, i.e. $\zeta^*:=\inf\{r\ge z\,:\, Y_r=0\}$ if $\delta_2^*<2$ and $\zeta^*=\infty$ otherwise.

    (i) The flow  $\cS^{+}$ is on $(-\infty,-r_0)$ a  ${\rm BESQ}(2-\delta_2^*-\delta_3\,|_{-\zeta^*}\, {2-\delta_3})$ flow driven by $\cW^{+}_Y$, killed on $(-\zeta^*,-r_0)$. 

    (ii) $\cS_{r,x}^-(a)\le Y_{-x}$ for any $ -\zeta^*<r\le x\le -r_0,\, 0\le a<Y_{-r}$.
    
    (iii)  Both $Y$ and $\cS^{-}$  are measurable w.r.t. $\cW_Y^{-}$.

    (iv) $\cW_Y^+$ is a white noise independent of $\cW_Y^-$.

body:
[Proposition eq:entropy limit property of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] For all odd $k \ge 3$ and any distinct $i,j \in [k]$, there exist asymmetric two-point distributions supported on $\{i,j\} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_k$ which are not symmetrization resistant. 

\begin{proof}
By affine invariance ((lem:affine_invariance of the paper)), we may take $p > 1/2$, and we may take our two-point PMF $f = f_k$ on $\mathbb{Z}_k$ to be such that $f_k(-1) = 1-p$ and $f_k(1) = p$ and zero elsewhere. 
We will construct a PMF $g = g_k$ for each $k$ such that $f * g$ is symmetric and 
\begin{equation} \lim_{p \downarrow \frac{1}{2}} H(g_k) = 0 . \end{equation}

We begin by writing $k = 2l + 1$ and $\delta = \frac{2p-1}{kp-l} = \frac{2p-1}{2lp+p-l}$. 
Define $g(0) = 1-l\delta$; the values of $g$ at the $2l$ remaining elements of $\mathbb{Z}_k = \mathbb{Z}_{2l+1}$ will be $\delta$ ($l$ times) and $0$ ($l$ times), according to the following pattern:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $k \equiv_4 1$, 
 $g_k(1) \coloneqq g_k(2) \coloneqq 0$ 
and $g_k(3) \coloneqq g_k(4) \coloneqq \delta$. 
\item If $k \equiv_4 3$, 
 $g_k(1) \coloneqq \delta$,
 $g_k(2) \coloneqq 0$;
and when $k > 3$, 
 $g_k(3) \coloneqq 0$ and 
 $g_k(4) \coloneqq \delta$. 
\item For all $k \ge 11$, for all integers $r \in [5,l]$, $g_k(r) \coloneqq g_k(r-4)$. 

\item Finally, for all $r \in [l]$, $g(-r) \coloneqq 0$ iff $g(r)=\delta$ and $g(-r)\coloneqq \delta$ iff $g(r)=0$. 
\end{enumerate}
Intuitively, $g$ consists of one large mass at the origin, and alternating pairs of zeros and $\delta$s on the rest of $\mathbb{Z}_k$. 

Note that $\lim_{p \downarrow \frac{1}{2}} \delta = 0$, so that
$\lim_{p \downarrow \frac{1}{2}} g_k = \mathds{1}_{0}$ and therefore $g_k$ satisfies (equation eq:entropy limit property of the paper). 
It remains to show that $g_k$ is a symmetrizer of $f_k$, i.e., that $(g_k * f_k)(r) = (g_k * f_k)(-r)$ for all $r \in [l]$. 

For $r \ge 2$, noting that $g(\pm(r-1)), g(\pm(r+1)) \in \{0, \delta\}$ with $g(-(r-1)) = \delta$ iff $g(r-1) = 0$ iff $g(r+1) = \delta$ iff $g(-(r+1))=0$, 
we have $g(-(r-1)) = g(r+1)$ and $g(-(r+1)) = g(r-1)$, so that
\[
(f * g)(r) 
= pg(r-1) + (1-p)g(r+1)
= pg(-r-1) + (1-p)g(-r+1) 
= (f * g)(-r) .
\]
Finally, noting that the values of $g_k(2) = 0$ and $g_k(-2) = \delta$ for all $k$, we compute
\begin{align*}
(f* g)(1) 
&= pg(0) + (1-p)g(2) \\

&= \frac{p^2}{2lp + p -l} \\
&= \frac{p^2 - (1-p)p + (1-p)p}{2lp + p -l} \\
&= \frac{p(2p - 1)}{2lp + p -l} + (1-p)g(0) \\
&= p \delta + (1-p)g(0) \\

&= (f* g)(-1). \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition eq:entropy limit property of arXiv:2607.29020

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] For \(\lambda,\mu\in[-\pi,\pi]\), recall that
\[
E_{n,f}(\lambda,\mu)
:=
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}

D_n(\lambda-\omega)\,D_n(\omega-\mu)\,\dd\omega.

\le
\frac{2\pi}{n}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
|f(\omega)-f(\lambda)|^2\,\Phi_n(\lambda-\omega)\,\dd\omega .
\]

body:
Fix input dimension d>=1 and a finite normalized training horizon T>=1. Data (x,y) are sampled independently at successive steps from a distribution P with bounded support in R^d times R. Let sigma be C^2, bounded and Lipschitz, with bounded first and second derivatives. Set sigma_*(x;(a,w))=a sigma(w.x), v(w)=-E[y sigma(w.x)] and u(w,w_prime)=E[sigma(w.x)sigma(w_prime.x)]; assume v and u are differentiable with bounded Lipschitz continuous gradients (Assumption 1). The initial neuron parameters (a_i,w_i) are iid with common bounded-support law rho_0 on R^(d+1), independently of the training samples. The two-layer mean-field network is f_N(x;theta)=N^(-1) sum_i a_i sigma(w_i.x). Use noiseless, unregularized SGD with source scaling xi=1/2, namely theta_i^(k+1)=theta_i^k+epsilon [y_k-f_N(x_k;theta^k)] grad_theta sigma_*(x_k;theta_i^k). The horizon here is the nonlinear-dynamics time k epsilon, as in Appendix B.2; this differs by a fixed factor from the sum of the source step sizes s_k=epsilon/2. These smooth-activation restrictions are an explicitly narrower case of the source; in particular ReLU is excluded. Train networks A and B independently using this same initialization law, training distribution and scheme, and stop them at k=floor(T/epsilon). For every delta in (0,1) and err>0 there is N_min such that for all N>=N_min there is epsilon_max(N)>0 such that for all 0<epsilon<=epsilon_max(N), with probability at least 1-delta there exists one permutation pi of all N neuron pairs (a_i,w_i) in B such that for P_x-almost every x, simultaneously for all t in [0,1], |t f_N(x;theta_A)+(1-t)f_N(x;theta_B) -f_N(x;t theta_A+(1-t)pi theta_B)|<=err. The permutation acts on both incoming weights and the corresponding output coefficients. No dimension-free width bound or trained deep-network conclusion is asserted.
fixed finite dimension and horizon; bounded training-data and initialization support
bounded smooth Lipschitz activation and bounded Lipschitz interaction gradients
mean-field normalization; iid initial neurons; fresh iid data at successive SGD steps
no gradient noise and no weight decay; constant source step size epsilon/2

[Lemma lem:exp-decay of arXiv:2411.10419, 'Lower bounds on the top Lyapunov exponent for linear PDEs driven by the 2D stochastic Navi'] In the same setting as in Theorem~(thm:main of the paper), for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a random constant $D_\varepsilon(\omega,u_0)$ satisfying $D_\varepsilon \in (0,1]$, $\mathbb{P}\times \mu$ almost surely, and a closed random subspace $F(\omega,u_0)\subset L^2_{*}$ with $\mathrm{codim}\,F(\omega,u_0) = m \in (0,\infty)$, such that for all $ \varrho_{0} \in L^{2}_{*}$ we have for all $t\geqslant 0$
\begin{equ}
   \|\varrho_t\| \geqslant  D_\varepsilon(\omega,u_0)\|\varrho_0\| \sin\angle(\varrho_0,F(\omega,u_0))e^{(\lambda^{\kappa}_1-\varepsilon) t}\;,
\end{equ}
where
\[
\sin\angle(\varrho_0,F) = \inf_{\varphi\in
F(\omega,u_0)}\frac{\|\varrho_0-\varphi\|}{\|\varrho_0\|}\;.
\]
title: Lemma lem:exp-decay of arXiv:2411.10419

body: [Thm 22 of arXiv:2609.00758, 'Deformations of Compact Calabi--Yau and Fano Varieties with Isolated Singularities'] Let $X,Y$ be compact complex spaces and $f:Y\to X$ a morphism with $f_*\O_Y=\O_X.$ Let $\cX\to S$ be a deformation of $X,$ $\cY\to S$ a deformation of $X,$ and $F:\cY\to\cX$ an $S$-morphism such that the diagram $\begin{tikzcd} \cY\ar[d,"F"] & Y\ar[l]\ar[d,"f"] \\ \cX& X\ar[l] \end{tikzcd}$ commutes. Let $\cX'\to S$ be another deformation of $X,$ and $F':\cY\to \cX'$ an $S$-morphism such that that the diagram $\begin{tikzcd} Y\ar[r]\ar[d,"f"]& \cY\ar[d,"F' "] \\ X\ar[r]&  \cX' \end{tikzcd}$ commutes. Then after making $S$ smaller if necessary, the deformations $\cX\to S$ and $\cX'\to S$ are isomorphic.

body: [Definition Vertex Separator, see e.g. \cite{RT23} Definition 4.8 of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] For any shape $\tau$, a vertex separator is a subset of vertices $S \subseteq V(\tau)$ such that there is no path from $U_\tau$ to $V_\tau$ in $\tau ~ \textbackslash ~ S$, which is the shape obtained by deleting $S$ and all edges adjacent to S. We write $S_\tau$ for a vertex separator of the minimum size.
title: Vertex Separator, see e.g. \cite{RT23} Definition 4.8

body:
[Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] Let $\C$ be a (locally small) monoidal category and $X,Y \in \text{Ob}(\text{Fun}(\C,\textbf{Set}))$. We define the \textit{Day convolution} of $X$ and $Y$ as the left Kan extension of their external product $$X\Tilde{\times}Y: (c,d) \mapsto X(c) \times Y(d)$$ along the bifunctor given by the internal monoidal law $\otimes$ of $\C$. 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\C \times \C} && \Set \\
	& {\C}
	\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{{X \Tilde{\times} Y}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\otimes"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{{\text{Lan}_\otimes (X\Tilde{\times} Y) =: X \otimes_{\mathrm{Day}}Y }}"', dashed, from=2-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shorten <=3pt, Rightarrow, from=0, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

The Day convolution, denoted by $\otimes_{\mathrm{Day}}$, assembles into a bifunctor and gives $\text{Fun}(\C,\Set)$ the structure of a closed monoidal category, as shown in Proposition 3.1 of \cite{nlab:day_convolution}.
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.29075

PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. For a continuous-time birth-death queue with birth rate lambda, death rate mu>lambda, killed on hitting zero, the expected busy duration from k>=0 is k/(mu-lambda) and the expected integral of queue length before extinction is k^2/[2(mu-lambda)]+(lambda+mu)k/[2(mu-lambda)^2]. The quadratic function has generator equal to minus k; negative drift gives exponential jump-count tails, which justify stopping and passage to the limit. These identities also average over a Poisson initial queue.
Constant birth and death rates
0<lambda<mu
Integer starting queue k>=0
Kill the process on hitting zero

Assume Poisson arrivals of rate lambda>0, independent exponential service of rate mu>lambda, FCFS, and a single server. After becoming empty, it remains on for a deterministic grace period g in [0,infinity], then switches off. An arrival to an off server starts a deterministic setup of duration tau>=0. Setup is not cancelled; arrivals during setup wait and are served when setup ends. Define p=exp(-lambda g) (p=0 for g=infinity), x=lambda tau, v=mu-lambda, and rho=lambda/mu.

The stationary mean queueing wait, excluding service, is

W(g)=lambda/[mu(mu-lambda)] + tau(1+lambda tau/2) p/(1+lambda tau p).

The long-run fractions of time busy, on-idle, off, and in setup are respectively

rho, (1-rho)(1-p)/(1+xp), (1-rho)p/(1+xp), (1-rho)xp/(1+xp).

If their powers are B,I,O,U, average power is

P(g)=rho B+(1-rho) I+(1-rho)[O+xU-(1+x)I] p/(1+xp).

F(k)=k^2/(2v)+(lambda+mu)k/(2v^2).

The generator satisfies LF(k)=-k and F(0)=0. Queue height is at most k plus the number of jumps. This tail makes the stopped quadratic boundary term vanish and the queue area integrable; apply the stopped generator identity and let the cutoff tend to infinity. The Poisson initial queue also has all moments and exponential moments sufficiently near zero, so the same formulas can be averaged over K.

C=mu/[lambda v] (1+xp),

and its expected queue area is

A=mu/v^2 [1+mu tau p+lambda v tau^2 p/2].

Renewal reward gives E[N]=A/C. Little's law gives response time E[N]/lambda, and subtracting 1/mu yields the displayed W. [Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.29486, 'Cabled braids and their crossing matrices'] Let $b, b' \in \mathcal{B}_n$. 
Let $\varphi$ be the braid permutation of $b$. 
Let $b_i, b'_{\varphi(i)} \in \mathcal{B}_{k_i}$ ($i=1, 2, \dots , n$). 
We have 
\begin{align*}
f(b_1, b_2, \dots , b_n;b) f(b'_{1}, b'_{2}, \dots , b'_{n};b') =
f(b_1 b'_{\varphi(1)}, b_2 b'_{\varphi(2)}, \dots , b_n b'_{\varphi(n)};bb').
\end{align*}

[Corollary corollary of arXiv:2412.06246, 'The smallest singular value for rectangular random matrices with Lévy entries'] Fix $\delta>1$, $\alpha\in(0,2)$ and let integers $N,n$ satisfy $N\geq \delta n$. Let $X=(x_{ij})$ be an $N\times n$ rectangular matrix with i.i.d. entries satisfying (equation stablelaw of the paper). Then for any $D>0$ we can find $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ and $C_4>0$ such that whenever $N\geq \max(N_0,\delta N)$, with probability at least $1-N^{-D}$ we have
    $$
X^*(B_1^N)\supset C_4 N^{\frac{1}{\alpha}-\frac{1}{2}}(\log N)^\frac{2(\alpha-2)}{\alpha}B_2^n,
    $$
    where $C_4,N_0$ depend only on $D,\alpha,\delta,C_\ell,C_u$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary corollary of arXiv:2412.06246

\end{align}

[Definition Entropy number of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space, and $\mathcal{M}\subseteq X$ be compact. For every fixed $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the entropy number $\varepsilon_n(\mathcal{M})_X$ is the infimum of all $\varepsilon > 0$ for which $2^n$ balls with centers from $X$ and radius $\varepsilon$ cover $\mathcal{M}$. Formally, we write
    \[
        \varepsilon_n(\mathcal{M})_X
        =
        \inf\left\{
            \varepsilon > 0 :
            \exists
            g_1,\cdots,g_{2^n} \in X,
            \
            \mathcal{M}
            \subseteq
            \bigcup_{j=1}^{2^n} B(g_j,\varepsilon)
        \right\}.
    \]
title: Entropy number

body: A smooth manifold of dimension n is a topological space M that is Hausdorff and second-countable, together with a smooth atlas: a collection of charts {(U_alpha, phi_alpha)} where the U_alpha are open sets covering M and each phi_alpha: U_alpha -> R^n is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of R^n, such that whenever U_alpha and U_beta overlap, the transition map phi_beta o phi_alpha^{-1} between open subsets of R^n is smooth (infinitely differentiable). Two atlases are considered to define the same smooth structure if their union is again a smooth atlas.

body:
[Lemma 28 of arXiv:2604.24684, 'Waning Immunity Fails to Restore a Positive Epidemic Threshold on Power--Law Networks'] Let $G=G(n,\tau)$ be a power-law random graph on $n$ vertices with exponent $\tau>2$. Then there exists a constant
$
M^{(0)}\ge 2
$
such that the following holds. For any $M\ge M^{(0)}$, if $v_1$ is a vertex with degree at least $M$, and
\(
k:=\left\lfloor \frac{\log n}{\log M}\cdot \min \left\{\frac{1}{32\tau}, \frac{\tau-2}{32(\tau-1)} \right\} \right\rfloor
\), and if $E$ is the event that there exist vertices
$v_2,\dots,v_k$ (not necessarily distinct)
such that, for every $i=1,\dots,k-1$,
\[
d(v_i)\ge M^i,
\qquad
\mathrm{dist}(v_i,v_{i+1})\le 4\tau(i+1)\log M.
\]
Then, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
\mathbb P(E)\ge \frac13 .
\]

body: [Definition of arXiv:2412.00279, 'Optimal local storage policy based on stochastic intensities and its large scale behavior'] Consider a local memory system with independent request processes $\{\Phi_i:i=1\ldots N\}$, aggregated natural history $\mathcal{F}_t$ and capacity $C$. A \emph{causal memory management} policy is a stationary $\mathcal{F}_t$-predictable stochastic process $\mathcal{C}(t)$, with values in the space $\mathscr{P}_C(N)$ of all subsets of $\{1,\ldots, N\}$ of size at most $C$ (equipped with the discrete $\sigma$-algebra).

[Defi def:Var of arXiv:2602.17579, 'Non-equilibrium functional inequalities for finite Markov chains'] For $f\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{|\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}|}$ we define the \emph{variance} and \emph{Dirichlet form} of $f$ 
respectively  as
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{var}_\pi(f)&\coloneqq  \mathbb E_\pi[f^2] - \bigl(\mathbb E_\pi[f]\bigr)^2 = (f^2,1)_\pi - \bigl((f,1)_\pi\bigr)^2, \\
     \mathscr{E}_\pi(f,M) &\coloneqq (f,-Mf)_\pi 
        = - \sum_{z,z'\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} f(z)f(z')M(z,z') \pi(z)
        = \frac12 \sum_{z,z'\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \big( f(z) - f(z') \big)^2 M(z,z') \pi(z). 
\end{align}

body: Let X be a normed vector space, X** its bidual (the dual of the dual X*), and J: X -> X** the canonical isometric embedding defined by J(x)(f) = f(x) for f in X*. Let B_X and B_{X**} denote the closed unit balls of X and X**. Then J(B_X) is dense in B_{X**} with respect to the weak-star topology sigma(X**, X*) on X**. When X is reflexive, J(X) = X** and the statement is immediate; the theorem's content is that weak-star density of J(B_X) in B_{X**} holds even when X is not reflexive. [Goldstine (1938); see Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis]
title: Goldstine's Theorem

body:
[Thm MO-as-colim of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The cocone $\sigma_{[0]}$ exhibits $\textbf{\textup{MO}}=\smash{\textbf{\textup{MOP}}^{[0]}}$ as the global colimit of $\smash{{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak J}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}|_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[0]}}}$.
    \begin{proof}
        We will more generally prove this for any $d\in{\mathbb{Z}}$, and similarly to before it will suffice to show that $\tilde\sigma_{[d]}$ exhibits $\textbf{\textup{BOP}}^{[d]}\hookrightarrow\textbf{\textup{BOP}}$ as a colimit.

        As $\ul\textup{VRep}=\coprod_{d\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\smash{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}$, we get an equivalence
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{\ul\textup{VRep}}\bar y_{\textup{top}} \simeq \coprod_{d\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}\,\bar y_{\textup{top}}|_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}
        \]
        in ${{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}[\textbf{\textup{BOP}}]$. As the left-hand side is terminal by Proposition~(prop:MOP-as-colim of the paper), so is the coproduct on the right-hand side. Thus, the coproduct of the maps 
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}\bar y_{\textup{top}}|_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}\to\big(\textbf{\textup{BOP}}^{[d]}\hookrightarrow\textbf{\textup{BOP}}\big)
        \]
        induced by $\tilde\sigma_{[d]}$ for all $d\in{\mathbb{Z}}$ is a map between terminal objects and hence an equivalence in ${{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}[\textbf{\textup{BOP}}]$. As a coproduct of maps in ${{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}[\textbf{\textup{BOP}}]\simeq({{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl}})_{/\textbf{\textup{BOP}}}$ (or any other $\infty$-topos) is an equivalence only if each summand is so, this completes the proof of the theorem.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm MO-as-colim of arXiv:2608.28504

[Theo 20 (Theorem 3.3 in \cite{Geiss:Ylinen:21}) of arXiv:2506.10213, 'Coupling of forward-backward stochastic differential equations on the Wiener space, and ap'] Let $n,d\ge 1$ and $(\Omega,\F,\P,W,\cP_T)$ be one of the quintuples
        $$
        (\Omega^i,\F^i,\P^i,W^i,\cP_T^i),\quad i = 0,1,
        $$
        as defined in Section~\ref{sec:coupling operator}. Consider the It\^o process
        \begin{equation}
         R_t = \xi  + \int_t^T f(s,K_s) \,\od s - \sum_{j=1}^d \int_t^T g_{j}(s,K_s) \,\od W_{s,j},
        \end{equation}
        where the following conditions are satisfied:
        \begin{enumerate}[$(S1)$]
            \item $\xi\in \cL^0(\Omega)$.
            \item The functions $f$ and each $g_j$ (for $j=1,\ldots,d$) are $(\mathcal{P_T},\mathcal{B}(C(\R^n)))$-measurable.
            \item The process $R=(R_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$, with $R_t:\Omega\to\R$, is continuous and $\F$-adapted.
            \item The process $K=(K_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$, with $K_t:\Omega\to\R^n$, is $\cP_T$-measurable.
            \item The integrability condition
            \[
            \E\int_0^T \Bigl[\,|f(s,K_s)| + |g(s,K_s)|^2\Bigr]\,\od s < \infty
            \]
            holds.
            \item The collections $(\xi,f,g,K,R,W)$ satisfies equation \eqref{eqn:theo:transference} for all $t\in[0,T]$ $\P$-a.s.
        \end{enumerate}
        
        Now, assume that the septuple $(\xi^0,f^0,g^0,K^0,R^0,W^0,\cP^0_T)$ satisfies conditions $(S1)$--$(S6)$. Let
        $\xi^1 \in \cC_0(\xi^0)$, and 
        $$
        f^1 \in \cC_T(f^0), \quad g_{j}^1 \in \cC_T(g^0_{j}),
        $$
        be $(\cP_T^1,\mathcal{B}(C(\R^n)))$-measurable modifications.
        Let
        $$
        R^1 \in \cC_T(R^0)
        $$
        be a continuous and $\F^1$-adapted process,
        and $K^1 \in \cC_T(K^0)$ be $\cP_T^1$-measurable.
        
        Then, the septuple
        $$
        (\xi^1,f^1,g^1,K^1,R^1,W^1,\cP_T^1)
        $$
        satisfies conditions $(S1)$--$(S6)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem main result of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] For any $\widehat G\subset\!\subset G$ with $G_0\subset \subset
\widehat G$ and $\kappa \in (0, \frac 12)$ being arbitrarily fixed,
there exists a constant ${\cal C}$ and a subdomain $\widetilde G \subset
\subset G$ with $\widehat G\subset \subset \widetilde G$, such that
for any solution $\tilde y$ to the equation (equation system-sp1 of the paper), it
holds that

\begin{align}\notag
    &   {\mathbb{E}} \int_{\frac T 2 - \kappa T}^{\frac T 2 + \kappa T}\int_{\widehat G}
    \big(|\nabla \tilde y|^2 + \tilde y^2\big)dx dt\\
    &   \leq {\cal C}\Big[ \exp\Big (\frac {\cal C}
    \varepsilon\Big ) {\mathbb{E}}\! \int_0^T\int_{G_0}\big( \tilde y^2 \!+ |\nabla \tilde y|^2\big)dx dt +
    \varepsilon{\mathbb{E}}\! \int_0^T  \int_{\widetilde G}(\tilde y^2 \!+\! |\nabla
    \tilde y|^2)dxdt\Big],
\end{align}
for all $ \varepsilon > 0 $. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

The Malliavin derivative on the Wiener-Poisson space is defined as the closed unbounded operator D = (D^{(1)}, D^{(2)}): D^{1, 2} subset L^2(Omega) -> L^2([0, T] x Omega) x L^2([0, T] x R_0 x Omega). For F in D^{(1)}, D_t^{(1)} F represents the stochastic gradient in the Brownian direction defined via directional perturbations along Cameron-Martin paths. For F in D^{(2)} with chaotic expansion F = sum_{n=0}^infinity I_n(h_n) with respect to Poisson integrals, D_{t, z}^{(2)} F = sum_{n=1}^infinity n * I_{n-1}(h_n(t, ., z)) denotes the difference operator F(omega + delta_{(t, z)}) - F(omega). The Hilbert space domain D^{1, 2} is equipped with the graph norm ||F||_{D^{1, 2}}^2 = ||F||_{L^2}^2 + ||D^{(1)} F||_{L^2([0, T] x Omega)}^2 + ||D^{(2)} F||_{L^2([0, T] x R_0 x Omega)}^2.
F in D^{1, 2} = D^{(1)} cap D^{(2)}

body:
[Satz thm:HigherOrderLSq of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on ${\mathbb R}^n$ which satisfies an $\mathrm{LS}_q$-inequality with constant $\sigma^q > 0$, and let $f\colon {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}$ be a $\mathcal{C}^d$-smooth function with ${\mathbb E} f = 0$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Assuming that $\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),1} \le \sigma^{d-j}$ for all $j=1,\ldots,d-1$ and $\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),\infty} \le 1$, it holds that
		\[
		\int \exp\Big\{\frac{c_{p,d}}{\sigma^p} |f|^{p/d} \Big\} d\mu \le 2,
		\]
		where a possible choice of the constant $c_{p,d}$ is given by
		\[
		c_{p,d} = \frac{2^{2p-3}(q^{1/p}-1)^p(p-1)^p}{eq \log^{p-1}(2)\max(q, p/d)}.
		\]
		\item For any $t\ge 0$, it holds that
		\[
		\mu(|f| \ge t)\le
		2 \exp\Big\{- \frac{C_p}{(d\sigma)^p} \min\Big(\min_{j=1, \ldots,d-1} \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),1}}\Big)^{p/j}, \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),\infty}}\Big)^{p/d}\Big)\Big\},
		\]
		where a possible choice of the constant $C_p$ is given by
		\[
		C_p = \frac{4^{p-1}(p-1)^p}{q\log^{p-2}(2) e^p}.
		\]
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 4 (Colored height function) of arXiv:2604.06532, 'Random permutations from $q$-Demazure products'] For a color threshold $c \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$, a row $S$, and a column $Y$, define
\[
  H(c;\, S,\, Y)
  \;:=\;
  \#\bigl\{\, Y' \ge Y : \text{the vertical arrow at column } Y',\, \text{row } S
  \text{ has color } \le c \,\bigr\}.
\]
At the top row $S = n$, this is related to the permutation height function by
$H(c;\, n,\, Y) = c - Y + 1 + n \cdot H_\sigma\!\bigl(\tfrac{Y-1}{n},\, \tfrac{c}{n}\bigr),$
since $H(c;\, n,\, Y)$ counts colors $\le c$ at positions $Y' \ge Y$, while $H_\sigma$ counts positions $i \le \lfloor nx \rfloor$ with $\sigma(i) > \lfloor ny \rfloor$.
title: Colored height function

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the annulus fields phi_k as exactly independent rather than approximately so, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the coupling error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the independence used in the concentric decomposition is an approximation that must be explicitly controlled, and skipping this step is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.
Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions
Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics
Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk
title: Technique: Concentric Decomposition of the 2D Gaussian Free Field

[Proposition prop:conditioned_Bernoulli2 of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph, $p_e\in(0,1), x_e>0$ for each $e\in E$. Let $\Omega = \{0,1\}^E$, $\Sigma \subset \Omega$ and $f(\omega)= \Sigma^{\uparrow}(\omega):=\{\eta \in \Sigma \mid \eta \supset \omega\}$, and 
	$$\rho[\omega] = \mathbb{P}_{p}[\omega], ~\forall \omega\in \Omega, ~\gamma[\eta] = \mathbb{P}_{\frac{x(1-p)}{1+x(1-p)}}[\eta \mid \Sigma]\propto \prod_{e\in \eta} x_e(1-p_e) , ~\forall \eta\in \Sigma.$$
    	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta]\propto \prod_{e\in \eta} x_e$. For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\mathscr{P}_\Omega[\omega] \neq 0$, the  conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]=\mathbb{P}_{\frac{x(1-p)}{1+x(1-p)}}[\; \cdot  \mid \Sigma^{\uparrow}(\omega)]$.
        \item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega} = \mathscr{P}_{\Sigma} \cap \mathbb{P}_{p}$.  
        For each $\eta\in\Sigma$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta] \neq 0$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta] = \mathbb{P}_p \cap \delta_{\eta} = \mathbb{P}_{\eta,p}. $ 
    \end{enumerate}

body: [Theorem thm:slow-switching-transience of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] In the \nameref{setting} Setting, suppose additionally that each CRN is endowed with mass-action kinetics and has at-most-monomolecular reactions. Suppose for each $i$ there exists a vector $v^i\in\mathbb R^d_{\ge0}$ such that $(v^iM_i)_m>0$ for each $m$ such that $v^i_m>0$, where $(v^iM_i)_m$ is the $m$-th entry of the vector $v^iM_i$. Suppose further that $\operatorname{supp}(v^i)=\operatorname{supp}(v^j)$ for each $i,j\in[n]$. Then as long as $\kappa>0$ is sufficiently small, $(x,i)$ is an evanescent state for the mixed Markov chain $Z_\kappa$ whenever $\operatorname{supp}(v^i)\cap\operatorname{supp}(x)\ne\varnothing$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:slow-switching-transience of arXiv:2507.09421

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Asymptotic influence bounds for polynomial thresholds exact calculation or structural obstruction Result: The desired C*d*sqrt(n) bound holds when the polynomial is a product of d affine linear forms with no cube zeros. Indeed its sign is a product of d threshold functions. If that product changes on a coordinate flip, at least one factor changes, so its influence is at most the sum of the factor influences. For a threshold g, unateness gives Inf_i(g)=|ghat(i)| and hence I(g)<=sqrt(n)*sqrt(sum_i ghat(i)^2)<=sqrt(n). Check: For a monotone coordinate of a Boolean function, its discrete derivative is either0 or1 after the conventional half-difference, so its expectation equals its flip probability. Cauchy-Schwarz and Parseval then give the threshold bound. A union bound gives the product estimate. Obstruction: A general multivariate polynomial need not factor into real affine forms. The argument supplies a genuine subclass result, not a reduction for arbitrary polynomial thresholds.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0173-asymptotic-influence-bounds-for-polynomial-thresholds
No independent review
title: Attempt on Asymptotic influence bounds for polynomial thresholds

body:
[Theorem 1 (Samuels' conjecture) of arXiv:2608.18392, 'On Samuels' Conjecture'] For every integer $n\geq1$, ordered mean vector $0\leq\mu_1\leq\cdots\leq\mu_n$, and $\lambda>\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_i$,
\begin{equation}
c(\bm{\mu},\lambda)
=
\min_{1\leq i\leq n} q_i(\bm{\mu},\lambda)
=
\min_{1\leq i\leq n} \prod_{j=i}^n \left( 1- \frac{\mu_j}{ \lambda-\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\mu_k } \right).

\end{equation}
The bound is sharp and is attained. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Samuels' conjecture

[Dfn 223 (relaxed domains) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\dist(\cdot,\cdot)$ denote the Euclidean distance in $\R^N$, and define
\beq
\begin{aligned}
    S_N(\iota)
    &\equiv\bigg\{\bx\in\R^N :
    \frac{\dist(\bx,S_N)}{N^{1/2}} \le \iota
    \bigg\}\,, &
    \Sigma_N(\iota)
    &\equiv\bigg\{\bx\in\R^N :
    \frac{\dist(\bx,\Sigma_N)}{N^{1/2}} \le \iota
    \bigg\}\,.
\end{aligned}\eeq
We call $S_N(\iota)$ the \textbf{$\iota$-relaxed spherical domain},
and $\Sigma_N(\iota)$  the \textbf{$\iota$-relaxed Ising domain}.\footnote{While these relaxed domains are needed in the Ising setting for the notion of a Lipschitz algorithm to make sense, any point in $S_N(\iota)$ or $\Sigma_N(\iota)$ can be rounded to a point in $S_N$ or $\Sigma_N$ with nearly the same performance; see Remark~\ref{r:relaxed-wlog}.}
title: relaxed domains

Let (M_k) be a martingale (or supermartingale for the upper tail) with respect to a filtration, with bounded increments |M_k - M_{k-1}| <= c_k almost surely. Then for all t > 0, P(M_n - M_0 >= t) <= exp(-t^2 / (2 sum of c_k^2)), and symmetrically for the lower tail: martingales with bounded steps concentrate like sums of independent bounded variables.

More explicitly, let (M_k)_{k=0}^n be an integrable real martingale with respect to a filtration (F_k), with |M_k-M_{k-1}| <= c_k almost surely for deterministic constants c_k >= 0. Write V = sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2. If V > 0 and t > 0, each of P(M_n-M_0 >= t) and P(M_n-M_0 <= -t) is at most exp(-t^2/(2V)), and P(|M_n-M_0| >= t) <= 2 exp(-t^2/(2V)). With the same increment bounds, the upper-tail inequality holds for supermartingales and the lower-tail inequality for submartingales. If V = 0 all increments vanish almost surely and all these tail probabilities are zero.
(M_k) a martingale for the given filtration
increments bounded: |M_k - M_{k-1}| <= c_k a.s.

[Proposition 4 (Equivariance of the flow-matching minimizer) of arXiv:2608.26961, 'Gromov--Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation'] Let $\pi\in\mathrm{c}_{\R^D}(\mu,\nu)$ be diagonally $G$-invariant and let
$v^\pi$ denote the minimizer of $J_\pi$ in \eqref{minvr}. Then $v^\pi$
admits a $G$-equivariant representative. More precisely, there exists a
jointly Borel field $\bar v:I\times\R^D\to\R^D$ such that
\[
\bar v_t=v_t^\pi
\qquad
\mu_t\text{-a.e. for a.e. }t\in I,
\]
and
\[
\bar v_t(gz)=g\bar v_t(z)
\qquad
\text{for every }g\in G,\ z\in\R^D,\ t\in I .
\]

[Dfn 46 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] Two separable representations $\pi$ and $\rho$ are \textbf{approximately equivalent}, written $\pi \simeq_\rm{a} \rho$, if there are unitary isomorphisms $U_1,U_2,\dots:H_\pi \to H_\rho$ such that
\[\|\pi(a) - U_n^\ast \rho(a) U_n\| \to 1 \qquad \hbox{as} \ n\to\infty \qquad \hbox{for every}\ a \in \A.\]

Similarly, $\pi$ is \textbf{approximately contained} in $\rho$, written $\pi \lesssim_{\rm{a}} \rho$, if there are unitary embeddings $V_1,V_2,\dots:H_\pi \to H_\rho$ such that
\[\|\pi(a) - V_n^\ast \rho(a) V_n\| \to 1 \qquad \hbox{as} \ n\to\infty \qquad \hbox{for every}\ a \in \A.\]
title: Definition 46 of arXiv:2507.08909

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $a:\mathbb{N}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $a(0_d)\neq 0$ and set $b:=a^{(-1)}$.
Then
\[
b(0_d)=\frac{1}{a(0_d)},
\qquad
b(k)=-\frac{1}{a(0_d)}\sum_{\substack{0_d\le_d \ell <_d k}} b(\ell)\,a(k-\ell),
\quad k\neq 0_d,
\]
where $\ell<_d k$ means $\ell\le_d k$ and $\ell\neq k$.

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2605.13727, 'Stochastic evolution equations\\ driven by arbitrary cylindrical Lévy processes'] Let $T>0$. On the space of \(H\)-valued, adapted, c\`adl\`ag processes on \([0,T]\), define a quasi-metric \(\rho_T^{\mathrm{em}}\) by setting, for each pair of processes \(X,Y\) in this space,
\[
\rho_T^{em}(X,Y)=  \sup_{\Gamma \in \mathcal{S}_{{\rm prd}}^{1, {\rm op}}}E\Bigg[
\norm{\Gamma(0)(X-Y)(0)+ \int_{(0,T]} \Gamma(s)\, \d(X-Y)( s)}\wedge 1 \Bigg].
\]
Then $\rho_T^{\rm em}$ and $d_T^{\rm em}$ generate the same topology on the space of $H$-valued, adapted, c\`adl\`ag processes on $[0, T]$.

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.27374, '\Large \bf Distribution-constrained optimal multiple stopping: the Root-type solution'] For every \(m\geq 1\), the measure \(\beta^m\) is supported on set of dyadic points $\{k2^{-m}:k\in\mathbb N_0\}$,
and this set meets every bounded interval in finitely many points.
Moreover, we have
$$
    \xi
    \leq_{st}
    \beta
    \leq_{st}
    \beta^m.
$$
For every \(T<\infty\), let 
$ \varepsilon_m(T)
    :=
    \sup_{0\le t\le T}
    \bigl(g_m(t)-g^\beta(t)\bigr)$. 
It follows that $ \varepsilon_m(T) \overset{m \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0$.
In particular, $\beta^m$ converges to $\beta$ weakly.

body:
[Definition 15 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Fix a set $\Sigma = \llbracket 1 , N \rrbracket$ with $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ and an interval $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}$.  A $\Sigma$-indexed line ensemble $\mathcal{L}$ on $\Lambda$ is said to satisfy the {\em partial Brownian Gibbs property} if and only if it is non-intersecting and for any finite set $K = \{k_1, k_1 + 1, \dots, k_2 \} \subset \Sigma$ with $k_2 \leq N - 1$, $[a,b] \subset \Lambda$ and any bounded Borel-measurable function $F: C(K \times [a,b]) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ we have $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E} \left[ F(\mathcal{L}|_{K \times [a,b]}) {\big \vert} \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} (K \times (a,b))  \right] =\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{avoid}}^{a,b, \vec{x}, \vec{y}, f, g} \bigl[ F(\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}) \bigr].
\end{equation}
On the left side of (\ref{Eq.PBGP}), we have that
$$\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} (K \times (a,b)) = \sigma \left \{ \mathcal{L}_i(s): (i,s) \in \Sigma \times \Lambda \setminus K \times (a,b) \right\},$$
and $ \mathcal{L}|_{K \times [a,b]}$ is the restriction of $\mathcal{L}$ to the set $K \times [a,b]$. On the right side of (\ref{Eq.PBGP}), we have $\vec{x} = (\mathcal{L}_{k_1}(a), \dots, \mathcal{L}_{k_2}(a))$, $\vec{y} = (\mathcal{L}_{k_1}(b), \dots, \mathcal{L}_{k_2}(b))$, $f = \mathcal{L}_{k_1 - 1}[a,b]$ with the convention that $f = \infty$ if $k_1 = 1$, and $g = \mathcal{L}_{k_2 +1}[a,b]$. In addition, $\mathcal{Q} = \{\mathcal{Q}_i\}_{i = 1}^{k_2 - k_1 + 1}$ has law $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{avoid}}^{a,b, \vec{x}, \vec{y}, f, g}$ as in Definition \ref{Def.fgAvoidingBE}, and $\tilde{\mathcal{Q}} = \{\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_{i}\}_{i = k_1}^{k_2}$ satisfies $\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_i = \mathcal{Q}_{i - k_1 + 1}$.
title: Definition 15 of arXiv:2603.24616

[Definition Tempered distribution of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] A \emph{tempered distribution} on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is a continuous linear functional
\[
  T: \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^d) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathbb{C}.
\]
The space of all tempered distributions is denoted by \(\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^d)\). That is,
\[
  \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^d)
  \;=\;
  \bigl\{\,T: \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^d)\to\mathbb{C} \text{ linear} 
  \;\bigm|\; T \text{ is continuous w.r.t.\ the Fréchet topology on } \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^d)\bigr\}.
\]
Continuity here means that whenever a sequence \(\{\varphi_j\}\subset\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) converges to zero (in the sense that each seminorm \(p_{\alpha,\beta}(\varphi_j)\to 0\)), we have \(T(\varphi_j)\to 0\).

\]
almost surely on non-extinction.

[Lemma lem:volume-cancel-matched of arXiv:2411.07809, 'Pirogov--Sinai Theory Beyond Lattices'] Suppose a graph $G$ satisfying Assumption~(as:2 of the paper) has a matched
  automorphism $\pi$ such that $\mathcal B$ is invariant under $\pi$.
  Suppose $Q$ is such that for all $v \in V_\textsf{e}$,
  \begin{equation}
    |Q^\textsf{e}_k(v)| \leq Q. 
  \end{equation}
  Then for any contour $\gamma$,
  \begin{equation}
    \left| \sum_{v \in \mathsf{Int}_\textsf{o} \gamma \cap V_\textsf{e}} Q^\textsf{e}_k(v) -
      \sum_{v' \in \mathsf{Int}_\textsf{o} \gamma \cap V_\textsf{o}} Q^\textsf{o}_k(v') \right|
    \leq Q |\gamma|. 
  \end{equation}
  The same result holds when replacing $\mathsf{Int}_{\textsf{o}}\gamma$ with
  $\mathsf{Int}_{\textsf{e}}\gamma$.

[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Let $T\in(0,\infty)$ and let $x^{(n)}_{t}$, $t\in[0,T]$, $n=0,1,2,...$,
be $\bR^{d}$-valued random functions measurable with respect to $(\omega,t)$. Assume that

(i) For any $\varepsilon>0$
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{T}P(|x^{(n)}_{t}-
x^{(0)}_{t}|\geq\varepsilon)\,dt=0;
$$

(ii) For any $R\in(0,\infty)$ there exist $N,p\in[1,\infty)$ such that
for any Borel $f(t,x)\geq0$
vanishing for $|x|\geq R$ and $n\geq1$ we have
\begin{equation}
                                 
E\int_{0}^{T} f(t,x^{(n)}_{t})\,dt
\leq  N\|f\|_{L_{p} }.
\end{equation}

Let a sequence $t^{(n)}\to0$ and let Borel $f^{n}(t,x)$, $n=0,1,2,...$, be given
on $\bR^{d+1}$ such that $f^{n}\to f^{0}$ in  measure
  on any bounded subset
of $\bR^{d+1}$ 
and
\begin{equation}
                                 
\lim_{c\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq0}
E\int_{0}^{T} |f^{n}(t^{(n)}+t,x^{(n)}_{t})|
I_{[c,\infty)}\big(|f^{n}(t^{(n)}+t,x^{(n)}_{t})|\big)\,dt=0.
\end{equation}

Then  
\begin{equation}
                                 
\lim_{n\to \infty}E \int_{0}^{T}
\big|f^{n}(t^{(n)}+t,x^{(n)}_{t})
-f^{0}(t,x^{(0)}_{t})\big|\,dt =0.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:bottle-events of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda\in (0,1)$. 
Let $i$ be a sufficiently large integer and let 
$j = \lfloor c_{\mathrm{b}} \log i \rfloor$. 
Let $Z$ be a generalised backoff process with send sequence $\overline{p}$ and start time~$\tau$.  
Let $\mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathcal{N}}_{\tau}$
and $\mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathbf{s}}_{\tau}$ be trivial events that always occur.
For all $t\geq \tau+1$
define the following events.
Let $\mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathcal{N}}_t$ be the event that 
$\mathcal{N}_{[j]}^Z(t)
\geq  \alpha_{\mathrm{b}}\log i$ 
and 
let $\mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathbf{s}}_t$ be the event that 
$\mathbf{s}^{{Z}}(t) \setminus \mathbf{B}_0^{{Z}}(t)$ is non-empty.   
Let $\mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathcal{N}}_{\leq t} = 
\bigcap_{t'\in \{\tau+1,\ldots,t\}} \mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathcal{N}}_{t'} $ and
let $\mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathbf{s}}_{\leq t} = 
\bigcap_{t'\in \{\tau+1,\ldots,t\}} \mathcal{E}^{Z,\mathbf{s}}_{t'}. $

[Proposition 46 (Several roots and toroidal refinement) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] For \(s\) normal variables and
\(R_s=\C[[h_1,\ldots,h_s]]\), tensoring the preceding retracts gives a
quasi-isomorphism.  Set
\begin{align*}
 \mathsf K_{\mathbf h}^\bullet
 &:=
 \left(
 R_s\otimes\bigwedge^\bullet\langle e_1,\ldots,e_s\rangle,
 \left(\sum_{j=1}^sh_je_j\right)\wedge
 \right),\\
 \widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\mathbf r,\mathbf h}^\bullet
 &:=
 \left(
 R_s[[r_1,\ldots,r_s]]
 \otimes\bigwedge^\bullet
 \langle\mathrm d\log r_1,\ldots,\mathrm d\log r_s\rangle,
 d_r+\sum_jh_j\mathrm d\log r_j\wedge
 \right).
\end{align*}
Then there is a natural quasi-isomorphism
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf K_{\mathbf h}^\bullet
 \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
 \widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\mathbf r,\mathbf h}^\bullet.

\end{equation}
The basis vectors \(e_I\) are indexed by subsets of the normal-crossing
boundary hypersurfaces, hence by the local nested forests.

If
\[
 r_i=\prod_{a=1}^{s}u_a^{M_{ia}},
 \qquad
 M\in\operatorname{GL}_s(\mathbb Z)
 \cap\operatorname{Mat}_{s\times s}(\mathbb N),
\]
then
\[
 e_i\longmapsto\sum_aM_{ia}e'_a,
 \qquad
 h'_a=\sum_iM_{ia}h_i
\]
defines an isomorphism of the finite Koszul complexes, and
\eqref{eq:NC-forest-dR} commutes with logarithmic pullback.  An arbitrary
matrix in \(\operatorname{GL}_s(\mathbb Z)\) gives the same statement on
the algebraic torus, but need not define a substitution of formal power
series at the boundary because negative exponents may occur.

body:
[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved finite special case and lower bound for Afonso S. Bandeira's Open Problem 11, How many deviations are needed afterall?, in Did just a couple of deviations suffice all along? (problems 10-14), Randomstrasse 101 (19 December 2024; https://randomstrasse101.math.ethz.ch/posts/HowManyDeviations/). For an n-by-n matrix A with entries in {+1,-1}, define disc(A)=min_{x in {+1,-1}^n} ||Ax||_infinity, where ||y||_infinity=max_i |y_i|, and let D_n=max_{A in {+1,-1}^{n-by-n}} disc(A). One has D_9=5. An attaining matrix is specified by its nine rows ---++++++; -+---++++; +---++-++; +++++--++; +-+----++; ++--+++-+; +--+-++-+; -+-+-+--+; --+-+---+, with + meaning +1 and - meaning -1. Every sign colouring has some row dot product of absolute value at least five; the next possible discrepancy level is excluded by the counting bound. Therefore sup_{n>=1} D_n/sqrt(n)>=5/3, attained as a finite-size lower bound by this matrix. This result does not determine the supremum over all n. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
All entries are signs; discrepancy uses all sign colourings.

Not by trusting a solver. Each entry has two halves and each half was verified on its own terms.

*Achievable.* The witness matrix is written out and its discrepancy recomputed by brute force over all

*Not more.* For every $n \le 11$ except one, the next level up is ruled out by counting alone: a single

of $2^{n-1}$. The exception is $n=10$ at level $6$, which the counting bound permits. That one case is

[Prop pasuniforme of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Consider $C_{w}(\pi)$ the convex hull of the distributions of variables of the form
    \[ \bigg\{ (\mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M}^{\omega}), \omega \text{ with finite expectation} \bigg\}   .\]
    Let $C_{\mathcal{U}}(\pi)$ to be the convex hull of subsequent Benjamini-Schramm limits of $(G_n,M_{n,\mathcal{U}}(G_n))$ where $(G_n)$ is any finite graph sequence converging in Benjamini-Schramm sense to $(\mathbb{T},o)$.
    For two distributions $\mu$ of a variable $(\mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M})$ and $\mu'$ of a variable $(\mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M}')$, set the total variation distance \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\mu')=\sup_{ \text{ events }A} | \mu(A)-\mu'(A)| .\]
    Then for any $\pi$ with finite expectation, satisfying $\hat{\pi} \neq \delta_0$ and $\hat{\pi}_0>0$, we have 
    \[ d_{\mathrm{TV}}(C_w(\pi),C_{\mathcal{U}}(\pi))> 0 . \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph with vertex degrees d(v), volume vol(S) = sum_{v in S} d(v), and for a vertex set S with 0 < vol(S) <= vol(V)/2 let phi(S) = e(S, V - S) / vol(S) be its conductance, where e(S, V - S) counts the edges leaving S. The conductance (Cheeger constant) of G is phi(G) = min over such S of phi(S). Let 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n <= 2 be the eigenvalues of the normalised Laplacian L = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}. CHEEGER'S INEQUALITY (Alon-Milman, Sinclair-Jerrum, Dodziuk; the graph form of Cheeger's 1970 Riemannian inequality): lambda_2 / 2 <= phi(G) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2). For a d-regular graph with adjacency eigenvalues d = mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ..., lambda_2 = (d - mu_2)/d and the edge expansion h(G) = min e(S, V-S)/|S| (over |S| <= n/2) satisfies (d - mu_2)/2 <= h(G) <= sqrt(2 d (d - mu_2)). Both sides are sharp up to constants: the cycle C_n has phi of order 1/n and lambda_2 of order 1/n^2 (so the square root is needed), while the hypercube and expanders have phi and lambda_2 of the same order. Consequences: a graph is an expander (phi bounded below) if and only if it has a spectral gap bounded below; the mixing time of the random walk is O(log(n) / lambda_2) and at least of order 1/phi; the sweep cut of the second eigenvector (the proof of the upper bound) is the spectral partitioning algorithm, with the guarantee phi(S) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2) for the set it returns; higher-order Cheeger inequalities (Lee-Oveis Gharan-Trevisan) relate lambda_k to k-way partitions, and the improved Cheeger inequality bounds phi by lambda_2 / sqrt(lambda_3).
G finite, connected, undirected, without isolated vertices (weighted graphs work verbatim with weighted degrees and volumes)
the spectral gap is that of the NORMALISED Laplacian; for regular graphs it is (d - mu_2)/d, and the unnormalised version scales by d
conductance is measured against volume; the vertex-count edge expansion h(G) is the same quantity only for regular graphs

[Lemma Ito formula of arXiv:2605.16963, 'Stochastic Euler Equations with Pseudo-differential Noise: Continuous and Discontinuous Pe'] Let \(\mathbb H\) be a Hilbert space and \(X\) a process given by
		\[
		X(t) = X_0 + \int_0^t a(t') \, \mathrm{d}t' + \int_0^t \int_{|l| \le 1} f(l,t') \, \widetilde{\eta}(\mathrm{d}l,\mathrm{d}t'), \quad t \geq 0,
		\]
		where \(a \in \mathscr{M}([0,\infty); \mathbb H) \cap L^1([0,\infty); \mathbb H)\) and \(f\) is a predictable \(\mathbb H\)-valued process satisfying
		$$
		\int_0^t \int_{|l| \le 1} \|f(l, t')\|_{\mathbb H}^2 \, \nu(\mathrm{d}l) \mathrm{d}t' < \infty\quad \text{for each } t > 0.
		$$
		Let \(\mathbb{S}\) be a separable Hilbert space and \(\phi: \mathbb H \rightarrow \mathbb{S}\) be a function of class \(C^1\) such that its Fr\'{e}chet derivative \(\phi': \mathbb H \rightarrow \mathcal{L}(\mathbb H; \mathbb{S})\) is locally Lipschitz continuous. Then, for every \(t > 0\), we have ${\mathbb P}\text{-}{\rm a.s.}$,
		\begin{align*}
			\phi(X(t)) - \phi(X_0) =\ & \int_0^t \Big[\phi'(X(t'-))\Big](a(t')) \, \mathrm{d}t'  + \int_0^t \int_{|l| \le 1} \bigg\{ \phi\Big(X(t'-) + f(l,t')\Big) - \phi(X(t'-))  \bigg\}\, \widetilde{\eta}(\mathrm{d}l,\mathrm{d}t')\\
			& + \int_0^t \int_{|l| \le 1} \bigg\{ \phi\Big(X(t'-) + f(l,t')\Big) - \phi(X(t'-)) - \Big[\phi'(X(t'-))\Big](f(l,t')) \bigg\}\, \nu(\mathrm{d}l)\mathrm{d}t'.
		\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma Ito formula of arXiv:2605.16963

Then we call a point process \textit{determinantal point process (DPP) with correlation kernel $K$} if its correlation functions~$\rho^{(n)}$ are given by 
   $$\rho^{(n)}(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \text{det}(K(x_i,x_j)_{i,j\in[n]}).$$

With notation as above,
set $d:=\dim R$.
Let $(R,\Delta)$ be a log $\Q$-Gorenstein pair, and let $E_R(k)$ be the injective hull of $k$ as an $R$-module.
Fix a canonical divisor $K_R \geq 0$.
Write
$K_R +\Delta=\frac{1}{m}\divi(f)$ for some $0\neq f\in R$ and some $m\in\Z_{>0}$.
Take a representing element $f^{\frac{1}{m}}\in R^+$.
Let $B$ be a perfectoid big Cohen-Macaulay $R^{+}$-algebra and
let $\phi:H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R)) \rightarrow H_{\m}^{d}(B)$ denote the morphism such that
the composition of the natural morphism $H_{\m}^{d}(R) \rightarrow H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R))$ and $\phi$ is identical to the morphism induced by the multiplication by $f^{\frac{1}{m}}$.

The BCM-test ideal of $(R,\Delta)$ with respect to $B$ is defined as
\[ \tau_{B}(R,\Delta) 
:= {\Image( E_R(k) \cong H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R)) \xrightarrow{\phi} H_{\m}^{d}(B))}^{\vee} \subset R, \]
where ${(-)}^{\vee}$ denotes Matlis duality.
The BCM-test ideal of $(R,\Delta)$ is defined as
\[ \taubcm(R,\Delta) := \bigcap_{B} \tau_B (R,\Delta) \subset R.\]
We say
that $(R,\Delta)$ is $\BCM_B$-regular if $\tau_B (R,\Delta)=R$
and
that $(R,\Delta)$ is BCM-regular if $\taubcm(R,\Delta)=R$.
These definitions are independent of the choices of $K_R$ and $f^\frac{1}{m}\in R^+$.

\infty.
\end{align*}
Then
\begin{align*}
d_W\left(
\mathcal L(X\mid Z\in B),
\mathcal L(Y\mid Y\in B)
\right)
\le
\frac{\E[\mathfrak d(X,Y)]}{p}
+
\frac{2D_B}{p}\,
\Pb\big[\{Z\in B\}\Delta\{Y\in B\}\big].
\end{align*}
title: Lemma 12 of arXiv:2606.30349

body:
[Proposition lem:preliminaries of arXiv:2607.07598, 'Universal Central Limit Theorem for non-exchangeable interacting diffusions'] Suppose Assumption (assum.main of the paper) holds with $k \ge 0$. Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item \emph{(Well-posedness)} For every $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$, the system (equation eq:X of the paper) admits a unique strong solution on $[0,T]$. Moreover, the McKean-Vlasov equation (equation eq:MKV of the paper) admits a unique strong solution $(Y_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$. In particular, the measure flow $(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is uniquely determined.
			
			
				\item \emph{(Uniform moment bounds)}
				For every $p\in[1,\infty)$, we have
				\begin{align} 
					\sup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}\max_{i\in[n]} \,
					{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\sup_{t\in[0,T]} |X_t^i|^p\Big]<\infty,
					\quad \text{and} \quad
					{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\sup_{t\in[0,T]} |Y_t|^p\Big]<\infty.
				\end{align}
				In particular, taking $p=2\lambda_d$,
				\begin{align} 
					\sup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}\max_{i\in[n]} \,
					{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\sup_{t\in[0,T]}w(X_t^i)\Big]<\infty,
					\quad \text{and} \quad
					{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\sup_{t\in[0,T]}w(Y_t)\Big]<\infty.
				\end{align}
			
			
			\item \emph{(Convergence of empirical measures)} As $n\to\infty$,
			\begin{align*}
				\sup_{t\in[0,T]}{\mathbb{E}}\bigg[{\mathcal{W}}_2^2\Big(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_t^i},\mu_t\Big)\bigg]\to 0.
			\end{align*} 
			\item \emph{(Poincar\'e inequality)} There exists $C< \infty$, independent of $t\in[0,T]$ and $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$, such that for any $g\in W^{1,2}(P_t)$,
			\begin{align*}
				\mathrm{Var}_{P_t}(g)
				:=
				\int_{({\mathbb{R}}^d)^n} g^2\,\mathrm{d} P_t
				-
				\Big(\int_{({\mathbb{R}}^d)^n} g\,\mathrm{d} P_t\Big)^2
				\le
				C\int_{({\mathbb{R}}^d)^n} |\nabla g|^2\,\mathrm{d} P_t,
			\end{align*}
			where $W^{1,2}(P_t)$ denotes the set of $g\in L^2(P_t)$ whose weak gradient $\nabla g$ belongs to $L^2(P_t)$.
			
			
			
			
			\item \emph{(Transport inequality for $\mu_t$)} There exists $\gamma_T<\infty$ such that for all $t\in[0,T]$ and all $\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$,
			\begin{align}
				{\mathcal{W}}_2^2(\nu,\mu_t)\le \gamma_T\,H(\nu\,|\,\mu_t).
			\end{align}
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition lem:preliminaries of arXiv:2607.07598

[Lemma 17 (Uniform Barnes, Stirling, and trigamma expansions) of arXiv:2608.20101, '\bfseries Largest bulk gap of the complex Ginibre ensemble'] Let \(0<c<C<\infty\).  Uniformly for \(y\in[cN,CN]\),
\begin{align}
 \log G(y+1)
 &=\frac{y^2}{2}\log y-\frac{3y^2}{4}
 +\frac y2\log(2\pi)-\frac1{12}\log y
 +\zeta'(-1)+O_{c,C}(N^{-2}),\\
 \log\Gamma(y)
 &=\left(y-\frac12\right)\log y-y+\frac12\log(2\pi)
 +\frac1{12y}+O_{c,C}(N^{-3}),\\
 \psi_1(y)
 &=\frac1y+\frac1{2y^2}+\frac1{6y^3}
 +O_{c,C}(N^{-5}).
\end{align}
The bounds are unchanged if \(y\) is perturbed by a quantity in a fixed
bounded interval.

body:
[Proposition prop:opmatch of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $(H_{t})$ be a Hermitian Brownian motion as in \S(sec:dyson of the paper) and let
$X^{N}$ solve the Hermitian SDE
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{d} X^{N}_{t}=b\big(X^{N}_{t}\big)\mathrm{d} t
  +\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\,f\big(X^{N}_{t}\big)\,\mathrm{d} H_{t}\,f\big(X^{N}_{t}\big).
\end{equation}
Then the eigenvalues satisfy
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{d}\lambda_{i}=b(\lambda_{i})\,\mathrm{d} t
  +\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{f(\lambda_{i})^{2}f(\lambda_{j})^{2}}
  {\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}}\,\mathrm{d} t
  +\frac{f(\lambda_{i})^{2}}{\sqrt N}\,\mathrm{d} B_{i},
\end{equation}
with $(B_{i})$ independent standard Brownian motions. Consequently, whenever
$L_{N}(0)\to\mu_{0}$, the empirical spectral distribution converges to the solution of
the continuity equation with velocity (equation eq:opvelocity of the paper); that is, the free
equation (equation eq:opsde of the paper) and the matrix equation (equation eq:opmatrix of the paper) have the same
spectral limit.

body:
[Lemma lem:Mstat of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For $\rho \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}$, take any half-space pre-landscape $\mathcal{M}^\rho$, continuously extended to $\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$, and  the half-space stationary horizon $\mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL} \in \mathcal D([2\rho \vee 0, \infty), \mathbb{R}, 2\rho \vee 0)$ from Theorem (T:half-stationary-horizon of the paper) (denoting that $\mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}_\lambda(x) = \mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}(\lambda,x)$).
Then for any $\lambda\ge 2\rho \vee 0$, we have
$$
\mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}_{\lambda}\diamond \mathcal{M}^\rho_{0, t} - (\mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}_{\lambda}\diamond \mathcal{M}^\rho_{0, t})(0)\stackrel{d}{=} \mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}_{\lambda} \stackrel{d}{=} \mathcal{M}^\rho_{0, t}\diamond\mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}_{\lambda} - (\mathcal{M}^\rho_{0, t}\diamond\mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}_{\lambda})(0) .
$$
Moreover, when $\lambda=2|\rho|$, $\mathcal{H}^\mathsf{DL}_{\lambda}$ is a Brownian motion with slope $-2\rho$.

[Corollary 5 (The value at the mode) of arXiv:2608.13631, 'The classical discrete laws near the mode:\\ complete local expansions for the negative bi'] Let $k^{*}=\lfloor(r-1)q/p\rfloor$ and $f=\{(r-1)q/p\}$, so that
	$t^{*}=k^{*}-\mu=-\tfrac qp-f$.  Then
	\begin{equation}
		\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}\;P(k^{*})
		=1+\frac{5}{12\,r}-\frac{B_2(f)}{2\sigma^{2}}+O(r^{-2}) :
	\end{equation}
	the fractional part of the mode threshold enters exactly through $B_2(f)$, and the constant
	$\tfrac5{12}$ is independent of $p$.

[Lemma lemma-linear-sphere of arXiv:2609.00108, 'The double sphere solution in the liquid drop model'] Let \(\beta\in(0,1)\). For \(\delta>0\) fixed sufficiently small,
		there exist
		\(
		\varepsilon_0>0,\) 
		\(
		C>0,
		\)
		such that, for every \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\) and every axially symmetric
		\[
		g_{S_R}\in C^{0,\beta}(S_R),
		\]
		problem (equation JJP of the paper) has a unique axially symmetric solution
		\[
		(h_{S_R},{\rm c})
		\in
		C^{2,\beta}(S_R)\times\mathbb R
		\]
		satisfying the normalization
		$$
		h_{S_R}\bigl((R+d)e_3+RP_S\bigr)
		=
		0.
		$$
		Equivalently, if
		\[
		h_{S_R}((R+d)e_3+R\omega)
		=
		Rh_S(\omega),
		\]
		then
		\(
		h_S(P_S)=0.
		\)
		Moreover,
		\begin{equation}
			\|h_{S_R}\|_{**}
			+
			|{\rm c}|
			\le
			C
			\|g_{S_R}\|.
		\end{equation}

Under the five hypotheses in assumptions, set b=E sigma'(Z), a=E[sigma'(Z)^2], q_l=(b^2)^(L-l), r_l=a^(L-l) for l=0,...,L-1, and r_plus=sum_(l=0)^(L-1)(r_l-q_l). Define M_n=r_plus*I_n+X_L^T X_L+sum_(l=0)^(L-1) q_l X_l^T X_l. Almost surely, n^(-1)*||K_NTK-M_n||_F^2->0, and ||K_NTK||_op is bounded eventually by a constant. Consequently K_NTK and M_n have the same weak limiting empirical spectral distribution whenever either limit exists. The source subsequently proves existence. If b=0, all q_l vanish, so the limiting NTK spectrum is that of r_plus*I_n+X_L^T X_L. This is an assertion about empirical spectral distributions at initialization, not convergence of individual extreme eigenvalues. The smoothness assumption excludes ReLU from this stated theorem.

All weights W_l in R^(d_l by d_(l-1)) and w in R^d_L have independent N(0,1) entries, independent of the input matrices.
sigma:R->R is twice differentiable with globally bounded first and second derivatives. For Z~N(0,1), E sigma(Z)=0 and E sigma(Z)^2=1.
X_0 is (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal as in the companion definition for constant B, epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0; the ESD of X_0^T X_0 converges to a deterministic probability measure mu_0.
X_l=d_l^(-1/2)*sigma(W_l X_(l-1)); scalar output f_theta(X_0)=w^T X_L; theta contains all hidden and readout weights; K_NTK=(grad_theta f)^T grad_theta f at random initialization.

[Definition D:substrateSpace of arXiv:2606.03079, 'Mean Field Limits for Stochastic, Underdamped Reactive Langevin Dynamics Models'] We define the substrate particle position and velocity product space analogously to $\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}$ as
$$\mathbb{X}^{(\ell)} \otimes \mathbb{V}^{(\ell)} \in (\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d)^{|\alpha^{(\ell)}|},
$$
with $\mathbb{X}^{(\ell)} \otimes \mathbb{V}^{(\ell)} \supseteq (\bm{x},\bm{v}) =\bigl((x_{1}^{(1)},{v}_{1}^{(1)}), \cdots, (x_{\alpha_{\ell 1}}^{(1)},{v}_{\alpha_{\ell 1}}^{(1)}), \cdots, (x_{1}^{(J)},{v}_{1}^{(J)}), \cdots, (x_{\alpha_{\ell J}}^{(J)},{v}_{\alpha_{\ell J}}^{(J)})\bigr)$. For $(\bm{x},\bm{v}) \in \mathbb{X}^{(\ell)} \otimes \mathbb{V}^{(\ell)}$, a sampled substrate position and velocity configuration for one individual $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ reaction, $x_{r}^{(j)}$ then labels the sampled position for the $r$th substrate particle of species $j$ involved in the reaction, and ${v}_{r}^{(j)}$ labels the sampled velocity for the same substrate particle. Let $d \bm{x}d \bm{v}=\bigl(\bigwedge_{j=1}^{J}(\bigwedge_{r=1}^{\alpha_{\ell j}} d x_{r}^{(j)}d v_{r}^{(j)})\bigr)$ be the corresponding volume form on $\mathbb{X}^{(\ell)}\otimes \mathbb{V}^{(\ell)}$ which also naturally defines an associated Lebesgue measure.

[Lem 20 of arXiv:2509.09589, 'Geometry of critical discrete structures: long-range percolation on the hierarchical latti'] Consider $\alpha\in(0, d)$ and $\theta\in(\alpha, \alpha + d/3)$.
Then
\begin{align}
0
\leq 
\bE\big( |\cT_n^{\sss(n)}| \big) - \bE\big( | \cC^-(0) | \big)
\lesssim
|\Lambda_n|^{2(\theta - \alpha)/d} \cdot \max\{ \Delta_n,\, \tilde\Delta_n \}\, .
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
0
\leq 
\bE\big( |\cT_n^{\sss(n)}| \big) - \bE\big( | \cC^-(0) | \big)
\lesssim
|\Lambda_n|^{-(d + 4\alpha - 4\theta)/d} 
\end{align}
if either 
(i) $\alpha\in (0, d/2]$ and $\theta\in(\alpha, \alpha + d/3)$, or
(ii) $ \alpha\in(d/2, 5d/6)$ and $2\alpha - d/2 < \theta <\alpha + d/3$.
On the other hand,
\begin{align}
0
\leq 
\bE\big( |\cT_n^{\sss(n)}| \big) - \bE\big( | \cC^-(0) | \big)
\lesssim
|\Lambda_n|^{-2(d - \theta)/d} 
\end{align}
if either 
(i) $\alpha\in(d/2, 5d/6)$ and $\theta\in(\alpha, 2\alpha - d/2]$, or
(ii) $\alpha\in[5d/6, d)$ and $\theta\in(\alpha, 2d - \alpha)$.
In particular,
\begin{align}
\bE|\cC^-(0)|
\gtrsim
|\Lambda_n|^{(\theta - \alpha)/d}
\end{align}
if either 
(i) $\alpha\in (0, 5d/6]$ and $\theta\in(\alpha, \alpha + d/3)$, or
(ii) $\alpha\in(5d/6, d)$ and $\theta\in(\alpha, 2d - \alpha)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
