[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We have the following formula,
$$e=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{1}{k!}$$
which can stand as an alternative definition for $e=2.71828\ldots$
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d5ea328b1533c512228f5a23439f02f3f4aaa53df3ca2df779e7ae35a831d242","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d5/d5ea328b1533c512228f5a23439f02f3f4aaa53df3ca2df779e7ae35a831d242.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f617b79a380b492a094cc3ee6eb5cbf54e76f335a27927756204526e6b3c8873","bundle_entry_key":"2608-10415-theorem-7-theorem-7","bundle_id":"population.tex-extract-s1_052","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"tex-extract-v2-20260907/bundle_s1_052.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:harvest.arxiv.mathematics:arxiv-2608-10415-theorem-7-theorem-7","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Paper's own proof, opening: This is something very standard, the idea being as follows:

\medskip

(1) In practice, we want to prove that we have the following equality:
$$\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{1}{k!}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n$$

For this purpose, the first observation is that we have the following estimate:
$$2<\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{1}{k!}<\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=3$$

In order to prove now that this limit is indeed $e$, observe that we have:
$$\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n
=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}\cdot\frac{1}{n^k}
\leq\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{1}{k!}$$

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2604.27485, 'On large deviation principles for general random processes \footnote{Research supported by'] {\rm 
We will say that the process $Z$ satisfies the l.d.p.\ if here exists a lower semi-continuous function  
$D\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,\infty]$, $D\not\equiv \infty,$  such that, for any Borel set $B\subset \mathbb{R}$ the following inequalities hold true for the ratio $z(T)=Z(T)/T$:
\begin{align}
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1{T}\ln\mathbf{P} (z(T)\in B) &\ge - D((B)),
\notag
\\
 \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac1{T}\ln\mathbf{P} (z(T)\in B) &\le - D([B]),

\end{align}
where 
$$
D(B):=\inf_{\alpha \in B}D(\alpha),
$$
$(B)$ is the interior of the set $B$ and~$[B]$ is its closure.
}

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2605.09706, 'A dyadic construction of a three-dimensional attractive point interaction Markov family'] Fix $T,\beta,\varepsilon>0$ and $x\in \overline E_\varepsilon$. The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The random time $\tau_\varepsilon^{\mathbb D_T}$ is a stopping time with respect to the dyadic filtration
$\{\mathcal F_t^{\mathbb D_T,\varepsilon}\}_{t\in\mathbb D_T}$.

\item The cemetery state is absorbing along the dyadic skeleton: whenever $s,t\in\mathbb D_T$ with $0\le s\le t\le T$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb P_x^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}\bigl[X_t=\Delta \,\big|\, \mathcal F_s^{\mathbb D_T,\varepsilon}\bigr]
=1
\quad
\mathbb P_x^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}\textup{-a.s. on }\{X_s=\Delta\}. \nonumber
\end{align}

\item At dyadic times, hitting the cemetery state is equivalent to having exited:
\[
\{\tau_\varepsilon^{\mathbb D_T}\le t\}
=
\{X_t=\Delta\}
\quad
\mathbb P_x^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}\textup{-a.s.}, 
\qquad t\in\mathbb D_T.
\]
\end{enumerate}
title: Proposition 7 of arXiv:2605.09706

[Definition def:stein of arXiv:2608.11084, 'Sharp Frobenius-Norm Concentration for Sample Moment Tensors'] Let \(Y\in\mathbb R^d\) be centered with
\(\mathbbm{E}\|Y\|_2^2<\infty\). A measurable map
\[
\tau:\mathbb R^d\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d\times d}
\]
with $\mathbbm{E}\|\tau(Y)\|_{\mathsf F}^2<\infty$
is called a \emph{Stein kernel} for \(Y\) if
\[
\mathbbm{E}\langle Y,\varphi(Y)\rangle
=
\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\tau(Y),\nabla\varphi(Y)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}
\]
for every smooth vector field
\(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) satisfying $\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft[
\|\varphi(Y)\|_2^2
+
\|\nabla\varphi(Y)\|_{\mathsf F}^2
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright]
<\infty$,
where
\[
\nabla\varphi
=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\frac{\partial\varphi_i}{\partial y_j}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)_{i,j=1}^d.
\]

\begin{align*}
	&\lim_{L \rightarrow \infty} \mathbb P_L^+((1-\varepsilon)\ell^* \le \tau_{\mathrm{cov}} \le \mathcal{L} \le (1+\varepsilon)\ell^*) = 1.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem.cap.extract of arXiv:2411.19145, 'On the intersection of critical percolation clusters and other tree-like random graphs'] There exists a constant $c>0$, such that for any $r\ge 1$, and any $2r$-well separated finite set $A\subset V$, one can find $U\subseteq A$, such that
$${\rm Cap}_\beta\big(B(U,r)\big) \ge c|U|\cdot r^\beta, \quad \textrm{and} \quad {\rm Cap}_\beta\big(B(U,r)\big)  \ge c \cdot {\rm Cap}_\beta\big( B(A,r)\big)  . $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 3 (The duality data are invariants) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The involution $\sigma$ and the weights $\kappa$ are uniquely
determined by the coupling functional: any two spectral
representations of the same pair $(\Delta_{m-1},C)$ share the same
$(\sigma,\kappa)$. Consequently every
object built from $(\sigma,\kappa)$ --- orbits, the constant $K$,
the invariant value $C^\ast$, the separatrix, the response span
--- is an invariant of the pair.

DRAFT: independent verification pending. Under iid finite nonnegative atomless weights on nearest-neighbor Z^2 with E[min(t1,t2,t3,t4)^2]<infinity, Ahlberg-Hoffman's fixed differentiability-direction exclusion implies that, on one probability-one event, both arms of every potential injective bigeodesic have direction limits. Intersect exclusions over a deterministic countable dense set of differentiability directions. Each ray escapes finite balls, so angular step sizes vanish and its direction cluster set is compact, nonempty, and connected. A nonsingleton connected cluster set would contain an arc hitting that dense set. Singleton directions may still be environment-selected; neither their simultaneous exclusion nor their antipodality follows here.

body:
[Theorem 6 (Full-law target entropy) of arXiv:2608.28827, 'Quantitative Target Convergence and Uniform-in-Time\\ Propagation of Chaos for Langevin-Re'] Under Assumption~\ref{ass:core-target} and either Assumption~\ref{ass:ksd-kernel} or Assumption~\ref{ass:W2},
the map \(t\mapsto H_N(t)\) is locally absolutely continuous and, for
\(0\le s\le t\),
\begin{align}
    H_N(t)-H_N(s)
    &=-N\int_s^t\E\KSD^2(\mu_u^N\|\pi)\,du
     -\varepsilon\int_s^t I(P_u^N\|\Pi_N)\,du
    \notag\\
    &\quad
     +\frac1N\int_s^t
       \E\sum_{i=1}^NC^\star(X_i^N(u))\,du.
    
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
    H_N(t)
    \le e^{-2\varepsilon\alpha t}H_N(0)
      +\frac{C^\star}{2\varepsilon\alpha}
       \{1-e^{-2\varepsilon\alpha t}\}.
\end{equation}
For $P_0^N=\mu_0^{\otimes N}$,
\begin{equation}
    \frac{H_N(t)}N
    \le e^{-2\varepsilon\alpha t}\KL(\mu_0\|\pi)
      +\frac{C^\star}{2\varepsilon\alpha N}.
\end{equation}

body:
[Thm smcprime-geo of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] Let $K_{\mathrm{SMC}'}$ be the Markov
jump kernel with density $q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(t\mid s)$ and invariant
law $\mu'$.
Then for every $n\ge1$,
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\bigl(K^{n}_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(x,\cdot),\mu'\bigr)\le\frac{x+\frac{11}{6}}{2^{ n-1}}.
\]
In particular, the SMC' jump chain is geometrically ergodic in total
variation.

[Proposition 18 ($\Sigma$ is a reflective submanifold) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] \begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] $R_L$ restricts to an isometric involution of
$S^{m-1}(2)$ whose fixed-point set is exactly
$L\cap S^{m-1}(2)$; thus $\Phi(\Sigma)$ is a \emph{reflective
submanifold} of the round sphere.
\item[\textup{(ii)}] The map
$\iota:=\Phi^{-1}\circ R_L\circ\Phi$ is defined on the open set
\[
U=\bigl\{\pi\in\Delta^\circ_{m-1}:\
2P_L\sqrt\pi-\sqrt\pi>0\ \text{componentwise}\bigr\},
\]
an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma^\circ$, on which
it is an involutive isometry of the Fisher--Rao metric with
$\operatorname{Fix}(\iota)=\Sigma\cap U$.
\item[\textup{(iii)}] $R_L$ reverses every transverse functional:
writing $\ell_O(x)=\kappa(z)^{1/4}x_z-\kappa(\sigma(z))^{1/4}
x_{\sigma(z)}$ for the linear form cutting out the orbit
hyperplane,
\[
\ell_O(R_Lx)=-\ell_O(x)\qquad\text{for every orbit }O.
\]
In particular the differential of $\iota$ along $\Sigma$ is $+1$
on $T\Sigma$ and $-1$ on the normal bundle, and for $r=1$ the
reflection exchanges the two connected components of
$S^{m-1}(2)\setminus\bigl(L\cap S^{m-1}(2)\bigr)$ --- a statement
about the \emph{full} sphere. Nothing is claimed about the number of
components of $S^{m-1}_+(2)\setminus\Phi(\Sigma^\circ)$: the octant
is not $R_L$-invariant, as Remark~\ref{rem:iota-domain} records. On
the octant one has only that, wherever both sides meet the domain,
the two sides are the sign regions of the orbit functional
$\ell_O$.
\end{enumerate}

[Thm 6 (Main result in spatial dimension $d=1$) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $\{K_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ denote an environment satisfying Assumption \ref{a1}, and let $\mathfrak H^N$ be as in \eqref{hn}. Assume as in Definition \ref{goodseq} that one has a good sequence of deterministic initial data $\mathfrak H^N(0,\bullet)$ converging weakly as measures to some limit $\mathfrak H_0$. There is an explicit Banach space $X$ of distributions on $\mathbb R$, which is continuously embedded in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R)$, such that the rescaled and recentered collection $\{ \mathfrak F^N\}_{N \ge 1}$ is tight with respect to the topology of $C([0,T], X)$. Furthermore any limit point as $N\to \infty$ is as follows. 
\begin{itemize} 
\item (Bulk fluctuations in $d=1$) If $N^{1/2}\varsigma_N \to \boldsymbol{\varsigma} \text{ as } N\to\infty$, then the limit point is unique and coincides with the law of $(t,x)\mapsto e^{\varsigma\bullet x +\frac12 |\varsigma|^2 t} \mathcal U(t,x+\varsigma t)$ where $\mathcal U$ is the solution of the additive-noise SPDE \begin{equation}\partial_t \mathcal U(t, x) = \frac12\partial_x^2 \mathcal U(t, x) + \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot \partial_x^p \big((\mathfrak H_0 *G_t)(x)\;\xi(t, x)\big),
\end{equation}started with initial data $\mathcal U(0, x)=0$. 

\item (Extremal fluctuations up to location scale $N^{1-\frac1{4p}}$ in $d=1$) If $N^{-1/2}\ll  |\varsigma_N|\ll  N^{-1/4p} \text{ as } N\to \infty,$ then the limit point is unique and coincides with the law of the solution of the additive-noise SPDE \begin{equation}\partial_t \mathcal U(t, x) = \frac12\partial_x^2  \mathcal U(t, x) + \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot   (\mathfrak H_0 *G_t)(x)\; \xi(t, x),
\end{equation}started with initial data $\mathcal U(0, x)=0$. 
\end{itemize} Here $G_t(x) = G(t,x)= (2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2t}$ is the standard heat kernel, $*$ denotes spatial convolution, and $ \xi$ is a standard space-time white noise defined on $\mathbb R_+\times \mathbb R.$ Furthermore in either case we have the noise coefficient $$\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}^2:=  \frac1{(2p)!}\int_{I} \bigg[ \int_{I^2}( x- y)^{2p}\mu(\mathrm d x)\mu(\mathrm d y)-\int_I ( a- z)^{2p} \pdif( z,\mathrm d a)\bigg]
\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathrm d z).
$$Here $\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}$ is the invariant measure of the Markov kernel $\pdif$, under its unit normalization (see Definition \ref{def:unit}). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Main result in spatial dimension $d=1$

[Lemma 4 (Point probability estimate) of arXiv:2605.08629, 'Moderate deviations for the Maki--Thompson rumour model'] Assume \eqref{bn-weak}. For any compact interval $K \subset \mathbb{R}$, the following holds uniformly for $z \in K$: define
    \[
    k_n(z) = \bigl\lfloor n x_\infty + z b_n \sqrt{n} \bigr\rfloor,
    \]
    then as $n \to \infty$,
    \[
    \log \mathbb{P}(X_n = k_n(z)) = -\frac12 \log n - \frac{z^2 b_n^2}{2\sigma^2} + o(b_n^2),
    \]
    where the $o(b_n^2)$ term is uniform for $z \in K$. Equivalently,
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(X_n = k_n(z)) = n^{-1/2} \exp\left(-\frac{z^2 b_n^2}{2\sigma^2} + o(b_n^2)\right)
    \]
  holds uniformity in $z \in K$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma delta*-cc of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The functor $\textup{diag}\colon {\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\textup{$G$-lvl}\to{{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}_\textup{$G$-gl}$ is cocontinuous.
    \begin{proof}
        It suffices that the pointset level functor $\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}\to\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ preserves homotopy pushouts and homotopy coproducts.

        Any cofibration $f$ in $\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}$ is an unbased level h-cofibration by Corollary~(cor:SpL-level-hcof of the paper), and so $\textup{diag}\,f$ is an unbased level cofibration in $\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$. Pushouts along the latter are homotopy pushouts by Theorem~(thm:G-gl-Sp-model-struct of the paper); as $\textup{diag}\colon\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}\to\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ evidently preserves pointset level pushouts, this shows that it also preserves homotopy pushouts.
        
        On the other hand, [schwede2018global]*{Corollary~3.1.37(i)} shows that coproducts in $\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ preserve $G$-global weak equivalences in full generality, so $\textup{diag}$ sends any coproduct of cofibrant objects to a homotopy coproduct.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma delta*-cc of arXiv:2608.28504

Work as d->infinity with integers N=N(d)->infinity and M=M(d)>=1. Let (X_d,nu_d) and (Omega_d,tau_d) be probability spaces and sigma_d in L2(nu_d times tau_d). Use its singular expansion sigma_d(x,theta)=sum_j sqrt(mu_j) psi_j(x) phi_j(theta), with ordered nonnegative mu_j, sum_j mu_j<infinity, positive mu_(M+1) and positive denominators in the displayed tail conditions, and orthonormal families psi_j in L2(nu_d), phi_j in L2(tau_d). Let D_d be the closed span of the psi_j and P_<=M its orthogonal projection onto the first M modes. Define the feature kernel U_d(theta,thetaprime)=E_x~nu_d sigma_d(x,theta)sigma_d(x,thetaprime), its spectral tail U_>r=sum_(j>r) mu_j phi_j phi_j^T, and kappa_r=sum_(j>r)mu_j>0 for each cutoff used. Draw theta_1,...,theta_N independently from tau_d and let K_ij=U_d(theta_i,theta_j). All stochastic rates below are as d->infinity. (H) There is one sequence u(d)>=M(d) such that, for every fixed real q>=1, all g in span{phi_1,...,phi_u} satisfy ||g||_(L2q(tau_d))<=C_q||g||_(L2(tau_d)), with C_q independent of d and g. (E) For the same u there is a fixed delta_E>0 such that N^(2+delta_E)<=kappa_u^2/sum_(j>u)mu_j^2 eventually. (Sa) There is a fixed delta_a>0 with N^(1+delta_a)<=kappa_M/mu_(M+1) eventually. Let Phi_ij=phi_j(theta_i) for j<=M, A=diag(sqrt(mu_1),...,sqrt(mu_M)), and Lambda=diag(U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M). Theorem6 gives a symmetric Delta such that K=Phi A^2 Phi^T+kappa_M(Lambda+Delta), and there exists a fixed delta_prime>0 with E||Delta||_op=O(N^(-delta_prime)). In particular the remainder is controlled in expectation, not only numerically. If additionally M<=N^(1-delta_h) for some fixed delta_h>0, then ||Phi^T Phi/N-I_M||_op=o_P(1). These conclusions do not require Dupper, Dlower, or the eigenvalue ratio part of Sb.

body: For an elliptic curve E over the rational numbers, the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture asserts that the rank of the finitely generated abelian group E(Q) of rational points equals the order of vanishing of the curve's L-function L(E,s) at s=1. A refined form further predicts the leading Taylor coefficient of L(E,s) at s=1 in terms of arithmetic invariants of E: the order of the Tate-Shafarevich group, the regulator, the real period, and the Tamagawa numbers. The conjecture is OPEN in general, one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, though proved when the analytic rank is 0 or 1 by Gross, Zagier, and Kolyvagin.
title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture

\]

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2604.07207, 'Mixing times of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $G=(\ZZ_L, +)$ where $L\geq 3$ is an odd number and assume that $\mu(1)=\mu(-1)=1/2$. Let $S$ be an SRRW on $G$ with reinforcement parameter $\alpha \in [0,1)$ and step distribution $\mu$. Fix $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[\bf (i)] 
    \item If $\alpha \in [0,1/2)$, then there exist two positive constants $c_1=c_1(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ and $C_1=C_1(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ such that for all large $L$,
    $$c_1  L^2 \leq t^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) \leq C_1 L^2.$$ 
\item If $\alpha = 1/2$, then there exist two positive constants $c_2=c_2(\varepsilon)$ and $C_2=C_2(\varepsilon)$ such that for all large $L$,
$$ \frac{c_2  L^2}{\log L} \le t^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)\leq  \frac{C_2  L^2}{\log L}.$$ 
\item If $\alpha \in (1/2,1)$, then there exist two positive constants $c_3=c_3(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ and $C_3=C_3(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ such that for all large $L$,
 $$c_3L^{\frac{1}{\alpha}} \leq  t^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) \leq C_3 L^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}.$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2604.07207

Let (X_t)_{t in T} be a stochastic process on a metric space (T, d) with SUB-GAUSSIAN INCREMENTS, meaning P( |X_s - X_t| > u ) <= 2 exp( - u^2 / (2 d(s,t)^2) ) for all s, t and u > 0. Then there is an absolute constant C with E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C integral_0^{diam(T)} sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) du, where N(T, d, u) is the covering number, the smallest number of d-balls of radius u needed to cover T. If the process is not centred one should read the statement for X_t - X_{t_0} with a fixed base point. Two standard cautions: the bound can be LOOSE - for a centred Gaussian process the sharp answer is Talagrand's generic chaining and the majorizing measure theorem, and Dudley's integral can overshoot by an unbounded factor; and the integral must converge, so a class with covering numbers growing faster than exp(u^{-2}) is not handled. Sudakov's minoration provides the matching lower bound E sup_t X_t >= c sup_{u > 0} u sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) for centred GAUSSIAN processes, so the two differ exactly by the integral versus the supremum. [Dudley (1967); see Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 8.1.6]

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2606.14564, 'Upper tails for irregular graphs \\ beyond the mean-field regime'] Suppose that $J$ is a nonempty subgraph of a connected graph $H$ with maximum degree at most $\Delta$. Then
 \[
   e_J \leq \Delta\cdot(v_J-\alpha_J^*)
   \leq
   \Delta\cdot\alpha_J^*.
 \]
 The first inequality is tight if and only if
 \begin{enumerate}[label=(Q\arabic*)]
 \item
   
   $J = H$ and $H$ is $\Delta$-regular or
 \item
   
   $J$ admits a bipartition $V(J) = A \cup B$ such that $\deg_Ja = \Delta$ for all $a \in A$.
 \end{enumerate}
 If both inequalities are tight, then $J = H$ and $H$ is $\Delta$-regular.
title: Lemma 9 of arXiv:2606.14564

Suppose $(n,p)$ is not critical, i.e., $[n - 2p + 1]_q \ne 0$. Then the Gram determinant satisfies the recurrence:

\]
where $d_{n-1,p-1} = \dim V_{n-1,p-1} = \binom{n-1}{p-1} - \binom{n-1}{p-2}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For positive differentiable unconditional and conditional densities p_t(x) and p_t(x|c), let s_u=grad_x log p_t(x), s_c=grad_x log p_t(x|c). At guidance strength gamma in R, the classifier-free guidance score is s_gamma=(1-gamma)*s_u+gamma*s_c. It is the gradient of log[p_t(x)^(1-gamma)*p_t(x|c)^gamma]. If the product has finite positive integral Z_(t,gamma), it is also the score of the normalized instantaneous density q_(t,gamma)=p_t^(1-gamma)*p_t(.|c)^gamma/Z_(t,gamma). This identity is pointwise in noise time t; it does not assert that the forward diffusion of q_(0,gamma) has marginals q_(t,gamma), or that a guided reverse process samples q_(0,gamma).

body:
[Proposition 1 (Dichotomy recurrence/transience for $\Tree_{\infty}$-walk) of arXiv:2608.30668, 'Recurrence and capacity of stable branching random walks'] Assume that \(\theta\) is not supported by a strict subgroup of \(\Z^d\). Consider the \emph{total escape} event
\(\esc= \bigl(W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u) \neq 0\ \forall u \in \Tree_{\infty}\!\setminus\! \{ c_0 \} \bigr)\).

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item
  If \(\P(\esc)=0\) then almost surely, for every \(x \in \Z^d\),
  \(\sum_{u \in \Tree_{\infty}} \1_{W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u)=x} = +\infty\)
  \emph{i.e.} \(x\) is visited infinitely often by
  \(W_{\Tree_{\infty}}\).
\item
  If \(\P(\esc)>0\) then almost surely, for every \(x \in \Z^d\),
  \(\sum_{u \in \Tree_{\infty}} \1_{W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u)=x} < +\infty\).
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, \[\P(\esc)=0 \text{ if and only if } \P(\esc_{+})=0,\] where
\(\esc_{+}= \bigl(W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u) \neq 0\ \forall u \in \Tree_{+} \bigr)\)
as in \eqref{eq:LinkFiniteInfinite}, and in the recurrent case we actually have that almost surely, for every \(x \in \Z^d\),
  \(\sum_{u \in \Tree_{+}} \1_{W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u)=x} = +\infty\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dichotomy recurrence/transience for $\Tree_{\infty}$-walk

[Proposition prop:largedeviation of arXiv:2510.13733, 'Internal Diffusion Limited Aggregation \\ with Critical Branching Random Walks'] For any $d\geq 1$ there exist positive constants $c $ and $\lambda_0$, depending only on the dimension $d$, such that for each $ \lambda \in (0,  \lambda_0]$ 
and for each $y \in B_R$
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E} \Big[  \exp\Big(  \lambda  \ell_{B_R}^y ( \partial B_R)  /R^2 \Big)  \Big]
  &  \leq e^{  c  \lambda / R^2 } \\

  \mathbb{E} \Big[\exp \Big(   \lambda  \ell_{B_R}^y ( \partial B_R) / R^2 \Big)  \Big| \ell_{B_R}^y ( \partial B_R) > 0 \Big] &  \leq e^{  c  \lambda }. 
\end{align}
Moreover, writing $ \bar \ell_{B_R}^y := \ell_{B_R}^y ( \partial B_R) - \mathbb{E} [ \ell_{B_R}^y (\partial B_R) ] $, we have that 
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb{E} \Big[\exp \Big(   \lambda \bar \ell_{B_R}^y  / R^2 \Big)  \Big| \ell_{B_R}^y ( \partial B_R) > 0 \Big]  \leq e^{  c  \lambda^2 / R^2 }. 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 15 (Barrier-regularized universality) of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Fix $N,n\ge1$, $K_{\rm feat}>0$, and $\beta,\gamma>0$.
	Let $W\in\R^N$ be a $(K_{\rm feat},\tau)$-regular feature with
		covariance matrix $\Sigma$, and set
		$\lambda_{\Sigma}=\|\Sigma\|_{\op}>0$.  Let $G$ be the centered Gaussian
	feature with covariance $\Sigma$, and let
	$W_1,\ldots,W_n$ and $G_1,\ldots,G_n$ be independent arrays of i.i.d.
	copies of $W$ and $G$, respectively.

	There are constants $C,n_0<\infty$, depending only on
	$K_{\rm feat}$, with the following property.  Let
	$\mathcal D\subset\R^N$ be nonempty, bounded, convex, and relatively
	open in its affine hull, and let
	$\mathcal B:\mathcal D\to[0,\infty)$ be a
	$\vartheta$-self-concordant barrier for some $\vartheta\ge1$.
	Define the reference scale
	\begin{equation}
		
		\Lambda_{\rm ref}
		:=\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)
		\left(
		1+\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal D}
		\{\lambda_{\Sigma}\|\theta\|_2^2+\gamma\mathcal B(\theta)\}
		\right).
	\end{equation}
	If $n\gamma\ge n_0$, then
		\begin{equation}
			
			\left|
			\E\Phi_W(\mathcal D,\mathcal B;\beta,\gamma)
			-
			\E\Phi_G(\mathcal D,\mathcal B;\beta,\gamma)
			\right|
			\le
			C\Lambda_{\rm ref}^2\left(
			\frac1{\sqrt{n\gamma}}
			+\frac{\sqrt{\dim\mathsf V_{\mathcal D}}(\tau/\lambda_{\Sigma}+1)}{n}
			\right).
		\end{equation}
	Moreover,
		\begin{equation}
			
			\Var\!\left(\Phi_W(\mathcal D,\mathcal B;\beta,\gamma)\right)
			+
			\Var\!\left(\Phi_G(\mathcal D,\mathcal B;\beta,\gamma)\right)
			\le C\frac{\Lambda_{\rm ref}^2}{n},
		\end{equation}
	and hence, for every $t>0$,
		\begin{equation}
			
			\P\left(
			\left|\Phi_W(\mathcal D,\mathcal B;\beta,\gamma)
			-\Phi_G(\mathcal D,\mathcal B;\beta,\gamma)\right|
			>C\Lambda_{\rm ref}^2\left(
			\frac1{\sqrt{n\gamma}}
			+
			\frac{\sqrt{\dim\mathsf V_{\mathcal D}}(\tau/\lambda_{\Sigma}+1)}{n}
			\right)+t
			\right)
			\le \frac{C\Lambda_{\rm ref}^2}{nt^2}.
		\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Barrier-regularized universality

body:
[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $\rho>0$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq \rho$, and let $B$ be a $(\rho,\zeta)$-Brownian motion on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$.  Let $(\A,\tau)$ be a $W^\ast$-probability space that contains a free multiplicative $(\rho,\zeta)$-Brownian motion $b$, and let $b_0$ be an operator in $\A$ that is freely independent from $b$.

Let $B_0=B_0^N$ be a sequence of random matrices in $\M_N(\C)$ independent from the process $B$ such that $B_0$ converges a.s.\ in $\ast$-distribution to $b_0$ as $N\to\infty$.

Then for any $t\ge 0$, $B_0 B(t)$ converges in $\ast$-distribution to $b_0b(t)$ a.s. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 3 of arXiv:2511.10535

C=C(\varepsilon,f,\eta).
\]

[Lemma of arXiv:2607.18011, 'From local giants to locality in long-range percolation'] \thlabel{lem:local_giant_density}
    Let $G$ be a transitive graph of polynomial growth with $d \geq 1$ and let $((\Tile{i}{j})_{j \geq 0})_{i \geq 0}$ be the renormalisation scheme in \thref{def:renormalisation_scheme}.
    
    Let $\Cell{i}{j}$ be a good level-$i$ cell and let $\Cell{i-1}{k}$ and $\Cell{i-1}{\ell}$ be two distinct good subcells of $\Cell{i}{j}$.
    
    The semi-cluster $\goodsize{i}{j}$ satisfies $\# \goodsize{i}{j} \geq \rho_0 r_i^{d(1 - \xi)}$. 
    
    The semi-clusters $\goodsize{i-1}{k}$ and $\goodsize{i-1}{\ell}$ satisfy $d_G(\goodsize{i-1}{k},\goodsize{i-1}{\ell}) \geq r_0/2$ and $\goodsize{i-1}{k},\goodsize{i-1}{\ell} \subset \Tile{i}{j} \subseteq B(\netvertex{i}{j},C_{\mathrm{vor}}{}r_i)$.

[Proposition of arXiv:2411.12315, 'A pursuit problem for squared Bessel processes'] The following limits hold as $\alpha\downarrow0$ :
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\theta(\alpha,\beta) \; \mathop{\sim}\limits\alpha / (2^{\frac{\beta}{2}}-2) &\qquad \text{if }\beta>2,\\
\theta(\alpha,\beta) \; \mathop{\sim}\limits  \sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2\ln(2)}}&\qquad \text{if }\beta=2,\\
\theta(\alpha,\beta) = 1-\frac{\beta}{2} +\alpha \left( \frac{1}{2-2^{\beta/2}}-\frac{1}{2} \right) +  \emph{o}(\alpha)&\qquad \text{if }0\leq \beta<2.\\
\end{array}$$
title: Unnumbered proposition of arXiv:2411.12315, 'A pursuit problem for squared Bessel processes'

[Definition of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'] Let $\gamma=\gamma_1\star\left(\gamma_2\star\left(\ldots\star\gamma_J\right)\ldots\right)$ be an admissible curve. Then, one defines the holonomy of the random connection $A$ along $\gamma$ as
$$
\mathbf{Hol}(\gamma):=\mathbf{Hol}(\gamma_J)\ldots\mathbf{Hol}(\gamma_2)\mathbf{Hol}(\gamma_1).
$$
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'

body:
[Corollary 6 (\textsf{Law of small numbers}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Let $(B_{n,k})_{1\leq k\leq N_n}$ be independent 
$\{0,1\}$-valued Bernoulli variables
with success probabilities $p_{n,k}$, and put

\noi
\begin{align}
 X_n:=\sum_{k=1}^{N_n}B_{n,k}
 \AND
 \theta_n:= \E[X_n] =\sum_{k=1}^{N_n}p_{n,k}.
\notag
\end{align}
If

\noi
\begin{align}
 \theta_n\to\lambda>0
\AND
 \max_{1\leq k\leq N_n}p_{n,k}\to0,
\notag
\end{align}
then $X_n$ converges to $\Pois(\lambda)$ in total variation and its
first four moments converge to those of the limit. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsf{Law of small numbers}
Strict local positivity

[Conjecture 1 (Samuels' Conjecture) of arXiv:2608.22816, 'A Cap-Move Reformulation of Ling's Proof of Samuels' Conjecture'] For every $\delta>0$, 
	\begin{align}
		\bP\pth{ \sum_{i=1}^n X_i < \delta + \sum_{i=1}^n \mu_i } \ge \min_{1\le i\le n} \prod_{j=i}^n \pth{1-\frac{\mu_j}{\delta + \sum_{k=i}^n \mu_k}}. 
	\end{align} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Samuels' Conjecture

body:
[Theorem intro-th:sec-order-main of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] (Theorem (th:sec-order-main of the paper))

  Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume that for every
  finite $r$ one has
  \begin{equation} 
  \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^2 \left( \frac{1}{N} \log \mathbb{E}[H
     \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A), \ldots, \lambda_N
     (A))] - \sum_{i = 1}^r \Psi (x_i) - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^r \Phi (x_i)
     \right) = \sum_{i = 1}^r \mathrm{T} (x_i), 
     \end{equation} 
  where $\Psi, \Phi, \mathrm{T}$ are smooth functions in a complex neighborhood of $0$ and
  the above convergence is uniform in a complex neighborhood of $0^r$. Then the $1 /
  N^2$ correction of the average empirical distribution of $N^{- 1} A$
  is given by
  \[ \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^2 \left( \frac{1}{N^{k + 1}}
     \mathbb{E}[\ensuremath{\operatorname{Tr}} (A^k)] -\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k - \frac{1}{N}
     \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'_k \right) =\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k
     +\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k, \]
  where $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}, (\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'_k)_{k \in
  \mathbb{N}}$ are given by ((intro-topg of the paper)),((intro-G of the paper)) respectively. The sequences
  $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}, (\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k)_{k \in
  \mathbb{N}}$ are given by
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k = \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 1} \frac{k!}{m! (m + 1) ! (k -
     m - 1) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi' (x))^{k - m - 1}
     \mathrm{T}' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{10em}}} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 2} \frac{k!}{m! (m
    + 1) ! (k - m - 2) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
    (x))^{k - m - 2} (\Phi' (x))^2) \right|_{x = 0} 
  \end{equation}
  and
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k = \frac{1}{24} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 3} \frac{k!}{m! (m
     + 1) ! (k - m - 3) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
     (x))^{k - m - 3} \Psi''' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \[ \text{{\hspace{4em}}} + \frac{1}{12} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 3} \frac{k!}{m! (m
     + 2) ! (k - m - 3) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
     (x))^{k - m - 3} \Psi''' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{10em}}} + \frac{1}{12} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 4} \frac{k!}{m! (m
    + 2) ! (k - m - 4) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
    (x))^{k - m - 4} (\Psi'' (x))^2) \right|_{x = 0} . 
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem intro-th:sec-order-main of arXiv:2412.09290

body:
[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21663, '\bf Variance lower bounds for geometric functionals of rotationally invariant log-concave '] Let $1 \leq i \leq m$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[{\rm (i)}] \[y_i=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^d y_i^j.\]
\item[{\rm (ii)}] For every $1 \leq j \leq d$, \[y_i^j-y_i \perp y_i.\] In particular, for fixed $i$, we can write \[y_i^j=y_i+w_j=r_nu_i+w_j,\] where \[w_j=y_i^j-y_i \in y_i^\perp, \quad \|w_j\|_2=ca_n.\]
\item[{\rm (iii)}]For every $1 \leq j \leq d$: \[\|y_i^j\|_2^2=\|y_i\|_2^2+\|w_j\|_2^2=r_n^2+c^2a_n=r_n^2+c^2r_nh_n.\] 
Therefore, \[y_i^j \in (r_n+h_n)B_2^d \setminus r_nB_2^d.\]
\item[{\rm (iv)}] For every $1 \leq j,k \leq d$: \[\langle y_i^j,y_i^k-y_i\rangle=\langle y_i^j-y_i,y_i^k-y_i\rangle= \langle w_j,w_k \rangle= \begin{cases}
c^2a_n^2 &, \text{ if } \, k=j\\
-\dfrac{c^2a_n^2}{d-1} &, \text{ if } \, k \neq j
\end{cases}.\]
\item[{\rm (v)}] For every $1\leq j \neq k \leq d$:  \[\|y_i^j-y_i^k\|_2=ca_n\sqrt{\frac{2d}{d-1}}.\]
\item[{\rm (vi)}] \[u_i^\perp=y_i^\perp={\rm span}\{y_i^j-y_i:1 \leq j \leq d \}={\rm span}\{w_j:1 \leq j \leq d \}.\]
\item[{\rm (vii)}] The vectors $w_1,\ldots,w_d$ are vertices of a regular $(d-1)$-simplex centered at $0$. Moreover, \[\frac{ca_n}{d-1}B_{u_i^\perp} \subseteq \conv\{w_1,\ldots,w_d\}.\]

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21663

body:
[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2608.18075, '2608.18075'] Let $a=A+r$, $b=B+s$ belong to $\mathfrak A$, where
$A,B\in\mathcal P_1$ and $r,s\in S_\Delta^{-1}$. Then
\begin{align}
 [T_{\boldsymbol m,a},T_{\boldsymbol n,b}]
 =T_{\boldsymbol m+\boldsymbol n,c},\qquad
 c(\boldsymbol j)=b(\boldsymbol j)a(\boldsymbol j+\boldsymbol n)
 -a(\boldsymbol j)b(\boldsymbol j+\boldsymbol m),
\end{align}
and $c\in\mathfrak A$. Its affine part is exactly
\begin{align}
 c_{\rm aff}(\boldsymbol j)
 =A_{\rm lin}(\boldsymbol n)B(\boldsymbol j)
 -B_{\rm lin}(\boldsymbol m)A(\boldsymbol j),
\end{align}
where $A_{\rm lin},B_{\rm lin}$ are the linear parts.

body:
(a) Let Z be standard Gaussian on R and f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| < infinity. Then E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ]. (b) Multivariate: if X is centred Gaussian on R^n with covariance Sigma and f is differentiable with the appropriate integrability, then E[ X_i f(X) ] = sum_j Sigma_{ij} E[ d f / d x_j (X) ]. (c) STEIN'S CHARACTERISATION: a real random variable Z is standard Gaussian IF AND ONLY IF E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ] for every bounded, continuously differentiable f with bounded derivative. This is the identity that makes Stein's method work: to show a law is close to Gaussian, one bounds E[ Z f(Z) - f'(Z) ] over a class of test functions f solving Stein's equation. (d) ISSERLIS-WICK FORMULA: for a centred Gaussian vector, E[ X_1 X_2 ... X_{2m} ] = sum over all PERFECT MATCHINGS of {1, ..., 2m} of the product of the covariances of the matched pairs, and any odd moment vanishes. For 2m = 4 this reads E[X_1X_2X_3X_4] = Sigma_{12}Sigma_{34} + Sigma_{13}Sigma_{24} + Sigma_{14}Sigma_{23}, and in particular E[Z^4] = 3 for a standard Gaussian, which is the '3' that the fourth moment theorem tests against. Centring is essential in (d); for a non-centred Gaussian one must first subtract the means. [standard; Isserlis (1918), Stein (1972); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Chapter 3]
(a) f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| finite
(c) the characterisation quantifies over a rich enough class of test functions
(d) the Gaussian vector must be CENTRED

[Lem 6 of arXiv:2604.13134, '\bf From Gaussian to Gumbel: extreme eigenvalues of complex Ginibre products with exact ra'] Let $\psi(x) = \Gamma'(x)/\Gamma(x)$ be the digamma function, with $\Gamma$ being the Gamma function.  
	\begin{enumerate}
			\item[\textup{(a)}.]  For any $s \geq 1$,
		\(
		\psi(j + s) - \psi(j) \leq \frac{s}{j}.
		\)
				\item[\textup{(b)}.]  For sufficiently large $z$, the following asymptotics hold:
		\begin{align*}
			\psi(z) &= \log z - \frac{1}{2z} + O(z^{-2}), \quad\quad
			\psi'(z) = \frac{1}{z} + \frac{1}{2z^2} + O(z^{-3});\\
			\psi^{(2)}(z)  &= -\frac{1}{z^2} - \frac{1}{z^3} + O(z^{-4}),\quad\quad
			\psi^{(3)}(z)  = \frac{2}{z^3} + \frac{3}{z^4} +  O(z^{-5}).
		\end{align*}
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 13 (The case \(g>1\)) of arXiv:2608.25725, 'Gr\"obner Bases for Alexander Fitting Ideals of Links'] Assume \(g>1\).  Then
\[
\mathcal D=
\{\delta>1:\,\delta\mid q,\ \delta\mid\lcm(m,k)\}.
\]
If \(\mathcal D=\varnothing\), then \(\AG_2(L)=\{1\}\).  Otherwise, the
Gr\"obner basis in Theorem~\ref{thm:pretzel-uniform} consists of
\(\{\Pi_0(x),y^g-h(x)\}\), together with \(\Pi_{g-1}Q_{g-1}\) when
\(g-1\in\mathcal S\), and with \(\Pi_{g-2}Q_{g-2}\) when
\(g\ge3\) and \(g-2\in\mathcal S\).  In particular, it has at most four
elements.  Its initial ideal is generated by \(y^g\) and
\(x^{\deg\Pi_0}\), together with \(x^{\deg\Pi_{g-1}}y^{g-1}\) when
\(g-1\in\mathcal S\), and with
\(x^{\deg\Pi_{g-2}}y^{g-2}\) when
\(g\ge3\) and \(g-2\in\mathcal S\).  Moreover,
\[
\Pi_{g-1}=
\prod_{\delta:\,\delta\in\mathcal D,\ \delta\nmid m,\ \delta\nmid k}\Phi_{2\delta}.
\]
When \(g\ge3\), one also has
\[
\Pi_{g-2}=
\prod_{\delta:\,\delta\in\mathcal D,\ \delta\nmid m\ \text{or}\ \delta\nmid k}\Phi_{2\delta}.
\]
Consequently, \(\AG_2(L)\) is obtained by interreducing an
at-most-four-element basis.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b06d9caf4499e373ff65611423270da513ac5c9944263938539642c041560074","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b0/b06d9caf4499e373ff65611423270da513ac5c9944263938539642c041560074.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:01206d6ebf0d8659f42bf613a2f917d326ca1cbcacd37d248ec55d046cb75c7a","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c5","bundle_id":"population.i0005-four-dimensional-parking-partials-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"interacting particle systems and random-walk potential theory","draft":"w661/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:i0005-c5-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C5 v1: multi-hole deletion bound and a Palm exponential-moment bound

Novelty: UNCHECKED. The source proves a two-hole deletion bound in Lemma 8.4. This is a strengthened two-hole constant and a multi-hole extension of that KNOWN argument. Literature search was limited to the source, companion paper, later author/title lists and relevant brain recalls; no assertion of priority.

For the iid sparse particle–hole initial law P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p and P(η=0)=1−2p, assume 0<p<1/2. Use synchronous nearest-neighbor simple random walks on Z^d, stationary holes of capacity one, and any d≥1. Let h_t=P(H_t(0)=1)>0 and q=p/(1−p)∈(0,1).

For distinct sites x_0,...,x_k and every finite integer t≥0,

P(H_t(x_i)=1 for every 0≤i≤k)≤h_t q^k.

In particular the source's two-hole constant p/(1−2p) can be replaced by p/(1−p). For any finite S⊂Z^d\{0}, N_t(S)=sum_{x∈S}H_t(x), and λ≥0,

E[exp(λN_t(S)) | H_t(0)=1]≤(1+q(e^λ−1))^{|S|}.

This is an exponential-moment inequality, not a claim of stochastic domination by a Bernoulli product process.

## Proof of the multi-hole inequality

Let E be the event that all k+1 specified holes are unfilled at time t. Then η(x_i)=−1 for every i, and no particle has arrived at any x_i by time t: with capacity one an arrival would fill that hole permanently.

Fix a subset J⊂{1,...,k}. Replace η(x_j)=−1 by 0 at the sites indexed by J, and leave every other initial variable and every walk/stack instruction unchanged. No particle ever visits one of these sites by round t in the original evolution. The changed evolution is identical away from these sites until its first putative arrival at any changed site. Before that arrival all particle moves are identical, so it would also be an arrival in the original evolution, a contradiction. Thus there is no such arrival, and all particles elsewhere evolve identically up to t. In particular the original hole at x_0 remains unfilled.

Call the image of E under this replacement E_J. The replacement map is injective on E after the fixed original −1 values are restored. These events E_J are pairwise disjoint: at x_j, their initial values are exactly 0 if j∈J and −1 otherwise. Each is a subset of {H_t(x_0)=1}. Conditional on all other initial variables and instructions, the probabilities of the specified coordinate assignments have ratio ((1−2p)/p)^{|J|}. Hence

P(E_J)=((1−2p)/p)^{|J|}P(E).

Only finitely many initial sites and instructions can affect the finitely many targets by time t (finite propagation and bounded initial particle count), so this change-of-variables identity can be understood entirely in a finite product space. Alternatively it follows by conditioning on all variables except the k changed initial coordinates.

Summing over the 2^k disjoint images gives

h_t≥sum_J P(E_J)
=P(E)(1+(1−2p)/p)^k
=P(E)((1−p)/p)^k.

Translation invariance gives P(H_t(x_0)=1)=h_t, proving the assertion. For k=0 the identity reduces to h_t=h_t.

## Proof of the exponential-moment inequality

For s=e^λ−1≥0 and binary H,

(1+s)^{N_t(S)}=product_{x∈S}(1+s H_t(x))
=sum_{J⊂S}s^{|J|}product_{x∈J}H_t(x).

Multiplying by H_t(0), taking expectations, and applying the multi-hole estimate term by term yields

E[H_t(0)(1+s)^{N_t(S)}]≤h_t sum_{J⊂S}(sq)^{|J|}
=h_t(1+sq)^{|S|}.

Divide by h_t. No independence of the surviving holes is used. Positivity of h_t follows, for finite t, by requiring all initial sites in a sufficiently large finite neighborhood of the target to contain holes and no particles.

## Limit of this result

The Palm expected number of other surviving holes in S is at most q|S|. This controls balls of radius O(p^−1/d), uniformly in time, but it does not control balls of radius O(h_t^−1/d), whose volume grows like h_t^−1. The missing time-dependent thinning/decorrelation input in C2 remains missing.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a717cab0408ba62fa14a8ae11b44e2c6621727ffa391b3ed98fd0857f08973f1","revision_digest":"sha256:1568d6f055efd1ea5822dd15d9b32a500c860bb2e3f333eef82afbe389f07225","source_id":"own-work:w661:I0005-C5:v1","source_revision":"v1; 2026-10-14T05:23:59.4615090+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
[Proposition 14 (Maximal common Gaussian factor) of arXiv:2607.10769, '\fontsize{14}{17}\selectfont\bfseries Sharp Poincar\'e interpolation along Wasserstein geo'] Let $\mu_i$ be $\kappa_i$-strongly log-concave probability measures
on $\R^n$, let $m_i=\int x\,\d\mu_i$, and define
\begin{equation}
	E=\left\{v\in\R^n:
		\int v\cdot\nabla\psi\,\d\mu_i
		=\kappa_i\int v\cdot(x-m_i)\psi\,\d\mu_i,\quad \forall\,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\R^n),\quad i=0,1\right\}.
\end{equation}
Then $E$ is a linear subspace. Moreover, under the orthogonal identification
$\R^n=E\oplus E^\perp$, there exist $\nu_i\in\mathcal P(E^\perp)$ such
that
\begin{equation}
 \mu_i=N_E(P_E m_i,\kappa_i^{-1}I_E)\otimes\nu_i,
 \qquad i=0,1.
\end{equation}
Here $N_E$ denotes a Gaussian law on $E$.  If a subspace $F\subseteq
\R^n$ admits such a factorization for both endpoints, with respective
covariances $\kappa_i^{-1}I_F$, then $F\subseteq E$.  Thus $E$ is the
unique maximal common Gaussian subspace.  Moreover, equality in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} at one (equivalently, every) time
$t\in(0,1)$ holds if and only if $E\neq\{0\}$.

For a nondegenerate centered real stationary Gaussian sequence X and any n>=1, rho(n)=r(n) and rho*(n)=r*(n). Here r(n) is the supremum of absolute normalized covariance of finite linear combinations supported in the past and future across gap n, and r*(n) is the same supremum for arbitrary finite separated index sets; complex coefficients are permitted and the norm of a linear form is (E|sum a_k X_k|²)^(1/2). Zero-norm forms are excluded. The rho coefficients instead allow arbitrary centered square-integrable functions of the respective coordinate sigma fields, including infinite sets. This Gaussian equality does not hold for general non-Gaussian sequences. Primary author formulation: Bradley (2005), equation (7.1), PDF p.27, with (6.7) and attribution to Kolmogorov-Rozanov (1960), Theorem1 on PDF p.28.

[Definition 41 (Oriented fusion cut profile) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] For dyadic $L,R,Q$, define
\begin{equation}

 \mu_{L,R}^{Q}
 :=P_Qm_h^{\mathrm{alg}}\big|_{H_L\otimes H_R}:
 H_L\otimes H_R\longrightarrow H_Q.
\end{equation}
This is a well-defined bounded map because its domain and target are
finite-dimensional.  Using the canonical unitary from
\eqref{eq:kernel-space}--\eqref{eq:flattening-map}, set
\[
 \mathbf m_{L,R}^{Q}
 :=\Theta_{H_L\otimes H_R,H_Q}^{-1}(\mu_{L,R}^{Q})
 \in\conj{H_L}\otimes\conj{H_R}\otimes H_Q.
\]
Put $E_1=\conj{H_L}$, $E_2=\conj{H_R}$, and $E_3=H_Q$.  For every
$I\subset\{1,2,3\}$, let
\[
 \Flat_I^{\mathrm{str}}(\mathbf m_{L,R}^{Q}):
 \conj{\bigotimes_{i\in I}E_i}
 \longrightarrow\bigotimes_{j\notin I}E_j
\]
be the canonical Hilbert-space linearization, and define
\begin{equation}

 \mathfrak f_{r,I}(L,R;Q)
 :=\norm{\Flat_I^{\mathrm{str}}(\mathbf m_{L,R}^{Q})}_{\Sch_r},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak f_r(L,R;Q)
 :=\max_{I\subset\{1,2,3\}}
 \mathfrak f_{r,I}(L,R;Q).
\end{equation}
The cut $I=\{1,2\}$ is exactly $\mu_{L,R}^{Q}$.  The two other
inequivalent nontrivial linearizations are its one-leg currying maps, and
the empty and full cuts give the Hilbert norm of the structure tensor.

body: The Banach–Tarski paradox is a theorem in set-theoretic geometry that states the following: Given a solid ball in three-dimensional space, there exists a decomposition of the ball into a finite number of disjoint subsets that can be put back together in a different way to yield two identical copies of the original ball. Indeed, the reassembly process involves only moving the pieces around and rotating them, without changing their original shape. The pieces themselves are not "solids" in the traditional sense, but infinite scatterings of points. The reconstruction can work with as few as five pieces.
title: Banach–Tarski paradox

On Z^4 let G be the full-space nearest-neighbor discrete-time SRW Green kernel, k_N(z)=G(z)1{|z|_2<=N}, sigma_N^2=sum_z k_N(z)^2, and xi_z independent standard Gaussians. Define Y_N(x)=sum_z k_N(x-z)xi_z/sigma_N and H_N(x)=1{Y_N(x)>=2sqrt(log N)}. Its density is (1+o(1))N^(-2)/(2sqrt(2pi log N)). For each fixed 0<beta<1/sqrt(2), the graph ball of radius floor(N^beta) contains no H_N hole with probability tending to one. For 1/2<beta<1/sqrt(2), its expected hole count nevertheless diverges. This is a Gaussian comparison field, not parking, and uses a spatial cutoff distinct from C11. Novelty: KNOWN Gaussian coarse/fine method; UNCHECKED exact cutoff statement. {"artifact_digest":"sha256:5a02b3868a47db55b6c952754e0268e213007ba978b87214b867a12bad064e55","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/5a/5a02b3868a47db55b6c952754e0268e213007ba978b87214b867a12bad064e55.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6cc85f6627aee7f83c3d1d43848b94925a2ddc088a5d0c34737969270e49bb92","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c16","bundle_id":"population.i0005-correlation-energy-and-active-moments-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:spatial-green-gaussian-hole-typical-void-scale-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C16 v1: typical Gaussian vacancy scale exceeds mean spacing

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN coarse/fine Gaussian method and
Green asymptotic; UNCHECKED prior appearance of this exact cutoff statement.
This is a comparison field, not the parking process. Its spatial cutoff
differs from C11's time cutoff; no equality of the fields is asserted.

For full-space discrete-time nearest-neighbor SRW on Z^4, let G be its
Green function, k_N(z)=G(z)1{|z|_2<=N}, and xi_z iid standard Gaussians.
Put sigma_N^2=sum_z k_N(z)^2 and

    Y_N(x)=sum_z k_N(x-z)xi_z/sigma_N,
    H_N(x)=1{Y_N(x)>=2 sqrt(log N)}, h_N=E H_N(0).

For every fixed 0<beta<1/sqrt(2),

    P(there is an H_N hole in B_floor(N^beta)) --> 0,

where B is a graph ball. Yet for 1/2<beta<1/sqrt(2), the expected number
of holes in the same ball tends to infinity. In particular mean intensity
does not determine typical nearest-hole distance, even at a polynomial
separation of scales. No active-particle field is defined here.

## Variance and marginal density

Lawler--Limic Theorem 4.3.1 gives
G(z)=(2/pi^2)|z|_2^(-2)+O(|z|_2^(-4)). Squaring and summing over lattice
annuli gives

    sigma_N^2=A log N+O(1),  A=8/pi^2.

Indeed sum_{1<=|z|_2<=N}|z|_2^(-4)=2pi^2 log N+O(1), by comparison
with unit cubes and the integrable derivative error; the sphere area in
four dimensions is 2pi^2. Terms from the Green error are summable. Normal
Mills bounds then give

    h_N=(1+o(1)) N^(-2)/(2 sqrt(2pi log N)).

The mean spacing h_N^(-1/4) is N^(1/2+o(1)). The unnormalized threshold
in the numerator field is

    s_N=2 sqrt(log N) sigma_N=2 sqrt(A) log N+O(1).

## Coarse noise is nearly constant on a smaller ball

Set r=floor(N^beta). Split the numerator field W_N(x) into F_x+C_x,
using respectively the noise sites |z|_2<=2r and |z|_2>2r. These are
independent centered Gaussian components. For all |x|_1<=r and sufficiently
large N, 3r<N, so

    Var(F_x)<=sum_{|w|_2<=3r}G(w)^2<=A beta log N+O(1).

We next show Var(C_x-C_0)<=C uniformly over |x|_1<=r. On the region
where both shifted kernels are inside their cutoff and |z|_2>2r,
the same Green asymptotic and the derivative of |z|^(-2) give

    |G(z-x)-G(z)|<=C r |z|_2^(-3)+C|z|_2^(-4).

Its squared lattice sum is bounded by
C r^2 sum_{|z|>2r}|z|^(-6)+C sum_{|z|>2r}|z|^(-8)<=C.
If exactly one shifted kernel is inside its cutoff, then
N-r<=|z|_2<=N+r. This shell has O(N^3 r) sites and each squared kernel
is O(N^(-4)), giving O(r/N)<=C. Else both kernels vanish. This proves
the asserted uniform increment variance without assuming differentiability
of a random field.

For any fixed epsilon>0, the Gaussian tail bound and a union bound yield

    P(max_{x in B_r}|C_x-C_0|>epsilon log N)
       <=C r^4 exp(-c epsilon^2 (log N)^2) -->0.

Also Var(C_0)<=A log N+O(1), so
P(|C_0|>epsilon log N)<=2N^(-epsilon^2/(2A)+o(1)) tends to zero.
Thus max_{x in B_r} C_x<=2epsilon log N with probability tending to one.

## Fine-noise maximum upper bound

Let u_N=(2sqrt(A)-3epsilon)log N, with epsilon small enough that u_N>0.
The fine variance bound and the cardinality |B_r|=O(N^(4beta)) give

    P(max_{x in B_r}F_x>u_N)
       <=N^[4beta-(2sqrt(A)-3epsilon)^2/(2A beta)+o(1)].

At epsilon=0 the exponent is 4beta-2/beta, which is strictly negative
exactly when beta<1/sqrt(2). Choose a sufficiently small fixed positive
epsilon so it remains negative. Then the fine maximum is at most u_N
with probability tending to one. Combining the two maximum bounds makes
max_{x in B_r}W_N(x)<s_N eventually with probability tending to one.
This proves the claimed vacancy probability.

## Diverging expectation despite the void probability

For beta>1/2, stationarity and the graph-ball count yield

    E sum_{x in B_r}H_N(x)=h_N |B_r|
      =N^(4beta-2+o(1)) -->infinity.

For beta additionally below 1/sqrt(2), the preceding result says the ball
is nevertheless empty with probability tending to one. The rare occupied
configurations account for this divergent expectation. This is an explicit
warning against treating an annealed expected hole count as a typical
spatial count in a logarithmically correlated comparison field.

## Limits of the comparison

The proof gives an upper bound on the probability of finding a hole in
these balls; it gives no matching upper bound on nearest-hole distance.
It does not identify the source parking field with this Gaussian field.
C9's finite-Palm criterion is sufficient, not proved necessary, and neither
a favorable interlacement proxy nor this unfavorable Gaussian proxy decides

[Proposition 30 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] The same compactness mechanism yields two useful crossover limits.

\textup{(i)} Let $m_\sigma$ be a real-valued function such that
\[
\delta_\sigma:=\sigma^{2-m_\sigma}\longrightarrow\delta\in(0,\infty).
\]
Consider
\[
\cA_{\sigma,m_\sigma,L}u=\frac1{\sigma^{m_\sigma}}\left(\int_{-L}^{L}J_\sigma(x-y)u(y)\,dy-u(x)\right)+q(x)u'(x)+a(x)u(x).
\]
Then
\[
\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m_\sigma,L})\longrightarrow\lambda_\delta,
\]
where $\lambda_\delta$ is the Dirichlet principal eigenvalue of $\delta d_Ju''+q(x)u'+a(x)u$
on $(-L,L)$. If the principal eigenfunctions are normalized in $L^2$, they converge strongly in $L^2$ to the normalized local principal eigenfunction. Moreover,
\[
\delta_\sigma E_\sigma(\phi_\sigma)\longrightarrow\delta d_J\int_{-L}^{L}|\phi_\delta'|^2\,dx.
\]

\textup{(ii)} Assume $q,a\in C^2([-L,L])$, $q\ge q_0>0$, let $m_\sigma\to2$, and suppose
\[
(2-m_\sigma)|\log\sigma|\longrightarrow\theta\in\R.
\]
Then $\delta_\sigma=\sigma^{2-m_\sigma}\to e^{-\theta}$ and
\[
\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m_\sigma,L})\longrightarrow
\lambda_1^D\left(e^{-\theta}d_J\partial_{xx}+q(x)\partial_x+a(x),(-L,L)\right).

[Lem 240 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,\delta>0$, and $\fq\in [1,2)$, there exists $c = c(\alpha,L,\delta) > 0$ such that the following holds for sufficiently large $N$. For any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$, we have
	\[
		\P\bigg(
			\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)
			\Big) \le \delta
		\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,,
	\]
for $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ as defined by \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}. The analogous estimate holds likewise for $\bbW_\fq(\mu_{\bG,\sym}(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))$ and $\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon))$, where the latter is defined by \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L.SYM}. 

\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof, $c$ denotes a constant that depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$, which can change line by line.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, for $C = C(\alpha)$ as defined therein, we have
	\beq
		\P\bigg(
			\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \in \cP_2(\R,C)
		\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
We now define
	\[
		S_\delta \equiv
		\Big\{ \mu \in \cP_2(\R,C) : \bbW_\fq(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta \Big\}
	\]
(note this differs slightly from the set $S_\delta$ defined in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.lip.trunc.to.ideal}). 
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_2(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_\fq$ metric, and therefore also compact. We may thus cover $S_\delta$ with finitely many $\bbW_\fq$-balls,
	\[S_\delta = \bigcup_{\mu \in T_\delta} \cB_{\fq,\delta/5}(\mu)
		\,,\]
	where $T_\delta \subseteq S_\delta$ is a finite set depending on only $\fq, \delta$, and
		\[\cB_{q,\delta/5}(\mu) 
		\equiv\bigg\{
			\mu' \in S_\delta : \bbW_\fq(\mu,\mu') \le 
			\frac{\delta}{5}
		\bigg\}\,.\]
	Note that for each $\mu \in S_\delta$, we have
	\begin{align*}
		\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) 
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu,\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon))
		- \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \\
		&\ge \delta - \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon))\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last term on the right-hand side above does not depend on $
\mu$, and is $o_N(1)$ by
	Proposition~\ref{p:confinement}. It follows that for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
		\inf_{\mu \in S_\delta} \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) \ge 
		\frac{4\delta}{5}\,.
	\]
	For each $\mu \in T_\delta$,  Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound} implies
	\[
		\E \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}}{\ge} \bigg(\Big[\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\Big]_+\bigg)^{1/2}
		\ge \frac{3\delta}{5}
	\]
	for sufficiently large $N$.
	Note that the $o_N(1)$ term above may depend on $\mu$; however, as $T_\delta$ is a finite set independent of $N$, the above estimate can be taken to hold simultaneously for all $\mu \in T_\delta$. By Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} combined with a union bound over
$\mu \in T_\delta$, we obtain
	\[
		\P\bigg(
			\min_{\mu \in T_\delta} \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux),\mu\Big)
			\ge \frac{2\delta}{5}
		\bigg)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.tail}}{=} 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\]
	(This $c$ depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$ only, as $\epsilon,\fq$ affect only the $N$-independent number of terms $|T_\delta|$ in the union bound.)
	On this event, we further have
	\[\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), S_\delta\Big)
		\ge \min_{\mu \in T_\delta} \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big) - \frac{\delta}{5}
		\ge 
		\frac{\delta}{5}\,,\]
	and therefore $\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \not\in S_\delta$.
	Combining with \eqref{e:confinement.mu.bG.to.P2} shows that 
	\[
		\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \in \cP_2(\R,C) \setminus S_\delta
	\]
with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ (again adjusting $c$ appropriately). 
	On this event, we obtain the desired estimate
	\[
		\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)
		\Big) \le \delta\,.
	\]

PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT, no independent review. Let Gamma be a finite group and Q a Gamma-equivariant positive contraction on l^2(Gamma) with 0 < Q < I, and let P_Q be the determinantal probability measure on subsets of Gamma with kernel Q. Let HM(Q) be the harmonic mean of the eigenvalues of Q. Then P_Q stochastically dominates the product Bernoulli measure of density HM(Q), and symmetrically P_Q is dominated by the product measure of density 1 - HM(I - Q). This is strictly weaker than Lyons's Conjecture 5.7 (ICM 2014), which asserts the same with the geometric mean (Fuglede-Kadison determinant) in place of the harmonic mean; the conjecture is the harmonic-to-geometric upgrade, and numerical monotone-coupling linear programs on Z/nZ, n <= 6 (102 random symmetric circulant contractions), satisfy the geometric-mean bound exactly, with density FK(Q) + 0.01 already failing on a tested instance.
Finite group Gamma
Q Gamma-equivariant with 0 < Q < I (strict contraction, invertible); the boundary cases follow by limits
Holley's inequality in its product-measure form

    with $0<\mathbb{E}[Y_1^2]<\infty$. Let $\{N_n\}$ be non-negative integer-valued, independent of $\{Y_n\}$,  with finite  variance. Let $\sigma_n^2$ be as in (\ref{sigmandefn}).\vskip3pt
    
   \noindent (i) If $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]\neq0$, and
    as $n\rightarrow\infty$, $\sigma_n^2\to \infty$,
    
    along with 
    $\sqrt{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[N_n]}=o(\sigma_n^2)$,
    
    then 
    \begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}\exp\Big[\iota t(\frac{S_{N_n}-\mathbb{E}[N_nY_1]}
    
    {\sigma_n})\Big]=\mathbb{E}\exp[\iota\delta_nt\tilde{N}_n]\mathbb{E}\exp[\iota t\sqrt{1-\delta_n^2}Z]+o(1),\ t\in\mathbb{R},
\end{equation}
where $\tilde{N}_n$ and $S_{N_{n}}$ are as in (\ref{Nndefn}) and (\ref{SNndefn}), respectively. \vskip5pt

\noindent (ii)  If $\mathbb{E}[Y_n]=0$, and as $n\rightarrow\infty$, $\mathbb{E}[N_n]\rightarrow\infty$, $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[N_n]}}{\mathbb{E}[N_n]}=:\xi\in(0,\infty)$, and 

$\tilde{N}_n$ converges weakly to a random variable $N$, 
then 

\begin{equation*}
    \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\exp\Big[\iota t\frac{S_{N_n}}
    {\sigma_n}\Big]
    
    =\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t^2x/2}\,\mu(dx), 
    
    \ t\in\mathbb{R},
\end{equation*}
where $\mu$ is the probability distribution of $1+N\xi$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In vector calculus, Green's theorem relates a line integral around a simple closed curve C to a double integral over the plane region D bounded by C. It is the two-dimensional special case of Stokes' theorem. In one dimension, it is equivalent to the fundamental theorem of calculus. In two dimensions, it is equivalent to the divergence theorem.
title: Green's theorem

A weak joint shape/length limit does not determine conditional shape at a prescribed lattice length. For even n, let L_n be uniform on {1/n,2/n,...,1} and let X_n=0 except at L_n=1/2. Choose X_n=+1 there in one sequence and -1 in another. Both joint laws tend to (0,U), where U is uniform on [0,1], and have identical length marginals. Their conditional features at L_n=1/2 are respectively +1 and -1; that atom has mass 1/n. Thus the required transfer must control relative conditional errors, not just a weak mixture limit. Author-derived explicit counterexample; independent review pending.

Status: proof (unaudited). Refutes monotonicity in the order; does not refute eventual mixability. Novelty not asserted.

Let 0<epsilon<1/2 and 0<p<1, and let F=(1-p)Uniform[0,epsilon]+p Uniform[1-epsilon,1]. Its mean is mu=p+(1/2-p)epsilon. Put r=n epsilon/[2(1-epsilon)]. If F is n-CM, then:

- If np is noninteger, r>=max({np},1-{np}), where {np} denotes its fractional part.
- If np is an integer and n>=2, F is in fact n-CM.

Proof of necessity. In any complete mix define K to be the number of coordinates in the high interval. Since the intervals are disjoint and every marginal has high mass p, E[K]=np. Pathwise,

    (1-epsilon)K <= sum_i X_i <= (1-epsilon)K+n epsilon.

The sum equals n mu=np(1-epsilon)+n epsilon/2, hence |K-np|<=r. Therefore np belongs to the convex hull of the allowed integers in [np-r,np+r] intersect [0,n]. If np is noninteger, this convex hull contains np only if both floor(np) and ceil(np) are allowed. The distances from np to these integers are {np} and 1-{np}; this gives the stated inequality. There is no independence assumption.

Proof of sufficiency when np is an integer k and n>=2. A centered uniform law is n-CM for every n>=2 by the explicit uniform triple plus symmetric pairs in D0007-C001 (even n consists of pairs, odd n one triple plus pairs). Thus choose U_1,...,U_n all uniform on [0,epsilon], with sum n epsilon/2. Add 1-epsilon to exactly k of their coordinates. The resulting sum is n epsilon/2+k(1-epsilon)=n mu. Apply an independent uniform coordinate permutation. Each marginal is the desired mixture F, because every coordinate receives a high label with probability k/n=p.

Concrete example. Take epsilon=1/10 and p=3/5, so F=(2/5)Uniform[0,1/10]+(3/5)Uniform[9/10,1] and mu=59/100. It is n-CM for every n>=2 divisible by five. It is not 6-CM: np=18/5, fractional part 3/5, while r=1/3<3/5. In particular it is 5-CM and not 6-CM, so successful fixed-order constructions do not imply monotonicity of n-CM. More directly at n=6, sum target 177/50=3.54 lies strictly between the largest sum with K=3 (33/10=3.3) and smallest with K=4 (18/5=3.6).

At n=7 the sum target lies in the possible K=4 interval, but no other K is possible; E[K]=21/5 is incompatible with K=4 almost surely. This demonstrates why support feasibility alone is weaker than exact marginal count feasibility.

In the sparse critical law of I0005-C3, now allow any fixed p in (0,1/4]. Let h_t=P(H_t(0)=1). For any fixed b>0 set r_t=floor(bh_t^−1/4), x_t=(r_t,0,0,0), and K_t(x)=sum_{n=0}^t(n+1)p_n(x). Then

K_t(x_t)=(4/π²)(log t + (1/2)log h_t − 2 log b)+O(1)
=(2/π²)log t+O(log log(t+2)).

The O(1) constant can depend on b and the initial law. Thus simply replacing equation (46)'s infinite-time kernel by a time-t cutoff, even if such a replacement were justified, does not restore bounded decorrelation at the mean hole spacing.

## Proof

Corollary 1.3, equation (8), gives c/(t+1)≤h_t≤C log(t+2)/(t+1), since EA_t(0)=h_t for the sparse law. In particular h_t→0. Consequently r_t→∞, r_t²=b²h_t^−1/2(1+o(1)), and r_t²/t→0 by the lower density bound. The log-positive branch in I0005-C1 is therefore eventually the ordinary logarithm, giving

K_t(x_t)=(4/π²)log(t/(1+r_t²))+O(1)
=(4/π²)(log t+(1/2)log h_t−2log b)+O(1).

The density bounds imply log h_t=−log t+O(log log(t+2)); inserting them proves the second formula. More precisely, the correction (1/2)log(th_t) is bounded below and at most (1/2)log log(t+2)+O(1).

## Scope of the obstruction

The source's pair bound in d≥5 has an exponential involving log(1/h_t) times a spatially decaying infinite-time kernel. At d=4 the displayed cutoff kernel is already of order log t at the mean spacing, so substituting it into that form yields an uncontrolled order-(log t)^2 exponent. This is a failure of that estimate, not a proof that true hole correlations are that large. Cancellation, conditioned killing, or another argument might still give the missing Palm pair-sum bound.

Multiplying the spacing by (log t)^α for a fixed real α only changes log(t/r_t²) by −2α log log t+O(1); it does not remove the leading logarithm. Moreover, positive density g_t≥c h_t of disjoint isolated-hole balls of radius R_t requires g_t|B_{R_t}|≤1 by translation invariance, hence R_t=O(h_t^−1/4). [Theorem thm:perturbed-first-order-solver of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Assume Assumptions~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) and
(ass:drift-multiplier of the paper).  Let $\alpha\geq0$, let $I=(r_0,r_1)$, let $w$
be a regular weight of order $\alpha$, and let $G\in L_w^2(I;\mathbb R^d)$ and
$\eta\in L^2(\mu_{r_1};\mathbb R^d)$.  There exists a unique
$p\in H_{x,w}^1(I;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfying
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal P_1p=G\quad\text{in distributions},\qquad
 \operatorname{Tr}_{r_1}^Xp=\eta(X_{r_1}).
\end{equation*}
There exists a constant
$C=C(\lambda,\Lambda_b,M_1(a),\operatorname{osc}_{\alpha,I}(w))>0$
such that, for every $\kappa\geq C$,
\begin{equation}
 \left(
   \kappa\left\lVert p\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
   +\left\lVert (D_xp)\sigma\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
 \right)^{1/2}
 \leq C\left(\kappa^{-1/2}\left\lVert G\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}
       +\sqrt{w_\kappa(r_1)}\norm\eta_{L^2(\mu_{r_1})}\right).
 
\end{equation}
Estimate~(equation eq:perturbed-first-order-energy of the paper) also holds in difference form
for two sets of data.

[Lemma t of arXiv:2602.18784, 'A note on the cooperative two-type SIR processes on Galton-Watson trees'] Assume all conditions in  Theorem (general of the paper). For all vertices $x$ in $GW (p)$,
    let $\tau_A(x)$ and $\tau_B(x)$ be the time
    that $x$ gets infected with $A$ and $B$, respectively. (Note that if the vertex $x$ is never infected by a disease, we let the corresponding time be $\infty$.)
    Let $y$ be a child of $x$.
    The conditional probability given
    $ \sigma (\tau_A(x), \tau_B(x))$ that $y$ is infected with both $A$ and $B$ is almost surely less than or equal to $1/m$.
title: Lemma t of arXiv:2602.18784

body: If a linear operator T is bounded from L^{p0} to L^{q0} with norm M0 and from L^{p1} to L^{q1} with norm M1, then for every theta in (0, 1) it is bounded from L^{p_theta} to L^{q_theta} with norm at most M0^{1-theta} M1^{theta}, where the intermediate exponents interpolate harmonically: 1/p_theta = (1-theta)/p0 + theta/p1 and likewise for q. The proof runs through the Hadamard three-lines theorem applied to an analytic family built from the duality pairing. Interpolation converts two endpoint estimates into the whole scale - the engine behind Hausdorff-Young and Young's convolution inequality.
title: Riesz-Thorin Interpolation Theorem

metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:800692cd47180d36b48bc5a16ddadef3ecc1ccc5604665005d3a36ac4b9c1d22","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/80/800692cd47180d36b48bc5a16ddadef3ecc1ccc5604665005d3a36ac4b9c1d22.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:58b27a1d22ff9ae3c0759205a139cc91f04d2b3f73db47604ee06aa55a081301","bundle_entry_key":"standard-adam-entry","bundle_id":"population.t421-standard-adam-p1-entry-and-center-graph-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"deterministic adaptive optimization","draft":"w706/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-bias-corrected-standard-moment-near-threshold-p1-entry-w706","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-006 v2; target 1; kind narrowed; rung proof (unaudited).

THE STATEMENT
There exist kappa>0 and a0>0 such that for every eta>0, epsilon=eta,
H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2) with 38<lambda_i<38+kappa, and standard m0=v0=0
with 0<|x_i,0|<eta*a0, ordinary bias-corrected full-batch Adam at
beta1=9/10,beta2=999/1000 approaches a nonzero product two-cycle by parity.
Both eta times the active curvature and eta times top preconditioned
sharpness tend to 38 as t->infinity. The eigenvalues are fixed during a run.
This does not assert arbitrary initialization or any p>1 behavior. kappa
and a0 are existential, not numerical bounds.

PRIMARY THEOREM USED
van den Berg, Hetebrij and Rink, More on the parameterization method for
center manifolds, arXiv:2003.00701, Theorem 1.1 pp.4-5 and Remark 1.4 p.6;
equivalently their arXiv:1905.00264 Theorem 2.1 pp.5-6.
The finite-dimensional special case used here: a C3 map fixing zero with
derivative diag(I_c,A_s), spectral radius(A_s)<1, has a locally invariant
C3 center graph tangent to the center subspace, parameterized by its center
coordinates (choose k_c=0). To match the theorem, choose an adapted norm
with ||A_s||<1; A_c=I satisfies all spectral-gap inequalities for n<=3;
the unstable space is zero. Subtract the linearization and multiply the
remaining O(||z||^2) nonlinearity by a smooth compact cutoff. Its derivative
supremum tends to zero as support shrinks, exactly as Remark 1.4 requires.
The cutoff changes nothing in the eventual local domain. This applies to
the parameter-augmented map (delta'=delta), so no separate parameter theorem
or stable-foliation theorem is needed.

SCALAR PROOF
Write b=9/10,d=999/1000,c=1/19,D=1/38. For scalar curvature lambda set
 X=x/eta, M=m/(eta lambda), V=v/(eta lambda)^2,
 rho=epsilon/(eta lambda)=1/lambda, delta=D-rho.
For X!=0 set y=|X|, q=M/X, r=V/X^2, and add clocks
alpha=b^(t+1), sigma=d^(t+1). Define u=dr+1-d, h=bq+1-b and
 A=1-h/[(1-alpha)*(rho+y*sqrt(u/(1-sigma)))].
On the open region A<0 this is the EXACT corrected recursion:
 (y,q,r,alpha,sigma)'=(-Ay,h/A,u/A^2,b alpha,d sigma).             (1)
All square roots and denominators are regular on a full open neighborhood
of z*=(0,-c,1,0,0,delta=0): u=1, rho=D>0, A=-1 there.
Thus (1), augmented by delta'=delta, extends C-infinity across y=0 locally.

The fixed-delta Jacobian at z* is
 [[1,0,0,0,0],[-4,.9,0,2/19,0],
  [152,-342/5,.999,-4,0],[0,0,0,.9,0],[0,0,0,0,.999]],
where the decimal entries denote the EXACT fractions 9/10 and 999/1000.
The center directions in (y,q,r,alpha,sigma;delta) are
 v_y=(1,-40,2888000,0,0;0),
 v_delta=(0,40,-2888000,0,0;1).
Their eigenvalue is 1; the other four eigenvalues are b,b,d,d. These
identities and invertibility are checked exactly in scripts/verify_center.py.

The subspace alpha=sigma=0 is invariant. Apply the primary center-graph
theorem to the restriction to this subspace with delta appended. Choose
center coordinates exactly (y,delta), since stable directions have zero
y and delta components. This gives q=Q(y,delta), r=R(y,delta), clocks=0,
with derivatives Q_y=-40,Q_delta=40,R_y=2888000,R_delta=-2888000 at zero.
View the same graph as an invariant center graph of the full clock map.
Denote its scalar center update by f_delta(y).

In coordinates e=(q-Q(y,delta),r-R(y,delta),alpha,sigma), the map has form
 y'=y B(y,e,delta),  e'=T(y,e,delta),  delta'=delta,
with T(y,0,delta)=0. At zero D_e T has eigenvalues b,b,d,d. Choose an
adapted e-norm and then shrink the neighborhood so
 ||T(y,e,delta)||<=theta||e||, theta<1.                           (2)
This follows from the mean-value formula and continuity of D_e T; no
phase projection or foliation theorem is being invoked.

We next identify the exact center normal form. The y=0 graph has y'=0,
so f_delta(0)=0. The extended full map has the EXACT fixed branch
 (y,q,r,alpha,sigma)=(delta,-c,1,0,0)                            (3)
for every sufficiently small real delta, including negative delta in the
smooth extension. Every such fixed point lies on our graph: its transverse
coordinate would otherwise satisfy e=T(y,e,delta) with ||e||<=theta||e||,
contradicting theta<1. Thus f_delta(delta)=delta.
Exact differentiation on the graph gives
 f_delta(y)=y+1444 delta*y-1444 y^2+O((|y|+|delta|)^3).
For example the y^2 coefficient is -76+(171/5)*(-40)=-1444,
and the delta*y coefficient is 76+(171/5)*40=1444.
These are exact symbolic checks, not floating-point estimates.
Two applications of Hadamard's lemma therefore give the EXACT factorization
 f_delta(y)=y+y(delta-y) K(y,delta), K(0,0)=1444,                 (4)
where K is C1. Choose a small interval |y|,|delta|<r_* on which K is
positive and f_delta is strictly increasing in y. For 0<delta<r_*/4,
f_delta maps (0,delta) into itself above the diagonal and (delta,r_*)
into itself below the diagonal. Every positive center orbit in that
interval consequently converges to delta.

NOW PROVE NEARBY ATTRACTION DIRECTLY, RATHER THAN ASSUMING A FOLIATION.
Smoothness of B implies, on a sufficiently small product neighborhood,
 |B(y,e,delta)-B(y,0,delta)|<=L||e||.
Along any orbit that remains there, (2) yields ||e_n||<=theta^n||e_0||,
so its amplitude satisfies
 y_(n+1)=f_delta(y_n)+y_n E_n,
 |E_n|<=L theta^n||e_0||.                                     (5)
The original map has A<0 throughout the neighborhood, hence y_n>0.

The neighborhood is forward invariant after shrinking the allowed initial
box. Indeed monotonicity and f_delta(delta)=delta imply
 f_delta(y)<=max(y,delta) for y>0 in the local interval. Equation (5) gives
 y_n<=max(y_0,delta)*exp[L||e_0||/(1-theta)].                    (6)
Choose y_0,delta<r_*/4 and ||e_0|| small enough that the exponential is <2
and the transverse coordinates remain strictly inside the local domain.
Induction using (2),(5),(6) gives y_n<r_*/2 and the required transverse
bound for all n. Apply the estimates on a slightly larger product box
to avoid circularity at the boundary; all its images are defined by the
cutoff center graph, which agrees with the original map on the smaller box.

For completeness, summable errors in (5) give y_n->delta, not just boundedness.
Fix 0<h<delta with delta+h<r_*/2. On y<=delta-h, for all sufficiently
large n the multiplier in (5),(4) is >=1+h*min(K)/2. On y>=delta+h
it is <=1-h*min(K)/2. These inequalities force finite exit from either
outer region. Moreover f_delta maps [delta-h,delta+h] strictly inside
itself at the endpoints: its endpoint margins are positive by (4).
For n large, the perturbation |y_n E_n| is smaller than these margins
and smaller than h/2. Strict monotonicity of f_delta prevents a step
from jumping across the entire middle interval. Hence the orbit enters
and remains in [delta-h,delta+h]. Since h is arbitrary, y_n->delta.
Then e_n->0 and continuity of Q,R imply q_n->-c,r_n->1,clocks->0.
This proves a uniform local positive-amplitude tube of attraction for
all sufficiently small delta>0. The tube may contain arbitrarily small
positive y; no lower bound depending on delta was assumed.

STANDARD ZERO MOMENTS ENTER THIS TUBE.
At m0=v0=0 the ratio values are q0=r0=0; clocks alpha0=b,sigma0=d.
Analyze first the extended boundary orbit y=delta=0. For q in [-c,0],
h=bq+1-b lies in [c,1-b] and
 A_t=1-h/[(1-b^(t+1))*D]<=-1.
Its q update maps [-c,0] into itself. Direct differentiation gives
 d(h/A_t)/dq=b/A_t^2<=b.
At q=-c the discrepancy from -c is 2c*b^(t+1)/(1+b^(t+1)). Thus
 |q_t+c|<=b^t*c+2c*t*b^t ->0.                                  (7)
Also 0<=r_t<=1 because r'=(d r+1-d)/A_t^2, and
 |r_(t+1)-1|<=d|r_t-1|+|1-A_t^(-2)| ->0.                       (8)
The convergence in (8) follows by splitting the geometric convolution
of its vanishing forcing into a finite initial part and a uniformly
small tail. The clocks vanish, so this boundary orbit approaches z*.

Choose a FINITE N placing it strictly inside the local tube's transverse
and amplitude upper bounds. Every preceding denominator is strictly
positive, u>=1-d>0, sigma_t<1, and A_t<=-1. By continuity of this
FINITE composition, some delta0>0 and a0>0 ensure that all physical
0<delta<delta0,0<y_initial<a0 have A<0 through time N and land inside
the same tube with y_N>0. Equations (2)-(8) then prove convergence to
(3). This establishes entry from actual time-0 ordinary bias correction,
without a warm-start or a stable-foliation hypothesis.

TWO COORDINATES AND CURVATURE.
Shrink delta0 further if needed and choose kappa>0 with
0<D-1/lambda<delta0 whenever 38<lambda<38+kappa.
The scalar maps are decoupled, with identical clocks. Each coordinate
converges by parity to |x_i|=eta*(D-1/lambda_i)>0,
m_i=opposite-sign lambda_i*|x_i|/19 and v_i=lambda_i^2*x_i^2.
Since the bias corrections tend to one,
sqrt(vhat_i)+epsilon ->eta*lambda_i*(D-1/lambda_i)+eta
                       =eta*lambda_i*D.
Each preconditioned eigenvalue therefore tends to 1/(eta D)=38/eta.
The active curvature is their Rayleigh average, and the limiting gradients
in both coordinates are nonzero. It and their maximum have the same limit.

WHAT WAS CHECKED / LIMITS
scripts/verify_center.py checks the complete augmented Jacobian, its spectrum,
both center tangent equations, the quadratic coefficients, the exact fixed
branch and boundary derivative. scripts/check_entry_cases.py checks 96 exact
physical/ratio identities and 1050 exact boundary invariance cases. Those
finite checks corroborate the identities; the formulas above prove them
on their full domains. Initial zero coordinates violate the nonzero-cycle
and top-curvature conclusion (they stay dormant with eta curvature=lambda).
lambda=38 collapses the cycle; below 38 the purported positive amplitude
is negative. Exact beta2=.999 is stronger than this local argument needs:
the center argument only needs 0<d<1; it is retained to match the target.
Numerical examples in logs/entry_numerics.json are diagnostics, not bounds.
Lean checks previously timed out; this is not a Lean-checked proof.

Hardest still-open part of target 1: p>1 from standard initialization,
and the remaining p=1 eigenvalue/initial-amplitude range. This theorem
does not prove or disprove o(1)-tracking there.

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix a concept $\alpha$ with $|S_\alpha|=L$, and let
	$T:=\|\eta^{(\alpha)}\|_1$
	denote the number of active coordinates in the clean cue
	$\eta^{(\alpha)}$. Then, under our standing assumptions for every $C>eL$  and all $N_f$ large enough,
	\[
	\mathbb P\bigl(T> C\log N_f\bigr)
	\le
	\exp\bigl(-c(C,L)\log N_f\bigr)
	= N_f^{-c(C,L)}
	\]
   In particular, for such $C$ we have 
	\[
\mathbb P\bigl(T\le C\log N_f\bigr)\xrightarrow[N_f\to\infty]{}1.
\]
