[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2511.13404, 'Asymptotic stability and mean ergodicity of Feller processes on Polish spaces'] Let $\mathfrak{F}\subset B(\X)$ be such that $L_b(\X)\subset\mathfrak{F}$ and satisfy Hypothesis $(\mathbf{H_1})$.
   Then the following statements are equivalent:
   \begin{itemize}
			\item[(\runum{1})] $\Phi$ is asymptotically stable with respect to $\mathfrak{F}$.
			\item[(\runum{2})] $\Phi$ is eventually continuous with respect to $\mathfrak{F}$ on $\X$, and there exists $z\in\X$ such that $\Phi$ satisfies the lower bound condition \eqref{eq:LBC_P} at $z$.
            \item[(\runum{3})] There exists $z\in\X$ such that $\Phi$ is eventually continuous with respect to $\mathfrak{F}$ at $z$ and satisfies the lower bound condition \eqref{eq:LBC_P} at $z$.
		\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 9 of arXiv:2606.11774, 'Martingale Solutions to a Stochastic Keller-Segel System with nonlocal Source and Super-li'] Let $d\ge 3$,  the constant $\alpha>1,\beta>1,\gamma\ge2$ and $ \alpha+1>\beta$. Under Assumption \ref{ass}, if \[\max\{3,\gamma,\alpha+1\}<\frac{2}{d+2}(\alpha-1+\beta),\]  then  
    for each $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and for every $T>0$, the equation  (\ref{equ2}) admits the pathwise  unique global nonnegative solution $u_n$ on $[0,T]$. There exists positive  constant $C(T)$, $C(T,k)$ independent of $n$   such that
    \begin{align}
\sup_{n\ge1}\mathbb{E}\Big(\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|u_n(t)\|_{L^2(\mathcal{O})}^2\Big)\leq C(T),
   \\
\sup_{n\ge1}\mathbb{E}\Big(\int_{0}^{T}\|\nabla u_n(t)\|_{L^2(\mathcal{O})}^2dt\Big)\leq C(T),
  \\
\sup_{n\ge1}\mathbb{E}\Big(\int_{0}^{T}\|u_n(t)\|_{L^{\alpha+1}(\mathcal{O})}^{\alpha+1}\|u_n(t)\|_{L^{\beta}(\mathcal{O})}^{\beta}dt\Big)\leq C(T),\\
\sup_{n\ge1}\mathbb{E}\Big(\int_{0}^{T}\|u_n(t)\|_{L^{k}(\mathcal{O})}^{k}dt\Big)\leq C(T,k),
 \end{align}
  where  $k\in[1,\frac{2}{d+2}(\alpha-1+\beta)+2)$.

[Lemma lm:homo_monot of arXiv:2605.10491, 'Zero-couplings of infinite measures with cyclically monotone support and multivariate regu'] Let $A \subset \reals^d\times\reals^d$ satisfy the following two properties:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item (monotonicity) 
        $\forall (x,y),(a,b)\in A: \langle{x-a,y-b}\rangle \geqslant 0$;
    \item (homogeneity) 
        $\exists \alpha,\beta > 0, 
        \forall \lambda>0,
        \forall (x,y)\in A: 
            (\lambda^\alpha x, \lambda^\beta y)\in A$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then $x \in \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{proj}_1 A)$ and $(0, b) \in A$ imply $\langle{x,b}\rangle \leqslant 0$.

body:
[Lemma lem: Bernstein poly of arXiv:2604.05941, 'Banach spaces of continuous paths with finite $p$-th variation'] For $x \in C([0,1])$, define its $n$-th Bernstein polynomial by
    \[
        x_n(t) := \sum_{k=0}^n x\Big(\frac{k}{n}\Big)\binom{n}{k} t^k(1-t)^{n-k}, \qquad t \in [0,1],
    \]
    so that $\|x_n\|_{\infty} \le \|x\|_{\infty}$ and $\|x_n - x\|_{\infty} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Then, for $\alpha \in (0,1)$, we have the following bound for the $\alpha$-H\"older norm of $x_n$:
    \[
        \|x_n\|_{C^{\alpha}} \le (2n+1)\|x\|_{\infty}, \qquad \forall \, n \in \mathbb{N}.
    \]

body:
Pourkamali-Macris Proposition2, with the standing spectral regularity made explicit. Let N<=M_N and N/M_N->alpha in (0,1]. Let mu be a probability density on [0,K] for a finite deterministic K. Its symmetrization mu_bar on R is assumed to have finite logarithmic energy integral integral log|x-y| dmu_bar(x)dmu_bar(y)>-infinity and integral log|x| dmu_bar(x)>-infinity, as in source Assumption2. Draw an infinite iid sequence of nonnegative singular values with law mu and, for each N, put its first N values (ordered if desired) on the diagonal of the rectangular N by M_N matrix Sigma_N. Condition on this singular-value sequence. The signal is S_N=U_N*Sigma_N*V_N^T, with independent normalized Haar orthogonal matrices U_N in O(N), V_N in O(M_N). Independently let Z_N have iid centered real Gaussian entries of variance1/N, and observe Y_N=sqrt(lambda)*S_N+Z_N for fixed lambda>0. In the partition function the candidate X has this same fixed-spectrum Haar prior P_N, and Zcal_N(Y)=integral exp(N*sqrt(lambda)*Tr(X^T*Y)-N*lambda*||X||_F^2/2) P_N(dX). Define F_N(lambda)=-(1/(N*M_N))*E[log Zcal_N(Y_N) | Sigma_N], where expectation includes the planted Haar orientations and Gaussian noise. Define I_N,M(A,B)=integral_{O(N)xO(M)} exp(N*Tr(A^T*U*B*V^T)) dU dV and J_N,M(A,B)=log I_N,M(A,B)/(N*M). Let mu_lambda be the pushforward of mu under x->sqrt(lambda)*x, and let nu_alpha be the limiting empirical SINGULAR-VALUE law of Z_N under this normalization. Write mu_lambda rectangular-free-plus_alpha nu_alpha for the singular-value law of sqrt(lambda)*Sigma_N+Z_N. Let J_alpha[mu_lambda,mu_lambda rectangular-free-plus_alpha nu_alpha] denote the corresponding deterministic limit of J_N,M_N(sqrt(lambda)*Sigma_N,sqrt(lambda)*Sigma_N+Z_N), in precisely this N*M normalization. Then for almost every singular-value sequence, F_N(lambda)->(lambda*alpha/2)*integral x^2 dmu(x)-J_alpha[mu_lambda,mu_lambda rectangular-free-plus_alpha nu_alpha]. This is the auxiliary quenched fixed-spectrum free energy in Section5.6.1, not an assertion that the original prior has iid singular values. Bounded support gives the bounded empirical second moments of source Assumption3. The source calls nu_alpha the Marchenko-Pastur law; here it is explicitly the nonnegative singular-value law, rather than confusing it with the law of squared singular values. No atomic, divergent-log-energy or unbounded-support extension is asserted.
N<=M_N, N/M_N->alpha in (0,1], fixed lambda>0; normalized real orthogonal Haar measures.
Nonnegative iid auxiliary singular values from a compactly supported density; finite symmetrized logarithmic energy and logarithmic moment.
Signal orientations, posterior candidate orientations, and centered Gaussian noise follow the matched fixed-spectrum model explicitly defined above; noise variance1/N.

[Lemma lem:strictly-perturbed-compactness of arXiv:2609.00556, 'Higgs--Demailly System and Positivity of Higgs Bundles'] Fix \(0<\gamma<1\).  Let
\[
 c_j\in C^{0,\gamma}(M,\mathbb R),
 \qquad
 F_j\in C^{0,\gamma}(M,\operatorname{End} E),
\]
and suppose that, for some constants \(c_-,c_+,C_0>0\),
\[
 0<c_-\leq c_j\leq c_+,
 \qquad
 \|c_j\|_{C^{0,\gamma}}
 +\|F_j\|_{C^{0,\gamma}}
 \leq C_0.
\]
Let \(g_j>0\) be \(h_{\rm ref}\)-Hermitian endomorphisms satisfying
\(\det g_j=1\) and
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 &\sqrt{-1}\Lambda_\omega
 \left(
  \bar\partial(g_j^{-1}\partial^{h_{\rm ref}}g_j)
  +[\theta,
    g_j^{-1}\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*g_j
    -\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*]
 \right)\\
 &\hspace{45mm}
 +c_j\log g_j=F_j.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
If
\[
 \|\log g_j\|_{C^0}\leq L,
\]
then
\[
 \|g_j\|_{C^{2,\gamma}}\leq C,
\]
where \(C\) depends only on the fixed background data,

body: Let K be a number field of degree n over the rationals, with r1 real embeddings and r2 pairs of complex conjugate embeddings, so n = r1 + 2 r2, and let O_K be its ring of integers. Dirichlet's unit theorem states the unit group of O_K, the elements with a multiplicative inverse in O_K, is isomorphic to the direct product of a finite cyclic group of roots of unity in K and a free abelian group of rank r1 + r2 - 1. Real quadratic fields thus have unit rank 1, generated modulo torsion by a fundamental unit, while imaginary quadratic fields have unit rank 0. Proved by Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet in 1846.
title: Dirichlet's unit theorem

body:
[Lemma lem:N(D) of arXiv:2607.01946, 'Second-order fluctuations for a phase transition in random partitions'] Suppose $\alpha\in(0,1),\theta = 0$. Then, 
\[
P_j^\downarrow = \pp{\frac{S_\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}}^{1/\alpha}\Gamma_j^{-1/\alpha} = \frac{\Gamma_j^{-1/\alpha}}{\sif \ell1 \Gamma_\ell^{-1/\alpha}},
\]
where $(\Gamma_j)_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$ is a sequence of arrival times of a standard Poisson process $(N(t))_{t\ge 0}$ (i.e., $N(t):=\max\{j\in{\mathbb N}:\Gamma_j\le t\}$). Then, 
\[
\nu(t) = N(Dt^\alpha) \quad\mbox{ with }\quad D := \frac{S_\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} = \pp{\sif\ell1\Gamma_\ell^{-1/\alpha}}^{-\alpha}.
\]
We have
\begin{equation}
\pp{\frac{ N(Dn t) - Dnt}{n^{1/2}}}_{t\in[0,\infty)}\Rightarrow \pp{{\mathbb B}_{Dt}}_{t\in[0,\infty)},
\end{equation}
in $D[0,\infty)$ as $n\to\infty$, where in the limit the Brownian motion ${\mathbb B}$ is independent of $D$.

body: Every strictly stationary phi-mixing Markov chain on a standard Borel space is interlaced rho-mixing, with rho*(n) <= min{1, 2 sqrt(2 phi(n))} and, for phi(n) <= 1/4, rho*(n) <= 2 sqrt(2 phi(n) (1 - 2 phi(n))). Route: a phi(n) bound puts every n-step transition row within phi of the marginal (row diameter 2 phi); the chi-square SDPI-versus-Dobrushin bound gives a robust channel coefficient kappa <= sqrt(2 phi) uniformly in the input law; merging same-colour observation times into alternating blocks makes the prefix-conditioned correlation matrix of Peyre's tensorization kappa times a path's bipartite adjacency (adjacent blocks keep their kernel, non-adjacent blocks decorrelate through a Markov separator); Peyre's N-against-M theorem gives ||E|| ^ 1 <= 2 kappa and the Z-against-Z theorem the arcsine bound; a finite-coordinate martingale approximation extends to infinite index sets. The reset chain P(i,0) = 1-q, P(i,i+1) = q is exponentially phi-mixing with psi'(n) = 0 for every n, so Bradley's 1997 lower-psi criterion does not cover it.

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2606.11068, '2606.11068'] Let \(G\) be positive, nonincreasing, and regularly varying at infinity with
index \(-\theta\), where \(\theta>0\). Then
\[
  \frac{\E[G(\tau_n^*)]}{G(n)}
  \longrightarrow
  v^\theta.
\]
If \(r>1/2\), then also
\[
  \frac{\E[G(\tau_n^+)]}{G(n)}
  \longrightarrow
  (2r-1)^\theta.
\]
If \(r<1/2\), then
\[
  \frac{\E[G(\tau_n^-)]}{G(n)}
  \longrightarrow
  (1-2r)^\theta.
\]

[Proposition c:clthardcore of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a  stationary process on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with summable exponential mixing correlations as in Definition (def.A2 of the paper) and having bounded Palm intensity functions as at ~(equation bdedreduced of the paper). Let \(\Psi = \Psi(\sim, \cdot)\) be a stabilizing interaction graph on \(\mathcal{P}\)
 and  satisfying the following a.s. connective constant bound: there exists $\Delta  \in [1,\infty)$ and $m_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all sets $B\in\mathcal{B}_b(r_0,n_0)$ with defined in~(equation e.particular-sets of the paper), $x\in\mathcal{P}\cap B$, and $m\ge m_0$ 
\begin{equation}
N(x, m; \Psi(\mathcal{P}\cap B)) \le\Delta^m.
\end{equation}
Consider the hard-core Gibbs model~(equation eqn:re-hardcore of the paper) with activity parameter \(\lambda\) such that 
\[
\lambda < \lambda_c(\Delta), 
\]
where the critical value \(\lambda_c(\Delta)\) is at ~(equation e.hc-critical-lambda of the paper). Under these conditions, the spin configuration \\
\( \{V_x(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n))\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n} \) satisfies the CLT as stated in Theorem~(spinmain of the paper), provided that the 
variance condition there is also satisfied.

body:
Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(A) Poincaré–Friedrichs inequality (zero boundary values). Suppose Ω is bounded in one direction: Ω ⊂ {x : a < x_1 < a + d} for some a and some finite d (in particular any bounded Ω, with d = diam Ω). Then for every u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω)
   ||u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∂_1 u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}.
For p = 2 the sharp constant for a slab of width d is d/π: ||u||_{L^2} ≤ (d/π)||∇u||_{L^2} for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω). NO regularity of ∂Ω is required and Ω need not be connected. Consequently ||∇u||_{L^p} is a norm on W^{1,p}_0(Ω) equivalent to the full W^{1,p} norm, the Dirichlet form ∫|∇u|^2 is coercive on H^1_0(Ω), and for bounded Ω the best constant C_P in ||u||_2 ≤ C_P||∇u||_2 satisfies 1/C_P^2 = λ_1(Ω), the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of −Δ.

(B) Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality (mean-zero functions). Suppose Ω is bounded, connected, and has Lipschitz boundary (or is bounded, connected and convex; more generally a bounded connected W^{1,p}-extension domain). Then there is C = C(Ω, p) with
   ||u − u_Ω||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ C ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}  for all u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω),  u_Ω = (1/|Ω|) ∫_Ω u dx.
For convex Ω and p = 2 the sharp constant is diam(Ω)/π (Payne–Weinberger). Consequently u ↦ ||∇u||_{L^p} + |∫_Ω u| is a norm on W^{1,p}(Ω) equivalent to the W^{1,p} norm, and the Neumann problem is coercive on the mean-zero subspace.

Where it fails. (A) fails without zero boundary values: constants lie in W^{1,p}(Ω) with zero gradient. (A) fails on any domain containing balls of arbitrarily large radius (R^n, half-spaces, exterior domains): dilating one test function shows no constant works. (B) fails for disconnected Ω (a function equal to different constants on two components). (B) fails on some bounded connected domains with bad boundary (rooms-and-passages domains, sufficiently sharp outward cusps), where functions that are ≈0 in one part and ≈1 in another can have arbitrarily small gradient energy; Lipschitz boundary rules this out. In (B) the constant depends on Ω and blows up as the domain degenerates (e.g. a thin neck).
1 ≤ p < ∞
(A): u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω), Ω contained in a slab of finite width d (no boundary regularity needed)
(B): Ω bounded, connected, Lipschitz boundary (or convex), u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω)

[Definition 1 (Entropy, relative entropy, and mutual information) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] All entropies in this paper are differential entropies with respect to the
Lebesgue measure on the affine span of the relevant polytope or cone.  If
\(p\) is a probability density, we write
\[
\ent(p):=-\int p(x)\log p(x)\,dx.
\]
If \(X\) has density \(p_X\), we also write \(\ent(X)=\ent(p_X)\).  For two
random variables \(X,Y\) with joint density \(p_{X,Y}\) and conditional
density \(p_{X\mid Y=y}\), the conditional entropy is
\[
\ent(X\mid Y)
:=
\mathbb E\bigl[\ent(p_{X\mid Y})\bigr]
=
-\int p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log p_{X\mid Y=y}(x)\,dx\,dy,
\]
whenever the conditional densities exist and the integral is well-defined.  For two
probability densities \(q,p\) on the same space, the relative entropy is
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)
:=
\int q(x)\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\,dx,
\]
with the usual convention that it is \(+\infty\) unless \(q\) is absolutely
continuous with respect to \(p\).  For random variables \(X,Y\), their mutual
information is
\[
I(X;Y):=
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(X,Y)\|
\operatorname{Law}(X)\otimes\operatorname{Law}(Y)\bigr).
\]
When the relevant conditional densities exist, this is equivalently
\[
I(X;Y)=\ent(X)-\ent(X\mid Y).
\]
title: Entropy, relative entropy, and mutual information

[Proposition 60 of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] Let $X$ and $(X_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be random elements on a metric space $(S,\rho)$.
	If there exists a sequence $\Big\{\big(X^k,(X^k_n)_{n\ge 1}\big):k\ge 1\Big\}$ of couplings of $X$ and $(X_n)_{n\ge 1}$ satisfying that for each $\varepsilon>0$,
	\begin{align}		\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\p\Big(\rho(X^k,X^k_n)>\varepsilon\Big)=0,
	\end{align}
	then $X_n\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}X$.

Let H be a complex Hilbert space (inner product linear in the first slot) and T: D(T) ⊂ H → H linear and densely defined. The adjoint T* has domain D(T*) = {y ∈ H : x ↦ ⟨Tx, y⟩ is bounded on D(T)}, and for y ∈ D(T*), T*y is the unique z ∈ H with ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, z⟩ for all x ∈ D(T) (uniqueness uses density of D(T); without density T* is not a well-defined operator). T is symmetric (Hermitian) if it is densely defined and ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ for all x, y ∈ D(T), i.e. T ⊂ T*. T is self-adjoint if T = T*, which includes the equality of domains D(T) = D(T*). T is essentially self-adjoint if it is symmetric and its closure T̄ is self-adjoint (equivalently, T is symmetric and has exactly one self-adjoint extension). For a closed symmetric T the deficiency subspaces are K_+ = ker(T* − i) = Ran(T + i)^⊥ and K_- = ker(T* + i) = Ran(T − i)^⊥, and the deficiency indices are n_± = dim K_± ∈ {0, 1, 2, ..., ∞}. A symmetric T is bounded below (semibounded) with bound c ∈ ℝ if ⟨Tx, x⟩ ≥ c‖x‖² for all x ∈ D(T); positive if c = 0 works. For symmetric T one always has T ⊂ T̄ ⊂ T* and T̄ = T**.
H is a complex Hilbert space
T is densely defined (needed for T* to be an operator)
title: Adjoint, Symmetric, Self-Adjoint and Essentially Self-Adjoint Operators

[Definition 17 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] \textbf{(Invariant GW trees)} Let $\nu$ be a supercritical offspring distribution whose mean is denoted by 
$\mathtt m_\nu$. 
Let $(\bT, \boo)$ be $\obbT^\bullet$-valued r.v.~It is distributed as an  
\emph{invariant GW($\nu$)-tree} if for all bounded Borel measurable function $F$ on $\obbT^\bullet$,
\begin{equation}

\bE \big[ F \big(\bT, \boo \big)\big]= \bE \Big[ \tfrac{\mathtt m_\nu + k_{\boo^\prime} (\bT^\prime) }{2\mathtt m_\nu  }F\big(\bT^\prime, \boo^\prime \big) \Big], 
\end{equation}
where $(\bT^\prime, \boo^\prime)$ is distributed as an infinite  GW($\nu$)-tree as in Definition \ref{GWptdef}. \cq
title: Definition 17 of arXiv:2605.02430

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.02771, 'Universality in Deep Neural Networks:\\ An approach via the Lindeberg exchange principle'] Let \(z^{(L+1)}\) and \(\tilde z^{(L+1)}\) be two DNNs in the sense of \textbf{Definition \ref{def:Deep_Neural_Network}}, with the same widths, with zero biases, and with an activation function \(\sigma\in C^{3\cdot2^{L-1}}_b\). Assume that the weights in \(z^{(L+1)}\) satisfy \textbf{Assumption \ref{assum:weights}} and \(\tilde z^{(L+1)}\) has Gaussian weights with matching first and second moments. Then
    \[
        \Bigl|\E[F(z^{(L+1)}(x))]-\E[F(\tilde z^{(L+1)}(x))]\Bigr|
        \leq C
        \sum_{k=1}^{L}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{k}}},
    \]
    for all \(F\in C^{3\cdot 2^{L-1}}_b(\R^{n_{L+1}})\).
    If the DNNs \(z^{(L+1)}\), \(\tilde z^{(L+1)}\) also have the same biases satisfying \textbf{Assumption \ref{assum:biases}}, and an activation function \(\sigma\in C^{3}_b(\R)\), then the same bound is true for all \(F\in L^\infty(\R^{n_{L+1}})\) with a  constant of the form \(C(L,n_{L+1,\sigma})\|F\|_{\infty}\). If instead, \(F\in C^1_b(\R^{n_{L+1}})\), the constant is of the form \(C(L,n_{L+1}, \sigma)\|\nabla F\|_{\infty}\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.02771

[Proposition LPprop of arXiv:2609.02213, 'Invariant subspaces for free linearizations of Lipschitz maps'] Let $f:M\to M$ be a Lipschitz map, let $e\in M$, and set $T=T_{f,e}$. Define
		$$
		\mathcal U:=\{\gamma\in\mathcal{F}(M,e):(T^n\gamma)_n\text{ has a w-convergent subsequence with non-zero limit}\}.
		$$
		If $\mathrm{int}(\mathcal U)\neq\emptyset$, then for every finite subset $S\subset M$ there exists an increasing sequence $(n_k)_k\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $(f^{n_k}(x))_k$ converges for every $x\in S$. In particular, $\mathcal U$ is dense in $\mathcal{F}(M,e)$.

[Defn weak_sol_Volterra clock of arXiv:2605.29073, 'Volterra clocks and their pure-jump limits: \\hitting times of curved boundaries'] We say that $(W\,, X)$ is a weak solution to (equation eq:Volterra_clock of the paper) on $[0\,,T]$ for the input $(G_0\,, K\,, f\,,\lambda\,, \nu)$ if there exists a filtered probability space $\left( \Omega\,, \mathcal F\,, (\mathcal G_t)_{t \geq 0}\,, \mathbb P\right)$ supporting a $(\mathcal G_t)_{t \geq 0}$-Brownian motion $W\,$, and a non-decreasing continuous process $(X_t)_{t \leq T}\,$, starting from $0\,$, such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item For every $t\in[0,T]\,$, $f(X_t)$ is a $(\mathcal G_t)_{t \geq 0}$-stopping time.
    \item $(W_{f(X_t)})_{t\leq T}$ is a martingale with respect to its own filtration.
    \item The Volterra equation (equation eq:Volterra_clock of the paper) holds $\mathbb P$-almost surely on $[0\,,T]\,$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Defn weak_sol_Volterra clock of arXiv:2605.29073

body: In mathematical logic, Goodstein's theorem is a statement about the natural numbers, proved by Reuben Goodstein in 1944, which states that every Goodstein sequence eventually terminates at 0. Laurence Kirby and Jeff Paris showed in 1982 that Goodstein's theorem is unprovable in Peano arithmetic. This was the third example of a true statement about natural numbers that is unprovable in Peano arithmetic, after the examples provided by Gödel's incompleteness theorem and Gerhard Gentzen's 1943 direct proof of the unprovability of ε0-induction in Peano arithmetic. The Paris–Harrington theorem gave another example.
title: Goodstein's theorem

[Definition def:constant-escape-coupling of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence~$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, $\lambda\in (0,1)$, 
and a high-level state $\Psi=(g,\tau',j,\overline{z},\mathcal{S},\textup{type})$.
Fix a (possibly random) tuple $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(\tau')$ of
disjoint sets
$\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(\tau') = (\mathbf{arr}_1^E(\tau'),\mathbf{arr}_2^E(\tau'),\ldots)$
where each $ \mathbf{arr}^E_{i}(\tau')\subseteq \mathcal{B}(\tau')$ and, 
for $i>j$, $\mathbf{arr}_i^E(\tau') = \emptyset$. 
Let $E$ be an escape process
with 
high-level state $\Psi$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, birth rate~$\lambda$, and
initial population $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(\tau')$.
Fix an integer  $\tau \ge \tau'$ and 
a real number $\nu \ge 0$. 
Let $\newsym{T-E-nu}{Decoupling time of a constant-escape process with start time $\tau$ and arrival rate $\nu$ from its parent escape process $E$}{T^E_{\nu,\tau}}$ be the first time $t \ge \tau$ such that $\nu^E(t) > \nu$. 
For all $i\geq 1$, let $\mathbf{arr}_i^{E^+}(\tau) = \mathbf{b}_i^E(\tau)$.
There is a constant-escape process~$E^+$ on~$[j]$ with
send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$, end-of-step arrival rate~$\nu$  
and and initial population $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{E^+}(\tau)$
such that there is a coupling satisfying the following invariants for every $i\geq 1$.
\begin{description}  
\item  [Inv-$\mathbf{b}_i(t)$:] For all $t$ with $\tau \le t \le T_{\nu,\tau}^E$, $\mathbf{b}_i^{E}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{b}_i^{E^+}(t)$.
\item  [Inv-$\mathbf{B}_i(t)$:] For all $t$ with $\tau+1 \le t \le T_{\nu,\tau}^E$, $\mathbf{B}_i^{E}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{B}_i^{E^+}(t)$.
\item [Inv-$\mathbf{s}_i(t)$:] For all $t$ with $\tau+1 \le t \le T_{\nu,\tau}^E$, $\mathbf{s}_i^{E}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{s}_i^{E^+}(t)$.
\end{description}
We refer to this coupling as the \emph{constant-escape coupling} of~$E$ with~$E^+$. 
The coupling is defined as follows. By construction, for every $i\geq 1$,
$\mathbf{b}_i^{E}(\tau) = \mathbf{b}_i^{E^+}(\tau)$ (these are empty for $i>j$). Thus, 
$\mathrm{Inv}$-$\mathbf{b}_i(\tau)$ is satisfied for every $i\geq 1$.

For integer~$t>\tau$, the coupling evolves as follows.
If $t > T^E_{\nu,\tau}$ then $E$ and $E^+$ evolve independently at time $t$.
If $t\leq T^E_{\nu,\tau}$ then
$\nu^E(t-1) \leq \nu$ and the coupling proceeds as follows.
For all $i\geq 0$, 
$\mathbf{B}_i^{E^+}(t)= \mathbf{b}_i^{E^+}(t-1)$ and 
$\mathbf{B}_i^{E}(t) = \mathbf{b}_i^{E}(t-1)$. By $\mathrm{Inv}$-$\mathbf{b}_i(t-1)$, we get $\mathrm{Inv}$-$\mathbf{B}_i(t)$.
For every $i\geq 0$, $\mathbf{s}^{E}_i(t)$ is determined 
by taking each element of $\mathbf{B}_i^{E}(t)$ independently with probability~$p_i$.
We define $\mathbf{S}^{E^+}_i(t)$ to be the random set formed by including each ball in 
$\mathbf{B}_i^{E^+}(t) \setminus \mathbf{B}_i^{E}(t)$ 
independently with probability~$p_i$, then take $\mathbf{s}^{E^+}_i(t) = \mathbf{S}^{E^+}_i(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{E}_i(t)$ to establish $\mathrm{Inv}$-$\mathbf{s}_i(t)$.
By the definitions, for all $i\in [j-1]$, $\mathbf{e}_i^{E}(t) = \mathbf{e}_i^{E^+}(t) = \emptyset$ and for all $i\geq j$, $\mathbf{e}_i^{E^+}(t) = \mathbf{s}_i^{E^+}(t)$ and
$\mathbf{e}_i^E(t) = \mathbf{s}_i^E(t)$.

We next define $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(t)$ and $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{E^+}(t)$. For each $i\in [j]$ independently,
\begin{itemize}
\item  with probability $\nu^E(t-1)$,
$\mathrm{arr}_i^E(t) = \mathrm{arr}_i^{E^+}(t) = 1$.
In this case, let $\mathbf{arr}_i^{E^+}(t) = \mathbf{arr}_i^E(t)$.
\item with probability $\nu - \nu^E(t-1)$,
$\mathbf{arr}_i^E(t)=\emptyset$ and $\mathrm{arr}_i^{E^+}(t)=1$.
\item with probability $1-\nu$, 
$\mathbf{arr}_i^E(t) = \mathbf{arr}_i^{E^+}(t) = \emptyset$.
\end{itemize}

body:
[Thm Free measure of arXiv:2411.13465, 'Height-offset variables and pinning at infinity for gradient Gibbs measures on trees'] \mbox{}\\
Let $Q: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow (0,\infty)$ be any positive symmetric transfer operator of gradient type such that $\sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}}j^2 Q(j) < \infty$.
Then the following holds true for the corresponding free state $\nu$ on the Cayley tree of order $d \geq 2$.
 \begin{itemize}
	\item[a)]\textbf{Existence.}\hypertarget{res: existence free}{} Let $(H_r)_{r \in \mathbb{N}}$ be as in Definition (def: SphericalAverage of the paper). Then $H:=\lim_{r \rightarrow \infty}H_r$ is a height-offset variable for $\nu$ in the sense of Definition (def: HeightOffset of the paper), where the limit holds almost surely and in $\mathcal{L}^2$ with respect to the same measure $\nu  \circ \left(\sigma^{\rho,0} \right)^{-1}$. In particular, the measure $\mu^H$ associated with $H$ and $\nu$ via Theorem (thm: DLR of the paper) is a proper Gibbs measure on the space of height configurations.
 \item[b1)]\textbf{Regularity of density of HOV.}\hypertarget{res: regularity density free}{} The corresponding distribution of $H^{\rho,0}$ obtained from Definition (def: SphericalAverage of the paper) under $\nu$ has an infinitely often differentiable Lebesgue-density $f_{H^{\rho,0}}$.\\
 Moreover, $f_{H^{\rho,0}}$ is strictly positive on $\mathbb{R}$.
 \item[b2)]\textbf{Localization of single-site marginal of pinned measure.}\hypertarget{res: localization free}{} Assume furthermore on the interaction $Q$ that there is some $R>0$ such that the moment generating function for a single gradient variable, $t \mapsto \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}\exp(tj)\frac{Q(j)}{\Vert Q \Vert_1}$ is finite for $t \in (-R,+R)$. \\
 Then, for every $A < (d+1)R$ there exists a $B(A) \in (0,\infty)$ such that the single-site marginal at the root satisfies the following exponential concentration:
 \[\mu^H(\vert \sigma_\rho \vert \geq s) \leq B(A)\exp(-As), \quad \text{for every } s \in \mathbb{N}.\]
  \item[c1)]\textbf{Peculiarity 1.}\hypertarget{res: peculiarity 1 free}{} The lifted measure Gibbs $\mu^H$ is necessarily not invariant under the translations of the tree.
 \item[c2)]\textbf{Peculiarity 2.}\hypertarget{res: peculiarity 2 free}{} The measure $\mu^H$ is not a tree-indexed Markov chain and in particular not extreme in the set of all Gibbs measures for the specification associated with $Q$ via (equation eq: GibbsSpecification of the paper).
 \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Pinning at infinity of the free gradient state: existence, regularity of density, loss of translation invariance and of Markov property

body:
[Defi Def:partition of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] For the positive integers $ \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_+ $ and the invertible elements $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_m \in \kappa^\times $,
 	we define: 
 	
 	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
 	\item 
 	For $ \alpha, \beta \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $ 
 	we say that 
 	$ (\ell_\alpha, \lambda_\alpha) $ and $ (\ell_\beta, \lambda_\beta) $ 
 	are {\em compatible}
 	if 
 	$ \alpha = \beta $ or if the following conditions hold:
 	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
 		\item
 		$ \ell_\alpha = 2 k_\alpha - 1 $ and $\ell_\beta = 2 k_\beta - 1  $ are both odd, 
 		for $ k_\alpha, k_\beta \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_+ $
 		and
 		
 		\item
 		$ \lambda_\alpha (-1)^{k_\alpha} = \lambda_\beta (-1)^{k_\beta}  $. 
 	\end{enumerate}
 
	\item 
	For $ \alpha \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $,
	we define 
	\[
		I_\alpha := 
		\{
			\beta \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \}
			\mid 
			 (\ell_\alpha, \lambda_\alpha) 
			\mbox{ and }
			(\ell_\beta, \lambda_\beta) 
			\mbox{ are compatible} 
			\,
		\}

	\]
	and $ \sigma(I_\alpha) := \inf\{ \beta \in I_\alpha \}  $.
	Note that $ I_{\sigma(I_\alpha)} = I_\alpha $ if $ I_\alpha \neq \emptyset $.
 	
 	\item
 	Define $ \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_s \in \{1, \ldots, m \} $ 
 	via:
 		for all $ \alpha \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $ with $ |I_{\alpha}| \geq 2 $ there is a unique $ \alpha_i $ with 
 		$ \alpha_i = \sigma(I_\alpha) $.
 	Moreover, we set $ I_0 := \{ 1, \ldots, m \} \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^s I_{\alpha_i} $. 
 	Hence, this defines a partition of the index set into disjoint subsets:
 	\[
	 	\{ 1 , \ldots , m \}  = I_0 \cup I_{\alpha_1} \cup \cdots \cup I_{\alpha_s}
	 	\ .
 	\]
 \end{enumerate}
title: Defi Def:partition of arXiv:2609.01501

[Definition 12 ($n$-good) of arXiv:2506.09609, 'Schramm-Loewner evolution contains a topological Sierpi\'nski carpet when $\kappa$ is clos'] We say that the origin is \textbf{$0$-good} if for any $u,v \in (-3/4, 3/4)^2$, the flow lines $\eta^L(u)$ and $\eta^R(v)$ do not intersect after leaving $B(u, \epsilon)$ and $B(v, \epsilon)$, respectively. More precisely, let $\tau_u$ denote the first exit time of $\eta^L(u)$ from $B(u, \epsilon)$, and let $\tau_v$ denote the first exit time of $\eta^R(v)$ from $B(v, \epsilon)$. The $0$-good property requires that $\eta^L(u)|_{[\tau_u,\infty)}$ and $\eta^R(v)|_{[\tau_v,\infty)}$ are disjoint for any $u,v \in (-3/4,3/4)^2$. Note that $u$ and $v$ are not necessarily different. Otherwise, we say the origin is \textbf{$0$-bad}.

For an integer $n \geq 1$ and $x \in \epsilon^n \mathbb{Z}^2 \cap (-3/4,3/4)^2$, we say that $x$ is \textbf{$n$-good} if for any $u,v \in B(x, 3 \epsilon^n)$, the flow lines $\eta^L(u)$ and $\eta^R(v)$ do not intersect after first leaving $B(u, \epsilon^{n+1})$ and $B(v, \epsilon^{n+1})$, respectively, and before leaving $B(x, 4 \epsilon^n)$. Otherwise, we say that $x$ is \textbf{$n$-bad}.
title: $n$-good

\thetag{i} 
Let $ \{ (\E ^n, \mathscr{D}^n) \}_{n\in\N } $ be an increasing sequence of non-negative symmetric closed bilinear forms on $\Lnu $.

\begin{align}	\notag &
\E ^{\infty } (f,f) = \limi{n} \E ^n (f,f) , 
\quad 
\mathscr{D}^{\infty} =
 \{ f \in \bigcap_{n \in\N } \mathscr{D}^n \, ;\, \limi{n} \E ^n (f,f) < \infty \}

It holds that $ (\E ^{\infty}, \mathscr{D}^{\infty} )$ is a closed symmetric bilinear form on $ \Lnu $. 
$ \{ (\E ^n, \mathscr{D}^n) \}_{n\in\N } $ converges to $ (\E ^{\infty}, \mathscr{D}^{\infty} )$ in the strong resolvent sense on $ \Lnu $.

[Thm RT of arXiv:2603.15323, '\Large \bf Small-time heat decay for stable processes on fractal drums'] Suppose that a map $f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$ satisfies the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) with
\[
\lim_{z\to-\infty}f(z)=0,
\]
and 
\[
|\phi(z)|\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}|z|}, \quad z\in {\mathbb R},
\]
for some constants $c_1,c_2>0$. Then, the solution of the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) is given by
\[
f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}L^{n}\phi(z)=\phi(z)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i_1,\cdots, i_n} 
c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_n}L_{\gamma_{i_1}}\cdots L_{\gamma_{i_{n}}}\phi(z),
\]
where $i_1,\cdots, i_n$ take values from 1 to $N$ and are not necessarily different.
Furthermore, if $\{\gamma_{j}\}$ is non-arithmetic, then 
$$
f(z)=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_{j}\gamma_{j}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(x)dx +o(1) \text{ as } z\to\infty.
$$ 
If $\{\gamma_{j}\}$ is arithmetic with span $\gamma$, then
$$
f(z)=\frac{\gamma}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_{j}\gamma_{j}}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(z-k\gamma) +o(1) \text{ as } z\to\infty.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$q(x,y)$ and total exit rate
\[
\Lambda(x):=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y).

Suppose Assumption~(ass:standing of the paper) holds. Then
\begin{equation}
\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\,\Lambda(x)=\mathbb{E}_\pi[\Lambda(X)]<\infty.
\end{equation}

[Definition 48 (Raw factor feedback) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] For a common graded module $M$, write $A=P_Mx$, $r=P_{M^\perp}x$.  For each input
weight $q$, let $\widehat Y_q$ be the branch-labeled direct sum of unsymmetrized
contraction output spaces and set
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\Lambda_q h
 =
 \left(
 r_{a,p}\otimes_s P_{M_q^\perp}h
 \right)_{\substack{a,p,s\\1\le s\le p\wedge q\$p,q,s)\ne(q,q,q)}}
 \oplus
 \left(
 A_{a,p}\otimes_s P_{M_q^\perp}h
 \right)_{\substack{a,p,s\\1\le s\le p\wedge q}} .
 
\end{equation}
All indices and contraction orders are separate orthogonal branch labels.  Put
\begin{equation}
 \widehat N_q=\widehat\Lambda_q^*\widehat\Lambda_q,
 \qquad
 \widehat{\mathfrak H}_Q(A,r)
 =
 \sum_{b,q}
 \ip{r_{b,q}}{\widehat N_qr_{b,q}}.
 
\end{equation}
The omitted residual branch is precisely total covariance; total mixed contractions vanish
by the grade-wise orthogonality of the active and residual modules.
title: Raw factor feedback

\[\be^{\eps}_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)

\be^{\eps}_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^0).\]

\[\ga_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
\ga_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^0).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2511.06414, 'Non-uniform Edgeworth expansions for weakly dependent random variables and their applicati'] Let Assumptions \ref{GrowAssum} and \ref{DerAss} hold with the same $m$. Then 
 there are polynomials $H_{j,n}$ with bounded coefficients whose degrees do not depend on $n$ so that with 
\begin{equation}
\Psi_{r,n}(x)=\Phi(x)+\varphi(x)\sum_{j=1}^{r}B_n^{-j}H_{j,n}(x)
\end{equation}
for all $r=1,2,...,m-2$ and $x\in\bbR$ we have\footnote{Namely, the non-uniform Edgeworth expansion or order $r$ and power $m$ holds true.}
$$
\left|F_n(x)-\Psi_{r,n}(x)\right|\leq C_nB_n^{-r}(1+|x|)^{-m}, \,C_n\to 0.
$$
In particular, for all $p>1/m$, 
$$
\left\|F_n-\Psi_{k,n}\right\|_{L^p(dx)}=o(\sig_n^{-k}).
$$
The coefficients of the polynomials are polynomial functions of $A_n$, $B_n-\sig_n$ and $\Lambda_n^{(j)}(0)\sig_n^{(j-2)}$ for $j\geq3$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2511.06414

Then, after exposing row $n-j+1$,

   \,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{n-j}
 \right)
 \geq1-C_0n^{-c_0}.
\end{equation}

body:
[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2609.03506, 'Divergence of decreasing rearranged Fourier series\\ on every infinite compact abelian gro'] Let \(q:G\to H\) be a continuous surjective homomorphism of compact
Hausdorff abelian groups. For \(f\in C(H)\),
\[
 \widehat{f\circ q}(\gamma)=
 \begin{cases}
 \widehat f(\lambda),&\gamma=\lambda\circ q,\quad\lambda\in\widehat H,\\
 0,&\gamma\text{ is nontrivial on }\ker q.
 \end{cases}
\]
These alternatives exhaust \(\widehat G\), and the descending
character is unique. Consequently
\[
 T_\delta^G(f\circ q)=(T_\delta^Hf)\circ q.
\]
Property \(\B(H)\) implies \(\B(G)\), and \(f\in\D(H)\) implies
\(f\circ q\in\D(G)\).

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2609.00867, '2609.00867'] In addition to Assumption~\ref{ass:kernel-density}, assume that \(\rho\) is
bounded below by a positive constant almost everywhere on some ball
\(D\subset\mathbb R^d\).
If \(s=0\), there exist \(\beta_0\ge1\) and constants
\(c_{d,\rho,D},C_{d,\rho}\in(0,\infty)\) such that, for every
\(\beta\ge\beta_0\),
\begin{equation}
 c_{d,\rho,D}\beta\log\beta
 \le\log\cZ_{\infty,\rho}(\beta;g_{d,0})
 \le\sup_{N\ge2}\log\cZ_{N,\rho}(\beta;g_{d,0})
 \le C_{d,\rho}\beta\log\beta.
\end{equation}
If \(0<s<d/2\), there exist \(\beta_0\ge1\) and constants
\(c_{d,s,m,\rho,D},C_{d,s,m,\rho}\in(0,\infty)\) such that, for every
\(\beta\ge\beta_0\),
\begin{equation}
 c_{d,s,m,\rho,D}\beta^{d/(d-s)}
 \le\log\cZ_{\infty,\rho}(\beta;g_{d,s}^{(m)})
 \le\sup_{N\ge2}\log\cZ_{N,\rho}(\beta;g_{d,s}^{(m)})
 \le C_{d,s,m,\rho}\beta^{d/(d-s)}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:quantile-mosaic of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $s = p/q$ in lowest terms. The phase
		$\chi(n) = e^{-2\pi in^{2}p/q}$ is periodic in $n$ with period $q$,
		and its discrete Fourier expansion yields the revival
		\begin{equation}
			u_{p/q}(z) = \sum_{r=0}^{q-1}\hat c(r)\,
			u_{0}\Big(z - \frac{2r}{q}\Big),
			\qquad
			\hat c(r) = \frac{1}{q}\sum_{n=0}^{q-1}
			e^{-2\pi i\left(pn^{2} - rn\right)/q},
			
		\end{equation}
		a finite superposition of translated square waves whose
		coefficients are generalized quadratic Gauss
		sums~[berndt1998]. Consequently $w_{p/q}$ is constant on the
		cells of the quantile lattice $\{l/q\}$, and for every law $f$,
		\begin{equation}
			f_{(p/q)\cdot 4/\pi} = w_{p/q}(F)\,f,
			
		\end{equation}
		a histogram reweighting of $f$ on at most $q$ of its own quantile
		cells, of total mass one. In particular the rational-time orbit of
		every law consists of explicitly computable histogram modulations
		of that law.

body: [Theorem ergodic_theorem_third of arXiv:2411.04795, 'Metastable Distributions of Semi-Markov Processes'] Consider a time scale $t= t(\varepsilon)$. If $ E, E' \neq \emptyset $ and $ E \bigcup E' =  \{1, \dots, M'\}$, then for each $i \in E,$ there is a probability measure $\mu(i, \cdot)$ concentrated on $E'$  such that $$ \lim \limits_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \mathbb P \left({ X^{x, \varepsilon}_{t(\varepsilon) } \in S_j }\right) = \mu(i, j)$$ uniformly in $x \in S_i.$  Moreover, if $t_1(\varepsilon) \le t_2(\varepsilon)$ are two time scales associated with the same sets $E$ and $ E'$, then the limit holds uniformly in all time scales $t(\varepsilon)$ satisfying $t_1(\varepsilon) \le t(\varepsilon) \le t_2(\varepsilon)$. body:
Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be $1$-periodic and of bounded variation on $[0,1]$ (hence bounded and integrable, with one-sided limits everywhere). Then for every $x$, $S_Nf(x)\to\frac12\big(f(x^+)+f(x^-)\big)$; in particular $S_Nf(x)\to f(x)$ at every point of continuity. The convergence is uniform on every closed interval on which $f$ is continuous at each point. By Riemann localization the conclusion at a single point $x$ only needs $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ together with bounded variation on some neighbourhood of $x$. Note that near a genuine jump the convergence cannot be uniform: the Gibbs phenomenon produces an overshoot of about $8.95\%$ of the jump on each side.

body:
[Problem prob:modal-cube-local-tabularity of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] Let $L$ be a logic with a language $\mathscr{L}$.
  For $\varphi, \psi \in \mathscr{L}$, let us write $\varphi \equiv_L \psi$ to mean $\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi \in L$, then $\equiv_L$ is clearly an equivalence relation.
  Then, $L$ is said to be \emph{locally tabular} if for any finite $P \subseteq \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}}$,
  the set $T(P) = \set*{ \varphi; \mathrm{V}(\varphi) \subseteq P } / \mathord{\equiv_L}$ is finite.
  For example, $\textbf{Cl}$ is locally tabular, while $\textbf{Int}$ is not.
  Here, it is known by Diego's theorem [diego_sur_1966] that the implicational fragment of $\textbf{Int}$ is locally tabular.
  It is also known that $\textbf{K}X$ ($X \supseteq \set{ \textsf{5} }$) is locally tabular (e.g.\ [CZ97]).
  Now, is the implicational fragment of $L\textbf{K}X$ ($L \in \set{ \textbf{C}, \textbf{W}, \textbf{I} }$, $X \supseteq \set{ \textsf{5} }$) locally tabular? (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Problem prob:modal-cube-local-tabularity of arXiv:2608.29708

[Theorem thm:cltholder of arXiv:2411.08848, 'Stationary random measures: Covariance asymptotics, variance bounds and central limit theo'] (CLT for H\"{o}lder continuous statistics)

Let $\alpha \in [0,1]$. Let ${\mathcal X}$ be a simple  stationary point process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying Assumption (asmpt:integrationofrhokT of the paper). Assume that for all $m \geq 2$ and for all $l_i \in \mathbb{Z}_+, \sum_{i=1}^{m-1} l_i= m$, 

\begin{equation}
    
 \int_{(\mathbb{R}^d)^{m-1}}  \prod\limits_{i=1}^{m-1} |z_{i}|^{\alpha l_i}\; |\kappa_{m-1}|(z_1,\ldots ,z_{m-1}) \, \mathrm{d} z_1\ldots \mathrm{d} z_{m-1} < \infty.
 \end{equation}

Suppose that $f \in C_0^{\alpha}$ and ${\rm Var}[{\mathcal X}_L(f)] \geq CL^{-2\alpha + \varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon,C > 0$.  Then CLT holds for ${\mathcal X}_L(f)$, i.e.,

\[  \frac{{\mathcal X}_L(f) - \mathbb {E} [{\mathcal X}_L(f)]}{\sqrt{{\rm Var}[{\mathcal X}_L(f)]}} \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow} N(0,1).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:cltholder of arXiv:2411.08848

[Theorem 18 of arXiv:2506.15037, '2BSDE with uncertain horizon and application to stochastic control in erratic environments'] Let Assumption \ref{assumption:isaac} be true. Let \((\underline Y, \underline Z, \underline U, \underline K)\) be the unique solution to \eqref{eq:2bsdecontr:-}. Then, the value function of the agent \eqref{value-} is given by
\[
\underline{V_0}(\xi) = \sup_{\alpha \in \mathcal{A}} \inf_{(\mathbb{P}, \beta) \in \mathcal{N}^\alpha} \mathbb{E}^\mathbb{P}[\underline Y_0].
\]

[Theorem main of arXiv:2609.00425, 'Individual and Uniform Eventual Positivity of Self-Adjoint Semigroups'] There exist a real self-adjoint $C_0$-semigroup $(\mathrm{e}^{tA})_{t \geq 0}$ on a Hilbert lattice $H$ and a strictly positive vector $u \in H$ such that the following assertions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[\upshape (i)]
        \item The generator $A$ has compact resolvent.
        \item The semigroup $(\mathrm{e}^{tA})_{t \geq 0}$ is individually eventually strongly positive with respect to $u$.
        \item The operator $\mathrm{e}^{nA}$ is not positive for each sufficiently large $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    In particular, $(\mathrm{e}^{tA})_{t \geq 0}$ is neither uniformly eventually positive nor uniformly eventually positive with respect to $u \otimes u$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:existence of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Under Assumption~(ass:params of the paper), the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \textbf{Well-definedness.}
  For each $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
  $f_n(t,\cdot;H,\alpha) \in L^\alpha(\mathbb{R})$,
  so $X^{(n)}_H(t)$ is a well-defined S$\alpha$S random variable.

\item \textbf{Finite-dimensional distributions.}
  For any $m \in \mathbb{N}^*$, $t_1,\ldots,t_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  and $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$:
  \begin{equation}
  
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
  \exp\!\Bigl(i\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)\Bigr)
  \right]
  = \exp\!\left(
  -\int_\mathbb{R}\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j f_n(t_j,u)\Bigr|^\alpha\,du
  \right).
  \end{equation}

\item \textbf{S$\alpha$S property.}
  For any $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  the linear combination $\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)$
  is S$\alpha$S. In particular, $(X^{(n)}_H(t_1),\ldots,X^{(n)}_H(t_m))$
  is a jointly S$\alpha$S random vector.

\item \textbf{Scale.}
  $\bigl\|X^{(n)}_H(t)\bigr\|_\alpha^\alpha
  = \int_\mathbb{R}|f_n(t,u)|^\alpha\,du < \infty$.

\item \textbf{Higher-order increment stationarity.}
  For $H$ constant ($H(t) \equiv H \in (n-1,n)$), the
  $n$-th order increment process
  \begin{equation}
  
  \Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)
  := \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}X^{(n)}_H(t+kh),
  \quad h \in \mathbb{R},
  \end{equation}
  is stationary in $t$. For functional $H(\cdot)$, the distribution
  of $\Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)$ depends on $t$ only through the
  values $H(t), H(t+h), \ldots, H(t+nh)$.
\end{enumerate}

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Aizenman-Barsky (1987), for Bernoulli percolation on Z^d (and general transitive graphs), work with the magnetisation M(p,h) = P(0 is connected to a ghost vertex attached to every site with probability 1 - e^{-h}) and prove two differential inequalities: M <= h dM/dh + M^2 + p M dM/dp and dM/dp <= |J| M dM/dh (|J| the coordination constant), the first of Simon-Lieb type via the pivotal decomposition, the second from Russo's formula. Integrating them gives: (i) sharpness of the phase transition, i.e. the susceptibility chi(p) is finite for every p < p_c, hence exponential decay of connectivities below p_c; (ii) the mean-field bounds M(p_c,h) >= c h^{1/2} (delta >= 2) and theta(p) >= c (p - p_c) for p > p_c (beta <= 1). What they do NOT prove: continuity of theta at p_c (theta(p_c) = 0 is open for 3 <= d <= 10), or the matching upper bounds beta >= 1, delta <= 2 (those need the triangle condition, i.e. the lace expansion in high dimensions). The same inequalities transfer to the Ising model via the random-current representation (Aizenman-Barsky-Fernandez). Typical failure: Conflating the auxiliary percolation ghost field h with an actual physical parameter of the underlying model, or applying the conclusion theta(p_c)=0 to a percolation variant where FKG fails for the ghost-augmented measure, such as certain dependent percolation models; the entire argument rests on FKG holding for the specific augmented construction, and this needs to be re-verified for each new model rather than assumed to transfer automatically from ordinary Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Aizenman and Barsky, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Aizenman, Kesten and Newman, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics.

body: In functional analysis and related branches of mathematics, the Banach–Alaoglu theorem states that the closed unit ball of the dual space of a normed vector space is compact in the weak* topology. A common proof identifies the unit ball with the weak-* topology as a closed subset of a product of compact sets with the product topology. As a consequence of Tychonoff's theorem, this product, and hence the unit ball within, is compact.
title: Banach–Alaoglu theorem

[Openproblem General anisotropic maximal correlation of arXiv:2609.02155, 'Exact Limits of Random Projections for Preserving Geometry:\\ Distance Recovery, Nearest-N'] \label[openproblem]{op:aniso}
For $D=\sum_i\lambda_iG_i^2$ observed through a rank-$m$ map, determine $\rho_{\mathrm{HGR}}(D;\mathcal{O})$ and the optimizing observation. We solve the problem for commuting projectors with balanced spectral retention in (thm:block-hgr of the paper), which also bounds every commuting block allocation. (thm:counterexample of the paper) shows that an unbalanced allocation can exceed $\sqrt{\alpha_m}$. For a noncommuting map, the observed quadratic form no longer splits along covariance eigenspaces, preventing direct use of the blockwise beta--gamma reduction or its tensorization. The unrestricted problem couples a weighted-gamma conditional-expectation operator with an optimization over row spaces. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2511.04938, 'Uniform dimension theorems for parabolic SPDEs'] Choose and fix some $T>S\ge 0$,
	and let $\{ Z(s\,,y) \}_{(s,y) \in [S,T]\times\T}$ be an $\R^p$-valued
	random field. Recall \eqref{def:rho} and \eqref{E:Z:N} with $\alpha=\frac12$,
	and suppose that:
	\begin{compactenum}[(i)]
	\item The following is finite for some $c,\, \gamma>0$:
		\[
			\mathcal{E}_0:=\E\left[ \exp\left(c\sup
			\left|\frac{\|Z(s\,,y)-Z(s',y')\|}{\rho((s\,,y)\,,(s',y'))\sqrt{\log_+
			(1/\rho((s\,,y)\,,(s',y')))}}\right|^\gamma\right)\right],
		\]
		where the sup is over all distinct points
		$(s\,,y),(s',y')\in[S\,,T]\times\T$;
	\item For every $\delta\in(0\,,1)$, there exist numbers $a,\kappa>0$ such that
		\[
			\P\left\{\mathcal{N}_n^\delta(s\,,B(\nu\,,2^{-n}))
			\ge 2^{an}\right\} \le 2^{-\kappa n^2},
		\]
		uniformly for all $n\in\N$, $s\in[S\,,T]$ and $\nu\in \R^p$.\smallskip
		\end{compactenum}
		Then, for every $\delta\in(0\,,1)$ and $R>0$, there exist 
		$K,L>0$ such that
		\[ 
			\P\left\{ \sup_{s \in [S,T]} \sup_{\nu \in B(0,R)}
			\mathcal{N}_n^\delta(s\,,B(\nu\,,2^{-n})) \ge K2^{an} \right\} \le L^n
			\e^{- n^2/L},
		\]
		uniformly for all $n \in \N$.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.19396, '\bf Penalisation of Two-Dimensional Brownian Motion'] Let $q$ be a nonnegative function from $
\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{R}$, compactly supported and such that its integral on $
\mathbb{C}$ is positive and finite. 
Then, there exists a unique continuous, strictly positive function $\varphi_q$ from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ satisfying the Sturm-Liouville equation $\Delta \varphi_q = q 
\varphi_q$ in the sense of Schwartz distribution, and such that the radial derivative of $\varphi_q$ at $z$ is well-defined for $|z|$ large enough 
and equivalent to $1/(\pi |z|)$ when $|z| \rightarrow \infty$. 
Under the Wiener measure $W^{(2)}$, and for 
$$A_s^{(q)} := \int_0^s q(X_u) du$$
the process 
$$\left( M_s^{(2,q)} = \frac{\varphi_q(X_s)}{
\varphi_q(0)} \exp \left(- \frac{1}{2} A_s^{(q)} \right) 
\right)_{s \geq 0}$$
is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_s)_{s 
\geq 0}$, and there exists a probability measure $W_{\infty}^{(2,q)}$ on 
$\Omega$, such that for all $s \geq 0$, its restriction to the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}_s$ has density 
$ M_s^{(2,q)}$ with respect to $W^{(2)}$. 
Moreover, under $ W_{\infty}^{(2,q)}$, $A_{\infty}^{(q)}$ is almost surely finite, and the $\sigma$-finite measure $
\mathbf{W}^{(2)}$ given by 
$$\mathbf{W}^{(2)} = \varphi_q(0) \exp 
\left( \frac{1}{2} A_{\infty}^{(q)} 
\right) 
\cdot W_{\infty}^{(2,q)} $$ 
does not depend on $q$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let sum a_n be a series of complex numbers. ROOT TEST (Cauchy): put L = limsup |a_n|^{1/n}. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges (the terms do not tend to 0); if L = 1 the test is inconclusive. RATIO TEST (d'Alembert): suppose a_n != 0 for large n. If limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1 the series converges absolutely; if liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| > 1 (in particular if |a_{n+1}/a_n| >= 1 for all large n) it diverges; otherwise the test is inconclusive. Comparison: for every sequence, liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| <= liminf |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n|, so whenever the ratio test decides, the root test decides the same way, and the root test is strictly stronger: for a_n = (1/2)^n for n even and (1/3)^n for n odd, the ratios oscillate between (2/3)^n -> 0 and (3/2)^{n} -> infinity so the ratio test says nothing, while |a_n|^{1/n} takes the values 1/2 and 1/3, limsup 1/2 < 1, and the series converges. Both tests are inconclusive for sum 1/n (divergent) and sum 1/n^2 (convergent), which have L = 1; the radius of convergence of a power series sum c_n z^n is 1 / limsup |c_n|^{1/n} (Cauchy-Hadamard), the root test in its most used form.
complex (or real) terms; the ratio test needs a_n != 0 eventually
limsup and liminf are taken in [0, infinity]; when the limits exist the tests read with the plain limit

body:
[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.27569, 'Laplace and Dolbeault operators on Sasakian manifolds'] On the $\left( 2n+1\right) $-dimensional
Sasakian manifold with Lefschetz operator $L$ and adjoint $\Lambda $ and operator $H$, we have for all positive integers $b$, 
\begin{align*}
[L^{b},H] &= 2bL^{b}, \\
[L^{b},\Lambda] &= (-bH-b(b-1))L^{b-1}.
\end{align*}
As a consequence, the map $L^b:\Omega^m\to \Omega^{m+2}$ is injective for $m\leq n-b$ and $\Lambda^b:\Omega^m\to \Omega^{m-2}$, for $m\geq n+2b$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition def:MST of arXiv:2605.01444, 'From second moments to pairwise negative correlation: \\applications to minimal and unifor'] The \emph{minimal spanning tree} $\mathrm{MST}$ on a finite, connected graph $G=(V,E)$ is defined as follows. Sample i.i.d.~random variables $\{W(e)\colon e\in E \}$ with uniform $(0,1)$ distribution. Let ${\ensuremath{\mathscr T}} (G)$ be the set of spanning trees of $G$; the minimal spanning tree $\mathrm{MST}(G)$ is the unique spanning tree that minimizes the total weight (sum of edge weights) among all trees in ${\ensuremath{\mathscr T}} (G)$. Denote by ${\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} _\mathrm{MST}={\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} _\mathrm{MST}^{(G)}$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathbb E}} _\mathrm{MST}={\ensuremath{\mathbb E}} _\mathrm{MST}^{(G)}$ the law and expectation of $\mathrm{MST}(G)$.

[Lemma lem:gutsclassification of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Assume that \(M\) is atoroidal and \(N\) is a component of \(M-F(z)\) where \(F(z)\) is a facet for \(z\).
Then \(\mathrm{Guts}(N)\) has only one connected component.
If there is a non-product annulus in \(N\), then \(\mathrm{Guts}(N)\) is a 4-ST or a non-longitudinal 2-ST.
If there is no non-product annulus in \(N\), then \(\mathrm{Guts}(N)\) is an acylindrical taut sutured manifold and admits a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric.

Let x_1,...,x_N be deterministic vectors in R^n, with integers N,n>=2, and let eps_1,...,eps_N be independent signs with probabilities1/2 for each of +/-1. Put r=min(N,n), M=max_i||x_i||_2 and H=sum_i x_i x_i^T. There is an absolute constant C such that E_eps||sum_i eps_i x_i x_i^T||_op<=C sqrt(log r) M ||H||_op^(1/2). The logarithm is natural. The N,n>=2 restriction makes the displayed logarithmic factor positive. This is the spectral-norm Rudelson inequality in Vershynin1011.3027v7, Corollary5.28 p19.

Assume that there exists $\alpha_\omega>0$ such that
\begin{equation}

\nu\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2
+

\ge
\alpha_\omega\|v\|_{L^2}^2,
\qquad \forall v\in V.
\end{equation}
Then the semigroup generated by $A_0-D_{K_{\min}}$ on $H$ is exponentially
stable in $L^2$, namely
\[
\|v(t)\|_{L^2}\le e^{-\alpha_\omega t}\|v_0\|_{L^2},
\qquad \forall t\ge0.
\]

body:
[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Let $\xi$ be the point process defined by \eqref{eq:DefXi}, and assume that $\mathbf{L}(\mathbb{Y})<\infty$, {\eqref{eqn:assumption_xS},} \eqref{eqn:assumption_g}, and \eqref{eqn:assumption_f} are satisfied. Let $\zeta$ be a Poisson process on $\mathbb{Y}$ with a finite intensity measure $\mathbf{M}$, and define
\begin{align*}
E_2 & := \frac{2}{(k!)^2} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \mathbbm{1}\{S_{\mathbf{x}}\cap S_{\mathbf{z}}\neq\varnothing\} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}})] \mathbb{E}[g(\mathbf{z},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x}) \\
E_3 & := \frac{2}{(k!)^2} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \mathbbm{1}\{S_{\mathbf{x}}\cap S_{\mathbf{z}}\neq\varnothing\} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) g(\mathbf{z},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x}) \\
E_4 & := \frac{2}{k!} \sum_{\varnothing \subsetneq I \subsetneq \{1,\hdots,k\}} \frac{1}{(k-|I|)!} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^{k-|I|}} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) g((\mathbf{x}_I,\mathbf{z}),\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^{k-|I|}(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x})
\end{align*}
with $(\mathbf{x}_I,\mathbf{z}):=(x_{i_1},\hdots,x_{i_m},z_1,\hdots,z_{k-m})$ for $I=\{i_1,\hdots,i_m\}$.
Then,
$$
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KR}}(\xi,\zeta) \leq \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathbf{L},\mathbf{M}) + E_2 + E_3 + E_4.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Defn defsto of arXiv:2606.24385, 'Gradient Mean-Field Dynamics with Measure-Valued States: Well-Posedness, Chaos, and Long-T'] Given $\phi\in {\mathcal H}_{Q}(L(X,X))$, and $t\in [0,T]$ we consider $T_{\phi}^{t}: X^{\ast}\rightarrow L^{2}(\Omega,{\mathscr{B}},{\mathscr{P}})$, $T_{\phi}^{t}x^{\ast}\coloneqq \int_{0}^{t}\nm{\phi^{\ast}(x^{\ast}),{\rm d} W(s)}$. We call  $T_{\phi}^{t}$ a generalized stochastic integral of the operator-valued random function $\phi$ with respect to $(W(s))_{s\in [0,t]}$ if $T_{\phi}^{t}$ defines a bounded linear operator. Furthermore, we say that $\xi:\Omega \rightarrow X$ is the stochastic integral of $\phi$ (if such an element exists) if $\nm{\xi,x^{\ast}}=T_{\phi}^{t}x^{\ast}$ for all $x\in X^{\ast}$.

Own work draft, proof (unaudited), no independent PASS; classical-method application with novelty unverified. Assume the C012 lower envelope E(alpha,theta)>=sin(theta)/(2*pi*e*alpha) for alpha>=1. If E<=A exp(-c alpha) with A,c>0 at some alpha>=1, then x exp(-x)>=eta for x=c alpha, eta=c sin(theta)/(2*pi*e*A). If eta>1/e this is impossible; if eta=1/e only x=1 works; if 0<eta<1/e, alpha is at most x_plus/c where x_plus>1 is the unique larger root x exp(-x)=eta. For eta<=exp(-2), L=log(1/eta)>=2 gives L+log L<=x_plus<=L+log L+2 log L/L. If A,c stay fixed as theta->0 this is a necessary O(log(1/theta)) upper endpoint. This conditional compatibility theorem does not establish an exponential regime, a matching power law, or the actual crossover point.
C012 retained-budget lower envelope accepted
theta in (0,pi/2], A,c>0
alpha>=1 and the stated exponential UPPER bound actually holds
Root statement requires 0<eta<1/e; eta>=1/e cases handled separately
A,c fixed as theta->0 for the stated logarithmic-scale interpretation

body: The random Schrodinger operator $H=-\Delta+\lambda V$ on $\mathbb Z^d$ with i.i.d. potential $V$ whose single-site law is not a point mass (the localization theorems assume more, e.g. a bounded density); it has localization (pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions) at large disorder and at band edges, while extended states are conjectured for $d\ge3$ at weak disorder; random band matrices interpolate between it and Wigner matrices.

body:
[Lemma lmm:smallest ev of arXiv:2411.10311, 'Planar Novikov-Shubin invariant for adjacency matrices of structured directed dense random'] Let $B_n \in \mathbb{R}^{nK \times nK}$ be a deterministic matrix with $\lVert B_n \rVert \le n^C$ for some constant $C>0$ and let $A_n$ be the adjacency matrix of the DSBM with connection probabilities $P$, where  $P$ has support. Then there are  constants $\widehat C,\alpha,\beta>0$, depending only on $C$ and $P$, such that
\[
\mathbb{P}\pB{\norm{(A_n+B_n)^{-1}}\ge \widehat C\1n^\beta} \le n^{-\alpha}
\]
hold for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

[Proposition 24 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\frac{1}{2}<\gamma_1\leq \gamma_2\leq 1$ and suppose that $v\in C^0([0,1]\times \R^d)$\footnote{We really mean here the usual meaning of $C^0$, that is, bounded continuous, as compared to $\mathcal{C}^0$, which means only bounded.} and $w^1,w^2\in \mathcal{C}^{\gamma_1}([0,1])$ with $w^1_0=w^2_0=0$. For $i=1,2$, let $X^i$ be any solution to
\[X^i_t=y^i+\int_0^t v(s,X_s^i)\,ds+w_t^i,\]
for $y^i\in\R^d$. Then, for any splitting $\mathcal{I}^{X^1}v(t,x)=I^1(t,x)+I^2(t,x)$, there exists a constant $C(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)>0$ such that
\[\|X^1-X^2\|_{\mathcal{C}^{\gamma_1}_t}\leq C\exp\Big(C \big(\|I^1\|_{\mathcal{C}^{\gamma_1}_t \mathcal{C}^1_x}^{1/\gamma_1}\vee \|I^2\|_{\mathcal{C}^{\gamma_2}_t \mathcal{C}^1_x}^{1/\gamma_2}\big)\Big)\big(|y^1-y^2|+\|w^1-w^2\|_{\mathcal{C}^{\gamma_1}_t}\big).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 24 of arXiv:2608.05931

Let M be a q-by-p real matrix, q<=p, of full row rank, whose q positive singular values are pairwise distinct. For any hidden width r>=1, let U be q-by-r, V be p-by-r, and g(U,V)=(1/2)||UV^T-M||F^2. Every local minimum of g is a global minimum over its factor domain. Every nonglobal critical point has a strictly negative Hessian eigenvalue. Consequently every second-order stationary point is globally optimal for rank-at-most-r approximation. This is the one-hidden-layer specialization of Kawaguchi, Deep Learning without Poor Local Minima, arXiv:1605.07110, section 2.3, Theorem 2.3 and Corollary 2.4 (printed p.3), with artificial data X=I_p,Y=M. It is a landscape theorem and does not itself assert convergence of a specified gradient-descent initialization.

Let T preserve a probability measure mu on X and let A have mu(A) > 0. By the Poincare recurrence theorem the first-return time n_A(x) = min { n >= 1 : T^n(x) in A } is finite for mu-almost every x in A. The INDUCED transformation T_A(x) = T^{n_A(x)}(x) preserves the normalised restriction of mu to A; Kac's formula says the integral of n_A over A with respect to mu equals mu of the union of the forward orbit of A, hence equals 1 when T is ergodic, so the mean return time is 1/mu(A). Conversely, the KAKUTANI TOWER (skyscraper) over T_A with height function n_A reconstructs T on the union of the orbit of A: the tower is the set of pairs (x,k) with x in A and 0 <= k < n_A(x), the map sends (x,k) to (x,k+1) below the top and (x, n_A(x)-1) to (T_A x, 0). Induced maps and towers are ergodic exactly when the original system restricted to the orbit of A is.
mu(A) > 0 and mu a finite invariant measure (Poincare recurrence).
Kac's formula in the form 'mean return time is 1/mu(A)' needs ERGODICITY;
without it the integral computes the measure of the orbit of A instead.
title: Induced (first-return) transformation and the Kakutani tower

		\begin{equation}

		Furthermore, $\kappa_1$ and $\kappa_2$ are explicitly computable in terms of $\Lambda_m$, $\Lambda_M$, $N_1$ and $N_2$. Specifically, if $\varepsilon, \delta \in (0,1)$ and $\kappa \in (0,\infty)$ satisfy

            \Lambda_m
            - \varepsilon \,(N_1+N_2+1)
              \bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{2\delta}\bigr)
            \geq \kappa
            \quad\textup{and}\quad
            \varepsilon\,
            \bigl(
              \tfrac{\Lambda_M}{1+\Lambda_M}
              - \tfrac{\delta}{2}(N_1+N_2+1)
            \bigr)
            \geq \kappa,
        \end{equation}
		then \eqref{eq:conv:abs} holds for $\kappa_1 = (\frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon})^{1/2}$ and $\kappa_2 = \frac{\kappa}{1+\varepsilon}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let f be a Schwartz function on the real line, smooth with all derivatives decaying faster than any polynomial, and let f_hat be its Fourier transform, f_hat(xi) equal to the integral over all real t of f(t) e^{-2 pi i xi t} dt. The Poisson summation formula states the sum over all integers n of f(n) equals the sum over all integers k of f_hat(k). It holds more generally for f in suitable Sobolev-type spaces, and generalizes to a lattice L in R^d, equating a sum over L with a sum over the dual lattice divided by the covolume of L. It underlies the functional equation of the Riemann zeta function and identities for theta functions.
title: Poisson summation formula

On
\[
 \Xi:=\left\{x\in B_{\frac{4}{5}}:\dist(u(x),\Sigma)

\]

\begin{equation}

\end{equation}

[Lemma of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] Let $\psi\in C^\infty(\mathrm{Cyl},\mathfrak{g})$. Define 
   \[\forall r_1,r_2,\theta_1,\theta_2, \ \ \ K_{r_1,r_2,\theta_1,\theta_2}\psi\coloneq \frac{1}{(r_2-r_1)(\theta_2-\theta_1)}\int_\Sigma \psi(u,\gamma)     1_{[\theta_1,\theta_2]}(\gamma)1_{[r_1,r_2]}(u) \mathrm{d} u\mathrm{d} \gamma .\]
    We have 
        \begin{eqnarray*}
        \mathbb{E}\left[\exp(i\langle \xi_N,\psi \rangle\right)]
        &=&\prod_{\theta\in \Theta^N_-}\left\{\prod_{r\in R^N_-}\left(1-\frac{\vert K_{r,r_+,\theta,\theta_+}\psi\vert ^2}{2}\sigma(\square(r,r_+,\theta,\theta_+))\right)+O_{N,\theta}\right\},
    \end{eqnarray*}
    where 
    $\sum_{\theta \in \Theta^N_-}\vert O_{N,\theta }\vert  \xrightarrow[N\to \infty]{}0$.

body:
[Proposition 33 (Monotonicity for Einstein--matter areal flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] 1. In the future-contracting regime $[t_0,t_1]\subset(-\infty,0)$, the conformal length~$\mathcal L$, the orbit area~$|t|$, the volume~$\mathcal V$ and its rescaling $|t|^{-3/4}\mathcal V$, and the energy $|t|\mathcal E_\chi$ are monotonically non-increasing in time.

2. In the future-expanding regime $[t_0,t_1]\subset(0,+\infty)$, the conformal length~$\mathcal L$, orbit area~$t$, volume~$\mathcal V$ and rescaled volume~$t^{-3/4}\mathcal V$ are monotonically non-decreasing, while the energy $t^{-2}\mathcal E_\chi$ is monotonically non-increasing.  In the Euler case, the exponent of~$t$ in the energy bound can be improved, namely $t^{-1}\mathcal E_{\rm E}$ is monotonically non-increasing.

As a result, the upper bound~\eqref{estimate-SE} on the energy~$\mathcal E_\chi(t)$ holds, and the upper/lower bounds~\eqref{estimate-LV} on $\mathcal L(t),\mathcal V(t)$ hold in the future-contracting/expanding regimes, respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Monotonicity for Einstein--matter areal flows

There is a full unnormalized linear-attention transformer with T+3 layers, two heads per layer and width 4d+3 whose first entry of the final output row is yhat=a_test^T X_T A^T y. Its n-token input has seven row blocks [J;J;J;A^T;a_test^T followed by n-d zeros;y^T;0_(1 by n)], where J=[I_d,0_(d by (n-d))]. [Lemma lem:tree-gauge-fixing of arXiv:2608.15923, 'Universality of two-dimensional Markovian holonomy fields'] Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite connected graph, let $T\subset E$ be a
spanning tree, and fix a root $o\in V$. If $\Phi:G^E\to\mathbb C$ is
integrable and invariant under the gauge action of $G^V$, then
\[
 \int_{G^E}\Phi(U)\,dU
 =
 \int_{G^{E\setminus T}}\Phi(U^T)\,dU,
\]
where $U^T_e=1_G$ for $e\in T$ and $U^T_e=U_e$ otherwise.
The same statement holds for the boundary-conditioned integrals of
Definition~(def:discrete-YM-measure of the paper).

Let X be a complex Banach space and T in K(X) compact. Then: (a) every nonzero point of the spectrum sigma(T) is an eigenvalue of T, of finite geometric multiplicity; (b) for each nonzero lambda in sigma(T) the operator T - lambda has finite ascent and descent p = p(lambda) >= 1, and X = N ⊕ R with N = ker (T - lambda)^p finite-dimensional and R = ran (T - lambda)^p closed, both T-invariant; T - lambda is nilpotent on N and invertible on R, and dim N is the algebraic multiplicity of lambda; (c) each nonzero lambda in sigma(T) is an isolated point of sigma(T), and the Riesz projection P_lambda = (1/(2 pi i)) times the contour integral of (z - T)^{-1} around a small circle about lambda is a projection of finite rank dim N onto N; (d) sigma(T) is at most countable and its only possible accumulation point is 0; equivalently, for every eps > 0 there are only finitely many eigenvalues with |lambda| > eps; (e) if dim X = infinity then 0 is in sigma(T); (f) sigma(T) = sigma(T'), and for lambda nonzero dim ker(T - lambda) = dim ker(T' - lambda) < infinity. (For real Banach spaces the statements about real nonzero lambda remain valid; the spectrum itself should be taken in the complexification.)
X is a complex Banach space
T: X -> X is compact
lambda is a nonzero scalar in the statements (a)-(c), (f)

[Question of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{B}(\Omega),\mathscr{P}_{\Omega})$ and $(\Sigma,\mathcal{B}(\Sigma),\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma})$ be Polish measure spaces and let $f:\Omega\to \mathcal{B}(\Sigma)$ be measurable\footnote{There is a natural $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma)$ generated by the Borel measures.}.
    What assumptions on $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}$, $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}$ and $f$ are needed for there to exist a probability measure $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega\times \Sigma$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}$ and $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}$ as marginals and such that the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]$ is supported on $f(\omega)$ almost surely? Do the graphical representations of the quantum Ising model satisfy any such assumptions? (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Unnumbered question of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'

body: Let (S, d) and (T, rho) be metric spaces and F a family of functions from S to T. F is equicontinuous at a point x_0 in S if for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that, for every f in F and every x in S with d(x, x_0) < delta, rho(f(x), f(x_0)) < epsilon; F is equicontinuous (on S) if it is equicontinuous at every point, and uniformly equicontinuous if a single delta works for every x_0 in S for each epsilon. The key feature is that the same delta serves every function in the family, not merely every point for a fixed function. [standard, e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis]
title: Equicontinuous Family of Functions

[Proposition prop:AGG of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Let $(I^{n}_i)_{i \in [n]}$ be indicator random variables with
$q^{n}_i = \mathbb{E}[I^{n}_i]$, $\lambda^{n} = \sum_{i=1}^n q^n_i$,
$W^n = \sum_{i=1}^n I^n_i$.
For each $i \in [n]$, let $B^n_i \subseteq [n]$ be such that $i \in B^n_i$. Then there exists a function $f_n$ with $||f_n||_{\infty} \leq 1$  such that
\[
  d_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(W^n,\, \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda^{n})\bigr)
  \leq  2 (b^n_1 + b^n_2 + b^n_3)
\]
with $$ 
b^n_1= \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in B^n_i} q^n_i\, q^n_j,  \quad  b^n_2 = \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in B^n_i \setminus \{i\}} \mathbb{E}[I^n_i I^n_j], \quad 
  b^n_3 = \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \left| \mathbb{E}\bigl[(I^n_i - q^n_i)\, f_n\big( 1 +\sum_{j\in [n]\setminus B^n_i} I^n_j\big)\bigr] \right|.
  $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Arratia, Goldstein \& Gordon

[Theorem thm:codiff-asymp of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Under Assumptions~(ass:params of the paper) and~(ass:limits of the paper), for fixed
$s \in \mathbb{R}$ and as $t \to +\infty$:
\begin{equation}

\tau\!\bigl(X^{(n)}_H(s),\, X^{(n)}_H(t)\bigr)
\sim C(s)\, t^{(\alpha-1)H_+ + H(s) - n},
\end{equation}
where the constant $C(s) > 0$ is given by
\begin{equation}

C(s)
= \frac{\alpha\,|\kappa_\infty|^{\alpha-1}\,|C_n(s)|}
{n - (\alpha-1)H_+ - H(s)},
\end{equation}
with
\[
\kappa_\infty := \frac{\binom{H_+-1/\alpha}{n}}{\Gamma(H_++1-1/\alpha)},
\]
and $C_n(s)$ is the leading tail coefficient of $f_n(s,\cdot)$ from
Lemma~(lem:kernel-asymp of the paper)(iii). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Asymptotic codifference of $n$-MFSM

[Lemma 4 (Theorem 1 in \cite{KL15}) of arXiv:2606.24090, 'Sparsity-adaptive concentration inequalities for random polynomials'] Let $(X_{i}^{(j)})_{i\le n, j\le d}$ be independent symmetric r.v.'s with log-convex tails such that $\mathbb{E}\vert X_{i}^{(j)}\vert^2=1$ for all $i , j$. For any multiindexed matrix $(a_\mathbf{i})_{\mathbf{i}\in [n]^d}$ and any $r\ge 2$ we have
    \begin{align}
        \Big\Vert \sum_{\mathbf{i}}a_{\mathbf{i}}X_{i_1}^{(1)}\cdots X_{i_d}^{(d)} \Big\Vert_{L_r}\asymp_{d} \sum_{I\subseteq [d]}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\in \Pi(I^c)}r^{|\mathcal{J}|/2} \big(\sum_{\mathbf{i}_{I}}\Vert (a_{\mathbf{i}})_{\mathbf{i}_{I^c}}\Vert_{\mathcal{J}}^r\prod_{j\in I}\Vert X_{i_j}^{(j)}\Vert_{L_r}^{r} \big)^{1/r}.
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 58 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Under the law \(\mu_H\) of
\eqref{eq:unique-entrance-mixture}, define
\begin{equation}
  J_\infty
  :=\int_0^Ue^{-L(s)}\,\mathrm ds
    +\int_0^\infty e^{-R(s)}\,\mathrm ds.
  
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
  0<J_\infty<\infty
  \quad\text{almost surely},
  
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  J_a\Longrightarrow J_\infty,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\EE}_a[J_a^{-1}]
  \longrightarrow
  D_H:=\EE_{\mu_H}[J_\infty^{-1}]
  \in(0,\infty).
  
\end{equation}
title: Theorem 58 of arXiv:2607.21374

The adaptive particle-weight system consists of $N$ agents with states $\bm{X}_i(t) \in \mathbb{D}$ (where $\mathbb{D} = \mathbb{R}^d$ or $\mathbb{T}^d$) and interaction weights $\bm{W}_{i, j}(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ co-evolving according to the coupled system of SDEs: $\mathrm{d}\bm{X}_i = \mu(\bm{X}_i) \mathrm{d}t + \nu \mathrm{d}\bm{B}_i + \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j \in [N] \setminus \{i\}} \bm{W}_{i, j} \sigma(\bm{X}_i, \bm{X}_j) \mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}\bm{W}_{i, j} = \alpha(\bm{X}_i, \bm{X}_j) \bm{W}_{i, j} \mathrm{d}t + \beta(\bm{X}_i, \bm{X}_j) \mathrm{d}t$ for all $i, j \in [N], i \neq j$, where $(\bm{B}_i)_{i \in [N]}$ are independent standard Brownian motions, $\nu \ge 0$, and $\mu, \sigma, \alpha, \beta$ are globally Lipschitz continuous functions.
\mathbb{D} is \mathbb{R}^d or \mathbb{T}^d
\bm{B}_i are independent Brownian motions
\mu, \sigma, \alpha, \beta are globally Lipschitz
title: Coupled Particle-Weight SDE System with Adaptive Plasticity

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2609.02415, 'Nef Cones of Hilbert Schemes of Orthogonal Grassmannians'] Let $X$ be a projective variety with Picard number $\rho(X) = n$. Suppose that the divisor classes $D_1, \ldots, D_n$ form a basis for the Néron-Severi group $\mathrm{NS}(X)$. If there exist irreducible curves $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_n \subset X$ satisfying the intersection conditions
\[
D_i \cdot \gamma_j = \delta_{ij} \quad \text{for all } 1 \leq i, j \leq n,
\]
then the Nef cone of $X$ is generated by $D_1, \ldots, D_n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 6 of arXiv:2609.02415

By taking the difference of two smooth increasing paths $L',L'':[0,T]\toS^{D}_+$, we can get a smoothed version of $a\mathbf{1}_{[0,t]}$ for every $a\in S^{D}_+$ and $t\in[0,T]$. Taking the differences of functions of this type, we can get a smoothed version of $a\mathbf{1}_{[t,t']}$ for $a\in S^{D}$ and $0\leqslant t<t'\leqslant T$. This procedure yields a family of test functions rich enough to determine $S^D$-valued measurable functions on $[0,T]$.

[Theorem 19 of arXiv:2506.10856, 'The space of multifurcating ranked tree shapes: enumeration, lattice structure, and Markov'] The tree $\ddot{T}_N$ with the maximum backwards degree in $\mathcal{MT}_N$ is the multifurcating tree with the following properties 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item It has $K=\lfloor \frac{N-2}{2} \rfloor+1$ internal nodes.
    \item Each of the $\lfloor \frac{N-2}{2} \rfloor$ non-root internal nodes subtend distinct cherries descending from the root.
    \item The rest of the $L=2 + (N \text{ mod } 2)$ tips are leaves descending from the root.
\end{enumerate}
The backwards degree of $\ddot{T}_N$ is \[ \text{deg}^-(\ddot{T}_N) = \big (3+ (N \text{ mod } 2) \big) 2^{\left \lfloor \frac{N}{2} \right \rfloor} - \left \lfloor \frac{N}{2} \right \rfloor - 3 .\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A power series sum a_n (x - c)^n has a radius of convergence R in [0, infinity] given by the Cauchy-Hadamard formula 1/R = limsup |a_n|^{1/n}: it converges absolutely for |x - c| < R and diverges for |x - c| > R (behavior on |x - c| = R varies). Within the open disk of convergence the series is infinitely differentiable and integrable term by term, and equals the Taylor series of its sum. This is the bridge from analytic functions to their coefficient sequences.
title: Power Series and Radius of Convergence

body: On four equally likely points {0, 1, 2, 3}, the systems A_1 = {0, 1}, A_2 = {0, 2}, A_3 = {1, 2} and B_1 = {0, 1}, B_2 = {0, 2}, B_3 = {0, 3} both have every event of probability 1/2 and every pairwise intersection of probability 1/4, so they share every bound computed from first and second order data, including the Gallot-Kounias value 3/4. But the first union has probability 3/4 and the second has probability 1. The first system attains the bound; the second falls short by 1/4.

[Lemma 56 (Complete shifts of every sign) of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:onechart}, let $\phi$ be the
function constructed there and put $m_0:=\inf_\Omega\phi$.  Then
$m_0>0$, and for every $t\in(-m_0,\infty)$ the metric
$g^{(t)}:=(\phi+t)^{4/(n-2)}\,g_{st}\big|_\Omega$ is smooth, complete,
and locally conformally flat, with
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}
 =n(n-1)\,t\,(\phi+t)^{-(n+2)/(n-2)},
 \qquad
 \lim_{t\to0}\int_\Omega|\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}|^{n/2}\,dV_{g^{(t)}}=0.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}$ is negative, zero, or positive
according as $t<0$, $t=0$, or $t>0$.  For $t>0$, the rescaled metric
$\bar g^{(t)}:=t^{-4/(n-2)}g^{(t)}
=\Bigl(1+\frac{\phi}{t}\Bigr)^{4/(n-2)}g_{st}\big|_\Omega$ satisfies
\[
 0<\mathrm{Sc}_{\bar g^{(t)}}<n(n-1),
 \qquad
 \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
 \sup_{\substack{x\in\Omega\\d_{g_{st}}(x,E)<\delta}}
 \mathrm{Sc}_{\bar g^{(t)}}(x)=0.
\]

body:
[Def weighted projective stack and curve of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Consider the $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$-weighted action of $\mathbb{G}_m$ on $n$-dimension affine space $\mathbb{A}^n$, i.e., \[t \cdot (x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (t^{a_1}x_1, \ldots, t^{a_n}x_n)\] where each $a_i > 0.$ 
Then, the {\em weighted projective stack} $\mathcal{P}(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ is given by the stack quotient
\[
\mathcal{P}(a_1, \ldots, a_n) := [(\mathbb{A}^n \setminus 0)/\mathbb{G}_m].
\]
When $n = 2$, we refer to the weighted projective stack $\mathcal{P}(a,b)$ as a {\em weighted projective curve}.
title: weighted projective stack and curve

body:
[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.04012, 'Hölder regularity for backward stochastic Volterra integral equations and applications to '] Suppose that $(\Psi, G)$ satisfy the assumptions in Theorem \ref{thm:well-posedness-BSVIE} with $p=2$, and let $(Y,Z)$ be the unique solution to \eqref{eq:bsvie-intro}. Let $(\Psi^\pi,G^\pi)$ satisfy the assumptions in Theorem \ref{theorem:energy-estimates} with $p=2$, with Lipschitz constant $[G^\pi]_L$ independent of $\pi$, and denote by $(Y^\pi,Z^\pi)$ the solution of the BSDE system \eqref{def:BSDE-app-BSVIE}.

Define the approximation errors
\begin{gather*}
    \varepsilon_{\Psi}^\pi
    \coloneqq
    \mathbb E\left[
    \int_0^T
    |\Psi(t)-\Psi^\pi(t)|^2\,dt
    \right], \quad \varepsilon_{G}^\pi
    \coloneqq
    \mathbb E\left[
    \int_0^T
    \left(
    \int_t^T
    \left|
    G(t,s,Y(s),Z(t,s))
    -
    G^\pi(t,s,Y(s),Z(t,s))
    \right|\,ds
    \right)^2
    dt \right].
\end{gather*}
Then there exists a constant $C>0$, independent of $\pi$, such that
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb E\Bigg[
    \int_0^T |Y(t)-Y^\pi(\tau(t),t)|^2\,dt
    +
    \int_0^T\int_t^T
    |Z(t,s)-Z^\pi(\tau(t),s)|^2\,ds\,dt 
    \Bigg]
    \leq
    C\big(\varepsilon_{\Psi}^\pi+\varepsilon_{G}^\pi\big). 
\end{align*}
In particular, if
$\varepsilon_{\Psi}^\pi+\varepsilon_{G}^\pi\to0$ as $|\pi|\to0$, then
\[
    (Y^\pi(\tau(\cdot),\cdot),Z^\pi(\tau(\cdot),\cdot))
    \longrightarrow
    (Y,Z) \quad \text{in $\mathcal H^2(0,T)\times\mathcal H_\Delta^2(0,T)$.}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.04012
