Method: Explicit calculation or obstruction with source-specific scope Result: The no-switch-over comparison has an exact simplification: if all jobs require deterministic time2 and arrivals are the superposition of independent Poisson streams, total workload is the workload of a work-conserving M/D/1 queue, independently of the polling order. Introducing deterministic switch-over times destroys work conservation even when the sum of a service time and a switch time remains2. Empty visits then consume capacity, and their boundary frequencies enter the two-dimensional reflected limit. Check: Total unfinished service decreases at unit rate whenever any work is present in the first system. In the second it is constant during each switch, including switches caused by an empty queue. Thus equal nominal time per saturated visit does not imply equal sample-path workload. Obstruction: The missing boundary occupation and reflection structure prevent identifying the limiting joint law from a scalar workload formula. The source suggests a two-dimensional transform boundary-value problem. No solution of that problem or valid interchange of its heavy-traffic limit is supplied.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0303-simultaneous-criticality-in-k-limited-polling

If g is a standard Gaussian vector in R^n and f : R^n -> R is L-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm, then P(|f(g) - E f(g)| > t) <= 2 exp(-t^2 / (2 L^2)) for all t > 0. An analogous inequality, with adjusted constants, holds for the uniform measure on the sphere; this isoperimetric concentration underlies laws of robustness.
f L-Lipschitz for the Euclidean norm
g standard Gaussian in R^n

[Theorem 43 (Sharp depth-only no-go and determinant blindness) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Fix $r\ge1$.  For every nonzero compact operator $K$ on a separable
Hilbert space $H$, there is a block-lower-triangular operator model of a
nonzero depth-$r$ primitive word whose only nonzero endpoint block is
unitarily equivalent to $K$.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 s_j(W_r)=s_j(K),\qquad j\ge1.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently primitive depth alone forces no Schatten membership, decay
law, regular variation, Mellin order, or Fredholm growth.

More explicitly, on
$\mathcal H=H_0\oplus\cdots\oplus H_r$, with $H_j\cong H$, choose
adjacent compact blocks $X_j:H_{j-1}\to H_j$ and set
$W_1=X_1$, $W_j=[X_j,W_{j-1}]$.  Then $W_r$ has only its $(r,0)$ block and
realizes the free normal word
\[
 \operatorname{ad}_{\mathsf q_r}\operatorname{ad}_{\mathsf q_{r-1}}
 \cdots\operatorname{ad}_{\mathsf q_2}(\mathsf q_1)
 \in\mathfrak L_r(Q^\sharp).
\]
Moreover $W_r^2=0$.  If $K\in\mathcal S_1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \det(I+zW_r)=1,
 \qquad
 \frac12\log\det(I+z^2W_r^*W_r)
 =\frac12\log\det(I+z^2K^*K).
 
\end{equation}
More generally, if
$D=\operatorname{diag}(D_0,\ldots,D_r)$ and $R_\triangle$ are trace
class, with $R_\triangle$ strictly block triangular, then
\begin{equation}
 \det(I+z(D+R_\triangle))
 =\prod_{j=0}^r\det(I+zD_j).
 
\end{equation}
Thus an ordinary Fredholm determinant can erase an entire strictly
triangular ancestry layer, while hermitized and labelled responses retain it.

[Prop contractionprinciple of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] Assume that $(X_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good\footnote{A rate function is said to be \textit{good} if its level sets $\{x \in E: \, I(x) \le M\}$ are compact.} rate function $I$ on some space $E$.   
 Let $F:E \rightarrow G$ be a bounded continuous function. 
 Then, the sequence of random variables $Y_n=F(X_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good rate function $J$ given, for any $y\in G,$ by
 \[ J(y) =  \inf\{ I(x) : F(x)=y\}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:correlation_branchingprocess of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] For all large enough $M, H > 0$, there is some $\lambda_0 > 1$ and $p, q > 0$ such that
for all $\lambda \geqslant \lambda_0$ the following holds.
Let $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ be independent infinite-line $\lambda$-tilted line ensembles on $[-2H,2H]$
with arbitrary boundary data subject to the restriction $X^1(\pm 2H) \leqslant H$.
Then there is a coupling between $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ and $\mathcal{P}^{p,q}_b$ such that,
for all $\tau \in \mathcal{T}_b$, $\tau \in \mathcal{P}^{p,q}_b$ implies $\mathsf{Reverse}_\tau(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Corollary cor: intro_multisection of arXiv:2609.00163, 'Decompositions and diagrams of symplectic surfaces in Weinstein domains'] Let $\Sigma$ be a multisection of a Lefschetz fibration $\Pi: W \to D^2$, where $W$ is a Weinstein domain. Then $\Sigma$ can be placed in a bridge-bisection-with-divides position with respect to the bisection-with-divides decomposition associated to this Weinstein structure.

body:
[Proposition ch-5-energy ensi of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] For any $z$ solving the equation (ch-5-system1 of the paper) and any $0\leq s,t\leq T$, it holds that

\begin{align}
    \notag
    & {\mathbb{E}}\int_G\big( |z_t(t,x)|^2 + |\nabla
    z(t,x)|^2 \big) dx 
    \\ \notag
    & \leq \displaystyle e^{{\cal C}\big(r_1^2 + r_2^{\frac{1}{2-n/p}}+1\big)T}
    {\mathbb{E}}\int_G \big(|z_t(s,x)|^2 + |\nabla z(s,x)|^2 \big) dx
    \\
    & \quad 
    + {\cal C}{\mathbb{E}}\int_0^T\int_G \big(f(\tau,x)^2 + g(\tau,x)^2\big)
    dxd\tau.
\end{align}
title: Proposition ch-5-energy ensi of arXiv:2411.05534

body: [Lemma lem:lift of arXiv:2609.02953, 'Alon's Question on Connectivity Graph-Codes: $f(d)=2^d$ for Every $d\geq 4$'] Let $B$ be a finite graph with an edge labelling in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{d}$ such that every selected graph $B_{a}$, $a\ne 0$, is connected, spanning and contains a cycle. Then there are infinitely many finite covers $\widetilde{B}$ of $B$ in which every lifted selected graph $\widetilde{B}_{a}$ is connected and spanning. If $B$ is finite, simple, bipartite and $d$-regular, the covers may be chosen with all of these properties.

        \forall \epsilon' >0 , \exists A_{\epsilon'} \subset \mathcal{C} ([0,T],\mathcal{S}) : \; \; \sup_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \mathbb{P}_k(A_{\epsilon'}) + \epsilon' \geq 1 \text{ and } \lim_{\delta \rightarrow 0} \sup_{v \in A_{\epsilon}}(m(v,\delta))=0. \nonumber

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent real random variables with densities bounded by K, A a real symmetric n x n matrix, b in R^n, c in R, and Q = X^T A X + b^T X + c. If A has five eigenvalues of modulus at least s > 0 (s_5(A) >= s), Q has a density bounded by 270 K^2/s, whatever n, the other eigenvalues, the signature of A, b and c; with three such eigenvalues, sup_a E|Q - a|^{-1/2} <= 77 K/sqrt(s), and one is not enough (X_1 uniform on [0,1] and Q = X_1^2 give E X_1^{-1} = infinity). The nine-eigenvalue bound 400 K^2/s and the 17- and 33-eigenvalue versions are special cases. The proof turns 2m - 1 large eigenvalues into m large singular values of one off-diagonal block by random sign decoupling on the eigenvectors and applies a Fourier decay bound for that block. The conjecture itself, with three eigenvalues of modulus at least 1 and a universal constant, and the case of four are open; the sign-decoupling route cannot go below five.

body: [Lemma fgt-unbased-h-cof of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, let $W$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space, and write $K$ for the class of all maps in $\cat{$\bm{({\textup{O}}(W)\times G)}$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}_*$ of the form $\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,W)\smashp_{{\textup{O}}(V)} i$ where we let $V$ run through finite-dimensional inner product spaces and $i$ runs through cofibrations of $\cat{$\bm{({\textup{O}}(V)\times G)}$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}_*$. [Theorem teo:2 of arXiv:2601.00291, 'The probability of connection between two vertices cannot be monotone with the distance fo'] For every $d \geqslant 2$, there exists a critical value $\lambda_c(\mathbb{Z}^d) \in (0,\infty)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[a)] If $\lambda > \lambda_c$, then $\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}\left(o\longleftrightarrow \vec{e}\, \right) > \mathbb{P}_{\lambda}\left(o\longleftrightarrow t\vec{e}\, \right)$ for all $t\in (0,1)$.
    \item[b)] If $0 < \lambda < \lambda_c$, then there exists
    $t = t(\lambda) \in (0,1)$ such that $\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}\left(o\longleftrightarrow \vec{e}\, \right) < \mathbb{P}_{\lambda}\left(o\longleftrightarrow t\vec{e}\, \right)$.
\end{enumerate}
Where $\vec e = (1,0,\ldots,0)\in\mathbb{Z}^d$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let p(x) = x^n + c_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + c_1 x + c_0 be a monic polynomial with complex coefficients. The companion matrix of p is the n by n matrix C(p) with 1 in every position (i+1, i) for i = 1, ..., n-1 (the subdiagonal), with -c_{i-1} in position (i, n) for i = 1, ..., n (the last column), and 0 elsewhere. The characteristic polynomial of C(p) equals p(x), so the eigenvalues of C(p), with multiplicity, are exactly the roots of p. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]
title: Companion Matrix of a Monic Polynomial

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] There exists a site $v_k \in V$ such that the $\Lambda_{v_k}$-coalescent does not come down from infinity.

        \item[(b)] There exist sites $v_2, \ldots, v_{k-1}$ such that for every $i = 1, \ldots, k-1$ either $M_{v_iv_{i+1}}(dz)$ or $R_{v_iv_{i+1}}(dz)$ is $\Lambda_{v_i}$-strong.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2512.21026, 'Minimax Duality in Game-Theoretic Probability\thanks{Work in progress: mistakes are likely'] Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\Omega$ be a linear space of bounded functions containing the constant functions.
  A \emph{(financial) risk measure} on $\Omega$ is a function $\rho:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $\rho(X+c) = \rho(X) - c$ for all $X\in\mathcal{X}, c\in\mathbb{R}$ (translation'),
  \item $X\leq Y \implies \rho(X) \leq \rho(X)$ for all $X,Y\in\mathcal{X}$ (monotonicity').
  \end{enumerate}
  The \emph{acceptance set} of $\rho$ is the set $\mathcal{A}_\rho := \{ X\in\mathcal{X} \mid \rho(X) \leq 0 \}$.

[Theo extremeredtheo of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] $\Omega^p$ is a Borel subset of $\varprojlim \mathcal M(\mathbb{G}^p_n)$. For every coherent system $\{M_n\}_n$ on $\mathbb{G}^p$ there exists the unique Borel measure $m$ on $\Omega^p$ such that
$$
M_n(\lambda)=\int_{\Omega^p} M_n^\omega(\lambda)m(d\omega)\qquad\forall \lambda\in\mathbb{G}^p_n.
$$
Conversely, for each Borel measure $m$ on $\Omega^p$ the relation above defines a coherent system on $\Omega^p$. This gives a one-to-one correspondence between Borel measures on $\Omega^p$ and coherent systems on $\mathbb{G}^p$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let epsilon=eta>0, beta1=9/10, beta2=999/1000, and H a fixed positive two-dimensional diagonal matrix with both eigenvalues in (38,13673160/358811). Use ordinary separate m/(1-beta1^(t+1)) and v/(1-beta2^(t+1)) corrections and add epsilon outside sqrt. There exist a sufficiently large absolute time T and an open full-state neighborhood U of a phase of the limiting uncorrected product two-cycle such that every corrected tail started in U at an absolute time t0>=T converges by parity to that cycle. Along these tails eta active curvature and eta top sharpness tend to 38. This is not an entry result for time-0 standard zero moments.

Suppose rho lies in the strict stable interval of claim 003. For every
fixed eta>0 and positive diagonal eigenvalues whose rho_i=epsilon/(eta lambda_i)
lie in that interval, consider the ordinary bias-corrected recursion
 m'=b m+(1-b)g, v'=d v+(1-d)g^2,
 x'=x-eta [m'/(1-b^(t+1))]/[sqrt(v'/(1-d^(t+1)))+epsilon].
There are an absolute time T and an open neighborhood U of a phase of the
uncorrected product two-cycle such that every run started at any sufficiently
large time t0>=T in U approaches that uncorrected cycle with the same parity.
Consequently eta C_t and eta S_t tend to 38 for such corrected tails.
This is a tail-basin theorem, not a claim about standard m0=v0=0.

Proof. In a compact neighborhood of either nonzero phase, v' stays strictly
positive, so all denominators and derivatives are bounded. The corrected
one-step map F_t and its derivative differ from the limiting map F by
O(d^t), uniformly there, since b=.9<d=.999<1. The two-step map G=F^2
has derivative spectral radius <1 at either phase, by claim 003.
Choose a vector norm in which its derivative operator norm is <1, then
shrink to a closed ball B around a phase on which G has Lipschitz
constant L<1. The corrected two-step map G_t=F_(t+1) o F_t obeys
sup_B ||G_t-G||<=A d^t for all sufficiently large t; its intermediate
images remain in the chosen other-phase neighborhood. For a smaller
ball U of radius r/2 choose T with A d^T< (1-L)r/2.
Then G_t maps B into B and, writing e_k for distance to the fixed phase,
 e_(k+1)<=L e_k+A d^(t0+2k).
Induction gives e_k<=L^k e_0+A d^t0 sum_(j=0)^(k-1)L^(k-1-j)d^(2j).
For any theta between max(L,d^2) and 1 the right hand side is O(theta^k).
Thus even iterates approach the phase; continuity and uniform F_t->F give
the other phase for odd iterates. The gradients are nonzero on the limit

[Theorem gaussian recursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] Let ${\bf x} \sim \gauss{0}{\mathbb{I}_n}$ and $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in [n]^d}$ be multi-indexed sequences of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a degree-$d$ homogeneous Gaussian polynomial random matrix as
$$
{\bf P}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in [n]^d} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b \in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf P}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf P}({\bf x})}_{2t}^{2t} ~\leq~ (2^d \sqrt{2}t)^{2t} \left( \sum_{1 \leq a+b \leq d}\norm{{\mathbb E} {\bf P}_{a,b}}_{2t}^{2t} \right).
$$

body:
[Lemma MorseChart of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] Let $f:\Sigma\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a Morse function. Then, for any $a\in \operatorname{Crit}(f)$, there exists a smooth chart $x\in U\subset M\mapsto (x_1(x),x_2(x))\in  \mathbb{R} ^2$ centered at $a$, called a \emph{Morse Chart near $a$}, in which the function $f$ reads
$$
f(x)=f(a)+\frac {1}{2}\left(\varepsilon_1x_1^2+\varepsilon_2 x_2^2\right),
$$
with $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in\{-1,1\}$. Moreover, 
\begin{itemize}
    \item If $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=1$, we say that $a$ has index $0$, or is a local minimum.
    \item If $\varepsilon_1=1,\varepsilon_2=-1$, we say that $a$ has index $1$, or is a saddle point.
    \item If $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=-1$, we say that $a$ has index $2$, or is a local maximum. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Morse Lemma

body: [Definition 2.2 of arXiv:2304.14793, 'Learning Graph Neural Networks using Exact Compression'] Two learning problems P and P′ are equivalent, written P ≡P′, if they share the same hypothesis space of GNNs S and, for every 𝐿∈S we have Loss(𝐿(𝐺),𝑇) = Loss′(𝐿(𝐺′),𝑇′). In other words, when traversing the hypothesis space for a GNN to return, no learning algorithm can distinguish between P and P′.
title: Definition 2.2 of arXiv:2304.14793: Learning Graph Neural Networks using Exact Compression

Uniformly over t,z when p M_t<=1/4, h_t(p)=p[1-p(M_t-1)+e1] with |e1|<=(5/2)p^2 M_t^2, and j_t(p,z)/h_t(p)^2=1+p I_t(z)+e2 with |e2|<=100p^2 M_t^2, I_t(z)=E|R_t intersect (R_t-z)|. At graph distance two I_2(z)=2p_2(z)>0, so the covariance is positive for sufficiently small p at time two, despite its negative sign at time one. For d>=3 only, I_t(z)/(t+1) tends to 2G(z)/[G(0)(G(0)+G(z))], with full-space SRW G. Fixed-p long times leave the dilute regime. Novelty: KNOWN rare-density expansion and capacity methods; UNCHECKED exact pair/range coefficient statement. Status: independently checked proof.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:1a56232c36428b14702ddca8c09e292a182c8a96e9f4abb905388a9231ab7b70","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/1a/1a56232c36428b14702ddca8c09e292a182c8a96e9f4abb905388a9231ab7b70.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6cc85f6627aee7f83c3d1d43848b94925a2ddc088a5d0c34737969270e49bb92","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c15","bundle_id":"population.i0005-correlation-energy-and-active-moments-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:sparse-parking-pair-survival-dilute-range-intersection-expansion-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C15 v3: finite-horizon sparse pair expansion and a time-two sign flip

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN elementary rare-density/product
expansion method; UNCHECKED separate prior appearance of the exact range
coefficient below. This is an actual particle-hole process statement at
fixed finite time, not a fixed-density long-time theorem.

For the source's sparse critical synchronous particle-hole process on Z^d,
d>=1, with signs +1 and -1 each having probability p, write h_t(p) for
one-hole survival probability and j_t(p,z) for joint survival at 0,z!=0.
Let R_t={X_0,...,X_t} be the range of one free nearest-neighbor SRW and
M_t=E_0|R_t|. For any integer t>=0 and z!=0 with p M_t<=1/4, uniformly in t,z,

    h_t(p)=p[1-p(M_t-1)+O(p^2 M_t^2)],
    j_t(p,z)/h_t(p)^2
      =1+p I_t(z)+O(p^2 M_t^2),
    I_t(z)=sum_y P_y(the path through t visits both 0 and z)
          =E_0 |R_t intersect (R_t-z)|.

In addition, for d>=3 only, with full-space escape-probability capacity
and g=G(0),

    I_t(z)/(t+1) --> 2/g-cap({0,z})
                  =2G(z)/[g(g+G(z))].

This limit concerns the first-order coefficient; the uniform remainder
is useful only in the dilute regime p M_t<=1/4.

The errors have absolute constants: at most (5/2)p^2 M_t^2 for the
singleton bracket and at most 100p^2 M_t^2 for the displayed pair ratio. In particular for |z|_1=2 and t=2,

    I_2(z)=2p_2(z)>0.

Thus these same-parity holes are positively correlated at time two for
all sufficiently small p. C14 proves they are negatively correlated at
time one for every p>0. Neither a blanket association statement nor a
time-propagated same-parity negative-correlation claim follows from the
one-round signs. This includes d=4.

## 1. Conditional survival and a finite product derivative

For a fixed finite target set K let phi_K(p) be the probability that no
particle enters K by time t, conditional on all its sites initially being
holes. The exact survival probability is p^|K| phi_K(p). Only initial
values and instructions in a finite backward time-t cone can affect this
event, by source finite propagation. After averaging the finitely many
relevant instructions, phi_K is a polynomial in p: each initial sign has
probabilities p,1-2p,p. In particular it has a Taylor remainder O(p^2)
at zero with a finite constant depending on K,t.

At p=0 all sites off K are empty and there are no particles, so phi_K(0)=1.
Differentiate the finite product law one coordinate y outside K at a
time. The derivative replaces that coordinate's empty state with +1 and
-1, each with coefficient one, and subtracts twice its empty state.
If its replacement is a hole, the configuration still has no particles
and the event has probability one. If it is a particle, it follows a free
SRW until its first visit to K, where it settles. There are no other
holes or particles. The no-arrival probability is therefore
1-P_y(T_K<=t). The coordinate contributes -P_y(T_K<=t). Summing gives

    phi_K(p)=1-p S_K(t)+O_{K,t}(p^2),
    S_K(t)=sum_{y outside K}P_y(T_K<=t).

The sum is finite because a walk takes at most t steps. The presence of
arbitrarily many random instructions creates no analytic issue: the event
averaged over them is a bounded function of a finite set of initial signs.

## 2. Singleton and pair coefficients

Translation of one free path and Tonelli give

    sum_y P_y(T_0<=t)=E_0|R_t|=M_t.

The y=0 term is one, hence S_{0}=M_t-1. For K={0,z}, inclusion-exclusion
for a single free path gives

    sum_y P_y(T_K<=t)=2M_t-I_t(z).

The y=0 and y=z terms of this union event are both one; therefore

    S_{0,z}=2M_t-I_t(z)-2=2S_0-I_t(z).

Substitution into p phi_{0} and p^2 phi_{0,z}, followed by expansion of
the strictly positive denominator phi_0(p)^2 near p=0, proves the displayed
ratio. For the range identity, fix one free path from 0 and translate it
by its starting point y. It visits both 0 and z exactly when -y is in
R_t and z-y is in R_t. The number of such y equals
|R_t intersect (R_t-z)|. Averaging proves the identity.

## 3. Time two and the correlation flip

If |z|_1=2, a two-step path visiting both targets must start at one target
at time zero and reach the other at time two. There is no time to visit
both from a different starting point, since their distance is two.
Therefore I_2(z)=P_0(X_2=z)+P_z(X_2=0)=2p_2(z).
For z=2e_i this equals 1/(2d^2); for z=e_i+e_j, i!=j, it equals 1/d^2.
The same constants hold after sign changes of coordinates. The coefficient
is positive, so the ratio exceeds one for all sufficiently small positive p.
At time one C14's exact ratio is [(1-2q)/(1-q)^2]^m<1, q=p/(2d).

## 4. Exact last-visit identity and capacity rate

For any finite K define M_K(t)=sum_y P_y(T_K<=t). On a path that visits
K through time t there is a unique last visit, at a site s in K and time
n between zero and t. The Markov property gives

    P_y(T_K<=t)=sum_{n=0}^t sum_{s in K}
                  P_y(X_n=s) P_s(T_K^+>t-n).

Sum over y. Each transition-kernel column sums to one by translation
invariance. Hence, after changing m=t-n,

    M_K(t)=sum_{m=0}^t sum_{s in K}P_s(T_K^+>m).

The summands decrease to sum_s P_s(T_K^+=infinity)=cap(K), so Cesaro
averaging gives M_K(t)/(t+1)->cap(K). This identity is valid in all
dimensions; in recurrent dimensions the limiting capacity is zero.

For d>=3, M_{0}(t)=M_t and cap({0})=1/g. Inclusion-exclusion from
Step 2 gives I_t(z)=2M_0(t)-M_{0,z}(t). The claimed rate now follows.
The two-point capacity identity 2/(g+G(z)) is Sznitman's Proposition 1.5,
equations (1.58)-(1.59), with the same full-space normalization.

## 5. Uniform dilute-regime remainder from free paths

Condition on initial holes at a finite K of size k. Give every possible
initial particle an independent full free walk, retaining its unused
suffix after actual settlement. A particle follows this prefix until
settlement; tie-breaking only chooses which arriving particle settles.
The no-arrival event for all free walks implies no actual arrival to K.
For y outside K put a_y=P_y(T_K<=t), S=sum_y a_y=S_K(t). Independence
of initial particle indicators and their free walks gives the free void
probability Q=product_y(1-p a_y). Bonferroni gives

    1-pS <= Q <= 1-pS+(pS)^2/2.

If there is a free arrival to K but no actual arrival, some free K-hitting
particle must have settled earlier at an initial hole outside K. A union
bound over those initial holes and particles, using p^2 for the opposite
signs at distinct outside sites, bounds this discrepancy probability by

    p^2 sum_{y outside K} E_y[1{T_K<=t}|R_t|]
       <=p^2 k E_0|R_t|^2.

The last inequality follows by fixing one translated free path: the
number of its translations hitting K is at most k times its range size.
Initial signs at the particle's own site or fixed target sites cannot
produce an outside hole and may harmlessly be included in the upper bound.

For completeness, E|R_t|^2<=2M_t^2. Sum over ordered pairs x,z of sites
visited. Every joint visit has either T_x<=T_z or T_z<=T_x. Strong Markov
at the first entrance to the earlier site bounds the respective sums by
sum_x P_0(T_x<=t) sum_z P_x(T_z<=t)=M_t^2. Including equal visit times
twice only enlarges the bound. Hence

    0<=phi_K(p)-(1-pS_K(t))
              <=(k^2/2+2k)p^2 M_t^2.

This establishes the singleton bracket error 5p^2 M_t^2/2 and pair
bracket error 6p^2 M_t^2, uniformly in time and separation.

Write a=M_t-1, I=I_t(z), b=2a-I, phi_0=1-pa+e_1,
phi_{0,z}=1-pb+e_2. Here 0<=e_1<=2.5p^2 M_t^2,
0<=e_2<=6p^2 M_t^2, 0<=a<=M_t, and 0<=I<=2M_t.
If pM_t<=1/4 then phi_0>=3/4. Expanding its square gives

    phi_0^2=1-2pa+r,   |r|<=6.4p^2 M_t^2.

Indeed the remainder is p^2a^2+2(1-pa)e_1+e_1^2, bounded by
(1+5+6.25/16)p^2M_t^2<6.4p^2M_t^2. Consequently

    |phi_{0,z}-phi_0^2(1+pI)|
        =|e_2-r+2p^2aI-pIr|<=20p^2 M_t^2.

Division by phi_0^2>=9/16 gives a ratio error below
36p^2M_t^2; the stated constant 100 is conservative.

## Quantifier limitation and sources

The uniform estimate requires p M_t<=1/4 and its error is quadratic in
p M_t. For fixed p>0, M_t tends to infinity, so the dilute regime ends.
The range-intersection coefficient therefore cannot be inserted into a
fixed-p long-time survival formula using this argument. This differs from C6's triangular-law
nonuniformity result and does not settle I0005.

Primary model and finite propagation: Bou-Rabee--Panagiotis,
arXiv:2609.02820v1, Sections 2 and 8.2. The finite-set conditional
survival identity is also proved in I0005-C13. All expansion and
inclusion-exclusion steps are given above explicitly.
The capacity normalization is additionally verified in Sznitman,
arXiv:0704.2560v3, (1.5)-(1.7) and Proposition 1.5. The last-visit
identity and Cesaro argument are proved here directly.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a1e8e0a4e9d3ea844deb3d838cd3e61ce199607ccdf1c6da584de03b25d96ae0","revision_digest":"sha256:1e11da4481898b83bd6939f334cb4fbf73268f079529b5d5ea351a666f4a7eee","source_id":"own-work:w661:I0005-C15:v3","source_revision":"v3; 2026-10-14T06:38:57.0934370+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Let F be a class of real-valued functions defined on a set X, and let S = (x_1, ..., x_n) in X^n. The empirical Rademacher complexity of F with respect to S is defined as R_S(F) = E_eps [ sup_{f in F} (1/n) * sum_{i=1}^n eps_i * f(x_i) ], where eps_1, ..., eps_n are independent Rademacher random variables. The population Rademacher complexity is R_n(F) = E_S[R_S(F)].

[Lemma lem:signed_ODE_analysis of arXiv:2508.18809, '{\bf Critical long-range percolation III: The upper critical dimension}'] Let $a,b>0$, let $h:(0,\infty)\to (0,\infty)$ be a measurable, regularly varying function of index $b$, and suppose that 
$f:(0,\infty)\to \mathbb R$ is a (not necessarily positive) differentiable function such that 
\begin{equation}

f'(r) = \frac{a \pm o(1)}{r}f(r) + \frac{A \pm o(1)}{r} h 
\end{equation}
as $r\to \infty$ for some constant $A\in \mathbb R$. If $b>a$ and $|f(r)|=O(h)$ as $r\to \infty$ then
\[
  f(r) = \frac{A \pm o(1)}{b-a} h(r)
\]
as $r\to \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: ODE analysis for signed functions

		f(P(B))P(C)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}&\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(P(B\cap T^{-i}C))\\
		&\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(P(B\cap T^{-i}C))\le f(P(B)P(C)).
	\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:1-a_SV of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\ell\in\mbox{SV}_\infty$ be $C^1$ with derivative $t\mapsto\wt\ell(t)/t$, where $|\wt\ell|\in\mbox{SV}_\infty$. Then, for each $x>0$, we have $(\ell(t)-\ell(xt))/\wt\ell(t)\to-\log x$ as $t\to\infty$. Defining $L_x(t) \coloneqq 1-\ell(x t)/\ell(t)$ for $t,x>0$, the function $|L_x|$  is  asymptotically equivalent to the quotient $|\wt\ell(t)\log x|/\ell(t)\sim |L_x(t)|$ as $t\to\infty$ and, if $x\neq 1$, slowly varying at infinity. Moreover,  for $x>0$, the function $\Sigma(x)\coloneqq \sup_{t>0, y\in [x\wedge 1,x\vee1]}\wt\ell(yt)/\wt\ell(t)$  satisfies
\[
\big|L_x(t)\big|
=\bigg|\frac{\ell(xt)}{\ell(t)}-1\bigg|
\leqslant \frac{|\wt\ell(t)|}{\ell(t)}
    \cdot\Sigma(x)|\log x|
\qquad \text{ for all }t,x>0.
\]
title: Lemma lem:1-a_SV of arXiv:2411.03609

[Definition def:r of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] Define the \emph{local KL retention ratio}
\[
  r(x):=
  \frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P(x,\cdot)\|\pi)}{\log(1/\pi(x))}.
\]
Define the \emph{typical retention} (stationary average)
\[
  \bar r_\pi:=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi}[r(X)]=\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\,r(x).
\]
By data processing applied to $\delta_x$, $0\le r(x)\le1$ for every state.
title: Local KL retention and typical retention

[Thm thm-fsop-quant of arXiv:2608.30548, 'Finite speed of propagation and waiting time phenomena for stochastic porous media equatio'] Let $u$ be the unique kinetic solution to (equation Eq_SPME_intro of the paper) with initial value $u_0$. For a given $x_0\in \mathbb T^d\setminus\mathrm{supp}(u_0)$ define the process $G:[0,T] \times \Omega\times \left[0,\frac{1}{2}\right) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ by 
    \begin{equation}
        G(t,\omega, r): = \sup_{s\in (0,t)} \, \int_{B_r(x_0)} u_s^{\alpha+1}.

        \lim_{t\rightarrow 0} \mathbb P\left( G(t,r) > 0 \right) = 0.
    \]
    If in addition the assumption (equation eq_flatness of the paper) of Theorem (Thm_fsop of the paper) holds, then 
    \[
         \lim_{t\rightarrow 0} \mathbb P\left( G(t,R_0) > 0 \right) = 0.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:hypercube_entropy}
Let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_d) \in_R \{\pm1\}^d$ with every $X_i$ asymmetric. 
Let $Y = (Y_1, \dots, Y_d) \in \Sym(X)$. 
Then, $H(Y) \ge \frac{1}{d} H(X)$, with equality if and only if the following conditions are all satisfied: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item There exists an index $i \in [d]$ such that both $f_{Y_i} = f_{-X_i}$ and $H(Y) = H(Y_i)$,
\item $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_1-\frac{1}{2}} = \dots = \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_d-\frac{1}{2}}$, 
\item the random variables $X_i$ are mutually independent. 
\end{enumerate}
\begin{proof}
Let $j \in \arg\max_{i \in [d]} H(X_i) = \arg\min_{i \in [d]} \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_i-\frac{1}{2}}$. 
Note that $Y_j$ is an independent symmetrizer of $X_j$ by (lem:Rd_projection_works of the paper). 
Thus we may apply (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) to $X_j$ and $Y_j$. 
Then, 
\begin{align}
H(Y) &\ge H(Y_j) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_a}\\
&\ge H(X_j) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_2}\\

&\ge \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d H(X_i) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_3}\\
&\ge \frac{1}{d} H(X) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_4}
\end{align}
where we used the entropy chain rule in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper)), 
(thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_2 of the paper)), 
and the entropy chain rule and the fact that conditioning reduces entropy in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)). 

Equality is attained in $H(Y) \ge \frac{1}{d} H(X)$ if and only if it is attained in each of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper)-

(ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)). 
The equality condition of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)) is $H(X) = \sum_{i=1}^d H(X_i) $
which is in turn equivalent to mutual independence of the $X_i$ (see e.g. [PW25:book]). 
The equality condition of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_3 of the paper)) is exactly (ii). 
Now consider the conditions

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $f_{Y_j} = f_{-X_j}$,
\item[(b)] $H(Y) = H(Y_j)$.
\end{itemize}
Equality is attained in (equation ineq:hypercube_entropy_2 of the paper) exactly when $H(X_j) = H(Y_j)$, which, in light of (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper), is equivalent to (a). 
Equality is attained in (equation ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper) exactly when (b) is true. 

We claim that (a-b,ii-iii) is equivalent to (i-iii). 
Clearly (a-b) implies (i); we need only show the converse. 
If (i-iii) is fulfilled, then
$$ H(X_j) = H(X_i) = H(Y_i) = H(Y) \ge H(Y_j) \ge H(X_j) $$
where we have used (in order), condition (ii), condition (i), condition (i) again, the entropy chain rule, and (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper). 
Thus, the last two inequalities are equalities, which forces (b) and also forces $H(Y_j) = H(X_j)$. 
The equality condition of (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) (applied to $X_j$ and $Y_j$) then implies (a). 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'

[Definition 2 (Borders and prefix--suffix lengths) of arXiv:2601.16580, 'Coin flipping and waiting times paradoxes \\ Why fair coins are exceptional'] Let \(T\) be a finite string of length \(L\). A \emph{border} of \(T\) is a substring that is both a prefix and a suffix of \(T\). We refer to the lengths \(\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}\) of these borders as the \emph{prefix--suffix lengths} of \(T\); formally, these are the lengths \(\ell\) such that:
\[
T[1..\ell] \;=\; T[L-\ell+1..L].
\]
We write \(\mathcal{B}(T)\) for the set of all such \(\ell\). (Some authors reserve “proper border’’ for \(\ell<L\); in this paper we \emph{include} \(\ell=L\).) The \emph{border polynomial} is
\[
H_T(y)\;:=\;\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{B}(T)} y^\ell .
\]
title: Borders and prefix--suffix lengths
Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.31070
Theorem thm.main_basic of arXiv:2606.13442

body: [Theorem thm:asymptotic slope of arXiv:2512.18435, 'Indistinguishability for recurrent clusters'] For every $\varepsilon>0$ and any $x$ in the cluster of $o$, with probability 1 there exists $R>0$ such that one of these three events is true: either the distance between $o$ and $x$ is less than $R$, or $q\neq 1/2$ and the slope of the straight line going through $o$ and $x$ is in $\big[\frac{2p-1}{1-2q}-\varepsilon, \frac{2p-1}{1-2q}+\varepsilon\big]$, or $q=1/2$ and the slope of the straight line going through $o$ and $x$ is in $(-\infty,-1/\varepsilon]\cup[1/\varepsilon,+\infty)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, the Riemann hypothesis is the conjecture that the Riemann zeta function has its zeros only at the negative even integers and complex numbers with real part ⁠1/2⁠. Many consider it to be the most important unsolved problem in pure mathematics. It is of great interest in number theory because it implies results about the distribution of prime numbers. It was proposed by Bernhard Riemann, after whom it is named. According to a 2026 survey, there is overwhelming numerical evidence for the hypothesis, but no proof is known.

body:
Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and F: Ω × R × R^n → R continuous. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 in Ω if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local maximum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity supersolution if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local minimum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. For the evolution equation u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,T) apply the definition in the variables (x,t), with test functions φ(x,t) of class C^1 and F((x,t), r, (p,s)) = s + H(x,p); so at a local maximum of u - φ one requires φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≤ 0, and at a local minimum φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≥ 0. Equivalent variants giving the same class: C^1 test functions may be replaced by C^2 or C^∞ ones, local extrema by strict local extrema, and one may normalize φ(x0) = u(x0). The definition is NOT invariant under F ↦ -F: in general the viscosity solutions of F = 0 and of -F = 0 differ. The correct symmetry is: u is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 iff -u is a viscosity supersolution of G(x,r,p) = 0, where G(x,r,p) := -F(x,-r,-p).
Ω ⊂ R^n open
F continuous on Ω × R × R^n
u continuous on Ω

On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. Let E_k be the span of the chi_S with |S| = k. For 0 < |rho| < 1, a linear operator A on functions on {-1, 1}^n commutes with T_rho iff A(E_k) is inside E_k for every k. For a permutation pi and signs eps, the map (U f)(x) = f(g x) with (g x)_i = eps_i x_{pi(i)} commutes with T_rho for every rho in [-1, 1]; for a finite group G of such maps, P_G = |G|^(-1) sum over g of U_g is the orthogonal projection onto the G-invariant functions and commutes with T_rho. [Lemma lem:applied-excess-conc of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence~$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$. Let $j$ be a sufficiently large positive integer.  Fix an integer $\tau \ge 0$ and a real number $\nu\ge 0$. Let $A_1,\dots,A_j$ be independent binomial random variables, 
and for each $i\in [j]$
let $m_i = \mathbb{E}(A_i)$. 
Let $\overline{A}=(A_1,\ldots,A_j)$.
Let~$E^+$ be a constant-escape process on $[j]$ with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time $\tau$, end-of-step arrival rate $\nu$, and $\overline{\mathrm{arr}}_{[j]}^{E^+}(\tau) = \overline{A}$. Let $\zeta$ and $\eta$ be real numbers with $\zeta \ge 1$ and $\eta \ge \xi^{-1/3}\zeta$. Fix $t \ge \tau$ such that, for all $k \in [j]$, $h_k^{\nu,\overline{m}}(t-\tau) \le \zeta P_kW_k$. Then with probability at least $1-e^{-500j/\lambda^2}$,
$\mathrm{excess}(\overline{b}_{[j]}^{E^+}(t),\eta) \le \lambda j/500$.

body:
Let $S$ be symmetric positive semidefinite and $w^*$ a solution of $\min_w w^T S w$ subject to $\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$, $w \ge 0$. Let $A = \{i : w^*_i > 0\}$ be its active set and $S_{AA}$ the principal submatrix on $A$. Then $w^*_A$ solves the equality-constrained problem on $A$ alone: if $S_{AA}$ is nonsingular, $w^*_A = S_{AA}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_A / (\mathbf{1}_A^T S_{AA}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_A)$, and $w^*_i = 0$ for $i \notin A$. The inactive rows and columns of $S$ enter only through the inequalities $(S w^*)_i \ge \lambda^*$ for $i \notin A$ that certify optimality, where $\lambda^* = w^{*T} S w^*$ is the optimal value. Consequently two covariance estimates that agree on $S_{AA}$ and both satisfy the inactive inequalities produce the same long-only weights, whatever they do to the eigen-directions supported on the inactive members.

[Lem 24 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Let \(s_0\geq0\), let \(d\in\C\) satisfy \(\left|d\right|\leq s_0\), and
let \((\mathbf{Y}_N)_{N\geq1}\) be any coupling such that, for each \(N\),
\(\mathbf{Y}_N\) is a centred elliptic Gaussian \(N\times N\) matrix with
mixed covariance \(s_0/N\) and holomorphic covariance \(d/N\), in the sense
of \eqref{EqGeneralMatrixCovariance}.  Write
\(d=|d|\mathrm{e}^{2\mathrm{i}\theta}\), taking \(\theta=0\) when
\(d=0\).  Let \((\mathscr{A},\varphi)\) be a tracial
\(*\)-probability space containing a free centred semicircular pair
\(\mathsf{s}_1,\mathsf{s}_2\) of variance one, and define
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{y}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}
       \left(\alpha\mathsf{s}_1+\mathrm{i}\beta\mathsf{s}_2\right),
 \qquad
 \alpha=\sqrt{\frac{s_0+\left|d\right|}{2}},
 \qquad
 \beta=\sqrt{\frac{s_0-\left|d\right|}{2}}.
\end{equation}
Then, simultaneously for every noncommutative polynomial \(R\) in two
indeterminates,
\[
 \tr_N R(\mathbf{Y}_N,\mathbf{Y}_N^*)
 \longrightarrow
 \varphi\!\left(R(\mathsf{y},\mathsf{y}^*)\right)
 \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]
In particular, \(\mathbf{Y}_N\) converges almost surely in
\(*\)-distribution to \(\mathsf{y}\).  Consequently, if
\((b_N)\) is deterministic and \(b_N\to b\in\C\), then
\(b_N\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Y}_N\) converges almost surely in
\(*\)-distribution to \(b\mathbf{1}+\mathsf{y}\).
title: Lem 24 of arXiv:2608.05185

PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT (revision 2), no independent review. Let Gamma be a finite group and Q a Gamma-equivariant positive contraction on l^2(Gamma) with 0 < Q < I, and P_Q the determinantal measure with kernel Q. Let HM(Q) be the harmonic mean of the eigenvalues of Q. Then P_Q stochastically dominates the product Bernoulli measure of density HM(Q), and P_Q is dominated by the product measure of density 1 - HM(I - Q). Precise chain: the minimal conditional ODDS of presence is s_min = 1/(J^{-1})_ee = HM/(1 - HM) with J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}, and the minimal conditional PROBABILITY is s_min/(1 + s_min) = 1/(Q^{-1})_ee = HM(Q) (revision 2 states the odds and the probability separately, after a reviewer noted the two had been conflated in a side note). This is weaker than Lyons's Conjecture 5.7 (geometric mean / Fuglede-Kadison determinant), which numerical monotone-coupling linear programs on Z/nZ, n <= 6, satisfy exactly, with FK + 0.01 failing on a tested instance; those LP results are floating-point evidence, not certificates.

[Theorem thm:liggett-construction of arXiv:2608.05105, 'Cluster-Cluster model in $\mathbb{Z}^d$'] Let \(S\) be a finite set and let \(\Omega=S^{\mathbb Z^d}\), equipped with the
product topology. 
Suppose that \(L\) is a pure-jump operator on \(D(\Omega)\) of the form
\[
    Lf(\eta)=\int_\Omega \bigl(f(\xi)-f(\eta)\bigr)c(\eta,d\xi),
\]
where \(c(\eta,d\xi)\) is a transition kernel on \(\Omega\). Assume that, for
every \(f\in D(\Omega)\), \(Lf\in C(\Omega)\), and that there exists a constant
\(C_0<\infty\) such that
\[
    \sup_{\eta\in\Omega}
    \int_\Omega |f(\xi)-f(\eta)|\,c(\eta,d\xi)
    \le C_0 |||f|||
    \qquad \text{for all } f\in D(\Omega).
\]
Then \(L\) is closable on \(C(\Omega)\), and its closure generates a
conservative Feller semigroup on \(C(\Omega)\). In particular, there exists a
càdlàg Markov process on \(\Omega\) with generator extending \(L\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Liggett's construction theorem; \cite{Liggett1985InteractingParticleSystems}, Chapter I, Proposition 3.2

	 \caL(\SNR) = \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2  /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right].
\eeq
Here, when $\| \bsx \| = 0$, we define $x_i x_j / \| \bsx \|^2 = 0$ for all $i, j$.

    \]where $B_n$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric random matrix independent of $G_n$ and whose upper-triangular entries are independent and verify, for all $i\le j$,
    \[
        (B_n)_{ij}=\begin{cases}
            \mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{1}{{K_n}}\right) & \mbox{if }\quad 0 < \min\big(|i-j|,\, n - |i-j|\big) \le \frac{K_n}{2}, \\
            0 & \mbox{otherwise,}
        \end{cases}
    \]
    with $\mathcal{N}\left(0,1\right)$ the standard normal distribution.

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.28307, 'Rigidity of closed $\lambda$-self-expanders'] \cite{okumura1974hypersurfaces}
Let $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \cdots, \lambda_n, n\geq 3$, be real numbers such that $\sum_i\lambda_i=0$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i^2=\mu^2$. Then
$$\frac{-(n-2)\mu^3}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}\leq \sum_i\lambda_i^3\leq \frac{(n-2)\mu^3}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}},$$
and equality holds if and only if at least $(n-1)$ of $\lambda_i$ are equal. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 11 (Total variation in terms of densities) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $(\XX,\XXA)$ be a measurable space, let $\lambda$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on
it, and let $f, g : \XX \to [0,\infty]$ be measurable, finite $\lambda$-almost
everywhere, with $\int_{\XX} f \dd\lambda = \int_{\XX} g \dd\lambda = 1$. Let
$\mu,\nu \in \Prob$ be given by $\mu(A) := \int_{A} f \dd\lambda$ and
$\nu(A) := \int_{A} g \dd\lambda$ for $A \in \XXA$. Then
\[
  \tv{\mu - \nu}
  \;=\; \int_{\XX} (f-g)^{+} \dd\lambda
  \;=\; \tfrac12 \int_{\XX} |f-g| \dd\lambda ,
\]
the integrands being defined $\lambda$-almost everywhere.

[Thm Product process of arXiv:2412.05999, 'Non-Archimedean GUE corners and Hecke modules'] Let $t=1/q$ and $n\ge 1$ be an integer.

\begin{enumerate}[left=0pt]
\item(Alternating case) Fix $\nu \in \Sig_n, \mu \in \Sig_{2n}$. Let $A\in\Alt_{2n}(F)$ be a random matrix with the unique $GL_n(\mathfrak{o})$-invariant distribution such that $\SN^{\alt}(A)=\nu $, and let $B\in \mathrm{GL}_{2n}(F)$ be any (fixed or random) matrix with singular numbers $\SN(B)=\mu $. Then $\SN^{\alt}(B^TAB)$ has distribution 

$$
\mathbf{P}(\SN^{\alt}(B^TAB)=\lambda)=c_{\mu,\nu}^{\alt,\lambda}(t)\frac{P_\lambda(1,t^2,\ldots,t^{2n-2};t^2)}{P_\mu(1,t,\ldots,t^{2n-2},t^{2n-1};t)P_\nu(1,t^2,\ldots,t^{2n-2};t^2)}.$$

\item(Hermitian case) Fix $\nu,\mu \in \Sig_n$. Let $A\in\Her_n(F)$ be a random matrix with the unique $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathfrak{o})$-invariant distribution such that $\SN^{\her}(A) = \nu$, and let $B\in \mathrm{GL}_{2n}(F)$ be any (fixed or random) matrix with singular numbers $\SN(B)=\mu $. Then $\SN^{\her}(B^*AB)$ has distribution 

$$
\mathbf{P}(\SN^{\her}(B^*AB)=\lambda)=c_{\mu,\nu}^{\her,\lambda}(t)\frac{P_\lambda(1,-t,\ldots,(-t)^{n-1};-t)}{P_\mu(1,t^2,\ldots,t^{2n-2};t^2)P_\nu(1,-t,\ldots,(-t)^{n-1};-t)}.$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Rowwise independent Gaussian martingale differences can have predictable variance one and conditional Lindeberg while every row sum equals the same normal Z. Weak convergence then holds, but stable convergence to a normal independent of the entire underlying sigma-field fails without further cross-row assumptions.
All rows share one underlying probability space
Natural row filtrations need not be nested across rows
Stable independent limit is relative to the full underlying sigma-field

    D_{n,k}=Z/n+(E_{n,k}-bar E_n)/sqrt(n).

Each row is jointly Gaussian. Its covariance is

    Cov(D_{n,i},D_{n,j})
    =1/n^2+(delta_{ij}-1/n)/n
    =delta_{ij}/n.

Hence each row consists of independent N(0,1/n) variables. With its natural filtration and trivial initial sigma-field it is a martingale-difference row. Its predictable total variance is exactly one. For a standard normal G, its conditional Lindeberg sum is

    E[G^2 1{|G|>epsilon sqrt(n)}] -> 0.

    E[H f(sum_k D_{n,k})] = E[1{Z>0} tanh(Z)] >0,

whereas independence of a new standard normal G would give E[H]E[tanh(G)]=0. Thus convergence of distributions does not establish asymptotic independence from all existing randomness. TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the scale walk S_k as an exact random walk with identically distributed increments, as if the field were an exact branching random walk, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the comparison of S_k with a random walk (scale-dependent variances, the bounded error terms (iii)) must be explicitly controlled, while the Gibbs-Markov pieces themselves are exactly independent; skipping this control is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.
Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions
Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics
Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk

A family $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ (or a sequence $K_N$ with $N\to\infty$; the same definition works on $\mathbb T$) is an approximate identity if (i) $\int K_\varepsilon=1$ for every $\varepsilon$; (ii) $\sup_\varepsilon\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty$; (iii) for every $\delta>0$, $\int_{|x|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. If $K\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ with $\int K=1$, the dilates $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\varepsilon)$ form an approximate identity. Standard examples: the Gauss-Weierstrass (heat) kernel $\varepsilon^{-d}e^{-\pi|x|^2/\varepsilon^2}$, the Poisson kernel of the half-space, the Fejer kernel $F_N$ and the Poisson kernel $P_r(x)=\sum_n r^{|n|}e^{2\pi i n x}$ ($r\uparrow1$) on $\mathbb T$. Non-example: the Dirichlet kernel $D_N$ satisfies (i) but not (ii), since $\|D_N\|_1\to\infty$; this is the root of the divergence phenomena for Fourier series. Some texts add the stronger condition $\sup_{|x|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\to0$, which is the convenient hypothesis for convergence at a point of continuity of a merely integrable $f$ (the tail is then controlled by $\|f\|_1$). Almost-everywhere convergence at Lebesgue points needs more than either condition: the usual hypothesis is the dilation structure $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\varepsilon)$ together with an integrable radially nonincreasing majorant of $|K|$.
each K_eps is Lebesgue integrable

[Definition def:second-var of arXiv:2608.21805, 'Logarithmic derivatives of variational and singular stochastic partial differential equati'] Under Assumptions~(ass:LR of the paper), (ass:diff2 of the paper), and~(ass:SC of the paper), the \emph{Malliavin--second variation} $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)$ (for $0 \leq s \leq t \leq T$ and $r \in [0, t]$) is the linear map $H \to L^2(\Omega; L_2(U, H))$, $v \mapsto \mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)v$, defined fibrewise in both arguments: for each $v \in H$ and each noise direction $a \in U$, the $H$-valued directional fibre
\[
  \mathcal{Z}^{a}(t,s;r)v \;:=\; \bigl[\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)v\bigr]a \;\in\; H
\]
is the unique variational solution of the $H$-valued linearised stochastic evolution equation obtained by applying both sides of
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  \mathrm{d}\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r) &+ \mathcal{A}'_u(t, X(t))\,\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
  &= -\mathcal{A}''_{uu}(t, X(t))\bigl(\mathcal{D}_r X(t),\,Y(t,s)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
  &\quad + \mathcal{B}'_u(t, X(t))\bigl(\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}W(t)
    + \mathcal{B}''_{uu}(t, X(t))\bigl(\mathcal{D}_r X(t),\,Y(t,s)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}W(t),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
to $v$ and to the direction $a$ (so that $\mathcal{D}_r X$ is read as $\mathcal{D}_r X(\cdot)\,a = Y(\cdot, r)\bigl(\mathcal{B}(r, X(r))a\bigr) \in V$ throughout), with initial condition
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{Z}(\max(s, r),\,s;\,r)\,v \;=\;
  \begin{cases}
    0, & r < s,\\
    \mathcal{B}'_u(r, X(r))\bigl(Y(r,s)v\bigr) \;\in\; L_2(U, H), & s < r \leq t,\\
    \mathcal{B}'_u(s, X(s))\,v, & r = s \ \text{in Regime A},\\
    0, & r = s \ \text{in Regime B},
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
read directionally as $\mathcal{Z}^{a}(\max(s,r), s; r)v = \bigl[\mathcal{B}'_u(r, X(r))(Y(r,s)v)\bigr]a \in H$ in the second branch, which is defined for every $r$ in Regime~A and, in Regime~B, for almost every $r > s$, namely wherever $Y(r,s)v \in V$. The value at $r = s$ is Lebesgue-negligible in the $r$-integrals where $\mathcal{Z}$ occurs and no statement below depends on it. The equation is posed at the initial time $\max(s,r)$, so that $\mathcal{Z}(\cdot,s;r)v$ is evolved on $[\max(s,r), T]$.

The right-hand side of~(equation eq:second-var of the paper) is well-defined because, by~(SC3),
\[
  \mathcal{D}_r X(t) = Y(t,r)\mathcal{B}(r,X(r)) \in L_2(U, V) \quad \text{for a.e.\ } t:
\]
one has $[\mathcal{D}_r X(t)](f) \in V$ for each $f \in U$, and the bilinear actions
\[
  \mathcal{A}''_{uu}(\mathcal{D}_r X, Y(t,s)) \in V^*, \qquad \mathcal{B}''_{uu}(\mathcal{D}_r X, Y(t,s)) \in L_2(U, H)
\]
are pointwise defined by~(D3)--(D4), using the $V$-valued character of $Y(t,s)v \in V$ for a.e.\ $t$.

The relation $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r) = \mathcal{D}_r Y(t,s)$, directionally $\mathcal{Z}^a(t,s;r)v = \mathcal{D}^a_r[Y(t,s)v]$ for every $a \in U$, is established in Lemma~(lemma:DtYts of the paper); well-posedness at the doubly-fibrewise level, together with the reconstruction of the $L_2(U,H)$-valued object $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)v$ from its directions, is Theorem~(thm:Z-wellposed of the paper). Every composition of $\mathcal{Z}$ with a Hilbert--Schmidt argument in the sequel is read directionally in the Malliavin slot: for $\Theta \in L_2(U, H)$, $\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r)\Theta$ denotes the map $(a, u) \mapsto \mathcal{Z}^{a}(t,s;r)(\Theta u)$, an element of $L_2(U, L_2(U,H))$ whenever the corresponding double column sum is finite. As with $Y(t,r)$, the shorthand ``$\mathcal{Z}(t,s;r) \in L(H)$'' refers only to the fibrewise action; almost-sure operator-norm membership is strictly stronger and not provided by the abstract framework.
title: Malliavin--second variation

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03187, 'Duality for a Martingale Transport Problem with Moment Constraints'] We consider a weak martingale optimal transport problem related to the martingale analogue of the Benamou--Brenier formula. In contrast to the classical setting, the second marginal is not given, but specified only through a finite number of moment constraints of a particular form. For this problem, we derive a finite-dimensional dual formulation and prove the absence of a duality gap under the specified interiority condition on the constraint vector. In addition, we describe the structure of the optimal martingale coupling and its relation to Bass martingales.

[Lem 5 of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] Let $A$ be a reduced $\F_p$-algebra and $\alpha:L\to W(A)$ be a pre-log structure such that 
$F_{W(A)}(\alpha(l))=\alpha(l)^p$ for $l\in L$, where $F_{W(A)}$ is the Witt vector Frobenius. 
Then, we have $\alpha=[-]\circ \alphab$, where

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2607.18862, 'Tamed Euler Schemes for Singular SDEs with Multiplicative L\'{e}vy Noise'] Let $(\sE,\|\cdot\|)$ be a normed vector space, $s_0,\zeta_i,\gamma_i\in[0,1]$, $i=1,\cdots,n$ be fixed numbers. Suppose $R:(0,1]\to \sE$ is a function such that 
	\be 
	\|R_t-R_s\|\leq \sum_{i=1}^{n}C_is^{-\zeta_i}(t-s)^{\gamma_i},~~\forall~s_0\leq s\leq t\leq 1,s\neq 0
	\ee 
	for some constants $C_i\geq 0$,  $i=1,\cdots,n$. Assuming that $\gamma_i-\zeta_i>0$ for each $i$,   it follows that 
	$$\|R_t-R_s\|\leq \sum_{i=1}^{n}C_i(1-2^{\zeta_i-\gamma_i})^{-1}(t-s)^{\gamma_i-\zeta_i},~\forall~s_0\leq s\leq t\leq 1,s\neq 0.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 14 of arXiv:2607.18862

[Theorem thm:alpham of arXiv:2609.02155, 'Exact Limits of Random Projections for Preserving Geometry:\\ Distance Recovery, Nearest-N'] For every rank-$m$ linear $L$ and every measurable estimator $g$,
\[
\frac{\Var\bigl(\E[D\mid\mathcal{O}]\bigr)}{\Var(D)}\le\alpha_m(\Sigma),
\qquad
\E\bigl[(D-g(\mathcal{O}))^2\bigr]\ge 8\sum_{j>m}\lambda_j^2.
\]
The variance bound is attained when the row space of $L$ is the top-$m$
eigenspace of $\Sigma$; for this map, the mean-square bound is attained by
$g=\E[D\mid\mathcal{O}]$. The same statements, with
$\Var(S)=12\tr(\Sigma^2)$, hold for the neighbor contrast
$S=\left\lVertX_0-X_1\right\rVert^2-\left\lVertX_0-X_2\right\rVert^2$ given
$(LX_0,LX_1,LX_2)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Sharp rank-$m$ limit for distance recovery

[Lem ptinc of arXiv:2604.12963, 'Shocks, instability, and the twenty networks\\ of infinite geodesics in the Directed Lands'] Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing. Let $I$ denote the set of its points of increase.
\begin{enumerate} [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}] \itemsep=1pt 
\item $I$ is closed.
\item If furthermore $f$ is continuous, then $x\in I$ is right-isolated in $I$ if and only if there exists $y>x$ such that $f(y)=f(x)$. Similarly, $x\in I$ is left-isolated in $I$ if and only if there exists $z<x$ such that $f(z)=f(x)$.
\item If $f$ is continuous, then each point $x \in I$ is either not left-isolated in $I$ or not right-isolated in $I$ {\rm(}or both{\rm)}.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:80d97294b8e92df1cf0787bcb370b1de67dd6b177e2773265a99c045c266fd6b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/80/80d97294b8e92df1cf0787bcb370b1de67dd6b177e2773265a99c045c266fd6b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:2f3275b96176775d8eb5dc40419f498be81655f87995faf6f4fc0f29ccdd72c9","bundle_entry_key":"haar-orbit-mi-mmse-comparison-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-finite-moment-and-orbit-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:haar-orbit-mi-mmse-comparison-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Orbit mixing and a dimension-uniform Gaussian comparison

Target 2. Proof draft of an abstract comparison lemma, unaudited.
The application to iid products requires a primary-source check of
their common limiting singular-value law and of the Gaussian reference
mutual-information limit. These are separate inputs, not assumed proved
by the finite-size Taylor expansion.

Let A_n and B_n be random N_n by P_n real matrices with finite second
moments, d_n=N_n P_n. Suppose B_n is invariant in law under independent
left and right orthogonal transformations. Let their singular-value
vectors, in the same decreasing order and padded to min(N_n,P_n), be
coupled so that

 e_n^2 = E sum_j (sigma_j(A_n)-sigma_j(B_n))^2/d_n -> 0.    (1)

Assume i_{B,n}(s)=I(B_n;sqrt(s)B_n+G_n)/d_n converges to a finite
function i_B(s) for all s>0. Gaussian noise has independent standard
entries and is independent of each signal. Write m_{A,n}(s) for the
normalized product-signal MMSE, and likewise for B.

Then the claimed conclusions are

 limsup_n i_{A,n}(s) <= i_B(s),                          (2)
 limsup_n m_{A,n}(s) <= 2 i'_{B,-}(s),   s>0.            (3)

At every differentiability point of i_B,

 m_{B,n}(s) -> 2 i'_B(s),
 limsup_n m_{A,n}(s) <= lim_n m_{B,n}(s).                (4)

The finite concave function i_B has at most countably many
nondifferentiability points on (0,infinity). Thus the MMSE comparison
holds outside at most a countable exceptional set. If i_B is
differentiable throughout (0,infinity), it holds everywhere there.

## 1. Gaussian-smoothed entropy is Lipschitz in input Wasserstein distance

For any coupled R^d-valued U,V with finite second moments and an
independent standard Gaussian G,

 |I(U;sqrt(s)U+G)-I(V;sqrt(s)V+G)|
    <= sqrt(sd) (E||U-V||^2)^(1/2).                     (5)

For bounded U,V, interpolate U_t=(1-t)U+tV and let p_t be the density
of sqrt(s)U_t+G. Differentiating the Gaussian kernel gives

 partial_t p_t(y)=-sqrt(s) div E[(V-U)phi(y-sqrt(s)U_t)].

The continuity equation and integration by parts yield

 |partial_t h(p_t)|
 <= sqrt(s) [E||U-V||^2]^(1/2) J(p_t)^(1/2).

Indeed the conditional velocity E[V-U|sqrt(s)U_t+G=y] has square
integral at most E||V-U||^2, by conditional Jensen. The score identity

 grad log p_t(sqrt(s)U_t+G)=-E[G|sqrt(s)U_t+G]

gives J(p_t)<=E||G||^2=d. Integrating in t proves (5); the Gaussian
conditional entropy h(G) is the same for both channels.

For finite-second-moment inputs truncate the coupled pair in L^2.
Their convolved densities converge pointwise, have a common Gaussian
lower bound on every tail derived from a fixed input ball, and are
bounded above by (2pi)^(-d/2). Convergence in L^2 of the inputs gives
uniform integrability of the squared output norms, hence convergence
of output entropies by the compact-plus-tail argument used in
finite_moment_expansion.md, Section C. Thus (5) passes to the limit.
All constants in (5) are explicit and the dimension dependence is
exactly sqrt(d).

## 2. Haar mixing increases both quantities exactly at finite dimension

Let tilde A=Q A R^T with independent Haar orthogonal Q,R, independent
of A. The input law of tilde A is a mixture of orthogonal images of
the input law of A. Output entropy is concave in the input law;
Gaussian noise and Frobenius loss are invariant under these images.
Therefore

    I(A;sqrt(s)A+G) <= I(tilde A;sqrt(s)tilde A+G).        (6)

The Bayes MMSE is the infimum, over estimators f, of a risk linear in
the input law. Hence it too is concave in the input law and

    mmse(A;sqrt(s)A+G) <= mmse(tilde A;sqrt(s)tilde A+G).  (7)

This uses no assertion that singular vectors of A are already Haar.

Under the singular-value coupling (1), draw the same independent Haar
left and right matrices for the rectangular diagonal singular-value
representatives of A_n and B_n. The first resulting matrix has the
law of tilde A_n; the second has the law of B_n by its assumed
bi-orthogonal invariance. Their squared Frobenius distance is exactly
the sum in (1). Equation (5), divided by d_n, gives

    |i_{tilde A,n}(s)-i_{B,n}(s)| <= sqrt(s) e_n.         (8)

Equations (6) and (8) prove (2). They also show that i_{tilde A,n}
converges pointwise to i_B, rather than merely lying below it.

## 3. Concavity transfers the MMSE comparison

For a Gaussian channel, I-MMSE gives i'_{tilde A,n}(s)=m_{tilde A,n}(s)/2;
this derivative is nonincreasing, so each i_{tilde A,n} is concave.
Its finite pointwise limit i_B is concave as well. For 0<h<s,

    m_{A,n}(s)/2 <= i'_{tilde A,n}(s)
       <= [i_{tilde A,n}(s)-i_{tilde A,n}(s-h)]/h.

Take limsup in n and then let h decrease to zero. The left difference
quotient tends to i'_{B,-}(s), proving (3). For the reference B_n,
the usual two secant bounds for a concave function give convergence of
its derivatives wherever i_B is differentiable. This proves (4).
No differentiation of a one-sided MI inequality is used.

## 4. Precise iid-product application still to be discharged

For centered iid unit-variance factors A_n=UV^T/sqrt(N), the normalized
matrix A_n/sqrt(N)=UV^T/N has a deterministic limiting empirical
singular-value law depending only on the two aspect ratios, under
the usual iid product-matrix spectral hypotheses. The Gaussian-factor
product B_n has the same law in the limit and is bi-orthogonally
invariant. To invoke the lemma it remains to attach a primary theorem
with exactly these iid rectangular dimensions and moment assumptions.

If the normalized empirical laws converge in W2 in probability and
their squared W2 distances are uniformly integrable, independent
singular-value samples can be coupled through their ordered quantiles
and the deterministic common limit. Writing r=min(N,P),

 E||tilde A_n-B_n||_F^2/(NP)
    = (r/P) E W2(mu_{A_n/sqrt(N)},mu_{B_n/sqrt(N)})^2 ->0.

This is condition (1). Finite factor fourth moments give a convenient
uniform-integrability estimate, since

 E[(||A_n||_F^2/(NP))^2] <= E[A_{11}^4]
   =3(M/N)^2+(M/N^2)(E U^4 E V^4-3),

which is bounded under fixed aspect ratios. Convergence of the
empirical second singular moment also needs to be justified, rather
than inferred from weak spectral convergence alone. Its variance is
computed from shared-row/shared-column covariances and is O(N^-2)
under fixed aspect ratios and finite factor fourth moments.

The other external input is the finite Gaussian-factor limiting MI,
treated in rotationally invariant rectangular denoising papers. The
all-SNR MMSE assertion further requires differentiability of that
limit; without it (2)-(4) are the exact conclusions.

Hardest unpaid step for a full application: verify the singular-law
theorem's hypotheses and the Gaussian reference regularity directly
from primary sources. The abstract lemma itself does not establish
these inputs. Finite-size reversal at SNR tending to zero with n is
compatible with all of (2)-(4).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:8f63ff0321a76b62e9dac113608ece73cd7dca48d071ce1c705e60d4b4dbfd27","revision_digest":"sha256:1e9902bf6f9a60114b953a59d6a753588520e4041acbe46cff07d15df14fb81b","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:haar-orbit-mi-mmse-comparison-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma l01 of arXiv:2412.04015, 'Linear fluctuation of interfaces in Glauber-Kawasaki dynamics'] There exist a finite constant $C_d$, depending only on the dimension
$d$, and, for all $\ell\ge 1$, a flow $\Phi_\ell$ connecting the Dirac
measure at the origin to the measure $m^{(2)}_\ell$. This flow is
supported in $\Lambda_{2(\ell-1)}$ and on nearest-neighbour bonds. That
is,
\begin{equation*}
\Phi_\ell(x,y) \;=\;0
\end{equation*}
if $\Vert y - x \Vert \not = 1$ or if $\{x,y\} \not\subset
\Lambda_{2(\ell-1)}$. 
Moreover,
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{j=1}^d  \sum_{x\in{\mathbb Z}^d}\Phi_\ell(x,x+e_j)^2
\;\le\; C_d\; g_d(\ell)\;,
\end{equation*}
where $(g_d(\ell) : \ell\ge 1)$ is the sequence introduced in
(equation 2-18 of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma l01 of arXiv:2412.04015

body:
[Theorem 18 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(n\ge2\).  For each \(j\), let
\[
 (M_j^{2n},g_j(s),J_j,\nu^j_s,x_j),\qquad -A_j\le s\le0,
\]
be a pointed compact K\"ahler--Ricci flow with its point conjugate heat
kernel based at \((x_j,0)\), in the standard real convention
  \(\partial_sg_j=-2\Rc(g_j)\), where $A_j\ge1$.  Assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item \(A_j\to\infty\), the pairs are uniformly \(H_{2n}\)-concentrated,
  and
  \[
            \inf_j\mathcal N^{g_j}_{x_j,0}(1)>-\infty;
  \]
\item the pointed metric-flow pairs converge in \(\mathbb F\) on every
  compact negative time interval to
  \((\mathcal Z,g_{\mathcal Z}(s),\nu^Z_s,z)\);
\item the limit is a connected noncollapsed metric soliton and convergence is smooth
  on its full regular spacetime;
\item on the regular convergence charts, \(J_j\) converges smoothly to a
  parallel K\"ahler complex structure \(J_Z\), while the distinguished
  point-kernel densities converge smoothly to the distinguished soliton
  density.
\end{enumerate}
Put \(Z:=(\mathcal Z_{-1},d_Z)\), let
\(\mathcal R:=\mathcal R_{-1}\), and denote the limiting regular
K\"ahler structure by \((g_Z,J_Z,\omega_Z)\).  Then the following two
conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item The space \(Z\) carries a compatible normal complex-analytic
structure with klt singularities.  Its analytic and metric topologies
agree, and its analytic regular locus is precisely \(\mathcal R\).
\item The form \(\omega_Z\) extends locally across \(\Sing Z\) as a
positive current with bounded potential.  Every \(p\in Z\) has a
neighbourhood \(U\), a closed holomorphic embedding
\(\iota_U:U\hookrightarrow\Omega_U\subset\C^L\), and \(c_U>0\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \omega_Z\ge c_U\,\iota_U^*\omega_{\C^L}
 \qquad\text{on }U\cap\mathcal R.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem {\cite[Theorem A of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] {LandryMinskyTaylor2025_TransverseSurfacesAndPseudoAnosovFlows_PUB}}, {[Landry2022_VeeringTriangulationsAndTheThurstonNorm_PUB]}]
Let \(\varphi\) be a pseudo-Anosov flow with no perfect fits on \(M\). Suppose that \(S\) is a properly embedded, oriented surface in \(M\). Then the followings are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(S\) can be isotoped to be almost transverse to \(\varphi\).
\item \(S\) is taut and pairs nonnegatively with the closed orbits of \(\varphi\).
\item \(S\) is taut and \([S]\in \mathcal{C}_{2}(\varphi)\).
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:critical_decay of arXiv:2605.15545, 'Crossover from subcritical to critical decay: \\ random walk, self-avoiding walk, percolat'] [Critical decay]

Let $d\ge 1$ and $\delta>0$.
Suppose that Assumptions~(ass:Omega of the paper) and~(ass:J of the paper) hold for $S_z$ for each $z\in [z_c-\delta,z_c)$, suppose that $m_z \to 0$ as $z \to z_c$,
and suppose that there are constants $M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta$ such that
$(J_z^{(\mu)},h_z^{(\mu)}) \in \mathcal{Q}_{M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta}$ uniformly in $\mu\in \overline\Omega_z$ and in $z \in [z_c-\delta,z_c)$.
If $z \to z_c$ and $\abs x \to \infty$ in such a way that $m_z \abs x_z \to s \in [0,\infty)$, with $s > 0$ if $d \le 2$, then we have
\begin{equation}
S_z(x)
= \frac { d } {  \sigma_z^2 \norm x_2^{d-2} } \mathbb{G}_{ s }(\hat x)
	[ \hat h_z (0) + o(1)] .

[Lem lem6.2 of arXiv:2411.15724, 'Wasserstein Convergence Rates for Empirical Measures of Random Subsequence of $\{nα\}$'] Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number such that $\| q \alpha \| \geq C q^{-\gamma}$ for any $q \in \mathbb N$ with some constants $\gamma \geq 1$ and $C > 0$. Given any $\theta > 1$ and $\tau > 0$ which satisfy $\theta = \gamma \tau$, then for $\varepsilon \in (0, 1/2)$,

Method: Exact conditioning, spectral integral estimate, deterministic graph comparison or order-statistic asymptotics Result: For the displayed kernel p(x,y)=min(x,y)*g2(y)*f0(y)/(beta0*f0(x)), the measure with density pi(x)=g2(x)*f0(x)^2 has symmetric pair flow pi(x)p(x,y)=min(x,y)*g2(x)*g2(y)*f0(x)*f0(y)/beta0. This recovers the credited reversibility by inspection. The obstacle to identifying it with ordinary unimodular rerooting is the reproductive f0 bias: unimodularity is a mass-transport identity for the root law, while the spine favors descendants through the right eigenfunction. One must construct and normalize a two-sided marked spine with the appropriate Radon-Nikodym factor before claiming an equivalence. Check: Cancel exactly one factor of f0(x), then exchange x and y. For an ordinary unimodular graph, stationary simple-random-walk rerooting instead uses degree bias, exposing the missing identification. Obstruction: No general equivalence, converse, or root-bias formula beyond this explicit kernel calculation is proved.

body: In mathematics, theta functions are special functions of several complex variables. Fundamentally, they are a family of continuous functions which encode the behavior of discrete multi-dimensional periodic systems, such as crystal lattices or points on a torus. Because they are smooth, they allow the study and manipulation of discrete combinatorial systems using the tools of analysis.

body:
[Theorem 24 (Critical arithmetic under tensor product) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Suppose \(p_A,p_B,r_A,r_B,C_A,C_B>0\), the functions
\(\ell_A,\ell_B\) are eventually positive and slowly varying, and
\(A,B\) satisfy
\[
 \mathcal N_A(R)\sim C_Ae^{p_AR}R^{r_A-1}\ell_A(R),
 \qquad
 \mathcal N_B(R)\sim C_Be^{p_BR}R^{r_B-1}\ell_B(R).
\]
If \(p_A>p_B\), then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal N_{A\otimes B}(R)
 \sim C_A\zeta_B(p_A)e^{p_AR}R^{r_A-1}\ell_A(R).
 
\end{equation}
The symmetric formula holds when \(p_B>p_A\).  If
\(p_A=p_B=p\), then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal N_{A\otimes B}(R)
 \sim p\,\mathrm B(r_A,r_B)C_AC_B
 e^{pR}R^{r_A+r_B-1}\ell_A(R)\ell_B(R),
 
\end{equation}
where
\(\mathrm B(a,b)=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)\).
Consequently the power exponent with larger value dominates, while equal
power exponents resonate and their Mellin orders add.

In the pure logarithmic case, if \(p,r,\rho,a,b>0\) and
\[
 s_N(A)\sim aN^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(r-1)/p},\qquad
 s_N(B)\sim bN^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(\rho-1)/p},
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 s_N(A\otimes B)
 \sim ab\left(
 \frac{\Gamma(r)\Gamma(\rho)}{\Gamma(r+\rho)}
 \right)^{1/p}
 N^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(r+\rho-1)/p}.
 
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(s_N(A_j)\sim a_jN^{-1/p}\), then
\begin{equation}
 s_N(A_1\otimes\cdots\otimes A_k)
 \sim\frac{a_1\cdots a_k}{\Gamma(k)^{1/p}}
 N^{-1/p}(\log N)^{(k-1)/p}.
 
\end{equation}
Finally, for any \(p,r,\rho>0\), existence of the coefficients on the
right-hand sides below implies existence of those on the left, and
\begin{align}
 \mathscr R_p^{(r+\rho)}(A\otimes B)
 &=\mathscr R_p^{(r)}(A)\mathscr R_p^{(\rho)}(B),
 \\
 \mathscr R_p^{(r)}(A\otimes C)
 &=\mathscr R_p^{(r)}(A)\operatorname{Tr}|C|^p,
 \qquad 0\ne C\in\mathcal S_p,
 \\
 \mathscr R_p^{(r)}(cA)
 &=|c|^p\mathscr R_p^{(r)}(A),\qquad c\ne0.
 
\end{align}

body:
[Lemma lem:nointersect of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $F_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}$ denote the event that at least two different odd CLE$_4$ gaskets of nested CLE$_4$ intersect both 
$\mathbb{D}(z_1, \varepsilon_1)$ and $\mathbb{D}(z_2, \varepsilon_2)$. Then
\begin{itemize}
    \item Let $E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k}(z_1,z_2)$ denote the event that the $k$-th odd nested CLE$_4$ gasket intersects 
    $\mathbb{D}(z_1,\varepsilon_1)$ and $\mathbb{D}(z_2,\varepsilon_2)$. Then there is a constant $C > 0$
    such that for all $k \geq 1$,
    $$\mathbb{P}(F_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2} \cap E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k}(z_1,z_2)) 
    \leq C(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/4}\left(\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k}) + 
    \1_{k \geq 2}\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k-1})\right).$$
    \item Further, for some $\widetilde C > 0$, 
    for all $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 > 0$ sufficiently small, 
$$\sum_{k \geq 1}\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm{odd},k}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)) < 
\widetilde C\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm odd}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)).$$
    \item In particular, $\mathbb{P}(F_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2})$ is bounded by 
    $C(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/4}\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm odd}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1, z_2))$ for some $C > 0$ as 
    $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2) \to 0$. 
\end{itemize}
Further, the same holds when we replace odd by even everywhere. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2607.28215, 'Almost stochastic dominance via optimal transport'] Assume that there is a class $\mathcal{F}$ of functions $f:E\to \R$ such that, for the random variables under consideration,
$$
\mathrm{OT}_c(X,Y) = \sup \{\E[f(X)-f(Y)]: f\in \mathcal{F}\}. 
$$
Then, for $X,Y\in \mathcal{L}_{c,g}(E)$,
\begin{equation} 
X \le_{\gamma,g} Y \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad  \E[f(X)] \le \E[f(Y)] \quad \mbox{ for all } f \in \mathcal{F}_{\gamma,g} \cup\{g\},
\end{equation}
where
$$
 \mathcal{F}_{\gamma,g} := \{ (1-\gamma) f + \gamma g: f \in \mathcal{F} \}.
$$

The bootstrap: Sigma^ := sum_{i=1}^n (X_i X_i^T + X_i X_{i+1}^T + X_{i+1} X_i^T) (11), Sigma~ := argmin over p x p positive semidefinite Sigma' of ||Sigma' - Sigma^||_inf (12), Y~ given X_[1,n] is N(0, Sigma~), and mu(X_[1,n], Y~) := sup over hyper-rectangles A in R_p of |P(X_[1,n] in A) - P(Y~ in A | X_[1,n])|. Here X_1, ..., X_n are centered random vectors in R^p with at least q >= 3 moments, max_i E[||X_i||_inf^q] < infinity, that are m-ring dependent (X_i independent of X_j whenever min{|i - j|, n - |i - j|} > m), coupled with independent centered Gaussian vectors Y_1, ..., Y_n with Var[(Y_1^T, ..., Y_n^T)^T] = Var[(X_1^T, ..., X_n^T)^T]; X_I := sum_{i in I} X_i and Y_I likewise (4), [i, j] := {i, ..., j}; mu(X_[1,n], Y_[1,n]) := sup over hyper-rectangles A in R_p of |P(n^{-1/2} X_[1,n] in A) - P(n^{-1/2} Y_[1,n] in A)| (5); sigma^2_{min,I} := min_{k in [p]} Var[Y_{I,k}] and ul(sigma)^2_{I|I'} := lambda_min(Var[Y_I | {Y_i : i in I'}]) (ul = the paper's underline); the assumptions, for constants sigma_min, ul(sigma) > 0 and all I, I' in [1, n], are (MIN-VAR) sigma^2_{min,I} >= sigma^2_min |I|, (MIN-EV) ul(sigma)^2_{I|I'} >= ul(sigma)^2 |I intersect I'^indep|, where I'^indep is the set of j with X_j independent of {X_i : i in I'}, and (VAR-EV) sigma_min <= ul(sigma) sqrt(log(4ep)/2); L_{q,i} := max_{k in [p]} E[|X_{i,k}|^q] + max_{k in [p]} E[|Y_{i,k}|^q] and nu_{q,i} := E[||X_i||_inf^q] + E[||Y_i||_inf^q] (6), Lbar_{q,I} and nubar_{q,I} their averages over i in I, Lbar_q := Lbar_{q,[1,n]} and nubar_q := nubar_{q,[1,n]} (7).

body:
[Lemma 6 (Linear-programming duality) of arXiv:2609.02080, 'Logarithmic basis number of graphs'] Let $G$ be a connected simple graph on $n\ge2$ vertices.  There is a probability distribution $p=(p_{\Bas})_{\Bas\in\mathfrak B(G)}$ on $\mathfrak B(G)$ such that
\[
    \sum_{\Bas\in\mathfrak B(G)}p_{\Bas}\ch_{\Bas}(e)
       \le a\log n
    \qquad\text{for every }e\in E(G),
\]
where $a$ is the constant from \cref{thm:weighted-basis}.
title: Linear-programming duality

body: [Theorem thm:law_of_quantum_lengths of arXiv:2412.04005, '$\SLE_{\kappa}(\rho)$ processes in the light cone regime on\\ Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\kappa$ and $\rho$ as above.  Let $\mathcal {W}$ be a quantum wedge of weight $\rho + 2$ and let $h$ be the corresponding field. Let $Y$ be the Bessel process encoding $\mathcal {W}$ and $(e_{j})_{j \in \mathbf{N}}$ be its excursions away from zero. Let $(h_{j})_{j \in \mathbf{N}}$ be the fields encoding the surfaces determined by the above excursions. Let also $t_{j}$ be the boundary quantum length associated with $h_{j}$ for all $j \in \mathbf{N}$. Then $(t_{j})$ has the law of a $\text{p.p.p.}$ with intensity measure given by $c( du \times t^{\alpha}dt)$ where $\alpha = -2 + \frac{2(\rho + 2)}{\kappa}$ and $c > 0$ is a constant depending only on $\alpha$ and $\rho$.
