[Lemma supportinequality of arXiv:2507.16188, 'The noisy voter model with general initial conditions'] {LubetzkySly14}}] 
For any $t \geq \hat t \geq 0$ and any set $W$ of vertices at time~$t$ in the space-time slab, if $\hat W$ denotes the (random) history of $W$ at time $\hat t$, we have
\[
\left\|\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}(X_{t}(W)\in \cdot)-\mu_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{W}\right\|_{\textsc{tv}} \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\big\|\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}(X_{\hat t}(\hat W)\in \cdot)-\mu_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{\hat W}\big\|_{\textsc{tv}}\right]\,,
\]
where the expectation is with respect to the update sequences along $[\hat t,t]$. Furthermore, if $\{X_t^{(i)}\}$ are i.i.d.\ copies of the dynamics, and $\tau_i\in[0,t]$ are stopping times for their backward dynamics, then
\[
\left\|\prod \mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}\big( X_{t}^{(i)}(W_i)\in \cdot\big)-\prod \mu^{(i)}_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{W_i}\right\|_{\textsc{tv}} \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\big\|\prod \mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}(X_{t-\tau_i}(\hat W_i)\in \cdot)-\prod \mu_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{\hat W_i}\big\|_{\textsc{tv}}\right]\,.
\]

[Thm 221 (\textbf{informal statement of main result}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] A measure $\mu$ can be approximated by $\mu_{\bG}(\bx)$, with $\bx$ the output of a Lipschitz algorithm \eqref{eq:algorithms-as-maps},
if and only if:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item  (for the spherical setting, where $\bx$ must lie near $S_N$)  $\mu$ lies in

$\bar{\cM}^{\Ising}(\alpha)$.

$\bar{\cM}^{\sph}(\alpha)$ and 
$\bar{\cM}^{\Ising}(\alpha)$
are specified by Definition~\ref{d:achievable-msrs}. Moreover they coincide with the sets
$\ocM^{\sph, \concave}(\alpha)$ and

[Proposition 25 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Length of the typical relaying zone.}

Let us consider $H$ a random variable distributed following $\mathcal{L}$. Let us further consider the landscape $\tilde{\landsc} := \landsc\cup \{(0, H)\}$. Then expectation of the length of the zone of the typical eventual relaying $\zone (0, H)$ is 
\[\e[\ell(\zone(0, H))] = \frac{1}{\lambda}\e[T],\]
where $T$ is the hitting time of the cemetery state $(-\infty, -\infty, -\infty)$ for the Markov chain $(\tilde{x}_n, \mathrm{t}_n, H_n)$ started at 
$(0, 0, +\infty)$:
\[\e[T] = \sum_{n\geq 1} \displaystyle\int_{\Half^{n+1}} g_n \delta_{(0, 0)}\displaystyle\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n} (\Leb \otimes \mathcal{L}).\]

[Theorem thm:intro-abstract-response of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] In the abstract setup above, suppose
Assumptions~(ass:admissible-forms of the paper)--(ass:spectral-borel of the paper) hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item The positive spectrum is almost surely simple:
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\!\left\{x\in\Omega_{\rm str}:
  \dim\ker(A_{\mu_x}-\Lambda_n^{\mu_x})=1
  \text{ for every }n\ge1
 \right\}=1.
 
\end{equation}
\item Fix $M\ge1$ and $1\le n_1<\cdots<n_M$.  If, for
$\mathbb P$-almost every $x\in\Omega_{\rm str}$, the selected positive
eigenvalues form a response-transverse family in the sense of
Definition~(def:abstract-response-transversality of the paper), then
\begin{equation}
 (\Lambda_{n_1}^{\mu_x},\ldots,\Lambda_{n_M}^{\mu_x})_\#\mathbb P
 \ll\mathcal L^M.
 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma sublemma of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] For $\omega \in \Omega$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$, define a measure $\mu_n^{\omega}$ by
\[
\mu_n^{\omega}\coloneqq \sum_{D\in \mathcal{D}_n}\nu(D)a_{n,D}\sum_{k=M_n}^{N_n} 
  \chi_{D\cap (C-V_k)}(\omega_k )\delta_{\omega_k}.
\]
Then $\mu_n^{\omega}\to \nu$ almost surely in the weak-$\ast$ topology.
title: Lemma sublemma of arXiv:2506.10448

Let S_t be the square-integrable Cox-CIR jump-diffusion asset price and X_t = ln S_t with running maximum M_T = sup_{0 <= t <= T} X_t. Then M_T admits the explicit Clark-Ocone martingale representation M_T = E[M_T] - int_0^T E[ 1_{[0, tau]}(t) * int_t^tau mu_bar_s D_t^{(1)} lambda_s ds | F_t ] dW_t + int_0^T int_{R_0} psi(t, z, M_t - J_{t, z}) d N_tilde^c(dt, dz), where mu_bar_s = int_{R_0} (e^{J_{s, z}} - 1) nu(dz), tau = inf{t : X_t = M_T}, and the jump kernel is given by psi(t, z, y) = 1_{J_{t, z} >= 0} int_y^{M_t} int_0^infinity F_bar_{t, x, r} dr dx - 1_{J_{t, z} < 0} int_{M_t}^y int_0^infinity F_bar_{t, x, r} dr dx, with joint tail probability F_bar_{t, x, r} = P(sup_{t <= s <= T} X_s > x, sup_{t <= s <= T} lambda_s > r | F_t).
S_t is square-integrable
Feller condition holds for CIR intensity lambda_t

[Proposition prop mdp y_t of arXiv:2604.10509, 'Nonequilibrium fluctuations and moderate deviations for the occupation time of the SSEP wi'] The sequence of processes $\{\mathcal{Y}_t / a_n, 0 \leq t \leq T\}_{n \geq 1}$ satisfies the large deviation principle with decay rate $a_n^2 $ and with rate function $\mathcal{Q}_T$. Precisely speaking, for any closed set $C$ and any open set $O$ in $D([0,T], \mathcal{D}^\prime (\mathbb T^d))$,
	\begin{align*}
		\limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{a_n^2} \log \mathbb P^n_{\rho_*} \Big( \{\mathcal{Y}_t/a_n, 0 \leq t \leq T\} \in C\Big) \leq - \inf_{\mu \in C} \mathcal{Q}_T (\mu),\\
		\liminf_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{a_n^2} \log \mathbb P^n_{\rho_*} \Big( \{\mathcal{Y}_t/a_n, 0 \leq t \leq T\} \in O\Big) \geq - \inf_{\mu \in O} \mathcal{Q}_T (\mu).
	\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop mdp y_t of arXiv:2604.10509

[Theorem 7 (Local-global relation for one function) of arXiv:2609.03976, '2609.03976'] Let $f\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a nonzero regular function. For every open subset $U\subseteq X$, $b_{f,U}(s)=\operatorname{lcm}_{x\in U}b_{f,x}(s)$.
		Consequently, if $V\subseteq U$ is open, then $b_{f,V}(s)\mid b_{f,U}(s)$
		and for every $x\in U$, $b_{f,x}(s)\mid b_{f,U}(s)$.
		In particular, $b_f(s)=\operatorname{lcm}_{x\in X}b_{f,x}(s)$,
		and hence $b_{f,x}(s)\mid b_f(s)$
		for every $x\in X$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Local-global relation for one function

[Theorem thm_longest_paths of arXiv:2606.09488, 'The temporal stochastic block model'] Suppose assumptions (ass1 of the paper) and (ass2 of the paper) hold. Fix $u,v \in V$. Then, 
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
    \item $|\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}| \in (e\theta\log n,\alpha(\theta)\log n)$ whp, where $$\alpha(\theta)\coloneqq \inf\left\{x>0: \log\left(\frac{x}{e\theta}\right)=1 \right\}  ;$$
	\item $|\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}(v)| \sim_p e\theta\log n$;
	\item if $\theta>1$, then $|\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}(u,v)| \sim_p \beta(\theta)\log n$ and $|\gamma_{\mathrm{min}}(u,v)| \sim_p \gamma(\theta)\log n,$, where
    $$\beta(\theta) \coloneqq \sup\left\{x>0:x\log\left(\frac{x}{e\theta}\right)=-1\right\},$$
    $$\gamma(\theta) \coloneqq \inf\left\{x>0:x\log\left(\frac{x}{e\theta}\right)=-1\right\}. $$
    However, if $\theta<1$, then whp there is no increasing path between $u$ and $v$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm_longest_paths of arXiv:2606.09488

body: [Definition 2 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] Given $0< t \le T$, we say that the process $X^\varepsilon$ does not jump from $0$ to $1$ during the time interval $(0,t)$ if and only if for any $r \in (0,t)$, we have $0 \le X_r^\varepsilon \le y_*^\varepsilon$, i.e. $e_1^\varepsilon \ge t$. This is equivalent to saying that for all $i\ge 1$ such that $\tau_i^\varepsilon \in (0,t)$, the condition $0<\tau^{\varepsilon}_{i+1} -\tau_i^\varepsilon<T_*^\varepsilon$ holds.

body:
[Corollary 100 (Hilbert-valued L\'evy entrance) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Every c\`adl\`ag Hilbert-valued L\'evy process with finite second moment has a
canonical degree-two critical split lift
\[
 (L_{s,t},A^L_{s,t},[L]_{s,t})
\]
with stopped Chen identities and finite-rank projection stability.  The lift
may be chosen as a shift-covariant Borel functional on the Skorokhod path
space.  Hence, after every bounded stopping time, the lifted future is
independent of the past and has the law of the original lifted process.
At stochastic weights above two the jump alphabet contains additional
power-jump primitives, which belong to the quasi-shuffle normal geometry.

[Definition 16 (Laplace transform order $\leq_{\textnormal{L}}$) of arXiv:2605.16560, 'Seasonal Statistics of Shannon Rate in a Dynamical Poisson-Voronoi Cellular Network'] We say that two non-negative random variables $X,Y$ satisfy {\em Laplace order} 

\[
X\leq_{\textnormal{L}}Y, \;\;\mbox{ if }\;\; \E_X\left[e^{-\gamma X}\right] \geq  \E_Y\left[e^{-\gamma Y}\right],
\]

for any $\g\geq 0$. The inequality is flipped because of the negative exponent.
title: Laplace transform order $\leq_{\textnormal{L}}$

[Lemma 10 (Replacement lemma) of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Let \(k\in\{1,2\}\). Fix \(x\notin\Sigma_n^{\varepsilon,R}\), and let
	\(\psi:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R\) be a uniformly bounded function whose support does not
	intersect the averaging box $ \{x+1,\ldots,x+\lfloor\varepsilon n\rfloor\} $.
	Then, for every \(t\in[0,T]\),
	\[
	\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
	\limsup_{n\to\infty}
	\mathbb E_{\mu^n}^n
	\left[
	\left|
	\int_0^t
	\psi(\tau_x\eta_s)
	\left(
	\eta_k^x(s)
	-
	\overrightarrow\eta_k^{\,\lfloor\varepsilon n\rfloor}(x,s)
	\right)
	\,\mathrm ds
	\right|
	\right]
	=0.
	\]
	The analogous estimate holds for the left average

Status: exact computational certificate plus a proved composition lemma; pending w346 KEEP. No novelty or full solution is claimed. Local status source is Garban and Steif, *Noise Sensitivity of Boolean Functions and Percolation* (2012), Exercise VIII.5 note, p. 97. The 7 September intake still labels the exponent unverified and unresolved.

Let f_k be iterated majority of three on 3^k independent fair bits. Algorithms query bits and must always return the exact output. Revealment is the largest probability that an individual bit is queried, under the uniform input and internal randomization.

For k=2, the minimum expected number of queries is 393/64 = 6.140625. Its minimum revealment is 131/192 = 0.6822916667. The usual recursive algorithm has expected cost 25/4 and revealment 25/36. Thus the verified finite-block cost decreases by 1.75%.

The certificate in check_majority.py examines all 19,683 partial assignments. At a partial assignment with m free bits, let A(s) be the sum of the remaining query counts over its 2^m compatible complete inputs. A(s)=0 if the function is forced; otherwise A(s)=2^m+min_i[A(s with bit i=0)+A(s with bit i=1)]. Every zero-error decision tree must choose an unqueried bit at a nonterminal state, so induction on m proves this recurrence gives the optimum. Randomization cannot beat the minimum of its deterministic trees. All computations use integers; the only division is by 2^9 at the root.

The independent checks use the 512-entry truth table to verify the terminal condition in every partial assignment, verify every Bellman residual and chosen action, and execute the complete policy on every input. All three error counts are zero; all outputs are correct and the sum of the 512 query counts is 3144. The policy is in majority_policy.json.

Randomize the policy by a uniform automorphism of the full ternary tree. This finite group preserves f_2 and acts transitively on its nine leaves. Each leaf then has revealment (393/64)/9 = 131/192. Conversely, any algorithm's maximum revealment is at least its expected query count divided by nine. This proves the finite-block optimum, subject to audit of the certificate.

For any k, evaluate each logical bit requested by this depth-two policy using a recursively composed policy on an independent descendant subtree. A logical subtree is selected before any of its own inputs are examined, so its selection event is independent of its bits and fresh internal randomness. At each block, the nine outputs are independent fair bits. A fixed leaf's query probability is consequently the product of the block probabilities. Hence

    delta_k <= (131/192)^floor(k/2) * (5/6)^(k mod 2).

For even k=2m this is n^(-0.17399134015245032), improving the exponent 0.16595623285353023 of the usual recursive construction. It is an achievable bound, not the exact asymptotic exponent. The former influence lower bound delta_k >= (2/3)^k still applies.

For NONNEGATIVE real numbers a_1, ..., a_n, (a_1 + ... + a_n)/n >= (a_1 a_2 ... a_n)^(1/n), with equality if and only if a_1 = ... = a_n. WEIGHTED FORM: if w_1, ..., w_n >= 0 with w_1 + ... + w_n = 1 and a_1, ..., a_n >= 0, then w_1 a_1 + ... + w_n a_n >= a_1^(w_1) ... a_n^(w_n), with the convention 0^0 = 1, and with equality if and only if all a_i with w_i > 0 are equal. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) nonnegativity is essential. With n = 2 and a_1 = a_2 = -1 the arithmetic mean is -1 while the product is 1 and its positive square root is +1, so the inequality as usually read reverses; the theorem is about nonnegative entries, never about arbitrary reals. (ii) With at least one zero entry and n >= 2 the geometric mean is 0 and the inequality is strict unless every entry is 0. (iii) The weights must be nonnegative AND sum to 1; dropping the normalisation makes the statement false, and the correct inhomogeneous relative is Young's inequality ab <= a^p/p + b^q/q with 1/p + 1/q = 1. (iv) The inequality is homogeneous of degree one, so it can be rescaled but never used to compare means of different orders; that is the power mean inequality, of which AM-GM is the limiting case as the exponent tends to 0.

in the weighted form the weights are nonnegative and sum to exactly 1
the geometric mean is the nonnegative real root of the product
the convention 0^0 = 1 is used for zero weights

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a space $X$ with a sum operation $+$, we can define the convolution of any two probability measures on it by the following formula:
$$(\mu*\nu)(E)=(\mu\times\nu)\left((x,y)\Big|x+y\in E\right)$$
Equivalently, in terms of the associated integrals, we must have 
$$\int_Xf(x)d(\mu*\nu)(x)=\int_{X\times X}f(x+y)d\mu(x)d\nu(y)$$
for any measurable function $f:X\to\mathbb R$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

(ass:bochner-regularity of the paper), the identities
(equation eq:occupation-current-splitting of the paper) hold in distributions.  Moreover,
for every $0<\varepsilon<T$,
\begin{equation}
 \left\lVert c\right\rVert_{0;(\varepsilon,T)}^2
 +\int_{(\varepsilon,T)\times\mathbb R^d}
 \left(|\operatorname{Ric}_g+\operatorname{Hess}_g\mathcal V|_g
       +|\partial_tg+\operatorname{Lie}_c g|_g\right)\,\mathrm d\mathfrak m<\infty.
 
\end{equation}
In addition, $c,D_xc\in L^{p_0}_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$, where $p_0$ is the fixed exponent
in Assumption~(ass:bochner-regularity of the paper).  Consequently, the tensor
$\mathscr R_{w,t}=w(t)\mathscr R_t+2w'(t)g_t$ is integrable over every
positive-time strip for every regular weight $w$.

[Introthm 6 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $M$ be a matroid and $F$ an inclusion-minimal modular flat in $M$ such that 
$M$ is a non-trivial modular join over $F$.
Write $M = P_{F}(M|_{F'}, M|_{F''})$ for some flats $F', F''$ of $M$ containing $F$.

[Theorem 2 (Linear exact equilibrium support) of arXiv:2608.24837, 'Strategic geometry of competing first-passage random walks'] For every \(k\geq 2\), the graph \(G_{k,2}\) has \(3k\)
vertices and every exact optimal strategy \(\mu\) satisfies

\[
\operatorname{supp}(\mu)=\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}.
\tag{3.3}
\]

Consequently

\[
\min_{\mu\in\mathcal O(G_{k,2})}|\operatorname{supp}(\mu)|
=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal O(G_{k,2})}|\operatorname{supp}(\mu)|
=k
=\frac{|V(G_{k,2})|}{3}.
\tag{3.4}
\]

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Local finiteness of scale-invariant network traffic measures structural attempt Result: For a bounded area A, translation invariance and Tonelli give expected full-network traffic through A equal to area(A)*integral_R2 |z|^-beta*E len R(0,z) dz. Scale invariance makes E len R(0,z)=Delta*|z|, yielding area(A)*2*pi*Delta*integral_0^infinity r^(2-beta) dr. This integral diverges for every beta: at infinity for beta<=3, at zero for beta>=3. Check: Translate each route by its source and integrate the length of its intersection with A over all source locations. Each infinitesimal route segment contributes area(A). This mass-transport identity uses nonnegative integrands, so it remains valid when the integral is infinite. Obstruction: The divergent full-network expectation neither disproves almost-sure local finiteness nor answers the restricted-major-road question. A proof must exploit the major-road restriction and separately control long routes and short routes which take large excursions.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0226-local-finiteness-of-scale-invariant-network-traffic-measures
No independent review

body: The real numbers are complete: every nonempty set of reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound (supremum) in R. This distinguishes R from Q (the rationals lack sup for e.g. {x : x^2 < 2}). Equivalent formulations: every bounded monotone sequence converges; every Cauchy sequence converges; nested closed bounded intervals have nonempty intersection; R has no gaps (Dedekind completeness). Completeness is the single axiom from which Bolzano-Weierstrass, the intermediate and extreme value theorems, and the whole convergence theory follow.
title: Completeness of the Reals (Least Upper Bound Property)

[Theorem thmluczak of arXiv:2411.18563, 'Lower tails for triangles inside the critical window'] Let $\Omega_0$ be a non-empty subset of $\Omega$, and let $(\alpha_i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a sequence of positive constants such that, for all $i$,
\[
\sup_{x,y\in \Omega_0: d(x,y)=1} d_W(\mu_i^{x}, \mu_i^{y})\leq \alpha_i\, .
\]
Let 
\[
\Omega_0^0=\{x\in \Omega_0 : y \in \Omega_0 \text{ whenever } d(x,y)=1\} .
\]
Let $f:\Omega\to \mathbb R$ be 1-Lipschitz. Then for all $x_0\in \Omega_0^0$, $u,t>0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\delta_{x_0}}\left(\{|f(X_t)-\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{x_0}}[f(X_t)]|\geq u\}\wedge \{X_s\in \Omega_0^0: 0\leq s\leq t\} \right)
\leq 
2e^{-u^2/(2\sum_{i=1}^t \alpha_i^2)}\, .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thmluczak of arXiv:2411.18563

When $\Adm^\star(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0)$ does not depend on some of these parameters we will sometimes omit them from the notation, writing e.g. $\cM^\BOGP(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) = \cM^\BOGP(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0)$ for all $L_0,\epsilon_0$. Define
    \[
        \sM^\star(\alpha,q_0) 
        = \adjustlimits 
        \bigcap_{\epsilon_0 > 0} 
        \bigcup_{L_0>0}
        \bigcap_{\epsilon>0}
        \bigcup_{L>0}
        \cB_{\epsilon_0}(\cM^\star(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0))\,.
    \]
Note that this order of quantifiers corresponds to the limit \eqref{e:control.problems.limiting.regime}.

Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H and let B be symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A), where 0 ≤ a < 1 and b ≥ 0. Then A + B, defined on D(A + B) = D(A), is self-adjoint, and it is essentially self-adjoint on every core of A. If in addition A is bounded below by M, then A + B is bounded below by M − max{b/(1 − a), a|M| + b}. (Wüst's theorem covers the borderline a = 1: if B is symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ ‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖, then A + B is essentially self-adjoint on D(A), though possibly not self-adjoint there.) Standard application (Kato): for n ≤ 3 and V ∈ L²(ℝⁿ) + L^∞(ℝⁿ) real valued, multiplication by V has −Δ-bound 0, so −Δ + V is self-adjoint on H²(ℝⁿ) and essentially self-adjoint on C_c^∞(ℝⁿ); this covers V(x) = −γ/|x| in ℝ³, the hydrogen Hamiltonian.

Normal approximation for a sum of locally dependent variables: when each summand is independent of all but a few others, Stein's method bounds the distance of the standardized sum from the normal law by the neighbourhood size and the third and fourth moments. Ross, Definition 3.1: a collection of random variables (X_1, ..., X_n) has dependency neighborhoods N_i ⊆ {1, ..., n}, i = 1, ..., n, if X_i is independent of {X_j}_{j∉N_i}. Theorem 3.5: let X_1, ..., X_n be random variables with E[X_i⁴] < ∞, E[X_i] = 0, σ² = Var(Σ_i X_i), and W = Σ_i X_i/σ; let (X_1, ..., X_n) have dependency neighborhoods N_i with D = max_i |N_i|. Then for Z a standard normal random variable, d_W(W, Z) ≤ (D²/σ³) Σ_i E|X_i|³ + (√26 D^{3/2}/(√π σ²)) √(Σ_i E[X_i⁴]) (3.8). Ross applies it to the number of triangles in the Erdős-Rényi graph G(n,p) (Section 3.2.1).

[Lemma lem:initial-robin of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $\kappa,R>0$, $\mathbf a_*\in D$, and $\rho>0$ satisfy
$B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)\Subset D$.
Then there exist
$\varepsilon_{\rm I}=\varepsilon_{\rm I}(D,\rho,\mathbf a_*,R)>0$ and
$C_{\rm I}=C_{\rm I}(D,\rho,\mathbf a_*,\kappa,R)>0$ such that whenever
$0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{\rm I}$,
$\mathbf a_\varepsilon\in B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)$, and a nonnegative
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(D)$ satisfies
\[
  \int_D\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=\kappa,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R\varepsilon}(\mathbf a_\varepsilon),
\]
one has
\begin{equation*}
  |\mathcal R(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})
  -\kappa^2H(\mathbf a_\varepsilon)|\leq C_{\rm I}\varepsilon.
\end{equation*}

body:
[Corollary 16 (Curvature raises ancestry) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] The exact identities
\begin{align}
 [\nabla_u,\nabla_v]&={\operatorname{ad}}_{\Omega(u,v)}|_D,
 \\
 \nabla_u\Omega(v,w)-\nabla_v\Omega(u,w)+\nabla_w\Omega(u,v)&=0
 
\end{align}
hold.  Moreover,
\(D\) is the smallest Lie subalgebra of \(L\) which contains
\(\Omega(\Lambda^2V)\) and is stable under every \(\nabla_u\), and
\begin{equation}
 \nabla_u\gamma_r(D)\subseteq\gamma_r(D),\qquad
 [\nabla_u,\nabla_v]\gamma_r(D)\subseteq\gamma_{r+1}(D),
 
\end{equation}
and curvature has the well-defined transverse symbol
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R^{(r)}_{u,v}:
 \gamma_r(D)/\gamma_{r+1}(D)\longrightarrow
 \gamma_{r+1}(D)/\gamma_{r+2}(D),
 \qquad[d]\longmapsto[\Omega(u,v),d].
 
\end{equation}
The induced \(V\)-actions on each fixed ancestry layer commute, and the
degree-one curvature class is
\(\kappa(1\otimes u\wedge v)\in Q\).

[Proposition 26 (Ambiguous leaves under parallel \(F\)) of arXiv:2608.29406, 'Partially Totally Real Submanifolds of Sasakian Manifolds'] Assume that \(F\) is parallel.  Then \(\Dtilde\) is integrable and its
leaves are totally geodesic in \(M\) if and only if
\begin{align}
 g(\nabla_X^\perp FY,\phi Z)&=0,
 \\
 g(PX,Y)&=0
 
\end{align}
for all \(X,Y\in\Gamma(\Dtilde)\) and
\(Z\in\Gamma(\Dperp)\).  In particular, if \(\Dperp\) is maximal and
\(\Dtilde\ne0\), these conditions cannot hold simultaneously.

Condition \eqref{eq:Fparallel-Reebcondition} is equivalent to
\(P|_{\Dtilde}=0\).  Maximality is used only in the final non-existence
conclusion, where \(P|_{\Dtilde}=0\) contradicts injectivity unless
\(\Dtilde=0\).

body:
[Corollary cor:MMi2 of arXiv:2606.24881, 'Queues with Correlated Service Times --- the $M/M_D/c$ Model'] Consider the $M/M_i/2$ queue obtained from the $M/M_D/2$ model by setting
\[
\mu_{12}=0.
\]
Assume the routing rule used throughout this paper: when both servers are
idle, an arrival is assigned to server \(1\) (equivalently, \(p=1\) in the
earlier \(M/M_D/2\) notation). Let
\[
\rho:=\frac{\lambda}{\mu_1+\mu_2},
\qquad \lambda<\mu_1+\mu_2.
\]
Then the stationary probabilities are given by
\begin{align}
\pi_{(1,0)} &= \frac{1+\rho}{1+2\rho}\,\frac{\lambda}{\mu_1}\,\pi_0, \\
\pi_{(0,1)} &= \frac{\rho}{1+2\rho}\,\frac{\lambda}{\mu_2}\,\pi_0, \\
\pi_2 &= \rho\bigl(\pi_{(1,0)}+\pi_{(0,1)}\bigr), \\
\pi_n &= \rho^{\,n-2}\pi_2, \qquad n\ge 2, 
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
\pi_0=
\left[
1+\frac{1+\rho}{1+2\rho}\frac{\lambda}{\mu_1}
+\frac{\rho}{1+2\rho}\frac{\lambda}{\mu_2}
+\frac{1}{1-\rho}\,
\frac{\rho\lambda}{1+2\rho}
\left(\frac{1+\rho}{\mu_1}+\frac{\rho}{\mu_2}\right)
\right]^{-1}.
\end{equation}
In particular, this coincides with Singh~[Singh:1970] for the

body: Define the Turing jump hierarchy above the empty set by 0^{(0)} equal to the empty set, and 0^{(n+1)} equal to the halting problem relative to an oracle for 0^{(n)}, so 0^{(1)} = 0' is the ordinary halting problem. Post's theorem states that a set B of natural numbers is definable by a Sigma^0_{n+1} formula of arithmetic if and only if B is computably enumerable relative to the oracle 0^{(n)}, and that 0^{(n+1)} has the same Turing degree as a complete Sigma^0_{n+1} set, and also as the set of true Sigma^0_{n+1} sentences. This aligns the syntactic arithmetical hierarchy with the effective Turing jump hierarchy. Proved by Emil Post.
title: Post's theorem

[Pro1 28 of arXiv:2608.29797, 'Mean-field branching SDEs: propagation of chaos, scaling limits and phase transitions'] Let $q_1,q_2:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be locally bounded
Borel functions. For $i=1,2$, let $Z^i$ be a nonnegative
nonexplosive solution of
\beqnn
Z_t^i
=Z_0^i+\int_0^t
\bigl(q_i(s)-\beta Z_s^i-b_2(Z_s^i)^2\bigr)\,\d s
+\int_0^t\int_0^{Z_s^i}W(\d s,\d u),
\eeqnn
where the two equations are driven by the same Gaussian white noise
$W$ with intensity $2\sigma\,\d s\,\d u$. If $Z_0^1\leq Z_0^2$ almost surely and $q_1(t)\leq q_2(t)$ for any $t\geq0,$
then $\mathbb P\bigl(Z_t^1\leq Z_t^2
\text{ for every }t\geq0\bigr)=1.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Exact conditioning, spectral integral estimate, deterministic graph comparison or order-statistic asymptotics Result: The local-limit argument controls the fraction of vertices in components above a fixed size; it does not put those vertices in one component. body:
[Definition 21 (Smoothed approximation of the initial Dirac mass) of arXiv:2607.19176, 'Exponential Convergence of the Sinkhorn Algorithm for the Schrödinger Bridge with Regime S'] Fix an initial point $(x,i)\in \mathbb R^d\times\mathcal I$ and let
$\varepsilon>0$. We define the smoothed initial distribution
$\mu_0^\varepsilon\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal I)$ by smoothing only
the continuous component and keeping the initial regime fixed. More precisely,
\[
\mu_0^\varepsilon(\mathrm dz,\{k\})
=
\mathbf 1_{\{k=i\}}
(2\pi\varepsilon)^{-d/2}
\exp\left(
-\frac{|z-x|^2}{2\varepsilon}
\right)
\mathrm dz,
\qquad k\in\mathcal I .
\]
Let $(X_t^\varepsilon,I_t^\varepsilon)_{t\ge0}$ be the solution of the same
regime-switching SDE with initial distribution $\mu_0^\varepsilon$, namely
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathrm dX_t^\varepsilon
=
b_{I_t^\varepsilon}\,\mathrm dt
+
\sigma_{I_t^\varepsilon}\,\mathrm dW_t,\\
(X_0^\varepsilon,I_0^\varepsilon)\sim \mu_0^\varepsilon,
\end{cases}
\]
where $(X_0^\varepsilon,I_0^\varepsilon)$ is independent of $W$, and
$I^\varepsilon$ evolves with the same constant transition rates
$(\lambda_{kl})_{k,l\in\mathcal I}$.

For each $k\in\mathcal I$, define the regime-wise marginal measure
\[
\mu_t^{\varepsilon,k}(A)
:=
\mathbb P(X_t^\varepsilon\in A,\ I_t^\varepsilon=k),
\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{app:lem_bound}, for every $t>0$, the measure $\mu_t^{\varepsilon,k}$ admits a
density $p_t^{\varepsilon,k}$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure, namely
\[
\mu_t^{\varepsilon,k}(\mathrm dz)
=
p_t^{\varepsilon,k}(z)\,\mathrm dz .
\]
Moreover,
\[
0\le p_t^{\varepsilon,k}(z)
\le
(2\pi\underline a t)^{-d/2},
\qquad t>0,\ z\in\mathbb R^d,\ k\in\mathcal I .
\]
The initial data are given by
\[
p_0^{\varepsilon,k}(z)
=
\mathbf 1_{\{k=i\}}
(2\pi\varepsilon)^{-d/2}
\exp\left(
-\frac{|z-x|^2}{2\varepsilon}
\right),
\qquad k\in\mathcal I .
\]
For $t>0$, the density vector
$p^\varepsilon=(p^{\varepsilon,k})_{k\in\mathcal I}$ satisfies the forward
system
\begin{equation}

\partial_t p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
=
-b_k\cdot\nabla p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
+
\frac{\sigma_k^2}{2}\Delta p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
-
\sum_{l\neq k}\lambda_{kl}p_t^{\varepsilon,k}
+
\sum_{l\neq k}\lambda_{lk}p_t^{\varepsilon,l},
\qquad k\in\mathcal I .
\end{equation}

body: [Definition of arXiv:2511.01058, 'Limit profiles and cutoff for the Burnside process on Sylow double cosets'] Let \(P\) be a transition kernel on a set \({\mathcal{X}}\) and let \(T:{\mathcal{X}} \to \mathcal{Y}\) be a function. The transition kernel \(P\) \emph{lumps under \(T\)} if for all Markov chains \((X_t)_{t \ge 0}\) generated by \(P\), the process \(Y_t = T(X_t)\) is a Markov chain on \(\mathcal{Y}\). The process \((Y_t)_{t \ge 0}\) is called a \emph{lumped process}.

body:
Let E be a family of subsets of a set X with the empty set in E and with X covered by countably many members of E, let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] satisfy rho(empty set) = 0, and define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k of rho(E_k) : E_k in E, A contained in the union of the E_k } for every subset A of X. Then mu* is an outer measure: mu*(empty set) = 0; A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B); and for EVERY countable family (A_n) of subsets of X, measurable or not, mu*(union of the A_n) <= sum of mu*(A_n). In particular Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is countably subadditive on all subsets of R^n, and finite subadditivity follows by padding the family with empty sets. WHERE THE INEQUALITY CANNOT BE IMPROVED: (a) equality fails in general even for pairwise DISJOINT sets. Let V be a Vitali set in [0,1] (one representative of each coset of the rationals) and let V_q = V + q for q in a countable enumeration of the rationals in [-1,1]. The V_q are pairwise disjoint, their union contains [0,1] and is contained in [-1,2], and by translation invariance all of them have the same Lebesgue outer measure; countable additivity would force that common value to be simultaneously 0 (giving outer measure 0 for [0,1]) and positive (to fill [0,1]), so the outer measure of the disjoint union is strictly less than the sum. Additivity is recovered exactly on the Caratheodory measurable sets. (b) Countable is sharp: the inequality does not extend to uncountable families - [0,1] is the union of its singletons, each of Lebesgue outer measure 0, while the union has outer measure 1. (c) No structure on rho is needed - rho need not be monotone, additive or a premeasure; that is why the construction is so robust, and also why mu* generally does not extend rho (mu*(E) <= rho(E) always, and equality for E in E requires rho to be a premeasure and E to be well behaved).
E contains the empty set and admits countable covers of X, so every subset has at least one admissible cover
rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; nonnegativity is essential for the rearrangement of the double sum
the family (A_n) is countable; the sets need not be measurable, disjoint or nested
the conclusion is an inequality only; additivity requires the Caratheodory criterion

[Theorem 40 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Suppose $\g\in C^{2L}(\us(R\e)), \z \in C^{2L+2}(\us(R\e))$, $R^4d^2/\la\leq\CR$, $R\geq1$, and
\bs
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla^\ell\z(x)\|_H&\leq C_{k,\z} d^{\lceil \ell/2\rceil-2}\qquad\forall \ell=3,\dots,2L+2,\\
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla^\ell\g(x)\|_H&\leq C_{\ell,\g} d^{\lceil \ell/2\rceil}\qquad\forall \ell=0,\dots,2L.
\es
Then
\bs
\frac{1}{\mathcal Z}\int_{\us(R\e)}\g(x)e^{-\la \z (x)}\dd x = \sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\nu_k(\g)\la^{-k} + \Rem_L,
\es where
\bs
\max_{k=0,\dots,L-1}d^{-2k}|\nu_k(\g)|&\leq C_{L,\z,\g},\\
|\Rem_L|&\leq C_{L,\z,\g,R}\left((d^2/\la)^L+e^{-(R-1)^2d/4}\right).
\es Here, $C_{L,\z,\g}$ depends on $L$, on $C_{\ell,\z}$, $\ell=3,\dots,2L+2$, and on $C_{\ell,\g}$, $\ell=0,\dots,2L$. The constant $C_{L,\z,\g,R}$ is analogous and also depends on $\CR$. We have $\nu_0(\g)=\g(0_d)$, and the formula for $\nu_k(\g)$, $k\geq1$ is given by $A_{2k}$ in~\cite[(2.20)]{A24}.

[Theorem Martingale Central Limit Theorem (\cite{HaHe80}, Theorem 3.2, p. 58) of arXiv:2605.10361, 'Limit shape of single-source stochastic sandpiles with $p$-topplings on $\Z$'] Let $(c_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence with $c_n \uparrow \infty$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$, let  $(\mathcal{F}_{n,i})_{n\in\mathbb{N},0\leq i\leq c_n}$ be sigma-fields and let $(S_{n,i})_{n\in\mathbb{N},0\leq i\leq c_n}$ be a zero-mean, square-integrable martingale array with differences $X_{n,i} = S_{n,i} - S_{n,i-1}$ for $1 \leq i \leq c_n$, where it is assumed that $S_{n,0}=0$. Let $C^2$ be a constant. Suppose that as $n \to \infty$:
    \begin{align*}
        \text{1) $\max_{1\leq i \leq c_n} |X_{n,i}| \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} 0$},&&
        \text{2) $\sum_{1\leq i \leq c_n} X_{n,i}^2 \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} C^2$},&&
        \text{3) $\mathbb{E}\big[\max_{1\leq i \leq c_n} X_{n,i}^2\big]$ is bounded in $n$}.
    \end{align*}
     Then $\sum_{1\leq i\leq c_n} X_{n,i} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{D}} Z$, where $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,C^2)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Martingale Central Limit Theorem (\cite{HaHe80}, Theorem 3.2, p. 58)

The process's name derives from the fact that the number of points in any given finite region follows a Poisson distribution. The process and the distribution are named after French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson. The process itself was discovered independently and repeatedly in several settings, including experiments on radioactive decay, telephone call arrivals and actuarial science.

body:
[Definition 1 of arXiv:2604.24390, 'Weak solutions to distribution-dependent stochastic Volterra equations'] A \textup{weak solution} to \eqref{eq:MVSVE} is a triple $((X,B),(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}),(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,T]})$ such that
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ is a probability space, $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,T]}$ is a filtration of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying the usual conditions,
    \item[(ii)] $X=(X_t)_{t\in [0,T]}\in L^1(\Omega~\times~ [0,T]; \mathbb{R}^d)$ is an $(\mathcal{F}_t)$-progressively measurable stochastic process, $B=(B_t)_{t\in [0,T]}$ is an $m$-dimensional Brownian motion w.r.t. $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,T]}$,
    \item[(iii)] $\int_0^t\big(|K_b(s,t)b(s,X_s,\mathcal{L}(X_s))| + |K_\sigma(s,t)\sigma(s,X_s,\mathcal{L}(X_s))|^2  \big)\dd s<\infty$ $\P$-a.s. for any $t\in[0,T]$,
    \item[(iv)] \eqref{eq:MVSVE} holds for $(X,B)$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$, $\P$-a.s., and
    \item[(v)] $X_0$ is $\mu_0$-distributed.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Definition 1 of arXiv:2604.24390

[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{unique_large_mass}
Let $f \in \Sym$ with $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\supp(f)} \ge 3$. 
At least one of of the following holds: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $H(f) > H(X)$
\item$f(0) \in (0,q) \cup (p,1)$, and for all $y \ne 0$, $f(y) \in (0,q)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Fix $y \in \mathbb{R}$. 
Define the \emph{Bernoulli entropy function} 
$H_B(t) = H(\Bern(t))$ for $t \in (0,1)$. 
It is easy to see that $H_B$ is concave, symmetric about $t=\frac{1}{2}$, and achieves its maximum at $t=\frac{1}{2}$. 

If there exists $y$ such that $f(y) \in [q, p]$, then, writing $Y \sim f$, we have $H(Y) > H(\mathds{1}\{Y=y\}) = H_B(f(y)) \geq H_B(p) = H(X)$. 
The result now follows from (no_atoms_bigger_than_p of the paper). 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.09904, 'Non-explosion principles for branched rough differential equations with unbounded coeffici'] A path \(\mathbf{Y} : [0, T] \to \CH_{N - 1} = \bigoplus_{n = 0}^{N - 1} \CH_{(n)}\) is a 
  \(\mathbf{X}\)-controlled rough path for some \(\gamma\)-H\"older branched rough path \(\mathbf{X}\) if 
  \begin{equation}
    R^{Y, f}_{st} = R^f_{st} = \< f, \mathbf{Y}_t\> - \< \mathbf{X}_{st} \curvearrowright f, \mathbf{Y}_s\>
  \end{equation}
  satisfies 
  \[\sup_{s < t \in [0, T]} \frac{|R^f_{st}|}{|t - s|^{(N - |f|)\gamma}} < \infty\] 
  for all \(f \in \CF_{N - 1}\). We denote \(Y_t = \< \mathbf{1}, \mathbf{Y}_t\>\) for the 
  path component of \(\mathbf{Y}\) and furthermore, for \(f \in \CF_{N - 1}\), denote 
  \(\partial^f_X Y_t = \< f, \mathbf{Y}_t\>\). We call \(\partial^f_X Y_t\) the \(f\)-th Gubinelli 
  derivative of \(\mathbf{Y}\) against \(\mathbf{X}\).

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the negative part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.4 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Problem 20.4 asks for a Gaussian extension of Theorem 7.12, the law of large numbers for fringe-subtree counts. Let T_n be the simply generated tree, equivalently the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, with n vertices. Let N_T be the number of vertices whose fringe subtree equals a fixed finite ordered rooted tree T, and let N_d be the number of vertices with d children. For the one-vertex tree bullet, N_bullet = N_0 exactly, since its occurrences are precisely the leaves. In both constructions of the companion memo on Problem 20.2, the subcritical law of its Theorem A (nu < 1) and the critical infinite-variance law of its Theorem B (nu = 1, sigma^2 = infinity), the bulk of the vertices has degree 0 or 1. Hence N_0 = n - N_1 + O(1), and N_bullet inherits the non-Gaussian limit of (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n): a two-point law in the first construction and a mixture of two Gaussians in the second. Assuming those two theorems, fringe-subtree counts are not asymptotically normal in general when nu < 1, nor when nu = 1 with sigma^2 = infinity. The finite-variance critical case is resolved in the literature by Janson (Random Structures Algorithms 48, 2016, Theorem 1.5) and is not included here as own work. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
T_n is an ordered rooted tree, and its one-vertex fringe subtrees are leaves.

body:
[Definition 15 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $M$ be a complex manifold  with a contact structure $H \subset TM$. 
\begin{itemize} \item[(i)]
For each $z \in M$, define $\fn_{z, 1} := H_z$ and $\fn_{z, 2} := T_z M/H_z$. Then $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ has a graded Heisenberg algebra structure given by Lie brackets of vector fields. We call it the {\em symbol algebra} of the contact structure $H \subset TM$ at $z \in M$.  Its universal enveloping algebra $U(\fn_z)$ has a grading coming from the grading $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ (this grading is not compatible with the natural filtration of the universal enveloping algebra), which we denote by $$U(\fn_z) \  = \ \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fn_z).$$  As $z$ varies, it defines a vector bundle $U(\fn)$ on $M$ with the fiber $U(\fn)_z = U(\fn_z)$  and a vector subbundle $U_k(\fn)$ for each $k \geq 0$ with the fiber  $U_k(\fn)_z = U_k(\fn_z)$.
\item[(ii)] For each $z \in M$,  define the {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z(\varphi)$ of a local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M, z}$ to be  zero.
The {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z (\xi)$ of a nonzero local vector field $\xi$ is defined to be 1 if it is a local section  of $H$ and 2 otherwise.  A local monomial  differential operator  on $M$ of the form $\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r$ has weighted order $${\rm ord}_z (\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r) \ := \ {\rm ord}_z (\xi_1) + \cdots + {\rm ord}_z(\xi_r).$$ A local differential operator on $M$ is {\em of weighted order $\leq k$} at $z$ if each of its monomial terms has weighted order at most $k$. 
\item[(iii)]
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ has {\em weighted vanishing order $\geq k+1$} at $z \in M$, if $P\varphi$ vanishes at $z$ for any local differential operator $P$ of weighted order $\leq k$. Denote by $\bm^k_z \subset \sO_z$ the ideal of local holomorphic functions with weighted vanishing order $\geq k$ at $z$ and set $ J^k_z := \sO_z / \bm^{k+1}_z.$ The vector bundle $J^k$ on $M$ whose fiber at $z$ is $J^k_z$ is called the {\em bundle of contact $k$-jets}. 
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ naturally determines a local section $j^k(\varphi) \in \sO(J^k)_z$, called the {\em contact $k$-jet} of $\varphi$ at $z$. 
There is a natural surjective homomorphism of vector bundles $ \pi^{k}_{k-1}: J^{k} \to J^{k-1}$ yielding an exact sequence of  vector bundles 
$$0 \to U_{k}(\fn)^* \longrightarrow J^{k} \stackrel{\pi^{k}_{k-1}}{\longrightarrow} J^{k-1} \to 0,$$ where $U_k(\fn)^*$ denotes the dual of the vector bundle $U_k(\fn)$.  \end{itemize}

[Definition 46 of arXiv:2609.00245, 'Higher-order Gaussian bounds for maximally subelliptic boundary value problems'] Let \(\sI\) be an index set, and for \(\iota\in \sI\) let \(W_1^\iota,\ldots, W_{r_\iota}^{\iota}\in \CbinftySpace[U][\Rn]\)
    be smooth vector fields on \(U\). We say that \(W_1^\iota,\ldots, W_{r_{\iota}}^{\iota}\)
    are \emph{H\"ormander vector fields on \(U\), uniformly for \(\iota\in \sI\)} if the following conditions hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \(\sup_{\iota\in \sI} r_\iota<\infty\).
        \item \(\left\{ W_j^\iota : \iota\in \sI, 1\leq j\leq r_\iota \right\}\subseteq \CbinftySpace[U][\Rn]\) is a bounded set.
        \item \(\exists m\in \Zg\) (independent of \(\iota\)) such that if \(X_1^\iota,\ldots, X_{q_\iota}^\iota\)
            is an enumeration of the commutators of \(W_1^\iota,\ldots, W_{r_\iota}^\iota\) up to order \(m\),
            then \(X_1^\iota,\ldots, X_{q_\iota}^\iota\) span the tangent space to \(U\),
            uniformly for \(\iota\in \sI\) (see Definition \ref{Defn::Scaling::UnitScale::SpanTangentSpaceUniformly}).
    \end{itemize}

body:
[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Fix $c > 0$ and let $Q_t$ be the birth-death process
  with
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $Q_0 \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(c)$;
    \item $n \mapsto n +1$ transitions of rate $c$; and
    \item $n \mapsto n - 1$ transitions of rate $n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then the first hitting time of $0$,
  \[
    \tau_c \coloneqq \inf\{ t \geqslant 0 \mid Q_t = 0 \},
  \]
  has Laplace transform
  \[
    \E e^{-s\tau_c} = e^{-c}
    \left[1 - c\int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^{s} e^{-cx} \, dx
    \right]^{-1},
    \quad s \geqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $s > 0$. By total expectation,
    \[
      \E e^{-s \tau_c}
      = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty
      \E\left(e^{-s\tau_c} \middle| Q_0 = n\right)
      \PP(Q_0 = n)\\
      = e^{-c} \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{c^n}{n!}\, \phi_n(s)
    \]
    where $\phi_n(s) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}(e^{-s\tau_c} \mid 
    Q_0 = n)$. So if $\Phi_s$ is defined on $[0, c]$ by
    \begin{equation}
      
      \Phi_s(y) \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty
      \phi_n(s) \, \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \quad \text{then} \quad
      \E(e^{-s\tau_c}) = e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c).
    \end{equation}
    Clearly $\phi_0(s) = 1$ and first-step analysis gives
    \[
      (c+n+s) \, \phi_n(s) = 
      n \, \phi_{n-1}(s) + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s),
      \quad n > 0.
    \]
    By taking a weighted sum of this recurrence,
    \[
      \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \left(c + n + s \right)
      \phi_n(s) = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \left[ n \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s)\right].
    \]
    The left-hand side is
    \[
      (c+s) \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_n(s)
      + y \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_n(s)
      =
      (c+s)\left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
    \]
    while the right-hand side is
    \[
      y \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_{n+1}(s)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[ \Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s)\right].
    \]
    We are left with the differential equation
    \[
      (c+s) \left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[\Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s) \right]
    \]
    or equivalently,
    the initial value problem
    \begin{align}
      
      \left(c-y\right) \Phi_s'(y)
      + \left(- c + y - s\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= \overbrace{c \, \phi_1(s) - c - s}^{-K}\\ \notag
      \Phi_s'(y) + \left(-1-\frac{s}{c-y}\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= -\frac{K}{c-y}
    \end{align}
    with condition $\Phi_s(0) = 1$.
    Use the integrating factor $I_s(y) = e^{-y} \, (c-y)^s$ to write
    \begin{align*}
      \left[e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)\right]'
      &= \frac{-K}{c-y} \, e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s\\
      e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)
      - e^{-0} \left(c - 0\right)^s \Phi_s(0) 
      &= \int_0^y \frac{-K}{c-x} \, e^{-x} \left(c - x\right)^s \, dx
      \intertext{for any $y < c$. It's clear from \eqref{eq:Phi} that
      $\Phi_s$ is continuous, so take the $y \uparrow c$ limit:}
      \frac{c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}
      &= K.
    \end{align*}
    Finally, the $y \uparrow c$ limit of \eqref{eq:IVP}
    informs us $-s \, \Phi_s(c) = -K$, thus
    \begin{align*}
      \E e^{-s\tau_c}
      &= e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c)
      = \frac{e^{-c}\, c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \, s \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}\\
      &= \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^s dx}
      = \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^1 c \, e^{-cx} \left(c-c\,x\right)^s dx}\\
      &= e^{-c} \left[1 - c \int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^s e^{-cx}\, dx \right]^{-1}.
      \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.03273, 'On the Asymptotic of Coupled Spherical Integrals: An Operator-Valued Extension of the Free'] Let $\left(\mathcal A, \mathcal E, \mathcal B_L\right)$ be an operator-valued probability space as defined in \cite[Chapter 9]{speicherFreeProbabilityTheory2009}, where $\mathcal A$ is the algebra of $L\times L$ block matrices composed of $N\times N$ blocks as $N$ tends to infinity and $\mathcal B_L$ is the algebra of all $L\times L$ matrices.
    Furthermore, the expectation operation $\mathcal E:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B_L$ applies the averaged normalized trace $\varphi$ to all $L^2$ blocks of its argument.
    Define matrix $Z_N$ as
    \begin{align}
        Z_N
        =
        \begin{bmatrix}
            E_{11} & \ldots & E_{1L} \\
            \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
            E_{L1} & \ldots & E_{LL}
        \end{bmatrix},
    \end{align}
    with blocks $E_{lk}\in\mathbb A^{N\times N}~\forall l,k$ where $N$ is finite.
    $Z_N$ is said to converge to $Z$ if all empirical operator-valued moments of $Z_N$ converge to the corresponding operator-valued moments of $Z$, defined on the operator-valued probability space $(\mathcal A, \mathcal E, \mathcal B_L)$, as $N\uparrow\infty$.
    That is
    \begin{align}
        \lim_{N\uparrow\infty}
        \mathrm{Tr}_L  [Z_N B_1 Z_N \ldots B_{n-1} Z_N]
        =
        \mathcal E[Z B_1 Z \ldots B_{n-1} Z]
        ,
        
    \end{align}
    for all $B_i\in\mathcal B_L$ and all $n\geq1$. 
    Note that we write with some abuse of notation, $Z_N B_i := Z_N (B_i\otimes \mathbb I_N)$.
    $\mathrm{Tr}_L$ is the normalized partial trace of order $L$, i.e. $\mathrm{Tr}_L[Z_N]$ returns an $L\times L$ matrix with entries $\mathrm{Tr}[E_{lk}]=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}\left(E_{lk}\right)$ at position $(l,k)$.

body: [Lemma CHL of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Let $a,b, x,y \in \mathbb{R}$, $a < b$, and suppose that $B$ is a Brownian bridge from $B(a) = x$ to $B(b) = y$ with variance $1$ as in ((S22E3 of the paper)). Let $U$ be an open set in $C([a,b])$ that contains a function $f$ such that $f(a) = x$ and $f(b) = y$. Then $\mathbb{P}(B \in U) > 0$.

[Theorem thm:spectralgap of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] There are some $\lambda_0 > 1$ and $\gamma > 0$ such that
for all $\lambda \geqslant \lambda_0$ and all $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
the spectral gap ${\gamma_n^\lambda}$ of the generator ${\mathscr{L}_n^\lambda}$
of the $n$-line $\lambda$-tilted diffusion is at least $\gamma$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Primary-source dependency map, W719-T295-C011 v1, source audit pending. In Ma, Wang, Chi and Chen, Implicit Regularization in Nonconvex Statistical Estimation (arXiv:1711.10467v3), consider iid real Gaussian sensing, a fixed unit signal x_*, noiseless observations, quartic loss f(x)=(1/(4m)) sum_j ((a_j^T x)^2-(a_j^T x_*)^2)^2, and the source local induction in its absolute region of incoherence. The omitted-row loss keeps denominator m, and its iterate is z_t=x_t^(l). Appendix A.4, PDF pp51-52, splits Delta_next into a full-gradient secant term and omitted-row forcing evaluated at z_t. Under the source induction and Gaussian row/projection events, it bounds the forcing norm by an absolute constant times C4(C4+5)(C4+10) eta (n log n/m) sqrt(log n/n), then makes this at most c eta sqrt(log n/n) by sufficiently large m/(n log n). Full-gradient segment contraction 1-eta/2 closes the static gap C3 sqrt(log n/n) in equation106. At linear m=alpha n the displayed proof coefficient grows as log n/alpha, and reducing eta alone cannot improve its ratio to the contraction budget. Appendix A.6, p53 equation112, uses the same factor n log n/m to control spectral-initialization leave-one-out perturbations. Separately, the segment-contraction geometry assumes m>=c0 n log n. Lemma4 p26 and equations53-55 control an absolute gap and absolute maximum projection C2 sqrt(log n); they do not prove a projection bound proportional to the current error norm. These are limitations of the displayed proof estimates, not a lower bound on actual perturbations or a necessity theorem for log oversampling. No linear-sample GD convergence or nonconvergence is established.

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix $\alpha$ and assume $T:=\|\eta^{(\alpha)}\|_1 \le C \log N_f$ for a $C >eL$. For $0 <\kappa <1$  set $\theta=\kappa\log N_f$. Then for a false stroke
	$\mu\notin S_\alpha$,
	\[
	q_+ := \mathbb P(x_\mu=1\mid \eta^{(\alpha)})
	\le
	\exp\bigl(-c(\log N_f)^2\bigr)
	\]
	for some $c=c(\kappa,L)>0$ and all $N_f$ large enough.
	In particular, $q_+$ is super-polynomially small in $N_f$.

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2506.13913, '2506.13913'] {Multidimensional Brownian motion}{}
   Let \(d \in \mathbb{N}\), and consider a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). A \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion is a stochastic process \(\{B_t\}_{t \geq 0} = \{(B_t^1, B_t^2, \dots, B_t^d)\}_{t \geq 0}\), where each component \(B_t^i\) (\(i = 1, \dots, d\)) is a Brownian motion defined on the probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\).

[Corollary 49 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\), let \(C\) be a smooth projective curve over \(k\), and let
\[
\pi\colon Y \to  C
\]
be a smooth projective morphism of relative dimension \(n\).
Assume that, for every geometric point $\overline{c} \to  C$, one has
\[
H^i\left(
Y_{\overline{c}},
\Omega^j_{Y_{\overline{c}}}
\otimes\omega_{Y_{\overline{c}}}
\right)=0
\]
for every  \(i<n\) and \(0\leq j\leq n\).
Then \(Y\) is HT-split.

metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:5fb7be4023d969b5af203fa968b9e1564657ac20f550bc911db90feba714b737","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/5f/5fb7be4023d969b5af203fa968b9e1564657ac20f550bc911db90feba714b737.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:582e938d316bd3d34c589b3a80a45bdb233a32e507f3c6bf8d8bdb2f6a801459","bundle_entry_key":"variance-hermite","bundle_id":"population.t311-positive-hermite-and-stein-spectral-order-001","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"analysis","draft":"w722/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:analysis.stein:w722-t311-variance-hermite","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Positive initial densities with algebraic Hermite profiles

Status: proof draft, unaudited. Target 1 construction, not a nonlinear convergence theorem.

Let pi be the standard normal density, h_n=He_n/sqrt(n!) its normalized probabilists' Hermite polynomials. For b>1/4 define

q_b(x) = integral from 0 to 1 of b(1-u)^(b-1) phi_(1+u)(x) du,

where phi_v is the centered Gaussian density of variance v. This is a strictly positive probability density. For 0<epsilon<1 the density rho_0=(1-epsilon)pi+epsilon q_b is also strictly positive. It has mean zero and variance 1+epsilon/(b+1).

For all m>=0 its q_b Hermite coefficients are

a_(2m) = Gamma(b+1) sqrt((2m)!)/(2^m Gamma(m+b+1)),
a_(2m+1) = 0.

For X conditional on U=u distributed as N(0,1+u), the Hermite generating function gives

E exp(tX-t^2/2) = exp(u t^2/2).

Equating derivatives at zero yields E He_(2m)(X) = (2m)! u^m/(2^m m!), while odd moments vanish. Each fixed derivative is integrable over u in [0,1]; this also follows directly since each polynomial moment is bounded uniformly in the variance interval [1,2]. Integrating in u and using

E U^m = b B(m+1,b) = Gamma(b+1) Gamma(m+1)/Gamma(m+b+1)

proves the coefficient formula. Stirling's formula, equivalently the central binomial asymptotic and the Gamma ratio, gives

sqrt((2m)!)/(2^m m!) ~ (pi m)^(-1/4),
Gamma(m+1)/Gamma(m+b+1) ~ m^(-b).

Therefore a_(2m) ~ Gamma(b+1) pi^(-1/4) m^(-b-1/4). Every exponent s>1/2 is realized by b=s-1/4. Nonconstant coefficients of rho_0/pi are epsilon a_n. The odd coefficients vanish; the asserted profile is on the even sector.

To justify the L2 expansion rather than only formal moments, Tonelli's theorem and direct Gaussian integration give

integral phi_(1+u)(x) phi_(1+v)(x)/pi(x) dx = (1-uv)^(-1/2),

for 0<=u,v<1. Thus the squared L2(pi) norm of q_b/pi is the integral of (1-uv)^(-1/2) against the two independent Beta(1,b) mixing laws. Set a=1-u and c=1-v. Then 1-uv=a+c-ac lies between (a+c)/2 and a+c. Near (0,0) the integrand is comparable to a^(b-1)c^(b-1)(a+c)^(-1/2). With r=a+c, z=a/r, the radial exponent is 2b-3/2; the z integral is finite for b>0. Integrability is therefore equivalent to b>1/4. Away from that corner the integrand is integrable. Completeness of the Hermite basis now identifies the actual L2 coefficients and gives finite chi-square divergence and hence finite KL for b>1/4.

This construction resolves positivity and normalization of the requested initial profile. It does not identify coefficients in the Stein eigenbasis. The Hermite basis does not diagonalize the Stein operator, as the dossier's eigenvector diagnostics already show. No decay exponent transfers between these two bases without an additional comparison theorem.

# Characteristic KL diagnostic

For h=1 the exact mean-field velocity and its spatial derivative are

v(x) = integral exp(-(x-y)^2/2) [(x-y)-y] rho_t(y) dy,
v_x(x) = integral exp(-(x-y)^2/2) [1-(x-y)((x-y)-y)] rho_t(y) dy.

Along characteristics X_t(a), set L_t(a)=log(partial_a X_t(a)). Then dX/dt=v(X), dL/dt=v_x(X), L_0=0. Conservation of mass gives log rho_t(X_t(a))=log rho_0(a)-L_t(a), and therefore

KL(rho_t|pi) = E_(a~rho_0) [log rho_0(a)-L_t(a)+X_t(a)^2/2+log(2pi)/2].

The script approximates this expectation and velocity integrals with Gaussian-mixture product quadrature. Unlike a KL computed from an atomic empirical law, this formula is defined for the continuum density. Its numerical quadrature still requires resolution checks, and its finite-time fits are evidence only. The Stein-information kernel used as an additional diagnostic is k(x,y)[xy+1-2(x-y)^2].","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:18618181c1e55723453d3fd0280a04028682b29877205fda162197655ca2b74e","revision_digest":"sha256:1fddbb037ca02911702eb3fd1b185f588a56ed9680b05ba54e4a44e3dd76ca40","source_id":"own-work:w722:T311:w722-positive-profile-v2","source_revision":"w722-positive-profile-v2","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition 23 (Maximum principle for Einstein--Euler flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Let $(\Phi,\Psi)$ be a sufficiently regular Einstein--Euler areal flow on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$ with $\mu>0$ throughout.
Then, for every $t\in[t_0,t_1]$ and $m=2,3$,
\bel{equa-widetildemax}
\aligned
\inf_{\Sbb^1}\Gammaun_m(t_0,\cdot)&\leq\Gammaun_m(t,x)\leq\sup_{\Sbb^1}\Gammaun_m(t_0,\cdot),\\
\inf_{\Sbb^1}\Gammazero_m(t_0,\cdot)&\leq\Gammazero_m(t,x)\leq\sup_{\Sbb^1}\Gammazero_m(t_0,\cdot).
\endaligned
\ee
Then the range of $\Gammaunpar(t,\cdot)$, respectively $\Gammazero(t,\cdot)$, coincides with the range of the corresponding initial map, namely the range is an invariant set.
The statement about $\Gammazero$ extends to vacuum.
The bound on~$\Gammaun$ extends to vacuum as the statement that if $C_1\hNumb\leq\hNumb\Gammaun_m\leq C_2\hNumb$ at initial time $t=t_0$ for some constants $C_1,C_2\in\RR$ then these inequalities hold for all times.
As a result, the convex hull of the range of $\Gammaunpar(t,\cdot)$ coincides with that at initial time. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Maximum principle for Einstein--Euler flows

For each $M \in \mathcal{R}_i$ for $i=1, \cdots, 6$, the shortest geodesic $\delta$ has an associated \textit{Corona insulator family} $\{\kappa_{ij}\}$ which is non-coalescable.
    \item
The set $\mathcal{R}_0$ consists of a single manifold $\text{\normalfont Vol} 3$, and $\delta$ in $\text{\normalfont Vol} 3$ has a non-coalescable insulator family.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def: wasserstein G of arXiv:2411.02917, '\hspace*{2mm}\\[-16mm] Stein's Method for Spatial Random Graphs'] The \emph{Wasserstein metric} $W_{\mathbb{G}}$ on $\mathcal{M}_{1}(\mathbb{G})$ based on $d_{\mathbb{G}}$ is defined as
$$W_{\mathbb{G}}(P,Q) = \inf_{\substack{(\Xi,\Sigma) \sim P \\ (\mathrm{H},\mathrm{T}) \sim Q}} \E \, d_{\mathbb{G}} \bigl( (\Xi,\Sigma), (\mathrm{H},\mathrm{T}) \bigr) = \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{G}}} \, \biggl| \int_{\mathbb{G}} f \, dP - \int_{\mathbb{G}} f \, dQ \biggr|, \quad P,Q \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{G}},$$

where $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{G}} = \bigl\{f \colon \mathbb{G} \to \R \bigm| \abs{f(\xi,\sigma) - f(\tau,\eta)} \leq d_{\mathbb{G}}((\xi,\sigma),(\tau,\eta)) \bigr\}$ and the second equality is due to the Kantorovich--Rubinstein theorem.

body:
Let X be a random variable with cumulant generating function psi(lambda) = log E[exp(lambda X)], finite on an interval containing 0 in its interior on the right. Then for every t, P(X >= t) <= exp(-psi^*(t)) where psi^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda t - psi(lambda)) is the (one-sided) Legendre transform of psi. If X = sum_{i=1}^n X_i with the X_i independent and identically distributed with cumulant generating function psi_1, then psi = n psi_1 and P(X >= n t) <= exp(-n psi_1^*(t)): the exponent is LINEAR in n with rate psi_1^*(t), the Cramer rate function. Cramer's theorem says this exponential rate is exactly right, that is (1/n) log P(X >= n t) -> -psi_1^*(t) for t > E[X_1] under a finiteness condition on psi_1 near 0, so the Chernoff bound loses nothing at the level of the exponential rate although it can lose polynomial factors. The method requires SOME finite exponential moment: without it psi^* is identically 0 for t above the mean and the bound is vacuous, which is the correct behaviour for heavy-tailed laws. [standard; e.g. Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Chapter 2]
psi(lambda) = log E e^{lambda X} finite for some lambda > 0 (otherwise the bound is vacuous)
for the i.i.d. rate statement: independent and identically distributed summands

Let Y be finite with a distinguished always-true empty fact bot, let n>=1 and |Y|>n+1, and let p be any probability law on Y with p(bot)=0. Put F=supp(p) union{bot} and H=Y\F. Given n iid samples from p, let O be the observed symbols union{bot}, U=Y\O, and GT the fraction of sample positions whose symbol occurs exactly once. Both O and U are nonempty. Define g(y)=(1-GT)/|O| on O and g(y)=GT/|U| on U. Let B(g) be the partition into nonempty equal-g-probability level sets, let p^B be uniform within each level set with its original p mass, and define Mis_infinity(g,p)=TV(p^B,g). Deterministically, g(H)<=GT and Mis_infinity(g,p)<=|p(U)-GT|. Hence, for every delta in(0,1], Pr(g(H)<=GT and Mis_infinity(g,p)<=3*sqrt(log(4/delta)/n))>=1-delta. This is a deliberately inefficient matching construction in the source calibration notion. If factoids have a surjective document representation, choosing one representative document per factoid realizes g as a document generator. The zero empty-fact mass and alphabet-size assumptions here make all singleton and denominator conventions explicit; no claim for arbitrary non-iid corpora is included. If the two assigned per-symbol scores are distinct, Mis_infinity(g,p)=|p(U)-GT| exactly. If they coincide, g is uniform, its exact score partition has one bin, and Mis_infinity(g,p)=0; unconditional equality with |p(U)-GT| is not asserted.
Finite alphabet with distinguished bot, p(bot)=0, n>=1 and |Y|>n+1.
IID samples; uniform two-level generator; exact score-level calibration.

[Theor* Informal statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:c4-finite-subgraph} of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Fix \(d\ge2\) and $\rho >0$. Consider three positive integers $r,k,n$ satisfying 
\( \rho k \le r\le k\le n.\) Let \(G=(I,J,M)\) be a \(C_4\)-free weighted bipartite graph with
\(
|I|=k,\qquad |J|=n,
\)
and right support degrees between \(2\) and \(d\).
Set
\[
\Lambda:=\min\left( \frac r2,\frac nk\right)
\quad\text{and}\quad
 m = \Theta\left( \frac{1}{d^3}\frac{\log\Lambda}{\log(\frac{d}{\rho}\log\Lambda)} \right).
\]
Then for a uniform right sample $\Omega$ of size $r$, we have
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\text{$G[\Omega]$ contains a \hyperref[def:weight-compatible-rooted-matching-tree]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{weight-compatible $m$-matching rooted tree}}}}
\right) \ge 1- O( \tfrac{d}{\log(\Lambda)}).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Informal statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:c4-finite-subgraph}

body:
[Theorem thm:main fluctuations of arXiv:2505.10256, 'Stochastic Oscillators out of equilibrium:\\ scaling limits and correlation estimates'] Let $m>5/2$ be fixed. 
Assume that the sequence of initial measures $\{\mu_N\}_{N\in\mathbb N}$ satisfies Assumption (assump:initial_measure of the paper). 
Moreover, assume that bounded measurable functions $v_0:\mathbb T\to\mathbb R$ and $e_0:\mathbb T\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $e_0(u)-v_0(u)^2\ge 0$ for any $u\in\mathbb T$.
Finally, assume that the sequence of initial density fields $\mathcal{V}_0^N$ converges in distribution to an $H^{-m}(\mathbb T)$-valued random variable $\mathcal{V}_0$ as $N\to\infty$.  
\begin{itemize}
\item[a)] 
Let $\mathcal{M}^N_t$ be a mean-zero martingale associated naturally to the volume fluctuation fields $\mathcal V^N_\cdot$ (see (equation eq:dynkin_martingale_definition of the paper) for the definition).  
The sequence $\{\mathcal{M}^N_t: t\in [0,T]\}_{N\in\mathbb N}$ is tight in $D([0,T],H^{-m}(\mathbb T))$, so that there exists a subsequence of $N$, which is again denoted by the same letter by abuse of notation, along which the sequence converges to a limit $\{\mathcal{M}_t ; t\in [0,T]\}$ in distribution:
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{N\to\infty} \mathcal{M}^N_\cdot = \mathcal{M}_\cdot 
\end{equation*}
where the limit $\mathcal{M}_\cdot $ is again a mean-zero martingale.
\item [b)]For any $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$, we have that
\begin{equation} 
\lim_{N\to \infty} \mathbb E_N[\langle \mathcal{M}^N(f)\rangle_t]  
= \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb T} 2 \chi(s,u) (\nabla f(u))^2 du ds
\end{equation}
where $\chi(t,u) = e(t,u) - v(t,u)^2$, and $(v,e)$ is the unique weak solution of (equation eq:hdl of the paper) with initial profile $(v_0,e_0)$.  
\item  [c)]
The sequence $\{\mathcal Q^N_m\}_N$ is tight and any of its limit points $\mathcal Q_m$ satisfies the identity 
\begin{equation}

\mathcal{V}_t(f) 
= \mathcal{V}_0(\mathcal T_tf) 
+ \mathcal{M}_t(f)
\end{equation}
for any $f\in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb T)$, where $\mathcal{M}_t$ is a mean-zero  martingale with continuous trajectories and $\mathcal T_t$ is the semigroup generated by the one-dimensional Laplacian $\Delta$. Moreover, $\mathcal V_0$ and $\mathcal M_t$ are uncorrelated in the sense that, for all $f,g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb T)$ and for all $t\in[0,T]$, it holds $E_{\mathcal Q_m}[\mathcal  V_0(g)\mathcal M_t(f)]=0$.
\item [d)] If $\mu_N$ is the invariant measure $\mu_{\rho,\beta}$ for some $\rho\in\mathbb R$ and $\beta>0$, then we can strength our result in the sense that we have the convergence of the sequence $\{\mathcal Q^N_m\}_N$ to the solution of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation
$$
d\mathcal V_t=\Delta \mathcal V_t dt+\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta}} \nabla \dot{\mathcal W_t} 
$$
again provided that $m>5/2$, where $\dot{\mathcal W_t}$ is a one-dimensional space-time white noise. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 6tmod8 of arXiv:2609.03926, 'Overcolored Partition $k$-tuples Restricted by Parity of the Parts'] We have
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item For all $n,r,s\ge 1$, some integer $\ell\ge 1$ and $k$ even,
		\[
		\bar{b}^k_{r,s}(n)\equiv
		\begin{cases}
			2rk\pmod 8, & \text{if } n=(2\ell)^2 \text{ or } 2(2\ell-1)^2,\\[4pt]
			2sk\pmod 8, & \text{if } n=(2\ell-1)^2,\\[4pt]
			6rk\pmod 8, & \text{if } n=2(2\ell)^2,\\[4pt]
			0\pmod 8,  & \text{otherwise }.\\[4pt]
		\end{cases}
		\]
		\item For all  $n,r,s\ge 1$, some integers $\ell, m\ge 1$ and $k$ odd,
		\[
		\bar{b}^k_{r,s}(n)\equiv
		\begin{cases}
			2sk\pmod 8, & \text{if } n=(2\ell-1)^2,\\[4pt]
			2k\left(s+(r+s)\left((r+s)k+1\right)\right)\pmod 8, & \text{if } n=(2\ell)^2,\\[4pt]
			2k(r+s^2k)\pmod 8, & \text{if } n=2(2\ell-1)^2,\\[4pt]
			2k(3r+s^2k+2s)\pmod 8,  & \text{if } n=2(2\ell)^2,\\[4pt]
			4s(r+s)\pmod 8,  & \text{if } n=\ell^2+2m^2,\\[4pt]
			0\pmod 8,  & \text{otherwise }.\\[4pt]
		\end{cases}
		\]
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.20026, 'Quasihelix properties\\ of selected Volterra Gaussian processes'] \leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[1),left=5pt]
\item 
 \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For any fixed $\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha\in(-1/2, 1/2)$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a local $(\alpha+\frac12, 0, T)$-quasihelix for any $T>0$.
    \item Let $\alpha = 1/2$. Then for any fixed $\lambda > 0 $ and any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a  local $(1, 1 - \varepsilon, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.  
    \item Let $\alpha > 1/2$. Then for any fixed $\lambda > 0$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a local $(\alpha+\frac12, 1$, $0, T)$-generalized quasihelix  for any $T>0$ and $(1, T_1, T_2)$-quasihelix  for any  \mbox{$0 < T_1 < T_2$}.
\end{enumerate} 

\item 
For any $T > 0$, the   process $U^{(3)}$ is local $(1, \alpha, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix in the case $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and local $(\alpha, 1, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix in the case $\alpha \in (1, 2)$. When $\alpha=1$, the process becomes standard Wiener process, and thus it is obviously a local $(\frac12, 0, T)$-quasihelix for all $T > 0$. For $\alpha \ge 2$ the process is a local $(\frac{\alpha}{2}, \frac12, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space and {X_i : i in I} a family of random variables. The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function G : [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) with G(t)/t -> infinity as t -> infinity such that sup_{i in I} E[G(|X_i|)] < infinity. The sufficiency direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on any superlinear moment, for example sup_i E[|X_i|^p] < infinity for a single p > 1, or sup_i E[|X_i| log^+ |X_i|] < infinity, forces uniform integrability. A uniform bound on the FIRST moment does not: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) the family X_n = n 1_{(0,1/n)} has E|X_n| = 1 for all n and is not uniformly integrable. [standard; e.g. Dellacherie and Meyer, Probabilities and Potential, or Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 13.3]
a probability space (or a finite measure space)
G convex, nondecreasing, superlinear at infinity; the constant sup_i E[G(|X_i|)] must be uniform over the family

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] A map $\Psi$ from a subshift $X \subset \mathcal{A}^{G}$ to a subshift $ Y \subset \mathcal{B}^G$ is called a \textbf{sliding block code}, if there exists a finite set $ F$ and a map $ \psi: L(X, F) \rightarrow \mathcal{B}$ such that $ \Psi(x)_g= \psi(x|_{g.F})$ for all $ x \in X$ and $ g \in G$.  The sliding block code is called a \textbf{factor} if it is surjective.

body:
For a real random variable X and l >= 0 let Q(X; l) = sup_x P(x <= X <= x + l) (Levy's concentration function). There is an absolute constant C such that for independent X_1,...,X_n, S = X_1 + ... + X_n and any 0 < l_i <= l (i = 1,...,n): Q(S; l) <= C l (sum_i l_i^2 [1 - Q(X_i; l_i)])^{-1/2}. Also Q(X_1 + X_2; l) <= min(Q(X_1; l), Q(X_2; l)) for independent X_1, X_2. If X_i has density <= 1 then Q(X_i; l_i) <= l_i, so 1 - Q(X_i; l_i) >= 1 - l_i.

Assumes: independence; 0 < l_i <= l

[Thm 12 of arXiv:2604.24189, 'Malliavin calculus and densities for chaos-driven stochastic differential equations'] Let $F$ be a real-valued chaos process on an abstract Wiener space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\P,\mathfrak{H})$.  
	Assume that $F$ verifies the hypothesis $\mathbf{(H_2)}$, with $H\in (\frac{1}{2},1)$. 
	For any \(h\in\HHH\), there exists a stochastic process $(\tilde F^{\,h}_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
	\item For any $t\in [0,T]$,  $\tilde{F}^{\,h}_t=F_t$ $\P$-a.s.;
	\item For all $\omega\in\Omega$, the map
	$
	\R_+\times\R \ni (t,\varepsilon)\longmapsto \widetilde F^{\,h}_t\big(\omega+\varepsilon\,j(h)\big)
	$
	is continuous.
	\item Let $\beta\in(0,H-\frac{1}{2})$ and $1-\alpha = H-\beta$. For all $\omega\in\Omega$, the mapping from $\R$ into $W_{2}^{1-\alpha}\left(0, T ; \mathbb{R}^{m}\right)$ defined by $\varepsilon\mapsto \tilde{F}^{h}_{\star}(\omega + \varepsilon j(h))$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ on $\R$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

	\mathbb{E}\big[\deg(X;\omega)^2\big] = 2 - \frac{2}{n} + d(d-1)p_1.
	\]

Every finite nonempty S in the square lattice Z^2 has |boundary_E S|>=4sqrt(|S|), while the edge-Cheeger constant of Z^2 is zero. Indeed, if S occupies a columns and b rows then its edge boundary is at least 2a+2b>=4sqrt(ab)>=4sqrt(|S|); square boxes of side r have boundary/volume=4/r. Thus an IP_2 inequality cannot be substituted for the uniform positive-Cheeger hypothesis in the explicit threshold proof. This does not refute the conjecture that finite isoperimetric dimension greater than one ensures p_c<1.

For an infinite connected graph of maximum degree D<infinity with edge-Cheeger constant h=inf_(finite nonempty S) |boundary_E S|/|S|>0, independent bond percolation satisfies

The lower bound is the union bound over at most D(D-1)^(r-1) simple paths of length r from a fixed vertex, for p(D-1)<1. After s successful discoveries and f failures, the discovered set has s+1 vertices, and at least h(s+1)-f boundary edges remain untested. Thus the exploration cannot finish while Z=h+hs-f>0. The tests are an independent Bernoulli(p) sequence: each success adds h to Z and each failure subtracts 1. If p>1/(1+h), its drift is positive. Fix -1<a<1 and sigma_a(t)=t for t>=0, sigma_a(t)=a*t for t<0, applied coordinatewise. A depth-L network has L affine layers, activation after the first L-1 layers, and an affine final output. Its squared parameter cost is sum_ell (||W_ell||_F^2+||b_ell||_2^2). For a function f and domain Omega, R_L is the infimum of this cost over all such finite-width networks equal to f on Omega; R_L=+infinity if the class is empty. Let Omega be a nonempty bounded open subset of R^d, and f:R^d->R^m a continuous function affine on each cell of a finite polyhedral decomposition. At every x in Omega at which f is differentiable, and for every integer L>=1, sum_(i=1)^rank(Jf(x)) s_i(Jf(x))^(2/L)<=R_L/L. The same lower bound applies if the hidden widths are prescribed, with their corresponding representation cost. It does not require the asymptotic cost to have a limit.

[Proposition 2 (Basic properties) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Under Assumption~\ref{ass:U}, the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item For every $\eps>0$,
    \[
        Z_\eps=\int_{\R^{3d}}e^{-H(z)/\eps} dz<\infty.
    \]
    Hence $\pi^\eps$ defined in \eqref{eq:pi} is a probability measure.

    \item The solution of \eqref{eq:sde} is non-explosive.

    \item For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\R^{3d})$,
    \[
        \int_{\R^{3d}}\calL_\eps f d\pi^\eps=0.
    \]

    \item The operator $\calL_\eps$ satisfies the H\"ormander bracket
    condition at every point of $\R^{3d}$.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Definition of arXiv:2609.02588, 'Ramsey-type results for Maker-Breaker games'] Given a $d$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$,
a vertex $v\in V(\mathcal{H})$ and a vertex set
$A\subseteq V(\mathcal{H})\setminus \{v\}$ we let
the $(d-1)$-uniform hypergraph
$$
\mathcal{H}_v[A] := \left( A, \left\{ f\in \binom{A}{d-1}:~ f\cup \{v\}\in E(\mathcal{H})\right\} \right)
$$
be the link of $v$ in $A$.

[Corollary 16 (Reciprocity of the common divisor of \(\AG_k\)) of arXiv:2608.25725, 'Gr\"obner Bases for Alexander Fitting Ideals of Links'] Let \(L\subset S^3\) be an oriented ordered link.  If
\(\AG_k(L)=\emptyset\), put \(\Delta_k=0\); otherwise, let \(\Delta_k\)
be a greatest common divisor of the elements of \(\AG_k(L)\).  Then
\[
 (\overline{\Delta_k})=(\Delta_k)
\]
as principal ideals of \(\Lambda\).  If \(\Delta_k\ne0\), there are
\(c\in\Q^\times\) and \(a_1,\dots,a_\ell\in\Z\) such that
\[
 \Delta_k(t_1^{-1},\dots,t_\ell^{-1})
 =c\,t_1^{a_1}\cdots t_\ell^{a_\ell}
  \Delta_k(t_1,\dots,t_\ell).
\]

body:
[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.30174, 'Exact counting of spherical metrics with one conical singularity on rectangular tori'] \
\begin{itemize}
\item[$(i)$] If $E\in\mathbb{R}$, then $\Delta_q(E)\in\mathbb{R}$. If $E\in\mathbb{C}\setminus \mathbb{R}$, then $\Delta_q(E)\notin [-2,2]$.
\item[$(ii)$] There are infinitely many periodic eigenvalues $\{E_0\} \cup\{E_{4n-1}, E_{4n}\}^{+\infty}_{n=1}$ and
infinitely many antiperiodic eigenvalues $\{E_{4n-3}, E_{4n-2}\}_{n=1}^{+\infty}$ that are all
real and can be ordered such that
\[
E_0 < \cdots < E_{2n-1} \leq E_{2n} < E_{2n+1} \leq E_{2n+2}<\cdots. \]
\item[$(iii)$] The spectrum $\sigma$ of the linear operator $-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+q(t)$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C})$ is given by
\[\sigma=\Delta_q^{-1}([-2,2])=\bigcup_{n=0}^{+\infty}[E_{2n}, E_{2n+1}].\]
\item[$(iv)$] $\Delta_q(E)>2$ for any $E<E_0$.
\item[$(v)$] For $n$ large, 
\begin{equation}E_{2n-1}, E_{2n}=\frac{n^2\pi^2}{L^2}+O(1).\end{equation}
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 15 (Resonant skew-Hermitian endpoint identity) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\Lambda\subset 2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, and choose $m\geq1$ such that
\[
m\omega\in2\pi\Z
\qquad(\omega\in\Lambda).
\]
Let $\Gamma=\gamma^{*m}$ be the $m$-fold concatenation of $\gamma$, naturally parametrised on $[0,mT]$.
Fix $r\geq1$, frequencies $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r\in\Lambda$, and real covectors $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r\in W^*$. No distinctness is assumed: the frequencies and covectors may repeat.
Choose real numbers $\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{j-1}-\sigma_j=\omega_j
\quad(1\leq j\leq r),
\qquad
m\sigma_j\in2\pi\Z
\quad(0\leq j\leq r).
\end{equation}
Set $D=i\diag(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r)$, write $I=I_{r+1}$, and, for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\in\R^r$, define
\begin{equation}
\rho_u(a)
 =\ell(a)D
  +\sum_{j=1}^r
   u_j\eta_j(a)(E_{j-1,j}-E_{j,j-1}),
\end{equation}
first as a real-linear map $V\to\uLie(r+1)$. Denote its complex-linear extension by
\[
\rho_{u,\C}:V_{\C}\longrightarrow M_{r+1}(\C).
\]
If $U^u$ is the right development
\[
\dd U_s^u=U_s^u\rho_u(\dd\Gamma_s),
\qquad U_0^u=I,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
U_{mT}^u=I
\qquad(u\in\R^r).
\end{equation}

[Corollary cor:convex-gap-density of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a symmetric open convex set
of finite Lebesgue measure. Then
\[
    D(\Omega)=2^{-d}\lambda_d(\Omega).
\]
Consequently, under the assumptions of
Theorem~(thm:density-bound of the paper),
\[
    \sigma_\eta(\Omega)=0
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \rho_\eta\geq2^{-d}\lambda_d(\Omega).
\]

\sqrt{\pi t}\,e^{\,-4\pi\beta |x|+16\pi^2\beta^2 t}\,

\int_0^\infty e^{4\pi\beta u}\,u\,e^{-\frac{(|x|+u)^2}{4t}}\,du

\erfc\!\Big(\frac{|x|}{2\sqrt t}-4\pi\beta \sqrt{t}\Big)
\,+\,

\end{align}

[Theorem thm:uniqueness of arXiv:2602.19192, 'Bakry--\'Emery Curvature of the Fractional Laplacian\\ via Fractional Brownian Covariance'] On $\mathbb{T}$, $\gamma = 1$ is the unique stability index for which
$\Gamma_2 \geq \kappa\,\Gamma$ holds with $\kappa \geq 1$
on all real trigonometric polynomials. The three regimes are:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\gamma < 1$: positive cross-sign coupling ($B > 0$),
  anti-persistent fBM dual ($H < 1/2$), $\kappa_{\mathrm{real}} < 1$.
\item $\gamma = 1$: zero cross-sign ($B = 0$),
  Brownian dual ($H = 1/2$), $\kappa_{\mathrm{real}} = 1$.
\item $\gamma > 1$: negative cross-sign ($B < 0$),
  long-range dependent dual ($H > 1/2$), $\kappa_{\mathrm{real}} < 1$.
\end{enumerate}
