body: In any bipartite graph, the maximum size of a matching (a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint) equals the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge). Both can be computed efficiently, and a minimum vertex cover can be extracted from a maximum matching via alternating paths from unmatched vertices. The equality can fail in non-bipartite graphs, where the minimum vertex cover can strictly exceed the maximum matching, for instance in an odd cycle. Proved by Denes Konig in 1931; equivalent to Hall's marriage theorem and a special case of the max-flow min-cut theorem.
title: Konig's theorem

\begin{align}
\exp(\tfrac{\kappa|\x-\y|}{N})\mathbf{H}^{N}_{\s,\t,\x,\y}&\lesssim_{\kappa}N^{-1}|\t-\s|^{-\frac12},\\
\exp(\tfrac{\kappa|\x-\y|}{N})|[\mathscr{S}^{N}\star\mathbf{H}^{N}_{\s,\t,\cdot,\y}]_{\x}|&\lesssim_{\kappa}N^{-1}|\t-\s|^{-\frac12},\\

body: [Corollary 1 (Overfitting implies a robust gap) of arXiv:2602.20971, 'Does Order Matter : Connecting The Law of Robustness to Robust Generaliz'] If $0<\varepsilon<\sigma^{2}$ and $\widehat{R}_{0}(f)\leq\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon,$ then $\operatorname{Gap}_{\rho}(f)\geq\Gamma_{\rho}(\varepsilon,L)$ where $\Gamma_{\rho}(\epsilon,L):=\sigma^{2}-\left(\sqrt{\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon}+L\rho\right)^{2}=\varepsilon-2L\rho\sqrt{\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon}-L^{2}\rho^{2}$. In particular, the lower bound is positive whenever $L\rho<\sigma-\sqrt{\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon}$.

[Lemma 73 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Suppose that Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}, \ref{Assumptions_basic} and \ref{Assumptions_offcrit}
 hold. Assume that $h = H$ and $\mathfrak{b} = +\infty$. Take an arbitrary $\mathfrak{a}$ such that
$[\mathfrak{a},+\infty)$ is included in a void. Then, for any $c>0$ there exists an interval $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2) \subseteq \amsmathbb{R}_{> 0}$ and $\eps > 0$ such that
\[
\forall x \in ( \mathfrak{a}+\zeta_2,+\infty) \qquad V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(x) - V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(\mathfrak{a}+\zeta_1)> c + \eps \log\big(1 + |x|\big),
\]
and
\[
 V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(\mathfrak{a}+\zeta_1)=\inf_{x\in [\mathfrak{a}+\zeta_1,+\infty)} V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(x).
\]
There exists $C>0$ depending only on $\mathfrak{a},c$ and the constants in the assumptions, such that the choice of $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$ can be made to obey $\zeta_2<C$ and $\zeta_2-\zeta_1> \frac{1}{C}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 (Bounded inclusion-minimal negative-support family and \texorpdfstring{$\bm{w}$}{w}-admissible exponent lattices) of arXiv:2609.02449, 'Finite Directional Coefficient Modules over Euler Fibers of $A$-Hypergeometric Systems'] The \emph{bounded inclusion-minimal negative-support family} is defined by
\[
\mathcal{M}_{\bm{w}}(\Lambda):=\MinNS(\Lambda)\cap\mathcal{B}_{\bm{w}}(\Lambda).
\]
An exponent lattice $\Lambda\in\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}$ is called \emph{$\bm{w}$-admissible} if $\mathcal{M}_{\bm{w}}(\Lambda)\neq\emptyset$.
Put
\begin{align}

\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta},\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{adm}}&:=\left\{\Lambda\in\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{M}_{\bm{w}}(\Lambda)\neq\emptyset\right\},\\

\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta},\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{null}}&:=\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}\setminus\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta},\bm{w}}^{\mathrm{adm}}.
\end{align}
title: Bounded inclusion-minimal negative-support family and \texorpdfstring{$\bm{w}$}{w}-admissible exponent lattices

body:
[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2606.17452, 'Optional Stopping for Superhedging Supermartingales'] Let $\tau$ be a stopping time, $f \in Q$ and fix $T \in \mathbb{N}\cup \{\infty\}$.
The following holds at all $S \in \mathcal{S}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item[i)]
\begin{equation} \nonumber
\overline{\sigma}_{\tau(S)}({\bf 1}_{\{\tau < T\}}~f)(S) \leq {\bf 1}_{\{\tau < T\}}(S)~\overline{\sigma}_{\tau(S)}f(S).
\end{equation}
\item[ii)]
\begin{equation} \nonumber
\overline{\sigma}_{\tau(S)}({\bf 1}_{\{\tau = T\}}~f)(S) \leq {\bf 1}_{\{\tau = T\}}(S)~\overline{\sigma}_{\tau(S)}f(S).
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}
Moreover, the above inequalities are actually equalities if
$\overline{\sigma}_{\tau(S)} 0(S) =0$
(which, as we have mentioned, it is equivalent to the fact that $(L_{(S, \tau(S))})$ holds).

body:
[Proposition 30 (Mean-field limit for exchangeable pair-repulsion systems) of arXiv:2605.23529, 'Generalized Bessel-Dunkl diffusions'] Assume that
\begin{equation*}
    \sigma_i(t,x)=\sigma(t,x),
    \qquad
    b_i(t,x)=b(t,x),
    \qquad
    H_{ij}(t,x,y)=H(t,x,y)=H(t,y,x),
\end{equation*}
where $\sigma,b$ and $H$ are continuous.  For each $N$, consider
\begin{equation}
    
    dX_i^{(N)}(t)
    =
    \frac1{\sqrt N}\sigma\bigl(t,X_i^{(N)}(t)\bigr)\,dB_i(t)
    +
    b\bigl(t,X_i^{(N)}(t)\bigr)\,dt
    +
    \frac1N
    \sum_{j\ne i}
    \frac{H\bigl(t,X_i^{(N)}(t),X_j^{(N)}(t)\bigr)}
         {X_i^{(N)}(t)-X_j^{(N)}(t)}\,dt .
\end{equation}
Suppose that the finite systems satisfy the existence and integrability assumptions
of Theorem~\ref{thm:mf:classical}; for example, this follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:example:GM-H} whenever the corresponding dominance, face sign,
and non-sticking conditions hold.  Assume also the coefficient growth and initial
moment hypotheses \ref{ass:mf:coeff}-\ref{ass:mf:initial}.  Then the empirical
measure processes
\begin{equation*}
    \mu_t^{(N)}
    =
    \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{X_i^{(N)}(t)}
\end{equation*}
are tight in $C([0,T],\mathcal P(\R))$ for every $T>0$.  Every subsequential limit
$\mu=(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ satisfies, for every $f\in C_b^2(\R)$,
\begin{align}
    \langle\mu_t,f\rangle
    &=
    \langle\mu_0,f\rangle
    +
    \int_0^t
    \langle\mu_s,b(s,\cdot)f'\rangle\,ds
     +
    \frac12
    \int_0^t
    \int_{\R^2}
    D_f^{-}(x,y)H(s,x,y)\,
    \mu_s(dx)\mu_s(dy)\,ds.
    
\end{align}

If the limiting equation \eqref{eq:example:GM-mean-field-limit} has a unique solution
in $C([0,T],\mathcal P(\R))$, then the whole sequence $\mu^{(N)}$ converges to that
solution.

Set
\[
 \theta_{\alpha,\gamma}:=
 \min\bigl\{1,q_{\gamma,\alpha},

Then
\begin{equation}

 \lesssim \mathfrak C_T(\norm{\mathbb X_{\alpha,\gamma}}_T),
\end{equation}
and the solution map is locally Lipschitz, uniformly over restart times on
compact intervals.
\end{samepage}

body: In probability theory, Chebyshev's inequality (also called the Bienaymé–Chebyshev inequality) provides an upper bound on the probability of deviation of a random variable (with finite variance) from its mean. More specifically, the probability that a random variable deviates from its mean by more than $k\sigma$ is at most $1/k^{2}$, where $k$ is any positive constant and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation (the square root of the variance).

The multi-season epidemic process is a discrete-time Markov chain on S_r subset Delta^{r-1} x [0, 1]^{r-1} with effective dimension 2r - 3. The state transition (p^{(k)}, iota^{(k)}) -> (p^{(k+1)}, iota^{(k+1)}) driven by (delta_k, tau_k) satisfies: p_1^{(k+1)} = z^{(k)}; p_j^{(k+1)} = p_{j-1}^{(k)} (1 - z_{j-1}^{(k)}) for 2 <= j < r; p_r^{(k+1)} = p_r^{(k)} (1 - z_r^{(k)}) + p_{r-1}^{(k)} (1 - z_{r-1}^{(k)}); iota_1^{(k+1)} = 1; and iota_j^{(k+1)} = iota_{j-1}^{(k)} (1 - delta_k) for 2 <= j < r.
Cutoff r >= 2
Shocks (delta_k, tau_k) are i.i.d.

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The orthogonal polynomials for $L^2[0,\infty)$, with scalar product
$$<f,g>=\int_0^\infty f(x)g(x)e^{-x}\,dx$$
are the Laguerre polynomials $\{P_k\}$, satisfying the following differential equation,
$$xP_k''(x)+(1-x)P_k'(x)+kP_k(x)=0$$
as well as the following order $2$ recurrence relation,
$$(k+1)P_{k+1}(x)=(2k+1-x)P_k(x)-kP_{k-1}(x)$$
and which are given by the following formula,
$$P_k(x)=\frac{e^x}{k!}\cdot\frac{d^k}{dx^k}\left(e^{-x}x^k\right)$$
called Rodrigues formula for the Laguerre polynomials.
title: Unnumbered theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

\[
 \|(x,A,Q)\|_{\mathrm{split},p}
 :=\|x\|_H+\|A\|_{p,\infty}+\|Q\|_1,
 \qquad
 \|A\|_{p,\infty}:=\sup_{n\geq1}n^{1/p}s_n(A).

\]
Its completion is canonically
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr G^{(p)}_0(H)
 :=H\times\mathcal S^0_{p,\infty}(H)_{\mathrm{skew}}
       \times\mathcal S_1(H)_{\mathrm{sa}}.
 
\end{equation}
The product \eqref{cc:eq-critical-split-product}, inverse, dilations, and
bounded pushforwards extend continuously, and
\[
 \mathscr G^{(p)}_+(H)
 :=\{(x,A,Q)\in\mathscr G^{(p)}_0(H):Q\succeq0\}
\]
is a closed submonoid.  An equivalent Aoki--Rolewicz power metric makes
each \(\mathscr G^{(p)}_0(H)\) a Polish group.  At \(p=1\) this is exactly
\(\mathscr G_{\mathrm{crit}}(H)\) with its previously defined topology.

[Thm relation static and dynamic SBP of arXiv:2411.13765, 'Schr\"odinger Bridge Problem for Jump Diffusions'] [follmer1988random]
The Schr\"odinger problems (equation Definition:DynamicSBP of the paper) and (equation Definition:StaticSBP of the paper) admit at most one solution $\hat{\mathbf{P}}$ and $\hat{\pi}$ respectively. Assume that the reference measure $R$ in the static problem (equation Definition:StaticSBP of the paper) and the reference path measure $\mathbf{R}$ in the dynamic problem (equation Definition:DynamicSBP of the paper) are such that $R=\mathbf{R}_{0T}$. Then, we have the following relations between the solutions: 
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\hat{\pi}$ is the solution to (equation Definition:StaticSBP of the paper), then
            \begin{equation}
                \hat{\mathbf{P}}(\cdot):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n}\mathbf{R}^{xy}(\cdot)\hat{\pi}(dxdy)
            \end{equation}
        is the solution to (equation Definition:DynamicSBP of the paper), which means that $\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{0T}=\hat{\pi}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{P}}$ shares its bridges with $\mathbf{R}$ in the sense that
            \[
                \hat{\mathbf{P}}^{xy}=\mathbf{R}^{xy} \text{ for $\hat{\pi}$-a.e. $(x,y)$}.
            \]
        \item Conversely, if $\hat{\mathbf{P}}$ is the solution to (equation Definition:DynamicSBP of the paper), then $\hat{\pi}:=\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{0T}$ is the solution to (equation Definition:StaticSBP of the paper).
        
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let f be the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous real functions on a metric space X (such an f is said to be of Baire class one). Then: (i) f is Borel measurable, indeed for every real a the set {f > a} is an F-sigma set; (ii) if X is completely metrizable, the set of points of continuity of f is a dense G-delta set, so f is continuous on a comeagre set. In particular a derivative, being a pointwise limit of continuous difference quotients, is Baire class one and is continuous on a comeagre set - the derivative of a differentiable function cannot be discontinuous everywhere.
Pointwise, not uniform, convergence;
completeness of X is needed only for the comeagre-continuity half.
Baire class one is strictly larger than the continuous functions and strictly smaller than the Borel functions.

body: In mathematical analysis, the Weierstrass approximation theorem states that every continuous function defined on a closed interval [a, b] can be uniformly approximated as closely as desired by a polynomial function. Because polynomials are among the simplest functions, and because computers can directly evaluate polynomials, this theorem has both practical and theoretical relevance, especially in polynomial interpolation. The original version of this result was established by Karl Weierstrass in 1885 using the Weierstrass transform.
title: Stone–Weierstrass theorem

body: [Theorem 3 of arXiv:2110.07472, 'Capacity of Group-invariant Linear Readouts from Equivariant Representations: How Many Obj'] Suppose a code which is equivariant to a finite group G is pooled to a new code which is equivariant to a finite subgroup H ⊆G. Suppose the number of trivial dimensions in the original G-equivariant code is N0. Then the fraction of linearly separable dichotomies on the G-invariant problem for the pooled code is at least f(P, ⌊N0/k⌋) where k = |G/H|. Similarly the fraction is at most f(P, N0).

\(L^2\), and that the families \(K_{n,t}\) and \(K_t\) satisfy the uniform increment bound
\[
    \|K_{n,t}-K_{n,s}\|_2^2+\|K_t-K_s\|_2^2\le C_T |t-s|^\beta .

        {(2\log\log N_j)^{m/2}}
        -
        \langle K_t,\xi^{\otimes m}\rangle
    \right|
    \longrightarrow0 .
\]

body: In mathematics, random graph is the general term to refer to probability distributions over graphs. Random graphs may be described simply by a probability distribution, or by a random process which generates them. The theory of random graphs lies at the intersection between graph theory and probability theory. From a mathematical perspective, random graphs are used to answer questions about the properties of typical graphs. Its practical applications are found in all areas in which complex networks need to be modeled – many random graph models are thus known, mirroring the diverse types of complex networks encountered in different areas. In a mathematical context, random graph refers almost exclusively to the Erdős–Rényi random graph model. In other contexts, any graph model may be referred to as a random graph.
title: Random graph

[Proposition 22 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] For every $\eps,\ka>0$,
the operator $H_{\ka,\eps}$ is self-adjoint on $L^2(D)$.
Its spectrum $\la_1(H_{\ka,\eps})\leq\la_2(H_{\ka,\eps})\leq\cdots$ is purely discrete, bounded below, and has no accumulation point.
Moreover, the corresponding eigenfunctions $\psi_1(H_{\ka,\eps}),\psi_2(H_{\ka,\eps}),\ldots$
form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(D)$. Finally, for any $f\in L^2(D)$,
\begin{align}

\mr e^{-t H_{\ka,\eps}}f=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mr e^{-t\la_n(H_{\ka,\eps})}\big\langle\psi_n(H_{\ka,\eps}),f\big\rangle\psi_n(H_{\ka,\eps}).
\end{align}

    \[
    \lim_{m \to \infty} \eta(\widehat{A} \cap A_m) = a \, \eta(\widehat{A}).
    \]
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition the existence of the pairing sigma of arXiv:2411.11341, 'Ultra high order cumulants and quantitative CLT for polynomials in Random Matrices'] Let $r\geq 2$ and $m_1,\dots,m_r\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $m=\sum_{i=1}^r m_i$. Let $\gamma\in \mathcal{P}(m)$ be the partition whose blocks are
\begin{align*}\{m_1+\cdots+m_{j-1}+1,\dots,m_1+\cdots+m_j\},\qquad 1\leq j\leq r
\end{align*}
with the convention $m_0=0$. Let $\tau\in \mathcal{P}(m)$ be a partition such that each block of $\tau$ has even size and $\gamma\vee\tau=1_m$. Then there exists a pairing $\sigma\leq \tau$ such that $\#(\sigma\vee\gamma)\leq r/2$.

body:
[Thm LDP-RWRS of arXiv:2608.13084, '\bf Branching random walk in random environment'] For any $\varepsilon\in (0, p\wedge (1-p))$, there exist positive constants $c_1(\varepsilon)$ and $c_2(\varepsilon)$ such that for any $x\in{\mathbb Z}^d$,
\begin{align*}
\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-\frac{d}{d+2}}\log \mathbb{Q}_x\left( \frac{T_n}{n} > p+\varepsilon\right) = &- c_1(\varepsilon),\\
\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-\frac{d}{d+2}}\log \mathbb{Q}_x\left( \frac{T_n}{n} < p-\varepsilon\right) = &- c_2(\varepsilon).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:volume-process-ext of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a real number $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$. 
Fix an initialising state 
$\Psi_0 = (0, \tau_0,j,\overline{z},\emptyset,\textup{initialising})$.
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be a transition rule on a set of high-level states which includes~$\Psi_0$. Let $\Psi^*$ be the $\Psi_0$-closure of~$\mathrm{hls}$. Suppose that $\mathrm{hls}$ is $\Psi^*$-valid.
A \emph{volume process} $V$ 
from $\Psi_0$ with transition rule~$\mathrm{hls}$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$ is defined as follows. 

Choose the initial population as follows.
Choose 
a random vector 
$\overline{\mathrm{arr}} = (\mathrm{arr}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{arr}_j)
\sim\mathsf{Po}(F_{[j]}^{\Psi_0}(\tau_0))$.
Let $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^V(\tau_0)$ be a tuple
of $j$~disjoint sets
$\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^V(\tau_0) = (\mathbf{arr}^V_1(\tau_0),\ldots,\mathbf{arr}^V_j(\tau_0))$ 
where each $\mathbf{arr}^V_i(\tau_0) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(\tau_0)$ and has size 
$\mathrm{arr}^V_i(\tau_0)$.

Let ${\overline{\mathbf{b}}}^V_{[j]}(\tau_0) = \overline{\mathbf{arr}}^V(\tau_0)$.
For all $i>j$, let   ${\mathbf{b}^V_i}(\tau_0) = \emptyset$. 

Let the initial high-level state $\Psi(\tau_0)$ be~$\Psi_0$. 
Crucially, we will show in Lemma~(lem:dist-volume of the paper) that the following invariant is maintained, conditioned on the value of $\Psi(\tau_0),\ldots,\Psi(t)$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Invariant: $
\mathrm{dist}( {\overline{b}}^{V}_{[j^{\Psi(t)}]}(t))= \mathsf{Po}(F_{[j^{\Psi(t)}]}^{\Psi(t)}(t))$. For $i> j^{\Psi(t)}$, $b_i^V(t)=0$.
 

\end{itemize}

For all $t> \tau_0$ the evolution of $V$ at step~$t$ is as follows, having 
already defined $\Psi(t-1)$ and  ${\overline{\mathbf{b}}}^V(t-1)$.

\begin{itemize}

\item Let $j = j^{\Psi(t-1)}$.

\item Let $Y_{t-1}$ be a $j$-jammed process with 
send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$t-1$, 
birth rate~$\lambda$, and initial population  $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{Y_{t-1}}(t-1) = {\overline{\mathbf{b}}}_{[j]}^V(t-1)$.

\item Explanation: 
Let $\overline{z} = \overline{z}^{\Psi(t-1)}$.
From the invariant, 
$\mathrm{dist}(\overline{\mathrm{arr}}^{Y_{t-1}}(t-1) ) =
\mathsf{Po}(F_{[j]}^{\Psi(t-1)}(t-1))  
$   which, by 
Definition~(def:F of the paper), is 
$\mathsf{Po}( f_{[j]}^{\overline{0},  
\overline{z}}(t-1 - \tau^{\Psi(t-1)}))$.  
By 
Lemma~(lem:f-track-jammed of the paper),
$\mathrm{dist}({\overline{b}}_{[j]}^{Y_{t-1}}(t)) = 
\mathsf{Po}(f_{[j]}^{\overline{0}, \overline{z}}(t-\tau^{\Psi(t-1)}))
$ which, by Definition~(def:F of the paper) again, is
$
\mathsf{Po}(F_{[j]}^{\Psi(t-1)}(t))
$.

 
\item  Let $\Psi(t) = \mathrm{hls}(\Psi(t-1), {\overline{b}}^{Y_{t-1}}_{[j]}(t), t)$.

\item Explanation:  
Let $\overline{X} \sim 
\mathrm{dist}({\overline{b}}_{[j]}^{Y_{t-1}}(t)) = 
\mathsf{Po}(F^{\Psi(t-1)}_{[j]}(t))$
and let $A = \mathrm{dist}(\overline{X} \mid \mathrm{hls}(\Psi(t-1), \overline{X}, t) = \Psi(t))$.
The function $\phi_{\Psi(t-1),\Psi(t),t}$ is  
$\phi_{A(\Psi(t-1),\Psi(t),t),
\mathsf{Po}(F^{\Psi(t)}_{[j]}(t))}$  in Definition~(def:valid of the paper) since $\mathrm{hls}$ is $\Psi^*$-valid.  
By construction  (from Definition~(def:phi of the paper)), for all $\overline{a}\in (\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0})^j$,  $\phi_{\Psi(t-1),\Psi(t),t}(\overline{a}) \leq \overline{a} $.
When
$\overline{a} \sim A$, 
the random variable 
$\phi_{\Psi(t-1),\Psi(t),t}(\overline{a})$
has distribution $\mathsf{Po}(F_{[j]}^{\Psi(t)}(t))$.

\item Let ${\overline{b}}^V_{[j]}(t) = \phi_{\Psi(t-1),\Psi(t),t}({\overline{b}}^{Y_{t-1}}_{[j]}(t))$.

\item Explanation: It will be the case that
$\mathrm{dist}({\overline{b}}^V_{[j]}(t)) = 
\mathsf{Po}(F_{[j]}^{\Psi(t)}(t))
$ and, for all $i \in [j]$,
$b^V_i(t) \leq b_i^{Y_{t-1}}(t)$.  

\item  For all $i\in [j]$,  let  $\mathbf{b}_i^{V}(t)$ be the lexicographically least
subset of $\mathbf{b}_i^{Y_{t-1}}(t)$ 
of size $b^V_i(t)$. 
 

\item {For all $i > j$, let $\mathbf{b}^V_i(t) = \emptyset$.}
\end{itemize}

[Thm beta-independent-2D-mixing-time of arXiv:2605.08052, 'Rapid phase ordering of Ising dynamics on $\mathbb Z^2$'] Consider the Ising model on $\Lambda_n = [- \frac{n}{2},\frac{n}{2}]^2\cap \mathbb Z^2$ with all-plus boundary conditions. There exist $\beta_0>0$ and $C>0$ such that for all $\beta > \beta_0$ and all $n\ge 1$, 
    \begin{align*}
        t_{\textsc{mix}} \le  \exp( C (1 \vee \log n)^3)\,.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] Let \(M\) be Seifert fibred with base \(S^2\) and exactly three exceptional fibres.
    Exactly one of the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $M$ is Haken, so $\pi_0 \Diff(M) \cong \Out(\pi_1(M))$;
        \item $M$ is geometric with $\mathbb{H}^2 \times \mathbb R$ geometry, and the standard maps induce isomorphisms
       \[ \pi_0\Isom(M)\xrightarrow{\cong} \pi_0\Diff^f(M) \xrightarrow{\cong} \pi_0\Diff(M) \xrightarrow{\rho,\cong} \Out(\pi_1(M));\]
        \item $M$ is geometric with $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ geometry, and the standard maps induce isomorphisms
       \[ \pi_0\Isom(M)\xrightarrow{\cong} \pi_0\Diff^f(M) \xrightarrow{\cong} \pi_0\Diff(M) \xrightarrow{\rho,\cong} \Out(\pi_1(M));\]
        \item $M$ is geometric with elliptic geometry, and the standard maps induce isomorphisms
       \[ \pi_0\Isom(M)\xrightarrow{\cong} \pi_0\Diff(M).\]
     \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, in each case the mapping class group $\pi_0 \Diff(M)$ is finite.
title: Unnumbered proposition of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'

[Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(E\) be an equivalence relation on a Polish space \(X\). If 
    \[E \leq_B E_{S_\infty}\]
    we say that \(E\) is \textit{classifiable by countable structures}. If 
    \[E \not\leq_B E_{S_\infty}\]
    we say that \(E\) is \textit{not classifiable by countable structures}.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a sequence of Wigner random matrices
$$Z_N\in M_N(L^\infty(X))$$
which by definition have i.i.d. complex normal entries, up to $Z_N=Z_N^*$, we have
$$Z_N\sim\gamma_t$$
in the $N\to\infty$ limit, where $\gamma_t=\frac{1}{2\pi t}\sqrt{4t-x^2}dx$ is the Wigner semicircle law.

[Theorem Wick formula 2 of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given independent variables $f_i$, each following the complex normal law $G_t$, with $t>0$ being a fixed parameter, we have the formula
$$E\left(f_{i_1}\ldots f_{i_k}f_{j_1}^*\ldots f_{j_k}^*\right)=t^k\#\left\{\pi\in S_k\Big|i_{\pi(r)}=j_r,\forall r\right\}$$
for the non-vanishing joint moments of these variables.

[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2605.02093, 'An analytic approach to the finite $R$-transform'] Let $\epsilon > 0$. Assume that $p_N \in \calP_N((-\infty, -\epsilon])$ is a sequence of polynomials whose empirical root distributions $\meas{p_N}$ converge weakly to a probability measure $\mu \in \calM((-\infty, -\epsilon])$.
Then, for each $s\in(0,\alpha)$, where $\alpha:=G_\mu(0)$, we have
\[
  L_{p_N}^{(N)}(s)-L_{p_N}^{(\infty)}(s)
  =O\!\left(\frac{\log N}{N}\right).
\]

In a finite bipartite graph the maximum size of a matching equals the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge). The inequality maximum matching <= minimum vertex cover holds in every graph; equality is special to bipartite graphs and fails already for a triangle (matching 1, cover 2). Equivalent to Hall's marriage theorem and to the max-flow min-cut theorem on the corresponding unit-capacity network; the dual statement (Konig's edge-colouring theorem) says a bipartite graph of maximum degree D can be properly edge-coloured with D colours.

For equality let G have parts L and R and let M be a maximum matching. Let U be the set of vertices of L not covered by M, and let Z be the set of vertices reachable from U by M-alternating paths (paths whose edges alternate between non-matching and matching edges, starting with a non-matching edge out of U). Put K = (L minus Z) union (R intersect Z). K is a vertex cover: an edge from L intersect Z to R minus Z cannot exist, since traversing it would put its R endpoint into Z (if the edge is not in M it extends an alternating path; if it is in M its L endpoint entered Z by a matching edge from R, which is that edge itself, so the R endpoint is already in Z). Every vertex of R intersect Z is matched (an unmatched one would end an M-augmenting path from U, contradicting maximality of M by Berge's lemma) and its partner lies in L intersect Z, while every vertex of L minus Z is matched (the unmatched vertices of L are exactly U, which lies in Z) to a vertex of R minus Z. body: [Definition 4 of arXiv:2609.03976, '2609.03976'] Let $f\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a nonconstant regular function. There exist $P(s) \in \mathcal{D}_{X}[s]$ and $b(s) \in \mathbb{C}[s]$, such that $P(s)f^{s+1}=b(s)f^{s}$, where $s$ is an independent variable(see, for example, \cite{Popa_ref}). All these possible $b(s)$ form an ideal, and since $\mathbb{C}[s]$ is a principal ideal domain, there exists a unique monic generator of this ideal. We will denote this polynomial by $b_{f}(s)$ and it is called the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of $f$.

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The integral of a function $f$ on $[a,b]$ is its normalized average
$$\int_a^bf(x)dx=(b-a)\times A(f)$$
that is, average $A(f)$ times the length of the interval $b-a$. Equivalently, 
$$\int_a^bf(x)dx=(b-a)\times\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^nf\left(a+\frac{b-a}{n}\cdot k\right)$$
which can stand as a formal definition for the integral.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

[Lem 13 of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] For any positive constants $\Lambda>1$, $c\in (0,\Lambda-1)$, there exists $c' > 0$, such that the following holds. Let $A \subseteq \Z^d$ be a finite set containing the origin, and let $\mathrm{diam}(A):=\max_{x,y \in A} \|x-y\|$ be its diameter. Then
\[\bP(x \xleftrightarrow{ Q_{0,2\Lambda\text{diam}(A)}} A) \geq c' \cdot (d(x,A))^{2-d} \cdot \mathrm{Cap}_{d-4}(A)\]
for any $x\in Q_{0,\Lambda \mathrm{diam}(A)}$ such that $d(x, A) \geq c \cdot \mathrm{diam}(A)$. Here, for $x \in \Z^d$ and a subset $A \subseteq \Z^d$, we define $d(x,A)=\inf_{a \in A}\|x-a\|$.
title: Lem 13 of arXiv:2607.24561

[Theorem th:main of arXiv:2601.06850, 'Explosion and non-explosion in pure birth Crump--Mode--Jagers branching processes'] ~

\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont(i)]
	\item If $\sum_{i=1}^\infty \lambda_i^{-1}<\infty$, then the process is explosive.
	\item If
	\begin{equation}
	
	\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{\lambda_i}i=\infty
	\end{equation}
	and
	\begin{equation}
	
	\liminf_{n\to\infty}\!\!\sum_{i=\lceil\varepsilon\log n\rceil}^n\!\! \lambda_i^{-1}>0\quad\text{for some $\varepsilon>0$},
	\end{equation}
	then the process is non-explosive.
	
	The same holds if $(\lambda_i)$ is dominated by a sequence satisfying (equation eq:lim1 of the paper) and (equation eq:lim2 of the paper).
	\item There exists a sequence $(\lambda_i)$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^\infty\lambda_i^{-1}=\infty$ and the process is explosive.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem th:main of arXiv:2601.06850

[Prop sturm-liouville of arXiv:2506.10623, 'Polynomial slowdown in an angle-dependent 2d branching Brownian motion'] Let $\alpha > 0$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$ is discrete and consists of the eigenvalues $0<\lambda_0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \cdots$ which all have multiplicity 1. 
		Let $\varphi_n$ be an eigenfunction associated to $\lambda_n$, then it has exactly $n$ zeroes, so it can be chosen uniquely such that $\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lVert\varphi_n\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rVert_2 = 1$ and $\varphi_n(x) > 0$ for any $x$ greater than its largest zero.
		Moreover, $(\varphi_n)_{n\geq 0}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. 
		
		\item Let $q > 0$. The previous point also holds for $\mathcal{L}_q$ with eigenvalues $(\lambda_{q,n})_{n\geq 0}$ and eigenfunctions $(\varphi_{q,n})_{n\geq 0}$ such that, for any $n \geq 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
	\begin{equation}
		\lambda_{q,n} = q^{2/(2+\alpha)} \lambda_n
		\qquad \text{and} \qquad
		\varphi_{q,n}(x) = q^{1/[2(2+\alpha)]} \varphi_n(q^{1/(2+\alpha)} x).
	\end{equation}
		
		\item Let $c_\alpha \coloneqq \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^1 \sqrt{1-u^\alpha} \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} u$. Then, as $n \to \infty$,
		\begin{equation} 
		\lambda_n \sim \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft( \frac{n}{c_\alpha} \aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{2\alpha/(\alpha+2)}.
		\end{equation}
		
		\item For any $n \geq 0$, the function $\varphi_n$ has the same parity as $n$.
		
		\item There exists $C >0$ depending on $\alpha$ such that, for any $n \geq 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, 
		\[
		\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lvert\varphi_n(x)\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rvert
		\leq C (n+1)^3 \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft[ 1 \wedge \exp \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft( - \frac{1}{2+\alpha} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft( \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lvertx\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rvert^{(2+\alpha)/2} -  Cn \aftergroup\egroup\originalright) \aftergroup\egroup\originalright) \aftergroup\egroup\originalright].
		\]
		
		\item There exist $C,c>0$ depending on $\alpha$ such that, for any $x \in \mathbb{R}$, 
		$\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lvert\varphi_0'(x)\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rvert
		\leq C e^{-c \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lvertx\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rvert^{(2+\alpha)/2}}$.
	\end{enumerate}

body:
[Theorem 7 (Hardness of exact quantile and lower-buffered quantile evaluation) of arXiv:2608.22227, '\fontsize{18pt}{20pt}\selectfont \bf Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Q'] The following decision problems are PP-hard under polynomial-time Turing
reductions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item exact finite-horizon QMDP evaluation, i.e., deciding whether
    \(Q_\tau(R^\pi)\le c\) for the return \(R^\pi\) of a fixed deterministic
    policy;
    \item exact lower-buffered quantile evaluation, i.e., deciding whether
    \(Q_\tau^\beta(R^\pi)\le c\) for the return \(R^\pi\) of a fixed
    deterministic policy.
\end{enumerate}
The hardness holds even for finite-horizon MDPs with two states, one action,
binary transition probabilities, and deterministic rational rewards in
\([0,1]\). Consequently, the corresponding exact planning problems are also
PP-hard under polynomial-time Turing
reductions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Hardness of exact quantile and lower-buffered quantile evaluation

body: [Corollary 3.7 of arXiv:2603.27659, 'Operator Norm Bounds for Multi-leg Matrix Tensors and Applications to Random Matrix Theory'] Let $m,N,a,b\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal{P}([m])$ be any permutations. With $M(\sigma,\tau;a,b)$ and $C(\sigma,\tau;a,b)$ as defined above, we have $\displaystyle N^{M(\sigma,\tau;a,b)}\leq\max_{\|A_{1}\|,\ldots,\|A_{m}\|\leq 1}\left|\left(\mathrm{Tr}_{\sigma}\otimes\mathrm{Tr}_{\tau}\right)\left(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\right)\right|\leq N^{C(\sigma,\tau;a,b)}.$ Here, for the graph $G_{\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k}}$ of the permutations, $M(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})$ is the maximum over blue-edge configurations of the number of directed cycles, and $C(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})=\min_{G^{\prime}}R_{G^{\prime}}$, the minimum over full simple partial graphs $G^{\prime}$ (partial graphs keeping every rectangle and containing no directed cycle for any blue-edge configuration) of the number $R_{G^{\prime}}$ of colored edges removed to obtain $G^{\prime}$ (Definition 2.1).

[Lem external-third-susceptibility of arXiv:2607.21428, 'Subcritical percolation and network archaeology on random recursive tree substrate network'] Assume  (equation eq:arch-q-range of the paper). Let $G_n^{(q)}$ denote the $q$-percolated
			observed graph, i.e.\ the graph on $[n]$ whose edge set consists of all
			retained edges of $G_n$, both tree and shortcut. Delete from $G_n^{(q)}$ the
			vertices of the root blob $\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}$ together with all retained shortcut
			edges having at least one endpoint in $\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}$, and call the connected
			components of the remaining graph the \emph{external components}. Enumerate
			them by an index $a$, and let
			\[
			S_{n,a} \;:=\; |\{\text{vertices of the $a$-th external component}\}|
			\]
			be their vertex masses. (Each external component is, in general, a union of
			several retained tree blobs joined by retained shortcut edges; it is not a
			single blob. The external components are precisely the candidate decorations
			of Lemma~(lem:singly-attached-decorations of the paper): an external component that is joined to
			$\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}$ by a retained shortcut edge in $G_n^{(q)}$ becomes part of a
			decoration $D_u$.) Then
			\begin{equation}
				
				\frac1n \sum_a S_{n,a}^2 \;=\; O_{\mathbb P}(1),
				\qquad
				\frac1n \sum_a S_{n,a}^3 \;=\; O_{\mathbb P}(1).
		\end{equation}

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2605.25715, '2605.25715'] Consider a general  $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ of real numbers, i.e.
\[
G=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\quad a,b,c,d\in \R.
\]
Then $G$ satisfies exactly one of the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $\mathrm{trace}(G)=a+d=0$.
\item[(ii)] $\mathrm{trace}(G)=a+d \neq 0$ and $G$ singular, i.e. $\det(G)=ad-bc=0$
\item[(iii)] $\mathrm{trace}(G)=a+d \neq 0$ and $G$ non-singular, i.e. $\det(G)=ad-bc\not=0$.
\end{itemize}
In particular, in the present case of $d=2$, $(iii)$ is equivalent to the condition of Theorem \ref{mainlapuin}.

[Proposition 29 (Strong error for tRLMC) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Assume \hyperref[ass:PJG]{\textup{(A1)}}, \hyperref[ass:PLC]{\textup{(A2)}}, and \hyperref[ass:D]{\textup{(A4)}}. Let \(X(t,x;t+\lambda)\) denote the solution of

\]

body: [Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:2110.09034, 'On the construction of cospectral nonisomorphic bipartite graphs'] [7, Lemma 3] Let A, B and C be (0, 1)-matrices. Let C be a non-zero matrix and A be a square matrix with no zero rows. Then, the matrices C ⊗A and C ⊗B are permutationally equivalent if and only if A and B are permutationally equivalent. Similarly, the matrices A ⊗C and B ⊗C are permutationally equivalent if and only if A and B are permutationally equivalent.

[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2609.01413, 'Sharp Threshold for Universality of Rational Canonical Forms over a Finite Field'] Let $f\in S$, let $k\ge 1$, and set
\[
R_f:=\F_p[t]/(f^k), \qquad K:=\F_p[t]/(f).
\]
Let $M$ be a finite $R_f$-module whose type at $f$ has largest part at most $k-1$.
Equivalently, as an $R_f$-module,
\[
M\cong \bigoplus_{j=1}^m \F_p[t]/(f^{\lambda_j})
\qquad\text{with}\qquad 1\le \lambda_j\le k-1.
\]
Then
\[
\#\Ext^1_{R_f}(M,K)=\#\Hom_{R_f}(M,K).
\]
More precisely, both groups are $K$-vector spaces of dimension $m$.

[Definition of arXiv:2608.26230, 'Comments on Choiceless Chain Conditions'] Given a set $X$ we say that it is $(a)$-uncountable, for $a\in\{1,2,3,4\}$, if it satisfies the corresponding statement:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $\aleph_1\leq|A|$.
  \item $\aleph_0<|A|$.
  \item $\aleph_0<^*|A|$.
  \item $|A|\nleq\aleph_0$.
  \end{enumerate}

 \left\lvert X_k(A)\right\rvert\geq\lambda.
\]
If $B\in\binom{[n]}{k+1}$ and $A\subset B$, $\left\lvert A\right\rvert=k$, then $A$ is called a parent of $B$, and $B$ is called a child of $A$.

[Lemm lemmZhou of arXiv:2412.08497, 'Time discretization of Quadratic Forward-Backward SDEs with singular drift'] Let $y_i(t) \in L^{2p}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^m)$ be an $\mathbb{R}^m\text{-valued}$ adapted martingale for all $0\leq i \leq r$ and $p\geq 1$. Then by the martingale representation theorem, there is a square integrable process $z_i(t)$ such that, $y_i(t) = \beta_i + \int_0^t z_i(s)\mathrm{d}W_s$. For any increasing function $\eta:\{0,1,\cdots,N-1\}\rightarrow \{0,\cdots,r\}$, we define $\tilde{\eta}:\{0,\cdots,r\} \rightarrow \{-1,0,1,\cdots,N-1\}$ as $\tilde{\eta}=\sup\{j; \eta(j)\leq i\}$ with the convention $\sup\emptyset = -1.$ Then, there is a constant $C(p,m)$ independent of $r$ such that 
				\begin{align*}
					\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big( \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}} \Big| \sum_{i=\eta(j)}^r z_i(s) \Big|^2\mathrm{d}s   \Big)^p\Big] \leq C(p,m)\mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|\sum_{i=0}^r y_i(t_{\tilde{\eta}(i)+1}) - y_i(0)\Big|^{2p}  \Big] .
				\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 49 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Suppose $u: \T^d \to \R^d$ is continuous, $\nabla \cdot u =0$, and for almost every $y \in \T^d$, the ODE
    \[\begin{cases}
    \dot \Phi_t(y) = u(\Phi_t(y)),\\
    \Phi_0(y) = y,
    \end{cases}\]
    admits a unique solution on $(-\infty,\infty)$. Then for any $f \in L^1(\T^d)$ with $f \geq 0$, the continuity equation
    \begin{equation}
    
    \begin{cases}
        \partial_t \phi + \nabla \cdot (u \phi) = 0,\\
        \phi(0,\cdot) = f(\cdot),
    \end{cases}\end{equation}
    admits a unique distributional solution on $(-\infty,\infty) \times \T^d$ such that $\phi \geq 0$ and for all $T>0,$ $\phi \in \mathcal{C}^0([-T,T],L^1(\T^d))$. Further
    \[\phi(t,\cdot) = (\Phi_t)_* f = f \circ \Phi_{-t},\]
    where $(\Phi_t)_* f$ denotes the pushforward of $f$ as a measure density with respect to Lebesgue, and hence $\phi$ is a renormalized solution in the DiPerna--Lions sense: that is, for all $\beta : \R \to \R$ such that $\beta \in C^1_b(\R)$, $\beta(\phi)$ is also a distributional solution to~\eqref{eq:continuity abstract} with initial data $\beta(f)$.

Let G = (V, E) be a countable locally finite directed graph. The particle system with hitting-time local interactions consists of health processes X_v(t) = x_v + Z_v(t) - sum_{u in N_G^-(v)} c_{uv} 1_{u in D_t} for v in V, where x_v >= 0 is initial capital, Z_v is a cadlag driving process with no positive jumps, N_G^-(v) is the in-neighborhood of v, c_{uv} >= 0 is default transmission impact, and D_t = {v in V : inf_{s in [0, t]} X_v(s) <= 0} is the cumulative default set.
G is countable and locally finite
Z_v are cadlag with Z_v(t) - Z_v(t-) <= 0
c_{uv} >= 0

[Theorem 8 (Hairer--Mattingly) of arXiv:2606.23222, 'A Route to Harris ergodicity for Non-Feller Markov Kernels'] Under the preceding drift and small-set assumptions, there exist
\(\beta>0\) and \(\bar\gamma\in(0,1)\) such that
\[
        \rho_\beta(\mu_1P,\mu_2P)
        \le
        \bar\gamma\,\rho_\beta(\mu_1,\mu_2)
\]
for all probability measures \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) with finite \(V\)-moment.
Consequently, \(P\) admits a unique invariant probability measure \(\pi\), and
there exist constants \(C<\infty\) and \(\rho\in(0,1)\) such that
\[
        \|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_V
        \le
        C(1+V(x))\rho^n,
        \qquad n\ge0 .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 18 of arXiv:2512.05687, '$L^p$-Boltzmann-Gibbs principle \\ via Littlewood-Paley-Stein inequality'] Assume $V''\ge -\a$ for some $\a>0$ and $\int_\R e^{-V(\eta)} d\eta<\infty$.
Let $p\in (0,\infty)$.  Then, there exist constants $c=c_{p,\a}, C=C_{p,\a}>0$, 
which are uniform in $\ell$ and $m$, such that

c\big\{ \|f\|_{L^p(\bar\mu_{\ell,m})} + \|D_\phi f\|_{L^p(\bar\mu_{\ell,m})} \big\}
&\le \|(1-L_{0,\ell})^{1/2}f\|_{L^p(\bar\mu_{\ell,m})} \\
&\le 
C\big\{ \|f\|_{L^p(\bar\mu_{\ell,m})} + \|D_\phi f\|_{L^p(\bar\mu_{\ell,m})} \big\},

for $f \in W^{1,p}(\mathcal{Y}_{\ell,m}, \bar\mu_{\ell,m})$, where

body:
[Thm THM52 of arXiv:2608.16170, '\bf On hitting time distributions of Markov processes with sub-Gaussian heat kernel bounds'] Let $X$ be a Borel right process on $(E,d)$ that satisfies (AC), (H2a) and (H2b).

 Further assume that $X$ admits the following short-time heat kernel lower bound at a fixed point $x\in E$: For some $T>0, \alpha>0,\beta>1$, there exist constants $C_1,C_2>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
p(t,x,y)\ge \frac{C_1}{t^{\alpha/\beta}}\exp\left\{-C_2\left(\frac{d(x,y)}{t^{1/\beta}}\right)^{\beta/(\beta -1)}\right\}, \quad \forall t\in (0, T], \, y\in E.
\end{equation}
Let $B\subset E$ be a nearly Borel set with compact closure $\overline{B}$. 
Then for any $\delta,\rho>0$ and any $\lambda>0$ ($\lambda\geq 0$ if $X$ is transient),
 \[
        \mathbb{P}^x[\sigma_B\leq t]\geq \frac{\nu^{(\lambda)}_{B_{x,\delta}}(\overline{B}_{x,\delta})}{\mathrm{e}^{\lambda T}}\cdot \frac{C_1C_3}{ t^{(\alpha-\beta)/\beta}}\exp\left\{-(1+\rho)C_2\left( \frac{\widetilde{d}(x,B)+\delta}{t^{1/\beta}}\right)^{\beta/(\beta-1)}\right\},\quad 0<t\leq T,
    \]
    where  $B_{x,\delta}:=\{y\in B:d(y,x)\leq \widetilde{d}(x,B)+\delta\}$, $\nu^{(\lambda)}_{B_{x,\delta}}$ is the measure obtained in Lemma~(LM51 of the paper), $C_1$ and $C_2$ are as in (equation eq:55 of the paper), and $C_3=(\beta-1)\rho\cdot \min\{(1+\rho)^{\alpha-\beta-\alpha/\beta}, 1\}>0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha, \beta,\rho$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Integrator-authored exact special-case argument and failure analysis after checking the incoming source Result: The coordinate-diagonal case is a sum of binary entropies, whose second derivatives are -1/[q(1-q)]. There is also an explicit non-diagonal line: for Q(c)=[[1/2,c],[c,1/2]], |c|<1/2, the empty and doubleton probabilities are a=1/4-c^2 and the two singleton probabilities are b=1/4+c^2. Hence H(c)=-2*a*log(a)-2*b*log(b), and Hsecond(c)=4*log(a/b)-8*c^2*(1/a+1/b)<=0. Continuity includes c=+-1/2. This verifies concavity on this affine kernel line. In general the determinant probabilities depend nonlinearly on Q, so concavity of Shannon entropy in a probability vector cannot be applied directly to an arithmetic kernel midpoint. Check: Inclusion-exclusion gives p11=det(Q), p10=Q11-det(Q), p01=Q22-det(Q), p00=det(I-Q); these are a,b,b,a and sum to one. Differentiating H first gives 4*c*log(a/b), independently confirming the second derivative and its sign. Obstruction: No joint concavity proof, no extension to arbitrary off-diagonal or noncommuting kernels, and no numerical trials treated as certification.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0461-entropy-concavity-for-determinantal-kernels
No independent review

Refuted inference, not a theorem: a positive order parameter in a Gibbs law conditioned on a selected crystalline branch does not by itself imply a positive vanishing-field response in the unrestricted zero-field law. The probability and entropy cost of that branch in the full partition function are missing hypotheses. The explicit three-state family in this bundle has branch response a>0 but full pressure slope zero.
A branch-conditioned law is different from the unrestricted law

Let X >= 0 with mu = E[X] > 0 and finite second moment, 0 <= theta < 1, t = theta mu and Y = (X - t)_+. Then P(X > t) >= E[Y]^2/E[Y^2] >= (mu - t)^2/E[X^2] = (1 - theta)^2 mu^2/E[X^2]. The two coefficients agree at theta = 0, and for 0 < theta < 1 the first is strictly larger.

[Theorem Theorem_optimal_stopping_times of arXiv:2608.08299, 'Non-linear optimal stopping with Bermudan strategies: the infinite horizon case'] \begin{enumerate}
    \item Assume that $\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \xi(\theta_n) <+\infty$.
    We assume that: if $\eta \in L^+_0(\mathcal{F}_{\infty})$, if 
  $(\tau_k)$ $\in \Theta^{\mathbb{N}}$ non-decreasing such that $\lim_{k \rightarrow +\infty} \tau_k  = +\infty$, then
  \[
  \limsup_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \limsup_{k \rightarrow +\infty} \rho_{\theta_n, \tau_k} [\eta] =  \eta.\]
    Let $\varepsilon >0 $. For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, we define: 
    \begin{equation}
    A_k^{\varepsilon}:=\{\tau \in \Theta_{\theta_k} : V(\tau) < \xi(\tau)+\varepsilon \,\,\, a.s. \}
   \,\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,\,
    \nu_k^{\varepsilon}:= \essinf A_k^{\varepsilon}.
   \end{equation}
    Then, $\nu_k^{\varepsilon}$ is a.s. finite and 
    \[
 V(\theta_k) \leq  \rho_{\theta_k, \nu_k^{\varepsilon}} [\xi(\nu_k^{\varepsilon})]+C\varepsilon,
    \]
    where $C>0$ is a positive constant (depending on $\rho$ only).
    \item
    Let us define: 
    \begin{equation}
    A_k:=\{\tau \in \Theta_{\theta_k} : V(\tau) = \xi(\tau) \,\,\, a.s. \}
   \,\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,\,
    \nu_k:= \essinf A_k,
   \end{equation}
    with the convention that $\essinf A_k = + \infty$ if $A_k=\emptyset$.
   It holds: \\ $\nu_k$ is optimal for the problem with value $V(\theta_k)$, if and only if, $\nu_k < +\infty$ a.s.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Fix finitely many inputs x^1,...,x^m in R^n_in and a finite T>0. For clarity restrict to a positive definite input Gram matrix V_0^{alpha beta}=<x^alpha,x^beta>/n_in. All layers have width n, zero biases, and mutually independent standard Gaussian weight entries. Equivalently, start from this deterministic V_0 and, conditional on V_l, draw n independent Gaussian m-vectors G_i with covariance V_l; update V_{l+1}^{alpha beta}=(c_n/n) sum_i phi_n(G_i^alpha)phi_n(G_i^beta). This is the covariance Markov chain of the Gaussian network, up to the harmless first-layer index shift. Let d_n/n tend to T. Let phi in C^4(R) satisfy phi(0)=0, phi′(0)=1 and |phi^(4)(x)|<=C(1+|x|^p) for some C,p>0. Fix a>0, put s=a sqrt(n), phi_n(x)=s phi(x/s), and c_n=(E[phi_n(g)^2])^(-1) for standard Gaussian g. The upper-triangular covariance process V_{floor(nt)} converges locally in distribution in the Skorohod topology to dV=b(V)dt+Sigma(V)^(1/2)dB, started at V_0, where Sigma_{alpha beta,gamma delta}(V)=V^{alpha gamma}V^{beta delta}+V^{alpha delta}V^{beta gamma} and b_{alpha beta}(V)=phi′′(0)^2/(4a^2) [V^{alpha alpha}V^{beta beta}+V^{alpha beta}(2V^{alpha beta}-3)] + phi′′′(0)/(2a^2) V^{alpha beta}(V^{alpha alpha}+V^{beta beta}-2). Local convergence means convergence of the processes stopped when the Euclidean norm of their upper-triangular vector first reaches any fixed finite radius, as in Definition 3.8. A global finite covariance limit is not asserted when explosion can occur. When the terminal covariance V_T is finite, the source describes the limiting scalar readout vector conditionally on V_T as centered Gaussian with covariance V_T; the output law is undefined on paths that explode before T.
A fixed finite collection of inputs with positive definite normalized Gram matrix (explicit restriction of the source)
Independent iid N(0,1) weights, no biases, constant width n
phi is C^4, phi(0)=0, phi′(0)=1 and the fourth derivative has polynomial growth
Fixed a>0 and s=a sqrt(n), exact Gaussian normalization, depth/width tends to finite T
Only locally stopped convergence is claimed in general

[Lemma 58 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] Let $\Sigma = \Sigma_{g,p}$ with $g\geqslant 2$ and $p\geqslant 2$. Let $\gamma$ be a separating simple closed curve in $\Sigma$ that separates $\Sigma$ into $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$, where $\Sigma_2$ has genus 0. Let 
        $s\in \{\pm 1\}^p$ and $n\in \big\{\chi(\Sigma) + p_+(s) , \dots, -\chi(\Sigma) - p_-(s)\big\}$, and 
        let $[\rho]\in \NHns\cap X^s_n$ such that $\rho(\gamma)$ is elliptic of infinite order with fixed point $x_0\in \mathbb{H}^2$. 
        \textcolor{black}{Let $x$} be a point on $\gamma$, and let $c_1$ be a preferred peripheral element of $\pi_1(\Sigma\textcolor{black}{, x})$ contained in $\pi_1(\Sigma_2\textcolor{black}{, x})$ that maps to a negative parabolic element.
        Suppose that there is a sequence $\{\delta_k\}_{k = 1}^\infty \subset \pi_1(\Sigma, x)$ of simple closed curves in $\pi_1(\Sigma_1,x)$ such that for each $k\in \mathbb{Z}_+$,
        \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
            \item $\delta_kc_1$ is simple, 
            \item $\rho(\delta_k)$ is hyperbolic, and
            \item the (oriented) axis $l_k$ of $\rho(\delta_k)$ turns positively around $x_0$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Assume further that 
        either every $\delta_k$ is non-separating, or every $\delta_k$ is separating and each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus [\delta_k]$
        has positive genus.
        In addition, suppose that the distance $d(l_k, x_0)\to \infty$ as $k\to \infty$.
        Then $\rho$ also sends a non-separating simple closed curve to an elliptic element.

[Maintheorem 1 (Empirical Fourier transforms under CPE) of arXiv:2608.22342, 'Completely Positive Entropy and Fourier Central Limit Theorems for Stationary Random Measu'] Let $\eta$ be a stationary random measure on $\bR^d$ with local second
moments. Assume that its translation action is essentially free and has CPE.
Then $\sigma_\eta\ll\lambda_d$. Moreover, for $\lambda_d$-almost every
$\xi\in\bR^d$, simultaneously for every $m\geq1$ and every
$h_1,\ldots,h_m\in C_c^\infty(\bR^d;\bC)$,
\begin{equation}

    \bigl(Z_R(\xi;h_1),\ldots,Z_R(\xi;h_m)\bigr)
    \dto (Z_1,\ldots,Z_m),
\end{equation}
where $(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is a complex Gaussian vector with mean zero and
\begin{equation}

    \E[Z_a\overline{Z_b}]
    =s_\eta(\xi)\int_{\bR^d}h_a\overline{h_b}\,d\lambda_d,
    \qquad \E[Z_aZ_b]=0.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Empirical Fourier transforms under CPE

[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2607.25645, 'Estimates of the total variation distance between laws of Sobolev mappings on Gaussian spa'] Let $k,d\in\mathbb N$ with $d\ge 2$, and let $a,b>0$. Set
\[
\varkappa:=\frac{1}{2k(d-1)}
\quad\text{and}\quad
s:=\frac{d}{2(d-1)}.
\]
Then, for every pair of mappings
\[
f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k),
\quad
g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k),
\quad
f_j,g_j\in \mathcal P_d(\gamma),
\]
satisfying
\[
\int_E \Delta_f\,d\gamma \ge a
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
\max_{1\le j\le k}\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(f_j)\le b,
\]
and for every $\beta\in(0,\varkappa)$, one has
\begin{equation}
d_{\rm TV}(f,g)
\le
C_1k^5d(\varkappa-\beta)^{-s}
\bigl(a^{-1}b^{\frac{2k-1}{2}}\max_{1\le j\le k}\|f_j-g_j\|_{L^2(\gamma)}\bigr)^\beta,
\end{equation}
where $C_1>0$ is an absolute constant.
	
In particular, optimizing over $\beta$, we obtain
\[
d_{\rm TV}(f,g)
\le
C_2k^5d
\bigl(1+\bigl|\ln\bigl(a^{-1}b^{\frac{2k-1}{2}}\max_{1\le j\le k}\|f_j-g_j\|_{L^2(\gamma)}\bigr)\bigr|\bigr)^s
\bigl(a^{-1}b^{\frac{2k-1}{2}}\max_{1\le j\le k}\|f_j-g_j\|_{L^2(\gamma)}\bigr)^\varkappa
\]
for some absolute constant $C_2>0$.

[Lemma Microscopic balls on $M$ are almost flat, see \cite{DGM26} of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[lemma]{lem:almostflat}
    For each $z \in M$ and $\eta > 0$ there exists $\delta_0 \in (0,1)$
	such that for every $0<\delta \le \delta_0$,
	any ball $U = B_M(z,\delta)$ in $M$ of radius $\delta$ has the following properties. 
	Let
	\[
	u : U \to B_{\mathbb{R}^d}(0,\delta)
	\]
	be geodesic normal coordinates. 
	Then $u$
	is a diffeomorphism with
	\[
	e^{-\eta} d_M(x,y) 
	\le d_{\mathbb{R}^d}( u(x), u(y) )
	\le e^{\eta}d_M(x,y)
	\]
	for all $x,y \in U$.
	Moreover if $\mathcal{L}$ is the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$ then the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the pushforward $u_\ast dM$ of the Riemannian volume measure $dM$ satisfies $$e^{-\eta} \leq \frac{u_\ast dM}{d\mathcal{L}} \leq e^{\eta}$$ on $u(U)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Microscopic balls on $M$ are almost flat, see \cite{DGM26}

[Lem 82 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] If the tuple $x_1$, \dots, $x_k$ is cyclic for $\pi$, then
\[\rmh^0_{\bspi}(\pi) = \rmh^0_{\bspi}(\Phi^\pi_{x_1,\dots,x_k}).\]
Equivalently, if $\phi \in \S_k(\A)$, then $\rmh^0_{\bspi}(\pi_\phi) = \rmh^0_{\bspi}(\phi)$.

[Lemma 40 of arXiv:2608.07239, 'Unified framework for asymptotically uniform iterative construction of generalised random '] Let $S$ be an FIS of $G$ of size $\alpha-k$ for some $k=O(M)$. Let $K:=|(V\setminus\overline{N}(S))\cap(F\cup R^*(S))|$ be the number of vertices $v\in V$ for which $S\cup\{v\}$ is still an independent set, but not an FIS. Finally, define $$\mathscr{P}_k(S):=\exp(P|F|+\tfrac12P|R^*(S)|+P\b(V)-\b(S))\prod_{t=k+1}^{\alpha}\frac{t-k}{n_t-K}.$$
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item If $k=0$, then $\mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol{S}_{\alpha-k}=S)=(1+O(\mathscr{E}))\mathscr{P}_k(S)$.
			\item If $k\geq1$ with $k=O(1)$, then $\mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol{S}_{\alpha-k}=S)\leq(1+o(1))\mathscr{P}_k(S)$.
			\item If $k\geq1$, then $\mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol{S}_{\alpha-k}=S)\leq\alpha^{o(k)}\mathscr{P}_k(S)$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:moment-char-ext of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Consider the following assertions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The convex set $Q$ is a face of $P$. 
Furthermore, we have $\ext Q\subset P_1$ or $\ext P=P_1$.
\item 
The convex set $Q$ is a simplex and $\ext Q\subset P_1$.
\item 
The convex set $Q$ is linearly compact and $\ext Q\subset P_1$.
\item 
We have $\ext G(C)\subset G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then: (1)$\Rightarrow$(2)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(4).

[Lemma lem:weighted-taylor-estimate of arXiv:2609.02710, 'Asymptotic Mean Value Laplacian\\ on equiregular sub-Riemannian manifolds'] There are a neighborhood $W$ of the origin
and a constant $C_N$ such that, for $z\in W$, $1\le i\le k$,
$1\le a\le n$, and every multi-index $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|_w\le2$,
\[
  \bigl|\partial_z^\gamma
    (f_a^i-f_a^{i,[N]})(z)\bigr|
  \le C_N\|z\|_w^{w_a+N-1-|\gamma|_w}.
\]
Consequently, after decreasing $h_*$ so that
$\delta_h\overline U_1\subset W$ for $0<h<h_*$,
\begin{equation}
  \max_{1\le i\le k}
  \|X_i^{x,h}-Y_i^h\|_{C^2(\overline U_1)}
  \le C_Nh^N,
  \qquad 0<h<h_*.
\end{equation}

Let $q\ge2$, let
$\varphi$ be of class $C^{q+1}$ near the origin, and set
\[
  P_q\varphi(z):=\sum_{|\alpha|_w\le q}
    \frac{\partial^\alpha\varphi(0)}{\alpha!}z^\alpha.
\]
Since $q-|\gamma|_w\ge0$, we have
$\partial^\gamma P_q\varphi=P_{q-|\gamma|_w}(\partial^\gamma\varphi)$.
Write $z=\delta_t\theta$, where $t=\|z\|_w$ and
$\|\theta\|_w=1$.  For $0\le j\le q-|\gamma|_w$,
\[
  \frac1{j!}\left.\frac{d^j}{d s^j}\right|_{s=0}
  \partial^\gamma\varphi(\delta_s\theta)
  =\sum_{|\beta|_w=j}

			\eta_{ct}^{(2)}\: \forall \: t\in [0,\infty) \right) =1.

Let (X_n)_{n=1}^\infty be i.i.d. random variables with \mathbb{E}[X_1] = 0 and \text{Var}(X_1) = 1. Define the linearly interpolated partial sum process S_t on [0, \infty), and for each n \ge 3, let \zeta_n(t) = \frac{S_{nt}}{\sqrt{2 n \log \log n}} for t \in [0, 1]. Then almost surely, the sequence of functions (\zeta_n)_{n \ge 3} in C([0, 1]) is relatively compact, and its set of limit points equals the Strassen compact set K = \{f \in C([0, 1]) : f(0) = 0, f \text{ is absolutely continuous}, \int_0^1 (f'(t))^2 dt \le 1\}.

[Thm 6 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional Finsler metric measure manifold. Assume that $\mathbf{S} \geq 0$. Given $p>\frac{n}{2}$, $\Xi>1$ and $0<r_{1} \leq r_{2} \leq R$.  Then there exists a constant $\varsigma >0$, such that when $\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R, 0}\leq \varsigma$,
the following inequality holds
\be
\frac{m(B^{+}_{r_{2}}(x_{0}))}{m(B^{+}_{r_{1}}(x_{0}))} \leq \Xi\left(\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}\right)^{n},
\ee
where $\varsigma:=\Big(\frac{1-\Xi^{-\frac{1}{2 p-1}}}{2 C_{2}(n,p,R)}\Big)^{\frac{2p-1}{p}} v(n,R)^{-\frac{1}{p}}$.

[Lemma 5 (Volterra-resolvent comparison) of arXiv:2608.19151, 'Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Controlled Hawkes Jump-Diffusions'] Let $k\in L^1([0,T];\mathbb R_+)$, and let $R$ be the solution of the Volterra equation
\[
    R(t)=k(t)+\int_0^t k(t-s)R(s)\,\dd s, \ t\in [0,T].
\]
Suppose $f,F$ are nonnegative integrable functions on $[0,T]$ and
\[
    f(t)
    \le
    F(t)+\int_0^t k(t-s)f(s)\,\dd s,
    \qquad 0\le t\le T.
\]

Then
\[
    f(t)
    \le
    F(t)+\int_0^t R(t-s)F(s)\,\dd s.
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \int_0^t f(u)\,\dd u
    \le
    \left(
        1+\int_0^T R(u)\,\dd u
    \right)
    \int_0^t F(s)\,\dd s,
    \qquad 0\le t\le T.
\]

In particular, in these cases the lifting property of Lemma~\ref{lem:lift-inclusions} holds.

body:
Own-work draft C015 v1, proof (unaudited); no novelty or independent-review claim. For finite d>=1 let Sigma and Gamma be PSD d-by-d matrices with traces at most one. Take two independent samples of m iid pairs with common product law a~N(0,1), w~N(0,Gamma). For rho((a,w),(aprime,wprime))=|a-aprime|+||Sigma^(1/2)(w-wprime)||, the expected minimum mean permutation cost is at most r_G(m)=inf over R>0 and positive integers k,q of [4R/q+2R/sqrt(k+1)+2sqrt(2)R*sqrt(q^(k+1)/m)+16exp(-R^2/8)]. In particular r_G(m)=O(log log m/sqrt(log m)), uniformly over dimension and admissible covariances. The Gaussian integral gives E exp(||w||^2/4)<=sqrt(2), using product_j(1-lambda_j/2)>=1-sum_j lambda_j/2>=1/2; the same applies to a. Thus norm clipping at radius R costs at most 8exp(-R^2/8) per pair, and C004 v2 covariance matching applies to the clipped pairs. Choosing R=sqrt(32 log log(m+exp(exp(1)))) proves the rate. This is an initial matching bound, not a trained-SGD theorem. The trace restriction excludes unscaled N(0,I_d) uniformly in growing d. C004 v2 is an unaudited dependency; all constants and the proof appear in proofs/C015_gaussian_covariance_matching.md.
Common independent iid product Gaussian pair samples; PSD Sigma,Gamma with trace <=1
d is finite and may vary with m under these trace constraints; matching uses the covariance pseudometric in the statement
title: Trace-bounded Gaussian initialization: dimension-free covariance-pseudometric matching (unaudited owner draft)

body: A Jordan normal form of a linear operator T on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field K is a block-diagonal matrix of Jordan blocks (equal eigenvalue down each block's diagonal, ones on the superdiagonal) representing T in some basis. Such a basis exists if and only if the characteristic polynomial of T splits into linear factors over K - automatic when K is algebraically closed, e.g. C, and false in general over R (a plane rotation by 90 degrees has no real Jordan form) - and the form is then unique up to the order of the blocks.
title: Jordan normal form

[Lemma general_order of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] Let $r \in [\delta_1], t \in [\delta_2]$. For any functions $f_1^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N},f_2^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$ and $w \in \mathds{N}$, if
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\delta_1, \delta_2 \in O(1)$
    \item $\forall (\vb*{y}, \vb*{z}) \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}\times \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} iy_i \leq \delta_1,  \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} jz_j \leq \delta_2$ and $ \|\vb*{y}\|_0 + \|\vb*{z}\|_0 \ge 2$:
    $$\mathds{E}[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} (f_1^{(i)}(U))^{y_i}\prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} (f_2^{(j)}(U))^{z_i}] \in o(n)$$
    \item $\forall k \in [\delta_1], \forall l \in [\delta_2]:$
    $$\mathds{E}[(f_1^{(k)}(U))^{\lfloor \frac{\delta_1}{k} \rfloor}],\mathds{E}[(f_2^{(l)}(U))^{\lfloor \frac{\delta_2}{l} \rfloor}] \in o(n)$$
    \item $\forall k \in [\delta_1]$ s.t. $\exists v \in V: f_1^{(k)}(v) > 0 $ and $ \forall l \in [\delta_2] $ s.t. $\exists v \in V: f_2^{(l)}(v) > 0 :\\
    \exists c>0 \textnormal{ s.t. }  \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}  \mathds{P}(f_1^{(k)}(U) \geq 1), \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathds{P}(f_2^{(l)}(U) \geq 1) \geq c$
\end{enumerate}
then
\begin{align*}
 &\sum_{\substack{\vb*{a} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}:\\\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} ia_i = \delta_1 }} \sum_{\substack{\vb*{b} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}:\\\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_2} ib_i = \delta_2}} \sum_{\gamma(\cdot) \in \hat{R}(\vb*{a},\vb*{b})} \hat{H}(\vb*{a},\vb*{b},\gamma(\cdot)) \\
 &= (\delta_1!\delta_2!)^w (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_2} \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{0.5cm}+ \Big( -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\delta_1!^{1+w}\delta_2!^w}{(\delta_1-2)!}(n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1-2} n\mathds{E}[(f_1^{(1)}(U))^2] (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2} \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm} -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\delta_1!^w \delta_2!^{1+w}}{(\delta_2-2)!} (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2-2} n\mathds{E}[(f_2^{(1)}(U))^2] \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm} - \frac{(\delta_1!\delta_2!)^{1+w}}{(\delta_1-1)!(\delta_2-1)!}  (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1-1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2-1} n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)f_2^{(1)}(U)] \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm} + \frac{1}{2^{1+w}} \frac{\delta_1!^{1+w}\delta_2!^w}{(\delta_1-2)!} (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1-2} n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(2)}(U)] (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2} \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm}+ \frac{1}{2^{1+w}} \frac{\delta_1!^w \delta_2!^{1+w}}{(\delta_2-2)!} (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2-2} n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(2)}(U)] \Big) (1+o(1))\\
   &= (\delta_1!\delta_2!)^w (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_2}(1+o(1)).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Own-work draft: proof (unaudited); independent mathematical and novelty review pending. Balanced four-point frozen-model spectral interpolation only; actual nonlinear transfer remains open.

# C017 v1: rescaled noise restores two roots in the iid-head frozen precursor
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: bound. Target:1. Novelty unestablished.
A supporting frozen-model result, not full Target1 and not yet a nonlinear-network result.

## 1. Model and precise limit
For 0<e<1/4 set D=1+e^2+e^4 and x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D), s,t=+/-1.
Use the uniform four-point population and teacher direction
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The letter u_e denotes this direction, not
nu, the fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Set c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)),
alpha=c_e/2, g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Its Walsh coefficients in modes
0,s,t,st are (0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Initialize independent neurons with W_j~N(0,I_3) and heads independently +/-nu.
First take width to infinity at every fixed e, obtaining initial Gaussian
Walsh coefficients Z_(e,h). This is the ordinary fixed-width CLT of C016.
Then train the FROZEN deterministic full kernel
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z]
with discrete step1/2. Write b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2) for the normalized
four-point eigenvalues lambda_h. Use the settled clock premises
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), b_0 bounded away from0.
Thus eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e and b_t/(b_t+b_st)->1/2.

For fixed kappa>0 choose effective Walsh noise variance alpha^2 rho_e,
 rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e).
Four independent errors +/-sigma_e with sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e)
realize exactly this variance. In particular sigma_e~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4),
so label noise remains <=1 for small e, but is not fixed as e decreases.
The noise-averaged clean risk conditional on initialization, in real-time
spectral interpolation of discrete GD, is
 Q_e(t)=sum_h [exp(-2b_h t)(Z_(e,h)-theta_h)^2
             +alpha^2 rho_e(1-exp(-b_h t))^2].             (1)
At integer t this is exactly discrete kernel GD. Real t is used only to
locate extrema of its spectral interpolation; no GD-to-flow limit is taken.

## 2. Joint initial-output covariance, on the relevant scales
Let phi_h(W)=(1/4)sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)), and
lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2. The initial covariance is diagonal in Walsh modes,
Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, by Gaussian coordinate sign symmetry.
In the Gaussian limit these modes are therefore independent.
C016 establishes lambda_s^RF/e^2->1/2 and the bounds
|phi_t|,|phi_st|<=e^2|W_2|/sqrt(D).
For W_0!=0, all four preactivations eventually have its sign. Consequently
phi_t/e^2 -> W_2 1{W_0>0}, and phi_st/e^2 ->0 almost surely.
Dominated convergence with the preceding bounds gives
 lambda_t^RF/e^4->1/2, lambda_st^RF/e^4->0.                (2)
On one probability space take independent standard normals G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st
and set Z_(e,h)=nu sqrt(lambda_h^RF)G_h for every e. This coupling has exactly
the required Gaussian law at each e. Since alpha~e^2/2, writing
A_(e,h)=(Z_(e,h)/alpha-theta_h/alpha)^2, we get almost surely
 e^2 A_(e,s)->a=2nu^2 G_s^2,
 A_(e,t)->(sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2, A_(e,st)->1.                (3)
Define B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2 >=1/2.
Here a>0 almost surely and a is independent of B. Independence is used only
after the joint Gaussian limit, not for finite-width output coefficients.

## 3. The new central derivative limit
For real s in a fixed compact interval set
 t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s, z=exp(-s).
Then q_s=exp(-b_s t_e(s))=e^(3/2)z exactly.
Normalize the risk derivative by 2alpha^2(b_t+b_st). Its fast contribution is
 [rho_e q_s-(A_(e,s)+rho_e)q_s^2]/eta
 =kappa(e/eta)z-[(e^2 A_(e,s))(e/eta)+kappa e^(5/2)/eta]z^2
 -> kappa z-a z^2.                                      (4)
For each slow mode q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)) uniformly on the compact interval.
Thus rho_e q_h(1-q_h)=O(sqrt(e)log(1/e))->0, while A_(e,h)q_h^2
has the limits in (3). The rate weights tend to1/2, giving their combined
contribution -B. The constant-mode contribution vanishes: its exponent
decays faster than every power of e and Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.
The same calculation after differentiating in s is valid: slow terms gain
a factor b_h/b_s=O(e), and even rho_e times that factor tends to0;
constant-mode exponentials dominate the additional polynomial factors.
Hence, almost surely in this coupling, uniformly on each compact s interval,

 Q'_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st)) -> H_kappa(s)
                                      =kappa exp(-s)-a exp(-2s)-B,
 and the derivatives in s converge too.                  (5)

## 4. Two-root criterion and peak time
On the event Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0 define
 z_+=(kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a), z_-=(kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a).
Both are positive and z_+>z_-. The classification is the elementary quadratic
criterion already used in C012, now with random coefficients a and B.
As s increases, H is negative, positive, then negative across
 s_min=-log z_+ and s_max=-log z_-.
The roots are simple. Uniform C1 convergence in (5) gives, for every such
fixed Gaussian realization, one nearby minimum and one nearby maximum of
the frozen interpolation for all sufficiently small e, converging to these
locations. Derivative convergence also gives strict decrease immediately
after the maximum. Thus there are two descents separated by a rise.
More precisely the peak satisfies
 b_s t_peak-(3/2)log(1/e) -> -log z_-,
 t_peak~(6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                         (6)
The statements are pathwise in the coupling, on Delta>0. Random compact
neighborhoods are allowed: convergence on every integer-sized compact set
holds on one probability-one event. No deterministic width rate is asserted.
On Delta<0, H is negative on every compact s interval; this only addresses
this particular time window, not global absence of DD. Delta=0 is not treated.

For value-based nonlinear transfer, a useful additional consequence is this:
 d/ds [Q_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2 eta)] converges to H_kappa(s).
Therefore differences of the normalized risks converge to differences of
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
Values across the two simple extrema have strict gaps of order alpha^2 eta.
An o(alpha^2 eta) uniform risk error over a containing compact interval would
preserve appropriately chosen decrease/rise/decrease witnesses and interval
peak localization. Such a nonlinear error is NOT supplied in this claim.

## 5. A tunable probability lower bound
The Gaussian independence in Section2 gives E a=2nu^2 and E B=1+nu^2,
so E[4aB]=8nu^2(1+nu^2). Markov's inequality yields
 P(Delta>0) >= 1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2.                   (7)
Choose kappa^2>8nu^2(1+nu^2)/delta for any prescribed delta in (0,1).
Then the frozen limiting construction has two simple central extrema with
probability greater than1-delta. The noise amplitude still tends to zero.
This is an initialization probability bound, with risk already averaged over
labels; it is not concentration for one realized label vector.
For fixed kappa the exact event probability need not equal this lower bound.

## 6. Scope and next unpaid step
C016's failed rho~1 route is avoided by changing BOTH noise scale and time
center; fixed nu and the unit-norm single-index teacher are retained.
This lemma concerns the balanced four-point frozen precursor only. It does
not yet prove the result for actual nonlinear GD, continuous iid input laws,
fixed label-noise amplitude, macroscopic feature learning, or full Target1.
The next step is a uniform-in-time risk transfer at order o(alpha^2 eta),
with nonzero iid initial output retained. C009's finite-horizon strategy is
a candidate; C015's zero-output paired argument cannot simply be substituted.
Independent mathematical and novelty review is pending. No paper-level
priority claim is made. Sources: own C009 clocks, C012 quadratic-root tool,
C016 Gaussian covariance and exact risk formula; the added slow-mode limits
and derivative scaling are proved above.
Every definition and fixed-nu spectral clock premise in the statement
Balanced four-point frozen full-kernel GD with independent Gaussian hidden weights and iid readouts +/-nu; fixed0<nu<=1
Width limit precedes e->0; unit-norm single-index teacher, noise-averaged risk with rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e)
Simple-root event kappa^2>4aB; peak location refers to real spectral interpolation of discrete GD
No claim of nonlinear transfer, continuous iid-input extension, fixed label-noise amplitude or full Target1 closure

[Definition 10 (Total variation distance) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] For $h \in \Sign$ put
\[
  \tv{h} := \sup_{A \in \XXA} \bigl| h(A) \bigr| \in [0,\infty),
\]
so that $\tv{\cdot} : \Sign \to [0,\infty)$ is a map; it satisfies the triangle
inequality $\tv{h_{1}+h_{2}} \le \tv{h_{1}} + \tv{h_{2}}$, since
$|h_{1}(A)+h_{2}(A)| \le |h_{1}(A)| + |h_{2}(A)|$ for every $A$. For
$\mu,\nu \in \Prob$ the number $\tv{\mu - \nu} \in [0,1]$ is called the \emph{total
variation distance} of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Recall the Hahn--Jordan decomposition: for $h \in \Sign$ there is a set
$E \in \XXA$, called a \emph{Hahn set for $h$}, such that $h(A) \ge 0$ for every
measurable $A \subseteq E$ and $h(A) \le 0$ for every measurable
$A \subseteq \XX \setminus E$; the two nonnegative measures
$h^{+}(A) := h(A \cap E)$ and $h^{-}(A) := -h(A \setminus E)$ then satisfy
$h = h^{+}-h^{-}$ and do not depend on the choice of $E$. If moreover $h(\XX) = 0$,
then
\[
  h^{+}(\XX) = h^{-}(\XX) = \tv{h} ,
\]
since $\sup_{A \in \XXA}h(A) = h^{+}(\XX)$ and
$\inf_{A \in \XXA}h(A) = -h^{-}(\XX)$.
title: Total variation distance

[Definition def:discrete-YM-measure of arXiv:2608.15923, 'Universality of two-dimensional Markovian holonomy fields'] Let $\Sigma$ be a compact surface of genus $g$ with boundary components
$b_1,\ldots,b_n$, endowed with an area measure $\mathrm{vol}$. Let
${\mathbb{G}}=(V,E,F)$ be a topological map embedded in $\Sigma$, let $G$ be a
compact group, and let $(Q_t)_{t>0}$ be a family of central continuous
probability densities on $G$. Fix conjugacy classes
$[t_1],\ldots,[t_n]$ and write
$\mathfrak t=([t_1],\ldots,[t_n])$.

For every $i$, choose an oriented edge $e_i$ contained in the $i$-th
boundary component; these edges are pairwise distinct. Once all variables
except $U_{e_i}$ are fixed, the boundary holonomy has the form
\[
 {\mathrm{Hol}}_{\partial b_i}(U)=a_i(U)U_{e_i}^{\varepsilon_i}b_i(U),
 \qquad \varepsilon_i\in\{\pm1\},
\]
so, for every $y_i\in G$, there is a unique value of $U_{e_i}$ for which
\[
 {\mathrm{Hol}}_{\partial b_i}(U)=y_it_iy_i^{-1}.
\]
Denote by $U^{\mathbf y}$ the resulting connection, where
$\mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$. The \emph{discrete Yang--Mills measure}
with weight $Q$ and boundary condition $\mathfrak t$ is the finite measure
characterized by
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \int_{\Omega^1({\mathbb{G}},G)}\! \Phi(U)\,
 d\mu_{{\mathbb{G}},G,Q,\mathrm{vol},\mathfrak t}(U)
 :=
 \int_{G^{E\setminus\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}}}\int_{G^n}
 &\Phi(U^{\mathbf y})
 \prod_{f\in F}Q_{|f|}\bigl({\mathrm{Hol}}_{\partial f}(U^{\mathbf y})\bigr)
 \,d\mathbf y\,dU
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
for every bounded measurable $\Phi$. This definition is independent of the
chosen boundary edges, by invariance of Haar measure under left and right
translations and inversion.
title: Definition def:discrete-YM-measure of arXiv:2608.15923

[Theorem thm:paley-wiener-schwartz of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Let \(T \in \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^d)\) by a tempered distribution of order $N$. Then \(\mathrm{supp}\,T \subseteq \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \lvert x\rvert \le R\}\) for some \(R \ge 0\) if and only if its Fourier transform \(\widehat{T}\) extends to an entire function on \(\mathbb{C}^d\) satisfying the following growth condition: there exists a constant \(C > 0\) such that
\[
  \bigl|\widehat{T}(z)\bigr|
  \;\le\;
  C\,\bigl(1 + \lvert z\rvert\bigr)^{N}\,
  \exp\bigl(R\,\lvert \mathrm{Im} z\rvert\bigr),
  \quad
  \forall\,z \in \mathbb{C}^d.
\]
Conversely, any entire function on \(\mathbb{C}^d\) satisfying such a bound is the Fourier transform of a unique tempered distribution of order $N$ supported in the closed ball \(\{x : \lvert x\rvert \le R\}\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Paley–Wiener–Schwartz, Theorem 7.3.1 of \cite{hörmander1983analysis}

[Lemma lem:toric of arXiv:2609.03448, 'Prime-power Diophantine tuples'] Let
\[
 D_0=24^4=331776.
\]
There exists a nonconstant polynomial
\[
 Q(T_1,\ldots,T_5)\in\mathbb Z[T_1,\ldots,T_5]
\]
with
\begin{equation}
 1\le q:=\deg Q\le5D_0<2^{21},
\end{equation}
and polynomials
\[
 G_i\in\mathbb Z[t_1,\ldots,t_4,T_1,\ldots,T_5]\qquad(1\le i\le5)
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
 (t_1t_2t_3t_4)^{12D_0}Q(T)
 =\sum_{i=1}^5G_i(t,T)\bigl(A_i(t)-T_iB_i(t)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The same polynomial $Q$ may be chosen so that
\begin{equation}
 \log_2 \bigl(h(Q)64^q\bigr)<2^{116}.
\end{equation}
Consequently every reduced labelled quintuple satisfying~(equation eq:AiBi of the paper)
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 Q(64\Lambda_1,\ldots,64\Lambda_5)\equiv0\pmod N.
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:isometric-conjugacy of arXiv:2609.00794, 'On operators whose adjoints or second adjoints attain their norms'] Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces, and let
\[
U\colon \ell_1\to X^*,
\qquad
V\colon \ell_1\to Y^*
\]
be surjective linear isometries. Given $T\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$, put $S:=U^{-1}T^*V\in\mathcal L(\ell_1,\ell_1)$.
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	{Y^* } && {X^*} \\
	{\ell_1} && {\ell_1}
	\arrow["{T^*}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{U^{-1}}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["V", from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow["S"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}    
    \end{equation*}
Then $\|S\|=\|T\|$, and $T \in \operatorname{NA}_2 (X,Y)$ if and only if $S^* \in \operatorname{NA} (\ell_\infty,\ell_\infty)$.

[Lem 19 of arXiv:2509.09589, 'Geometry of critical discrete structures: long-range percolation on the hierarchical latti'] We have,
\begin{align*}
\Delta_n

body:
[Theorem thm:Z4 of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] The symmetrization resistant distributions on $\mathbb{Z}_4$ are exactly the two-point distributions supported on $\{0,1\}$, $\{1,2\}$, $\{2,3\}$, and $\{3,0\}$, as shown in (fig:Z4 symmres of the paper).

\begin{proof}
Let $f$ be a PMF on $\mathbb{Z}_4$ with support $F$. 
If $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{F}=1$, $f$ is symmetric. 
If $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{F}=4$, $f$ is not symmetrization resistant by (thm:no_symmetrizers_in_interior of the paper). 

If $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{F}=2$, Note that $F \coloneqq \supp(f)$ cannot be a coset of the subgroup $\{0,2\}$, 
otherwise there is a constant $c$ such that $F - \{c\} = \{0,2\}$ and
$f$ is symmetric. 
Since we do not have multiplicative inverses for all the nonzero elements in $\mathbb{Z}_4$, we do not have affine invariance; 
however, we do still have translation invariance ($g \in \Sym(f)$ iff $g(\cdot +c) \in \Sym(f(\cdot -c))$) 
and, by (lem:automorphisms of the paper), invariance under additive inverses ($g \in \Sym(f)$ iff $g_- \in \Sym(f_-)$). 
Thus the only example we need to consider is $F = \{0,1\}$ with $p \coloneqq f(1) \ge \frac{1}{2}$. 
Since $\Sym(f)$ is formed by the intersection of a hyperplane with $\Delta_4$, $\dim(\Sym(f)) \le 2$ and the elements $g$ of ${\rm Ex}(\Sym(f))$ must have at most two nonzero entries; that is, for $G \coloneqq \supp(g)$, $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{G} \le 2$. 
Since there are no constants which symmetrize $f$, we consider the cases where $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{G} = 2$. 
When $G = \{0,1\}$ or $G = \{2,3\}$ it is readily observed that there is no solution.
When $G = \{0,2\}$ or $G = \{1,3\}$ the unique solution is $g(x) = \frac{1}{2}$ for $x \in G$; that is, $H(g) = 1 \ge H(f)$. 
When $G = \{0,3\}$ the unique solution is $g = f_-$, and
when $G = \{1,2\}$ the unique solution is $g = g^*$ with $g^*(1) = p$, $g^*(2) = 1-p$, $g^*(0) = g^*(3) = 0$. 

Therefore $f$ is symmetrization resistant as long as its support is not contained in a coset of $\{0,2\}$. 

It remains only to consider the case $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{F} = 3$. 
By invariance under shifts, we may take $F = \{0,1,2\}$. 
PMFs with this support exist in the triangle depicted in (fig:Z4_012 of the paper). 
Note that for any such $f$ we have $\{\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}_{\{0,2\}},\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}_{\{1,3\}}\} \subseteq \Sym(f)$. 
We will treat in turn the elements of $A$,$B$, $C$, and $C'$ supported on $3$ points. 

The central region $B$ is the simplest: since ${\rm Ex}(B) = \{\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}_{\{0,1\}},\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}_{\{0,2\}},\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}_{\{1,2\}}\}$ consists of two-point distributions with entropy $1$, any $f \in B \setminus {\rm Ex}(B)$ is a nontrivial convex combination of the extreme points and therefore satisfies $H(f) > 1 = H(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}_{\{0,2\}})$.
Therefore $\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}_{\{0,2\}}$ is an entropy-reducing symmetrizer and $f$ is not symmetrization resistant.  

Note that we treated the edges of $B$, and the remaining edges of $A$, $C$, and $C'$ consisted of two-point distributions, so we now need only treat the interiors $A^{\circ}$, $C^{\circ}$, and $(C')^{\circ}$. 

In the case $f = (1-a-b, a, b, 0) \in C^{\circ}$, we have $a+b < \frac{1}{2}$. 
The unique nontrivial symmetry equation satisfied by $g = (g_0, g_1, g_2, g_3) \in \Sym(f)$ is 
\[ g_1f_2 + g_2 f_1 + g_3 f0= (f * g)(-1) = f * g)(1) = g_0 f_1 + g_1 f_0 + g_3 f_2, \]
which reduces to
\[ g_3(1-a-2b) + g_2a = g_1(1-a-2b) + g_0a. \]
In this last equation, every term is nonnegative, so we readily see that there are symmetrizers (which are necessarily extreme points) supported in $\{0,2\}$, $\{0,3\}$, $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,3\}$ (since the intersection of a hyperplane with the simplex $\Delta_4$ can have at most four corners, these are actually all of the extreme points of $f$, though we will not use this fact). 
The extreme point with support $\{1,2\}$ is $g = (0, \frac{a}{1-2b}, \frac{1-a-2b}{1-2b}, 0)$.
