[Prp 20 of arXiv:2608.13976, 'Boundary Harnack principle for diffusion with jumps on metric measure spaces'] Assume that the metric measure space $(\sX, d , m)$ satisfies
${\rm (VD)}$ and ${\rm (RVD)}$,
the scale functions $\phi_c$ and $\phi_j$ satisfy  \eqref{polycon} and \eqref{e:1.11}.
Suppose $X$ is the $m$-symmetric Hunt process associated with the regular Dirichlet form $(\mathcal E,\mathcal F)$ in \eqref{e:E} and satisfies
the condition ${\rm HK(\phi_c, \phi_j)}$. Let $D$ be an  open subset in $\sX$. Then  for each $z_0\in \partial D$ and $R>0$
so that $\overline{B(z_0, 2R)}\subsetneq \sX$,
there exists a constant  $C=C(z_0, R)\geq 1$  independent of the geometry of $D$  such that   for   any  nonnegative  regular harmonic functions $f$ and $g$
on $D\cap B(z_0, R)$   vanishing  on  $(D^c)^r\cap B(z_0, R),$
\begin{equation}
f(x)g(y)\leq Cf(y)g(x)  \quad \hbox{for } x, y\in D\cap B(z_0, R/32).
\end{equation}
Furthermore, if in addition we assume there exist a positive constant $c$ and a positive function $V_1$ on $\R_{+}$ such that
 $V(x, r)\geq cV_1(r)$ for any $x\in \sX$ and $r>0,$  then  BHP  \eqref{e:4.11} holds
   with $C=C(R)\geq 1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'] Define $\theta:= 1-\|\varphi\|_{L^2(\Bbb R)}^2 = 1-\varphi *\varphi (0)>0$, where $\varphi$ is as in Theorem (mr3 of the paper). Define the following second-order elliptic operator on $C^2(\Bbb R^n)$: $$L^{(n,\epsilon)}_{\mathrm{Cen}}f(y_1,...,y_n):= \frac12 \sum_{i,j=1}^n \big( \theta \delta_{i,j}+\epsilon \Phi_\epsilon(y_i-y_j)\big)\cdot (\partial_{ij}f)(y_1,...,y_n).$$ 
    Denote by $ \mathbf E^{(x_1,...,x_n)}_{\mathrm{Cen}(\epsilon)}$ the expectation with respect to the Markov process $X$ on $\Bbb R^n$ with generator $L^{(n,\epsilon)}_{\mathrm{Cen}}$.
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'

[Definition 27 (Upper \(\Gamma\)-convergence) of arXiv:2608.27374, '\Large \bf Distribution-constrained optimal multiple stopping: the Root-type solution'] Let \(b_n,b:\mathbb R_+\to[-\infty,\infty]\) be upper
semicontinuous. We say that \(b_n\) upper-\(\Gamma\)-converges to
\(b\), and write
\[
    b_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma^+}b,
\]
if:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item for every sequence \(t_n\to t\),
    $
        \limsup_{n\to\infty}b_n(t_n)\le b(t)$;
    \item for every \(t\ge0\), there exists \(t_n\to t\) such that
    $
        b_n(t_n)\longrightarrow b(t)$.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26618, 'A Unified Descriptive-Complexity Framework for Model Selection under Correlated Designs'] Assume that $\eta_n \to \infty$ and that the descriptive complexity satisfies the Kraft inequality
$
\sum_{S\in\mathcal M_n} e^{-C_S}\le 1.
$
There exists a constant $\lambda_{\mathrm{sel}}$ depending only on $\alpha$ and $\zeta$ such that, for every $\lambda \geq \lambda_{\mathrm{sel}}$, if the following conditions hold:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(\romannumeral 1)]
For every \(S\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sup}}\), \(C_S\ge C_{S^*}\). In addition, there
exist constants \(0<\tilde c_1<c_1\) such that, for every \(j\ge 1\),
\begin{equation}
\sum_{S\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sup}}, \Delta^+(S)=j}
\exp\!\left\{
-c_1\lambda^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\bigl(C_S-C_{S^*}\bigr)
\right\}
\le
\exp\!\left\{\tilde c_1(\eta_n j)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\right\}.
\end{equation}

    \item[(\romannumeral 2)]
    There exists a sufficiently large constant $c_2>1$ such that, for every
    $S\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sub}}$,
    \begin{equation}
    \mathrm{APP}(S)\ge c_2\Bigg(
    \eta_n(s^*-s)
    +\lambda\bigl(C_{S^*}^{\frac{2}{\alpha}}-C_S^{\frac{2}{\alpha}}\bigr)_+
    +\log^{\frac{2}{\alpha}} N\Bigl(\Delta^-(S)\Bigr)
    \Bigg).
    \end{equation}

    \item[(\romannumeral 3)]
    For every $S\in\mathcal M_w$ satisfying $2B_S>u_S$, we have
    $\mathrm{APP}(S)\ge 2(2B_S-u_S).$
\end{itemize}
Then
\[
\Pr\!\left(
\min_{S\in\mathcal M_n,\;S\neq S^*}\mathrm{DCIC}(S)>\mathrm{DCIC}(S^*)
\right)\to 1
\qquad \text{as } n\to\infty.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26618

such that for all $n\ge N$ and all $E\subseteq B^{\Lambda_n}$,
\[
\nu(E)\,\ge\, \e^{-(2n+1)^d\delta}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\nu([E]_\varepsilon)\,\ge\, 1-\varepsilon.
\]
title: Blowing-up property

[Definition eq:K-differences of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] We say that $K \colon \mathcal{V} \to \mathrm{End}(H)$ is \emph{dressing
compatible} with $(\Psi, \Phi)$ if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., leftmargin=*]
\item For every $u \in \mathcal{V}$ and $i \in \mathbb{N}$:
\begin{align}
K(Tu) - K(u) &= \Psi(Tu)\Phi(Tu), \quad 
K(S_i u) - K(u) = \Psi(Tu)C_i(u)\Phi(S_i u). 
\end{align}
\item There exists $z \in \mathbb{F}$ such that the resolvent
exists at every vertex:
\[
R(u) \vcentcolon= (I - zK(u))^{-1} \in \mathrm{End}(H),
\qquad u \in \mathcal{V}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

Own-work draft, independently checked proof, T326-w697-C04 v1; reviewer urn:mb-agent:d6ca7a10ae76247b PASS on this exact version recorded in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. In the Lu et al. reduced linear-attention model, hold v21=0 fixed and train v=v22 and the independent raw block U=[M11^T,m21] by Euclidean gradient flow with no ridge. The effective matrix is Gamma=vUR, R=diag(I_d/d,1); M is a directly trained block, not further factored into K^TQ. In exactly infinite context, fix a pool of M iid N(0,I_d) tasks w_i; z(w)=(w,||w||^2/d+rho), rho>=0, J=[I_d,0]. Let P_R project onto the span of {Rz(w_i)}, Q_R=I-P_R, r=rank P_R, q=(Q_R)_(d+1,d+1), A_0=r-1+q. For balanced raw initialization v_0=epsilon, U_0=epsilon J/sqrt(d), 0<epsilon<1, define D=epsilon^2(1-A_0/d), z_*=(D+sqrt(D^2+4d^2 A_0))/2 and a_raw=epsilon sqrt(z_*)/(d sqrt(d)). The global zero-loss limit is Gamma_infinity=J+(a_raw-1)dJ Q_R R. For an independent fresh standard Gaussian task and query N(0,I_d/d), its normalized excess prediction risk equals (1-a_raw)^2 B_d,M, where B_d,M=[d+1-r-q+(d^2 eta-1)q(1-q)]/d and eta=(1+rho)^2+2/d. The scaling d^2 eta is essential. If M>=d+1 the risk is zero. If M<=d, W=[w_1,...,w_M], G=W^TW, s=(||w_i||^2/d+rho)_i and beta=s^T G^(-1)s give q=1/(1+d^2 beta). For any 0<delta<1, with probability at least 1-delta-8/(dM), 0<=B_d,M-(d-M)/d<=1/d+4sqrt(3)eta/sqrt(M delta). This follows from E tr G=dM, Var tr G=2dM, E tr G^2=dM(d+M+1), Chebyshev, Markov and a union bound; no independence between the two concentration events is assumed. Thus at fixed epsilon,rho, every sequence M->infinity with M/d->kappa has conditional fresh-task risk ->(1-kappa)_+ in probability over the task pool. If M instead stays a fixed positive integer, G/d->I_M and s->(1+rho)1_M give d beta->M(1+rho)^2 and d q->1/[M(1+rho)^2], so the risk tends to 1+1/M. A single task therefore gives limit 2, while a diverging sublinear pool gives limit 1, although both have M/d->0. These are in-probability limits, not expectation-over-pool claims. Exact finite identities passed 1456 rational assertions over 99 cases; the general probability statement rests on the written proof. No Lean certificate or general K,Q,V result is claimed.

[Theorem thm1 of arXiv:2411.03942, 'Asymptotic expansions relating to the distribution of the product of correlated normal ran'] Let $\mu_X,\mu_Y\in\mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_X,\sigma_Y>0$, $-1<\rho<1$ and $n\geq1$. 

\vspace{2mm}

\noindent 1. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $x\rightarrow\infty$,
\begin{align}f(x)&\sim\frac{s^{-(n+1)/4}C_n}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{|r_X+r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\exp\bigg(\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X-r_Y)^2\bigg)\nonumber \\
&\quad\times x^{(n-3)/4}\exp\bigg(\frac{|r_X+r_Y|}{1+\rho}\sqrt{\frac{nx}{s}}-\frac{x}{s(1+\rho)}\bigg)\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty c_\ell(r_X,r_Y,\rho,n)\frac{s^{\ell/2}}{x^{\ell/2}}, 
\end{align}
where 

$c_0(r_X,r_Y,\rho,n)=1$ 
and, for $\ell\geq1$,
\begin{align*}
c_\ell(r_X,r_Y,\rho,n)
=\exp\bigg(-\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X-r_Y)^2\bigg)\sum_{j=0}^\ell h_{j,\ell}(r_X,r_Y,\rho,n), 
\end{align*}

with, for $j\geq0$ and $\ell\geq1$,
\begin{align*}
h_{j,\ell}(r_X,r_Y,\rho,n)&=\frac{((3-n)/2)_{\ell-j}((n-1)/2)_{\ell-j}}{(\ell-j)!2^{\ell-j}n^{(\ell-j)/2}}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{|r_X+r_Y|}\bigg)^{\ell-j}\sum_{i=\lceil j/2\rceil}^j\bigg(\frac{n}{2}\bigg)_i\bigg(\frac{1-\rho^2}{2}\bigg)^i\\
&\quad\times M\bigg(\frac{n}{2}+i,\frac{n}{2},\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X-r_Y)^2\bigg) g_{i,j}\bigg(\frac{n-3}{4}-\frac{\ell-j}{2},\frac{|r_X+r_Y|}{1+\rho}\sqrt{n}\bigg).
\end{align*}

\noindent 2. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y=0$. Then, as $x\rightarrow\infty$,
\begin{align}f(x)\sim \frac{x^{n/2-1}}{(2s)^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}\exp\bigg(-\frac{nr_X^2}{2}-\frac{x}{s(1+\rho)}\bigg)\sum_{k=0}^\infty d_k(r_X,\rho,n)\frac{s^k}{x^k}, 
\end{align}  
where $d_0(r_X,\rho,n)=1$ and, for $k\geq1$,
\begin{align}
d_k(r_X,\rho,n)&=(-1)^k\frac{(1-n/2)_k(n/2)_k}{k!}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho^2}{2}\bigg)^k\exp\bigg(-\frac{n}{2}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)r_X^2\bigg)\nonumber\\
&\quad\times M\bigg(\frac{n}{2}+k,\frac{n}{2},\frac{n}{2}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)r_X^2\bigg)  \\
&=(-1)^k\frac{(1-n/2)_k(n/2)_k}{k!}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho^2}{2}\bigg)^k\sum_{j=0}^k\frac{(n/2)^j}{(n/2)_j}\binom{k}{j}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)^jr_X^{2j}. 
\end{align}

\noindent 3. Suppose that $r_X-r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $x\rightarrow-\infty$,
\begin{align}f(x)&\sim\frac{s^{-(n+1)/4}C_n}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{|r_X-r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\exp\bigg(\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}\bigg)(r_X+r_Y)^2\bigg)\nonumber \\
&\quad\times |x|^{(n-3)/4}\exp\bigg(\frac{|r_X-r_Y|}{1-\rho}\sqrt{\frac{n|x|}{s}}+\frac{x}{s(1-\rho)}\bigg)\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty c_\ell(r_X,-r_Y,-\rho,n)\frac{s^{\ell/2}}{|x|^{\ell/2}} .
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 23 (Cut factorization for ordered contractions) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Identify the output stochastic legs with
\[
 ([m]\setminus A(P))\sqcup([n]\setminus B(P))
\]
in that order, and let
\[
 \iota_K:[m]\setminus A(P)\longrightarrow[q(P)],
 \qquad
 \iota_L:[n]\setminus B(P)\longrightarrow[q(P)]
\]
be the resulting order-preserving injections.  Every output cut is uniquely
\[
 U=\iota_K(S)\cup\iota_L(T),
\]
with
$S\subset[m]\setminus A(P)$ and
$T\subset[n]\setminus B(P)$.  Then
\begin{equation}

 \norm{\Flat_U(L\circ_PK)}_{\Sch_r}
 \le
 \norm{\Flat_S(K)}_{\Sch_r}
 \norm{\Flat_{T\cup B(P)}(L)}_{\Sch_r},
 \qquad 1\le r\le\infty.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}

 \Prof_{q(P),r}(L\circ_PK)
 \le\Prof_{n,r}(L)\Prof_{m,r}(K).
\end{equation}

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d89b9f9730df61ec17959fa9b292442425633dc4dfbc0612adf0326eebcc064e","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d8/d89b9f9730df61ec17959fa9b292442425633dc4dfbc0612adf0326eebcc064e.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:7a227421e00876a248597cbf36dfbba44a60bc949d0cea2e2f293692750825be","bundle_entry_key":"phase-retrieval-angular-transfer","bundle_id":"population.t321-radial-angular-transfer-unaudited","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability and statistical learning","draft":"w724/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.functional.inequalities:t321-phase-retrieval-angular-transfer-w724-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# A uniform radial gap and an explicit angular reduction

Status: proofs (unaudited) of two lemmas toward Target 2. Neither lemma is a polynomial upper bound for the full empirical sign quotient. No scored frontier move is claimed.

## 1. Conditional radial Poincare bound

For an integer d>=2, a>0, beta>0 and any real b, let rho have density

    p(r)=Z^{-1} r^{d-1} exp(-beta(a r^4-2b r^2)), r>0.

Then, with the ordinary radial derivative as energy,

    C_P(rho) <= pi/(2 sqrt(beta a(d-1))).                 (1)

This is uniform in b; it does not require global convexity of minus log p.

**Proof.** Put k=d-1>0, tau=beta a>0 and q=b/a. For V(r)=tau r^4-2 tau q r^2-k log r, let z>0 and -s<0 be the two roots of t^2-q t-k/(4tau)=0. Thus z s=k/(4tau), z-s=q, s>0. Set r_*=sqrt(z). Direct factorization gives, for every r>0,

    V'(r)=(r-r_*) A(r),
    A(r)=4tau (r+r_*)(r^2+s)/r
         >=8tau r_* sqrt(s)=4sqrt(tau k)=:kappa.        (2)

The inequality uses r+r_*>=r_* and r+s/r>=2sqrt(s). It is valid also for negative q. At r=r_* the factored identity still holds; no division by r-r_* is performed.

For r>=r_*, V'(r)>=kappa(r-r_*). For r<=r_*, multiplication by the negative factor reverses the comparison: V'(r)<=kappa(r-r_*). Integrating outward from any r>=r_* therefore gives

    V(r+u)-V(r)>=kappa u^2/2, u>=0.

Similarly for r<=r_* and 0<=u<r,

    V(r-u)-V(r)>=kappa u^2/2.

Let F(r)=rho((0,r]). The Gaussian integral consequently yields

    (1-F(r))/p(r)<=sqrt(pi/(2kappa))       if r>=r_*,
    F(r)/p(r)<=sqrt(pi/(2kappa))           if r<=r_*.

Since min(F,1-F) is no larger than either of these tails, for every r>0,

    p(r)/min(F(r),1-F(r))>=sqrt(2kappa/pi)=:h.           (3)

Here is the full Poincare implication of (3), so no external Cheeger convention is needed. Let m be the unique median, F(m)=1/2, and take a locally absolutely continuous f with finite weighted H1 norm. Put g=f-f(m), so g(m)=0. Integrate the bound |g(r)|^2<= integral between m and r of 2|g g'|. Tonelli, first over each side of m, gives

    integral g^2 p <=2 integral_0^m |g g'| F
                       +2 integral_m^infty |g g'|(1-F)
                  <=(2/h) integral |g g'| p
                  <=(2/h)(integral g^2 p)^(1/2)
                          (integral |g'|^2 p)^(1/2).

All integrands before applying Cauchy-Schwarz are nonnegative; no unproved interchange of signed integrals is used. Weighted H1 functions have a locally absolutely continuous representative because p is strictly positive on every compact subinterval. The finite H1 norm makes g square-integrable. If its norm is zero the conclusion is immediate; otherwise divide by its positive norm and square. Since Var(f)<=integral g^2 p, we obtain C_P<=4/h^2=2pi/kappa, which is (1). Normalization is finite because d>0 at zero and tau>0 controls the quartic tail.

## 2. Polar disintegration of the empirical loss

For a fixed sample a_1,...,a_m and a unit teacher v, define on the unit sphere

    A(u)=m^{-1}sum (a_i.u)^4,
    B(u)=m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^2(a_i.u)^2,
    B0=m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^4.

Then L(ru)=A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2+B0. If the sample covariance S satisfies S>=lambda I with lambda>0, Cauchy-Schwarz gives A(u)>=(u^T S u)^2>=lambda^2 for every u. Let nu be the spherical marginal, with surface density proportional to

    Z(u)=integral_0^infty r^{d-1}
                   exp(-beta(A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2)) dr.

Its radial conditional rho_u is the measure of Section 1 with a=A(u), b=B(u). Let a0 be any positive lower bound on A, and set

    C_r=pi/(2sqrt(beta a0(d-1))).

Simultaneously for every u, C_P(rho_u)<=C_r. For the sample event used in C003, lambda=1/2 and a0=1/4, so C_r=pi/sqrt(beta(d-1)). This uses a fourth-moment LOWER bound only; the known failure of a dimension-free uniform fourth-moment UPPER bound is irrelevant.

For a smooth compactly supported even f, write f_r(u)=f(ru) and g(u)=E_{rho_u} f_r(u). Exact variance disintegration gives

    Var_mu f <= C_r E_mu |partial_r f|^2 + Var_nu g.     (4)

Both the conditional law and nu are invariant under u -> -u, and g is even. Thus the second term is on the real projective sphere. This is the term not yet bounded polynomially.

## 3. A quantitative transfer bound if the angular gap is supplied

Assume, in addition to A>=a0>0, the deterministic spherical bounds

    0<=B<=b0, |grad_S A|<=a1, |grad_S B|<=b1.

Let C_nu be the Poincare constant of nu restricted to even functions, using the ordinary round-sphere gradient. Define the following finite constants:

    q0=b0/a0, e0=d/(4beta a0),
    U2=1+q0+e0,
    U4=e0+q0 U2,
    U6=(d+2)U2/(4beta a0)+q0 U4,
    T=32(a1^2 U6+b1^2 U2).

Then the full even-function Poincare constant obeys

    C_even(mu) <= C_r+2C_nu(U2+beta^2 C_r^2 T).          (5)

If C_nu is infinite this is understood only as a conditional statement; it does not assert a finite useful bound. For finite C_nu the proof is as follows.

Radial integration by parts, whose boundary terms r^{d+j}exp(-beta(Ar^4-2Br^2)) vanish at both endpoints for j=0,2, gives

    4beta A E r^4=d+4beta B E r^2,
    4beta A E r^6=(d+2) E r^2+4beta B E r^4.

Jensen gives (E r^2)^2<=E r^4. Solving the resulting quadratic inequality yields

    E r^2<=B/A+sqrt(d/(4beta A))<=q0+sqrt(e0)<=U2.

The same identities give E r^4<=U4 and E r^6<=U6. All these estimates are uniform in u.

Differentiate the normalized conditional expectation at fixed radius:

    grad_S g=E grad_S f_r-beta Cov(f_r,H),
    H=r^4 grad_S A-2r^2 grad_S B.                       (6)

Differentiation under the radial integral is justified by the uniform lower bound A>=a0 and finite smooth spherical coefficient bounds: every derivative is dominated by a polynomial in r times exp(-beta a0 r^4+2beta b0 r^2), integrable against r^{d-1}dr. The same domination applies to the compactly supported smooth f and its derivatives. The normalizer is positive and has a positive minimum on the compact sphere.

Weighted Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    |E grad_S f_r|^2<=U2 E(r^{-2}|grad_S f_r|^2).

At a fixed u use an orthonormal tangent basis. Scalar radial Poincare for each component of H gives

    E|H-EH|^2<=C_r E|partial_r H|^2<=C_r T,

since |partial_r H|^2=|4r^3 grad_S A-4r grad_S B|^2
<=32(r^6 a1^2+r^2 b1^2). Vector Cauchy-Schwarz and radial Poincare for f give

    |Cov(f_r,H)|^2<=Var(f_r) E|H-EH|^2
                       <=C_r^2 T E|partial_r f|^2.

Consequently (6) and |x+y|^2<=2|x|^2+2|y|^2 imply

    |grad_S g|^2<=2U2 E(r^{-2}|grad_S f_r|^2)
                 +2beta^2 C_r^2 T E|partial_r f|^2.

Apply the even-function spherical Poincare inequality to g, integrate over u, and use (4). The Euclidean polar identity

    |grad f|^2=|partial_r f|^2+r^{-2}|grad_S f_r|^2

shows that the resulting constant is at most the right side of (5). Smooth even functions are sufficient for this variational inequality and extend by closure to the even weighted Sobolev domain. Alternatively (5) may be read first on this smooth core; the Gibbs density is positive smooth and coercive, so symmetric mollification and smooth radial cutoffs give the usual weighted H1 approximation.

## 4. The comparison coefficients are polynomial on the existing sample event

The C003 event includes

    S>=I/2,
    m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^2|a_i|^2<=4d,
    m^{-1}sum |a_i|^4<=2d(d+2).

Therefore one may use

    a0=1/4, b0=4d, a1=8d(d+2), b1=8d.

For example |grad_S A| is at most the full ambient gradient norm, bounded by 4m^{-1}sum |a_i.u|^3|a_i|<=4m^{-1}sum |a_i|^4. Similarly B and its gradient are bounded by the trace of m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^2 a_i a_i^T and twice that trace. These are crude polynomial bounds; no dimension-free directional upper bound is asserted.

Thus every coefficient in (5) is bounded polynomially in d, beta and beta^{-1} (square roots can be bounded by 1 plus their arguments). In a specified polynomial beta(d,epsilon) regime, a polynomial C_nu would imply the desired polynomial C_even. The remaining unpaid step is precisely a polynomial Poincare bound for the even spherical marginal nu, whose density is the explicit radial integral Z(u). Ordinary compactness gives only finiteness; a generic density-oscillation comparison can cost exp(O(beta)) and does not close Target 2.

## Checks and limits of the claim

Equation (2), the direction reversal below r_*, the two Gaussian-tail integrations, and the median argument are separate load-bearing steps. The radial result requires d>1 and beta a>0; b need not be nonnegative. The empirical transfer uses B>=0, the uniform coefficient bounds, and a specified finite angular constant. No independence of radial and angular variables is asserted. Equation (4) is conditional variance, and (6) includes the conditional score covariance that would be lost by treating the variables as independent. [Prop of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Both $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}^\otimes$ and $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}^\otimes$ are cartesian.
    \begin{proof}
        It is clear from the definitions that the unit of $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}$ is terminal and that the derived functors ${{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_G\times{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_G\to{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_G$ of the product functors admit left adjoints (namely, the derived functor of the diagonal) for every $G$. Thus, $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}^\otimes$ is cartesian by Remark~(rk:what-it-means-to-be-cartesian of the paper). The statement for $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}^\otimes$ follows in the same way using Lemma~(lemma:box-product-vs-product of the paper).

[Lemma 32 of arXiv:2609.02808, 'Minimizers of Laplace eigenvalues under a lower curvature bound'] Let $j\ge1$, let $u_j$ be the $j$-th eigenfunction, and put
$\mu=\mu_j(\varphi)$. Set
\[
\psi(s):=\varphi(D-s),\qquad
\hat\tau(s):=\pi-\tau(D-s),\qquad
\hat\gamma(s):=j\pi-\gamma(D-s).
\]
Then $\hat\gamma$ is the phase of the reflected natural-at-$0$ solution and
$\hat\tau$ is the density clock for $\psi$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\hat\gamma(s)
\le
\bar\gamma(\hat\tau(s);\mu_j)
\qquad\text{for all }s\in(0,D).
\end{equation}

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] The derivative bounds~\eqref{forq},~\eqref{forw} of Proposition~\ref{prop:main} imply 
\begin{align}
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla_x^\ell\z(x,0)\|_H&\leq C_{\z}d^{\lceil\ell/2\rceil-2},\quad\ell=3,\dots,2N+2,\\
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla_x^\ell\g_k(x)\|_H&\leq C_{\z,\g}d^{\lceil\ell/2\rceil},\quad \ell=0,\dots,2(N+1-k),\;k=1,\dots,N,\\
\sup_{x\in \us(R\e),y\in[0, (R\e)^2]}|D_{\z}^{k-1}\g(x,y)|&\leq C_{\z,\g},\quad k=1,\dots,N+1.
\end{align} The constant $C_{\z}$ depends on $C_{\z,\ell}$, $\ell=0,\dots,2N+2$ from~\eqref{forw}. The constant $C_{\z,\g}$ is similar and also depends on $C_{\g,\ell}$, $\ell=0,\dots,2N$ from~\eqref{forq}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let Gamma have terminals a_0,a_1,..., joining a_{n-1} to a_n by n^2 2^{n+1} internally disjoint length-(n+1) paths, with all internal vertices distinct across paths and blocks. Independent Bernoulli bond percolation has p_c=1/2 and theta_Gamma(1/2)>3/5. For A_N={a_0 connects to a_N}, for every fixed t>=0 the conditional exponential moment E_{1/2}[exp(t N_{A_N})|A_N] is bounded uniformly in N; the conditional mean is less than 3. Yet for every 0<a<1/2 its integrated conditional pivotal cost from a to 1/2 tends to infinity. There is almost surely one infinite critical cluster. [Proposition prop:fluctuation-identities of arXiv:2608.22910, 'A Commutator Framework for Selective Spectral Alignment in Deep Neural Networks'] Let \(x,x'\) be independent with law \(\mu\). Then
\begin{align}
\mathcal V_{\ell+1}
&=
\mathbb E_\mu\|S_{\ell+1}\|_F^2
-\|\mathcal S_{\ell+1}\|_F^2\\
&=
\frac12\mathbb E_{\mu\otimes\mu}
\|S_{\ell+1}(x)-S_{\ell+1}(x')\|_F^2.

\end{align}
If \(g_{\ell+1}=\nabla_{a_{\ell+1}}F\), so that
\(S_{\ell+1}=g_{\ell+1}g_{\ell+1}^\top\), then
\begin{align}
\mathcal V_{\ell+1}
&=
\mathbb E_\mu\|g_{\ell+1}\|^4
-\left\|
\mathbb E_\mu[g_{\ell+1}g_{\ell+1}^\top]
\right\|_F^2
\\
&=
\frac12\mathbb E_{\mu\otimes\mu}
\bigl[
\|g_{\ell+1}(x)\|^4+\|g_{\ell+1}(x')\|^4
-2\langle g_{\ell+1}(x),g_{\ell+1}(x')\rangle^2
\bigr].

\end{align}
In particular, \(\mathcal V_{\ell+1}=0\) if and only if
\(S_{\ell+1}(x)=\mathcal S_{\ell+1}\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\).

[Defn Radial SLE($\kappa,\rho$) of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\xi$ be the growth point on the unit circle, and let
\[
\boldsymbol{\rho} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \rho_j \delta_{u_j} + \sigma_0 \cdot \delta_0 + \sigma_{\infty} \cdot \delta_{\infty}
\]
be a divisor on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, where $\rho_j \in \mathbb{C}$, and the divisor $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ is symmetric under inversion, i.e.,
\[
\boldsymbol{\rho}(z) = \overline{\boldsymbol{\rho}\left(\frac{z}{|z|^2}\right)} \quad \text{for all } z \in \widehat{\mathbb{C}}.
\]
We say $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ satisfies the neutrality condition for $\mathrm{SLE}(\kappa,\rho)$ if
\[
\int \boldsymbol{\rho} = \kappa - 6.
\].

Define the radial $\operatorname{SLE}(\kappa, \xi, \boldsymbol{\rho})$ Loewner chain by

\begin{equation}
\partial_t g_t(z)=g_t(z)\frac{\xi(t)+g_t(z)}{\xi(t)-g_t(z)}, \quad g_0(z)=z.
\end{equation}

Let $\xi(t)=e^{i\theta(t)}$, $u_j=e^{iq_j}$ and $h_t(z)$ be the covering map of $g_t(z)$ (i.e. $h_t(z)=g_t(e^{iz})$) , then the Loewner differential equation for $h_t(z)$ is given by
\begin{equation}
\partial_t h_t(z)=\cot(\frac{h_t(z)-\theta(t)}{2}), \quad h_0(z)=z,  
\end{equation}
 the driving function $\theta(t)$ evolves as

\begin{equation}
d\theta(t)=\sqrt{\kappa}dB_t+\sum_j \rho_j \cot( \frac{\theta(t)-q_j(t)}{2}).
\end{equation}
title: Radial SLE($\kappa,\rho$)

Dominated extension form: let V be a real vector space, p : V -> R a sublinear functional (p(x + y) <= p(x) + p(y) and p(t x) = t p(x) for t >= 0), U a linear subspace of V, and f : U -> R a linear functional with f(u) <= p(u) for all u in U. Then there is a linear functional F : V -> R extending f with F(x) <= p(x) for all x in V. Normed form: if X is a real or complex normed space, U a subspace, and f a bounded linear functional on U, then f extends to a bounded linear functional on X with the same norm. Consequently, for every nonzero x in X there is a functional of norm one with F(x) = ||x||, so the dual separates points.
p sublinear (real case); in the complex case dominate |f| by a seminorm
the proof uses Zorn's lemma / the axiom of choice in general; no choice is needed for separable spaces

[Definition of arXiv:2509.23496, 'Crossing probabilities in geometric inhomogeneous random graphs'] An event $E$ is called a \emph{finite-crossing event} for a graph $\mathscr G$ with vertex set $V\subset\mathbb R^d \times [0,1]$ if there exists $k\ge 1$, and a Borel subset $A \subset (\mathbb R^d \times (0,1])^k$ 
    such that
    \[
    E=\big\{\exists (\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_k)\in V^k\cap A, \forall 1\leq i\leq k-1,\, \mathbf{x}_i=\mathbf{x}_{i+1}\text{ or }\,\mathbf{x}_i\sim \mathbf{x}_{i+1}\big\}
    \]
    We also use this definition for rooted graphs
    $(\mathscr G, \mathbf{x}_0)$ adding the requirement $\mathbf{x}_0\sim \mathbf{x}_1$
    to the definition of $E$. Given $k$ and $A$ we say $E$ is the finite-crossing event associated with~$(k,A)$.
    \pagebreak[3]
    
    The set
    $A$ is called \emph{downward-closed} if, for all  $((x_1,u_1),\ldots,(x_k,u_k)) \in A$ and $u_1' \leq u_1, u_2' \leq u_2, \ldots, u_k' \leq u_k$ it follows that $((x_1,u_1'),\ldots,(x_k,u_k')) \in A$. The event $E$ is called downward-closed if $A$ is.

[Cor 11 of arXiv:2604.25964, 'Strong convergence rate of Euler-Maruyama approximations in temporal-spatial H\"older-norm'] Let $p \ge 2,$ 
    
    $T\in (0, \infty),$ $\mu, \sigma, \gamma  \in C^2(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})$, $(\Om, \mf, \pr, (\mathcal{F})_{t\in [0, T]})$ be a filtered probability space which satisfies the usual conditions. 
    For every $n \in \mathbb{N}, x\in \mathbb{R}$, let $Y^{n,x} = \left(Y^{n, x}_t \right)_{t\in [0, T]}: [0, T] \times \Om \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy for all $k \in \{0, \dots, n-1\},$ $t\in \left( \frac{kT}{n}, \frac{(k+1)T}{n} \right]$ that $Y_0^{n, x}=x$ and 
    $$Y_{t}^{n, x} = Y_{\frac{kT}{n}}^{n, x}+\mu \left(Y_\frac{kT}{n}^{n, x}\right) \left (t- \frac{kT}{n} \right) +\sigma \left(Y_\frac{kT}{n}^{n, x}\right) \left(W_{t}- W_{\frac{kT}{n}}\right) +  \gamma (Y_\frac{kT}{n}^{n, x})\left(Z_{t}- Z_{\frac{kT}{n}}\right).$$ 
    Then for 
    every $x\in \mathbb{R}$, there exists an uniqueness adapted stochastic process with c\`adl\`ag sample paths $(X_t^x)_{t\in [0, T]}: [0, T]\times \Om \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $t\in [0, T]$, it holds a.s that $$X_t^x=x+\int^t_0\mu(X^x_s)ds+\int^t_0\sigma(X^x_s)dW_s + \int^t_0 \int_{\bR_0} \gamma (X^x_{s-})z \widetilde{N}(d s, d z),$$ and 
    for any $p \geq 2$ and $m > 1$, there exists a constant $C> 0$ such that for all $n\in \mathbb{N},$  $x \in \mathbb{R},$ $y\in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{x\}$, $t\in [0, T]$, it holds that 
        \begin{align*}
        &  \dfrac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|X^x_{t}-X^{y}_{t}\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{|x-y| n^{\frac{1}{mp}}} 
        + \frac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|Y^{n,x}_{t}-Y^{n,y}_{t}\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{|x-y| n^{\frac{1}{mp}}}\\
&+\dfrac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|X^x_{t}-Y^{n, x}_t\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{1+|x|}+\dfrac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\left(X^x_{t}-Y^{n, x}_t\right)-\left(X^y_{t}-Y^{n, y}_t\right)\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{|x-y|(1+|x|+|y|)} \leq \dfrac{C}{n^{\frac{1}{mp}}}.
        \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor 11 of arXiv:2604.25964

[Lemma lem:stoch-conv of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Let $K_T\to K$ in $L^2([0,1])$, and assume that $K_T$ satisfies the uniform
$L^2$-shift bound~(equation eq:L2-shift of the paper).  Let $M^T$ be square-integrable
martingales whose jumps vanish in probability, and suppose that
$(M^T,\langle M^T\rangle)$ converges in law to $(M,\langle M\rangle)$ in the
Skorokhod topology, where $M$ is continuous.  If
$d\langle M^T\rangle_t=q_t^Tdt$ and the densities $q^T$ satisfy the moment
bound~(equation eq:moment-density of the paper), then
\begin{equation}
\int_0^\cdot K_T(\cdot-s)\,dM_s^T
\Longrightarrow
\int_0^\cdot K(\cdot-s)\,dM_s
\qquad\text{in }C([0,1]).
\end{equation}

Write

\qquad
A_t^T:=\int_0^t(K_T-K)(t-s)\,dM_s^T,
\]
where $B^T$ denotes the same expression with the fixed kernel $K$ and the
martingales $M^T$ and $M$.

body:
[Lemma skewed of arXiv:2412.08334, 'Maker-Breaker on Galton-Watson trees'] In the case $I(v)=|T_v|$ and given the non-trivial situation, where $|T_\mathbf{0}|=\infty$, the number of external nodes with infinite progeny at Maker's turns can be described as the random walk
	\[S_0=c,\quad S_{n}=S_{n-1}+(\xi'_n-2)\quad\text{for}\ n\in\mathbb{N},\]
	where $(\xi'_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is an i.i.d.\ sequence with marginal probability mass function
	\[\mathbb{P}(\xi_1'=k)=\frac{1}{1-q}\, \sum_{n\geq k} p_n \binom{n}{k}(1-q)^kq^{n-k}\quad\text{for }k\in\mathbb{N},\]
	where $(p_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is again the pmf of the offspring distribution corresponding to the underlying supercritical GW-process. As before, $c=1$ corresponds to Breaker starting, $c=2$ corresponds to Maker starting the game.
title: Lemma skewed of arXiv:2412.08334

[Lem construction of Gmp from coding functions and binomial pointset of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{[Berry_Broutin_Goldschmidt_12_The_continuum]}] 
  Fix $p \in (0,1)$.
  Let $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$ to be a tilted tree as defined above
  and $\mathcal{Q}^{p}$ be a binomial pointset of intensity $p$, independent of $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$.
  Let $v_{0}, v_{1}, \ldots, v_{m-1}$ be the vertices of $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$ in depth-first order.
  Write $\mathscr{T}(\mathcal{Q}^{p}, X_{\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}}) = \{(x_{i}, y_{i}) : 1 \leq i \leq s \}$
  (recall its definition from (equation eq: def of time markers from excursion and pointset of the paper)).
  We define a graph $G(\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}, \mathcal{Q}^{p})$
  by attaching an edge between $v_{x_{i}}$ and $v_{y_{i}}$ on $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$.
  (If $\mathscr{T}(\mathcal{Q}^{p}, X_{\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}})$ is empty, we define $G(\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}, \mathcal{Q}^{p}) \coloneqq  \tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$.)
  Then, $G(\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}, \mathcal{Q}^{p})$ has the same distribution as $G_{m}^{p}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem construction of Gmp from coding functions and binomial pointset of arXiv:2412.08236

[Lem annuli_lemma of arXiv:2604.14122, 'The scaling limit of random walk and\\ the intrinsic metric on planar critical percolation'] Fix $m\in \mathbf{N}$, and let $i,j\in \mathbf{N}$ with $i\leq j-10$. Let $B(0,R^{-i}/2)$ be the box centered at the origin with side length $R^{-i}$, and tile it with boxes of side length $n^{-1}R^{\kappa-j}$. Let $K$ be the set of centers of such boxes that are fully contained inside $B(0,R^{-i}/2)$. Suppose that $z_1,\ldots, z_m\in K$ are distinct. Then there exist $n_{u}\in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ 
for each $1\leq u\leq m$ and $s_{u,l},r_{u,l} \in \mathbf{R}_{\geq 0}$ such that $0<s_{u,l}<r_{u,l} \leq n^{-1}R^{\kappa-i}$ for $1\leq l\leq n_{u}-1$ and $0=s_{u,n_{u}}< \frac{1}{2}n^{-1}R^{\kappa-j}\leq r_{u,n_{u}}$ so that all the annuli $A(z_u;s_{u,l},r_{u,l})$ are pairwise disjoint and
\[ \prod_{u=1}^{m} \frac{\prod_{l=1}^{n_{u}-1} s_{u,l}}{\prod_{l=1}^{n_{u}} r_{u,l} } \leq C(R,m)\prod_{u=1}^{m} \frac{1}{R^{-i} \wedge \min_{1\leq v<u} |z_{u}-z_v|} , \]
where $C(R,m)$ is a constant depending only on $R,m$. We use the convention that $\prod_{l=1}^{n_{u}-1} s_{u,l}=1$ if $n_{u}=1$, and the minimum of an empty set is infinite.
title: Lem annuli_lemma of arXiv:2604.14122

body:
[Lem uniform-mixture of arXiv:2605.13004, 'Orientation in Poisson Cluster Processes via Imaginary Bispectra'] Let $h$ be a nonincreasing probability density on $(0,\infty)$, and let $X$ have density $h$. Then there exists a nonnegative random variable $Z$ and an independent $Y\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ such that
\[
X\stackrel d=YZ.
\]
Equivalently, $h$ admits the representation
\[
h(x)=\int_{(x,\infty)} z^{-1}\,G(dz)
\quad\text{for a.e. }x>0,
\]
where $G=\mathcal{L}(Z)$. Moreover, for every $p>0$,
\[
\mathbb{E} X^p=\frac{1}{p+1}\mathbb{E} Z^p
\]
whenever either side is finite. Finally,
\[
h(x)=a^{-1}\1_{(0,a)}(x)\quad\text{a.e.}
\]
if and only if $Z=a$ a.s.

[Corollary cor:spectral-clustering of arXiv:2507.12502, 'Quantitative Edge Eigenvector Universality for Random Regular Graphs: Berry-Esseen Bounds '] Consider the spectral embedding $\Psi: V \to \mathbb{R}^K$ defined by
\[
\Psi(v) = \left(\frac{u_2(v)}{\lambda_2}, \ldots, \frac{u_{K+1}(v)}{\lambda_{K+1}}\right)
\]
for $K \leq N^{1/10-\delta}$. Then for any two disjoint vertex sets $A, B$ of size at least $N^{3/4}$:
\[
\left\|\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{v \in A} \Psi(v) - \frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{v \in B} \Psi(v)\right\|_2 = \Omega\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\right)
\]
with probability at least $1 - N^{-c}$ for some $c > 0$.

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Let $t>0$ and $x\in\mbb R^2$ be fixed. For every $\eps>0$ and $A\subset[0,t]^2$,
\[\be^{\eps}_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)

\be^{\eps}_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^0).\]

\[\ga_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
\ga_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^0).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary fourier2 of arXiv:2412.04013, 'Rate estimates for total variation distance with applications\thanks{The author gratefully'] Let $E[|X_{1}|^{k}]+E[|X_{2}|^{k}]\leq K_{k}<\infty$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Assume also that for all $l\in\mathbb{N}$ there is
$C_{l}>0$ such that the corresponding characteristic functions $\phi_{1},\phi_{2}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
|\phi_{1}(u)|+|\phi_{2}(u)|\leq \frac{C_{l}}{(1+|u|)^{l}},\ u\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
\end{equation}
Then for all $0<\epsilon<1$ there is a constant $C_{\epsilon}$
(which depends on $d$ and on the sequences $K_{k},C_{l}$ but not on $X_{1},X_{2}$)
such that
$$
d_{TV}(X_{1},X_{2})\leq C_{\epsilon}d_{FM}^{1-\epsilon}(X_{1},X_{2}).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary fourier2 of arXiv:2412.04013

[Cor Gint2 of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] Let $\lambda$ be a partition and $k$ be an integer such that $\lambda_1\leq k$. Let $\mathcal C$ be a positively-oriented simple complex contour encircling both $0$ and $-\mathfrak b$. Then
 \begin{equation*}
G^{(0,\mathfrak b)}_{\lambda}(x_1,\dots, x_n)\\
=(-1)^{-|\lambda|}\oint_{\mathcal C}\frac{du_1}{2\pi\mathbf i u_1}\dots\oint_{\mathcal C}\frac{du_k}{2\pi\mathbf i u_k}\prod_{i<j}\frac{u_i-u_j}{u_i}\prod_{i=1}^k\(\frac{1}{(u_i+\mathfrak b)^{\lambda'_i}}\prod_{j=1}^n(1-u_ix_j)\).
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In linear algebra, eigendecomposition (also known as eigenvalue decomposition or EVD) is a factorization of a matrix $A$ into a canonical form given by $A=QDQ^{\mathsf {-1}}$, where $D$ is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of $A$ on the diagonal, and $Q$ is a matrix whose columns are the corresponding eigenvectors of $A$. Only diagonalizable matrices can be factorized in this way. When the matrix being factorized is a normal or real symmetric matrix, the decomposition is called "spectral decomposition", derived from the spectral theorem.

[Proposition sec1aC of arXiv:2606.07353, 'The Gaussian structure of a perturbed KPZ'] Suppose that $t\ge0$. Then, the probability measure $\mu_{t,V}(F)$ is
 absolutely continuous w.r.t. the measure $\nu$.  
 We denote its respective
 Radon-Nikodym derivative   by ${\mathcal
  P}_t^VF$. As a result, the family $\big({\mathcal P}_t^V\big)_{t\ge0}$ forms a strongly continuous
semigroup of linear operators on $L^1(\nu)$ which  satisfies
\begin{equation}
  
  \begin{split}
    &{\mathcal P}_t^VG\ge0,\quad\mbox{if }G\ge0,\\
&  \int_{\rm H}{\mathcal P}_t^VGd\nu=\int_{\rm H} Gd\nu,\quad G\in
L^1(\nu).
\end{split}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition sec1aC of arXiv:2606.07353

body:
[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.14564, 'Upper tails for irregular graphs \\ beyond the mean-field regime'] The following holds for every nonempty $J \subseteq H$ without isolated vertices, all $x \in (0, \infty)$, and every $G \subseteq K_n$ with at most $xf$ edges.
  Writing
  \[
    \pi(x) \coloneqq \max\{(2x)^{v_J-\alpha_J^*},(2x)^{\alpha_J^*}\} \le \max\{2x, (2x)^{v_J}\},
  \]
  we have:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item
    
    If $J \in \cJ$, then, for all $p$,
    \[
      \frac{N(J,G)}{n^{v_J}p^{e_J}} \le \pi(x).
    \]
  \item
    
    If $J \in \cJ \setminus \cJ^*$, then, for all $p < n^{-1/\Delta}$,
    \[
      \frac{N(J,G)}{n^{v_J}p^{e_J}} \le \pi(x) \cdot (np^\Delta)^{\gamma_H},
    \]
    where $\gamma_H$ is a positive constant that depends only on $H$.
  \item
    
    If $J \notin \cJ$ and $\eps_H = \infty$, then, for all $p$,
    \[
      \frac{N(J,G)}{n^{v_J}p^{e_J}} \leq \pi(x) \cdot \max\{p^{1/2}, n^{-1/(2\Delta)}\}.
    \]
  \item
    
    If $J \notin \cJ$ and $\eps_H<\infty$, then, for every $L \ge 1$ and all $p \ge Ln^{-1/\Delta-\eps_H}$,
    \[
      \frac{N(J,G)}{n^{v_J}p^{e_J}}\leq \pi(x) \cdot \max\{p^{1/2}, n^{-1/(2\Delta)}, L^{-\beta_H}\},
    \]
    where $\beta_H$ is a positive constant that depends only on $H$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.14564

[Prop moment of arXiv:2412.09471, 'On the moderate deviation principles in the sparse multi-type Erd\H{o}s R\'enyi random gra'] When $\Sigma(\kappa,\mu)\neq 1$, under the Assumption~(assump1 of the paper), and assuming $|\mu^n-\mu|=O(\frac1n)$, for all $0<\alpha\leq\mu^n$ and any  $r\in{\mathcal S}$, we have
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item Normalization Constant:
    \begin{equation}
      Z_n^{\alpha}=|c|-\frac{1}{2}c^T\kappa c+O\left(\frac1{n}\right).
    \end{equation}
    \item First Moments:
     \[
    {\mathbb E} X^{n,\alpha}_r=\frac{c_r}{|c|-\frac{1}{2}c^T\kappa c}+O\left(\frac1{n}\right),
\]
    \item Second Moments: let $\Psi^\alpha$ be the $d\times d$ symmetric matrix with entries $\Psi^\alpha_{ij}={\mathbb E} X^{n,\alpha}_iX^{n,\alpha}_j$ for all $i,j\in{\mathcal S}$. Then we have 
\begin{equation}
\Psi^\alpha_{ij}=\frac{1}{|c|-\frac{1}{2}c^T\kappa c}\Phi_{ij}+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),
\end{equation}
where $\Phi$ is the matrix given by~(equation cor3 of the paper).
\item Probability Mass Function: for any $k\in{\mathbb N}^d$,  
    \begin{equation}
    {\mathbb P}(X^{n,\alpha}=k)=\frac{h(k)}{|c|-\frac{1}{2}c^T\kappa c}+O\left(\frac1{n}\right).
    \end{equation}
    \item Logarithmic Moment Generating Function: there exists $\eta\in(0,\infty)^d$ such that
\[
\sup_n\log{\mathbb E} \exp\langle\eta, X^{n,\alpha}\rangle<\infty.
\]
\end{enumerate}
title: Prop moment of arXiv:2412.09471

body:
[Defi 13 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] A family of non-commutative random variables $ x=(x_1,\dots ,x_m)$ in a $W^*$-probability space $(\A,\tau)$ is called 
		a {\bf free semicircular system} if $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ are freely independent, 
		selfadjoint ($x_i=x_i^*$, $i=1 \dots m$), and for all $k\in\N$ and $i=1,\dots,m$ one has
		\begin{equation}
        
			\tau( x_i^k) =  \int t^k \,\varsigma(dt),
		\end{equation}
		with $\varsigma(dt) = \frac 1 {2\pi} \sqrt{4-t^2} \ \mathbbm{1}_{|t|\leq2}\, dt$ the semicircle distribution. For an explicit construction of such operators, we refer to \cite[Lecture 7]{SpeicherNicaBook}.
        
        A {\bf free semicircular Brownian motion} $(x(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is a family of semicircular variables such that $x(t)/\sqrt{t}$ has the semicircle distribution for each $t>0$, and the additive increments of $x$ are stationary and freely independent: for $0 \leq t_1 < t_2 < \infty$, $x(t_2)-x(t_1)$ has the same law as $ x(t_2-t_1)$, and $x(t_2) - x(t_1)$ is freely independent from $(x(t))_{0\leq t\leq t_1}$.   See \cite{BianeSpeicher1998} for a detailed construction and properties.
title: Definition 13 of arXiv:2511.10535

[Lemma lem:eta_func of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] For $\eta$ defined in~(equation eq:defn_eta of the paper), it follows that $\eta(x)=0$ for $x \in [0,(a+b)/2)$, $\eta(x)=1/2$ for $[(a+b)/2,a)$, $\eta(a)=1$ and  
    \begin{equation}
        \eta(x) =
            1+\frac{1}{x-a} \bigg( \int_0^{x-a} \eta(t) \,\mathrm{d} t + \int_0^{x-\tfrac{a+b}{2}} \eta(t)\,\mathrm{d} t\bigg), \quad \text{ for all } x > a,
    \end{equation} where $\eta$ is a non-decreasing function on $(0,\infty)$, and continuous on $(a,\infty)$, specifically $\eta$ is locally absolutely continuous on $(a,\infty)$.

[Lem 20 of arXiv:2607.06242, 'Exponential mixing and Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle for Markov cocycles'] Suppose for any $M>0$, there is a finite measurable $C_M:\Sigma\to \mathbb R_+$ such that for any $t>0$, any controlled path $u
       =\Phi^{\varphi_u}_{0,\cdot, \xi}u_0
       $ satisfying 
       \[
      {\frac 12} \int_0^t
      \|\varphi_u (s)\|^2 ds  \leq M, \quad d(u_0, \mathcal{A}(\xi))<1,\]
      and any $v_0 \in \mathcal{A}(\xi)$, there is a controlled path $v
      =\Phi^{\varphi_v}_{0,\cdot, \xi}v_0
      $ such that 
      \begin{align}
        \sup _{0 \leq s \leq t}\|u(s)-v(s)\|^2 \leq C_M(\xi)\left\|u_0-v_0\right\|^2
      \end{align}
      and 
      \begin{align}
        \int_0^t\left\|\varphi_u(s)-\varphi_v(s)\right\|^2 d s \leq C_M(\xi)\left\|u_0-v_0\right\|^2. 
      \end{align}

body:
[Lemma lem:formula of arXiv:2412.03450, 'On intermediate levels of nested occupancy scheme in random environment generated by stick'] Let $\gamma>0$ and $\eta$ be a positive random variable with the Laplace transform $\ell$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E} \eta^{-\gamma} = \frac{\gamma}{\Gamma(1+ \gamma)} \int_0^\infty s^{\gamma-1}\ell(s) {\rm d} s,
$$
where $\Gamma$ is the Euler gamma-function. Here, both sides of the equality may be infinite. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:formula of arXiv:2412.03450

body:
[Theorem workload-optimality of arXiv:2505.04942, '\textbf{Randomized Routing to Remote Queues}'] Assume the conditions of Theorem~(theorem:load-balancing of the paper) hold for a sequence of GBC systems where the customers' origins are known. Then for $T > 0$, $ \sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \tilde{\Gamma}^{\dagger}_{n}(t) \Rightarrow 0 $ as $ n \to \infty $. If conditions~(equation eq:fourth-moments of the paper) and (equation eq:log-log-n-bound of the paper) also hold, then there exist two positive numbers $ C^{\dagger} $ and $ C^{\ddagger} $ such that with probability 1,
	\[
	\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \tilde{\Gamma}^{\dagger}_{n}(t) < \max \Big\{ C^{\dagger} \chi_{n}, C^{\ddagger} \frac{\log \log n + \log (n \chi_{n}^{2})}{\sqrt{n} \chi_{n}} \Big\} \quad \mbox{for $n$ sufficiently large.}
	\]
	The order of this upper bound is minimized with $ \chi_{n} = C'' n^{-1/4}\sqrt{\log n} $ for $ C'' > 0 $, in which case $ \sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \tilde{\Gamma}^{\dagger}_{n}(t) = O(n^{-1/4}\sqrt{\log n})$ with probability 1. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem workload-optimality of arXiv:2505.04942

[Lemma phi_bound of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Fix $\lambda, \alpha > 0$. Let $y > 0$ satisfy
    \begin{equation}
    
        \upsilon(\lambda y) \le \alpha y^\alpha.
    \end{equation}
    If $\alpha < 1$, let $\tau > 0$ satisfy (equation eq:condition_on_y of the paper) as well, i.e., $\upsilon(\lambda \tau) \le \alpha \tau^\alpha$.

    Then for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ in case $\alpha \ge 1$ and for all $x \le \tau$ in case $\alpha < 1$ it holds that
    \[
    \phi(\lambda x) \le x^2 \frac{\phi(\lambda y)}{y^2} + \rho_{\lambda, \alpha}(y) \exp\left\{x_+^\alpha \right\} \ind[x > y],
    \]
    where $\rho_{\lambda, \alpha}(x)$ is defined by~(equation def:rho of the paper).

Let G be a finite undirected loopless multigraph on n vertices with positive edge weights w_e, L its weighted Laplacian, and t > 0. A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). Z(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests, and Q_t = (I + tL)^-1. If i and j lie in the same connected component, t (e_i - e_j)^T Q_t (e_i - e_j) tends to the effective resistance R(i, j) = (e_i - e_j)^T L^+ (e_i - e_j) as t -> infinity (conductances w_e). If they lie in different components, the quantity tends to infinity.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The probability for a random permutation $\sigma\in S_N$ to be a derangement, that is, to have no fixed points, is given by the following formula:
$$P=1-\frac{1}{1!}+\frac{1}{2!}-\frac{1}{3!}+\ldots+(-1)^N\frac{1}{N!}$$
Thus we have the estimate $P\simeq1/e$, in the $N\to\infty$ limit.
title: Unnumbered theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

Use fresh IID samples and the Heavy Ball recursion w_(k+1)=w_k-delta*a_(k+1)*<a_(k+1),w_k-w_star>+alpha*(w_k-w_(k-1)), with delta>0, alpha in[0,1], and initial pair independent of the samples with finite second moments. Fix coordinate j, put x=delta*sigma_j^2 and h=1+alpha-x. For e_k=w_k^(j)-w_star^(j), form m_k=E[(e_k^2,e_k*e_(k-1),e_(k-1)*e_k,e_(k-1)^2)^T]. Then m_(k+1)=B*m_k, where B=[[h^2+(c-1)*x^2,-alpha*h,-alpha*h,alpha^2],[h,0,-alpha,0],[h,-alpha,0,0],[1,0,0,0]]. Its characteristic polynomial det(z*I_4-B) is D(z)=z^4-[h^2+(c-1)*x^2]*z^3+(2*alpha*h^2-2*alpha^2)*z^2+alpha^2*[-h^2+(c-1)*x^2]*z+alpha^4. These are raw second moments, with no zero-mean assumption on the error. An eigenvalue of B alone does not assert a matching lower bound for every particular initial pair.
The stated IID realizable two-axis distribution and fourth moment c>=2.

Let A_1, ..., A_n be events with S = sum_i P(A_i) > 0 and let N = 1_{A_1} + ... + 1_{A_n} be the number that occur. Then P(A_1 or ... or A_n) >= S^2 / sum_{i,j} P(A_i and A_j) (Chung and Erdős, 1952). The sum runs over all ordered pairs, i = j included, so the denominator is E[N^2] = S + sum over i != j of P(A_i and A_j), which is at least S > 0. Equality holds if and only if N is almost surely constant on the event {N > 0}. No independence is assumed.

body: In combinatorics, Ramsey's theorem, in one of its graph-theoretic forms, states that one will find monochromatic cliques in any edge labelling, with a fixed finite number of colours, of a sufficiently large complete graph. Precisely: for all positive integers r and c there exists a positive integer N = R_c(r) such that every labelling of the edges of a complete graph on at least N vertices with at most c colours contains a set of r vertices all of whose connecting edges carry the same colour. The finiteness of the number of colours is essential: with unboundedly many colours available (for example, a fresh colour on every edge) no monochromatic clique on 3 or more vertices need appear, however large the graph.

body:
[Theorem thm: main 1 of arXiv:2607.20097, 'Phase transition for the asymptotic entropy of branching random walks on groups'] Let $G$ be a countable group and let $\textsf{BRW}(G,\pi,\mu)$ be a branching random walk with step distribution $\mu$ on $G$ and offspring distribution $\pi$ with mean $\mathbb{E}[\pi]=\rho>1$. If $\mu$ has finite entropy, $\pi(0)=0$, and $\pi$ has a finite second moment, then the following holds for the entropy $H(\widehat{M}_n)$ of the empirical distribution $\widehat{M}_n$ of $\textsf{BRW}(G,\pi,\mu)$\textcolor{blue}{:}
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
\setlength\itemsep{0em}
    \item \textbf{Small-$\rho$ regime.} If $\rho\leq \mathsf{e}^{\textsf{h}(\mu)}$, then almost surely
    $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(\widehat{M}_n)}{n}=\log\rho.$$
    \item \textbf{Large-$\rho$ regime.} If $\rho > \mathsf{e}^{\textsf{h}(\mu)}$, then almost surely
    $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(\widehat{M}_n)}{n} = \textsf{h}(\mu),$$
    where $\textsf{h}(\mu)$ is the asymptotic entropy of the random walk $(G,\mu)$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Branching random walks

[Theorem 1 (Exact Variance Representation of Hölder Deficit) of arXiv:2607.23255, '2607.23255'] Let

\[
1<p,q<\infty,
\qquad
\frac1p+\frac1q=1,
\]

and let

\[
f,g\geq0
\]

satisfy

\[
0<
\int f^p dx<\infty ,
\qquad
0<
\int g^q dx<\infty .
\]

Define

\[
F=f^p,
\qquad
G=g^q,
\]

and

\[
Z(\theta)
=
\int
F^{1-\theta}G^\theta dx .
\]

Let

\[
d\mu_\theta
=
\frac{
F^{1-\theta}G^\theta
}{
Z(\theta)
}
dx .
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\log
\frac{
\|f\|_{L^p}
\|g\|_{L^q}
}{
\int fg dx
}
=
\int_0^1
K_{1/q}(s)
\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_s}
\left(
\log G-\log F
\right)
ds ,
}
\]

where

\[
K_{1/q}(s)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s}{p},
&
0\leq s\leq\dfrac1q ,
\\[2ex]
\dfrac{1-s}{q},
&
\dfrac1q\leq s\leq1 .
\end{cases}
\]

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02595, 'Minimal Radial Sub-Gamma Envelopes for Infinitely Divisible Random Vectors'] Let \(X\) be a centered infinitely divisible random vector with finite second moment and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). We define the radial pole \(C_X(t)\) as the smallest scale in a right sub-gamma bound for \(\ip{t}{X}\) whose quadratic proxy is fixed at the true variance \(t^\top\Sigma t\). A canonical directional measure and an independent \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,2)\) multiplier give an exact variational formula for \(C_X\). The resulting extended-valued function is positive homogeneous and is pointwise least among all homogeneous denominators compatible with the covariance quadratic form. We prove linear-map, convolution, and L\'evy-time rules, and show that the full family of directional remainders determines the law of \(X\). Geometrically, \(C_X\) lies between the Minkowski functional of the moment-generating-function domain and one third of the positive support function of the L\'evy measure; the upper constant is sharp, and the zero set is a polar cone. The pole need not be subadditive. It is continuous on the sphere under global exponential moments and positive-definite covariance, whereas finite variance alone permits a jump from zero to infinity in nearby directions. For additive gamma-ray models, \(C_X\) equals the domain gauge and has a finite-polytope formula.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02595: Minimal Radial Sub-Gamma Envelopes for Infinitely Divisible Random Vectors

body:
[Lem EsNoi of arXiv:2411.06974, '{\bf Distribution dependent SDEs with multiplicative fractional noise}'] Let $\beta\in (\frac 1 2,H)$, $\beta_1\in [\beta,H)$ and $1-\beta<\alpha<\beta$.
Assume that  $\mu,\nu\in\mathscr{P}_{2,\beta}(W_{S,T}^d)$ and $\sigma_{ij}\in  C_b^{2,(2,0)}(\mathbb R^d\times\mathscr{P}_2(\mathbb R^d)), 1\leq i,j\leq d$.
Let $X^\mu$ and $X^\nu$ be respectively the solutions of equation (equation X-mu of the paper) with the frozen distribution parts $\mu$ and $\nu$.
Then for any $S\leq s<t\leq T$ with $t-s\leq 1$,
\begin{align*}
&\left|\int_s^t\left(\sigma(X_r^\mu,\mu_r)-\sigma(X_r^{\nu},\nu_r)\right)\text{\rm{d}} B^H_r\right|\cr
\le&\|B^H\|_{s,t,\beta_1} \left(\Lambda_1 (t-s)^{\beta_1}+\Lambda_2  (t-s)^{\alpha+\beta_1}\right)\|X^\mu-X^\nu\|_{s,t,\infty}\cr
&+\Lambda_3 \|B^H\|_{s,t,\beta_1} (t-s)^{\beta+\beta_1}\|X^\mu-X^\nu\|_{s,t,\beta}\cr
&+\|B^H\|_{s,t,\beta_1} \left(\Lambda_4 (t-s)^{\beta_1}+\Lambda_5 (t-s)^{\alpha+\beta_1}\right)\mathbb{W}_{2,S,T,\beta}(\mu ,\nu),
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
&\Lambda_1 := \frac {C_0\mathcal{B}(1-\alpha,\alpha+\beta_1)} {\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \|\nabla\sigma\|_\infty, \\
&\Lambda_2 := \frac {2^{3-\frac {\alpha} {\beta}} \beta C_0\|\nabla\sigma\|_\infty^{\frac {\beta-\alpha} {\beta}}} {(\beta-\alpha)(\alpha+\beta_1)\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\Big[\left( \|\nabla^2\sigma\|_\infty \left( {\|X^\nu\|_{s,t,\beta}\vee\|X^\mu\|_{s,t,\beta}} \right)\right)^{\frac {\alpha} {\beta}}\cr
&\qquad +\left( \|D^L\nabla\sigma\|_\infty \left(\mathbb{W}_{2,S,T,\beta}(\mu,\delta_{\bf 0})\wedge \mathbb{W}_{2,S,T,\beta}(\nu,\delta_{\bf 0})\right)\right)^{\frac {\alpha} {\beta}} \Big], \\
&\Lambda_3 :=\frac {\alpha C_0\|\nabla\sigma\|_\infty\mathcal{B}(\beta-\alpha+1,\alpha+\beta_1)} {(\beta-\alpha)\Gamma(1-\alpha)}, \\
&\Lambda_4 :=\frac {C_0\|D^L \sigma\|_\infty } {\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \left( \mathcal{B}(1-\alpha,\alpha+\beta_1)+\frac {\alpha  \mathcal{B}(\beta-\alpha+1,\beta_1+\alpha)} {\beta-\alpha} \right), \cr
&\Lambda_5 :=\frac {2^{3-\frac {\alpha} {\beta}} \beta C_0 \|D^L\sigma\|_\infty^{\frac {\beta-\alpha} {\beta}}} {(\beta-\alpha)(\beta_1+\alpha)\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \Big[ (\|\nabla_1 D^L\sigma\|_\infty (\|X^\nu\|_{s,t,\beta}\wedge\|X^\mu\|_{s,t,\beta}))^{\frac {\alpha} {\beta}}\cr
&\qquad + \left((\|D^{L,2}\sigma\|_\infty+\|\nabla_2 D^L\sigma\|_\infty)( \mathbb{W}_{2,S,T,\beta}(\mu,\delta_{\bf 0})\vee\mathbb{W}_{2,S,T,\beta}(\nu,\delta_{\bf 0})) \right)^{\frac {\alpha}{\beta}}  \Big],
\end{split}
\end{equation}
in which $C_0:=\frac{\beta_1}{\Gamma(\alpha)(\alpha+\beta_1 -1)}$, $\nabla_1 D^L\sigma$ and $\nabla_2 D^L\sigma$ stand for the gradient operators of $D^L\sigma(x,\cdot)(\mu)(y)$ on $x$ and $y$, respectively.
title: Lem EsNoi of arXiv:2411.06974

body:
[Op of arXiv:2506.15949, 'On the passage times of self-similar Gaussian processes on curved boundaries'] In the case $\nu=0$, one can show in like manner that
	\begin{align*}
		&\textstyle\mathrm{E}\left(\left| X(t) - \sum_{j=1}^n a_j X(s_j)\right|^2 \right)\\

		&\textstyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} {\rm d} \xi \,\|\xi\|^{\beta-d-2\gamma} 
			\left[ (1-{\rm e}^{-t\|\xi\|^\gamma}) - \sum_{j=1}^n a_j(1-{\rm e}^{-s_j\|\xi\|^\gamma}) \right]^2.
	\end{align*}
	Let $\phi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a test function and define
	\[\textstyle
		\mathcal{I} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} {\rm d} \xi \,\left[ (1-{\rm e}^{-t\|\xi\|^\gamma}) 
		- \sum_{j=1}^n a_j(1-{\rm e}^{-s_j\|\xi\|^\gamma}) \right] \hat{\phi}(\xi).
	\]
	Then
	\[\textstyle
		\mathcal{I} = \left[ (2\pi)^d\phi(0) - \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} {\rm e}^{-t\|\xi\|^\gamma} 
		\hat{\phi}(\xi) {\rm d} \xi \right] - \sum_{j=1}^n a_j \left[
		(2\pi)^d\phi(0)-\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} {\rm e}^{-s_j\|\xi\|^\gamma}\hat{\phi}(\xi)\, {\rm d} \xi\right].
	\]
	It seems that there is no natural choice of $\phi$ that makes all the terms in 
	$\sum_{j=1}^n (\cdots)$ vanish.
	Therefore, it is unclear to us whether or not $X$ satisfies (equation SLND of the paper) when $\nu=0$,
	and the validity (or not) of (equation SLND of the paper) when $\nu=0$ is  an open problem. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Unnumbered OP of arXiv:2506.15949, 'On the passage times of self-similar Gaussian processes on c'

[Corollary 6 (Dirichlet spectral and Cheeger bounds) of arXiv:2607.13210, 'Punctured Wilson--Evolving Sets and Root Identities for Massive Kirchhoff Forests'] For distinct $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ elements of $V$, we find:
\begin{equation}
  \Pp(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\Root)
  \leq
  \prod_{i=1}^k\frac{q}{q+\lambda_1(D_{i-1})}.
\end{equation}
If $ \phi_D
  :=\inf_{\varnothing\neq A\subset D}
  \frac{Q(A,V\setminus A)}{\pi(A)},$ then, we get:
\begin{equation}
  \Pp(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\Root)
  \leq
  \prod_{i=1}^k
  \frac{q}{q+\phi_{D_{i-1}}^2/2}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dirichlet spectral and Cheeger bounds

[Thm 9 of arXiv:2606.21759, 'A Note On Gaussian Random Fields \& Underlying Markov Processes Through a Central Limit Th'] {(An OU$\mathcal{L}(1_\pi^\perp)$-Process Limit)}

Assume that $A$ satisifies {\bf RFA1}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item{} Then, the stationary UGRF $Z$ 
 in Theorem \ref{statugrfthm} is a version of the unique
OU$\mathcal{L}(1_\pi^\perp)$-process

for arbitrary Lamperti parameter $\gamma<0$,

 $\{U_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges under $P_\pi$ in
  finite dimensional distribution to 
It\^o's infinite dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck 
$\mathcal{L}(1^\perp_\pi)$-process with characteristic
(dissipative) operator
$\Gamma =\gamma{\mathbf I}$, and $C=-2A^{-1}$. 
\end{enumerate}

body: In abstract algebra, a composition series provides a way to break up an algebraic structure, such as a group or a module, into simple pieces. The need for considering composition series in the context of modules arises from the fact that many naturally occurring modules are not semisimple, hence cannot be decomposed into a direct sum of simple modules. A composition series of a module M is a finite increasing filtration of M by submodules such that the successive quotients are simple and serves as a replacement of the direct sum decomposition of M into its simple constituents.
title: Composition series

body: In mathematics, specifically in differential topology, Morse theory enables one to analyze the topology of a manifold by studying differentiable functions on that manifold. According to the basic insights of Marston Morse, a typical differentiable function on a manifold will reflect the topology quite directly. Morse theory allows one to find CW structures and handle decompositions on manifolds and to obtain substantial information about their homology.

  Let $T$ be an arithmetical theory with a computable set of axioms,
  and let $A$ and $B$ be arithmetical sentences.
  We write $A \lewis_T B$ if, for every $\Sigma_1$-sentence $S$,
  \[
    T \vdash S \to A \quad \Longrightarrow \quad T \vdash S \to B.
  \]
  Let $\operatorname{Pres}_T(x,y)$ be an arithmetical formula formalizing this relation.
  An \emph{arithmetical realization} $*$ of $\mathscr{L}_\lewis$ maps each propositional variable to an arithmetical sentence,
  commutes with the propositional connectives, and satisfies
  \[
    (\varphi \lewis \psi)^*
    \coloneq
    \operatorname{Pres}_T(\ulcorner \varphi^* \urcorner,\ulcorner \psi^* \urcorner).
  \]
  The \emph{($\Sigma_1$-)preservativity logic of $\operatorname{Pres}_T(x,y)$}
  consists of the formulas $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_\lewis$
  such that $T \vdash \varphi^*$ for every arithmetical realization $*$.

[Theorem 54 (Canonical Markov chain) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Assume \hyp{A}{A}. For every $\mu \in \Prob$ there is a unique
probability measure $\Prb_{\mu}$ on $(\XX^{\Nz},\XXA^{\otimes\Nz})$ with
\[
  \Prb_{\mu}\bigl( X_{0} \in A_{0},\dots,X_{m} \in A_{m} \bigr)
  = \int_{A_{0}}\int_{A_{1}} \cdots \int_{A_{m}}
      T(\dd x_{m} \mid x_{m-1}) \cdots T(\dd x_{1} \mid x_{0})\, \mu(\dd x_{0})
\]
for all $m \in \Nz$ and $A_{0},\dots,A_{m} \in \XXA$. Here the differentials appear,
as usual, in the order opposite to that of the integral signs, so that
$\int_{A_{0}}$ goes with $\mu(\dd x_{0})$ and $\int_{A_{m}}$ with
$T(\dd x_{m} \mid x_{m-1})$. Read from the right, the measures then occur in the
order in which they act, matching the composition $T^{m}\circ\mu$ of
\ref{conv:kernelnotation}. Writing
$\Prb_{x} := \Prb_{\delta_{x}}$ and denoting by $\Ex_{\mu}$ the corresponding expectation,
one has moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item the map $x \mapsto \Prb_{x}(B)$ is measurable and
        $\Prb_{\mu}(B) = \int_{\XX} \Prb_{x}(B)\,\mu(\dd x)$, for every $B \in \XXA^{\otimes\Nz}$;
  \item \emph{(Markov property)} for every bounded measurable
        $F : \XX^{\Nz} \to \R$ and every $m \in \Nz$,
        \[
          \Ex_{\mu}\bigl[ F \circ \vartheta^{m} \mid \sigma(X_{0},\dots,X_{m}) \bigr]
          = \Ex_{X_{m}}[F] \qquad \Prb_{\mu}\text{-almost surely};
        \]
  \item the law of $X_{n}$ under $\Prb_{\mu}$ is $T^{n}\circ\mu$;
  \item the shift $\vartheta$ preserves $\Prb_{\pi}$, that is $\Prb_{\pi}\circ\vartheta^{-1} = \Prb_{\pi}$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:isomVG of arXiv:2601.10359, 'An Operator It\^o Formula for Volterra Gaussian Processes:\\ The Intrinsic Bracket via Cau'] Under the Decreusefond--\"Ust\"unel conditions, the Skorokhod isometry with trace correction holds~[DU]: for $u \in \Dom(\delta^X)$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[(\delta^X(u))^2] = \mathbb{E}[\left\|u\right\|_{\mathcal{H}_X}^2] + \mathbb{E}[\left\|D^X u\right\|^2_{\mathrm{HS}}],
\]
where $\left\|D^X u\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$ denotes the Hilbert--Schmidt norm of the two-parameter Malliavin derivative of $u$. For adapted processes $u$ satisfying H\"older regularity, the trace correction $\mathbb{E}[\left\|D^Xu\right\|^2_{\mathrm{HS}}]$ is controlled: over a short interval $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, it is $O(|\Delta t|^{1+\gamma})$ where $\gamma$ depends on the regularity of $u$. For standard Brownian motion ($H=1/2$), the trace correction vanishes identically for adapted $u$, recovering the classical It\^o isometry. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:vc-dimension of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a class of binary classifiers on a space $Z$. 
A set $S \subseteq Z$ is \emph{shattered} by $\mathcal{H}$ if for every subset $T \subseteq S$, there exists $h \in \mathcal{H}$ such that $h(z) = 1$ for $z \in T$ and $h(z) = 0$ for $z \in S \setminus T$. 
The \emph{VC-dimension} of $\mathcal{H}$, denoted as $\mathsf{VCdim}(\mathcal{H})$, is the size of the largest set shattered by $\mathcal{H}$. 
If arbitrarily large sets can be shattered, $\mathsf{VCdim}(\mathcal{H}) = \infty$.
title: VC dimension

body:
[Corollary cor:scalar-dyadic-interval-formula-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let \(W\ge0\) satisfy
\[
    \mathbb{E} W=1,\qquad
    \mathbb{E}[W\log_2^+W]<\infty,\qquad
    \mathbb{E}[W\log_2 W]<1.
\]
Let \(W_0,W_1\) be independent copies of \(W\), define
\[
    X_i=\frac{W_i}{2},
    \qquad i=0,1,
\]
and let \(\mu\) be the corresponding scalar dyadic Mandelbrot cascade measure
on \([0,1]\).  Set \(M=\mu([0,1])\).  Then, almost surely on \(\{M>0\}\),
\begin{equation}
    \dim_{\mathrm F}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_{\mathrm E}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_2(\mu)
    =
    D^+(W),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
D^+(W)
=
\sup_{1<q<2}
\max\left\{
0,\,
2-\frac2q\bigl(1+\log_2\mathbb{E}[W^q]\bigr)
\right\},
\end{equation}
with the convention that the corresponding term is interpreted as \(0\)
whenever \(\mathbb{E}[W^q]=\infty\).  In particular, on the same event, if
\(D^+(W)>0\), then for every \(0<\sigma<D^+(W)\) there are finite random
constants \(C_\sigma(\omega),R_\sigma(\omega)<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
    |\widehat{\mu}(\xi)|
    \le
    C_\sigma(\omega)|\xi|^{-\sigma/2}
    \qquad (|\xi|\ge R_\sigma(\omega)).
\end{equation}
If \(D^+(W)=0\), the decay assertion is vacuous.

[Lemma 6 (Mollification) of arXiv:2609.01403, '2609.01403'] Let $w\in\mathcal L^{2s}(\mathbb R^n)$ and
$f\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$.  If
\[
\mathscr{L}_sw\le f
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega),
\]
then
\[
\mathscr{L}_sw^\delta\le f^\delta
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega^\delta),
\qquad
\Omega^\delta=\{x\in\mathbb R^n\mid B_\delta(x)\subset\Omega\}.
\]
The same statement holds with $\mathscr{L}_s$ replaced by
$\mathscr{L}_s+c_0$ for any constant $c_0\in\mathbb R$, and the analogous assertions hold with all inequalities reversed.
title: Mollification

[Definition eq:integral-equation-path-dependent-SDE of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\in [0,T]},\mathbb{P})\) be a filtered probability space equipped with a
	\(d\)-dimensional Wiener process \(W\) and \(\mathcal{F}_0\)-measurable random variables \(X_0, \lambda, \bar{\lambda}\).
	A stochastic process \(X\) is called a \emph{strong solution} if \(X\) is \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\)-adapted, has continuous
	paths, and satisfies the following integral equation \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s.:
	\begin{equation} 
		X(t)=X_0 + \int_{0}^{t} b(s,X,\lambda) ds + \int_{0}^{t} \sigma(s,X,\bar{\lambda}) dW(s),\quad t\in [0,T].
	\end{equation}
	\emph{Strong uniqueness} holds for equation (equation eq:path-dependent-SDE of the paper) if, for any two strong solutions \(X\) and \(Y\) (defined on the same probability space with the same \(W, X_0, \lambda, \bar{\lambda}\)), their paths are indistinguishable; that is,
	\[
		\mathbb{P}\big( \Vert X-Y \Vert_{\ast,T} = 0\big)=1.
	\]
title: Strong solution and uniqueness

body: In mathematics, Tychonoff's theorem states that the product of any collection of compact topological spaces is compact with respect to the product topology. The theorem is named after Andrey Nikolayevich Tikhonov, who proved it first in 1930 for powers of the closed unit interval and in 1935 stated the full theorem along with the remark that its proof was the same as for the special case. The earliest known published proof is contained in a 1935 article by Tychonoff, "Über einen Funktionenraum".
title: Tychonoff's theorem

body: Let (M,g) be a connected Riemannian manifold with induced geodesic distance d. The Hopf-Rinow theorem states the following are equivalent: (1) (M,d) is a complete metric space; (2) M is geodesically complete, i.e. every geodesic extends to be defined on all of R (equivalently the exponential map at some, hence every, point is defined on the whole tangent space); (3) every closed bounded subset of M is compact. If these hold, any two points of M can be joined by a minimizing geodesic whose length realizes the distance d between them. Due to Heinz Hopf and Willi Rinow.
title: Hopf-Rinow theorem

[Defn 24 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] Fix $\omega\in\Omega_{0}$. We construct a legal
path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{2n+1}=\omega_{2n}^{x_{2n}-1,x_{2n}}=\omega^{-1,0}$
(with $n$ depending on $\omega$). We do it in three phases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Begin with a path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{n}=\omega_{n-1}^{x_{n-1}-1,x_{n-1}}$,
whose last configuration satisfies $c(-1,0,\omega_{n})\neq0$ (here
$c=c^{\land}$ by Observation \ref{obs:D_and}). Recall Lemma \ref{lem:and_move_0},
and that $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega)<l(\omega)$. If $c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$
we are done (taking $n=0$). Otherwise, there exists $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$
with $\omega(x)=0,\ \omega(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega)=1$. Set $x_{0}$
to be the minimal such $x$, and $\omega_{1}=\omega^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}}$.

Continue by induction: assume that we constructed $\omega_{m}$. If
$c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$ we move to phase 2. Otherwise, set $x_{m}$
to be the minimal $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$ such that $\omega_{m}(x)=0,\ \omega_{m}(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega_{m})=1$,
and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.

This procedure is valid, since we only exchange sites in $[1,l(\omega)]$,
so the condition $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega_{m})<l(\omega)$ holds
for all $m$. Moreover, it must end: at each step the center of mass
$\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\eta(x)$ increases by $1$, and it cannot
exceed $\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\cdot1\le l(\omega)^{2}.$
\item Next, exchange $-1$ and $0$, choosing $x_{n}=0$ and $\omega_{n+1}=\omega_{n}^{-1,0}$.
\item Finally, wind back the path of phase 1: for $m\in\{n+1,\dots2n\}$
we set $x_{m}=x_{2n-m}$, and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.
Since all these transitions are in $[1,L]$ they do not depend on
the configuration at $-1$ and $0$, hence they are all legal and
end at $\omega_{2n+1}=\omega^{-1,0}$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 24 of arXiv:2608.13208

[Lemma key_est of arXiv:2412.07690, 'A law of large numbers concerning the distribution of critical points of random Fourier se'] Fix $r_0\in (0,1)$ and  a box $B=B^\infty_{r_0/2}(0)=[-r_0/2,r_0/2]^m$. Then the following hold.
  
  \begin{enumerate}
  
  \item For any $\ell\in {{\mathbb N}}_0$ and any $p>m$ there  exists $C=C(p,m,\ell,\mathfrak{a})>0$, independent of $R$,  such that, $\forall R>2$
  \[
  \big\Vert\, {\boldsymbol{K}}^R_\mathfrak{a}-{\boldsymbol{K}}_\mathfrak{a}\,\big\Vert_{C^\ell(RB)}\leq CR^{-p}
  \]
  \item For any $\ell\in {{\mathbb N}}_0$ and any $p>m$ there  exists $C=C(p,m,\ell,\mathfrak{a})>0$, independent of $R$,  such that, $\forall R>2$, $\forall {\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}}\in RB$
  \[
  \big\vert\, D^\ell {\boldsymbol{K}}^R_\mathfrak{a}({\boldsymbol{x}}-{\boldsymbol{y}})\,\big\vert \leq\frac{C}{\big(\, 1+|{\boldsymbol{x}}-{\boldsymbol{y}}|_\infty\,\big)^p}.
  \]
  \end{enumerate}

[Definition Edge-rooted unimodularity of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Let $\hat{\mu}$ be a probability measure on decorated edge-rooted graphs.
    Let $(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_-,\mathbf{o}_+))$ be a random edge-weighted decorated graph with law $\hat \mu$. Let $\overset{\rightarrow}{e}_1$ be a uniformly picked directed edge of the form $(\mathbf{o}_+,\mathbf{v})$ for $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{o}_-$. 
    We say that $\hat{\mu}$ is:
    \begin{itemize}
    \item stationary if $(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_-,\mathbf{o}_+))\overset{\mathcal{L}}{=}(\mathbb{G},\overset{\rightarrow}{e}_1)$
    \item revertible if $(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_-,\mathbf{o}_+))\overset{\mathcal{L}}{=}(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_+,\mathbf{o}_-))$ 
    \item unimodular if it is both revertible and stationary.
    \end{itemize}
    The subspace of unimodular laws on edge-rooted graphs will be noted $\mathcal{L}_U(\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{\star})$
title: Edge-rooted unimodularity

[Lemma Kepsilon of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] Let $M\in \mathbb{N}$. \[\|f\|^p_{s,p} \coloneq \int_{[0,1]^2}\frac{\vert f(t)-f(s)\vert_\mathfrak{g} ^p}{\vert t-s\vert ^{1+ps}}\mathrm{d} t\mathrm{d} s\leqslant \frac{12^p}{M^{1-ps}}\sum_{0\leqslant k < l \leqslant M}\frac{\left\vert f(\frac{k}{M})-f(\frac{l}{M})\right\vert^p}{(k-l)^{1+ps}}.\]

[Definition 34 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] (\textbf{Snake-trees, ${\boldsymbol \alpha}$-stable Brownian cactus}) Let $\zeta \ino (0, \infty)$, let $(h,w)\ino \fSigma ([0, \zeta])$ and $d_{h,w} \ino \MMT([0, \zeta])$ be as in Definition~\ref{defsnkme}.

\noi
$(\mathbf a)$ We denote by 
$(T_{h,w}, d_{h,w}, r_{h,w}, \mu_{h,w})$ the pointed measured compact metric space induced by the pseudometric $d_{h,w}$ as defined in (\ref{quotient}). We call it the \textit{snake-tree} associated with $(h,w)$. To simplify, we denote by $p_{h,w}: [0, \zeta] \! \rightarrow \! T_{h,w}$ the canonical projection.

\smallskip

\noi
$(\mathbf b)$ Let $\alpha\ino (1, 2]$ and let $(H, W)$ be a one-dimensional Brownian snake with $\alpha$-stable branching mechanism as defined in Proposition \ref{Holdsnake}. Then the random real tree 
$(T_{H,W}, d_{H,W}, r_{H,W}, \mu_{H,W})$ is called a \emph{Brownian cactus with $\alpha$-stable branching mechanism}.  \cq

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.20714, 'High Minima of Gaussian Processes: Overshoots and Minimizer Locations'] The probability measure
\(\mu\in\cM(K)\) is optimal
if and only if

\[
        k_\mu(t)\ge \mathcal E_R(\mu),
        \qquad t\in K.
\]

Moreover, if \(\mu\) is optimal, then
\[
        k_\mu(t)=\mathcal E_R(\mu),
        \qquad t\in\supp(\mu).
\]

In particular, if \(k_\mu\) is constant on \(K\), then \(\mu\) is
optimal. If, in addition,
\[
        \mathcal E_R(\eta)>0
\]
for every nonzero finite signed measure \(\eta\) on \(K\) satisfying
\(\eta(K)=0\), then the optimal measure is unique.

Consequently, if \(\supp(\mu)=K\), then \(\mu\) is optimal if and only if
\(k_\mu\) is constant on \(K\).

body: [Theorem 3.4 of arXiv:2607.29403, 'Strong invariants and Tverberg numbers in convexity spaces'] Let $(X,\mathcal{C})$ be a convexity space with generator family $\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$. The following are equivalent. 1. $\textup{VC}(\mathcal{C})\leq d$. 2. Every subset of $X$ in convex position has size at most $d$. 3. The comatching number of $\mathcal{C}$ is at most $d$. 4. Every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ has a subfamily $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ of size at most $d$ with $\bigcap\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\bigcap\mathcal{F}$. 5. Every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{G}$ has a subfamily $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ of size at most $d$ with $\bigcap\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\bigcap\mathcal{F}$. 6. Every $(d+1)$ -element set $S\subseteq X$ has a nontrivial partition $S=S_{1}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}S_{2}$ such that $\operatorname{conv}(S_{1})\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(S_{2})$. 7. Every finite $S\subseteq X$ has a subset $S^{\prime}\subseteq S$ of size at most $d$ with $\operatorname{conv}(S^{\prime})=\operatorname{conv}(S)$. 8. Every finite $Y\subseteq X$ has a partition into nonempty blocks $Y=Y_{1}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}\cdots\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}Y_{t}$, each of size at most $d$, such that $\operatorname{conv}(Y_{1})\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(Y_{t}).$ 9. Every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{G}$ has a partition into nonempty blocks $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}_{1}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}\cdots\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}\mathcal{F}_{t}$, each of size at most $d$, such that $\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{t}.$ 10. The same statement as in 9 holds for every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$.

P and Q are probability measures on one measurable space with densities p, q with respect to a sigma-finite measure dominating both; d_TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) - Q(A)| = (1/2) integral |p - q| and H^2(P, Q) = (1/2) integral (sqrt p - sqrt q)^2 = 1 - integral sqrt(pq), so 0 <= H^2 <= 1 and H = sqrt(H^2). Then H^2(P, Q) <= d_TV(P, Q) <= H(P, Q) sqrt(2 - H^2(P, Q)) <= sqrt(2) H(P, Q). The bounds are sharp: mutually singular P, Q give H^2 = d_TV = 1, and the pair P_e = (1/2 + e, 1/2 - e), Q_e = (1/2 - e, 1/2 + e) on two points, 0 < e < 1/2, has d_TV = 2e = H sqrt(2 - H^2) exactly, with d_TV / H -> sqrt(2) as e -> 0.

Method: Fixed-degree random Cayley graphs with optimal spectral gap structural calculation Result: Abelian groups cannot supply even a uniform fixed-degree gap in a basic test case. For arbitrary r generators a_i of Z/pZ, divide the r-dimensional phase cube into M^r boxes with M^r<p. Two of the p points k*(a_1,...,a_r)/p fall in one box. Their nonzero difference k gives a nontrivial character for which all generator phases have distance at most2*pi/M from zero. Hence its adjacency eigenvalue is at least2r-4*pi^2*r/M^2. Check: Use cos(x)>=1-x^2/2 in the eigenvalue2*sum_i cos(2*pi*k*a_i/p). Taking M tending to infinity at order p^(1/r) forces the gap to0, regardless of how the generators were chosen. Obstruction: The argument identifies a structural obstruction to abelian candidates but supplies no optimal bound for the nonabelian special-linear families.

[Corollary cor:LRPexplicit of arXiv:2608.25279, 'Provable Non-Acceleration of Standard Strang\\ Splittings of Kinetic Langevin Dynamics'] Set
\begin{equation}
 h_\star=\frac{2}{\sqrt{26}},\qquad
 \beta_\star=\frac49,\qquad
 \gamma_\star=-\frac1{h_\star}\log\frac49.
\end{equation}
There exist a potential $U\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$1\le U''\le25$ and a constant $C>0$ such that the following holds
for every $R\ge1$. Let
\[
 U_R(x)=R^2U(x/R),
 \qquad
 Q_R=Q_{h_\star,\gamma_\star}^{U_R}.
\]
Then $U_R\in\mathcal U_{25}^1$, $Q_R$ has a unique invariant law $\pi_R$, and at least one of
the two explicit initial states defined in Section~(sec:LRP of the paper),
denoted by $z_R$, satisfies
\begin{equation}
 W_2(\delta_{z_R},\pi_R)\le CR,
 \qquad
 \norm{\delta_{z_R}Q_R^n-\pi_R}_{\mathrm{TV}}\ge\frac38,
 \qquad
 0\le n\le
 \left\lfloor\frac1{16}e^{R^2/8000}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Check which steps of the DGFF proof use only the covariance asymptotics and which use the Gibbs-Markov property of the DGFF specifically. Result: The intermediate-level-set moment calculations (Theorem 2.7) use only the two-point Gaussian densities, which are determined by the covariance asymptotics, plus a coarse Gibbs-Markov decoupling at one scale used to identify the limit as unique; for a general field the decoupling can be replaced by the comparison of the field with the DGFF plus an independent bounded-variance field via Kahane-type interpolation, provided the covariance difference is bounded uniformly. Under the hypothesis (16.12) with an additional uniform bound sup |C_N(x,y) - G_N(x,y)| < infinity this gives the Theorem 2.7 analogue by a Gaussian comparison of the exponential moments. The extremal-process part is harder: the cluster law at the maximum depends on the local covariance limit (16.12) and is model-dependent, so universality can only be of the form: same Poisson structure, model-dependent cluster law and constant, which is what the DRZ maximum result already indicates. Obstruction: Without uniform boundedness of C_N - G_N the interpolation fails; with it, the level-set statement follows but the cluster law remains model-dependent.

[Proposition 16 (Max-plus propagation) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $(\Theta_R)_{R\ge1}$ be a family of $N$-linear operations between fixed

satisfying
\[
 \mathsf M_{\Theta_R}^{(r)}(T;S_1,\ldots,S_N)
 \lesssim
 R^{\delta_{T;\mathbf S}}\log(e+R)^{\eta_{T;\mathbf S}}.

Then
\begin{equation}

 \norm{\Flat_T(\Theta_R(K_1(R),\ldots,K_N(R)))}_{\Sch_r}
 \lesssim R^{\alpha_T}\log(e+R)^{\kappa_T},

    \kappa_{j,S_j}\right).
 
\end{align}

On Q_d, d>=2, adding a perfect matching of new edges has optimal ordinary SRW gap 4/(d+1), uniquely attained by antipodal pairs.
