[Definition defHN of arXiv:2605.10617, 'Logarithmic scaling of selective sweep curves:\\ from tents to houses'] The \emph{logarithmic population sizes} $H^N=(H^N_0,H^N_1)$ are defined by
    $$
      H^N_i(t)
        = \log_N^+\big(X^N_i(\tfrac{t\log N}{\varphi_N})\big),
        \ i\in\{0,1\},
    $$
    where $\log_N^+(\cdot):= \max\{\log_N(\cdot), 0\}$ denotes the positive part of the logarithm to the base $N$.

    Throughout we will assume that $(X_0, X_1)$ satisfies for $t\ge 0$ the Moran dynamics~(equation Morandyn of the paper) with $a>0$ and starting condition $(X_0(0), X_1(0)) = (N-1, 1)$ where selection is moderate  or quasi-strong in the sense of Definition~(def:moderate-selection of the paper).
    With a view towards part II of Theorem~(thm:house of the paper) we extend $X^N$ to the negative time axis by putting $(X_0(t), X_1(t)) = (N,0)$ (and consequently $(H_0^N(t), H_1^N(t)) = (1,0)$) for $t<0$.

    where $w(t) \in H$, with $H$ being the real vector space defined by
    $$H \coloneqq \{w : \mathbb{Z}^2_{\star,N}\to\mathbb{C} \mid w_k = \overline w_{-k} \} \,,$$
    
    and $W^k_t$ are $\mathbb{C}$-valued Brownian motions which are independent except for the reality condition
   $W^k = \overline{W^{-k}}$. Let $H_I \coloneqq \{w \in H \mid  w_k = 0 \text{ for all } k \notin I\}$, where $I \coloneqq \{k \in \mathbb{Z}^2 \mid |k| = 5\}$. Then for all $N$ large enough there are $0 < \nu_* \le \nu^* < \infty$
    (possibly depending on $N$) such that:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item When $\nu < \nu_*$, (equation eq:stoch-navier-stokes of the paper) has multiple invariant measures, at least one of which gives $H_I$ measure $0$. Furthermore, for all $\delta > 0$ there is some $\eta > 0$ such that for all $w(0) \notin H_I$,
        \begin{equation}
            \limsup_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t}|\{s \leq t \mid d(w(s), H_I) < \eta \}| < \delta \quad a.s.\,,
        \end{equation}
        where $|\cdot|$ denotes Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and $d(w,H_I) \coloneqq \inf_{z \in H_I} \|w - z\|$ is the distance from $w$ to $H_I$.
        \item When $\nu > \nu^*$, (equation eq:stoch-navier-stokes of the paper) has a unique invariant measure, and it is supported on $H_I$. Furthermore, almost surely
        $$\limsup_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t}\ln d(w(t),H_I) < 0 \,.$$
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Consider the initial value problem y' = f(t, y), y(t_0) = y_0, with f continuous on a rectangle around (t_0, y_0) and Lipschitz in y uniformly in t there. Then there is an interval around t_0 on which the problem has exactly one solution. Continuity of f alone (Peano) gives existence but not uniqueness: y' = 2 sqrt(|y|), y(0) = 0 has infinitely many solutions.

body:
There is an integer N(n), depending only on the dimension n, with the following property. Let A be a bounded subset of R^n and suppose that to each x in A is assigned a closed ball B(x, r(x)) with r(x) > 0 centred at x. Then one can select from that family countable subfamilies G_1, ..., G_{N(n)}, each consisting of PAIRWISE DISJOINT balls, whose union covers A. Consequence for measures: if mu is a Radon measure on R^n and the balls are a fine cover of a set A, one may extract a countable disjoint subfamily covering mu-almost all of A; this is what makes the differentiation theorem for Radon measures work without any doubling assumption.
Centres must be the points of A themselves (the theorem is FALSE for balls merely containing the points), radii positive and bounded, A bounded.
The constant N(n) depends only on dimension, not on the set or the radii;
unlike the Vitali covering lemma no enlargement of balls is needed and no doubling property of the measure is used.

[Proposition 17 of arXiv:2608.26300, 'Coordinate-Deletion Bundles from Composition Algebras: Hopf Defects, $KO$-Classes, and Rea'] After scalar extension to an algebraic closure $\overline F$, the norm
	$N_D$ is isotropic. Consequently, on a scheme-theoretic overlap
	$U_i\cap U_j$ the divisor
	\[
	N_D(q_j)=0
	\]
	is in general nonempty after scalar extension, and the entries of
	\[
	M(q_j)^{-1}
	=\frac{1}{N_D(q_j)}M(\overline{q_j})
	\]
	are not regular along that divisor. Thus anisotropy on $F$-rational
	points alone does not make the coordinate-deletion cocycle a regular
	$\GL_d$-valued cocycle on the full standard cover of $\PP^d_F$.

On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. Let S(rho) = Stab_rho[f] with f not identically 0, 0 < rho <= 1, and nu_rho(k) = W_k rho^k/S(rho). Then mu(rho) = rho S'(rho)/S(rho) = E_{nu_rho}[K] and rho mu'(rho) = Var_{nu_rho}(K) >= 0, so mu is nondecreasing on (0, 1], strictly iff the weight sits on at least two levels; mu(rho) -> k_min as rho -> 0 and mu(1) = sum_k k W_k / sum_k W_k. With k_min and k_max the least and largest levels carrying weight, a^{k_max} <= S(a rho)/S(rho) <= a^{k_min} for 0 < a <= 1, with equality for some a < 1 iff k_min = k_max; and for fixed 0 < a < 1 the ratio rho -> S(a rho)/S(rho) is nonincreasing, strictly unless one level carries all the weight.

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2609.01996, 'Baumslag--Solitar Subgroups Obstruct Model Companions for Fields with Group Actions'] If \(N\geq1\) is coprime to \(mn\), there is a canonical surjective homomorphism of additive groups
  \[
    \operatorname{red}_N:\Z\left[\frac1{mn}\right]\longrightarrow\Z/N\Z
  \]
  whose kernel is
  \[
    N\Z\left[\frac1{mn}\right].
  \]
  Moreover, if \(S\subseteq\Z[1/(mn)]\) is finite, then \(\operatorname{red}_N\) is injective on \(S\) for all but finitely many primes \(N\) coprime to \(mn\).

body: [Lem 32 of arXiv:2607.27535, 'Universal topological statistics on \\ triangulated singular spaces'] Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots A_6 \in \RR^5$ be points in a general position. Let $K_1, K_2$ be the 2nd (ordered) FK triangulation of the ordered simplices $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$, where $\sigma_i$ are given by $\sigma_1 =(A_1 A_2 A_3 A_4 A_5)$ and $\sigma_2 =(A_2 A_3 A_4 A_1 A_6)$. Then the simplicial complexes $K_1, K_2$ restrict to two different complexes in the 3-simplex $(A_1 A_2 A_3 A_4)$. In other words, $K_1, K_2$ cannot be glued at their common (3-dimensional) face to form a single simplicial complex.

body: [Lemma lem:independence-across-bands-moduli-proof of arXiv:2606.10973, 'Quasisymmetric rigidity of the Brownian sphere'] For each $\alpha > 0$ and $M > 0$, there exists $\lambda_\ast = \lambda_\ast(\alpha, M) \in (0,1)$ such that, for each $\lambda \in (0,\lambda_\ast]$, the following is true. Let $(\BC, \Phi; 0, \infty)$ be a $\sqrt{8/3}$-LQG cone. Let $\{t_j\}_{j \in \BN}$ be a decreasing sequence of positive real numbers such that $t_{j + 1}/t_j \le \lambda$ for every $j \in \BN$. Then, for each finite subset $J \subset \BN$, with probability at least $1 - (\lambda^{\alpha})^{\#J}$, there exists $j \in J$ for which $\Mod(A_{\lambda t_j,t_j}^\bullet(0; D_\Phi)) \ge M$.

body:
[Theorem thm:sech-stability of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] For the canonical kernel:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\roman*), leftmargin=*]
			\item the translates of the profile~(equation eq:sech of the paper) are the only
			steady states of the equation~(equation eq:cdf-equation of the paper) that are
			laws: the secant law is the unique steady probability law of the
			diffusive dynamics, up to translation;
			\item the linearization at the secant law is, in the similarity
			variable $\xi = x/\sqrt D$, the P\"oschl--Teller operator
			\begin{equation}
				\mathcal{L} = \partial_{\xi\xi} - 1 + 2\operatorname{sech}^{2}\xi,
				\qquad
				\operatorname{spec}\mathcal{L} = \{0\}\cup(-\infty, -1],
				
			\end{equation}
			with simple eigenvalue $0$ carried by the translation mode
			$\operatorname{sech}\xi$ and reflectionless essential
			spectrum~[deift1979]: the spectral gap equals $1$ in the
			original time units, for every diffusivity $D$;
			\item the secant law attracts every law whose data approach the
			limits $0,1$ exponentially: there is a limit position $x_{0}$ with
			\begin{equation}
				\big\Vert F(\cdot,t) - F^{*}(\cdot - x_{0})\big\Vert_{\infty}
				\;\le\; C e^{-\mu t},
				
			\end{equation}
			for some $\mu > 0$, and with every rate $\mu < 1$ once the
			solution enters a neighborhood of the front family; the densities
			converge in $L^{1}$, the only memory of the datum being the phase
			$x_{0}$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title:
Uniqueness, spectrum, and stability of the secant
		law

[Def 19 of arXiv:2609.01389, 'K-stability and birational rigidity of Fano 3-fold weighted complete intersections'] For a linear system $\mcM$ on $X$, we denote by $n (\mcM)$ the positive rational number such that $\mcM \sim_{\mbQ} - n (\mcM) K_X$.
Let $\varphi \colon Y \to X$ be an extremal divisorial contraction.
We say that $\varphi$ is a \textit{Sarkisov extraction} if there is a Sarkisov link (in the Mori category) initiated by $\varphi$.
We say that $\varphi$ is a \textit{maximal extraction} if there is a movable linear system $\mcM$ such that $\ord_E (\mcM) > n (\mcM) a_X (E)$.
We say that $\varphi$ is a \textit{strong maximal extraction} if there is a movable linear system $\mcM$ on $X$ such that 
\[
\frac{1}{n (\mcM)} > c (X, \mcM) = \frac{a_X (E)}{\ord_E (\mcM)},
\]
where $c (X, \mcM)$ is the canonical threshold of the pair $(X, \mcM)$.

A subvariety $\Gamma \subset X$ is said to be a \textit{Sarkisov center} (resp.\ \textit{maximal center}, resp.\ \textit{strong maximal center}) if there is a Sarkisov extraction (resp.\ maximal extraction, resp.\ strong maximal extraction) $\varphi \colon Y \to X$ whose center is $\Gamma$.
We say that a subvariety $\Gamma \subset X$ is a \textit{weak maximal center} if there is a movable linear system $\mcM$ on $X$ such that $\Gamma$ is a center of non-canonical singularities of the pair $(X, \frac{1}{n (\mcM)} \mcM)$.
title: Definition 19 of arXiv:2609.01389

[Proposition 36 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ with $\alpha + \beta/2>1$. Suppose for some $\lambda \in [0,1]$ and $K \geq 1$, we have that for all $j \in \N, n \in \{0,1,2\}, p \geq 1$,
    \[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega \mathcal{C}^0_{t,x}} \leq K p^\lambda 2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
    Then for any $N \in \N$, there exists a splitting
    \[\iop^{N} U^N := \sum_{j=0}^N \big(I^{1,j,N} + I^{2,j,N}\big)\]
    such that for all $0< \ep < C(\alpha,\beta)^{-1}$,  there exists $C(\ep,\alpha,\beta,d)>0$ such that for all $p \geq 1$,
    \begin{align}
        \|I^{1,j,N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^0_y L^p_\omega \mathcal{C}^{1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\beta} -\ep}_t \mathcal{C}^{1}_x } &\leq C K p^{\lambda \lor 1/2} 2^{- C^{-1} j}, \\
        \|I^{2,j,N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^0_y L^p_\omega \mathcal{C}^{1-\ep}_t \mathcal{C}^1_x} &\leq C K^{4(\frac{2-\alpha}{\beta} \lor 1)}  p^{((\frac{2-\alpha}{\beta} \lor 1) + \ep) \lambda} 2^{- C^{-1} j},
            \\
            \|I^{1,j,N}\|_{ W^{1,2p}_yL^p_\omega  \mathcal{C}^{1}_t \mathcal{C}^{1}_x } &\leq CK p^\lambda 2^{2j}  \|\nabla \Phi^N\|_{L^{2p}_\omega L^{2p}_y\mathcal{C}^0_t},
            
            \\
            \|I^{2,j,N}\|_{ W^{1,2p}_yL^p_\omega  \mathcal{C}^{1}_t \mathcal{C}^{1}_x } &\leq CK p^\lambda 2^{2j}  \|\nabla \Phi^N\|_{L^{2p}_\omega L^{2p}_y\mathcal{C}^0_t},
                           
    \end{align}
    where $\Phi^N$ is given by~\eqref{eq:truncated ODE flow}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 36 of arXiv:2608.05931

body:
[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.12475, 'Central limit theorem for the homozygosity of the hierarchical Pitman-Yor process'] Under the limiting procedure $\theta_0, \theta \to \infty$ such that $\frac{\theta_0}{\theta} \to c \in (0,\infty)$,
the homozygosity of the HPYP with $L$ groups satisfies
\bal
\tilde{H}_{m,L}(\alpha, \theta_0, \beta, \theta) &= \frac{\sqrt{\theta}}{f(\alpha, \beta, \theta; m, L, c)} \left( H_{m,L}(\alpha, \theta_0, \beta, \theta) - \frac{\sum_{j=1}^m A_j(\beta, m, L) \frac{ \prod_{s=1}^{j-1} (\theta + s\beta) (1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)} }{ \beta^j \theta_0^{j-1}} }{L^m \theta^{m-1}} \right) \\
&\xrightarrow{D} N(0, \sigma_{c,m,L}^2)
\eal
for all $m \geq 2$, where the variance is given by
\bal
&\sigma_{c,m,L}^2 = \sigma_{X,m,L}^2 + \sigma_{T,m,L}^2 + \sigma_{1,m,L}^2 + \sum_{k=1}^L \left( \sum_{\bm{m} \in M_{m,L}} C_{\bm{m}} m_k \right)^2 \\
&- 2\sum_{k=1}^L \left( \frac{ \sum_{j=1}^m \left[\left(\sum_{\bm{m} \in M_{m,L}} \sum_{\bm{j} \in M_{j, L}} (m_k - \beta j_k) \prod_{\ell = 1}^L \Cs(m_\ell, j_\ell, \beta) \right) + \beta j A_j(\beta, m, L) \right] \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}} }{\sum_{j=1}^m A_j(\beta, m, L) \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}}} \right)^2
\eal
where
\bal
\sigma_{1,m,L}^2 &= \frac{\sum_{1 \leq i,j \leq m} \frac{A_i(\beta, m, L)A_j(\beta, m, L)\left[ (1 - \alpha)_{(i+j-1)} + (\alpha - ij)(1 - \alpha)_{(i-1)}(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)} \right]}{\beta^{i+j} c^{i+j-1}}}{\left( \sum_{j=1}^m A_j(\beta, m, L) \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}} \right)^2} \\
\sigma_{T,m,L}^2 &= \beta \frac{ \sum_{1 \leq i,j \leq m} \frac{ A_i(\beta, m, L)A_j(\beta, m, L) (1 - \alpha)_{(i-1)}(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)} }{\beta^{i+j} c^{i+j-2}} \cdot ij}{\left( \sum_{j=1}^m A_j(\beta, m, L) \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}} \right)^2} \\
\sigma_{X,m,L}^2 &= \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{2m} \tilde{A}_j(\beta, m, L) \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}} -  \sum_{1 \leq i,j \leq m} A_i(\beta, m, L) A_j(\beta, m, L)  \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(i+j-1)}}{\beta^{i+j} c^{i+j-1}}  }{\left( \sum_{j=1}^m A_j(\beta, m, L) \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}} \right)^2}
\eal
and the coefficients $\{A_j(\beta, m, L)\}_{1 \leq j \leq m}$, $\{\tilde{A}_j(\beta, m, L)\}_{1 \leq j \leq 2m}$, and $\{C_{\bm{m}}\}_{\bm{m} \in M_{m,L}}$ are defined, respectively, as
\bal
A_j(\beta, m, L) &= \sum_{\bm{m} \in M_{m,L}} \sum_{\bm{j} \in M_{j,L}} \prod_{k=1}^L \Cs(m_k,j_k,\beta) \\
\tilde{A}_j(\beta, m, L) &= \sum_{\bm{m}_1 \in M_{m,L}} \sum_{\bm{m}_2 \in M_{m,L}} \sum_{\bm{j} \in M_{j,L}} \prod_{k=1}^L \Cs(m_{1k} + m_{2k}, j_k, \beta) \\
C_{\bm{m}} &= \frac{\sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{\bm{j} \in M_{j,L}} \prod_{\ell = 1}^L \Cs(m_\ell, j_\ell, \beta) \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}}}{\sum_{j=1}^m A_j(\beta, m, L) \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}}{\beta^j c^{j-1}}}.
\eal (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Prop 26 of arXiv:2608.28148, 'Flows and homotopies of Banach Lie algebroids'] Let $(A,\pi,M,\rho,\LB_A)$ be a Banach Lie algebroid which satisfies Assumption {\rm \textbf{(H)}}. For $k\geq 2$ fix a $C^k$-map $\g\colon [0,1]^2 \rightarrow M$ together with $J:=[-\eta,1+\eta]$ and an extension $\hat{\g}\colon [0,1] \times J \rightarrow M$ as in \Cref{timedepend}.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item For $s \in [0,1]$ there is $\delta_s >0$ and an open neighborhood $\mathcal{W}_s\subseteq J \times M$ of the graph of $\hat{\g}_\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon\in I_s := [0,1] \cap [s-\delta_s,s+\delta_s]$.
 
 Then for every  $C^\ell$-map ${c}\colon [0,1]^2\to A$, $\ell \leq k$, with $\g=\pi\circ c$, there is $C^{\ell,\infty}$-map ${\mathfrak{u}^s} \colon I_s \times \mathcal{W}_s \rightarrow A$, such that $\pi \circ \mathfrak{u}^s(\varepsilon , t,y)=y$ and  $\mathfrak{u} (\varepsilon, t,\g_\varepsilon(t))=c_\varepsilon(t)$ for $(\varepsilon, t)\in I_s \times [0,1]$.
 
 Further, we can choose $\mathfrak{u}_\varepsilon$ constant on $\left(\left([-\eta, -\frac{\eta}{2}] \cup [1+\frac{\eta}{2},1+\eta]\right) \times M\right) \cap \mathcal{W}_s$. If $c_\varepsilon(0)=0$ (or $c_\varepsilon(1)=0$) for $\varepsilon\in I_s$, then also ${\mathfrak{u}_\varepsilon}(0)=0$ (or $
  {\mathfrak{u}_\varepsilon}(1)=0$).
 \item  If $M$ is smoothly paracompact, the section $\mathfrak{u}$ can be defined on $[0,1] \times J\times M$.
  \end{enumerate}

body: [Defn 2 (Fat Tree) of arXiv:2604.26499, 'Spectrum of Random Matrices with Exploding Moments'] A directed graph $T=(V, E)$ is called a fat tree if it is a connected graph without loops and all the edges have multiplicity more than one. Additionally, the underlying simple graph $\mathcal{T}=(V, \mathcal{E}),$ obtained by ignoring orientation and multiplicity satisfies $|V|=|\mathcal{E}|+1$.
title: Fat Tree

body: [Lem edge-concentration of arXiv:2606.01627, 'The geometry of the giant component of random geometric graphs'] Let $M$ be a connected compact $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold of volume $1$.  For each $n$ let $G_M^n(r)$ be the Poisson random geometric graph with expected average degree $\Delta \in [1,n/2]$.  Then for each $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $c = c(\varepsilon,M) > 0$ so that if $e(G_M^n(r))$ is the number of edges in $G_M^n(r)$ then $$\mathbb{P}\left(\left| e(G_M^n(r)) - n\Delta/2 \right| > \varepsilon n\Delta \right) \leq \exp\left(-c \log^2 n \right)\,.$$
title: Lem edge-concentration of arXiv:2606.01627

body:
[Theorem 8 (Verification under measure superharmonicity) of arXiv:2606.17517, 'Killed resolvents and measure-valued stopping gains for reflected optimal stopping with ma'] Let $u:\R^2_+\to\R$ be continuous and of polynomial growth. Assume:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(V1)}] $u\ge G$ on $\R^2_+$.
\item[\textup{(V2)}] $u=G$ on $\R^2_+\setminus\mathcal O$.
\item[\textup{(V3)}] For some $p>2$, $u\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal O)$,
and $(\mathcal L-r)u-c=0$ a.e.\ in $\mathcal O$.
\item[\textup{(V4)}] On $\interior{\R}^2_+$, the distribution
$(\mathcal L-r)u-c$ extends to a signed Radon measure $\mu_u$ satisfying
$\mu_u\le0$ in the sense of measures; equivalently, for every nonnegative
$\phi\in C_c^\infty(\interior{\R}^2_+)$,
$\langle(\mathcal L-r)u-c,\phi\rangle\le0$.
\item[\textup{(V5)}] $u$ belongs to the generalized It\^o class of
Definition~\ref{def:generalized-ito-class}, and the reflected boundary
contribution is nonpositive in the supermartingale calculation. In particular,
this holds if $u$ satisfies the normal-reflection condition $\partial_i u=0$
on $\{x_i=0\}$, $i=1,2$, in the relevant trace sense.
\item[\textup{(V6)}] The localization and uniform-integrability conditions
needed to take expectations and pass to the limit hold for $u(X)$, $G(X)$,
$c(X)$, and the additive functional $A^{\mu_u}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $u\ge V$ on $\R^2_+$. If, in addition, $\tau_{\mathcal O^c}<\infty$
$\mathbb P_x$-a.s.\ for every $x$, and the stopped It\^o formula is exact on
$[0,\tau_{\mathcal O^c}]$, then $u=V$ on $\R^2_+$ and $\tau_{\mathcal O^c}$ is
optimal.

DRAFT; independent check by w395 pending. On nearest-neighbor Z^2 with finite strictly positive edge weights, let S_R={x: ||x||_infinity=R}. Let E_R mean some globally minimizing finite simple path between distinct vertices of S_R passes through 0. First-exit truncation makes E_R decreasing. An infinite branch of the finite sets of oriented simple witnesses truncated inside [-R,R]^2 shows that intersection_R E_R is exactly existence of a bigeodesic through 0. For a stationary random law, absence everywhere follows if P(E_R) tends to zero. Equation (4.25) of Auffinger-Damron-Hanson, arXiv:1511.03262, already uses this boundary-pair reduction; no novelty is asserted. This global event need not be measurable from inside edges alone at fixed R.
Nearest-neighbor undirected Z^2
Finite strictly positive weights
Global path minimization; simple paths
Stationarity only for the final everywhere-absence consequence

Then, for every fixed  $T>0$ and every $\delta>0$,
\[

        >\delta
    \right)
    =
    0.
\]
In particular, as $\varepsilon\to 0$,
\[

    \quad\text{in probability}.
\]

[Thm T_UB of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] Fix a graph $H$, with $\rho=\rho(H)>1$. 
If $\rho$ is rational, let $a/b$ be its expression as an irreducible fraction. 
If $\rho$ is irrational, let $b$ be arbitrarily large.  
Suppose that $np^\rho=A\log^{2+2/b} n$.
Then, for large enough $A$, with high probability, we have that 
$\langle\mathcal{G}_{n,p} \rangle_H=K_n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary 66 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let $X$ be a Noetherian scheme such that every closed point of $X$ is contained in the closed fiber $X_{\F_p}$.
If $X$ is lim-perfectoid split, then \(X_{\F_p}\) is HT-split.

In particular, if $X$ is smooth and projective over $W(k)$ for a perfect field $k$ of characteristic $p$, then for every ample line bundle $L$ on $X$, we have
\[
H^i_{(p)}(X,\Omega^j_{X/W(k)} \otimes L^{-1})=0 \quad (i+j<\dim X).
\]

body:
[Theorem 22 of arXiv:2605.25715, '2605.25715'] [Explicit construction]
Let $A \in M_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ be symmetric and positive definite.
Let $G \in M_{d}(\mathbb{R})$. Let $\sigma(G) = \{ \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d \} \subset \mathbb{C}$ be the set of eigenvalues of $G$ counting multiplicities. Assume that
\begin{equation*}
    \lambda_i + \lambda_j \neq 0 \quad \text{for all } 1 \leq i, j \leq d.
\end{equation*}
Then, there exists a $d\times d$ symmetric and invertible matrix $S$ such that \eqref{SOHHDlinalg1} holds. In particular, $S$ is explicitly given by
\[
S = (-P)^{-1},
\]
where $P$ is determined by the vectorized equation \eqref{vectorialmap}.
Moreover, 
$$
\mu=\exp\left( \langle Sx, x \rangle  \right) dx
$$
is an infinitesimally invariant measure for $\left(\frac12 \mathrm{trace}(A \nabla^2) + \langle Gx,\nabla \rangle,\; C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d)\right)$ and
$$
\tilde Gx=Sx+(G-AS)x
$$
is in fact a SOHHD for $\tilde G x$.

[Definition 40 (Batch-size exponent) of arXiv:2609.02728, 'Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improv'] For a sequence of training problems with \(D\to\infty\), the batch size has exponent \(b\in[0,1)\) if
\[
B=D^{b+o(1)},
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
b=\lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\log B}{\log D}.
\]
title: Batch-size exponent

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] An exponential variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ experiences loss of memory:
$$P(f>s+t|f>s)=P(f>t)\quad,\quad\forall s,t>0$$
Conversely, the only continuous variables having this property are the exponential ones.

[Theorem 32 of arXiv:2609.02785, 'Characterization of Stanley-Reisner varieties by their automorphism group'] Let $\Delta$ be a simplicial complex on $[n]$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item The standard torus $T_0=(\KK^*)^n$ embeds into $\Aut(X_\Delta)$ as a closed algebraic subgroup.
\item Every algebraic torus $D\subseteq\Aut(X_\Delta)$ satisfies $\dim D\leq n$.
\item Every algebraic torus of dimension $n$ in $\Aut(X_\Delta)$ is conjugate to $T_0$.
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition prop:pn-tree-properties of arXiv:2607.24018, 'Jeu de taquin forests \\ and the inverse infinite RSK correspondence'] The trees of $\Phi(T)$ satisfy:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(T\arabic*)]
		\item 
		Each tree $\tau$ in $\Phi(T)$ has an asymptotic direction
		\[ z_{\tau} := \alpha_\textnormal{asym}(\tau)  \in [0,1]. \]
		
		\item 
		Distinct trees have distinct asymptotic directions.
		
		\item 
		The set of asymptotic directions of the trees coincides with
		the set of inverse-RSK values:
		\begin{equation}
			
			\{z_{\tau} : \tau \text{ a tree in } \Phi(T)\}
			= \{z_n : n \geq 1\}.
		\end{equation}

		\item 
		The set
		$\{z_{\tau} : \tau \text{ a tree in } \Phi(T)\}$ is dense in
		$[0,1]$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Asymptotic directions for all jeu de taquin forest trees

[Lemma of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] Assume that \(\lambda<\mu^*\).
There exists \(r>1\) such that the function
\[
V(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N r^{x_i}, \qquad x\in\mathbb N^N,
\]
satisfies the Foster--Lyapunov drift condition
\[
\mathcal LV(x)\leq \mathcal L^{FB}V(x)\leq -cV(x)+b\mathbf 1_C(x),
\]
for some constants \(c,b>0\) and some finite set \(C\subset \mathbb N^N\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Critical window for fixed-outdegree preferential attachment structural reduction Result: Local weak convergence alone cannot determine macroscopic cluster sizes. A single cycle on n vertices and a disjoint union of cycles whose lengths are about sqrt(n) have the same local weak limit, the two-sided infinite path, but their largest components have orders n and sqrt(n). Check: For every fixed radius r, once each cycle length exceeds2r+1 all rooted radius-r neighborhoods are identical. Their total component sizes remain explicitly different. Obstruction: This prevents deriving the critical window from the Polya-point local limit alone. A growing-scale exploration argument must retain age and fixed-outdegree dependencies.

body:
[Corollary ribbon tiling slope of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] Let $ X \subset \mathcal{A}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ be a strongly irreducible subshift for $ d \geq 2$. Let $G = G_1\times G_2\times\cdots\times G_r$, where each $G_i$ is a hyperbolic group with the CIC property and $ c: X \times \mathbb{Z}^d \rightarrow G$ is a cocycle with respect to the subgroup $W \leq \mathbb{Z}^d$ of finite index. Then there exists a homomorphism $ \theta: W \rightarrow G$ and a constant $ C$ such that for all $ x \in X\text{ and } w \in W$, there exist $h_1= h_1(x, w)$ and $h_2 = h_2(x, w)$ with $ \max(|h_1|, |h_2|) \leq C$ such that
   $$c(x, w ) = h_1 \theta(w) h_2.$$

[Theorem 20 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] There is a unique probability law \(Q\) on \(\mathcal X\) whose marginal on
every finite nonempty \(T\subset\mathbb D\) is \(\mu^T\) from
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-dimensional-entrance-law}.  For every sequence
satisfying \eqref{eq:wall-parameter-limit}, the laws \((Q_n)\) are tight in
\(\mathcal X\) and converge weakly to \(Q\).  The convergence is uniform in
the sequential sense over all dyadic, grid-aligned parameters.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  Q\bigl(f(0)=0,\ f(t)\leq0\text{ for every }t\in\mathbb R\bigr)=1.
  
\end{equation}

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2609.03282, 'Characteristic-free characterizations of projective space for smooth toric varieties'] In the above setting, assume $m<n$. For $1\leq q\leq m$ and $J\subset\Sigma(1)$ with $|J|=m-q$, one has
\[
H^q\bigl(X,\cO_X(D_J-D)\bigr)=0.
\]
Consequently, $H^q(X,\cK_q)=0$ for $1\leq q\leq m$.

[Proposition propexplog of arXiv:2411.06827, 'The Exponential Lie Series and a Chen--Strichartz Formula for L{\'e}vy Processes'] The degree $n$ component $y_n$ of the logarithm $\log^\ast(\exp(x))$ in $\widehat{GL(x)}$ is an element of the completion of the free pre-Lie algebra $PL(x)$ given by
$$
	y_n=\sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{j_1+\cdots + j_k=n} \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k}x^{j_1} * \cdots  * x^{j_k}.
$$
Therefore, we also have
$$
	\nu(y_n)=\bar\mu((\bar i^{(n)})^0)=V_{i^{(n)}}.
$$ 
In particular, we see that $V_{i^{(n)}}$ is a vector field. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition propexplog of arXiv:2411.06827

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Borel-Cantelli over the Hermitisation: identify which estimate is only in probability. Result: The proof of Theorem 6.2 has three inputs: (i) convergence of the singular-value distributions of n^{-1/alpha}X - z for each z, which is almost sure by the objective method (the local weak convergence to the PWIT holds a.s.); (ii) uniform integrability of log at infinity, a.s. from moment bounds; (iii) uniform integrability of log near zero, i.e. a lower bound on the small singular values, which is where only an in-probability bound s_n(n^{-1/alpha}X - z) >= n^{-c} with probability 1 - o(1) is available. To make (iii) almost sure one needs the failure probability summable in n, i.e. a bound like P(s_n <= n^{-c}) <= n^{-1-eps}. For heavy tails the row norms are not concentrated and the Rudelson-Vershynin small-ball argument gives only polynomial failure probabilities with exponent that is not obviously above 1. If the failure probability were shown to be O(n^{-1-eps}) (for instance via an Esseen-type anti-concentration in the alpha-stable domain, which gives exponent depending on alpha), Borel-Cantelli finishes the a.s. statement. So the problem reduces to a quantitative smallest-singular-value bound for heavy-tailed matrices with summable failure probability; the bound is plausible but I did not prove it. Obstruction: Need P(s_n(n^{-1/alpha}X - z) <= n^{-c}) summable in n for heavy-tailed entries.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0031-almost-sure-convergence-in-the-heavy-tailed-circular-law
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

[Definition 67 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] Given $(\md,q,\omega,L)$ as above, and a point $w_0$ satisfying the properties in \Cref{def:w0},
          we define two subsets $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \overline{\mathfrak{X}}$ and $\mathcal{Y}^- \subseteq \overline{\mathfrak{X}}$ as follows. Set
   	\begin{flalign}
          & \mathcal{Y} = \big\{ z \in \overline{\mathfrak{X}} : \dist_{\bm{v}_{w_0}} (z, w_0) \le L^2 (\mathfrak{d}_{w_0} \mathfrak{e}_{w_0;q})^{1/2}, \dist_{\bm{w}_{w_0}} (z, w_0) \le L^5 \mathfrak{d}_{w_0} \mathfrak{e}_{w_0;q} \big\}, \qquad \text{if $\bd = \mathfrak{d}$}; \\
          & \mathcal{Y} = \big\{ z \in \overline{\mathfrak{X}} :
          \dist_{\bm{v}_{w_0}} (z, w_0) \le L^2 N^{B\delta} \bd,\mathfrak{d}_z^2 \le L^5 N^{2B\delta} \bd^2
          \}, \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad
            \text{otherwise}.
            
	\end{flalign} 

        
	\noindent Then define $\mathcal{Y}^- \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$ by 
	\begin{flalign*}
		& \mathcal{Y}^- = (1/L) \cdot (\mathcal{Y} - w_0) + w_0, \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \text{if $\bm{d} = \mathfrak{d}$}; \\
		& \mathcal{Y}^- = \big\{ z \in \overline{\mathfrak{X}} :
		\dist_{\bm{v}_{w_0}} (z, w_0) \le L \bd,\mathfrak{d}_z^2 \le L^4 \bd^2
		\}, \qquad 	\text{otherwise}.
              \end{flalign*}
title: Definition 67 of arXiv:2605.26664

body: In mathematics, particularly in differential topology, there are two Whitney embedding theorems, named after Hassler Whitney:The strong Whitney embedding theorem states that any smooth real m-dimensional manifold can be smoothly embedded in the real 2m-space, ⁠⁠ if m > 0. This is the best linear bound on the smallest-dimensional Euclidean space that all m-dimensional manifolds embed in, as the real projective spaces of dimension m cannot be embedded into real (2m − 1)-space if m is a power of two. The weak Whitney embedding theorem states that any continuous function from an n-dimensional manifold to an m-dimensional manifold may be approximated by a smooth embedding provided m > 2n. Whitney similarly proved that such a map could be approximated by an immersion provided m > 2n − 1. This last result is sometimes called the Whitney immersion theorem.
title: Whitney embedding theorem

[Theorem 12 (Probability-generating function) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The \textsc{pgf} of $T_{m,p}$ is
  \[
    G_{T_{m,p}}(z)
    \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty \PP \left(T_{m,p} = n\right) z^n
    = \left[
        \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \binom{m-m/z}{\ell}
        (-1)^\ell
        \left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right)^\ell
      \right]^{-1}.
  \]
  As an analytic expression,
  both sides agree on an open ball around the origin
  with radius (strictly) greater than $1$,
  upon defining $G_{T_{m,p}}(0)$ by its limit $0$.
  \begin{proof}
    By Proposition \ref{thm:concatenation}, Remark \ref{rem:lgf is pgf},
    Lemma \ref{thm:H ogf} and Lemma \ref{thm:G ogf},
    \begin{align*}
      G_{T_{m,p}}(z) =
      \phi_J(z) = \frac{\phi_H(z)}{\phi_G(z)}
      &= \left(1-p\right)^m \binom{m/z - 1}{m}^{-1}
        \left[\sum_{\ell=0}^m \binom{m}{\ell} 
        \binom{m/z-1}{\ell}^{-1} \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1} \\
      &= \left(1-p\right)^m
        \left[ \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \binom{m/z - 1}{m}
        \binom{m}{\ell} 
        \binom{m/z-1}{\ell}^{-1} \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1} \\
      &= (1-p)^m
        \left[
        \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \frac{\left(m/z-1\right)^{\underline{m}} m^{\underline{\ell}}
        }{
          m! \left(m/z-1\right)^{\underline{\ell}}}
          \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1}\\
      &= (1-p)^m
        \left[
        \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \binom{m/z - \ell - 1}{m - \ell}
        \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1}.
    \end{align*}
    Reverse the summation order via $\ell \mapsto m - \ell$
    then use $\binom{-\nu}{\ell} = (-1)^\ell \binom{\nu + \ell - 1}{\ell}$.
    This concludes the formal result.

    Let $E_k$ be the event that coupons
    $1, 2, \dots, m$ are collected on
    the days $k\,m + 1, k\,m+ 2, \dots, k\,m + m$ respectively.
    Then $\{ E_k \}_{k \geqslant 0}$ is a collection of
    independent events, each with positive probability $q = ((1-p)/m)^m$.
    The random variable $G = \inf_{k \geqslant 0} \1_{E_k}$
    is geometric with parameter $q$ and thus
    \[
      \PP(T_{m, p} = n) \leq \PP(T_{m, p} \geq n)
      \leq \PP(m\,G + m \geq n)
      = (1-q)^{\left\lceil\frac{n-m}{m}\right\rceil}.
    \]
    The radius of convergence is no less than $(1-q)^{-1/m} > 1$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Probability-generating function

Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Assuming stationary-density concentration at rho, the lower bound at every t<(rho-epsilon)N follows immediately and sharply from the particle-count test. Starting empty, S_t<=t deterministically. For A={S>(rho-epsilon/2)N}, the time-t law gives probability zero whereas stationarity gives probability tending to one. Therefore the total-variation distance tends to one. This reduces the unresolved direction to forgetting the configuration just above rho*N. Check: The TV lower bound is the difference of probabilities of the single event A, with the intermediate threshold strictly between t/N and rho. No spectral approximation or mixing definition change occurs. Obstruction: Need the matching upper bound after (rho+epsilon)N additions, including spatial activation coverage or a successful coupling. A small relaxation time and the density lower bound do not by themselves prove this upper bound.

body: [Definition \bf Acyclic and cyclic vertex of arXiv:2603.28936, 'Composition of random functions and word reconstruction'] A vertex $x\in [n]$ is \emph{$w$-acyclic} (or just \emph{acyclic} if $w$ is clear from the context) if $B_{w^2}(x)$ is a rooted directed tree, and it is \emph{$w$-cyclic} (or just \emph{cyclic}) otherwise. We denote by $\mathcal{T}_n=\mathcal{T}_n^w$ the (random) set of acyclic vertices and by $\mathcal{C}_n=\mathcal{C}_n^w$ the (random) set of cyclic ones.

body:
[Lemma asymptotics of arXiv:2609.02871, 'Estimating the number of real zeros of linear combinations of radicals of polynomials'] Let $\beta>-\frac{1}{2}$ and let $d\mu$ be the length measure on $\partial \mathbb{D}$. Then
\begin{itemize}
    \item  \begin{equation} 
u(z)
:= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}
\left(\frac{|z-\zeta|^2}{1-|z|^2}\right)^{\beta} \, d\mu(\zeta)
\end{equation}
is the unique radial solution to $\Delta_\mathbb{D} u-\beta(\beta+1)u = 0$ in $\mathbb{D}$ such that $u(0)=1$. As $|z|\to 1-$ the function $u$ has the following asymptotic properties (for $\beta > -1/2$):
\[
u(z)
= C_1(\beta)\,(1 - |z|^2)^{-\beta}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr),
\]
where $C_1(\beta)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}
|1-\zeta|^{2\beta} \, d\mu(\zeta)$ is a positive numerical constant.
   
    \item A function 
    \begin{equation} 
    g(z)= g(|z|)= \frac{u(|z|)}{2\pi}\int
    \limits_{|z|}^{1}\frac{1}{u^2(r)r}dr
    \end{equation}
      is radial fundamental solution to
    $\Delta_\mathbb{D} g+\lambda g = -\delta_0$
    in $\mathbb{D}$ (see (equation eq:distributions of the paper) in Appendix for the precise meaning).  As $|z|\to +0$ $$g(z)= \frac{-\log|z|}{2\pi}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr)$$
    and as $|z|\to 1-$ 
\[
g(z)
= C_2(\beta)\,(1 - |z|^2)^{\beta+1}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr), \quad C_2(\beta) >0.
\]
    
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma asymptotics of arXiv:2609.02871

[Lem technical facts about G of arXiv:2605.05631, 'Wandering Exponents and the Free Energy of the High-Dimensional Elastic Polymer'] Fix $t>0$ and $x\in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\mathbb{G}_{x,t}(\mu)$ is a negative, increasing, strictly concave function of $\mu\in (0,\infty)$. This function and its derivative have 
				\[\lim_{\mu \to \infty}\mathbb{G}_{x,t}(\mu)=\lim_{\mu \to \infty}\mathbb{G}_{x,t}'(\mu)=0,\]
				\[\lim_{\mu\to 0}\mathbb{G}_{x,t}(\mu)=-\frac{|x|}{2}, \;\;\;\;\;\lim_{\mu\to 0}\left(\mathbb{G}_{x,t}'(\mu)-\frac{x^2}{8\sqrt{\mu t^3}}\right)=-\frac{|x|^3}{12t^2}.\]
				In particular, for $t,x\in (0,\infty)$, the function $\mathbb{G}_{x,t}(\mu)$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$, while $\mathbb{G}_{x,t}'(\mu)=O(\mu^{-1/2})$ as $\mu \to 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem technical facts about G of arXiv:2605.05631

[Thm 7 of arXiv:2604.24624, 'Limit distributions of the threshold radius for the maximum degree and the associated poin'] Under the assumptions of Theorems \ref{MainResult.02} and \ref{MainResult.03}, assume also that $(r_n)_{n \in \BN}$ is chosen so that $E[\sum_{j=k_n}^\infty W_{j,n}'] \to \beta \in (0,\infty)$ and $n\theta r_n^d = o(k_n)$.
    Then, in the uniform case, $\Phi_{k_n,n}$ converges in distribution, with respect to the vague topology, to a Poisson point process $\CQ$ with intensity measure $\beta \text{Leb}(\cdot \cap [-1/2,1/2]^d)$.
    In the non-uniform case, $D_{k_n^{1/(2m)}}\Phi_{k_n,n}$ converges in distribution, with respect to the vague topology, to a Poisson point process $\CQ$ with intensity measure $\Lambda(B) = \beta \gamma^{-1} \int_B \exp(\partial^{2m}f(\bm{0})[z]/((2m)!)) \,dz$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
What the lemma says: $f\in L^1$ implies $\hat f(n)\to0$ (on $\mathbb T$) or $\hat f(\xi)\to0$ as $|\xi|\to\infty$ (on $\mathbb R^d$), with $\hat f$ continuous and bounded by $\|f\|_1$. What it does not say. (i) No rate is implied: for every even sequence $(a_n)$ of nonnegative reals with $a_n\to0$ that is convex for $n\ge1$ ($a_{n-1}+a_{n+1}-2a_n\ge0$), there is a nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ with $\hat f(n)=a_n$ for all $n$; taking $a_n=1/\log(|n|+e)$ shows the decay can be as slow as one likes. So an estimate like $|\hat f(n)|\le Cn^{-\alpha}$ must come from extra regularity: e.g. $\alpha$-Holder continuity gives $|\hat f(n)|\le\frac{C}{2}(2|n|)^{-\alpha}$ via $\hat f(n)=\frac12\int(f(x)-f(x+\tfrac1{2n}))e^{-2\pi inx}dx$, and bounded variation gives $|\hat f(n)|\le V(f)/(2\pi|n|)$. (ii) The converse fails: not every null sequence is the sequence of Fourier coefficients of an $L^1$ function. For odd $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ with sine coefficients $b_n$, the series $\sum_nb_n/n$ must converge; since $\sum_{n\ge2}\frac1{n\log n}=\infty$, the everywhere-convergent series $\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\sin(2\pi nx)}{\log n}$ is not the Fourier series of any integrable function. (iii) Consequently 'the coefficients tend to 0' is never evidence that a given trigonometric series is a Fourier series, and never by itself a convergence statement.

claims about rates require stated regularity of f

	$I = I(x): \mathbb{R} \rightarrow [0,\infty]$ and the normalizing function
	$\psi(T)$, such that $\lim\limits_{T\rightarrow\infty}\psi(T) = \infty$,
	if the following equality holds for any  $x \in  \mathbb{R}$,
	$$
	\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\limsup_{T\rightarrow \infty}\frac{1}{\psi(T)}
	\ln\mathbf{P}(\xi_T(1)\in U_\varepsilon(x))
	=\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\liminf_{T\rightarrow \infty}\frac{1}{\psi(T)}
	\ln\mathbf{P}(\xi_T(1)\in U_\varepsilon(x))=-I(x),
	$$
	where
	$
	U_\varepsilon(x):=\{y\in \mathbb{R}: \ |x-y|<\varepsilon\}.
	$

[Definition def:Omegai of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] For a transposition $\tau_{ij} = (i\,j)$ with $1 \le i < j \le n$, define the
associated direction set
\[
  \Omega_{ij}
  :=
  \Bigl\{
    \eta = \tau_{ij} h :
    h \in S_{[n]\setminus\{i,j\}},
    \text{ and every cycle of } h \text{ has odd length}
  \Bigr\},
\]
where
\[
  S_{[n]\setminus\{i,j\}}
  :=
  \bigl\{\, h \in S_n : h(i)=i,\ h(j)=j \,\bigr\}
  \cong S_{n-2}.
\]
A permutation $\eta \in S_n$ is called \emph{shiftable} if
$\eta \in \Omega_{ij}$ for some $1 \le i < j \le n$. A direction law $q$ on $S_n$
is called shiftable if its support is contained in
\[
  \Omega := \bigcup_{1 \le i < j \le n} \Omega_{ij}.
\]
title: Shiftable directions

Own-work research draft; status proof (unaudited), independent review and novelty assessment pending. Let k>=2, D>=1, F:[0,1]^k -> R^D extend C2 to a neighborhood of the cube, sup ||DF||_op<=L, sup ||D2F||_bilinear<=M, and let f>=0 integrate to one with Euclidean Lipschitz constant <=H. Define beta=2/(2k-1), C=L*(sqrt(k-1)+sqrt(k))/2+L*H/4+M/8 and K=8*C+L*sqrt(k). For every N>=1 there is a continuous N-piece affine generator of one-dimensional uniform noise with W1 error <=K*N^(-beta) to F_#(f dx). Use n^(2(k-1)) transverse rows spaced n^(-2), n chords per row, and positive-time connectors; zero-mass chords are omitted. For an (a,b)-bi-Lipschitz C2 chart, uniform surface law is covered with L=b and H=k*b^(k-1)*M/a^k through the area Jacobian. On F_k(x)=(x,|x|^2), b_k=sqrt(1+4k), A_k=8^k+2^k*sqrt(2*(1+8*sqrt(k))). Uniform parameter law has error >=(1/2)*(2*A_k*N)^(-beta); uniform surface law has the same bound with A_k replaced by b_k*A_k. Both have matching upper exponent beta. Thus the suggested universal curved-image exponent 2/(k+1) fails when k>2, although it agrees at k=2. This is a worst-case rate for the stated controlled C2/Lipschitz-density class, not a lower bound for every image. Merely upper/lower bounded densities are not covered by the upper construction, and no claim of originality or sharp unrestricted-deep rate is made.
k>=2; C2 chart with finite uniform derivative bounds L,M; nonnegative probability density with finite Lipschitz constant H; scalar uniform source; all positive-time connectors counted. Surface law additionally requires a>0 bi-Lipschitz chart.

\[
(X_1,D_1)

Then the pair
\[
\left(

is log HT-split.

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] A stochastic process $(X_{g})_{g \in G}$ is \textbf{$k$-dependent} if for any subsets $ A, B \subset V$ with $d(A, B) > k$, the restrictions $X_{A} = (X_g)_{g \in A}$ and $X_B = (X_g)_{g \in B}$ are independent. A process $(X_g)_{g \in G}$ is \textbf{finitely dependent} if it is $k$-dependent for some $k \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'

[Own-work draft: T407-WEDGE-008 v2, proof (unaudited); not independently checked; priority unestablished.] For independent Gaussian a,b in R^d and wedges where sign((exp(tG)a) dot b) differs from sign(a dot b), a coordinate-plane tangent has probability c_d t+o(t), c_d=Gamma(d/2)/(2sqrt(pi)Gamma((d+1)/2)). For d>=3 the distinct orthogonal tangents G12,G13 have pair intersection (1-1/sqrt(2))c_d t+o(t); for d>=4 the disjoint-coordinate tangents G12,G34 have intersection (c_d/4)t+o(t). Thus their overlaps are Theta_d(t), not O_d(t^2). In d=2 a single rotation wedge has probability t/pi exactly, but there is only one tangent direction. In d=4 the disjoint-plane intersection is exactly cot(t/2)[1-(t/2)cot(t/2)]/pi for 0<t<pi, with small-t coefficient 1/(6pi). These are coordinate-route obstruction results, not a sample-complexity lower theorem.
Fixed integer d>=3 or d>=4 as specified, t downarrow0, noiseless bilinear Gaussian classifiers; standard coordinate-plane generators with unit operator norm; no dimension-uniform remainder asserted.
For the exact d4 formula additionally 0<t<pi.
No independent reviewer PASS has been received.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:38196447624834cd27390838109fb9fda0f3887f3c2188a08c3b5c0a58eae29b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/38/38196447624834cd27390838109fb9fda0f3887f3c2188a08c3b5c0a58eae29b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:415d1aa5a7951d740e65355b7715963d1b626a19fd4d0b33d34d2aea6b4a167c","bundle_entry_key":"gaussian-bilinear-tangent-overlap","bundle_id":"population.t407-draft-gaussian-tangent-wedge-overlap","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning theory","draft":"w693/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.sample_complexity:draft-gaussian-bilinear-tangent-wedges-linear-overlap","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Definitions and exact Gaussian identity


Let a,b be independent N(0,I_d). Put h_0(a,b)=sign(a dot b), h_i(t)(a,b)=sign((R_i(t)a) dot b), with R_i(t)=exp(t G_i) and G_i skew-symmetric. These are members of {sign(a^T U b): U in O(d)} because U=R_i(t)^T. Let W_i(t)={h_i(t)!=h_0}. The sign convention at zero is immaterial: each relevant nonzero linear form in b has zero Gaussian probability of vanishing, for a!=0, and a=0 is null.

For any two nonzero deterministic normals v,w and standard Gaussian b,
  P_b(sign(v dot b)!=sign(w dot b))=angle(v,w)/pi.
Proof: project b to the plane of the normals. Its angle is uniform on a circle; the two disagreement sectors have total angle 2 angle(v,w). Divide by 2pi. Collinear cases have angle zero or pi and satisfy the same identity.

Consequently, with u=a/||a|| uniform on S^(d-1),
  P(W_i(t))=E_u angle(u,R_i(t)u)/pi.
For ANY three binary classifiers, pointwise
  1_(W_1 intersection W_2)=(1_(W_1)+1_(W_2)-1_(h_1!=h_2))/2.
If exactly one wedge occurs, the last disagreement indicator is one; if both occur, h_1=h_2 is opposite to h_0; if neither occurs, all agree. Therefore
  P(W_1 intersection W_2)
   =E_u[angle(u,R_1u)+angle(u,R_2u)-angle(R_1u,R_2u)]/(2pi).       (A)
This is an exact probability identity with shared Gaussian b, not an independence assumption.

## 1. d=2: requested first diagnostic and exact answer

For the planar rotation R(t) and 0<=t<=pi,
  P(W(t))=t/pi,
because the angle of every nonzero normal and its rotation is t. For 0<=t<=pi/2, identity (A) gives
  P(W(t) intersection W(-t))=0,
  P(W(t) intersection W(2t))=t/pi.
There is only one tangent direction in O(2), since its local dimension is one. Opposite signs of that direction are not two independent tangent directions.


Tangent first variations and shared-coordinate pair


For a skew G and unit u,
  lim_(t downarrow0) angle(u,exp(tG)u)/t=||G u||.
Indeed exp(tG)u=u+tGu+O(t^2), Gu is perpendicular to u, and angle=2 arcsin(chord/2) for unit vectors. The same chord identity gives
  lim_(t downarrow0) angle(exp(tG_1)u,exp(tG_2)u)/t
    =||(G_1-G_2)u||.
For coordinate-plane generators below ||G_i||op=1. The curve exp(sG_i)u has speed ||G_i exp(sG_i)u||<=1, so its spherical angular distance from u is at most t. The angle between the two rotated normals is at most 2t by the triangle inequality. In particular each scaled term has a uniform integrable bound, and the nonnegative overlap integrand in (A), divided by t, is at most 1/pi. Dominated convergence is therefore justified:
  lim P(W_i(t))/t = E||G_i u||/pi,
  lim P(W_1(t) intersection W_2(t))/t
   =[E||G_1u||+E||G_2u||-E||(G_1-G_2)u||]/(2pi).                (B)
No exchange of an unbounded derivative and expectation is used.

## 3. Distinct Frobenius-orthogonal tangents sharing a coordinate

For d>=3 choose G_1=G_12=e_1 e_2^T-e_2 e_1^T and
G_2=G_13=e_1 e_3^T-e_3 e_1^T. Their Frobenius inner product is zero and each has operator norm one. Set
  c_d=Gamma(d/2)/(2 sqrt(pi) Gamma((d+1)/2))>0.
Then E||G_12 u||=pi c_d. To see this, ||G_12u||=sqrt(u_1^2+u_2^2); for d>2 the squared quantity has Beta(1,(d-2)/2) distribution. The beta integral gives its mean square root as
  Gamma(3/2) Gamma(d/2)/Gamma((d+1)/2)=pi c_d.
This beta distribution follows by writing u=g/||g|| for independent standard Gaussian coordinates: the first-two sum of squares and remaining sum are independent chi-squares. In d=2 the quantity equals one and c_2=1/pi, consistent with the formula.

Now G_12-G_13=e_1(e_2-e_3)^T-(e_2-e_3)e_1^T is orthogonally conjugate to sqrt(2) G_12. Uniform-sphere rotation invariance gives
  E||(G_12-G_13)u||=sqrt(2) pi c_d.
Substitution into (B) proves
  P(W_i(t))=c_d t+o(t),
  P(W_12(t) intersection W_13(t))=(1-1/sqrt(2)) c_d t+o(t).    (C)
The coefficient is strictly positive. Thus the intersection is Theta_d(t) and is NOT O_d(t^2). The subscript d means that d is fixed in the t limit; no dimension-uniform remainder is asserted.

In d=3, c_3=1/4. One can avoid gamma functions entirely: u_3 is uniform on [-1,1], and E sqrt(1-u_3^2)=pi/4 is a semicircle integral. Thus
  lim_(t downarrow0) P(W_12 intersection W_13)/t=(2-sqrt(2))/8.
This is approximately .0732233, a positive constant.


Disjoint-coordinate pair


For d>=4 instead take G_1=G_12 and G_2=G_34. These tangent matrices act on disjoint coordinates and are Frobenius-orthogonal. Pointwise,
  ||(G_12-G_34)u||=sqrt(u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2+u_4^2).
Its expectation is (3/2) pi c_d: for d>4 use Beta(2,(d-4)/2) and Gamma(5/2)/Gamma(2)=3sqrt(pi)/4; in d=4 the quantity is one, and pi c_4=2/3 gives the same ratio. Equation (B) now yields
  P(W_12(t) intersection W_34(t))=(c_d/4)t+o(t).               (D)
In d=4 the coefficient is 1/(6pi)>0. Disjoint coordinates in the perturbations do not make the events independent: both wedges concern the same base decision boundary a dot b=0.



## 5. Exact intersection formula for disjoint planes in d=4

For d=4, G_1=G_12 and G_2=G_34, there is also an exact finite-angle expression. Put z=t/2 with 0<t<pi. Then
  P(W_12(t) intersection W_34(t))=cot(z)(1-z cot(z))/pi.        (E)

Proof: for u uniform on S^3, S=u_1^2+u_2^2 is uniform on [0,1]. For the first plane rotation,
  angle(u,R_12(t)u)=2 arcsin(sin(z) sqrt(S)).
The conditional single-wedge probability is this angle divided by pi. Writing alpha=sin(z) and integrating over S gives
  E angle =4 integral_0^1 v arcsin(alpha v) dv
          =2z-z csc(z)^2+cot(z).
For completeness, integration by parts gives
  integral_0^1 v arcsin(alpha v)dv
   =z/2-[z-alpha sqrt(1-alpha^2)]/(4alpha^2),
which proves the evaluated expression. Symmetry gives the same expectation for the second plane. On the other hand,
  (R_12(t)u) dot (R_34(t)u)=cos(t)||u||^2=cos(t),
so the angle between those normals is exactly t. Equation (A) therefore makes the intersection equal to the single-wedge probability minus t/(2pi). Using csc(z)^2=1+cot(z)^2 gives (E).

For 0<z<pi/2, tan(z)>z, by integrating derivative sec(z)^2>1 from zero. Thus 0<z cot(z)<1 and the exact overlap in (E) is strictly positive. Finally cot(z)=1/z-z/3+O(z^3) yields
  P(W_12 intersection W_34)=t/(6pi)+O(t^3).
The displayed expansion is an analytic Taylor expansion at zero of smooth trigonometric quotients after their removable singularities are canceled; it is not a floating-point estimate. This exact formula strengthens the same overlap obstruction and makes no sample-complexity claim.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:84c6ed35e6d39ff33b26530b4fb31b1a0ec3838f775ec6c4cdd5752b45b2e677","revision_digest":"sha256:2bfbe9f5ac9b892595ae02a14536ccf15fa76fa102dbfd11dc7f313f881c1c05","source_id":"own-work:w693:T407-WEDGE-008:v2","source_revision":"2026-10-20T11:46:47.545360+03:00; v2; proof unaudited; no priority established","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2607.23585, 'The one-period Kyle model has one equilibrium'] Set $V^{(0)}:=V$. On an extension of the underlying probability
	space, there exists a random variable $V^{(1)}$ such that $V^{(0)}$
	and $V^{(1)}$ are conditionally independent and identically
	distributed given $Y$. Moreover, the following hold:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item
		      the triples $(V^{(0)},V^{(1)},Y)$ and
		      $(V^{(1)},V^{(0)},Y)$ have the same law;

		\item
		      the pairs $(V^{(1)},Y)$ and $(V,Y)$ have the same law;

		\item
		      $\E[V^{(1)}\mid Y,V^{(0)}]=P(Y)$ almost surely;

		\item
		      $\E[V^{(1)}\mid V^{(0)}]
			      =F\bigl(\phi(V^{(0)})\bigr)$ almost surely.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def.hepp_2 of arXiv:2607.10105, 'The four-dimensional Anderson model: a case study for critical SPDEs'] Let $\mathcal T$ be a Hepp tree (Definition (def.hepp of the paper)), possibly with a marking $(N_\mathfrak n)$ and multiplicities $(m_\mathfrak l)$. We define the following notations:
\begin{enumerate}[{(1)}]
\item Recall $\mathfrak n^+$ is the parent of $\mathfrak n$. Define $\mathcal C_\mathfrak n$ to be the set of children of $\mathfrak n$, and $\mathcal T_\mathfrak n$ to be the subtree rooted at $\mathfrak n$ (with $\mathcal T_\mathfrak n=\{\mathfrak n\}$ when $\mathfrak n$ is a leaf), and write $\mathfrak m\leq\mathfrak n$ if $\mathfrak m\in \mathcal T_\mathfrak n$. Define $\mathcal B$ to be the set of branching nodes, $\mathcal L$ the set of leaves, and $\mathfrak r$ the root. We also write $\mathcal L_\mathfrak n=\mathcal L\cap \mathcal T_\mathfrak n$ and $\mathcal B_\mathfrak n=\mathcal B\cap\mathcal T_\mathfrak n$ etc. 
\item For $\mathfrak n\in\mathcal B$, define $\gamma_\mathfrak n=|\mathcal C_\mathfrak n|$ to be the number of children of $\mathfrak n$ (leaves are counted \emph{without} multiplicity; later we also need to treat leaves \emph{with multiplicity}, which will be clearly indicated below).
\item Finally, for $\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m'\in\mathcal T$, define $\mathfrak m\vee\mathfrak m'$ to be the lowest common ancestor of $\mathfrak m$ and $\mathfrak m'$. Note that $\mathfrak m\vee\mathfrak m'\in\mathcal L$ if and only if $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m'\in\mathcal L$; otherwise $\mathfrak m\vee\mathfrak m'\in\mathcal B$.
\end{enumerate}

We usually denote $r$ to be the total number of leaves of $\mathcal T$ without multiplicity; it is easy to see that $\sum_{\mathfrak n\in\mathcal B}(\gamma_\mathfrak n-1)=r-1$. We may also denote by $m=\sum_{\mathfrak l\in\mathcal L}m_\mathfrak l$ the total number of leaves of $\mathcal T$ with multiplicity (each leaf $\mathfrak l$ counted $m_\mathfrak l$ times).

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.09121, 'Truncated Signature Information for Mixed Fractional Brownian Paths'] Let $\mathcal H$ consist of distinct positive scales.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Assume Assumption~\ref{ass:compact}.  If $L\ge2K$, then for every $\epsilon>0$,
\[
    \delta_2(\epsilon;\Theta_K,\mathcal H)>0.
\]
If $L\ge K$, then for every $\epsilon>0$,
\[
    \delta_3(\epsilon;\Theta_K,\mathcal H)>0.
\]
\item For every $\theta_0\in\mathcal P_K$, if $L\ge2K$, then there exist $r_2,c_2>0$ such that
\[
    \|\Psi_{\mathcal H}(\theta)-\Psi_{\mathcal H}(\theta_0)\|
    \ge c_2\|\theta-\theta_0\|
\]
whenever $\theta\in\mathcal P_K$ and $\|\theta-\theta_0\|\le r_2$.  If $L\ge K$, then there exist $r_3,c_3>0$ such that
\[
    \|\Gamma_{\mathcal H}(\theta)-\Gamma_{\mathcal H}(\theta_0)\|
    \ge c_3\|\theta-\theta_0\|
\]
whenever $\theta\in\mathcal P_K$ and $\|\theta-\theta_0\|\le r_3$.

[Proposition prop:separated-loop of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Suppose \(r\) is fixed and \(C_V^\delta=\bigcup_{j=1}^rC_{j,V}^\delta\), with each \(C_{j,V}^\delta\) connected.  Put

\(C=\bigcup_jC_j\) (note that every $C_j$ is a continuum).
If \(B\Subset D\), \(\mathrm{dist}(C,B)>0\), and $m_D(C,B)=m_D(C,B^\circ)$,
then for \(B_V^\delta=\{v\in D^\delta:\mathrm{dist}(v,B)\leq2\delta\}\),
\begin{equation}
 m_{D^\delta}^\delta(C_V^\delta,B_V^\delta)
 \longrightarrow m_D(C,B).
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:transform_BR of arXiv:2601.08184, 'Wasserstein-p Central Limit Theorem Rates: From Local Dependence to Markov Chains'] Under the assumptions and notation of Lemma~(lem:BR_Hilbert of the paper), let
\((a_k)_{k\ge 1}\) be a real-valued predictable sequence, i.e.,
\(a_k\) is \(\mathcal F_{k-1}\)-measurable for each \(k\ge 1\). Define
\[
T_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k d_k,\qquad n\ge 1.
\]
Then, for every \(p\ge 2\), the same constant \(C_p\) as in
Lemma~(lem:BR_Hilbert of the paper) satisfies
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\|T_n\|^p
\le
C_p\left\{
\mathbb{E}\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^2\,\mathbb{E}[\|d_k\|^2\mid \mathcal F_{k-1}]\Bigr)^{p/2}
+
\mathbb{E}\sum_{k=1}^n |a_k|^p\,\|d_k\|^p
\right\},
\qquad n\ge 1.
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(\tau\) is a stopping time taking values in
\(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\), then $a_k:=\mathbf 1_{\{k\le \tau\}}$ is predictable, and $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^{\tau} d_k = M_\tau.$ Consequently,
\[
\mathbb{E}\|M_{\tau}\|^p
\le
C_p\left\{
\mathbb{E}\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{\tau}\mathbb{E}[\|d_k\|^2\mid \mathcal F_{k-1}]\Bigr)^{p/2}
+
\mathbb{E}\sum_{k=1}^{\tau}\|d_k\|^p
\right\}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:transform_BR of arXiv:2601.08184

body:
[Prop of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] Let $d, n$ be positive integers and $d\le n/2$.  
    Let $M$ be an $n\times n$ random matrix where each row is independently and uniformly chosen from all $n$-dimensional binary vectors $\{0,1\}^n$ with exactly $d$ ones. Let $X$ denote the number of zero columns in $M$. Then the following holds.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Assume that $d=\log n - g(n)$ for some non-negative function $g$ satisfying $g(n) \longrightarrow \infty$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Then,
        \[
        \lim_{n\to \infty} \mathbb{P}(X\ge 1)=1.
        \]
        That is, asymptotically (in $n$) the matrix $M$ almost surely has at least one zero column. In particular, it holds for 
        $d\le (1-\varepsilon)\log n$ (for  any fixed $\varepsilon>0$). 
        \item For any fixed $d\geq 1$ and fixed $\theta \in (0,1)$,
        \[
         \liminf_{n\to \infty} \mathbb{P}(X > \theta \mathbb{E} X ) 
         \geq (1-\theta)^2.
        \]
        In particular, 
        \[
         \liminf_{n\to \infty}\mathbb{P}(X>\theta  e^{-d} n /2) 
         \geq (1-\theta)^2,
        \]
        that is, for large enough $n$, the nullity of the matrix $M$ is bounded from below by  a constant proportion of $n$ with a positive probability.
    \end{enumerate}

[Theorem theorem_ipm_geom_random_graphs of arXiv:2606.03442, 'Stein's method in network analysis'] Let $(H,T) \sim \mathbf{PP}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_1) \otimes Q^{\kappa_1}$ and $(\Xi,\Sigma) \sim \mathbf{PP}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_2) \otimes Q^{\kappa_2}$ 
    be random geometric graphs. 
    Define
\[
     \Delta\kappa(\xi,x) \ :=\  \sum_{y \in \xi}|\kappa_1(x,y) - \kappa_2(x,y)|.
\]
    Then, for all $h\colon \mathbb{G} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ bounded and measurable,
    
    
    
    
    
    \begin{align*}
        \vert \mathbb{E}[h(&\Xi,\Sigma)] - \mathbb{E}[h(H,T)] \vert \\
        &\ \le\   \mathbb{E} \biggl[  \int_{\mathbb{X}} \Delta_V^{\kappa_2} f_h(\Xi, \Sigma) \vert \boldsymbol{\lambda}_1(dx) 
                  - \boldsymbol{\lambda}_2(dx) \vert \biggr] 
         + \mathbb{E} \biggl[  \int_{\mathbb{X}} \Delta_E f_h(\Xi, \Sigma) \Delta\kappa(\Xi,x)  \boldsymbol{\lambda}_1(dx)  \biggr].
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let G = (V, E) and H = (W, F) be graphs. A graph homomorphism from G to H is a function phi: V -> W such that {u,v} in E implies {phi(u), phi(v)} in F, that is, phi maps adjacent vertices to adjacent vertices. A graph G has a homomorphism to the complete graph K_k if and only if G is properly k-colorable, so graph homomorphisms to K_k generalize proper colorings. [standard, e.g. Hell and Nesetril, Graphs and Homomorphisms]
title: Graph Homomorphism

[Lem 1 of arXiv:2604.25964, 'Strong convergence rate of Euler-Maruyama approximations in temporal-spatial H\"older-norm'] (\cite[Corollary 2.2]{HN22})

Let $t_0 < T$, and let $a, x : [t_0, T] \to [0,\infty)$ and
$\delta : [t_0, T] \to [t_0, T]$ be measurable functions such that
$\delta(t) \le t$ for all $t \in [t_0, T]$. Assume that, for some
constants $c_\star > 0$ and $p \ge 1$,
\[
x(t) \le a(t) + \left( \int_{t_0}^t |c_\star x(\delta(s))|^p \, ds \right)^{1/p}
< \infty, \quad t \in [t_0, T].
\]
Then, for all $t \in [t_0, T]$, it holds that
\[
x(t) \le 2^{1-\frac{1}{p}}
\left( \sup_{s \in [t_0, t]} a(s) \right)
\exp\left( \frac{2^{p-1} c_\star^p (t - t_0)}{p} \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 1 of arXiv:2604.25964

Own-work; CONJECTURE, not a theorem; novelty UNCHECKED. For iid finite nonnegative teeth with tail C*t^(-1/3)*(log t)^kappa, the predicted backbone-collision threshold for two independent walks started together is kappa=2/3: infinite for kappa<=2/3, including equality, and finite for kappa>2/3. The heuristic balanced rectangle has height h_R of order R^(3/2)*(log R)^(3kappa/4), volume V_R of order R^2*(log R)^(3kappa/2), and time t_R of order R^3*(log R)^(3kappa/2). Inverting yields R(t) of order t^(1/3)*(log t)^(-kappa/2) and V(t) of order t^(2/3)*(log t)^(kappa/2). Reciprocal-volume kernel and horizontal-range predictions give squared backbone return sum density of order 1/[t*(log t)^(3kappa/2)], so the logarithmic exponent is 3kappa/2. At equality the expected return sum grows like log log T, and the predicted geometric-scale collision chances are of order 1/(m log m). These quenched estimates are unproved. Summability of backbone returns cannot establish finite total collisions in the teeth; a separate tooth-cluster bound is necessary. The full calculation and source estimates requiring revision are in I0012-H1 v1.

[Theorem thm:critical-toppling-d4 of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Fix $\nu_{0}>0$, $\theta_{0}>0$, and $K_{0}<\infty$. There are
			constants $c=c(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})>0$,
			$C=C(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})<\infty$, and
			$t_0=t_0(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})<\infty$ such that, for every mean-zero i.i.d.\ field
			$(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^4}$ satisfying
			\[
				\Var(\zeta(0))\geq\nu_{0}^2\, ,
				\qquad
				\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_{0}|\zeta(0)|}\leq K_{0}\, ,
			\]
			and every $t\geq t_0$,
			\begin{equation}
				c\log t\leq \mathbb{E} u_t(0)\leq C\log t\, .
			\end{equation}
			Moreover, for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}^4$, $t\geq2$, and $s\geq0$,
			\begin{equation}
				\mathbb{P}\left(|u_t(x)-\mathbb{E} u_t(0)|>s\right)
				\leq
				C\exp\left\{
					-c\min\left(\frac{s^2}{\log t},s\right)
				\right\}\, .
			\end{equation}
			Consequently,
			\[
				\frac{u_t(x)}{\mathbb{E} u_t(0)}\longrightarrow1
				\qquad\textup{in $L^2$ and almost surely}
			\]
			for every fixed $x$.

[Definition def-Skorohod of arXiv:2603.01823, 'on a fractional stochastic heat equation arising from the disordered pinning model'] Let $D=\{1,\cdots,\mathrm{max(D)}\}$ be finite or let $D=\mathbb N$, and $U=\left(u_k\in L^1, k\in D\right)$ be a sequence of random variables measurable with respect to $\sigma(\xi_k:k\in D)$. We say that $U$ is $L^1$-Skorohod integrable if there exists a random variable $S \in L^1$
 such that for any $n\in D$ and any bounded differentiable $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ with bounded $\nabla f$, we have
$$ \mathbb E\left[Sf(\xi_1,\cdots,\xi_n)\right]=\mathbb E\left[U\cdot \nabla f(\xi_1,\cdots,\xi_n)\right],$$ then $S$ is called the $L^1$-Skorohod integral of $U$ and is denoted by 
\[S:=\int{\raisebox{-.82em}{\hspace{-1.18em}\scriptsize \bf o}}\hspace{.7em} U\xi.\]

Target 2 source obstruction; proof draft, unaudited. This is a standard
conditional-expectation identity and a counterexample to a literal finite-size
argument, not a refutation of an asymptotic formula or a novelty claim.

## Corrected finite-dimensional identity

Let S be a square-integrable random real matrix and Y an observation. Let
B_1(Y),...,B_k(Y) be a Y-measurable Frobenius-orthonormal family. Set
a_j=<S,B_j(Y)> and O=sum_j a_j B_j(Y). Suppose E[S|Y] lies in their span.
For any positive deterministic normalization c, put
R_B=E||S-E[S|Y]||_F^2/c and R_O=E||S-O||_F^2/c. Then

    R_B - R_O = sum_j E Var(a_j|Y)/c >= 0.             (1)

Indeed <E[S|Y],B_j>=E[a_j|Y], by measurability and conditional
expectation (localize if the observation-dependent coefficients are used).
Pointwise orthogonal projection gives
||S-O||^2=||S||^2-sum_j a_j^2. The assumed span condition and the
L2 projection identity give
E||S-E[S|Y]||^2=E||S||^2-sum_j E(E[a_j|Y]^2).
Subtract. All terms are integrable since sum_j a_j^2<=||S||^2.

Thus an oracle using the true coefficients is not an observation-only
competitor in the definition of Bayes risk. Asymptotic equality requires
the normalized conditional-variance sum in (1) to vanish; equivariance alone
does not prove this. For a biorthogonally invariant prior and isotropic
Gaussian noise the posterior mean is equivariant. At an observation with
distinct positive singular values, its stabilizers force the posterior mean
to lie in the observed singular-vector span, so (1) applies there. Gaussian
convolution makes the exceptional algebraic set of repeated or zero
singular values null. Formula (1) itself needs only the stated span condition.

## Exact scalar counterexample to the finite-size conclusion

Take N=P=1, S,Z independent standard normal, and Y=S+Z. The prior is
invariant under the left and right groups O(1). If Y=u sigma v is a real
singular value decomposition, u,v are signs. The oracle coefficient in
equation (4) of the source is a=u S v. Its reconstructed matrix is
u a v=S, so its squared error is zero almost surely.

The posterior density of S given Y=y is proportional to
exp(-(x^2+(y-x)^2)/2)=exp(-(x-y/2)^2-y^2/4).
It is N(y/2,1/2), hence the Bayes estimator is Y/2 and its MSE is 1/2.
The risk gap equals Var(a|Y) averaged, namely 1/2, in agreement with (1).
This example uses signal variance one and SNR one; all moments are finite.

The conclusion also fails with bounded signal: let S be uniform on {-1,1}.
The same oracle still returns S. Both posterior weights are positive for
every finite y, E[S|Y=y]=tanh(y), and Var(S|Y=y)=sech(y)^2>0.
Consequently Bayes MSE is strictly positive while oracle risk is zero.

## Primary-source locator and exact scope

Pourkamali and Macris, *Rectangular Rotational Invariant Estimator for
High-Rank Matrix Estimation*, arXiv:2403.04615v1 (7 March 2024), equation
(4), and Section 2.3, PDF page 4. The page says:

> Therefore, the oracle estimator is Bayes-optimal under bi-rotational invariant prior and achieves the MMSE.

The displayed comparison on that page treats the truth-dependent oracle
as a Bayes competitor. The rendered PDF page was visually checked, rather
than inferring the inequality direction from text extraction; evidence:
papers/2403_oracle_claim_page.png. The counterexample disproves that literal
finite-size sentence and identifies the missing step in its proof.

It does not disprove asymptotic Statements 1 or 3. Those require a separate
vanishing-conditional-variance argument or another direct proof. In

Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with distribution function F, and let F_n(x) = (1/n) sum_{i <= n} 1{X_i <= x} be the empirical distribution function. Then sup_{x in R} | F_n(x) - F(x) | -> 0 almost surely. NO regularity of F is assumed: F may have atoms, may be singular, may be anything. The strong law alone gives only F_n(x) -> F(x) almost surely for each FIXED x, with a null set depending on x, and the union over uncountably many x of those null sets need not be null; the content of the theorem is that monotonicity upgrades pointwise convergence to UNIFORM convergence with a single null set. The quantitative companion is the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality, P( sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)| > t ) <= 2 exp(-2 n t^2) with Massart's sharp constant 2, valid for every n and t. The abstract generalisation replaces the class of half-lines by a general class of sets or functions, and then a combinatorial condition such as finite Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension is required - uniform convergence over an ARBITRARY class of sets is false. [Glivenko and Cantelli (1933); Massart (1990) for the sharp DKW constant; see van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 19.1]
i.i.d. real observations
no assumption whatsoever on F
the uniformity is over half-lines; for a general class of sets a complexity condition is required

[Lem bessel of arXiv:2602.22342, 'Sum of Gaussian vectors and large sets'] [$\sqrt{\log d}\,$-Bessel sequence]

Given $C>0$, there is a positive integer $q=O(C)$ depending only on $C$ such that the following holds. 
Let $\Lambda\geq 1$, let $d,d_0$ be positive integers.
Given a linear map $F:\R^{d}\to \R^{d_0}$ with $\|F\| \leq C$,
define  $\hat{Z}_F$ to be the random vector uniformly distributed on the vectors 
$F(\sqrt{\log d} \, e_1)$, ..., $F(\sqrt{\log d}\,e_d)$.
Then $\hat{Z}_F-\E[\hat{Z}_F] \in \sum^q\mathcal{G}(\R^{d_0}).$

body: [Lemma lem:three-pointed-sphere of arXiv:2606.10973, 'Quasisymmetric rigidity of the Brownian sphere'] Let $(\widehat\BC, \Phi_1; 0, 1, \infty)$ be a three-pointed $\gamma$-LQG sphere with unit area. Let $\Phi_2$ be a whole-plane GFF. Then for each bounded open subset $U \Subset \BC \setminus \{0, 1\}$, the laws of $\Phi_1|_U$ and $\Phi_2|_U$, viewed as random Schwartz distributions modulo additive constants, are mutually absolutely continuous.

[Lemma lem:vec_KP of arXiv:2604.28068, 'Mean-square Stability and Bifurcations for Dissipative SDEs'] If $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}$, then 
\[
\mathrm{vec}(AB)=(B^T\otimes\mathbb{I}_d)\,\mathrm{vec}(A)=(\mathbb{I}_d\otimes A)\mathrm{vec}(B).
\]
Moreover,  if $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is a column vector, then $\mathrm{vec}(x)=x$ and $\mathrm{vec}(x^T)=x$.

body: Consider $D$ related regressions whose coefficient vectors $w_d \in \mathbb{R}^p$ are modelled hierarchically, $w_d = w_0 + \delta_d$ with $\delta_d \sim N(0, T)$ independent across $d$, observed through $\hat w_d = w_d + z_d$ with known noise $z_d \sim N(0, \Sigma_d)$ (the sampling covariance of row $d$'s least-squares estimate). The posterior mean of $w_d$ given $\hat w_d$ is the matrix shrinkage $$\tilde w_d = w_0 + T\,(T + \Sigma_d)^{-1}(\hat w_d - w_0),$$ which shrinks fully in the directions where the prior spread $T$ is small relative to the noise and not at all where it is large. Empirical Bayes estimates the unknowns from the rows themselves: $w_0$ by the row mean (or by a pooled fit such as the global convex weights of a stacking problem), and $T$ from the row covariance of the residuals $\hat w_d - w_0$, whose expectation is $T + \bar\Sigma$: with a common noise covariance one whitens by $\bar\Sigma^{-1/2}$, forms the $p \times p$ residual covariance $\hat R = \frac{1}{D}\sum_d r_d r_d^T$ of the whitened rows, and takes $\hat T = (\hat R - I)_+$ (eigenvalues below one set to zero - the same 'subtract the noise level, keep the positive part' as the spiked-covariance debiasing, now at the aspect ratio $p/D$ of the row covariance, which is a random-matrix problem in its own right). The scalar positive-part James-Stein rule toward $w_0$ is the special case $T \propto \Sigma$. Two facts decide whether the construction helps in practice: the noise model $\Sigma_d$ must be right (under heteroscedastic residuals the homoscedastic $\sigma_d^2 (X_d^T X_d)^{-1}$ can understate the noise by a large factor in the ill-conditioned directions, making the estimated amount of shrinkage collapse to zero where cross-validation would shrink substantially - the sandwich covariance is the repair), and the gain is a variance reduction only, so it is largest when the rows are noisy relative to their spread, i.e. at small calibration sizes.

[Lemma lem_transition_asymptotics of arXiv:2411.08846, 'On the Number of Crossings and Bouncings\\ of a Diffusion at a Sticky Threshold'] Consider the setting of Theorem~(thm_main of the paper). 
Let $ (f_n,k_n,g_n,h_n;\,n\in\IN) $ be the functions defined for all $n \in \IN$ and $x\in \IR $ by 
$f_n(x) := \Prob_{x} \left(  X_{1/n} = 0 \right) $, 
$k_n(x) := \mathbbm{1}_{\{x\not = 0\}} f_n(x/\sqrt n) $, 
$g_n(x) := \Prob_{x} \left( x X_{1/n} < 0 \right) $, 
$h_n(x) := \sqrt n g_n(x/\sqrt n) $.
It holds that 
\begin{enumerate}
	[label={\upshape (\roman*)}]
	\item  $\lim_{n \rightarrow  \infty} f_n(0) = 1 $ and 
	$\lim_{n \rightarrow  \infty} \sqrt n (1- f_n(0)) = 
	{2 \sqrt{2}}/{\rho \sqrt \pi} $,
	\item  the sequence $(k_n)_n $ satisfies~(equation eq_connd_gn_aggreg of the paper) and $\lim_{n \rightarrow  \infty} m_{\sqrt n \rho}( k_n )  =  2 \sqrt{{2}/{\pi}} $,
	\item  the sequence $(h_n)_n $ satisfies~(equation eq_connd_gn_aggreg of the paper) and $\lim_{n \rightarrow  \infty} m_{\sqrt n \rho}( h_n )  = 1/{\rho} $.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In computational complexity theory, the Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem states that nondeterministic space complexity classes are closed under complementation. It was proven independently by Neil Immerman and Róbert Szelepcsényi in 1987, for which they shared the 1995 Gödel Prize. In its general form the theorem states that NSPACE(s(n)) = co-NSPACE(s(n)) for any function s(n) ≥ log n. The result is equivalently stated as NL = co-NL; although this is the special case when s(n) = log n, it implies the general theorem by a standard padding argument. The result solved the second LBA problem.
title: Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem

body: [Corollary 11 of arXiv:2609.03951, 'Generalized Semi-Riemannian Submersions and Foliations'] Let $U$ be a conformal, irrotational observer vector field on a spacetime $(M,g)$, let $S$ be a restspace of $U$, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $U$-stationary, codimension-one lightlike foliation on $M$. Then $\mathcal{F}_S := \mathcal{F} \cap S$ is a codimension-one Riemannian foliation on the Riemannian manifold $(S, h)$, where $h = g|_S$. Furthermore, if $S$ is a closed manifold with strictly positive sectional curvature, then there exists no $U$-stationary, codimension-one lightlike foliation on $M$.

Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), Target 3 route obstruction. On uniform S^(d-1), let Z=sqrt(d)*x.u and p=w/sqrt(d). Train all original Euclidean mean-field parameters of a exp(b+w.x), with square loss against a fixed target of L2 norm <=Y, Y>=1, from a=b=0 and a rotation-invariant probability law of p. Assume an existing characteristic solution satisfies |a|,|b|,||p||<=K uniformly in time and dimension, K>=1. Then ||p_t.u||_L2 <=s_d(t)=K/sqrt(d)+B_K Y t/d, B_K=3^(1/4) K exp(K+2K^2). The actual degree-1 output coefficient is at most K exp(K+K^2/2)s_d(t). Any axial exponential approximant with coefficients bounded by C to Z with a fixed L2 error delta in [0,1), independent of d must have C>=(1-delta)exp(-K^2/2)/s_d(t). Thus a t=o(d) phase with one fixed K cannot generate the dimension-uniform bounded-coefficient or fixed interval-density handoff used by the prepared-axis C11-C13 proofs. This uses only initial rotational invariance, not later invariance, and allows off-axis neurons. Uniform parameter control is assumed, not derived; longer phases or dimension-growing parameters remain open. This is not an unrestricted learning-time lower bound or a refutation of Target 3. No novelty or independent audit is asserted.

Let f be twice continuously differentiable near a root r with f(r) = 0 and f'(r) nonzero. Then for starting points sufficiently close to r, Newton's iteration x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k) converges to r quadratically: |x_{k+1} - r| <= C |x_k - r|^2 for a constant C depending on bounds for f'' and 1/f' near r.

f(r) = 0, f'(r) nonzero
x_0 sufficiently close to r

On a separable complete metric (Polish) space, a family of probability measures is tight (for every epsilon there is a compact set carrying at least 1 - epsilon of every measure) if and only if it is relatively compact in the topology of weak convergence (every sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence with a probability-measure limit).

	$N=|Q|\geq2$. For $F=(F_z)_{z\in Q}$, set
	\[
		L_Q(F)\coloneqq
		\max_{\Gamma}
		\min_{z\in\Gamma}F_z\, ,
	\]
	where the maximum is over simple paths $\Gamma$ in
	$Q$ from the left to the right. For every
	$\beta\geq1$ there is a $C^\infty$ function $L_{Q,\beta}$ of the
	coordinates $(F_z)_{z\in Q}$ such that, with an absolute constant $C<\infty$, uniformly over~$F$, 
	\begin{equation}
		|L_{Q,\beta}(F)-L_Q(F)|
		\leq C\frac{(\log N)^2}{\beta} \, , 
	\end{equation}
	and, for $k=1,2,3$,
	\begin{equation}
		\sum_{z_1,\ldots,z_k\in Q}
		|\partial_{z_1}\cdots\partial_{z_k}L_{Q,\beta}(F)|
		\leq C\beta^{k-1}(\log N)^{k-1} \, . 
	\end{equation}

[Theorem thm:rmulmc-spacetime of arXiv:2506.23062, 'Shifted Composition IV\@: \\ Toward Ballistic Acceleration for Log-Concave Sampling'] Let $\hat{\boldsymbol{P}}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{P}}{}'$ denote the kernels for~(eq:rm-ulmc of the paper) and~(eq:ULMC of the paper) respectively, and let $\boldsymbol{P}$ denote the kernel for~(eq:ULD of the paper) run for time $h$.
    Assume that $\pi$ satisfies~(equation eq:pi of the paper) with constant $1/\alpha$, $0 \preceq \nabla^2 V \preceq \beta I$, $\gamma \asymp \sqrt{\alpha}$, and $\kappa \coloneqq \beta/\alpha$.
    Write $\chi^2 \coloneqq \chi^2(\bs\mu\mathbin{\|}\bs\pi)$.
    Then, for all $\varepsilon \in (0, \widetilde O(\log^{1/2}(1+\chi^2))]$ and $h =\widetilde{\Theta}(\frac{\varepsilon^{2/3}}{\beta^{1/2} \kappa^{1/3} \,(d^{1/3} + \log^{1/3}(1+\chi^2)) \log^{1/3}(\chi^2/\varepsilon^2)})$, we have $\KL(\bs\mu\hat{\boldsymbol{P}}{}^{N-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{P}}{}' \mathbin{\|} \bs\pi) \leqslant {\varepsilon^2}$ provided that
    \begin{align*}
        N = \widetilde{\Theta}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa^{5/6}\,(d^{1/3} + \log^{1/3}(1+\chi^2))}{\varepsilon^{2/3}} \log^{4/3} \frac{\chi^2}{\varepsilon^2}\Bigr)\,.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
