[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] \cite[Lemma 2.13]{ryu}
        For $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ and a parabolic element $\widetilde{A}\in \mathrm{Par}_n$ of $\univcover,$ let  $s(\widetilde{A})\in\{\pm\}$ be its sign, i.e., $s(\widetilde{A})=+$ if $\widetilde{A}\in \mathrm{Par}^+_n,$ and $s(\widetilde{A})=-$ if $\widetilde{A}\in \mathrm{Par}^-_n.$ Let $A$ be the projection of $\widetilde{A}$ to $\SL$, and for $i,j\in\{1,2\}$ let $a_{ij}$ be the $(i,j)$-entry of $A.$ Then either $a_{12}\neq0$ or $a_{21}\neq 0.$  Furthermore,
        
        \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
       \item If $n$ is even, then $s(\widetilde{A})=sgn(a_{12})$ if $a_{12}\neq 0,$ and $s(\widetilde{A})=-sgn(a_{21})$ if $a_{21}\neq 0.$
       
    \item If $n$ is odd, then $s(\widetilde{A})=-sgn(a_{12})$ if $a_{12}\neq 0,$  and $s(\widetilde{A})=sgn(a_{21})$ if $a_{21}\neq 0.$

[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.27374, '\Large \bf Distribution-constrained optimal multiple stopping: the Root-type solution'] For $r >0$ and $x \in \R$, define
$$
\overline{v}^\xi(r,x):=\P\left[\sigma^\xi > r,\ X_r\le x\right],\qquad 0\le r<\infty.
$$
For $0\le s\le t$, let $\overline{V}_s^t:=\overline{v}^\xi(t-s,Y_s)$.
Then $(\overline V_s^t)_{0\le s\le t}$ is a $\P^x$-submartingale with respect to
$(\mathcal F_s^Y)_{0\le s\le t}$.
title: Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.27374

body: Every symmetric positive semidefinite kernel k on a set X is the reproducing kernel of a unique RKHS of functions on X: the space is built as the completion of finite linear combinations of the functions k(x, .) under the inner product determined by <k(x, .), k(y, .)> = k(x, y). body:
The load-bearing hypothesis in uniqueness for the Cauchy problem $u_t=\Delta u$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, $u(\cdot,0)=g$, is the growth bound $|u(x,t)|\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ with $A,a$ independent of $t$ (the Tychonoff class); smoothness of $u$ and continuity down to $t=0$ are not enough. Tychonoff's counterexample ($n=1$): let $g(t)=e^{-t^{-2}}$ for $t>0$, $g(0)=0$, and $u(x,t)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{g^{(k)}(t)}{(2k)!}x^{2k}$. The Cauchy estimates for $g$ ($|g^{(k)}(t)|\le k!\,(\theta t)^{-k}e^{-\frac12t^{-2}}$ for some $\theta>0$) make the series converge locally uniformly together with all its derivatives, and termwise differentiation gives $u_{xx}=u_t$; $u$ is continuous on $\mathbb R\times[0,\infty)$ with $u(x,0)\equiv0$, yet $u\not\equiv0$. So the zero initial datum admits the two distinct solutions $0$ and $u$, and by the uniqueness theorem $u$ cannot satisfy any uniform bound $|u|\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ on a strip. Two corollaries an auditor should apply: (1) a solution of the heat equation is not determined by its initial data unless a class is specified -- 'the' solution of a Cauchy problem is meaningless without one; (2) the Tychonoff solution necessarily changes sign, because nonnegative solutions with zero initial data are unique by Widder's theorem, so one-sided bounds are an alternative (and weaker) substitute for the growth class. The class is essentially sharp: the counterexample family with $g(t)=e^{-t^{-\alpha}}$, $\alpha>1$, shows uniqueness fails as soon as growth $e^{a|x|^{2+\varepsilon}}$ is allowed, while $|u|\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ suffices.
The growth bound must be uniform in t on the time strip
Continuity at t = 0 and smoothness for t > 0 do not substitute for it
Nonnegativity (Widder) is an alternative hypothesis
title: Pitfall: Uniqueness for the Heat Cauchy Problem needs a growth condition (Tychonoff)

Let $(X, \mathcal{A}, \mu)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{B}, 
u)$ be $\sigma$-FINITE measure spaces and let $f: X	imes Y 	o [0, \infty]$ be measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}$ (the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the measurable rectangles $A	imes B$). Then: (i) for every $x \in X$ the section $y \mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\mathcal{B}$-measurable and for every $y$ the section $x \mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\mathcal{A}$-measurable; (ii) the functions $x \mapsto \int_Y f(x,y)\,d
u(y)$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)$ (with values in $[0,\infty]$) are $\mathcal{A}$- resp. $\mathcal{B}$-measurable; (iii) $\int_{X	imes Y} f\,d(\mu	imes
u) = \int_X\Big(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d
u(y)\Big)d\mu(x) = \int_Y\Big(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\Big)d
u(y)$, all three possibly $= +\infty$, where $\mu	imes
u$ is the (unique, by $\sigma$-finiteness) product measure with $(\mu	imes
u)(A	imes B) = \mu(A)
u(B)$. Fubini's theorem is the companion for signed/complex $f$: if $f \in L^1(\mu	imes
u)$ - which by Tonelli applied to $|f|$ can be checked by ONE iterated integral of $|f|$ - then the sections are integrable for a.e. $x$ (resp. $y$), the partial integrals are integrable, and the three integrals agree as finite numbers. Sharp edges: (1) $\sigma$-finiteness cannot be dropped: $X = Y = [0,1]$, $\mu$ = Lebesgue, $
u$ = counting measure, $f = \mathbf{1}_{\{x = y\}}$ (measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra since the diagonal is closed hence Borel); then $\int_X\int_Y f\,d
u\,d\mu = 1$ while $\int_Y\int_X f\,d\mu\,d
u = 0$; (2) nonnegativity (or integrability) cannot be dropped: $f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$ on $(0,1)^2$ has iterated integrals $\pi/4$ and $-\pi/4$, and $f(x,y) = \mathbf{1}_{\{x = y\}} - \mathbf{1}_{\{x = y+1\}}$ on $\mathbb{N}	imes\mathbb{N}$ with counting measures has iterated sums $1$ and $0$ - in both $\int|f| = \infty$; (3) joint measurability cannot be dropped: assuming the continuum hypothesis there is a set $S \subset [0,1]^2$ (Sierpinski) with every vertical section countable and every horizontal section co-countable, so the iterated integrals of $\mathbf{1}_S$ are $0$ and $1$ - $S$ is not Lebesgue measurable in the plane; (4) for the COMPLETED product (Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ is the completion of $\mathcal{L}^m\otimes\mathcal{L}^n$) the sections are measurable only for a.e. $x$ and the partial integral is defined a.e.; the equalities in (iii) still hold with this proviso; (5) the theorem gives equality of the iterated integrals with the DOUBLE integral - the existence and equality of the two iterated integrals of a signed function does not by itself imply integrability (example (2) reversed: symmetrise to make both iterated integrals 0).

[Thm distance of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] Let  $1\leq k<n$ and $p\in (0,1)$ satisfy $p(1-p)(n-k)\geq 1$. 
Let $V \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a (fixed) subspace of dimension $k$ 
and  $u\in \mathbb{C}^n$ be a (fixed) vector. 
Let $\delta=(\delta_1,\cdots, \delta_n)$ be a random vector consisting 
of i.i.d. Bernoulli($p$) random variables, and denote the distance from 
$\delta + u$ to $V$ by $r$. Furthermore, denote 
$$
   E(p) = \mathbb{E} r \quad \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \quad D(p)= \sqrt{p(1-p)(n-k) + d^2_{u'}},
$$
where $u'=u+p\, \1=u+\mathbb{E} \delta$ and $d_{u'}$ is the distance from $u'$ to $V$. 
Then  
$$
          \tfrac{1}{2}  D(p)\leq     E(p)\leq D(p)
$$
and for any $t>0$, 
\[
 \mathbb{P}_{\delta}\left( \left|r- E(p) \right|\geq t\right) \leq Ce^{-ct^2},
\]
where $C,c$ are positive absolute constants.
title: Thm distance of arXiv:2604.10446

[Theorem thm:xiphi of arXiv:2605.15545, 'Crossover from subcritical to critical decay: \\ random walk, self-avoiding walk, percolat'] Let $d\ge 1$ and $\delta >0$.
Suppose that Assumptions~(ass:Omega of the paper) and~(ass:J of the paper) hold for $S_z$ for each $z\in [z_c-\delta,z_c)$, suppose that $m_z \to 0$ as $z \to z_c$,
and suppose that there are constants $M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta$ such that
$(J_z^{(\mu)},h_z^{(\mu)}) \in \mathcal{Q}_{M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta}$
and $\hat h_z^{(\mu)} (0)  \ge M^{-1} > 0$
uniformly in $\mu\in \overline\Omega_z$ and in $z \in [z_c-\delta,z_c)$.
Suppose further that $\lim_{z\to z_c}\sigma_z = \sigma_{z_c}$
and $\lim_{z\to z_c}\hat h_z(0) = \hat h_{z_c}(0)$.
Then for every $\phi \ge 0$,
as $z \to z_c$ we have
\begin{equation} 
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb Z^d}} \| x\|_2^\phi S_z(x)
\sim A_\phi \frac { d \hat h_{z_c}(0) } {  \sigma_{z_c}^2   }
\frac {1} {    m_z^{2+\phi} }
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\xi_\phi(z)
\sim \Bigl(\frac{A_\phi}{A_0}\Bigr)^{1/\phi} \frac 1 m_z
= 2 \biggl(\frac{\Gamma( \frac{\phi+2}{2})\Gamma( \frac{\phi+d}{2} )}{\Gamma(\frac d2)}\biggr)^{1/\phi}
	\frac 1 m_z .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 8 (Representation Power of (Smooth) HyCNNs) of arXiv:2608.22746, 'Generative Neural Networks for Sinkhorn Distributionally Robust Hypothesis Testing'] For any $L_f$-Lipschitz convex function $f: \mathbb{R}^d  \to \mathbb{R}$, compact convex set $\mathbb{D} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, and $\varepsilon > 0$, assume that $\mathbb{D}$ has a diameter $D\in(0,\infty)$ such that $\|\boldsymbol{x}_1 - \boldsymbol{x}_2\| \le D$ for any $\boldsymbol{x}_1, \boldsymbol{x}_2 \in \mathbb{D}$, and then: 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There exists a hyper input convex neural network $\widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}$ with maxout activation functions satisfying $\sup_{\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{D}} | \widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}(\boldsymbol{x}) - f(\boldsymbol{x}) | \le \varepsilon$ and $L \cdot h = \mathcal{O}((\frac{DL_f} {\varepsilon})^d)$. 
        \item There exists a smooth HyCNN with a sufficiently small parameter $\tau>0$, denoted by $\widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}^{\tau}$, satisfying $\sup_{\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{D}} | \widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}^{\tau}(\boldsymbol{x}) - f(\boldsymbol{x}) | \le \varepsilon$ and $L \cdot h = \mathcal{O}((\frac{DL_f} {\varepsilon})^d)$. 
        \item There exists a sequence of smooth HyCNNs, denoted by $\{\widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}_n^{\tau}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$, satisfying  $\widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}_n^{\tau}\to f$ uniformly on $\mathbb{D}$, 
        when $\tau$ is sufficiently small and $L \cdot h = \mathcal{O}((\frac{DL_f} {\varepsilon})^d)$. 
        
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Representation Power of (Smooth) HyCNNs

[Theorem 11 (Implicit Function Theorem) of arXiv:2606.15178, 'The distribution of the de Moivre experiment'] Assume that $ \Omega $ is an open subset of $ \mathbb{R}^2 $ and that $ f : \Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ is a function of class $ C^k $. Assume also that $ (a,b) $ is a point in $ \Omega $ such that 
	$$ f(a,b)=0 \qquad\qquad \text{ and }\qquad\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(a,b)\neq 0. $$
	Then there exist an open neighborhood $ U $ of $ (a,b) $ in $ \mathbb{R}^2 $, an open interval $ I $ of $ \mathbb{R} $ which contains $ a $, and a function $ g:I\rightarrow\mathbb{R} $ of class $ C^k $ such that, for any $ (x,y)\in U $, we have 
	$$ f(x,y)=0\Leftrightarrow y=g(x). $$
	Moreover, for all $ x \in I$, we have
	$$ g'(x)=-\dfrac{\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,g(x))}{\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,g(x))}. $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Implicit Function Theorem

[Prop evprop of arXiv:2608.30518, 'Grow-up rates of inhomogeneous semilinear heat equations in the critical dimension'] Assume that (equation katei-f of the paper), $N\ge 10$ and $f\le f_H$ in $B_1$. Then, we obtain the following.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] The operator $\mathcal{L}$ has a countable sequence of discrete eigenvalues, and the corresponding eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(B_1)$. Moreover, the first eigenvalue is simple.
    \item[(ii)]  The restriction of $\mathcal{L}$ to $L^{2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(B_1)$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions $\{\varphi_k\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ with corresponding eigenvalues $\{\mu_k\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$. Each eigenspace is one-dimensional. Thus,
    after the normalization $\varphi_k(r)>0$ near $r=0$, $\varphi_k$ is uniquely determined. Moreover, $\mu_1$ and $\varphi_1$
    coincide with the principal eigenvalue and a corresponding eigenfunction of $\mathcal{L}$ in $L^2 (B_1)$, respectively. Furthermore, $\varphi_1>0$ in $B_1$.
    \item[(iii)] Let $m=N+2\gamma$, where $\gamma$ is that in (equation defgam of the paper). We define
    \begin{equation*}
   \psi_k(r):=(\frac{N\omega_N}{m\omega_m})^{1/2}r^{\gamma}\varphi_k,
    \end{equation*}
    where $\omega_{N}$ is the volume of the $N$-dimensional unit ball.
    Then, $\psi=\psi_k$
    is an orthonormal basis in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(B_{1}^m)$ 
    for the following eigenvalue problems
    \begin{equation*}
    -\Delta\psi - K(r) \psi=\mu\psi \quad \text{in $B_{1}^m$} \quad \psi=0 \quad \text{on $\partial B_{1}^m $}
    \end{equation*}
    with $\mu=\mu_k$.
 Moreover, $\psi_k\in C^2(\overline{B_{1}^m})$ and $\psi_1>0$, $\psi_1'\le 0$ in $B_{1}^m $.
\item[(iv)]  In the case $f=f_h$, we have $\mu_1=H-h$. Moreover, if $f_1\le f_2\le f_H$ and $f_2\not\equiv f_H$ in $B_1$, then $\mu_1(f_1)\ge \mu_1(f_2)> 0$. Finally, $\mu_1\downarrow 0$ as $f\uparrow f_H$ uniformly in $B_1$.  
\item[(v)] The following maps are continuous:
\[\mathrm{Lip}[0,1]\cap \{f\le f_H \} \ni f\mapsto \mu_1 \in [0,\infty), \hspace{2mm} \mathrm{Lip}[0,1]\cap \{f\le f_H \} \ni f\mapsto  \psi_1(0) \in (0,\infty).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Biane density-cube regularity. For any Borel probability measure mu on R and any t>0, let p_t be the continuous density of mu free-additive-convolved with the centered semicircle of variance t. At every x with p_t(x)>0, its ordinary derivative exists and |p_t(x)^2*p_t_prime(x)|<=1/(4*pi^3*t^2). Consequently the globally continuous function x maps to p_t(x)^3 is Lipschitz on R with Lipschitz constant at most 3/(4*pi^3*t^2). The derivative bound is sharp: for mu a point mass at zero, equality holds at x=plus or minus sqrt(2*t). Neither compact support nor an initial density or finite moment is assumed. The derivative is asserted only on the positive-density set; the global cube-Lipschitz conclusion uses continuity through the zero set. This is Biane1997 Proposition4 and its elementary global consequence, not an entropy-differentiability or matrix mutual-information theorem.
Arbitrary Borel probability measure mu on R; t>0 is the semicircular variance, not its standard deviation.

[Lemma 36 (Uniform $2p$-moment bounds for \ref{eq:LSDE}) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Let Assumptions~\hyperref[ass:PJG]{\textup{(A1)}}--\hyperref[ass:D]{\textup{(A4)}} hold,
and let $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ solve~\ref{eq:LSDE} with $X_0=x$.
Then for any $p\in\mathbb{N}$ there exist constants $c_p>0$ and $C_p>0$ such that
for all $t\ge0$,
\[
  \E\|X_t\|^{2p}
  \;\le\;
  e^{-c_p t}\,\|x\|^{2p}
  \;+\;
  C_p,
\]
where one can take
\[
  c_p = p a,
  \qquad
  C_p = C\Bigl(b + \tfrac{1}{\beta}(d+2(p-1))\Bigr)^p
\]
for a constant $C>0$ depending only on $p$.

[Theorem 7 (Theorem 1.1 in \cite{MR3106501}) of arXiv:2606.12670, 'The censored stochastic six-vertex model and parabolic Kazhdan--Lusztig $R$-polynomials'] Consider Glauber dynamics on a monotone spin system. 
    Let $\nu$ and $\tilde{\nu}$ both be obtained by starting from the minimal configuration of the spin system and running a censored Glauber dynamics where the set of transitions censored for $\tilde{\nu}$ contains the set censored for $\nu$.
Then we have that
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\nu}\preceq\nu\preceq\pi\,,
\end{equation}
where $\pi$ is the stationary measure of the Glauber chain. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\begin{itemize}
    \item If $\lambda_1 < n-M$, then $\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda) = 0$.

\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary cor:endpoint-acm-type-two of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq4$.  The lower bound in (equation eq:endpoint-local of the paper) already counts
distinct degree-$h$ Hilbert values of arithmetically Cohen--Macaulay
projective monomial curves in $\mathbb P^{k-1}$ of Cohen--Macaulay type two.
More precisely, for $t=k-4$ and with $\xi$ recording homological degree, the
witnesses have graded Betti polynomial
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal B_{A_t}(\xi,z)
 ={}&\bigl(
  1+\xi(z^p+z^{q+s}+z^{r+s})
  +\xi^2(z^{p+s}+z^{q+r+s})
 \bigr)\\
 &\hspace{18mm}\cdot
 \prod_{i=1}^t(1+\xi z^{\ell_i}).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Writing $\beta_i(A_t)=\sum_j\beta^{A_t}_{i,j}$, their total Betti polynomial
depends only on $k$:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \sum_{i=0}^{k-2}\beta_i(A_t)\xi^i
  &=\mathcal B_{A_t}(\xi,1)=(1+2\xi)(1+\xi)^{k-3},\\
  \beta_i(A_t)&=\binom{k-3}{i}+2\binom{k-3}{i-1}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here out-of-range binomial coefficients are zero.  In particular, the
homogeneous prime toric ideal $I_{A_t}$ has
\[
 \operatorname{ht}I_{A_t}=k-2,
 \qquad
 \mu(I_{A_t})=k-1=\operatorname{ht}I_{A_t}+1,
\]
so it is an almost complete intersection.  Thus the witnesses have ACM
coordinate rings of type two.  Their defining ideals are prime toric almost
complete intersections, all with the same total Betti format.  As
$h\to\infty$, they realize $h^{k-1+o_k(1)}$ distinct degree-$h$ Hilbert
values; at $k=4$, they realize a positive proportion of the ambient interval.
The internal degree shifts in
(equation eq:endpoint-betti-tower of the paper) vary with the parameters.
Their Hilbert numerator is obtained by setting $\xi=-1$ in
(equation eq:endpoint-betti-tower of the paper); equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{HS}_{R_{A_t}}(z)=
 \frac{
  (1-z^p-z^{q+s}-z^{r+s}+z^{p+s}+z^{q+r+s})
  \prod_{i=1}^t(1-z^{\ell_i})}
 {(1-z)^k}.
\end{equation}

For all integers n >= 0 and k >= 0, binom(n, k)^2 = sum_{j=0}^k c(k, j) binom(n, 2k - j), where c(k, j) = (2k - j)!/(j! ((k - j)!)^2) = binom(2k - j, j) binom(2k - 2j, k - j) and binom(n, r) = 0 for r > n. Hence E[binom(N, k)^2] = sum_{j=0}^k c(k, j) E[binom(N, 2k - j)] for any random variable N with values in the nonnegative integers.

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2604.07697, 'Stochastic fractional heat equation with general rough noise'] \cite[Lemma 4.6]{HW2022} 
Assume that the  random fields $\{u_{\varepsilon}(t,x), {t\in[0,T],\,x\in\mathbb R}\}_{\varepsilon>0}\subset \mathcal{Z}_{\lambda,T}^p$ with
 $$
\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|u_{\varepsilon}\|_{\mathcal{Z}_{\lambda,T}^p}=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\left(\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\left\|u_{\varepsilon}(t,\cdot)\right\|_{L_{\lambda}^p(\Omega\times\mathbb{R})}
+\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathcal{N}_{\frac12-H,p}^*u_{\varepsilon}(t)\right)<\infty.
  $$
  If $u_{\varepsilon}\to u$ almost surely in $\left(\mathcal{C}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}),d_{\mathcal{C}}\right)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$, then $u\in \mathcal{Z}_{\lambda,T}^p$.

[Prop polymom of arXiv:2606.16259, 'Super-Arrhenius relaxation of the triangular plaquette model in any dimension'] A finite set \(W \subset \mathbb{Z}^d\) is admissible if and only if the Laurent polynomial
\[
\sum_{(t_1,\dots,t_d)\in W} \prod_{i=1}^d x_i^{t_i}
\]
is divisible in \(R_d\) by \(1+x_1+\cdots+x_d\).

[Thm 0103383 of arXiv:2606.29143, 'Comonotonic and moment matching approximations for sums of lognormal random variables'] Let $A = (a_1, ..., a_m)^{'}$ and $Q = (q_1, ..., q_m)^{'}$ be two numerical vectors with $\min(a_1, ..., a_m) \geq 0, \max(a_1, ..., a_m) > 0$ and $0 = q_0 < q_1 < q_2 < ... < q_m = 1$. Then for any continuous random variables $X_1, ..., X_n$ we have that $$(S^c)_{\omega} \stackrel{d}{=} (S_{\omega})^c$$

where $\stackrel{d}{=}$ stands for equality in distribution and $X_{\omega}$ denotes the step-weighted version of a continuous random $X$ associated with the step-weight function $\omega(x) = \omega_{A, Q, X}(x)$.

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2511.02725, 'Mixing of general biased adjacent transposition chains'] Consider $\Mnn$ with parameters $\vec p$ satisfying $\ep$-positive bias.

[Proposition 29 (Annealed space-time average exists, Step
	2.c)) of arXiv:2605.28677, 'Weak universality for stochastic reaction-diffusion models\\ with long-range correlated no'] Let $[\beta]\geq0$ and $ | \beta| < 2$.
	Assume that $\eqref{Pi-_shift}_\beta$ and $\eqref{Pi-_recentre}_\beta$ hold,
that $\eqref{est_Gamma}_\beta^\gamma$ holds for all $\gamma$ populated and not purely polynomial, 
and that $\eqref{est_Pi-}_{\beta'}$ holds for all populated $\beta'\prec\beta$. Then for all $T>0$

\begin{equation}
\int_T^\infty dt\, \Big| \frac{d}{dt}\EE \Pi^-_{x\beta t}(y) \Big|
\lesssim \ve^{|\beta|-\langle\beta\rangle} (\sqrt[4]{T})^{\alpha-2} (\sqrt[4]{T}+|x-y|)^{\langle\beta\rangle-\alpha} \, .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem LLTT of arXiv:2411.04590, 'Singular stochastic delay equations driven by fractional Brownian motion: Dynamics, longti'] Assume \(\mathcal{B}\) is a Banach space, and let \((T_t)_{t \geq 0}\) be a \(\mathcal{C}_0\)-semigroup acting on \(\mathcal{B}\). Assume further that for \(t \geq r\), this semigroup is compact. Let \(L: \mathcal{D}(L) \to \mathcal{B}\) denote the infinitesimal generator of this semigroup. Then, if \(\mu \in P\sigma(L)\), there exists some \(j \geq 1\) and \(b \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\mu = \lambda_j + ib\), where \(\lambda_j\) is the Lyapunov exponent of the semigroup as stated in the previous proposition. Furthermore, for every \(\lambda_j \neq -\infty\), there exists \(b \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\lambda_j + ib \in P\sigma(L)\).

body: [Theorem 1.1 (Main Theorem, Informal) of arXiv:2304.07612, 'A Cheeger Inequality for Small Set Expansion'] Let G = (V, E) be a finite, undirected, degree-regular graph, and δ, ǫ ∈ (0, 1/4). Suppose G is such that sets of density up to δ have expansion at least ǫ. Then, let V1−ǫ denote the direct sum of eigenspaces of G with eigenvalue at least 1 −ǫ. For any 2 ≤p ≤q ≤∞, the p →q norm of the eigenspace of G, ∥V1−ǫ∥p→q ≤ 1 √ δ. Our main theorem describes the “hard direction” (combinatorial to algebraic) of the equivalence.

[Thm theta-n-L1-nondegenerate of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be $p$-harmonic in $B_R(x_0)\subset \mathbb R^n$, $n\ge 3$, and assume
that $Du(x_0)=0$. Suppose that $u$ has a nondegenerate homogeneous tangent
$P$ of degree $\lambda>1$ at $x_0$, with rate $\delta>0$, in the sense of
Definition~(def:nondegenerate-homogeneous-tangent of the paper). Then, for all sufficiently
small $r>0$, $H(r)>0$, $N_\ast(r)$ is well-defined, and
$$
N_\ast(r)=\lambda+O(r^\delta).
$$
Moreover, $  \Theta(r)=O(r^{-1+\delta}). $
Consequently,
$  \Theta\in L^1(0,r_0) $
for some $r_0>0$, and the gauge-corrected frequency
$$  r\mapsto  \exp\left(\int_{r_0}^r \Theta(s)\,ds\right)N_\ast(r)
$$
is nondecreasing on $(0,r_0)$.

[Lemma lem:rebolledo of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Let $(V^1,V^2)$ be a limit point of $(V^{T,1},V^{T,2})$ in
$C([0,1];\mathbb R^2)$.  Along the same subsequence, the martingales
$(\widehat M^{T,1},\widehat M^{T,2})$ are tight in $D([0,1];\mathbb R^2)$, and
any joint limit $(W^1,W^2)$ is a pair of continuous local martingales satisfying
\begin{equation}
\langle W^i\rangle_t=\int_0^t V_s^i\,ds,
\qquad
\langle W^1,W^2\rangle_t=0.
\end{equation}
Consequently, possibly after enlarging the probability space, there exist two
independent Brownian motions $\beta^1,\beta^2$ such that
\begin{equation}
W_t^i=\int_0^t\sqrt{V_s^i}\,d\beta_s^i,
\qquad i=1,2.
\end{equation}

[Definition def:stability of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] A \textbf{stability condition} on $(\cC,\Gamma,\mathrm{cl})$ is given by 
\begin{itemize}
\item an additive map $Z\colon \Gamma\to\bC$, the \textit{central charge},
\item full additive subcategories $\cC_\phi\subset\cC$, $\phi\in\bR$, the \textit{semistable objects of phase $\phi$},
\end{itemize}
such that:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $\cC_{\phi+1}=\cC_\phi[1]$.
\item $\operatorname{Hom}(E_2,E_1)=0$ for $E_i\in\cC_{\phi_i}$, $\phi_1<\phi_2$.
\item Any $E\in\cC$ has a \textit{Harder--Narasimhan (HN) filtration}: A tower of triangles 
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=tiny]
0=E_0 \arrow{rr} & & E_1\arrow{rr}\arrow{dl} & & E_2\arrow{rr}\arrow{dl} & &\cdots \arrow{rr} &  & E_{n-1} \arrow{rr} & & E_n\cong E \arrow{dl} \\
& A_1 \arrow[dashed]{ul} & & A_2 \arrow[dashed]{ul} & & & &  & & A_n \arrow[dashed]{ul}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
with \textit{semistable factors} $0\neq A_i\in\cC_{\phi_i}$, $\phi_1>\phi_2>\ldots>\phi_n$;
\item $Z(E)\coloneqq Z(\mathrm{cl}(E))\in\bR_{>0}e^{\pi \sqrt{-1}\phi}$ for $E\in\cC_{\phi}$, $E\neq 0$.
\item The \textit{support property} (from~[KS_motivicdt]): There is a norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $\Gamma\otimes_{\bZ}\bR$ and $C>0$ such that
\[
\|\gamma\|\leq C|Z(\gamma)|
\]
for any $\gamma\in\Gamma$ which is the class of a semistable object. 
\end{enumerate}

Fix a finite Netsor program. Its inputs are fixed real vectors of fixed dimensions and independent matrix variables W of shape n by m with independent N(0,1/m) entries. Its only instructions are MatMul g=W h and coordinatewise NonLin h=phi(h_1,...,h_k), with matching dimensions; a matrix variable may be reused, but transposition is not an instruction. Let n_hidden be the program collection of dimensions internal to chains of matrix contractions, and n_output the output dimensions; input dimensions remain fixed. Fix one matrix variable W of shape n by m. Let F_(ell-1) be the sigma-algebra generated by all vector variables constructed before line ell. Stack the parent vectors previously multiplied by this W as columns of H, and their observed products W h as the corresponding columns of G. If line ell is g=W h, then h is F_(ell-1)-measurable and the conditional law of g given F_(ell-1) is Gaussian with mean G H^+ h and covariance [h^T(I_m-H H^+)h/m] I_n. Here H^+ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. H H^+ is the orthogonal projector onto the span of H, so R=I_m-H H^+ is a projector with operator norm at most one. If h lies in that span, the conditional covariance is zero and the product is determined by the previous products. Empty H,G give mean zero and covariance (|h|^2/m) I_n. The claim allows rank-deficient histories and causal reuse of W; it does not assert a formula for programs using W^T.

[Lem 13 of arXiv:2607.27535, 'Universal topological statistics on \\ triangulated singular spaces'] Suppose that $(\dist_1, \dist_2)$ are metrics on a metrizable space $M$ and let $\Delta = \Delta(\dist_1, \dist_2)$ be their distortion \eqref{eqn:metric_distortion}. Let $K_\bullet^{(i)} = \filt_\bullet(\ptx; \dist_i)$, where $\filt$ is either the Vietoris-Rips or the \v Cech filtration and $\ptx \subset M$. Then the following holds for every $\alpha > (1+\Delta)^2$:
    \begin{align*}
        \bigg| \Pi_k( K_\bullet^{(1)}) (\alpha) - \Pi_k( K_\bullet^{(2)} )(\alpha) \bigg| \le \min_{i=1, 2} \bigg( \Pi_k( K_\bullet^{(i)} )((1+\Delta)^{-2} \alpha, (1+\Delta)^2 \alpha) \bigg).
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] Let $L \supseteq \textbf{FIK}$, then we define $\mathfrak{M}_L^* = (W_L^*, \leq^*, \sqsubset^*, V^*)$, the \emph{canonical model} for $L$, by the following:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $W_L^*$ is the set of all maximal $L$-consistent theory.
    \item $(\Gamma_x, \Delta_x) \leq^* (\Gamma_x', \Delta_x')$ iff $\Gamma_x \subseteq \Gamma_x'$.
    \item $(\Gamma_x, \Delta_x) \sqsubset^* (\Gamma_y, \Delta_y)$ iff $\Box^{-1} \Gamma_x \subseteq \Gamma_y$ and $\Diamond^{-1} \Delta_x \subseteq \Delta_y$.
    \item $V^*(p) = \set{ (\Gamma_x, \Delta_x) \in W_L^*; p \in \Gamma_x }$.
  \end{itemize}

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $\mathcal B$ be a field of characteristic $0$. Let $\mathcal C$ be a $\mathcal B[G]$-module.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} We say that $\mathcal C$ is rational if it is definable over $\mathbb Q$, i.e., there exists a $\mathbb Q[G]$-module $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q}$ whose extension $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q}\otimes_{\mathbb Q} \mathcal B$ to $\mathcal B$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal C$.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} Suppose that $\mathcal B$ contains a primitive $m$-th root of unity $\zeta_m$ (e.g., $\mathcal B$ contains $B_0$). We say that $\mathcal C$ is almost rational if it is definable over $\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$, i.e., there exists a $\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)[G]$-module $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)}$ whose extension $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)}\otimes_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)} \mathcal B$ to $\mathcal B$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal C$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} A lift $\mathcal V$ of a $k[G]$-module $V$ to $R$ is called rational (resp.\ almost rational) if the $B[G]$-module $\mathcal V\otimes_R B$ is rational (resp.\ almost rational).

[Definition Percolation configuration on $\Zd$ of arXiv:2604.24743, 'The impact of disorder and non-convex interactions on delocalisation of height functions'] A site percolation configuration on a subset $\Lambda \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^d$ is a function $r \in \{ 0 , 1\}^\Lambda$. We say that a site is open in the percolation configuration $r$ if $r_x = 1$ and closed if $r_x = 0$. We implicitly extend all the site percolation configurations defined on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ (or on a subset of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}^d}$) to the extended graph $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}^d}_n$ by setting $r_x = 1$ for $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}^d}_n \setminus \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ (see Figure~(fig:extrendedperco of the paper)).
    
    An edge percolation configuration on a subset $\Lambda \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^d$ is a function $\omega \in \{ 0 , 1\}^{E(\Lambda)}$. We extend this definition to the multigraph $\mathbb{Z}^d_{n\mathrm{-mult}}$ (N.B. in this case, any edge of the multigraph is allowed to be open or closed).

[Theorem thm:convbls2 of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] For $z_1, \dots, z_n \in D$ distinct points, and 
$\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n > 0$, let 
$D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)$ be the 
$n+1$-connected domain 
$D \setminus \bigcup_{j = 1}^n \overline{\mathbb{D}(z_j,\varepsilon_j)}$. 
Let $\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}$ be the corresponding approximating metric graphs.

In these domains consider the Brownian loop soup 
$\mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}$ at the critical intensity, and the metric graph loop soup 
$\widetilde \mathcal{L}_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}}$, also at the critical intensity. 
Let 
$\widetilde \Xi^a_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}}$ denote the PPP of Brownian boundary to boundary excursions of intensity equal to $a \geq 0$ on the outer boundary and equal to $0$ on the inner boundaries on the metric graph 
$\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}$. 
We let $\Xi_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}^a$ denote the corresponding PPP of Brownian boundary to boundary excursions in the continuum.

Finally, let 
$(\widetilde C_k^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n, m})_{k \geq 1}$ 
be the clusters of 
$\widetilde \Xi^a_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}} 
\cup \widetilde \mathcal{L}_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}}$, 
and $(C_k^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n})_{k \geq 1}$ the clusters of $\Xi_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}^a 
\cup \mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}$,  
listed say by the order of decreasing diameter. 
Let $\widetilde \gamma, \gamma$ denote closed paths on the metric graph and in the continuum respectively.

Then we have that the probabilities
$$\tilde p^{\rm mult}_{a,m} := \mathbb{P}\left(\nexists \widetilde C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n, m}\text{ with }\widetilde \gamma \in \widetilde C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n, m}\text{ such that} \sum_{j=1}^{n}
\indx_{\widetilde \gamma}(z_j)
\text{ odd}
\right),$$ 
converge, as $m \to \infty$, to 
$$p^{\rm mult}_a := \mathbb{P}\left(\nexists C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}\text{ with }\gamma \in C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}\text{ such that} \sum_{j=1}^{n}
\indx_{\gamma}(z_j)
\text{ odd}\right).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:convbls2 of arXiv:2604.15146

[Proposition 36 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(q\in Y^{\rm rv}\), choose a relatively compact holomorphic
coordinate neighbourhood \(U\Subset Y^{\rm rv}\), coordinates
\(a=(a^1,\ldots,a^m):U\to\C^m\) with \(a(q)=0\), and
\[
                         q\in U_0\Subset U_1\Subset U.
\]
Let \(\xi=(\mu_t)_{t<T}\) be a fixed limiting point based at \(q\),
and let \(\tau_i\searrow0\) realize a tangent space at \(\xi\), whose
time-\((-1)\) model is
\((Z,d,\cR,g,J,f,\mathfrak m)\).  On \(\pi^{-1}(U)\), set
\begin{equation}
                             F_i=\tau_i^{-1/2}a\circ\pi.
\end{equation}
Assume $(\mathrm S)_U$.  After passing to a further subsequence still
realizing the same tangent space, the maps $F_i$ converge
smoothly on every compact time-$(-1)$ regular chart to a holomorphic map
\begin{equation}
                              F:\cR\longrightarrow\C^m.
\end{equation}
The limit \(F\) has bounded differential and therefore extends uniquely
to a globally Lipschitz map \(F:Z\to\C^m\).  This extension is
holomorphic on the normal complex space \(Z\).

If $(\mathrm Q)_U$ also holds, then on $\cR$
\begin{equation}
 cI_m\le
 \left[\langle dF^\alpha,d\overline{F^\beta}\rangle_{g^{-1}}
 \right]_{\alpha,\beta=1}^m
 \le CI_m.
\end{equation}

[Definition def:gaussian:measure of arXiv:2605.28106, 'Gaussian Processes with Sample Paths in Reproducing Kernel Banach Spaces'] A probability measure \( \gamma \) on \( (X,\mathcal{C}(X)) \) is called a \emph{Gaussian measure} if the characteristic functional of \( \gamma \) has the form
    \begin{equation} 
        \widehat{\gamma}(f) =
        \exp\left(ia(f)-\frac{1}{2}R(f,f)\right),
        \qquad \forall f\in X^*,
    \end{equation}
    where \( a : X^* \to \mathbb{R} \) is a linear functional and \( R : X^* \times X^* \to \mathbb{R} \) is a symmetric, positive bilinear form.
title: Definition def:gaussian:measure of arXiv:2605.28106

[Definition def:strong-local-minimizer of arXiv:2608.30904, 'Entire monotone solutions of the anisotropic Allen--Cahn equation in dimension 5'] A function $u\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^4)$ is an
\emph{$L^\infty$-local minimizer} of $E_\varepsilon$ if, for every bounded
Lipschitz domain $\Omega\Subset\mathbb R^4$, there exists $\eta>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
E_\varepsilon(u;\Omega)\le E_\varepsilon(w;\Omega)
\end{equation}
whenever $w-u\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$ and $\|w-u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}<\eta.$

It is \emph{strict} if equality implies $w=u$ almost everywhere in
$\Omega$.

[Proposition prop:randomcluster-Ising of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected graph. Let $\Omega:=\{0,1\}^E$ be the space of bond configurations and $\Sigma:=\{-1,+1\}^V$ be the space of spin configurations. Define $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ by 
$
      f(\omega) = \{ \sigma \in \Sigma \mid \omega_e = 0, \forall e \not \in S(\sigma) \}.
$ 
For any $A\subset V$ with $|A|$ even, let
	\[\rho[\omega] \propto 1\! \!1[\omega\in\mathcal{F}_A]\mathbb{P}_p[\omega],~\forall \omega\in\Omega,~\gamma[\sigma]\propto 1, ~\forall \sigma\in \Sigma,\]
    where $p=(1-e^{-2J_e})_{e\in E}$.
	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\mu^A$ defined by
		$\mu^A[\sigma] \propto \mu[\sigma] \mathbb{P}_{S(\sigma),p}[\mathcal{F}_A].$
		 For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\omega\in\mathcal{F}_A$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]$ on $\Sigma$ is realized by tossing independent fair coins to get $\pm$ for each open cluster.
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is $\phi_p[\;\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_A]$.  For each $\sigma\in\Sigma$ with $S(\sigma)\in\mathcal{F}_A$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \sigma]$ on $\Omega$ is the independent Bernoulli percolation on $S(\sigma)$ with parameter $p$ conditioned on $\mathcal{F}_A$,  $\mathbb{P}_{S(\sigma),p}[\;\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_A]$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma lem:subset of arXiv:2609.01998, 'New Upper bounds on the Mondrian Art Problem'] Let $m, \ell$ be positive integers such that $m > \ell \geq \sqrt{2m}+1$. Fix $r \in \{0, 1, \ldots, m-1\}$ and let $s$ be the smallest positive integer such that $s(s + 1)/2 \geq r$. Then for any integer $k$ with $s \leq k \leq 2\ell - s$ there exists a subset of $\{m-\ell, \ldots, m+\ell\}$ summing to $mk+r$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 35 (Time-dependent $T_2$ inequality) of arXiv:2608.28827, 'Quantitative Target Convergence and Uniform-in-Time\\ Propagation of Chaos for Langevin-Re'] Take any $\varepsilon>0$. Let $\rho_t$ be the law of
\[
    dZ_t=a_t(Z_t)\,dt+\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\,dW_t,
    \qquad Z_0\sim\rho_0.
\]
Assume that \((t,x)\mapsto a_t(x)\) is measurable and that, for every
\(T<\infty\), there exist \(L_T,C_T<\infty\) such that
\[
    \|a_t(x)-a_t(y)\|\le L_T\|x-y\|,
    \qquad
    \|a_t(x)\|\le C_T(1+\|x\|),
\]
for all \(t\in[0,T]\) and \(x,y\in\R^d\). Moreover, assume that
\begin{equation}
    \langle x-y,a_t(x)-a_t(y)\rangle\le L\|x-y\|^2
\end{equation}
uniformly in $t$.  If $\rho_0\in T_2(C_0)$, then $\rho_t\in T_2(C_t)$, where
\begin{equation}
    C_t=C_0e^{2Lt}+2\varepsilon\int_0^t e^{2L(t-s)}\,ds.
\end{equation}
Thus
\[
    C_t=
    \begin{cases}
      C_0e^{2Lt}+\dfrac{\varepsilon}{L}(e^{2Lt}-1),&L\ne0,\\[1ex]
      C_0+2\varepsilon t,&L=0,
    \end{cases}
\]
and $C_t\le C(1+C_0)e^{\ell t}$ for some finite $C$ and some \(\ell\ge0\).

[Theorem 22 of arXiv:2609.01436, '2609.01436'] Assume \cref{ass:CL}, and let $F_t$ be a conservative isotropic measure
solution with conserved mass $N>0$ and energy $E>0$; set
$c_0=\sqrt{NE}$.  Fix $t_0\geq0$, $h\in(0,N]$,
$\delta\in(0,1/2)$, and an integer $j\geq k_0$, where
$k_0=k_0(N)$ is supplied by \cref{lem:scales}.  Suppose
$N_{0,2}(F_{t_0},\varepsilon_j)\geq h$.
Set
\begin{equation}
 \tau_j(h,\delta)
 =2e^{2c_0}\delta^{-2}h^{-2}\Theta_j(h)^2.
\end{equation}
If $\tau_j(h,\delta)\leq1$, then there exists
$T\in[t_0,t_0+\tau_j(h,\delta)]$ such that
\begin{equation}
 F_T(\{0\})
 \geq(1-\delta)e^{-c_0(T-t_0)}h>0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, every $t\geq T$ satisfies
$F_t(\{0\})\geq(1-\delta)e^{-c_0(t-t_0)}h$.
The interval length also satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \tau_j(h,\delta)
 \lesssim_{h,\delta,N,E,b_0,\eta}
 (1+j)^2\varepsilon_j^{1-\eta}\to 0.
\end{equation}

[Proposition prop:decomp of arXiv:2606.05377, 'The Clark-Kushner condition for interacting reinforced random walks on finite graphs'] For every $k \geq 0$,
\begin{equation}
U(k+1) = D(k+1) - \big(H(k+1) - H(k)\big) + C(k+1),
\end{equation}
where
\[
D(k+1) = \xi(k+1)\mathcal{P}(X(k)) - \xi(k)Q(X(k))\mathcal{P}(X(k)),
\qquad
H(k) = \xi(k)Q(X(k))\mathcal{P}(X(k)),
\]
\[
C(k+1) = \xi(k+1)\big[Q(X(k+1))\mathcal{P}(X(k+1)) - Q(X(k))\mathcal{P}(X(k))\big].
\]
Moreover $D(k+1)$ is a martingale difference with respect to $\mathcal{F}_k$, and
$D$ and $H$ are uniformly bounded: $\|H(k)\| \leq C_\mathcal{P}$ and
$\|D(k+1)\| \leq 2C_\mathcal{P}$, with $C_\mathcal{P}$ as in~(equation eqn:P_bound of the paper).
title: Proposition prop:decomp of arXiv:2606.05377

[Theorem sufcond2 of arXiv:2505.11721, 'Variational principles for Hausdorff and packing dimensions of fractal percolation on self'] Let $h\in (1,2]$ and $(b_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be an unbounded increasing positive sequence such that  
$$
\sum_{n\ge 1}\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}W^{(n)}_i |\log W^{(n)}_i|^h)}{b_n^h }<+\infty.
$$
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\liminf_{N\to +\infty} b_N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N H(W^{(n)})>0$, then $\mathbb{E}(\|\nu\|)=1$.   Moreover, if for all $v\in \mathcal{I}^*$ one has $\mathbb{P}(W_i(v)>0)=\mathbb{P}(c_i(v)=1)$, then conditional on $K_\omega\neq\emptyset$, $K_\omega=\supp(\mu_\omega)$; equivalently, $\supp(\mu_\omega)=K_\omega$ almost surely.

\item If $\liminf_{N\to +\infty} b_N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N H(W^{(n)})<0$, then $\nu=0$ almost surely. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 9 (Averaged kernel) of arXiv:2606.23222, 'A Route to Harris ergodicity for Non-Feller Markov Kernels'] Assume that \(P\) is quasi-Feller and \(\psi\)-irreducible, with
\[
        \operatorname{Int}(\operatorname{supp}\psi)\neq\varnothing .
\]
Assume also that \(P\) satisfies the coercive geometric drift
\eqref{eq:drift}. Then every Lyapunov sublevel set
\(C_R=\{V\le R\}\) is petite.

Consequently, if \(R>2K/(1-\gamma)\), there exists a probability distribution
\(a=(a_n)_{n\ge1}\) on \(\mathbb N^*\) such that the averaged kernel
\[
        K_a=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nP^n
\]
has \(C_R\) as a small set. Moreover \(K_a\) satisfies a geometric Lyapunov
drift for which the same threshold \(R>2K/(1-\gamma)\) is sufficient in the
Hairer--Mattingly theorem. Hence \(K_a\) is geometrically ergodic in weighted
total variation.

## Reviewed v1 proof text

# Linear hardness with bounded covariance condition number

Status: proof (unaudited). Target 2, endpoint-qualified result.
The hardest step is transferring the distributional score guarantee under
contamination; its complete argument is in clipped_oracle_transfer.md.

## Precise model and conclusion

Fix a polynomial per-round query budget P(d) and inverse-polynomial
0<e(d)<=1. The oracle is a fixed jointly measurable field satisfying
E_{Q*Gaussian(sigma^2 I)}||f_sigma-s_{Q,sigma}||^2<=e^2/sigma^2
for EVERY sigma>0. Queries may use arbitrary points and positive noise
levels, and the algorithm has no hidden-instance information beyond the
oracle and public parameters. No pointwise-error or Lipschitz promise is
imposed. The result below does not assert an absolute error bound uniform
over sigma.

There is a family Q^theta in R^d with E||Y||^2<=2 and
kappa(Cov(Q^theta))<=3, with such legal fixed oracles, so every randomized
algorithm using fewer than d adaptive rounds has TV error at least
0.9-eta on at least 0.9 of the hidden instances. Here
B=4(d+1)/e and eta=e^2/[4(B+d)^2]. Thus eta is inverse polynomial,
eta<=1/(2d), and eta<1/4 (indeed <=1/324 for d>=1).

The same lower bound, less 1/200, holds for sampling the Gaussian-smoothed
law Q^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I) whenever 0<tau<=h_d/(100d).
This is exponentially fine smoothing, with
log(1/tau)=O(d log q + log(Md)) for tau chosen at the displayed boundary.
For these smoothed laws the second moment is at most 3 and condition
number at most 3. This is NOT a fixed-smoothing dimensional lower bound.

## Construction and proof

1. Invoke Kou--Wang, arXiv:2610.09166v1, Theorem 4.1, with original
score tolerance e0=e/4 and query budget P(d). Their fixed public box
parameters (Appendix B.1, (61)--(62)) are
M=ceil(100(dP+1)), q=100Md/e0, a_i=q^{-(i-1)}/4,
h_i=a_i/(100M), and centers a_i+(k-1/2)a_i/M. Write P^theta for the
uniform box law and a^theta for their fixed legal oracle.

The supplied theorem says: for every randomized algorithm using fewer
than d rounds, TV(output,P^theta)>=0.9 on a set of theta of probability
at least 0.9. Public parameters and oracles are independent of the sampler.
This theorem is used as settled ground, not re-proved.

2. Their Lemma B.1 gives support in the unit ball and
Cov(P^theta)=diag(h_i^2/3). In particular
||Cov(P^theta)||op=h_1^2/3=1/(480000 M^2)<=1/d,
since M>=100d for integer P>=1. Let H=N(0,I/(eta d)), public and
independent of theta, and Q^theta=(1-eta)P^theta+eta H.

Writing mu=E P^theta and Sigma=Cov(P^theta), the covariance identity is
Cov(Q^theta)=I/d+(1-eta)Sigma+eta(1-eta)mu mu^T.
It follows in quadratic form order that I/d<=Cov(Q^theta)<=3I/d.
Also E_Q||Y||^2=(1-eta)E_P||Y||^2+1<=2.

3. Supply f^theta_sigma=projection_{ball(B/sigma)} a^theta_sigma.
The clipping-transfer lemma gives score error at most e^2/(2sigma^2),
hence the requested e^2/sigma^2 guarantee. All parameters are public,
and f is fixed and jointly measurable. A batch of queries to f is
simulated by exactly the same batch to a, then deterministic clipping.
No extra information, extra adaptive round, or hidden density is used.

4. Given any sampler for Q using f, simulate it using a as just described.
Its output law L^theta is exactly the same. Theorem 4.1 gives
TV(L^theta,P^theta)>=0.9 on at least 0.9 of theta. As
TV(P^theta,Q^theta)<=eta, triangle inequality yields
TV(L^theta,Q^theta)>=0.9-eta there. This proves the unsmoothed conclusion.
For sequential samplers, at least d rounds implies at least d queries.

5. For a one-dimensional uniform law U on an interval of half-width h,
TV(U,U+z)=min(1,|z|/(2h)). Convexity under mixtures gives
TV(U,U+tau Z)<=tau E|Z|/(2h)<=tau/(2h).
For products, the telescoping product bound (or independent coupling)
gives TV(P^theta,P^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I))
<=sum_i tau/(2h_i)<=d*tau/(2h_d)<=1/200.
This uses no false multiplication of conditional query probabilities.
Therefore TV(Q^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I),P^theta)<=eta+1/200.
The same simulated output lower bound is now 0.9-eta-1/200.
Adding tau^2 I to a positive covariance can only reduce its condition
number, and the second moment increases by d*tau^2<=1.

6. If one treats R^theta=Q^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I) as the base target,
its legal oracle at additional noise sigma is f^theta_{sqrt(tau^2+sigma^2)}.
Its squared error is at most e^2/[2(tau^2+sigma^2)]<=e^2/sigma^2.
Again one original query suffices. Thus the construction also yields
smooth positive densities, with intrinsic smoothing tau exponentially small.

7. For the OU convention X_t=e^{-t}Y+sqrt(1-e^{-2t})Z, set
sigma=sqrt(e^{2t}-1). Its score is
e^t s_{Q,sigma}(e^t x), and the corresponding oracle is
e^t f_sigma(e^t x). Its error bound is e^2/(1-e^{-2t}).
To target the OU endpoint at time t, rescale the sampler's output by e^t.
The Gaussian endpoint argument applies when sqrt(e^{2t}-1)<=h_d/(100d).
Any stronger OU error normalization requires an additional argument.

## What this moves, and what remains open

Covariance conditioning alone does not prevent the linear box mechanism:
rare public mass repairs it while clipped approximate oracles preserve
hardness. The targets are neither log-concave nor uniform convex-body laws;
this does not answer the source paper's near-isotropic convex-body question.
Their fourth moments grow as eta decreases; bounded second moment is the
only tail assumption used here.

The fixed or inverse-polynomial smoothing endpoint is the unpaid step.
The box coordinates below that smoothing scale can be discarded in TV,
so this construction does not close T306's dimension exponent at that
endpoint. It is a complete lower bound for unsmoothed targets and for the
explicit fine endpoint above. The reviewer must decide how Target 2's
unstated endpoint dependence should be scored; the row must not be closed
on the strength of this qualified result.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:02ed4e3e9471762e0c7b668ebd062aacf59e2c7858ef371bcde0c00af522059d","revision_digest":"sha256:2e56818e86f2f7ad5ae3c3fb468643d4d7ae566a5992507c769ae33bb5e065ac","source_id":"own-work:w720-T306-C03","source_revision":"C03 v2; scope-only clarification, proof (unaudited); v1 PASS by urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28; 2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
[Defn 2 (continuous R\'enyi and Tsallis entropies) of arXiv:2607.17576, 'How much randomness is needed to symmetrize a random variable?'] Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable with density $f$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure. For $\alpha\in (0, 1)\cup (1, \infty)$, the R\'enyi entropy $h_\alpha(X)$ of order $\alpha$ is defined by
$$
h_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log \int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)^\alpha dx
$$
and the Tsallis entropy $T_\alpha(X)$ of order $\alpha$ is defined by
$$
T_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)^\alpha dx-1\right).
$$
Taking the limit $\alpha\to 1$, both entropies are reduced to the Boltzman-Shannon entropy 
$$
h(X)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)\log f(x)dx.
$$
title: continuous R\'enyi and Tsallis entropies

The global Fourier entropy-influence conjecture asks for one finite absolute C with H(f)<=C sum_i I_i(f) for every Boolean f in every dimension; none of the accompanying local drafts asserts that conjecture is proved.

[Proposition 5 (Minimization over equivariant fields) of arXiv:2608.26961, 'Gromov--Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation'] Let $\pi\in\mathrm{c}_{\R^D}(\mu,\nu)$ be arbitrary. Then the
field $v^{\pi^G}$ associated with $\pi^G$ minimizes $J_\pi$ over all
$G$-equivariant fields:
\[
v^{\pi^G}\in
\argmin_{\substack{v:I\times\R^D\to\R^D\ \mathrm{jointly\ Borel}\\
v_t(gx)=gv_t(x)\ \forall\,t,g,x}}
J_\pi(v).
\]
In particular, the constrained problem is the ordinary
flow-matching problem for the diagonally symmetrized coupling $\pi^G$.

body:
[Lemma lem:h_inverse of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] The characteristic sub-gamma function $h(u) = 1 + u - \sqrt{1+2u}$ 
is a strictly increasing
function from $[0,\infty)$ onto $[0,\infty)$ with inverse
\begin{align}
  h^{-1}(v) = v + \sqrt{2v},
  \qquad 
  v\geq 0.
  
\end{align}
Consequently, for any $v \geq 0$,
$h(u) \geq v$ if and only if $u \geq v + \sqrt{2v}$.

		$X_h(r,\theta)$ as in (equation sphere-h of the paper). Then
		\[
		H_h
		=
		\frac2R
		-
		\left(
		\Delta_{S_R}h
		+
		\frac{2}{R^2}h
		\right)
		+
		\mathcal Q_{S_R}[h],
		\]
		where
		\[
		\mathcal Q_{S_R}[h]
		=
		Q_2(h)
		+
		\mathcal R(h),
		\]
		with
		\[
		Q_2(h)
		=
		\frac{2}{R}h\Delta_{S_R}h
		+
		\frac{2}{R^3}h^2.
		\]
		Moreover,
		\[
		|\mathcal Q_{S_R}[h]|
		\lesssim
		\left( |{h \over R}|^2 +			|\nabla_{S_R}h|^2 \right)
		|\nabla_{S_R}^2h|
		+
		\frac1R
		\left(
		\frac{|h|}{R}
		+
		|\nabla_{S_R}h|
		\right)^2.
		\]
		Assume in addition that
		\[
		\frac{|h|}{R}
		+
		|\nabla_{S_R}h|
		+
		R|\nabla_{S_R}^2h|
		\leq \delta
		\]
		for some sufficiently small universal constant $\delta>0$. Then the
		cubic remainder satisfies
		$$
		\begin{aligned}
			|\mathcal R(h)|
			\leq{}&
			\frac{C}{R}
			\left[
			\left(
			\frac{|h|}{R}
			\right)^2
			+
			|\nabla_{S_R}h|^2
			\right]
			R|\nabla_{S_R}^2h|

			&+
			\frac{C}{R}
			\left[
			\left(
			\frac{|h|}{R}
			\right)^3
			+
			\frac{|h|}{R}|\nabla_{S_R}h|^2
			+
			|\nabla_{S_R}h|^4
			\right].
		\end{aligned}
		$$
		In particular,
		\[
		|\mathcal R(h)|
		\leq
		\frac{C}{R}
		\left(
		\frac{|h|}{R}
		+
		|\nabla_{S_R}h|
		+
		R|\nabla_{S_R}^2h|
		\right)^3.
		\]

\begin{itemize}

    \item $G$ admits a dominating set $D=\{u,v\}$ such that 
    \[
    N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset 
    \quad \text{and} \quad 
    \deg(u)+\deg(v)=|V(G)|.
    \]
\end{itemize}

[Corollary 55 of arXiv:2604.09933, 'Explicit cutoff profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random shuffles'] For \(1\le q<\infty\),
\[
\left\|\frac{\widetilde Q_{\mu,p}(\cdot)}{U(\cdot)}-1\right\|_{L^q(U)}^q
=
\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}U\{L_p=\ell\}\,|S_\mu(\ell)-1|^q.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\left\|\frac{\widetilde Q_{\mu,p}(\cdot)}{U(\cdot)}-1\right\|_{L^q(U)}^q
=
\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}
\left(\frac{1}{\ell!\,p^\ell}-\frac{1}{(\ell+1)!\,p^{\ell+1}}\right)|S_\mu(\ell)-1|^q
+\frac{1}{n!\,p^n}|S_\mu(n)-1|^q.
\]
title: Corollary 55 of arXiv:2604.09933

body: Let (M,g) be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension n with Ricci curvature Ric >= (n-1) K for a constant K, and let M_K be the complete simply connected model space of constant sectional curvature K. For p in M, let V(p,r) be the volume of the geodesic ball of radius r about p, and V_K(r) the volume of a radius-r ball in M_K. The Bishop-Gromov inequality states that the ratio V(p,r)/V_K(r) is a nonincreasing function of r > 0 (if K > 0, for 0 < r <= pi/sqrt(K), the diameter of M_K, which by Bonnet-Myers also bounds the diameter of M), with limit 1 as r -> 0; consequently V(p,r) <= V_K(r) for every such r. Due to Richard Bishop and Mikhail Gromov.
title: Bishop-Gromov inequality

body:
[Theorem thm:mPAM of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For each $\epsilon>0$, we take $d_\epsilon>0$, such that $d_\epsilon\epsilon^{1/2}|\log(\epsilon)|\to 0$ as $\epsilon\to 0$.
Then consider the following function defined on $\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$:
\begin{equation}   
\mathcal{M}^{\rho,\epsilon}(x, s; y, t):= -\epsilon^{1/2}H_{d_\epsilon}^-(\lfloor 2\epsilon^{-1}x \rfloor, 2\epsilon^{-3/2}s;  \lfloor 2\epsilon^{-1}y \rfloor, 2\epsilon^{-3/2}t) + \epsilon^{-1}(t-s),
\end{equation}
where either (1) fixed $\alpha\ge \frac{1}{2}$ and $\rho=-\infty$, or (2) $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}-\rho\epsilon^{1/2}/2$ for some $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$.
Then as $\epsilon\to 0$, the above function converges to $\mathcal{L}^\rho$, weakly under the uniform-on-compact topology.

[Theorem thm_main of arXiv:2411.08846, 'On the Number of Crossings and Bouncings\\ of a Diffusion at a Sticky Threshold'] Let $X$ be the sticky Brownian motion of stickiness parameter $\rho>0$ defined on the filtered probability space $(\Omega, \bF, (\bF_t)_{t\ge 0},\Prob_x) $ such that $\Prob_x$-a.s., $X_0 = x$ (in particular, $X$ is $(\bF_t)_{t\ge 0}$-adapted),  
and let $\loct{X}{0}{} $ be the right local time at $0$ of $X$.
Then, the following convergences holds, 
\begin{enumerate}
	[label={ (\roman*)}]
	\item  for every diverging sequence $u_n$, it holds that:  
	$ \cC{0}{n,\cdot}(X)/u_n  \convergence{\Prob_x\text{-}\mathrm{ucp}} 0 $, 
	\item 
	$ \cD{1}{n,\cdot}(X) /\sqrt n \convergence{\Prob_x\text{-}\mathrm{ucp}}
	4 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \loct{X}{0}{} $ 
	and $ \cC{1}{n,\cdot}(X) /\sqrt n \convergence{\Prob_x\text{-}\mathrm{ucp}}
	4 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \loct{X}{0}{} $, 
	 
	\item 
	$ \cD{2}{n,\cdot}(X) /n \convergence{\Prob_x\text{-}\mathrm{ucp}} \rho \loct{X}{0}{} $
	and 
	$ \cC{2}{n,\cdot}(X) /n \convergence{\Prob_x\text{-}\mathrm{ucp}} \rho \loct{X}{0}{}$, 
\end{enumerate}
where as per~(equation eq_txt_sticky_pathwise of the paper), $\rho \loct{X}{0}{t} = \int_{0}^{t} \mathbbm{1}_{\{X_s = 0\}} \,\mathrm{d} s  $, for all $t\ge 0 $. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 8 of arXiv:2609.01020, '2609.01020'] Let $Y\subset X$ be a complex analytic subset of $X$. 
A stratification $Y=\bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A}Y_\alpha$ of $Y$ is called a Whitney 
stratification if it satisfies the following conditions (a) and (b): 
\begin{enumerate}
\item [(a)]
Assume that a sequence $x_i\in Y_\alpha$ of points converges to a point $y\in Y_\beta \ 
(\alpha \neq \beta)$ and the limit $\mathbf{T}$ of the tangent spaces $T_{x_i}S_\alpha$ exists. 
Then we have $T_y Y_\beta \subset \mathbf{T}$. 
\item [(b)] 
Let $x_i \in Y_\alpha$ and $y_i \in Y_\beta$ be two sequences of points which converge to 
the same point $y\in Y_\beta \ (\alpha \neq \beta)$. Assume further that the limit $\ell$ 
(resp. $\mathbf{T}$) of the complex lines $\ell_i$ joining $x_i$ and $y_i$ (resp. of the 
tangent spaces $T_{x_i}Y_\alpha$) exists. 
Then we have $\ell \subset \mathbf{T}$. 
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 8 of arXiv:2609.01020

body: [Cor prop:implication of arXiv:2605.10908, 'On Talagrand's Convexity Conjecture'] Suppose that for any $n\geq 1$, any random vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ which is dominated in convex order by a standard Gaussian random vector is the sum of three standard Gaussian vectors. Let $b, c \in (0, 1)$ satisfy $2b +c \leq 1$. Then for any closed set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $\gamma_{n}(A) > \frac{5}{6}$, the set $b^{-1}(A+A+A)$ contains a symmetric convex body $K$ with $\gamma_{n}(K) \geq c$.

\]
Here and throughout this theorem, for $2<p<\infty$,

$C_w([0,T];W^{1,p})$.

Moreover, for every $2<p\le\infty$, if $w_0\in W^{1,p}$, there exists

\[
\sup_{t\ge0}\|\nabla w(t)\|_{p}<\infty,

\]

body:
[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $P$ be the transition matrix of a reversible Markov chain; That is, $P$ satisfies,
   \[\pi(x) P(x,y) = \pi(y)P(y,x),\quad \forall x,y\in \Omega\]
   where $\pi$ is the stationary distribution. Then,
   \[\langle Pf,g\rangle_\pi = \langle f,Pg\rangle_\pi,\quad \forall f,g \in \mathbb{R}^\Omega\]
   \begin{proof}
     \begin{align*}
      \langle Pf, g\rangle_\pi &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}(Pf)(x)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}\sum_{y\in \Omega}P(x,y)f(y)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}\sum_{y\in \Omega}P(x,y)f(y)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{y\in \Omega}\sum_{x\in \Omega}P(y,x)g(x)f(y)\pi(y)\tag{By reversibility}\\
      &= \sum_{y\in \Omega}(Pg)(y)f(y)\pi(y)\\
      &=  \langle f, Pg\rangle_\pi
     \end{align*} 
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 12 of arXiv:2604.07478

body:
[Thm random coordinate change of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] Assume the setting of Theorem~(Loewner coordinate change in H of the paper), and suppose the driving function \( W_t \in \mathbb{R} \) evolves according to the stochastic differential equation
\begin{equation}
dW_t = \sqrt{\kappa} \, dB_t + b\left(W_t; \Psi_t(W_1), \ldots, \Psi_t(W_n)\right)\, dt,
\end{equation}
where \( B_t \) is standard Brownian motion, and \( b \) is a drift term depending on the conformal images of marked points under the time-dependent conformal map
\[
\Psi_t := \widetilde{g}_t \circ \Psi \circ g_t^{-1},
\]
with \( \Psi \) conformal near \( W_0 \in \mathbb{R} \) and \( g_t \), \( \widetilde{g}_t \) the Loewner flows before and after coordinate change, respectively.

Define the transformed driving function \( \widetilde{W}_t := \Psi_t(W_t) \), and introduce the reparameterized time
\[
s(t) := \int_0^t |\Psi_u'(W_u)|^2 \, du.
\]
Then the time-changed process \( \widetilde{W}_s := \widetilde{W}_{t(s)} \) satisfies the stochastic differential equation
\begin{equation}

d\widetilde{W}_s = \sqrt{\kappa} \, dB_s 
+ \frac{b\left(W_s; \Psi_{t(s)}(W_1), \ldots, \Psi_{t(s)}(W_n)\right)}{\Psi_{t(s)}'(W_s)} \, ds 
+ \frac{\kappa - 6}{2} \cdot \frac{\Psi_{t(s)}''(W_s)}{[\Psi_{t(s)}'(W_s)]^2} \, ds.
\end{equation}
title: Stochastic Loewner chain under coordinate change

body:
[Maintheorem 3 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] There is a probability law \(\mu_H\) on
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal Y
  :=\mathbb R_+^2\times C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R_+)^2
  
\end{equation}
equipped with its product topology, with local uniform convergence in each
path coordinate,
such that
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L_{\widehat{\PP}_a}
  (U_a,V_a,\overline L_a,\overline R_a)
  \Longrightarrow \mu_H.
  
\end{equation}
Let \((U,V,\overline L,R)\) denote the coordinate random element under
\(\mu_H\).
The left horizon \(U\) is finite almost surely, whereas \(R\) is defined on
the whole half-line.  The path \(\overline L\) is constant on
\([U,\infty)\) almost surely.  Write \(L\) for the restriction of the
constant-extended path \(\overline L\) to \([0,U]\).  Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  J_\infty
  :=\int_0^Ue^{-L(s)}\,\mathrm ds
    +\int_0^\infty e^{-R(s)}\,\mathrm ds
  
\end{equation}
satisfies \(0<J_\infty<\infty\) almost surely and
\begin{equation}
  J_a\Longrightarrow J_\infty,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\EE}_a[J_a^{-1}]
  \longrightarrow
  D_H:=\EE_{\mu_H}[J_\infty^{-1}]\in(0,\infty).
  
\end{equation}
Finally, the persistence probability satisfies
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{T\to\infty}{T^{1-H}}{\PP\bigl(B_t\leq1\text{ for every }0\leq t\leq T\bigr)} = \mathsf C_H,
  
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf C_H
  =\frac{H\,\EE[M]}{\Gamma(1/H)D_H}.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Maintheorem 3 of arXiv:2607.21374

[Maintheorem 1 (Stationary product limit and avalanche sharpness) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] For each $\gamma\in\{\mathrm{os},\mathrm{iso}\}$,
\[
        t_{\mathrm d}^\gamma
        =t_{\mathrm{sus}}^\gamma
        =t_\infty^\gamma
        =:t_c^\gamma.
\]

The critical values satisfy
\[
        1\leq t_c^{\mathrm{os}}\leq2\log2,
        \qquad
        \frac13\leq t_c^{\mathrm{iso}}
        \leq t_c^{\mathrm{os}}.
\]
Moreover, for every fixed collection of distinct sites
$x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\in\mathbb Z$, viewed as elements of $\Lambda_N$ for sufficiently large $N$,
\[
        \bigl(
        F_{N,x_1}^\gamma,\ldots,F_{N,x_\ell}^\gamma
        \bigr)
        \xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{\mathrm d}
        \nu_{t_c^\gamma}^{\otimes\ell}.
\]
Equivalently, in the original uniform parametrisation, the limiting
fitnesses are independent and uniform on $[q_c^\gamma,1]$, where
$q_c^\gamma:=1-e^{-t_c^\gamma}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stationary product limit and avalanche sharpness

exists.  Consequently, for every $f\in C_c^\infty(M)$,
\begin{equation}
  A_hf(x)\longrightarrow\mathcal A_\mu f(x),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal A_\mu$ is given by
(equation eq:general-limit-operator of the paper) and
\begin{equation}
  \Gamma_i(x)=J_x(0)\Lambda_i(x)
  +\sum_{j=1}^kM_{ij}(x)\beta_j(x).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop: approx_ample of arXiv:2412.07690, 'A law of large numbers concerning the distribution of critical points of random Fourier se'] Suppose that ${\boldsymbol{U}}$ is a Banach space with norm $\Vert-\Vert$, ${\boldsymbol{T}}$ is a compact metric space, $N\in {{\mathbb N}}$ and 
\[
G: {\boldsymbol{U}}^N\times {\boldsymbol{T}}\to [0,\infty) ,\;\;(u_1,\dotsc, u_N,t)\mapsto G(u_1,\dotsc, u_N,t) \in [0,\infty)
\]
is a continuous  function. We  define
\[
G_* : {\boldsymbol{U}}^N\to [0,\infty),\;\; G_*(u_1,\dotsc, u_N):= \min_{t\in {\boldsymbol{T}}} G(u_1,\dotsc, u_N, t).
\]
Suppose that there exist $v_1,\dotsc, v_N\in {\boldsymbol{U}}$ such that  $G_*(v_1,\dotsc, v_N)=r_0>0$.  Then,  for any $r\in (0,r_0)$, there exists ${\varepsilon}={\varepsilon}(r)>0$ such  that
\[
\forall u_1,\dotsc, u_N\in {\boldsymbol{U}},\;\;\forall  i=1,\dotsc N,\;\;\Vert u_i-v_i\Vert<{\varepsilon}\Rightarrow G_*(u_1,\dotsc, u_N)>r.
\] 
In particular if
\[
U_1\subset U_2\subset\cdots 
\]
is an increasing  sequence  of  finite dimensional subspaces of  ${\boldsymbol{U}}$ whose union is a dense subspace of ${\boldsymbol{U}}$, then there exists $\nu\in {{\mathbb N}}$ and
\[
u_{1,\nu},\dotsc, u_{N,\nu}\in U_\nu
\]
such that  $G_*\big(\, u_{1,\nu},\dotsc, u_{N,\nu}\,\big)>0$.

body:
[Lem 100 (comparison of Fokker--Planck equations) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$
where $(\sss,\xxx)\sim\varphi$.
Let $\hvX$ be the SDE solution from Definition~\ref{d:intro.SDE.coefs}.
Assume the coefficients $B^i$ and $\Sigma^{ij}$ of \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv} are bounded and Lipschitz. Then the processes $\hvX$ and $\hvY$ satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations. Consequently, for each fixed $t$, the marginal law of $\hvX(t)$ agrees with the marginal law of\/ $\hvY(t)$.

\begin{proof}
Abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation density of $\vY$, and recall from Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr} that $\hvY$ has occupation density $\nu\equiv\rho_{\vY}*\varphi$.
Let $\mu$ denote the occupation density of $\hvX$.
 Let $f:\R^d\to\R$ be a smooth compactly supported test function. 
\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for $\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$.} We will calculate
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\vY(T))-f(\vY(0))\Big]
	= \int_{s,x} \varphi(s,x)
	\bE\Big[ f(Y(T-s)+x)
	-f(Y(-s)+x)\Big]
	\,ds\,dx
	=\textup{(dr)}+\textup{(qv)}
	\]
where $\textup{(dr)}$
and $\textup{(qv)}$
denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(dr)}^i
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i f(Y(t)+x)\,dD^i(t)
	\,ds\,dx \,,\\
	\textup{(qv)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(qv)}^{ij}
	= \frac12
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i\partial_j
	f(Y(t)+x)\,dQ^{ij}(t)
	\,ds\,dx\,.
	\end{align*}
Abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as follows:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}^i
	&= \int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{t,y} I_T(t+s)
	\partial_i f(y+x)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)\,ds\,dx \\
	&=
	\int_{s',x'}
	I_T(s')\partial_i f(x')
	\bigg\{\int_{t,y} 
	\varphi(s'-t,x'-y)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)
	\bigg\}\,ds'\,dx'\\
	&=
	\int_{t,y}
	I_T(t)\partial_i f(y)
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,y)}
	{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}
	\nu(dt\,dy)\,,
	\end{align*}
recalling at the last step that $\nu=\rho*\varphi$ is the occupation density of $\hvY$.\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for SDE solution $\hvX$.}
 If $f:\R^d\to\R$ is a smooth compactly supported test function, define
	\[
	L_t f(x)
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	B^i(t,x)
	\partial_i f(x)
	+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	A^{ij}(t,x)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(x)
	\]
Then, by It\=o's formula, the process
	\[
	N(t)
	= f(\hvX(t))-f(\hvX(0)) - \int_0^t L_s f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	\]
is a local martingale. Since we assumed the coefficients are bounded, we can conclude that $N$ is a true martingale, and the optional stopping theorem gives
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\hvX(T))-f(\hvX(0))\Big]
	= \bE \int_0^T L_t f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	= \textup{(Dr)}+\textup{(QV)}\,,
	\]
where $\textup{(Dr)}$ and $\textup{(QV)}$ denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(Dr)}^i
	=\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T \partial_i f(\hvX(t))
	B^i(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T 
	\partial_i\partial_j f(\hvX(t))
	A^{ij}(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,.
	\end{align*}
Again abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}^i
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i f(y) 
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,x)}
		{\rho*\varphi(t,x)}
	\mu(dt\,dy)\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(y) 
	\frac{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi(t,x)}
		{\rho*\varphi(t,x)}
	\mu(dt\,dy)
	\end{align*}
recalling that $\mu$ is the occupation density of $\hvX$, and using the definitions \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv} of $B^i$ and $A^{ij}$.

Comparing the expressions for $\hvX$ and $\hvY$ shows that $\mu$ and $\nu$ satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations. We now apply \cite[Lem.~2.3]{MR2375067}: this is a general result applying to $\R^d$-valued stochastic differential equations
such as \eqref{e:abstract.sde}, with a given law fo (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $n,k,d\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge k$, and $d\ge2$. There exists a constant
$C(k,d,n)>0$, depending only on $k,d,n$, such that, for every isotropic
log-concave measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^n$, every
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in\mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$, and every
$\psi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ with $0\le \psi\le1$, one has
\[
\biggl(\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Delta_f\,d\mu\biggr)^{\frac{1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}
\biggl(\int_{\mathbb R^n}\psi(f)\,d\mu\biggr)
\le
C(k,d,n)
\|\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^k)}^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+1}}.
\]

		\qquad(c\in\Hh^n,\ s\ge0),

\|u_{g,\alpha}\|_{\M_{\beta_0},k}\le C_1\|g\|_{\M_{\beta},k}.
$$

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. For a bounded-density probability eta on [0,R] with density <=C, midpoint quantiles have spacing >=1/(Cn), normalized squared-singular-value Vandermonde log energy converges to the logarithmic energy of the symmetrized law, and boxes of coordinate radius 1/(4Cn^3) preserve that energy up to 1/n^2 while having log volume o(n^2). An explicit uniform negative-log tail bound is Cd(1+log(1/d)); arbitrary bounded weakly converging profiles have the matching energy limsup. Standard technical lemma for the square reference-MI calibration; novelty unestablished.
eta has a Lebesgue density bounded by finite C and support [0,R], R finite.
n>=2; midpoint generalized inverse quantiles; natural logarithms.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b8e5531524507c787243bb49650bb55afc480f7f8efee959147d95d5b310cbd5","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b8/b8e5531524507c787243bb49650bb55afc480f7f8efee959147d95d5b310cbd5.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:26ccb837dbba6c98e5cddc0e0c215c36f68708f1bc45cd1754c64b87d2b36f37","bundle_entry_key":"bounded-density-quantile-vandermonde-boxes-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-square-calibration-and-oracle-gap-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:bounded-density-quantile-vandermonde-boxes-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Bounded-density quantiles: Vandermonde energy and small boxes

Target 2 supporting lemma for the square spectral-density calibration.
Proof draft, unaudited. These are elementary logarithmic-potential
estimates; no novelty is claimed for the general technical lemma.

Let eta be a probability measure on [0,R], R>0, with a Lebesgue density
bounded by C<infinity. Necessarily C>0. Let F be its distribution function,
and for n>=2 set x_i=F^(-1)((i-1/2)/n), 1<=i<=n, with the left quantile
convention. Put

    V_n(x)=n^(-2) sum_(i<j) log|x_j^2-x_i^2|,
    nu=(eta+reflection(eta))/2,
    Sigma(nu)=integral integral log|u-v| nu(du)nu(dv).

The conclusions are:

1. x_i>0, x_j-x_i >= (j-i)/(Cn), and x_i>=(i-1/2)/(Cn).
2. For every 0<d<1,

   n^(-2) sum_(i<j: x_j-x_i<d) log(1/(x_j-x_i))
       <= C*d*(1+log(1/d)).                           (1)

3. V_n(x)->Sigma(nu), a finite number.
4. Let delta_n=1/(4Cn^3). Every y with |y_i-x_i|<=delta_n is positive
   and increasing, and

   product_(i<j)(y_j^2-y_i^2)
     >= (1-1/(2n^2))^(n(n-1)) product_(i<j)(x_j^2-x_i^2),
   V_n(y) >= V_n(x)-1/n^2.                            (2)

   The corresponding product box has volume (1/(2Cn^3))^n, whose
   logarithm divided by n^2 tends to zero.
5. For any positive profiles z^(n) in a fixed [0,R'] with empirical
   measures converging weakly to eta,

       limsup_n V_n(z^(n)) <= Sigma(nu).              (3)

   Coincident coordinates give V_n=-infinity and do not cause an exception.

## Proof of spacing and the uniform logarithmic tail

Absolute continuity makes F continuous, and F(x_i)=(i-1/2)/n, including
when F has flat intervals. The density bound gives
F(v)-F(u)<=C(v-u). Apply this to two quantiles and to zero and x_i to get
conclusion 1. The empirical quantile laws converge weakly to eta; bounded
support also gives convergence of all bounded continuous kernels below.

Write k=j-i. If x_j-x_i<d, then k<Cnd and
log(1/(x_j-x_i))<=log(Cn/k). There are at most n pairs for each k. Let
K=min(n-1,floor(Cnd)); including an endpoint pair only increases this
upper bound. If K=0 the sum is empty. Otherwise

    left side of (1) <= (1/n) sum_(k=1)^K log(Cn/k)
      <= (1/n) integral_0^K log(Cn/u) du
      = (K/n)[1+log(Cn/K)].

The integral is finite at zero, and the sum bound uses a decreasing
integrand on each unit interval. Put a=K/(Cn). Since 0<a<=d<1, the function
a*(1+log(1/a)) is increasing on (0,1]. This proves (1).

For the second logarithm, x_i+x_j>=x_j-x_i>0. Thus the analogous negative
log tail for x_i+x_j<d is bounded by the same right side of (1). This also
handles quantiles approaching zero; no hard-edge gap is assumed.

## Convergence of the energy, with the cutoff paid

For a fixed d>0, the kernels log(max(|u-v|,d)) and
log(max(u+v,d)) are bounded continuous on [0,R]^2. Their double empirical
integrals converge to the corresponding double eta integrals. The
diagonal terms are bounded by a constant depending on d,R divided by n,
so half of each double empirical sum equals its i<j sum up to o(1).

Replacing the truncated pair logs by the true logs changes the normalized
sums by at most C*d*(1+log(1/d)) for each kernel, by (1). The continuum
negative log tails tend to zero too: the bounded density gives uniform
local integrability of log|u-v|, while log(u+v)>=log|u-v| controls the
other negative tail. Positive parts are bounded on the compact square.
Take n->infinity first, then d->0. This proves

    V_n(x)->(1/2) integral integral
           [log|u-v|+log(u+v)] eta(du)eta(dv).

For u,v>=0 off the null singular set, |u^2-v^2|=|u-v|(u+v).
Expanding the four quadrants of the symmetrization shows that the last
display equals Sigma(nu). All involved logs are integrable, so these
identities are not a cancellation of undefined infinities.

## Stability throughout the boxes

If |y_i-x_i|<=delta_n, each positive difference x_j-x_i and each sum
x_i+x_j changes by at most 2delta_n. Conclusion 1 bounds each of these
original quantities below by 1/(Cn). Hence each new difference or sum
is at least (1-1/(2n^2)) times its old value. Also
y_1>=1/(2Cn)-1/(4Cn^3)>0. The squared differences factor into these
positive sums and differences. Multiply their bounds over n(n-1)/2
pairs to obtain the first part of (2). With u=1/(2n^2)<=1/2, the
elementary inequality log(1-u)>=-2u gives a total log loss at most
n(n-1)/n^2<=1. Dividing this log loss by n^2 proves the second part of
(2). The box is inside the ordered positive chamber, and its stated
volume and subexponential logarithmic scale follow directly.

## Upper bound for arbitrary nearby profiles

Truncate both logarithmic kernels below as above. The untruncated pair
sums are no larger than the truncated ones. For fixed cutoff, weak
convergence on [0,R'] gives their limit, with diagonal corrections O(1/n).
Then decrease the cutoff to zero. Integrability under eta identifies the
limiting energy, proving (3). The same argument gives a uniform upper
bound in a sufficiently small weak neighborhood of eta for all large n:
fix the cutoff first, use continuity of its bounded double integral,
and only then remove it. This is the form used in the Laplace argument.

The proof is analytic. The accompanying Fraction script checks the
polynomial box inequality on finite rational profiles and all their
corners, and detects a collision in a deliberately oversized box. Those
finite checks do not certify the general convergence argument.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:f91ebbe6b88f8d0da76d7a95800245ceda66ac687a4f50d4d4c01642933be55d","revision_digest":"sha256:2ecfea7de06b18284b31dd76bb8e4c02ca3e283bd8b91f83cf7e9d2571d78496","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:bounded-density-quantile-vandermonde-boxes-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 claim w718-T287-017 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Definition 9 of arXiv:2605.30616, 'Brownian motion: the hyperbolic number setting'] Let $\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu_{t}\right)$ be a $\mathbb H$-valued-probability
space, and $A,B\in\sigma\left(X\right)$.

(1) $A$ is said to be independent of $B$, if $\mu\left(A\mid B\right)=\mu\left(A\right)$.

(2) $B$ is said to be independent of $A$, if $\mu\left(B\mid A\right)=\mu\left(B\right)$.

(3) $A$ and $B$ are said to be mutually independent, if both $A$
is independent of $B$, and $B$ is independent of $A$.

[Lemma 32 (Verification of the rare-success hypotheses) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] Assume either
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\rho_n\to\rho\in(0,1)$, or
\item $\rho_n\sim\lambda/n$ for some fixed $\lambda>0$.
\end{enumerate}
Then the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:reset-rare-success} hold.  In addition, the optional right-tilt condition \eqref{eq:reset-right-tilt-condition} holds for every fixed $a\in(0,1)$.

[Theorem thm:AGG-3.2 of arXiv:2609.01776, 'On the Cuspidal Cohomology of Iwahori Congruence Subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(3, \mathbb{Z})$'] Let $n = 2, 3, $ or $4$.  Let $N = \frac{1}{2} n (n-1)$.  Suppose $\Gamma \subseteq \mathrm{SL}(n, \mathbb{Z})$.  Then, there is a natural isomorphism 
\[\Phi \colon W(\Gamma) \to H_N(\Gamma, \mathbb{C}).\]  
If $\Gamma$ is normal in $\mathrm{SL}(n, \mathbb{Z})$, this is an isomorphism of $\mathrm{SL}(n, \mathbb{Z})$-modules, with $W(\Gamma)$ given the structure of an $\mathrm{SL}(n, \mathbb{Z})$-module by the action 
\[(m_2 \cdot f)(m_1) = f(m_1 m_2) \quad \text{ for } m_1, m_2 \in \mathrm{SL}(n, \mathbb{Z}),\]
which factors through $\mathrm{SL}(n, \mathbb{Z}) / \Gamma$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2607.25949, 'Block-hierarchical covariance decompositions for finite-block additive functionals'] (Reversible marginal spectrum).\\
Assume that the stationary Markov chain is reversible, and let \(K\) denote the
transition operator of the base chain acting on \(L^2_0(\nu)\).  For every 
\(\lambda\in Spec(K)\backslash\{1\}\), define
\begin{equation}
\theta_k(\lambda)
=
\frac{k-(k-2)\lambda}{1-\lambda}.
\end{equation}
Then, on the marginal subspace generated by one-coordinate functions in the  \(k\)-window space, the operator 
\(B_k\)  admits \(\theta_k(\lambda)\) as eigenvalues. More precisely, 
 if \(h\in L^2_0(\nu)\) satisfies \(Kh=\lambda h\), then the boundary-corrected function
\[
M_{\lambda,k}(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
=
\frac{1}{1-\lambda}h(x_1)
+
\sum_{i=2}^{k-1}h(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{1-\lambda}h(x_k)
\]
is an eigenfunction of \(B_k\) with eigenvalue \(\theta_k(\lambda)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2607.25949

[Theorem 39 of arXiv:2604.03213, 'Asymptotic expansion for transport maps \\ between laws of multimatrix models'] With $\bX$ the solution to Equation \eqref{skvjdnand}, assuming $\bJ\in (\cC^{k+1}(\cB))^d$, and that for all $p\in [1,d]$, $\norm{\bJ_p - X_p }_{\cC^k,\infty} <\infty$, then we set
    $$\kappa \coloneqq \sup_{R>0}\ \left\{ \sum_{1\leq i\leq d} \norm{\partial_i\bJ_p - \1_{i=p} 1\otimes 1}_{0,R} + \norm{\widetilde{\partial}_i \bJ_p }_{0,R} \right\},$$
    where $\norm{\cdot}_{0,R}$ is in Definition \ref{def.norms-of-derivatives}.  And there exists a constant $C_{\bJ}$ such that for any $j_0,\dots,j_n$ with $j\coloneqq j_0+\dots+j_n \in [1,k]$, $R>0$, and $i,p\in [1,d]$,
    \begin{align}
        
        \norm{ \la e_i| \widetilde{\partial}^{(j_n)}\circ\cdots\circ \widetilde{\partial}^{(j_1)}\circ \partial^{(j_0)} \bX_{t,p}}_{{0,c,R}} &\leq C_{\bJ} (1+t)^{2j} \times e^{-\frac{1-j\kappa}{2}t}, \\
        \norm{\widetilde{\partial}^{(j_n)}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\partial}^{(j_1)}\circ\partial^{(j_0)} \bX_{t,p}}_{0,c,R} &\leq C_{\bJ} (1+t)^{2j} e^{\frac{\kappa j}{2}t}.          
    \end{align}

[Lemma L:two-point-TASEP of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Fix $\alpha_0 \in \mathbb{R}$. 
There are constants $C_0, c > 0$ depending only on $\alpha_0$ such that the following holds. Take $0 < t_1 \le t_2 < \alpha_0 t_1$, and $x_1, x_2, y \in \II{0, \alpha_0 t_1^{2/3}}$, and $\alpha \ge 1/2 - \alpha_0 t_1^{1/3}$.  Then 
\begin{align*}
	\mathbb{P}\Big(|\bar h^\alpha(x_1, t_1; \delta_y) - \bar h^\alpha(x_2, t_2; \delta_y)| \ge a (|x_1 - x_2|^{1/2} + |t_2 - t_1|^{1/3})\Big) &\le 2\exp(-c a^{1/2}),
\end{align*}    
for any $a > 0$ satisfying
$$
C_0\log^2 \left( \frac{t_1^{1/3}}{|x_1 - x_2|^{1/2} + |t_2 - t_1|^{1/3}}\right) < a < t_1^{1/4}.
$$
title: Lemma L:two-point-TASEP of arXiv:2604.10020
