[Lemma lem:chebyshev-minimax of arXiv:2605.17082, 'Spectral Purification in Reversible Markov Chains: Hidden Parameters, Observable Equivalen'] Let $[a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}$ be an interval and let $\xi \notin [a, b]$. Among all polynomials $Q_m$ of degree at most $m$ satisfying $Q_m(\xi) = 1$, the unique minimizer of
\[
\max_{x \in [a,b]} |Q_m(x)|
\]
is the rescaled Chebyshev polynomial
\[
Q_m^\ast(x) = \frac{T_m(\varphi(x))}{T_m(\varphi(\xi))},
\]
where $\varphi$ is the affine map sending $[a,b]$ to $[-1, 1]$, defined by
\[
\varphi(x) = \frac{2x - (a+b)}{b - a},
\]
and $T_m$ is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, $T_m(\cos \theta) = \cos(m\theta)$.

body: Blum's speedup theorem, from machine-independent complexity theory, produces computable functions with no best program. For any total computable function r, there is a computable 0-1 valued function h such that for every program P1 computing h with complexity Phi_1, there exists another program P2 also computing h whose complexity Phi_2 is so much smaller that r(Phi_2(x)) <= Phi_1(x) for all but finitely many inputs x. So for h, any candidate optimal program is beaten, by an arbitrarily large computable factor r, by another program that is itself beatable the same way, with no program ever asymptotically optimal. Proved by Manuel Blum in 1967 from the Blum axioms for complexity measures.
title: Blum's speedup theorem

[Prop 41 (Moment-transfer form) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $Q$ be an $\So{n}$-valued random matrix, let $H\sim\haarOdist_{n}$, and let $\mathcal X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$. Let $0<\varepsilon<1$ and let $r$ be a positive integer with $r\leq c_0\ell$, where $c_0$ is the constant in Lemma \ref{lem:jl_haar_moment}. Suppose that, for every $v\in\mathcal V_{\mathcal X}$,
\be 
\left|\mathbb{E} Z_v(Q)^{2r}-\mathbb{E} Z_v(H)^{2r}\right|\leq \alpha.
\ee
Then
\begin{align}
&\mathbb{P}\left(\exists\,i<j:\left|\frac{\|A_Q(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2}{\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2}-1\right|>\varepsilon\right) \notag\\
&\hspace{2cm}\leq
\binom{N}{2}\left[\left(C_0\frac{r}{\varepsilon^2\ell}\right)^r+\frac{\alpha}{\varepsilon^{2r}}\right]. 
\end{align}

[Definition 8 of arXiv:2608.30059, 'Multihomogeneous Measures and Stochastic Polar Representations'] A measurable map
\[
\tau=(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_q):
E\longrightarrow[0,\infty)^q
\]
is called a \emph{product gauge} if
\begin{equation}

\tau(S_rx)=r\tau(x),
\qquad r\in G,\quad x\in E.
\end{equation}
It is \emph{admissible for \(\nu\)} if
\[
E_\tau
:=
\bigcap_{i=1}^q\{\tau_i>0\}
\]
is \(\nu\)-conull.

Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random elements and let F be a countable class of measurable real functions (countability, or a suitable separability/measurability condition, is needed so the suprema are measurable). Let eps_1, ..., eps_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of the X_i. Then E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i f(X_i) |, and in the other direction E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) |. The constant 2 in the first inequality is the standard one and is not claimed sharp. Symmetrization is what allows one to work CONDITIONALLY on the data, replacing an empirical process by a Rademacher process whose conditional law is sub-Gaussian with an explicit variance proxy, which is the entry point for chaining bounds and Rademacher complexity. The X_i need not be identically distributed. Note the direction of the useful inequality: it bounds the centred empirical process by the Rademacher process, which is the one that can be chained. [standard; e.g. van der Vaart and Wellner, Weak Convergence and Empirical Processes, Lemma 2.3.1]
X_i independent (not necessarily identically distributed)
F countable, or measurable in the sense that the suprema are measurable
eps_i Rademacher, independent of the sample

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Denote by \(\ParaHoelder{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R)\) the parabolic H\"older space.
The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item 
  The map \(\bm{\Psi}:\Opendenseset_\alpha \rightarrow \ParaHoelder{\alpha}([0,1]\times\mathbb R)\) defined by
  \[
  \bm{\Psi}(\gamma)(s,x)=\Psi^\gamma(s,x)-\log\cosh x,
  \qquad (s,x)\in [0,1]\times \R,
  \]
  is \(C^2\) in the Fr\'echet sense.
  \item 
  Fix $\gamma\in \Opendenseset_\alpha$ and $h\in \Hoelder{\alpha/2}([0,1])$. 
  Then, for all $s\in [0,1)$,
  \[
  D^2\Psi^\gamma[h,h](s,0)\leq 0.
  \]
  \item 
  Fix $\gamma\in\Opendenseset_\alpha$ and fix $h_1,h_2\in \Hoelder{\alpha/2}([0,1])$ where $h_1\geq 0$ and $h_2\geq 0$.
  Then, for all $s\in [0,1)$,
  \[
  D^2\Psi^\gamma[h_1,h_2](s,0)\leq 0.
  \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.15432

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^∞} ≤ (4π|t|)^{−n/2}‖f‖_{L¹} measures the data in L¹ (or in L^{p'} with p' ≤ 2 for the interpolated version). It does not say that the solution of a Schrödinger equation with L² data becomes small in L^∞ as time passes. Concrete counterexample: fix any t ≠ 0, pick g ∈ L²(R^n) \ L^∞(R^n), and set f = e^{−itΔ}g. Then ‖f‖_{L²} = ‖g‖_{L²} < ∞, while e^{itΔ}f = g ∉ L^∞ — so e^{itΔ} is not even a bounded operator from L² to L^∞, at any time, let alone a decaying one. Since the group is unitary, ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L²} = ‖f‖_{L²} for all t: no norm decay occurs in L²; dispersion is a spreading of a fixed amount of mass, and it can only be seen in norms that punish spreading. Related traps: (i) the decay factor is |t|^{−n/2} pointwise in t and is not integrable near t = 0 for n ≥ 2, so it cannot be used naively inside a Duhamel integral — that is exactly the role of Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev in the Strichartz proof; (ii) the wave analogue ‖e^{it|∇|}f‖_{L^∞} ≲ |t|^{−(n−1)/2}‖f‖_{L¹} is false without frequency localization (or a loss of (n+1)/2 derivatives), because the wave kernel is a measure on the light cone; (iii) with a potential, decay estimates require spectral hypotheses (no zero-energy eigenvalue or resonance), not just decay of the potential.
title: Pitfall: The Dispersive Decay Estimate Needs L¹ Data — There Is No L² → L^∞ Decay

[Lemma lem:degenerate-endpoints of arXiv:2608.09368, 'A proof of Ross's conjecture for two-site moving-target search'] If $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=1$, every policy has infinite total cost for every
initial belief, so any threshold selector is optimal in the extended-real
sense.  If $\alpha_1=1$, $\alpha_2<1$, and $a=1$, the stationary rule
that always searches site~2 is optimal and is a threshold rule with
$p^*=1$.  Symmetrically, if $\alpha_2=1$, $\alpha_1<1$, and $b=1$, the
rule that always searches site~1 is optimal and has $p^*=0$.

body: [Definition Amalgamation of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] For every $i,j\in [k]$, let $G_{i,i}=(V_{i,i},E_{i,i})$ be a multigraph on the vertex set $\mathcal N^{(i)}$ and $G_{i,j}=(V_{i,j},E_{i,j})$ be a bipartite multigraph on the bipartitioned vertex set $\mathcal N^{(i)}\cup \mathcal N^{(j)}$. Given graphs $G_{i,j}$ for every $i,j \in [k]$, we define the multigraph $\mathcal G(G_{i,j}:i,j\in [k])$ to be the simply the graph on $V_n=\mathcal N^{(1)}\cup \dots \cup \mathcal N^{(k)}$ whose edge set is the union $\cup_{i,j\in [k]}E_{i,j}$. We call $\mathcal G(G_{i,j}:i,j\in [k])$ the \emph{amalgamation} of the graphs $G_{i,j}$ for $i,j\in [k]$.
title: Amalgamation

[Theorem BTP-thm-intro of arXiv:2608.30747, 'Compact homogeneous complex manifolds'] Let $(M=G/K,J)$ be a complex C-space fibering over a flag $F=G_1/H_1\times\dots\times G_s/H_s$ and assume that $G_i\ne \Eg_6, \Eg_7, \Eg_8$ for all $i=1,\dots,s$.  Then a metric $g=g_\ag+g_\qg$, $g_\qg=(x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Delta_\qg^+}$ is BTP if and only if 
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm (i)}]
\item either $g_\qg=g_b|_\qg$ for some bi-invariant metric $g_b$ on $[\ggo,\ggo]$ (i.e., $x_\alpha=x_\beta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Delta_{\qg_i}$, $i=1,\dots,s$, see (equation decp-intro of the paper)),   

\item or $g_\qg$ is K\"ahler on the flag $F=G_f/H_f$ (i.e., $x_{\alpha+\beta}=x_\alpha+x_\beta$ for all $\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta\in\Delta_\qg^+$) and $\tfrac{1}{x_\alpha}A_\alpha= \tfrac{1}{x_\beta}A_\beta$ for all $\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta\in\Delta_\qg^+$, where $A_\alpha$ is the $Q$-orthogonal projection of $H_\alpha$ on $\ag^c$.      
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem BTP-thm-intro of arXiv:2608.30747

[Lemma 31 (TV bound via the shifted construction) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Assume \eqref{eq:reg-framework} and \eqref{eq:tv-local-error}. Let
\[
  d_n^2:=\E\|\bar Y_n-Y_n'\|^2.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  \TV(\widetilde\mu_N,\nu_N)
  \le
  \overline C_{\mathrm{TV}}\,\lambda
  +\sqrt{\tfrac{c}{2}}\,d_{N-1}
  +\sqrt{\tfrac{c}{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N-2}\eta_n^2\,d_n^2},
\end{equation}
where \(c=\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{-1})\).

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4783e35d35a9d3f83fc21575d97ce32b2d708346464c354e701a49e075dedd1d","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/47/4783e35d35a9d3f83fc21575d97ce32b2d708346464c354e701a49e075dedd1d.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:b293482c92228bb1fde3c6b8b850040915501d62a52386da925c88dba9fb3ec1","bundle_entry_key":"scalar-stability","bundle_id":"population.t250-scalar-and-tanh-correlation-stability-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w712/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:concave-scalar-kernel-relative-noise-stability-w712","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Concave scalar kernel stability with conditional relative noise

T250-w712-C003 v1. Target 1. Status: proof (unaudited).

The depth dependence is polynomial whenever the following scalar conditions hold. No claim about a general covariance-matrix recursion follows from these conditions.

Let n>=1, c>0, kappa>0, and let (Q_l,F_l) be an adapted process taking values in [0,1], with Q_0=q_0 deterministic in (0,1]. Suppose F:[0,1]->[0,1] is increasing and concave, F(0)=0, and F(q)>0 for q>0. Assume, throughout [0,1],

    F(q) <= q-c q^2,
    E[Q_(l+1)|F_l] = F(Q_l),
    Var(Q_(l+1)|F_l) <= (kappa/n) F(Q_l)^2.

Write s_0=q_0 and s_(l+1)=F(s_l). Then, for every integer l>=0,

    E(sqrt(Q_l)-sqrt(s_l))^2 <= 4 kappa/(c n).       (1)

This is an abstract stability lemma, not an assumption of independent layers. Only conditional moments are used.

Proof. All s_l are strictly positive. Put R_l=Q_l/s_l, S_l=F(Q_l)/F(s_l), and v_l=E(R_l-1)^2. These moments are finite since R_l<=1/s_l at each fixed l.

Concavity with F(0)=0 and monotonicity imply that S_l lies between R_l and 1: for Q_l<=s_l, Q_l/s_l<=F(Q_l)/F(s_l)<=1; for Q_l>=s_l, the inequalities reverse. Consequently

    (S_l-1)^2 <= (R_l-1)^2,
    S_l^2 <= 2(S_l-1)^2+2.

The second inequality follows because its right side minus its left side is (S_l-2)^2. Conditional centering, rather than independence, gives

    v_(l+1) = E(S_l-1)^2 + E Var(R_(l+1)|F_l)
             <= (1+2 kappa/n)v_l + 2 kappa/n.

Starting at v_0=0, induction gives v_l<=(1+2 kappa/n)^l-1. If 2 kappa l/n<=1, then log(1+x)<=x and exp(x)-1<=2x on [0,1] give v_l<=4 kappa l/n.

Let mu_l=E Q_l. Taking the conditional mean and using the drift assumption and Jensen for the square gives

    mu_(l+1) <= mu_l-c mu_l^2.

The same inequality holds for s_l. The assumptions imply c a<1 at every positive deterministic iterate; for a positive mean with positive next mean the drift inequality likewise implies c a<1. Hence reciprocal comparison is legitimate:

    1/[a(1-c a)] >= 1/a+c.

If a next mean is zero, all subsequent Q values vanish almost surely, because F(0)=0 and the conditional mean is nonnegative. In either case the resulting upper bounds remain valid:

    mu_l, s_l <= 1/(q_0^(-1)+c l) <= 1/(c l), l>=1.

For 1<=l<=n/(2 kappa), |sqrt(r)-1|<=|r-1| for r>=0 yields

    E(sqrt(Q_l)-sqrt(s_l))^2 <= s_l v_l
                  <= (1/(c l))(4 kappa l/n).

For l>n/(2 kappa), use (sqrt(a)-sqrt(b))^2<=a+b to bound the same expression by mu_l+s_l<=2/(c l)<4 kappa/(c n). At l=0 it is zero. These ranges cover integer depths even when n/(2 kappa)<1. This proves (1).

Gaussian chain corollary. If the process is driven by successive fresh standard Gaussian vectors g_j, the finite preactivation is h_j=sqrt(Q_(j-1))g_j, and the deterministic comparison is hbar_j=sqrt(s_(j-1))g_j, then the same fresh Gaussian vectors couple the complete trajectories. With the product Euclidean metric on the vectors normalized by sqrt(n),

    W2((h_j/sqrt(n))_(j=1)^L,
       (hbar_j/sqrt(n))_(j=1)^L)^2 <= 4 kappa L/(c n).

Here Q_(j-1) must depend only on preceding innovations, so g_j is independent of it. This requirement is explicit; arbitrary post hoc Gaussian vectors do not establish the original network's joint law.

Application. The critical one-input tanh chain satisfies c=1/6 and kappa=48, as proved in tanh_depth_uniform.md. Thus the abstract bound is 1152/n, and the joint bound is 1152 L/n. The only ingredients involving tanh are concavity, quadratic signal decay, and bounded conditional relative variance; this pinpoints what a different scalar activation or stable chain must supply.

Limits. The ratio contraction is scalar. A matrix analogue does not follow by applying concavity entrywise, nor by replacing conditional centering with marginal variance bounds. The unpaid step for several inputs is a covariance/shape stability statement that remains uniform as the deterministic signal decays.

Verification. Every denominator is positive where inverted; Q=0 is included in the ratio contraction, while q_0=0 is the separate identically-zero case. The supplied tanh application has the exact-rational boundary checks and numerical diagnostics in logs/verification.json. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:LFH-ins of arXiv:2510.16431, '\Large Liouville quantum gravity: from random planar maps to conformal field theory'] Let $\beta_i\in\mathbb{R}$  and $s_i\in \partial\mathbb{H}$ for $i = 1, ..., M$ where $M\ge 1$ and all the $s_i$'s are distinct.
    Sample $(h, \mathbf c)$   from  $C_{\mathbb{H}}^{(\beta_i, s_i)_i}P_\mathbb{H}\times [e^{(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^M\beta_i - Q)c}dc]$ with $C_{\mathbb{H}}^{(\beta_i, s_i)_i} =		\prod_{i=1}^M  |s_i|_+^{-\beta_i(Q-\frac{\beta_i}{2})} \exp(\frac{1}{4}\sum_{j=i+1}^{M}\beta_i\beta_j G_\mathbb{H}(s_i, s_j))$.   
Then  \[\phi = h - 2Q\log|\cdot|_++\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^M\beta_i G_\mathbb{H}(s_i, \cdot)+\mathbf{c}\] is called the  \emph{Liouville field on $ \mathbb H$ with insertions $(\beta_i,s_i)_{1\le i\le N}$}. We denote its law by $\mathrm{LF}_{ \mathbbm{H}}^{(\beta_i,s_i)_i}$.
title: Definition def:LFH-ins of arXiv:2510.16431

[Theorem 4 ({\cite{KiM_strong}}, but with a few technical conditions on the drift removed, see remark below) of arXiv:2608.28528, 'Strong solutions of SDEs with critical discontinuities in diffusion coefficients'] Let $d \ge 3$, $T>0$. Assume that $b \in \mathbf{F}_{\delta, g}$ and that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that the function $g_\delta$ from \eqref{fbb_inhom} additionally satisfies
$$
g_\delta \in L^{1+\varepsilon}(\mathbb{R}).
$$
Let $\{b_n\} \subset (C^\infty \cap L^\infty)(\mathbb R^{1+d},\mathbb R^d)$ be a sequence of vector fields such that
$$
b_n \rightarrow b \quad \text{ in } [L_{\loc}^2(\mathbb R,L^2_{\rho}(\mathbb R^d))]^d,
$$
are form-bounded with the same form-bound $\delta$ having $\sup_n\|g_{\delta,n}\|_{L^{1+\varepsilon}(\mathbb R)}<\infty$. (For example, the standard mollifier in $\mathbb R^{1+d}$ applied to $b$ yields $b_n$, see Appendix \ref{Conv_b_n} for details.) 

If the form-bound $\delta$ of drift $b$ is sufficiently small, then 
 the following are true:

\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] There exists a subsequence $\{b_{n_k}\}$ such that for any initial time $r \in [0,T[$ and every initial point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the approximating strong solutions $\{X^{x,n_k}_{r,t}\}_{k=1}^\infty$ to
\begin{equation*}
X_{r,t}^{x,n}=x+\int_r^t b_n(s,X_{r,s}^{x,n})ds + W_t-W_r, 
\end{equation*}
considered on a fixed complete probability space $(\Omega,\{\mathcal F^W_t\}_{0 \leq t \leq T},\mathcal F^W,\mathbf{P})$,
	converge for every $t \in [r,T]$ $\mathbf{P}$-a.s.\,to a strong solution $X^x_{r,t}$ of SDE 
	\begin{equation*}
X_{r,t}^{x}=x+\int_r^t b(s,X_{r,s}^{x})ds + W_t-W_r, \quad t \in [r,T]. 
\end{equation*}

\item[(ii)] 
The constructed strong solution $X^x_{r,t}$ satisfies the following Krylov-type bound. For every $q \in(d,\delta^{-1/2})$ and any vector field $f \in \mathbf{F}_{\beta}$, $\beta < \infty$, there exists a constant $C$, depending only on $d$, $q$, $\delta$, $g_\delta$, $\beta$, $g_\beta$ and $T$, such that
    \begin{equation} 
        \mathbf{E}\int_r^T
        \big|fh\left(\tau,X_{r,\tau}^x\right) \big| d\tau  \le C\left\| f |h|^{q/2} \right\|_{L^2([r,T],L^2_{\rho}(\mathbb{R}^d))}^{2/q} \quad  \text{for all }   h \in C_c \left([r,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\right).
\end{equation}

\item[(iii)] 
The constructed solution $X_{r,t}^x$ is pathwise unique among strong solutions to \eqref{sde_b} that satisfy \eqref{kr1} for some
$q \in (d,\delta^{-1/2})$, with $|f|=1$ and with $|f|=|b|$. 

    \item[(iv)] The operators
    \begin{equation}

    T_b^{r,t}f(x) := \mathbf{E}[f(X^x_{r,t})], \quad f \in C_\infty,
    \end{equation}
    constitute a backward Feller propagator on $C_\infty$, 
and, furthermore, we have
$$
T_b^{r,t}=s\mbox{-}C_\infty\mbox{-}\lim_n T_{b_n}^{r,t} \quad \text{loc.\,uniformly in $r,t \in [0,T]$}
$$
regardless of the choice of the sequence $\{b_n\}$ as long as it satisfies the preceeding uniform form-boundedness assumptions. In this sense, the law of $X^x_{r,t}$ does not depend on the choice of the subsequence in {\rm (\textit{i})}.

\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: {\cite{KiM_strong}}, but with a few technical conditions on the drift removed, see remark below

[Thm main-use-result-cline-hsing of arXiv:2605.29095, 'Asymptotics of the number of components of random polynomial lemniscates'] Let $\{Y_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ be an i.i.d. family of random variables with common distribution $F$ and $S_n = Y_1 + Y_2 + ...+ Y_n$. Assume that $\mathbb{P}[|Y_1| >x]$ is regularly varying with index $-2$ and $\sup_{x \geq 0} F(-x)/(1-F(x)) <\infty$. Assume $Y_1$ has mean zero\footnote{Note that the mean of $Y_1$ is well defined since the tail of $Y_1$ is regularly varying with index $-2$.} and let $t_n$ be a sequence such that 
    
    \[ \lim_{n\to \infty} n(1-F(t_n)) = \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{n \log t_n \mathbb{E}[Y_1^2 1_{|Y_1| \leq t_n }]}{t_n^2}= 0.\]

Then, \[ \lim_{n\to \infty} \sup_{s \geq t_n} \biggl|\frac{\mathbb{P}[S_n >s]}{n (1 - F(s))} -1 \biggr| =0.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In computational complexity, problems that are in the complexity class NP but are neither in the class P nor NP-complete are called NP-intermediate, and the class of such problems is called NPI. Ladner's theorem, shown in 1975 by Richard E. Ladner, is a result asserting that, if P ≠ NP, then NPI is not empty; that is, NP contains problems that are neither in P nor NP-complete. Since it is also true that if NPI problems exist, then P ≠ NP, it follows that P = NP if and only if NPI is empty.
title: NP-intermediate

# C020 v2: a shifted peak for ONE realized label vector
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
General T267 remains open. This is a restricted four-atom width-first theorem.

## 1. Model and precise probability statement
For 0<e<1/4 put D=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D),
s,t in {-1,1}. The population is uniform on these four atoms and the
training set contains one observation at each atom (stratified, not iid).
Set u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2,
and g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Thus ||u_e||=1 and its four Walsh
coefficients (0,s,t,st) are (0,alpha_e,alpha_e,alpha_e).
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. Independently draw four noise signs xi_(s,t),
each uniform {-1,1}, and label y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, where
 sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e))~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4).
Initialize f_m(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x), with iid w_j~N(0,I_3)
and independent iid a_j uniform {-nu,nu}. Both layers undergo simultaneous
GD with step gamma=1/2 on loss (1/8)sum_i(f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2, using gate
derivative zero at zero. The individual clean risk is
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
There is NO noise average anywhere in the claim.

Let H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z], and let
lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of H(X,X)/4, b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2),
eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s. C009's clock premises are
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), eta_e~e,
with b_0 bounded away from zero.
For epsilon>0 let E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon) mean that there exist integer
k0<k1<k2<k3 with k0>=0, satisfying
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),                   (1)
 |k1/((3pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
 |k2/((9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
and k2 is an interior maximum on a nontrivial integer interval [l,k3]
with k1<l<k2<k3 and both endpoint risks strictly below R(k2).
Ties between interior maximizing indices are allowed. The claim is
 liminf_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P_(xi,initialization)(E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon)) >= 1/16.       (2)
For each fixed chi in {-1,1}, conditional on xi_(s,t)=chi*s, the lower
bound over initialization alone is 1/2. The time k1 is a low-risk
cancellation WITNESS, not a claimed uniquely located stationary minimum.
The time k2 is an interval peak, not a unique stationary point theorem.
Equation (1) is the finite-witness meaning of two descents separated by a rise;
no monotonicity of every intervening nonlinear GD step is asserted.

## 2. Gaussian-width precursor and its exact unaveraged risk
C016/C017 supply, after the fixed-e width limit, independent Gaussian
Walsh initial outputs Z_(e,h) with covariance nu^2 lambda_h^RF. Couple them
for all e using independent standard G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st. Set
 U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e.
Then almost surely
 e U_(e,s)->L=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1.
These convergences are uniform when the four Gaussian coordinates range
over a fixed bounded set; the scalar variance coefficients are deterministic.
The constant initial output Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

Fix the single label branch xi_(s,t)=chi*s. Its only nonzero normalized
noise Walsh coefficient is N_s=d e^(-1/4), d=2sqrt(kappa)chi;
N_0=N_t=N_st=0. Write N=N_s. The exact frozen clean risk is
 Q_(e,chi)(t)=alpha_e^2 sum_h [q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h]^2,
 q_h=exp(-b_h t).                                       (3)
At integer times this is discrete kernel GD, not gradient flow. In real
time it is only the spectral interpolation used to select integer witnesses.
Use the favorable initialization event chi*L<0, of probability1/2.
Every assertion below first refers to a fixed Gaussian realization in
this event, then is made probabilistic through compact exhaustion.

## 3. Early cancellation and two large value gaps
For small e, N and U_(e,s) have opposite signs. Thus
 q_*=-N/(U_(e,s)-N) belongs to (0,1),
 q_*~(-d/L)e^(3/4).
The fast residual N+q_*(U_(e,s)-N) is EXACTLY zero. Define
 t_1=-log(q_*)/b_s, t_0=-log(2q_*)/b_s.
Both are nonnegative for small e, t_0<t_1, and
 b_s t_1=(3/4)log(1/e)-log(-d/L)+o(1).                 (4)
Round these to nearest integers k0,k1. Their separation is (log2)/b_s,
which tends to infinity, so rounding preserves their order. A time change
of at most1/2 multiplies q_s by exp(O(b_s))=1+O(e). The residual error at
k1 is therefore O(|N|e)=O(e^(3/4)); at k0 it is -N+O(|N|e).
Slow-mode q_h tend to1 at both times and their U_h stay bounded. The
constant-mode residual is negligible faster than every power of e because
its initial normalized coefficient is O(e^(-2)) and b_0 is positive.
It follows that
 Q(k1)/alpha_e^2 -> L_t^2+1=2B,
 Q(k0)/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa,
where B=(L_t^2+1)/2>=1/2. In particular Q(k0)>Q(k1).
This proves the first descent witness and its leading clock; no derivative
argument or minimum uniqueness is needed.

## 4. The later single-label peak
Set t_e(v)=((9/4)log(1/e)+v)/b_s and z=exp(-v). Then q_s=e^(9/4)z.
Differentiate (3), using the exact derivative identity of C019:
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st))
 =sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
   [q_h N_h(N_h-U_h)-q_h^2(U_h-N_h)^2].                 (5)
The fast term -q_s N U_s/eta_e converges to -dL z=A z,
with A=-dL>0. Its other four expansion terms vanish uniformly on bounded
v intervals. Their orders are respectively e^(3/4), e^(3/2), e^(9/4), e^3,
for q_s N^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s N/eta_e,
and q_s^2 N^2/eta_e. The slow terms, with N_t=N_st=0, tend to -B,
since their weights tend to1/2 and q_t,q_st=1-O(e log(1/e)).
The constant term is again exponentially negligible. Hence locally uniformly
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st)) -> A exp(-v)-B.         (6)
Integration on bounded intervals gives convergence of centered risk differences:
 [Q(t_e(v))-Q(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
 -> V(v)-V(0), V(v)=-A exp(-v)-Bv.                     (7)
The function V is strictly concave, with its unique maximum at
 v_*=log(A/B), and has strict value gaps to either endpoint of any compact
interval containing v_* in its interior. Also, uniformly on compact v sets,
 Q(t_e(v))/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa.            (8)
Indeed q_s U_s=O(e^(5/4)) is negligible relative to N=O(e^(-1/4));
slow risk is O(alpha_e^2) and the constant-mode risk is negligible.
Equations (8) and Section3 give the second strict gap Q(peak)>Q(k1).
Equation (7) gives the third strict gap to a later time, now of order
alpha_e^2 eta_e. It is much smaller than the two early value gaps.

Round all central t_e(v) to the integer grid. The mesh in v is b_s->0,
so (7) remains uniform on the grid. On a fixed compact interval containing
v_* inside, an integer maximizing index is interior and its v coordinate
tends to v_*. This uses the positive gap between V(v_*) and the compact
complement of any neighborhood of v_*, not derivatives of nonlinear GD.
The central maximizing time consequently has leading term
 (9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                              (9)
The early cancellation witness (4) precedes the entire central interval,
since their b_s-scaled time separation is (3/2)log(1/e)+O(1).
This completes the Gaussian frozen-array witness construction.

## 5. Probability and transfer to the actual BOTH-layer nonlinear updates
For an integer M>=1 restrict to the compact Gaussian event
 K_M={chi L<=-1/M, |G_0|,|G_s|,|G_t|,|G_st|<=M}.
These increasing events exhaust {chi L<0}. On K_M, A is bounded above
and away from zero and B is bounded above and below. Thus v_*, the offset
in (4), and all coefficients used above lie in deterministic bounded sets.
All estimates in Sections3-4 are uniform on K_M: the U limits have deterministic
coefficients linear in bounded G, the denominator L is bounded away from0,
and the exponentially small constant-mode bounds are uniform as well.
Choose a deterministic central v interval [-J,J] whose interior contains
all possible v_* on K_M, with a margin of at least1. Strict concavity and
compactness give uniform positive endpoint gaps for V. The two large early
gaps are also uniform. For small e, the entire central grid interval lies
inside the relative time tolerance epsilon in (2), and the cancellation
indices lie inside the stated earlier relative tolerance.

For each fixed e choose a finite integer horizon T_e(M) containing the
central grid interval and the possible earlier witnesses. C009 Section3,
as applied in C018 Section3, gives joint weak convergence of all actual
individual risks through that finite horizon to (3) when m tends to infinity.
The proof retains the actual nonzero initial output and controls both-layer
motion and gate-crossing remainders. The finite sixteen-label family is
covered, although here only the fixed single branch is used. Risk squaring
is continuous on the finite array, and the prediction arrays are tight.
No finite-width Gaussian-mode independence or e-uniform width bound is used.

For clarity about maxima and weak convergence, take the deterministic
central interval just specified. The event that there exist k0<k1 before
it and a grid index j in its interior, with the two early witness gaps
strictly positive and R(j) strictly above BOTH central endpoint values,
is open in the finite risk array: it is a finite union of finite intersections
of strict inequalities. Restrict k1 to its required relative time band.
The frozen arrays on K_M satisfy this open event for sufficiently small e.
Any maximum k2 over that central interval then lies in its interior;
replacing j by k2 only increases the witness gaps. The right endpoint is
k3, and k1 precedes the central interval. The entire central interval is
already in the required peak-time band, so all maximizers qualify.
The open-set Portmanteau inequality transfers the LOWER probability bound
to actual nonlinear risk arrays for each fixed e. Thus the two ordered
liminf limits have conditional probability at least P(K_M). Let M increase
to infinity to obtain the conditional lower bound1/2. This argument sends
width to infinity separately at every e and finite horizon, before e tends
to zero. No infinite-horizon NTK statement or interchange of limits occurs.

Finally the two noise events xi=+s and xi=-s are disjoint and each has
probability1/16 under the original four independent sign errors. Noise is
independent of initialization. Summing their conditional lower bounds gives
(1/16)(1/2)+(1/16)(1/2)=1/16, proving (2). Other sign patterns might add
probability, but they are not analyzed or counted in this claim.

## 6. Limits and unresolved piece
This is a single REALIZED label vector result, unlike C017/C018. It is
consistent with C019: its peak is at the later (9/4)log(1/e) clock, while
C019 addresses bounded offsets around (3/2)log(1/e).
The four input atoms cluster as e decreases; training inputs are stratified,
noise amplitude shrinks, width is taken first, and only a positive-probability
noise/initialization event is proved. No full typical-data theorem, macroscopic
feature learning, fixed-noise theorem, unique stationary points or complete
noise window is claimed. The hardest unpaid step is a general single-dataset
result beyond this shrinking four-atom, positive-probability construction.
Dependencies C009,C016,C017,C018,C019 and this claim all remain unaudited.
Independent correctness and novelty review are pending; no priority claim
is made. Sources: the named own proof files; the full ReLU kernel and clock
premises come from C009, with Heckel-Yilmaz 2007.10099v2 Section3 as its
primary kernel source. No new external literature result is claimed here.
Exact stratified four-point shrinking-input model and finite-witness meaning in proofs/SINGLE_LABEL_SHIFTED_PEAK.md
Unit-norm single-index centered ReLU teacher; four independent Rademacher errors with sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e))
Fixed0<nu<=1 and kappa>0; iid Gaussian hidden weights and independent iid signed heads; both layers trained by simultaneous step1/2 GD
Width tends to infinity at each fixed e and finite horizon before e decreases

[Prop pr:wick_renormalization of arXiv:2411.03482, 'Ergodicity of 2D singular stochastic Navier--Stokes equations'] Let $X_{N} := \mathcal{L}_{N} X$. Then there exist a stochastic process $\Wick{X^{\otimes 2}}$ such that for any $T>0, \kappa>0$,
    \begin{equ}
    
        \big(\Wick{X_N^{\otimes 2}}\big) := X_N^{\otimes 2} - \mathbb{E} X_N^{\otimes 2} \rightarrow \Wick{X^{\otimes 2}} \quad\text{in}\quad C([0,T]; \mathcal{C}^{-\kappa})\;.
    \end{equ}
    Since $X_N$ is stationary in space, we have in particular 
        $\div(X_N^{\otimes 2}) \rightarrow \div(\Wick{X^{\otimes 2}})$ in $C([0,T]; \mathcal{C}^{-1-\kappa})$.
    Moreover, for any $0<\eta<\frac{1}{2}$, $p\geq 1$ and small $\kappa'>0$, we have 
    \begin{equs}
    
        \mathbb{E} \sup_{s \leq t}\|X[s]\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-2\eta}}^p &\leq C(p,\eta, \kappa') \alpha_0^p t^{p(\eta-\kappa')}\;, \\
    
        \mathbb{E} \sup_{s \leq t}\|\div(\Wick{X^{\otimes 2}[s]})\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-1-2\eta}}^p &\leq C(p,\eta,\kappa')\alpha_0^{2p} t^{p(\eta-\kappa')}\;.
    \end{equs} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop pr:wick_renormalization of arXiv:2411.03482

body:
[Lemma lem:eb-exponential of arXiv:2608.25551, 'Beyond Optimal Rates in Stochastic Optimization: Trajectory-Adaptive Stopping Rules'] For every $\theta \in [0,1)$ and every $x \ge -1$,
\begin{equation}

    \exp\left(
        \theta x - \psi_{\mathrm E}(\theta) x^2
    \right)
    \le
    1+\theta x.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}

    \psi_{\mathrm E}(\theta)
    \le
    \frac{\theta^2}{2(1-\theta)}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, let $\mathcal G$ be a sigma-field, let $X$ be an integrable real-valued random variable satisfying $|X| \le b$ almost surely for some deterministic $b > 0$, and let $\lambda \in [0,1/b)$. Then
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{E}\left[
        \exp\left(
            \lambda \bigl(X - \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal G]\bigr)
            -
            \frac{\lambda^2 X^2}{2(1-\lambda b)}
        \right)
        \,\middle|\,
        \mathcal G
    \right]
    \le 1
    \qquad
    \text{almost surely}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Conditional exponential moment bound

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to derive the tail exponent from the Gibbs-Markov fixed-point equation as for smoothing transforms (Durrett-Liggett classification). Result: The Gibbs-Markov property along dyadic square partitions gives a fixed-point equation of smoothing type Z^D =_d sum_i e^{alpha Phi_i} Z^{D_i} with Gaussian binding field Phi and 4 pieces; Durrett-Liggett gives, for such equations, that non-trivial solutions have tails whose exponent is the root of a structure equation, here forcing E[Z^D(A)^s] finite iff s < 1. This yields the correct tail EXPONENT (P(Z^D(A) > t) decays like t^{-1} up to slowly varying factors) but not the precise Laplace asymptotic E e^{-lambda Z} = 1 - c lambda log(1/lambda)(1+o(1)) demanded by property (5); the slowly varying factor is exactly the content of the conjecture and the Durrett-Liggett theory does not fix it. Obstruction: Smoothing-transform theory fixes the power in the tail but not the logarithmic correction; the log factor is what (5) asserts.

body: In topology, a discipline within mathematics, the Jordan curve theorem (JCT), formulated by Camille Jordan in 1887, asserts that every Jordan curve divides the plane into two regions: the interior, bounded by the curve, and an unbounded exterior, containing all of the nearby and faraway exterior points. Every continuous path connecting a point of one region to a point of the other intersects with the curve somewhere.

[Lemma 7 (Bound on exceedance probability) of arXiv:2604.11434, 'Maxima of stationary systems of randomly time-changed L\'evy particles'] Let $\alpha$ be a mass function satisfying Assumption~\ref{asu:alpha}, let $(L_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be a L\'evy process satisfying Assumption~\ref{asu:levy}, and let $(X_t)_{t\ge 0}$
  be the time-changed process in the sense of Lemma~\ref{lem:existence_tcp}.
  Then, for all $t\ge 0$, there exists $v>0$ and $C_{v,t}>0$ such that
  for all $u,x\in\RR$ satisfying $u-x > v$ it holds that
  \begin{align*}
    \PP
    \left[
    \sup_{s\in[0,t]}
    X_s(x)
    \ \ge \ u
    \right]
    \ \le \
    C_{v,t}
    \cdot
    \PP
    \left[
    L_{t\cdot \overline{\alpha}}
    \ge
    u - x - v
    \right]
    \,.
  \end{align*}
title: Bound on exceedance probability

body:
[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\beta >0$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$ such that $\alpha + \beta/2 > 1$. Suppose $U:[0,1] \times \T^d \to\R^d$ is a $C^0([0,1],C^{\alpha-}(\T^d))$ multiscale finite range random velocity field; that is, $U$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{asmp:main for refreshing}, and \eqref{eq:refreshing theorem hypothesis} holds for some $p >\frac{ \beta}{\alpha + \beta/2-1} \lor \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$.
    
    Then almost surely:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item  for all $y \in \T^d$ and $s \in [0,1]$, the ODE~\eqref{eq:main refreshing ODE s} admits a unique solution on $[0,1]$, and thus the two-parameter flow $\Phi_{s,t}$ given by~\eqref{eq:main refreshing flow} is uniquely defined,
        \item  $\Phi_{s,t}$ is uniformly-in-time Lipschitz-in-space, $\sup_{0 \leq s,t \leq 1} \|\Phi_{s,t}\|_{W^{1,\infty}_y} < \infty$,
        \item  and the continuity equation~\eqref{eq:continuity} admits unique positive measure-valued solutions, that is, if $\phi \in TV(\T^d)$ is a positive measure, then there exists a unique distributional solution to~\eqref{eq:continuity} such that for all $t \in [0,1], f(t,\cdot) \in TV(\T^d)$ is a positive measure.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.05931

body:
[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] The image of the lifted product map $\ev: \Par\times \Par\to \univcover$ is as follows:
     \[
        \begin{aligned}
        \ev(\Par^+\times \Par^+) &= \Par_0^+\cup \Ell_1 \cup \Par_1^-\cup \Hyp_1,\\
        \ev(\Par^+\times \Par^-) &= \Par_0\cup \Hyp_0 \cup \{\mathrm{I}\},\\
        \ev(\Par^-\times \Par^-) &= \Par_0^-\cup \Ell_{-1} \cup  \Par_{-1}^+\cup \Hyp_{-1}.
        \end{aligned}
    \]
 Two parabolic elements $\pm P_1$ and $\pm P_2$ commute if and only if $\ev(\pm P_1, \pm P_2)$ belongs to $\Par_0 \cup \{\mathrm{I}\}$.
 Moreover, for $s_1, s_2 \in \{\pm\}$, $\ev$ satisfies the strong path-lifting property on the set $$S_{s_1,s_2} = \big\{(\pm P_1,\pm P_2) \in \Par^{s_1}\times \Par^{s_2}| \pm P_1P_2 \neq \pm P_2P_1\big\}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2609.02065

[Lemma lem:normals of arXiv:2607.06249, 'Extreme least singular values of Gaussian row submatrices and a phase retrieval stability '] Fix distinct $S,T\in\mathcal{S}$. Let $r=|S\cap T|$ and $D=m-r$. Then $D\ge2$. Conditional on the rows indexed
by $S\cap T$, the two normal lines $\mathbb{F} u_S$ and $\mathbb{F} u_T$ are independent Haar-distributed lines in the
$D$-dimensional space $E^\perp$, $E=\operatorname{span}_\mathbb{F}\{b_i:i\in S\cap T\}$. Equivalently, for all
phase-invariant events one may take $u_S,u_T$ to be independent Haar unit vectors in $E^\perp$.

[Prop of arXiv:2411.09988, 'A Study in Markov Chains, Loop-Erased Random Walk and Loop Soups'] The complete graph on n+1 vertices $\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$ is the (undirected) simple graph with the maximal number of edges. That is, every pair of distinct vertices is connected by an edge. In particular, each vertex has degree $n$. The number of spanning trees of the complete graph on $n + 1$ vertices is
    \[(n+1)^{n-1}.\]

[Theorem 9 (Uniqueness criteria for viscosity and entropy solutions) of arXiv:2605.13512, '2605.13512'] Assume that the speed function $\tilde c(x,y)$ satisfies Assumption \ref{ass:pde-speed} and
is dependent on $x$ only, that is to say that $\tilde c(x,y) = \tilde c(x)$. 

(HJ) Then, the limiting current $v = v(x,t)$ is the unique solution in the class of non-decreasing Lipschitz-1 functions in the space variable, in the sense of Definition \ref{defn: classical viscosity solution}.

    (SCL) Moreover, suppose that $\lambda(x,t)$ is a non-negative, locally bounded measurable function on $\bR \times \bR_+$ lying inside the interval $[0,1]$, that is also a weak solution to \eqref{SCL} in the sense of \eqref{weak soln integral form}. Let $\rho(x,t) = v_x(x,t)$ where $v$ solves \eqref{eq:no-t-HJ}. 
    
    Then, for any fixed $t > 0$, we have that for almost every $x \in \bR$,
    \be 
    \int^t_0 G(x, \lambda(x,s)) ds \leq \int^t_0 G(x, \rho(x,s)) ds.
    \ee
    Furthermore, if equality in \eqref{maximum principle} holds for almost all $(x,t)$, it implies that $\lambda(x,t) = \rho(x,t)$ for almost all $(x,t)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniqueness criteria for viscosity and entropy solutions

[Lemma 35 (Macroscopic Gram gap and energy capture) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $\mathfrak H=\mathfrak H_Q(A,r)>0$.  The reduced promotion satisfies
\begin{align}
 \lambda_{q_*}&\ge\frac{\mathfrak H}{dQ},
 \\
 \norm{\mathcal N_{q_*}R_{q_*}c}
 &\ge\frac{\lambda_{q_*}}{R}\norm c,
 \qquad c\in L_{q_*},
 \\
 \sum_{b,q}\norm{P_{V_q^{\mathrm{red}}}r_{b,q}}^2
 &\ge\frac{\mathfrak H}{dQa_QR^2}.
 
\end{align}
In particular, $\mathcal N_{q_*}R_{q_*}$ is injective on $L_{q_*}$,
$\dim V_{q_*}^{\mathrm{red}}\le d$, and
$V_{q_*}^{\mathrm{red}}\subset M_{q_*}^{\perp}$.

[Proposition 101 (Finite-cutoff reconstruction) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $Z_\Lambda=(X_{\W,\Lambda},X_{\K,\Lambda},
Y_{\W,\Lambda},Y_{\K,\Lambda})$ solve the finite-cutoff fixed-point equation for an
adapted localization pair, and set
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 u_\Lambda^{\chi,\rho}
 &=\rho(\Psi_{\W,\Lambda}+V_{\W,\Lambda})
   +X_{\W,\Lambda}+Y_{\W,\Lambda},\\
 v_\Lambda^{\chi,\rho}
 &=\rho(\Psi_{\K,\Lambda}+V_{\K,\Lambda})
   +X_{\K,\Lambda}+Y_{\K,\Lambda}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Then, in the sense of finite-cutoff distributions,
\begin{equation}
 \chi u_\Lambda^{\chi,\rho}v_\Lambda^{\chi,\rho}
 =\chi\Theta_\Lambda
  +\mathscr F_{X,\Lambda}^{\chi,\rho}(Z_\Lambda)
  +\mathscr F_{Y,\Lambda}^{\chi,\rho}(Z_\Lambda).
\end{equation}
Consequently the reconstructed fields solve the finite-cutoff auxiliary system
\eqref{eq:cutoff-system}.  Conversely, suppose that a solution of
\eqref{eq:cutoff-system} can be written as
\[
 u_\Lambda=B_{\W,\Lambda}^\rho+R_{\W,\Lambda},
 \qquad
 v_\Lambda=B_{\K,\Lambda}^\rho+R_{\K,\Lambda},
\]
with
\[
 R_{a,\Lambda}\in C_TH^r\cap C_T^1H^{r-1}
 \quad(a\in\mathfrak C)
\]
for some $r>3/2$.  Then it determines a unique solution of the finite-cutoff fixed-point equation

body:
Let X_1, X_2, ... be INDEPENDENT AND IDENTICALLY DISTRIBUTED. Call an event A EXCHANGEABLE if it is invariant under every permutation of finitely many indices, that is A is unchanged when the values of any finite set of coordinates are permuted. Then P(A) is 0 or 1 for every exchangeable A. This is strictly stronger than Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, which applies to TAIL events: every tail event is exchangeable, but not conversely. The standard separating example is A = { S_n = 0 for infinitely many n } for a simple random walk, which is exchangeable but NOT a tail event, since changing X_1 changes every partial sum. Identical distribution is essential and cannot be relaxed to mere independence. Minimal counterexample: let X_1 be Bernoulli(1/2) and let X_n = 0 deterministically for every n >= 2. These are independent but not identically distributed, and the event A = { x : x_n = 1 for some n } is invariant under every finite permutation of the coordinates, hence exchangeable, yet P(A) = P(X_1 = 1) = 1/2. The proof below breaks exactly where one needs it to: the permutation swapping the first n coordinates with the next n is not measure preserving unless the coordinates share a law. A standard use: for an i.i.d. sequence the events {limsup S_n = + infinity} and {liminf S_n = - infinity} are exchangeable, because permuting finitely many summands changes S_n for only finitely many n, so each has probability 0 or 1; for a non-degenerate mean-zero law a short further argument then shows both probabilities are 1, but that conclusion is NOT delivered by the 0-1 law alone. [Hewitt and Savage (1955); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.1]

body: [Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.29615, 'A Characterization of the Cumulants\\ as Continuous Moment-Based Statistics'] Let $F:L^n\to\R$ be such that there exists a continuous function $f:\R^n\to \R$ with $F(X)=f(\E[X], \dots, \E[X^n])$. Suppose that $F$ is additive, i.e., for all independent $X,Y\in L^n$, $F(X+Y)=F(X)+F(Y)$. Then $F$ is a linear combination of cumulants of order at most $n$, equivalently $f$ is (in the appropriate domain) a linear combination of logarithmic Bell polynomials. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let Sigma be a p by p positive semidefinite matrix and n >= 1 an integer, and let X be a p by n random matrix whose n columns are independent and identically distributed as the p-dimensional Gaussian N(0, Sigma). The Wishart distribution W_p(Sigma, n) is the probability distribution of the p by p random matrix X X^T. When Sigma is positive definite and n >= p, a matrix distributed as W_p(Sigma, n) is almost surely positive definite (invertible). [standard, e.g. Muirhead, Aspects of Multivariate Statistical Theory]

[Definition 11 (positive survival datum) of arXiv:2609.03736, '2609.03736'] A positive survival datum for $\Theta_\Omega$ is a
pair $(\rho,\Lambda)$ with $0\ne\rho\succeq0$ in
$\mathcal H_{E,\Omega}$ and $\Lambda\in\RR$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \Theta_\Omega(\rho)\succeq\Lambda\rho.
 
\end{equation}
When we wish to make the underlying homogeneous data explicit, we say that
$(\rho,\Lambda)$ is a positive survival datum for
$(\mathsf G,\mathsf H,E,\ell,\Omega)$.
Its global support dimension and basepoint support dimension are
\begin{equation}
 D_\rho=\rank\rho,\qquad
 r_\rho=\rank K_\rho(o,o).
 
\end{equation}
Invariance makes the last rank independent of the point, and positivity
makes it nonzero.  Thus $D_\rho/r_\rho$ compares the global support of the
operator on $\mathcal I_{E,\Omega}$ with the support visible in one geometric
fiber.
title: positive survival datum

[Prop 23 of arXiv:2510.23423, 'One-arm exponents of the high-dimensional Ising model'] Let $d\geq 2$ and $\beta>0$. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a subgraph of $\mathbb Z^d$ with $0\in V$. Let $S\cap B=\emptyset$ be finite subsets of $V$, with $S$ containing $0$. Assume that $\partial S$ is separating $0$ and $B$ in the sense that every path from $0$ to $B$ has to visit $\partial S$. Then,
\begin{equation}
	\phi_{G, \beta}^0[0 \connect{} B] \leq \sum_{\substack{u\in S\\ v\notin S\\ u\sim v}} \phi_{S, \beta}^0[0 \connect{} u]\beta\phi_{G, \beta}^0[v \connect{} B]. 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

A subset Ω′ ⊆Ωis said to be shattered by F if any function g : Ω′ →{0, 1} can be obtained by restricting some function f ∈F onto Ω′. The VC dimension of F, denoted by VC(F), is the size of the largest subset Ω′ ⊆Ω that can be shattered by F.

        \[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega \continuous^0_{x}} \leq K \sqrt{p}2^{(n-\alpha+\ep)j}.\]
        \item[(iii)] For all $j \in \N, \nabla \cdot u^j =0.$
        \item[(iv)] $\P(\forall x \in \T^d, |U(x)| \geq 1) = 1.$

    However, 
     \begin{enumerate}
        \item 
        There exists $y \in \T^d$ such that for all $h>0$
         \[\P\big(\text{\eqref{eq:main ODE autonomous data} has a unique solution on } [0,h]\big) = 0.\]
        Further, there exists $y \in \T^d$ such that almost surely in $U$, for all $\ep>0$ sufficiently small, 
        \[\limsup_{t\to 0} t^{-\frac{1}{1 -2\alpha  -\ep}} \mathrm{diam}\{X_t : X \text{ is a solution to~\eqref{eq:main ODE autonomous data}}\} = \infty.\]
        \item 
        Almost surely, $U$ admits nonunique bounded solutions on $[0,1]$ to~\eqref{eq:continuity} for some bounded initial data.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 4.30 (p. 137) asks whether there is an explicit function psi(b,s) tending to 0 as s tends to infinity, not depending on the chain, with sup_x |P(S_t/(sigma sqrt t) <= x) - P(Z <= x)| <= psi(||g||_inf, t/tau2) for standardized g and continuous-time reversible chains. Our result (id P0209, 2026-09-08): NO such psi exists. Take two independent reversible chains: Y two-state with rates epsilon and 1 - epsilon (spectral gap exactly 1) and Z a fair sign flip at rate R/2; set epsilon = s^-2, R = s^4, A = 2 epsilon + sqrt((1-epsilon)(1-4 epsilon)), B = (2-A)/(1-epsilon) and g = A Z + B (Y - epsilon). Then exactly, at every s: E g = 0, E g^2 = 1, ||g||_inf = 2 and tau2 = 1. Taking t = s sends t/tau2 to infinity with the sup norm pinned at 2, yet normality fails: S_t is compound Poisson with vanishing intensity (the mean number of visits to the rare state is epsilon t = 1/s, tending to 0), so with probability 1 - O(1/s) no visit occurs and S_t sits near the deterministic value -B epsilon t while the whole variance is carried by one rare excursion. Verification as the source words it: the identities were checked to seven decimals at every s, and the measured Kolmogorov distance to N(0,1) is 0.478, 0.505, 0.509, 0.506 at s = 30, 100, 300, 1000 - flat at about 1/2, not decreasing, while t/tau2 rises from 30 to 1000. Prior art not cleared.

body: In mathematical analysis, a function of bounded variation, also known as BV function, is a real-valued function whose total variation is bounded (finite): the graph of a function having this property is well behaved in a precise sense. For a continuous function of a single variable, being of bounded variation means that the distance along the direction of the y-axis, neglecting the contribution of motion along x-axis, traveled by a point moving along the graph has a finite value. For a continuous function of several variables, the meaning of the definition is the same, except for the fact that the continuous path to be considered cannot be the whole graph of the given function, but can be every intersection of the graph itself with a hyperplane parallel to a fixed x-axis and to the y-axis.

[Theorem thm:dim_free_unbounded of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_n \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ be a martingale difference sequence adapted to a filtration $(\mathscr{F}_i)^n_{i=0}$ with $\mathscr{F}_0 = \{\varOmega, \varnothing\}$. 
    Fix $\alpha > 0$ and set for all $i \in [n]$
    \[
    \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i \coloneqq \E\lrs{\mathbf{X}^2_i \middle| \mathscr{F}_{i-1}},
    \quad
    U_i \coloneqq \norm*{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{X}_i)_+ \big| \mathscr{F}_{i-1}}_{\psi_{\alpha}}.
    \]
    
    Fix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \succcurlyeq 0$, $U \ge K > 0$ and define the event
    \begin{equation}
    
        E \coloneqq \lrc{\sum^n_{i = 1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i \preccurlyeq \boldsymbol{\Sigma},
        \quad
        \sum^n_{i = 1} U^{2}_i \le U^2,
        \quad
        \max_{i \in [n]} U_i \le K}.
    \end{equation}
    Let $\sigma^2 \coloneqq \lambda_{\max}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, and $z$ be as in (equation eq:def_z of the paper). Then for any $\mathrm{x} > 0$ with probability at least $\mathbb{P}(E) - (e\cdot r(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) +1) e^{-\mathrm{x}} - e^{-\mathrm{x}} \ind[\alpha < 1]$, it holds for any $0 < \varepsilon\le 1$
    \begin{align}
        \max_{k \in [n]} \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{S}_k) \le& (1 + \varepsilon)\sigma \sqrt{2\mathrm{x}} + \frac{7 \lr{\ln \frac{8}{\varepsilon}}^{1/\alpha} Kz \mathrm{x}}{\min\lrc{2 \alpha z^{\alpha}, \hspace{0.2em}\underline{\log}\hspace{0.2em}\lr{\lr{\frac{K z}{\sigma}}^2 \mathrm{x}} }} \nonumber \\
        &+ \frac{3 K}{\alpha} \left(2 \mathrm{x} + 2\ln\lr{\frac{4 U}{K}}
        + \frac{4}{\alpha}\ln \lr{\frac{4}{\alpha e}} \right)^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}} \ind[\alpha < 1] ,
    \end{align}
    and moreover,
    \begin{align}
       \max_{k \in [n]} \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{S}_k) \le& (1 + \varepsilon)\sigma \sqrt{2 \mathrm{x}} + 2 \lr{\ln \frac{8}{\varepsilon}}^{1/\alpha} Kz \mathrm{x} \nonumber \\
       &+ \frac{3 K}{\alpha} \left(2 \mathrm{x} + 2\ln\lr{\frac{4 U}{K}}
        + \frac{4}{\alpha}\ln \lr{\frac{4}{\alpha e}} \right)^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}} \ind[\alpha < 1] .
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 15 (Lipschitz control of spectral observables) of arXiv:2606.21137, 'A Sudakov--Fernique proof of Lehner-type edge bounds for matrix-valued GUE sums'] On the real vector space
	\(\bigl(M_M(\C)_{\mathrm{sa}}\bigr)^n\), the maps
	\[
		(G_1,\ldots,G_n)\mapsto\lambda_{\max}(H_M),
		\qquad
		(G_1,\ldots,G_n)\mapsto\lambda_{\max}(-H_M),
		\qquad
		(G_1,\ldots,G_n)\mapsto\|H_M\|_{\op}
	\]
	are Lipschitz with respect to the real Euclidean norm on the GUE inputs induced
	by the Frobenius norm,
	\[
		\|(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_n)\|_{\mathrm{Euc}}
		=
		\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\|\Delta_i\|_F^2\right)^{1/2},
	\]
	with constant
	\[
		L
		\le
		\frac{\Arow}{\sqrt M}.
	\]

Let X be a continuous random vector in R^n with finite variance and let Z ~ N(0, I_n) be independent of X. Let X_t = X + sqrt(t) * Z. Let h(X_t) = - int p_t(x) log p_t(x) dx be the differential entropy of X_t. Then d/dt h(X_t) = (1/2) * J(X_t), where J(X_t) = int ||nabla log p_t(x)||^2 p_t(x) dx is the Fisher information of X_t.

body:
[Definition def:above_below_waterfall of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] Denote by $\mathcal{W}^{\pm}$ the regions above and below the waterfall, that is,
	\begin{equation*}
		\mathcal{W}^{+}\coloneqq
		\begin{cases}
			\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
			\mathsf{x}>\mathsf{N}+(\mathsf{t}-\mathsf{T}+\mathsf{S})^+\},&\textnormal{if $\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{T}$};\\
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
			\mathsf{t}_l<\mathsf{t}<\mathsf{t}_r,\ \mathsf{x}>\tfrac12(\mathsf{S+\mathsf{t}+\mathsf{N}})
		\}\\\hspace{20pt}
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\le \mathsf{t}_l,\
					\mathsf{x}>\mathsf{N}
			\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{S}}
			\\\hspace{20pt}
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\ge \mathsf{t}_r,\
					\mathsf{x}>\mathsf{S}+\mathsf{N}+\mathsf{t}-\mathsf{T}
				\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{S}+\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{T}}
		,
		&\textnormal{if $\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}$},\\
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation*}
	and
	\begin{multline*}
		\mathcal{W}^{-}\coloneqq
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
			\mathsf{t}_l<\mathsf{t}<\mathsf{t}_r,\ \mathsf{x}<\tfrac12(\mathsf{S+\mathsf{t}-\mathsf{N}})
		\}
			\\
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\le \mathsf{t}_l,\
					\mathsf{x}<\mathsf{t}
			\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{S}}
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\ge \mathsf{t}_r,\
					\mathsf{x}<\mathsf{S}
				\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{S}+\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}}.
	\end{multline*}
	Here the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{S}}$ means that the
	subset in the union is present only if $\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{S}$, and similarly for all
	other indicators.
	In the samples in (fig:waterfall_region of the paper), right,
	the regions $\mathcal{W}^{\pm}$ are the lighter-colored ones. They consist solely of the horizontal lozenges
	\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline = (current bounding
		box.south),scale=.25]
	\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,1)--++(1,0)--++(-1,-1)--cycle;
	\end{tikzpicture}.\footnote{The below region $\mathcal{W}^-$ exists only if
	$\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}$. In (sec:asymptotic_clustering_of_nonintersecting_paths of the paper) below,
	we show that for
	$\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{T}$, the nonintersecting paths stay
	as low as they can: First, they go straight with
	slope $0$ until $\mathsf{t}=\mathsf{T}-\mathsf{S}$, and then
	continue diagonally with slope $1$.}

	Also denote $\mathcal{P}\coloneqq \mathcal{H}\setminus(\mathcal{W}^+\cup \mathcal{W}^-)$,
	this is the region inside the hexagon where we expect the nonintersecting paths to cluster together.
	We call $\mathcal{P}$ the \emph{saturation band}. It has constant width~$\mathsf{N}$
	and includes the waterfall region.
title: Definition def:above_below_waterfall of arXiv:2507.22011

body: [Definition def:contours_whole_plane of arXiv:2605.03896, 'Dimer models on astroidal zig-zag graphs'] For \(v\in V(N)\) and \(\zeta\in \Sigma_+^\circ\), let \(C_v^\zeta\) be a curve from \(\sigma(\zeta)\) to \(\zeta\) intersecting \(A_0\) exactly once in the component of \(A_0\setminus\bm \alpha\) corresponding to \(v\), and such that \(\sigma_*(C_v^\zeta)=-C_v^\zeta\). body:
[Lemma 7 (Joint score orthogonality and Fisher-energy decomposition) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Under the joint law of $(X_t,R)$, assume the relevant squared scores are
integrable and that differentiation may be passed under the \(\nu\)-integral
in \(p_t(x)=\int p_t(x,r)\,\dd\nu(r)\).  Write
$s_t^R(X_t)=s_t^r(X_t)|_{r=R}$.  Then
\begin{equation}

\E[g_t(X_t,R)\mid X_t]=0,
\end{equation}
and therefore the score second-moment matrices obey
\begin{equation}

\E\!\left[s_t^R(X_t)s_t^R(X_t)^\top\right]
=
\E\!\left[s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)^\top\right]
+
\E\!\left[g_t(X_t,R)g_t(X_t,R)^\top\right].
\end{equation}
Taking the trace gives
\begin{equation}

\E\|s_t^R(X_t)\|^2
=
\E\|s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)\|^2
+
\E\|g_t(X_t,R)\|^2,
\end{equation}
and, for every deterministic vector $v$,
\begin{equation}

\E|v^\top s_t^R(X_t)|^2
=
\E|v^\top s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)|^2
+
\E|v^\top g_t(X_t,R)|^2.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Joint score orthogonality and Fisher-energy decomposition

[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $\beta>0$, $\lambda>0$, $p\geq 1$ and let, for all $j\geq 0$, $u^j$ be defined by~\eqref{eq:refreshing poisson}. Suppose there exists $M\geq 1$ such that for all $j\geq 0$, $n\in\{0,1,2\}$, and $s\in[0,1]$,
\[\|\nabla^n f^j_s\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_{t,x}}\leq M 2^{(n-\alpha-\beta /p)j}.\]
Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item the $u^j$ are mutually independent with $\E u^j =0$,
\item for each $j\geq 1$, $u^j$ has a finite temporal range of dependence $2^{-\beta j}$,
\item and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$ and $n\in\{0,1,2\}$,
\[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_{t,x}}\leq CM(\lambda+p)2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 19 of arXiv:2608.05931

Let A0,A1 be real Hurwitz 2x2 matrices. Fix lambda in (0,1) such that Alambda=(1-lambda)A0+lambda A1 has real eigenvalues -lambda_minus<0<lambda_plus. For beta>0 let I switch 0->1 at rate beta*lambda and 1->0 at rate beta*(1-lambda), and let Xdot=AI X. For every initial probability law assigning no mass to X=0, t^-1 log||Xt|| converges almost surely to an initial-law-independent real chi(beta). There exist 0<beta1<=beta2<infinity such that chi(beta)<0 for beta<beta1 and chi(beta)>0 for beta>beta2. Consequently the norm tends respectively to zero or infinity. The theorem does not assert beta1=beta2, monotonicity, or a single instability interval. Source: Benaim, Le Borgne, Malrieu and Zitt, arXiv:1204.1921, Section 1 standing Hurwitz assumption, Assumption 1.1, rates preceding Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.6, PDF pp.1-2.

[Lemma Planar two-disk logarithmic capacity and
boundary-layer profile, \(d = 2\) of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] For
\(0 < \varepsilon \ll \delta\) the logarithmic capacity of the
union of two disks of radius \(\varepsilon\) whose centers are at
distance \(2\delta\) is
\(\operatorname{cap}_{\log} = \sqrt{2\varepsilon\delta}\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right)\).
Consequently, writing
\(\delta_{\varepsilon} = \operatorname{dist}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\partial M \right)\)
and assuming
\(\log\delta_{\varepsilon}/\log\varepsilon \rightarrow \theta \in \lbrack 0,1\rbrack\),
the reflected half-plane condenser energy of
\(B\left( x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon \right) \cap M\) is
\(E_{H} = B(\theta)\, E_{0}\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right)\) with the
planar profile

\[B(\theta) = \frac{1}{1 + \theta},\quad\quad B(1) = \frac{1}{2},\quad B(0) = 1.\]

[Theorem thm:lower of arXiv:2608.23638, 'Replicable Conformal Prediction'] Fix an integer $n\ge1$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $0<\varepsilon\le\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)/4$, $0<\rho\le1$, $0\le\delta\le\tfrac1{16}$. Let $\mathcal{A}:[0,1]^n\times\mathsf R\to\mathbb{R}$ be jointly measurable, with a shared seed $r\sim\nu$ independent of the data. If, for \emph{every} atomless Borel law $P$ on $[0,1]$ with CDF $F_P$, $\mathcal{A}$ is $\rho$-replicable and $\mathbb{P}[F_P(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D};r))\in[1-\alpha\pm\varepsilon]]\ge1-\delta$, then
$n\;\ge\;\tfrac{9(1-8\delta)^{2}}{4096}\,\tfrac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{\varepsilon^{2}\rho^{2}}\;\ge\;\tfrac{9}{16384}\,\tfrac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{\varepsilon^{2}\rho^{2}}$.
The proof is self-contained, incurs no logarithmic loss, and uses accuracy only at the two endpoints of the hard family, each satisfying Assumption~(ass:margin of the paper) with $\kappa=1$, $\Delta=\varepsilon$, constant density in $[2\min(\alpha,1-\alpha),2]$; the whole family satisfies it with $\Delta=\tfrac14$, $f_{\min}=\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$, $f_{\max}=2$. The bound concerns exact replication of the scalar threshold; Appendix~(app:lower of the paper) states the exact scope (set-map-only replicability is not automatically covered). (Proof: Appendix~(app:lower of the paper).) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:dub of arXiv:2603.28161, 'Boundary four-point connectivities of conformal loop ensembles'] {dubedat2015}}]
Let $n\ge1$, $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,...,x_n)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Let $U=\{(y_1,y_2,\mathbf{x}):|y_1-u|<\varepsilon, 0\le y_2-y_1<\varepsilon,\|\mathbf{x}-{\bf x}_0\|<\varepsilon\}$, and $\Delta=\{(y_1,y_2,\mathbf{x})\in U:y_1=y_2\}$. For $\rho,\tau,\sigma\in\mathbbm{R}$, consider the differential operator
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{M}=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{y_1}^2+\left(\frac{\rho}{y_1-y_2}+a(y_1,y_2,\mathbf{x})\right)\partial_{y_1}+\left(\frac{\tau}{2(y_2-y_1)}+b(y_1,y_2,\mathbf{x})\right)\partial_{y_2}+{\bf X}+\left(-\frac{\tau \sigma}{2(y_1-y_2)^2}+\frac{d(y_1,y_2,\mathbf{x})}{y_2-y_1}\right)
\end{equation}
where ${\bf X}:=\sum_{i=1}^nc_i(y_1,\mathbf{x})\partial_{x_i}$, and $a,b,c,d$ are smooth on $U$. Suppose $\alpha_-<\alpha_+$ are the two roots of the indicial equation $\alpha(\alpha-1)+(\tau+2\rho)\alpha-\tau \sigma=0$.

Suppose $f$ is a real-valued smooth function on $U\setminus\Delta$ such that $\mathcal{M} f=0$ and $f=O((y_2-y_1)^{\alpha_-+\delta})$ for some $\delta>0$. Further, assume that for ${\bf Y}:=\partial_{y_1}$ and ${\bf Y},{\bf X}$ satisfies the H\"ormander's condition on $U\setminus\Delta$. Then there exists a smooth function $g$ on $U$ such that $f=(y_2-y_1)^{\alpha_+}g$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 5 (Localized cutoff heat-kernel bound) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Let $\mathsf O\subset\R^{3d}$ be a bounded smooth open set, and let
$Z^{\delta,\mathsf O}$ denote the cutoff process constructed in
Lemma~\ref{lem:chain-compatible-cutoffs}.  After the reordering
\[
    X^1=r,\qquad X^2=p,\qquad X^3=\theta,
\]
the cutoff drifts preserve Pigato's triangular dependence structure
\[
    B_j=B_j\left(x^{j-1},\ldots,x^3\right),\qquad j=2,3.
\]
Then, for every $0<t_0<M<\infty$ and compact sets
$K_0,K_1\subset\mathsf O$, the transition laws of
$Z^{\delta,\mathsf O}$ admit densities
$p_\delta^{\mathsf O}(t,z,y)$ satisfying
\[
    \sup_{\substack{
        0\le\delta\le1\\
        t\in[t_0,M]\\
        z\in K_0,\ y\in K_1}}
    p_\delta^{\mathsf O}(t,z,y)<\infty .
\]
The same estimate holds for the adjoint cutoff family.

[Proposition prop:caractHolder of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] Let $s\in (0,1)$, $\alpha \in [0,1]$ and consider $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $f \in \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$.    Then $f \in T^{s, \alpha}C(\mathbb{R}^2)$ if and only if its hyperbolic wavelet coefficients satisfy
$$ 
\sup_{\bar{j}\in (\mathbb{N}\cup\{-1\})^2,\bar{k}\in \mathbb{Z}^2} 2^{( (1+\alpha)\max (\bar{j})+(1-\alpha) \min(\bar{j})) s}  | c_{\bar{j},\bar{k}} | < + \infty.$$

DRAFT, mathematical review pending. Let P be a finite probability law on simple paths and F_k the prefix filtration, with completed paths retained and a finite deterministic horizon N. For nested forbidden sets A subset B let E_A,E_B be full-path avoidance events, so E_B subset E_A, and r(A)=P(E_A), r(B)=P(E_B). Put M_k^A=P(E_A|F_k), M_k^B=P(E_B|F_k). For every lambda>0, P(max_(0<=k<=N)(M_k^A-M_k^B)>=lambda)<=min(1,(r(A)-r(B))/lambda). This applies to exact fixed-length SAW kernels and to all-length finite endpoint-constrained SAW laws; no independence or path-length loss is required.

[Prop upscale of arXiv:2609.03033, 'An Overview of Einstein $4$-Manifolds'] Let $(M^4,g)$ be a smooth compact oriented Riemannian manifold,
 and suppose, for a fixed spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak{c}$,  that there is a solution of the unperturbed Seiberg-Witten equations  ((drc of the paper)--(sd of the paper))  for every 
 metric $\widehat{g}$ in the conformal class of  $g$.  
Then the scalar curvature 
$s$ and self-dual Weyl curvature $W_+$ of $g$ must satisfy
\begin{equation}

\int_M \left(s-\sqrt{6}|W_+|\right)^{2}d\mu_g  \geq  72\pi^2 [c_1^+]^2 .
\end{equation}
 Moreover, if $c_1^+:= c_1(L)^+$ is non-zero, equality can only occur  if $g$ is an almost-K\"ahler metric for which $s-\sqrt{6}|W_+|$ is a  negative constant,  for which the 
 symplectic form everywhere belongs to the bottom eigenspace of $W_+$,  and for which the two highest eigenvalues of $W_+$ are everywhere equal.

body: The hairy ball theorem of algebraic topology (formally, the Sphere Vector Field Theory, sometimes called the hedgehog theorem) states that there is no non-vanishing continuous tangent vector field on even-dimensional n-spheres. For the ordinary sphere, or 2‑sphere, if f is a continuous function that assigns a vector in ℝ3 to every point p on a sphere such that f(p) is always tangent to the sphere at p, then there is at least one pole, a point where the field vanishes (a p such that f(p) = 0).
title: Hairy ball theorem

# Positive entrances for the rescaled-correlation SDE

Status: proof draft (unaudited), Target1 architecture step. This is a theorem about a specified SDE, not a correction to Li-Nica Theorem4.1 and not a proof of finite-width network convergence. The result includes both disputed constant drifts, so it does not require deciding C012's source correction.

Let c>0, gamma be real, and B be standard Brownian motion on [0,T] with B_0=0 on a usual filtered probability space. Consider finite, continuous, adapted processes q_t>0 for t>0 satisfying on every compact positive-time interval

    dq_t = 2q_t[(1-c sqrt(q_t))/t+gamma]dt+2sqrt(2)q_t dB_t.   (Q)

Put a=c/sqrt(2), b=3-gamma. Every such solution corresponds to a finite nonnegative F_0-measurable variable u_0 through

    E_t=exp((b-1)t-sqrt(2)B_t),
    U_t=E_t[u_0+a integral_0^t E_s^(-1)ds],
    q_t=t^2/(2U_t^2), t>0.                                  (R)

Conversely every finite u_0>=0 in F_0 gives a strictly positive solution on positive times by (R). For u_0=0 its unique continuous entrance is q_0=1/c^2. For u_0>0 its continuous entrance is q_0=0, and q_t/t^2->1/(2u_0^2). Thus the unique solution having a strictly positive finite entrance value has necessarily q_0=1/c^2 and is pathwise unique for a given B. Merely assigning the value q_0=0 does not select a unique positive solution.

For the ReLU coefficient c=sqrt(2)/(3pi), the positive entrance is q_0=9pi^2/2. The source's displayed Eq4.7 has gamma=-1 (b=4); its displayed log equation4.8 corresponds to gamma=+1 (b=2). The entrance classification above applies separately to both. C004's checked compact generator selects gamma=+1 in its coordinate transformation, but the source-theorem correction remains for the Claude reviewer.

## Reciprocal transformation and classification

For t>0 define U=t/sqrt(2q). Its derivatives are U_t=U/t, U_q=-U/(2q), U_qq=3U/(4q^2). Ito's formula gives

    dU=[U/t-U((1-c sqrt(q))/t+gamma)+3U]dt-sqrt(2)U dB
       =[a+bU]dt-sqrt(2)U dB.                                (U)

The constant term uses U c sqrt(q)/t=c/sqrt(2)=a. The coefficients of (U) are globally Lipschitz, and its integrating factor is E_t as above. On any positive-time interval the variation-of-constants identity says E_t^-1 U_t-a integral_0^t E_s^-1 ds is constant in t. Evaluating at one positive time shows that this constant u_0 is finite. Since E is continuous, positive, and E_0=1, it follows that U_t->u_0 as t decreases to zero. Positivity of U at every positive time forces u_0>=0. Its measurability at zero follows from the usual right-continuity of the filtration and adaptedness of U_t. This proves that every positive solution must have representation (R).

Conversely the representation solves (U), is positive at every t>0 since a>0, and is finite on every finite interval. Applying Ito to t^2/(2U^2) away from t=0 proves (Q). Thus the representation covers exactly the positive solutions.

If u_0>0, U_t->u_0 immediately gives the stated q_t/t^2 limit. If u_0=0, continuity of B implies uniformly for 0<=s<=t that E_t/E_s->1 as t->0. Consequently

    U_t/(a t)=(1/t) integral_0^t E_t/E_s ds ->1 almost surely,
    q_t ->1/(2a^2)=1/c^2 almost surely.

This also proves continuity and strict positivity at the canonical entrance. Uniqueness follows from the integrating-factor formula, with no choice of an initial Brownian correlation or independent marginal limits.

## Integral interpretation through the singular time

The canonical extension also satisfies the integral SDE from time0; its singular drift is locally integrable. To see this directly without an unstated regularity assumption, set M_t=sup_(s<=t)|B_s|. On a fixed Brownian path and finite T, the exponential-ratio estimate gives

    |U_t/(at)-1| <= C(omega)(t+M_t)

near zero. Since the ratio tends to1, it follows that |q_t-1/c^2|<=C(omega)(t+M_t). The function q(1-c sqrt(q)) is locally Lipschitz and vanishes at 1/c^2, so the absolute singular drift is bounded by C(omega)(1+M_t/t). Doob's L2 inequality gives E M_t<=2sqrt(t), and therefore

    E integral_0^T M_t/t dt <=4sqrt(T)<infinity.

Tonelli's theorem makes the latter integral finite almost surely. The remaining drift is continuous and the noise coefficient q is bounded near zero on each path. Localize by these path bounds and let the lower integration endpoint decrease to zero; the stochastic integral has a continuous extension. Thus the integral equation is well defined with q_0=1/c^2. For u_0>0, q_t=O(t^2), making the drift integrable even more directly.

## Why this is not a full q-chain convergence statement at time0

For the network observable q_l=l^2(1-rho_l), the literal value at l=0 is0. The canonical positive-time limit instead has continuous extension 1/c^2>0. Hence the unmodified q_floor(nt) paths cannot converge in the usual Skorohod topology on [0,T] to that continuous extension: evaluation at0 preserves the value0 under Skorohod convergence. Changing only the value at the first time point also does not address the whole shrinking initial layer.

The natural continuous entrance variable is U_n=1/(n theta_floor(nt)), whose initial value tends to0. Once its network convergence is established, q_t=t^2/(2U_t^2) on positive times selects u_0=0 and thus the canonical q entrance. C005-C006 attempt precisely that network step but remain unaudited. body: In the random recursive tree, the layer of a vertex is the number of rounds of leaf-stripping until it is a leaf, and l_k is the limiting fraction of vertices at layer k. Conjecture 1 of arXiv:2608.04303, l_k = exp[-k/e - (3/(2e)) log k - O(1)], holds: the paper's recursion s_0 = 1, s_i(y) = 1 - exp(-int_0^y s_{i-1}) is exactly the Poisson product formula P(M_i <= y) for the generation-i minimum M_i of the branching random walk on the Poisson-weighted infinite tree, so lbar_k = E[e^{-M_k}], and the velocity 1/e with the (3/(2e)) log k correction is Addario-Berry and Ford (Ann. Appl. Probab. 2013, Theorem 1.1). With Aidekon (2013) the O(1) is a genuine limit: lbar_k e^{k/e} k^{3/(2e)} -> C* ~ 1.42 and l_k / lbar_k -> 1 - e^{-1/e} ~ 0.3078. The layer half of Conjecture 2 also holds: the maximum layer is floor(diameter/2), so L_n = e log n - 1.5 log log n + O_P(1).

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2608.28528, 'Strong solutions of SDEs with critical discontinuities in diffusion coefficients'] Define occupation measures: for a Borel measurable set $A \subset [s,t] \times \mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\mu_m^{s,x}(A):=\mathbf{E}\int_s^t \mathbf{1}_A(r,X_{s,r}^{x,m})dr, \quad m=1,2,\dots
$$
and
$$
\mu^{s,x}(A):=\mathbf{E}\int_s^t \mathbf{1}_A(r,X_{s,r}^{x})dr.
$$
The following are true:
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\rm (\textit{i})}] For every function $0 \leq F \in C_c([s,t] \times \mathbb R^d) \cap \mathbf{F}_\mu$,
\begin{align*}
\int F d\mu_m^{s,x} & = \mathbf{E}\int_s^t F(r,X_{s,r}^{x,m})dr \\
& \rightarrow \int_s^t \int_{\mathbb R^d} F d\mu^{s,x} = \mathbf{E}\int_s^t F(r,X_{s,r}^{x})dr \text{ as } m \rightarrow \infty
\end{align*}
and
\begin{equation}

\mathbf{E}\int_s^t F(r,X_{s,r}^{m,x})dr,\;\; \mathbf{E}\int_s^t F(r,X_{s,r}^{x})dr \leq C \|F\|_{L^2([s,t], L^2_{\rho}(\mathbb R^d))}^{\frac{2}{q}},
\end{equation}
where constant $C$ depends on $\mu$, but does not depend on the smoothness or the support of $F$.

\item[{\rm (\textit{ii})}] The limiting occupation measure $\mu^{s,x}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the weighted Lebesgue measure $dr \times \rho(x)dx$ on $[s,t] \times \mathbb R^d$.

\smallskip

\item[{\rm (\textit{iii})}] For every function $0 \leq F \in L^2([s,t] \times L^2_{\rho}(\mathbb R^d)) \cap \mathbf{F}_\mu$,
$$
\mathbf{E}\int_s^t F(r,X_{s,r}^{x})dr \leq C \|F\|_{L^2([s,t], L^2_{\rho}(\mathbb R^d))}^{\frac{2}{q}}.
$$ 
\end{itemize}

body:
[Corollary 18 (Unitriangular standard-monomial Wick--Jacobi gauge) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] On a fixed standard-monomial stratum, fix a monomial order and let
\[
 b_1,\ldots,b_\mu
\]
be the standard monomials for the quotient by the initial ideal of
\((\partial_1P_m,\ldots,\partial_dP_m)\), and put
\[
 \mathcal W
 =
 \exp\!\left(-\frac12\Delta\right),
 \qquad
 \Delta=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.
\]
Choose the section \(\iota\) in
\cref{thm:jacobi-normal-form-transfer} to be their standard polynomial
representatives.
The classes represented by
\[
 \mathcal Wb_1,\ldots,\mathcal Wb_\mu
\]
form a Jacobi-enriched Wick basis of the twisted de Rham module.  Relative
to \(b_1,\ldots,b_\mu\), its algebraic comparison matrix is triangular by
increasing polynomial degree, has diagonal equal to one, and therefore
\begin{equation}
 \det B_{\mathrm{Jac}}^{\mathrm{std}}=1.
 
\end{equation}
Its inverse is induced by
\(\exp(\Delta/2)\), the positive finite sum over Wick pairings.
For a nonquadratic phase, \(\mathcal W\) is here a triangular change of
cohomology frame; it is not asserted to be a chain map for
\(\nabla_{P,t}\).
The equality of the determinant to one belongs to this specified gauge;
the invariant statement under arbitrary rational frame changes is the
nonvanishing in \cref{cor:jacobi-comparison-determinant}.

[Lemma lem:moment_bound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{X}$ be a L\'evy process with 
generating triplet $(\bm{\gamma_X},\bm{\Sigma_X}\bm{\Sigma_X}^{\scalebox{0.6}{$\top$}},\nu_{\bm{X}})$.
 Recall the Blumenthal--Getoor index $\beta$ from~(equation eq:BG of the paper) and the associated quantity $\beta_+\in [\beta,2]$. Assume that, for some $p>0$, we have
$\int_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus B_{\bm{0}}(1)}|\bm{w}|^p\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})<\infty$.
 Then there exist constants $C_i\in[0,\infty)$, $i=1,\ldots,4$, such that
\[
\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{s\in[0,t]}|\bm{X}_s|^p\bigg]
\leqslant \1_{\{\bm{\Sigma_X}\neq\bm{0}\}}C_1 t^{p/2} 
+C_2 t^p + C_3 t^{\min\{1,p/\beta_+\}},
\quad \text{ for } t\in[0,1].
\]
If $\int_{B_{\bm{0}}(1)\setminus\{\bm{0}\}}|\bm{w}|\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})< \infty$ and $\bm{X}$ has zero natural drift, i.e. $\bm{\gamma_X}=\int_{B_{\bm{0}}(1)\setminus\{\bm{0}\}}\bm{w}\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})$, then $C_2=0$ in the inequality above. [Proposition prop:fourier of arXiv:2607.12564, 'Power-law and log-periodic degree tails for a family of probability generating function eq'] Let $\chi:=2\pi/\log\lambda$, $s_m:=\rho+1+i\chi m$, and
$\mathcal{M}_j(s):=\int_0^\infty w_j(x)x^{s-1}dx=\mathbb{E}[V_j^{\,s-1}]$, finite and analytic for

\begin{equation}
  \widehat\Psi_j(m):=\int_0^1\Psi_j(u)e^{2\pi i m u}\,du=\frac{2p}{a\log\lambda}\,\mathcal{M}_j(s_m).
\end{equation}
In particular $\widehat\Psi_j(0)=\overline\Psi_j=\frac{2p}{a\log\lambda}\mathbb{E}[V_j^{\,\rho}]>0$.

[Theorem thm.odlyzko_richmond of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] If $\{p_j\}$ is a discrete distribution with $p_j = 0$ for $j < 0$ and $j > d$, while $p_0 > 0, p_d > 0$, and
    \[
        \gcd\{j: p_j \ne 0\} = 1,
    \]
    then for any $\delta > 0$ there is an $n_0^{OR} = n_0^{OR}(\delta)$ such that if $a_{k,n}$ denotes the value of the
    $n$-fold convolution $\{p_j\}^{*_n}$ at $k$ then for $n \ge n_0^{OR}$,
    \[
        a_{k,n}^2 \ge a_{k-1,n} a_{k+1,n}
    \]
    for $\delta n \le k \le (d-\delta) n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Proposition 3.3 (Proposition 2.1, [PR19]) of arXiv:2604.02746, 'Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant'] Fix $\Delta\geq 3$.
