body:
[Defi Def:star of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] Let $ \mathcal{Q} = (\mathcal{Q}_0,\mathcal{Q}_1) $ be a totally mutable quiver. 
	We say that $ \mathcal{Q} $ is of {\em type star-shaped} if it is mutation equivalent to a star-shaped quiver $ \mathcal{Q}_\star $,
	i.e., a quiver that   
	is made up from the following components:
	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
		\item 
		finitely many quivers $ \mathcal{Q}^{(\alpha)}_\star $ of type $ A_{\ell_\alpha} $ with 
		respective set of vertices $ \{ 1^{(\alpha)}, \ldots, \ell_\alpha^{(\alpha)} \} $ 
		and $ \ell_\alpha \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_+ $, 
		for $ \alpha \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $,
		and
		
		\item 
		an additional, distinguished vertex, say $ 0 $, 
		and there exists a single arrow between $ 0 $ and $ 1^{(\alpha)}  $, 
		for all $ \alpha \in \{ 1, \ldots, m \} $. 
	\end{enumerate} 
	We call 
	$ \mathcal{Q}^{(\alpha)}_\star  $ the {\em rays} of $ \mathcal{Q}_\star $,
	$ \ell_\alpha $ the {\em length of the ray} $ \mathcal{Q}^{(\alpha)}_\star $,
	and
	$ m $ the {\em number of rays} of $ \mathcal{Q}_\star $.
title: Defi Def:star of arXiv:2609.01501

body:
[Theorem 19 (Pathwise centered operator and full cutoff convergence) of arXiv:2606.26065, 'Localized Centered Second-Chaos Operators'] Assume the Galerkin-state finite-state condition in Assumption~\ref{ass:time} and
\[
 \mathfrak S_H^{(\eps)}(\beta,\sigma)
 +\mathfrak S_B^{(\eps)}(\zeta,\sigma)<\infty.
\]
Then on the full-probability event $\Omega_*$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:BC}, for every cutoff $\Lambda$ the series~\eqref{eq:assembled} defines a bounded operator
\[
 \cB^\circ_\Lambda(\omega):\Xspace_T^\sigma\to\Yspace_T^{\beta,\zeta},
\]
and
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{\Lambda\in\Dyd\cup\{\infty\}}
 \norm{\cB^\circ_\Lambda(\omega)}_{\Xspace_T^\sigma\to\Yspace_T^{\beta,\zeta}}
 \le C_*(\omega)
 \left[\mathfrak S_H^{(\eps)}+\mathfrak S_B^{(\eps)}\right].
\end{equation}
Moreover the entire Galerkin sequence, not merely a subsequence, satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \cB^\circ_\Lambda(\omega)\to\cB^\circ(\omega)
 \quad\text{in }\cL(\Xspace_T^\sigma,\Yspace_T^{\beta,\zeta}).
\end{equation}
For every fixed input and output test vector, the limiting scalar pairing belongs to the centered second Wiener chaos.

body:
[Definition def:continuous_process_min_max_construction of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] (Continuous
  process) Let $\ell>0$,  $x_0 \in [0, \ell]$ and
  $\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0 \in \{-1, 1\}$ (resp.
  $\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0 \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$) be given. Consider two
  independent Markov jump processes $\sigma^1$ and $\sigma^2$ with the
  transition rates of figure
  (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper)
  (resp. (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)) and
  respective initial states $\sigma^1_0$ and $\sigma^2_0$.

  Using the jump times $(T_i)_{i \ge 0}$ of the couple
  $(\sigma^1, \sigma^2)$, recursively define $x(t)$ by $x(0) = x_0$
  and
\begin{equation*}
x(t) = \max \left[0,  \min \left[\ell, x(T_i) + (\sigma^2(T_i) - \sigma^1(T_i)) (t - T_i) \right] \right] \text{ for } t \in [T_i, T_{i+1}[.
\end{equation*}
The process $X(t) = (x(t), (\sigma^1(t), \sigma^2(t)))$ is referred to as {continuous process}.
title: Definition def:continuous_process_min_max_construction of arXiv:2411.13964

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.19832, 'Sharp Convex Concentration for Symmetric Random Tensors with Subgaussian Coordinates'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\R$. Assume that
\[
 \int e^{x^2/K^2}\,d\mu(x)\le2.
\]
Let $g\ge0$, and put
\[
 a=\int g\,d\mu,\qquad
 b=\int g\log_+g\,d\mu.
\]
If $0<a\le1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \int x^2g(x)\,d\mu(x)
 \le K^2\left[b+a\log\left(\frac{2}{a}\right)\right].
\end{equation}
Also,
\begin{equation}
 \int x^4\,d\mu(x)\le C K^4.
\end{equation}

[Lem Lemma: Invariant polynomials of arXiv:2605.16921, '${\ASL_n}(\mathbb Z)$ invariant random subsets of $\mathbb Z^n$'] Let $n \geq 0$ and let $P: Z^0(X) \to \mathbb{R}_{\leq n}[X_1, \ldots, X_d]$ be a measurable map such that, for every $\gamma \in \SL_d(\mathbb{Z})$, every $t \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, and $\nu$-a.e.\ $x \in Z^0(X)$,
    $$ P(\gamma \cdot x)(t) = P(x)(\gamma(t)) \quad \text{(up to a uniformly bounded error)}.$$
    Then $P(x)$ is the constant polynomial for $\nu$-a.e.\ $x$.

Let S0,S1 be finite sets of the same size N with intersection size N-k,where0<=k<N. Let1<=r<N. For b=0,1 let P_b be the law of an ordered r-tuple sampled uniformly without replacement from S_b,viewed on the common ambient space(S0 union S1)^r. Then ||P0-P1||_TV=1-(N-k)_r/(N)_r<=min(1,r*k/(N-r)),where(a)_r denotes the falling factorial and is0 when the nonnegative integer a<r. In particular,the bound r*k/(N-r) is LemmaA.10(with r denoted n there).

Uniform ordered sampling without replacement;both laws embedded in the same tuple space.

[Proposition prop:mono of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item \emph{(Attractiveness.)} On a fixed marked configuration, if $A\subseteq B$ are initial
  infected sets then $A_t\subseteq B_t$ for every $t\ge0$.
\item \emph{(Monotonicity in the configuration.)} Let $\omega\subseteq\omega'$ be marked
  configurations carrying the same trajectories, the same recovery marks and the same transmission
  marks on the particles, respectively the ordered pairs, that they have in common. Then every
  open path of $\omega$ is an open path of $\omega'$. Consequently $I_t(\omega)\subseteq
  I_t(\omega')$ for every $t$, and every event which is the existence of an open path with
  prescribed properties is increasing.
\item \emph{(Monotonicity of the survival probability.)} The map
  $\eta\mapsto\mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\mu}_\eta(\text{survival})$ is non-decreasing,
  $\lambda\mapsto\mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\mu}_\eta(\text{survival})$ is non-decreasing, and
  $\mu\mapsto\mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\mu}_\eta(\text{survival})$ is non-increasing. The three statements are
  at a fixed recovery rule $\mathfrak r$. Hence $\eta_c$ is well
  defined by (equation eq:etac of the paper) and is non-decreasing in $\mu$, and $\mu_c$ is well defined by
  (equation eq:muc of the paper) and is non-decreasing in $\eta$ and in $\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact minimum stationary cover time for reversible chains structural calculation Result: The assertion holds for two states. Write P(0,1)=a and P(1,0)=b,0<a,b<=1. Stationarity gives pi=(b,a)/(a+b), and E_pi C=b/[a(a+b)]+a/[b(a+b)]=(a^2+b^2)/[ab(a+b)]>=1, since a^2+b^2>=2ab and a+b<=2. Equality requires a=b=1. Check: The initial state is already visited at time0, so the two-state cover time is exactly the first hit of the other state. This fixes the common off-by-one and laziness errors. A deterministic directed cycle would violate the general bound for large n but is nonreversible and is not a counterexample. Obstruction: A many-state coupon-collector argument needs to control the distribution of the next unvisited target; its selection is biased by the history. Individual stationary hitting-time inequalities cannot simply be summed in random discovery order.

[Corollary 14 of arXiv:2607.04012, 'Hölder regularity for backward stochastic Volterra integral equations and applications to '] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assumption-Holder-BSVIE} holds for some $p>2$,
    and let $0<\gamma<\frac12-\frac1p$. Then there exists a version of $Z$,
    still denoted by $Z$, and a random variable $C_\gamma$ satisfying
    $\mathbb E[|C_\gamma|^p]<\infty$, such that, almost surely,
    \begin{gather*}
        \bigg(
        \int_0^{s\wedge r}
        |Z(t,s)-Z(t,r)|^2\,dt
        \bigg)^{\frac12}
        \leq
        C_\gamma |s-r|^\gamma,
        \qquad s,r\in[0,T].
    \end{gather*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma pro: singleEdge vs Tree of arXiv:2411.13465, 'Height-offset variables and pinning at infinity for gradient Gibbs measures on trees'] The following relation holds true for the moment generating function $\hat{\varphi}^{\nu}_r$ and any $t$ in the interval $(-R,R)$, where $\hat{\psi}^{free}(t)$ exists as a finite number.
\begin{enumerate}[a)]
    \item In case of $\nu$ being the free measure,
\[\hat{\varphi}^{free}_r(t)=\prod_{l=0}^{r-1} \hat{\psi}^{free}\left(\frac{t}{(d+1)d^{l}}\right)^{(d+1)d^l}.\]
    \item For the $\nu$ being a GGM of height-period $2$ with associated fuzzy chain $\bar{\mu}$, for real $t$ we have
    \[ \hat{\varphi}_r^{\bar{\mu}}(t)  \leq \prod_{l=0}^{r-1} \hat{\psi}_\star^{\bar{\mu}}\left(\frac{t}{(d+1)d^{l}}\right)^{(d+1)d^l}.\]
\end{enumerate}
Note that the Statements (a) and (b) remain true if we replace the moment generating functions by the respective characteristic functions, i.e., substitute $t=is$ for any $s \in \mathbb{R}$, and consider absolute values in (b).

Then

and
\[
 \sum_i\mathsf C_i^2=(1-N^{-1})I_W.
\tag{3.3.1w$_2$}

Consequently every assertion of
(lem:singleton-renewal of the paper),
(lem:singleton-order-sum of the paper), (lem:typed-pass of the paper), and
(lem:haar-passive-zero of the paper) remains valid with $W_i^\circ$ replaced by
$\mathsf C_i$ and with the better seed parameter
\[
 \eta_C=\left\|\frac1N\sum_i\mathsf C_i^2\right\|
 =\frac{N-1}{N^2}\le\frac1N.
\tag{3.3.1w$_3$}
\]

For $q\ge1$ there are scalars $\alpha_q,\beta_q$ such that
\[
 \mathsf C_i^q=\alpha_q\mathsf C_i+\beta_qI,\qquad
 |\alpha_q|\le2,\quad \beta_1=0,\quad
 |\beta_q|\le\frac3N\quad(q\ge2).
\tag{3.3.1w$_4$}
\]
More generally, for $2\le q\le L\log n$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
 \left\|\frac1N\sum_i\mathsf C_i^{\otimes q}\right\|_\mathrm{op}
 \le\frac2N.
\tag{3.3.1w$_5$}
\]
After latest-pivot exposure, the same bound, with $A_L^q/N$ on the
right, survives powers on individual rails and fixed flips, dualities,
and normalized Brauer maps.  Thus a
fused nonroot full-deposit block is either one passive singleton, an
explicit scalar child of size $A_L^q/N$, or a hard intact block carrying
one $A_L^q/N$ resource.  If an intact rank-one pinch remains after
latest-pivot exposure and Ward evacuation, so that its exterior map
$T\in\operatorname{End}(W)$ is fixed with respect to the fresh plane, then
\[
 \left\|\frac1N\sum_i\mathsf P_iT\mathsf P_i\right\|_\mathrm{op}
 \le\frac1N\|T\|_\mathrm{op}.
\tag{3.3.1w$_6$}
\]

[Definition 1 (Asymptotically Flat manifold) of arXiv:2608.29427, '\small Positive mass and rigidity \\ for asymptotically flat tangent bundles'] A complete Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is called asymptotically Flat (AF) if there exists a compact set $K\Subset M$ such that
	\[
	M\setminus K=M_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup M_k,
	\]
	where each end $M_a$ is diffeomorphic to the complement of a closed Euclidean ball in $\mathbb R^n$, and, in the corresponding coordinates near infinity,
	\[
	g_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\in\mathcal O_2\left(|x|^{-\sigma_a}\right)
	\]
	for some $\sigma_a>0$.

[Lemma lem-propertieschi of arXiv:2604.14318, '\large The free energy of the interacting Bose gas:\\\medskip a variational description \\'] Suppose that the interaction potential $v$ satisfies Assumption (V), in particular (equation LowBoundAss of the paper). Then the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The set $K$ in (equation Kdef of the paper) is compact, and for any $\rho_1,\rho_2$, the infimum in the definition (equation chidefneu of the paper) of $\chi(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ may be restricted to $K$, not changing its value for any sufficiently large $L$. Furthermore, the maps $P\mapsto \langle P,\mathfrak N_U^{\ssup{\ell,{\mathcal L }}}\rangle$ and $P\mapsto\langle P,\mathfrak N_U^{\ssup{\ell,{\mathcal S }}}\rangle$ are continuous on $K$. 

\item The maps  $[0,\infty)^2 \ni (\rho_1,\rho_2)\mapsto \chi(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ and $[0,\infty)\ni\rho \mapsto \overline\chi(\rho)$ are convex. Furthermore, for any $\rho_1$, respectively $\rho_2\in[0,\infty)$, $\lim_{\rho_2\to\infty}\chi(\rho_1,\rho_2)=\infty$ and $\lim_{\rho_1\to\infty}\chi(\rho_1,\rho_2)=\infty$.

\item The map $\rho_1\mapsto \chi(\rho_1,0)$ is  continuous at $\rho_1=0$ with $\chi(0,0)=\chi^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({v=0}})}}}(0,0)=\overline q=(4\pi\beta)^{-d/2}\zeta(1+d/2)$ and $\partial_{ \rho_1}\chi(\rho_1,0)|_{\rho_1=0}=-\infty$. 

\item For any $\rho_1, \rho_2 \in[0,\infty)$, there is at least one minimiser $P$ in the formula for $\chi(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ on the right-hand side of (equation chidefneu of the paper).

\item For any $\rho\in[0,\infty)$, there is at least one minimiser $P$ in the formula for $\overline\chi(\rho)$ on the right-hand side of (equation chifreeenergy of the paper). 

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:dom1 of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda >0$ and a send sequence~$\overline{p}$.
Let $X$ be the backoff process with birth rate $\lambda$ and send sequence $\overline{p}$.
Let $J$ be a positive integer.
Let $\overline{p}'$ be the send sequence 
such that, for all $i\geq 0$, $p'_i = p_{i+J}$.
There is a real number $\lambda'\in (0,\lambda)$ and a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on non-negative integers with  $\mathcal{D} \gtrsim \mathsf{Po}(\lambda')$ such that 
the following holds.
Let $X'$ be the backoff process with 
birth distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and  send sequence $\overline{p}'$. Then 
there is a coupling of $X'$ and~$X$ such that, 
for all non-negative integers~$i$ and $t$,
$\mathbf{b}^{X'}_{i}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{b}^{X}_{i+J}(t+J)$.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2604.07207, 'Mixing times of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $S$ be an SRRW on $(\ZZ_2^d, +)$ with reinforcement parameter $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and step distribution $\mu$ given by
     $$\mu(e_G)=\frac{1}{2}, \quad \text{and }\quad \mu(e_k)=\frac{1}{2d}, \ k=1,2,\dots,d.$$
  Then for any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$,
$$ \lim_{L\to \infty}\frac{t^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)}{d\log d} = \frac{1}{(1-\alpha) \ _2F_1(1,\alpha^{-1};\alpha^{-1}+1; \frac{1}{2})}.$$
where
$$
_2F_1(a,b;c;z):=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{(a)_m (b)_m}{(c)_m} \frac{z^m}{m!}
$$
is the hypergeometric function, and $(a)_m$ is the rising Pochhammer symbol given by $(a)_0=1$ and $(a)_m=a(a+1)\cdots (a+m-1)$ for $m\geq 1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2604.07207

[Lemma 33 of arXiv:2608.26953, '2608.26953'] Let \(M\) be a finite-dimensional left \(A_S\)-module and \(p\geq 0\). Then
\[ \Theta_p: M^\vee\otimes_{A_S}\Omega_S^p\otimes_{A_S}M \rightarrow \prescript{}{A_S}{\operatorname{Hom}} \bigl(M,\Omega_S^p\otimes_{A_S}M\bigr), \qquad \Theta_p(\varphi \otimes \beta \otimes m)(x) = \varphi(x)\beta\otimes m, \]
is an isomorphism of \(A_S\)-bimodules, where the bimodule structures are induced by the left and right \(A_S\)-actions on \(\Omega_S^p\). Moreover,
\[ \prescript{}{A_S}{\operatorname{Hom}} \bigl(M,\Omega_S^p\otimes_{A_S}M\bigr) \cong \bigoplus_{\sigma = [v_0, \ldots, v_p]\in S_p} \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk} \bigl( M_{v_0} , M_{v_p}\bigr), \] under which a family \(U_\sigma \colon M_{v_0} \to M_{v_p}\) corresponds to \( x \to  \sum_{\sigma=[v_0, \ldots, v_p] \in S_p} \rho_\sigma\otimes U_\sigma( \delta_{v_0} x).\)

[Theorem thm:Lagrange of arXiv:2411.14556, 'Emergence in Graphs with near-extreme constraints'] Let $g$ be an entropy-maximizing graphon, subject to the constraints $\varepsilon(g)=e$ and $\tau(g)=t$.
If the function $G(x,y)$ is not constant on the set of points $(x,y)$ where 
$0 < g(x,y) < 1$, then there exist unique Lagrange multipliers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that 
\begin{equation}  H'(g(x,y)) = \alpha + \beta G(x,y) \end{equation}
almost everywhere. Furthermore, the function $g(x,y)$ is bounded away from 0 and 1.

[Proposition eq:Gaussian-jet-law of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:Gaussian-jet}
Let the disorder be standard Gaussian.  For every deterministic frame \(O\),
\begin{equation}
 (h_G(O),g_G(O),A_G(O))\stackrel d=
 \left(
 \frac{Z_0}{\sqrt N},
 \sqrt p\,(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n),
 \gamma_{N,p}M_n-\frac{pZ_0}{\sqrt N}I_n
 \right),
 \qquad
 \gamma_{N,p}=\sqrt{\frac{2p(p-1)n}{N}}.
\end{equation}
Here \(Z_0,Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) are independent standard Gaussians and \(M_n\) is an independent GOE matrix.

body:
[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] For the genus-two surface \(\Sigma_2\) considered in
Lemma~\ref{lem:lr-secants-extremal-length}, there is no strictly increasing
function \(F:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) such that
\(
  t\mapsto F\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{X_t}(\lambda)\bigr)
\)
is convex for every \(\lambda\in\mathcal{ML}(\Sigma_2)\) and every
Teichm\"uller geodesic \(X_t\subset\mathcal T(\Sigma_2)\). Consequently,
after allowing equivariant harmonic maps to
$\mathbb R$-trees as targets, there is no universal strictly increasing
transformation $F$ that makes all harmonic-map energy functions convex along
all Teichm\"uller geodesics. In particular, no fixed power $F(s)=s^k$,
$k>0$, has this property.

[Proposition 23 (Endpoint tail inequalities) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] For every $0\leq s\leq t$ and $k\geq2$,
\begin{equation}

h_k(t)-h_k(s)
\geq
\int_s^t\Phi_k(h(u))\,du.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $h_k$ is continuously differentiable on
$[0,t_{\mathrm{sus}}^{\mathrm{iso}})$ and, for every
$t<t_{\mathrm{sus}}^{\mathrm{iso}}$,
\begin{equation}

h_k'(t)
\leq
\sum_{u=1}^{k-1}h_u(t)h_{k-u}(t)
+\ell(t)h_k(t).
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:geodesics_are_maximizers of arXiv:2605.22787, 'Invariant measures for half-space geometric LPP: classification and the one force--one sol'] Assume that $b$ is an eternal solution. For $(m,n) \in \mathbb{Z}^2_{\mathrm{HS}}$, define the path $\gamma_{(m,n)}$ by (equation eq:gamma_path of the paper). For $j \in \mathbb{Z}_{< n}$, define 
    \[
    i_j^* := \max\Bigl\{i \in \mathbb{Z}: \gamma_{(m,n)}(-k) = (i,j-1) \text{ for some }k \in \mathbb{N} \Bigr\}.
    \]
    That is, $i_j^\star$ is the rightmost location on horizontal level $j-1$ that the path $\gamma_{(m,n)}$ crosses. Then,
    \begin{equation} 
    i_j^\star = Z_{b({\hspace{1.1pt}\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.5}{\bullet}}\hspace{1.1pt}},j-1),j}(m,n) = \max \Biggl\{\argmax_{j \le i \le m} \Bigl[b(i,j-1) + G\bigl((i,j),(m,n)\bigr)\Bigr]\Biggr\}.
    \end{equation}

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] \textup{(i)} For every bounded interval $\Omega=(\alpha,\beta)$, $\Lp(\cA_\Omega)$ is finite and is associated with a positive eigenfunction $\phi_\Omega\in C^1(\Omega)\cap C(\overline \Omega)$ satisfying $\phi_\Omega(\beta)=0$. It is unique up to a positive factor. If $q\in C^1(\overline \Omega)$, the adjoint eigenfunction is positive in $\Omega$ and vanishes at $\alpha$. Increasing exhaustions converge to the generalized principal value on every bounded or unbounded interval. For $\Omega_L=(-L,L)$, assume $J\in C_c^2(\R)$, $q,a\in C^2(\R)$ and $q\ge q_0>0$, write $\lambda_p(L):=\Lp(\cA_{\Omega_L})$, and normalize $\int_{-L}^{L}\phi_L\phi_L^*=1$. Then $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ belongs to $C^1((0,\infty))$ and
\[
\lambda_p'(L)=
q(L)\phi_L'(L)\phi_L^*(L)
-d\phi_L(-L)\int_{-L}^{L}J(x+L)\phi_L^*(x)\,dx<0.
\]

\textup{(ii)} Let $\mathcal L\subset(0,\infty)$ be open. Assume that the pulled-back coefficients satisfy the analytic hypothesis $\mathrm{(A_{an})}$ of Section~5: locally uniformly for $L\in\mathcal L$, the functions $J(z(\xi-\eta))$, $q(z\xi)$ and $a(z\xi)$ admit bounded holomorphic extensions with respect to the complex length variable $z$ in a neighborhood of $L$, uniformly for $\xi,\eta\in[-1,1]$. Then $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is real analytic on $\mathcal L$. After pull-back to $(-1,1)$ and normalization at the origin, the direct eigenfunction is real analytic as a $C^1([-1,1])$-valued map; the normalized adjoint eigenfunction is analytic as well. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:calYzero_representation}
The set $\{ \hat{f}_i^0 \mid i \in \mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, \dots \}$ is a basis for ${\rm aff}(\Sym^0)$. 
Moreover, the coefficients in an expansion $f = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0$ with respect to this basis
are given by the formula
$\alpha_i^0 = \frac{2(p f(-2i) - q f(2i))}{p-q}.$

\begin{proof}
Fix $f \in \Sym^0$. 
Note that for all $z \not\in S^0 = 2\mathbb{Z}$ and positive integers $i$, $f(z) = \hat{f}_i^0(z) = 0$. 

Solving the symmetry equation $pf(0) + qf(2) = pf(-2) + qf(0)$ for $f(0)$, we obtain
\(
f(0) = \frac{pf(-2) - qf(2)}{p-q},
\)
so that defining 
\(
\alpha_1^0= 2f(0) 
\)
results in 
\( f(0) 
= \alpha_1^0 \hat{f}_1^0(0) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \alpha_k^0 \hat{f}_k^0(0)\). 
Since 
$f(z)=0$ for all other $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} < 2$, this is the unique value of $\alpha_1^0$ satisfying the formula $f(z) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \alpha_k^0 \hat{f}_k^0(z)$ when $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} < 2$. 

We proceed by induction on $k$. 

Our inductive hypothesis is that 
\(
\alpha_i^0 = \frac{2(pf(-2i) - qf(2i))}{p-q}
\)
(where $i \in [k]$) is the unique solution to $f(z) = \sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(z)$ for $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} < 2k$. 
We compute
\begin{align*}
f(2k) = \sum_{i \ge 1} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(2k) 
&= \alpha_{k}^0 \hat{f}_{k}^0(2k) + \alpha_{k+1}^0\hat{f}_{k+1}^0(2k) \\
&= \left(\frac{2(pf(-2k) - qf(2k))}{p-q}\right)\left(\frac{q}{2}\right) + \alpha_{k+1}^0 \frac{p}{2} 
\shortintertext{thus}
\alpha_{k+1}^0 &= \left(\frac{2}{p}\right)\left(f(2k) - \left(\frac{pqf(-2k) - q^2f(2k)}{p-q}\right)\right) \\
&= \frac{2((p-q+q^2)f(2k) - pqf(-2k))}{p(p-q)} \\

&= \frac{2(pf(2k) -qf(-2k))}{p-q} .
\end{align*}
where we have used the identity $p - q +q^2 
= p^2$. 

Note that the symmetry equation 
\[ pf(2k) +qf(2k+2) = pf(-2k-2)+qf(-2k) \]
may be arranged as 
\[pf(2k) - qf(-2k) = pf(-2(k+1)) - qf(2(k+1)) \]whence the desired formula 
\(
\alpha_{k+1}^0 = \frac{2(pf(-2(k+1)) - qf(2(k+1)))}{p-q} 
\).
A similar argument shows that the same value of $\alpha_{k+1}^0$ is the unique solution to $f(-2k) = \sum_{i\ge1} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(-2k)$. 
Since $f(z) = \hat{f}_i^0(z) = 0$ for all $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{z} \in (2k,2(k+1))$,

this completes the induction step; 

consequently $f = \sum_{k \ge 1} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0$ everywhere on $\mathbb{R}$. 

Finally, note that 
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 
= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat{f}_i^0(2k) 
= \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0(2k) 
= \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} f(2k) = 1. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'

body:
[Theorem 16 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] The Krawtchouk polynomial $K_{m,d,n} = K_m$ is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\lambda_m = 1 - \frac{nm}{d(n-1)}$ of the RWBD chain's transition matrix $P$.
   \begin{proof}
      By Lemma \ref{krav_orth}, the Krawtchouk polynomials are orthogonal wrt the inner product,
      \[\langle A,B\rangle = \sum_{i=0}^n {d \choose i}(n-1)^i A(i) B(i)=\langle A,B \rangle_\pi\]
      The transition probabilities of the RWBD chain are affine so by Theorem \ref{eig-orth}, the Krawtchouk polynomials are eigenfunctions as required. Therefore, for each $K_m$ there exists $\lambda_m$ such that,
      \[PK_m = \lambda_m K_m\]
      Specializing to the $0^\text{th}$ coordinate we have,
      \[(PK_m)(0) = \lambda_mK_m(0)\]
      Now, consider $(PK_m)(0)$
      \begin{align*}
      (PK_m)(0) &= \sum_{y\in \Omega} P(0,y)K_m(y)\\
      &= P(0,0)K_m(0)+P(0,1)K_m(1)\\& = K_m(1)
      \end{align*}
      Therefore,
      \[\lambda_m = \frac{K_m(1)}{K_m(0)}\]
      Evaluating $K_m(0)$ and $K_m(1)$,
      \begin{align*}
            K_m(0) &= \sum_{j=0}^{m}{(-1)}^j{0 \choose j}{d-0 \choose m-j}{(n-1)}^{m-j}\\
            &= {d \choose m}{(n-1)}^{m}\\
            K_m(1) &= \sum_{j=0}^{m}{(-1)}^j{1 \choose j}{d-1 \choose m-j}{(n-1)}^{m-j}\\
            &= {d-1 \choose m}(n-1)^m - {d-1 \choose m-1} {(n-1)}^{m-1}
      \end{align*}
      Recall the standard binomial coefficient identities,
      \[\frac{d}{d-m}{d \choose m}={d-1 \choose m} \quad \text{and}\quad \frac{m}{d}{d\choose m} = {d-1 \choose m-1} \]
      Therefore,
      \begin{align*}
         \lambda_m &= \frac{\frac{d}{d-m}{d \choose m}(n-1)^m - \frac{m}{d}{d \choose m} (n-1)^{m-1}}{{d \choose m}(n-1)^{m}}\\
         &= \frac{d}{d-m} - \frac{m}{d(n-1)} \\
         &= 1 - \frac{mn}{d(n-1)}
      \end{align*}
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 25 of arXiv:2512.07202, 'Hitting Probabilities for Hypoelliptic Differential Equations Driven by Fractional Brownia'] Let 
\[
\rho_{s,t}(u) := \mathbb{P}\left( \mathbf{U}_{s,t} \in du ~\big|~ \mathcal{F}^W_s \right), \quad u \in \mathfrak{g}^{(l)}(\mathbb{R}^d)
\]be the conditional density of \( \mathbf{U}_{s,t} \) given \( \mathcal{F}^W_s \).
There exist a constant \( C > 0 \), depending only on \( d \) and \( H \), and a family of positive random variables \( \{\Psi_{s,t}\}_{0 \leqslant s < t} \) such that
\[
\rho_{s,t}(u) \leqslant \frac{C}{(t-s)^{H\nu}} \exp\left( -\frac{\|u\|_{\mathrm{CC}}^2}{C(t-s)^{2H}} \right) \Psi_{s,t},
\]
for all \( 0 \leqslant s < t \leqslant T \), where the Malliavin-Sobolev norm of \( \Psi_{s,t} \) does not depend on \( s \) or \( t \), and \( \nu=\sum_{k=1}^l k \dim(\mathcal{L}_k) \) is the homogeneous dimension of \(\mathfrak{g}^{(l)}(\mathbb{R}^d) \). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 25 of arXiv:2512.07202

[Conjecture 2 (Variance-sensitive Matrix Spencer) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] There exists a universal constant $C$, such that for any choice of $n$ symmetric matrices $A_{1}, \dots, A_{n} \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfying $\|A_i\|_{\op}\le 1$ there exists a coloring $x\in\{\pm1\}^{n}$, such that
\begin{equation}

\Bigl\|\nlsum_{i=1}^n x_i A_i\Bigr\|_{\op} \le C \Bigl\|\nlsum_{i=1}^n A_i^2\Bigr\|_{\op}^{1/2}.
\end{equation} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Variance-sensitive Matrix Spencer

[Lemma 14 (Curvature in a controlled cone corridor) of arXiv:2609.02788, '\textbf{Quantized Einstein Metrics on \(S^7\) with \(SU(3)\)-Symmetry}'] Let
\[
 g=dt^2+\sum_{i=1}^3 f_i(t)^2Q|_{\mathfrak m_i}
\]
be an $SU(3)$-invariant diagonal metric satisfying $\Ric(g)=6g$ on an
interval $I\subset(0,T]$.  Suppose that, for constants $c_0,C_0>0$,
\begin{equation}
 c_0t\le f_i(t)\le C_0t,
 \qquad |tL_i(t)|\le C_0,
 \qquad i=1,2,3.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 |\Rm(g)|(t)\le C t^{-2}\qquad(t\in I),
\]
where $C$ depends only on $c_0,C_0,T$ and the fixed homogeneous
normalization $Q$.

Independent derivation pending w440 review. For every fixed integer n>=1, the supremum of the critical probability of reaching graph distance n, over roots of infinite connected locally finite quasi-transitive graphs of maximum degree at most 3 with p_c<1, is 1. Indeed, for the uniformly L-subdivided 3-regular tree with L>=n, that probability is 1-(1-2^(-n/L))^3 and tends to 1 as L grows. No single f(n) tending to zero can bound the entire class. A degree-only C/n bound fails already at n=L since the probability is 7/8. This does not exclude graph-dependent bounds and does not address the smaller vertex-transitive class. The family has p_c tending to 1, growing orbit count, and volume-growth rate tending to 1.

[Thm 6.2 of arXiv:2608.16170, '\bf On hitting time distributions of Markov processes with sub-Gaussian heat kernel bounds'] Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional complete Riemannian manifold with non-negative Ricci curvature and $\Delta _M$ be the Laplace-Beltrami operator on it. 
 Let $X=(X_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be the Brownian motion on $M$ associated with the generator $\frac{1}{2}\Delta _M$. Then for any $x\in M$ and nearly Borel set $B\subset M$, 
\[
    \lim_{t\downarrow 0}\left(-t \cdot \log \mathbb{P}^x[\sigma_B\leq t] \right)=\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{d}(x,B)^2,
\]
where $\widetilde{d}(x,B)$ is defined as (equation eq:63 of the paper).

body: exact_full_dual(points): compute $r=\operatorname{qrank}(\text{points})$, greedily keep $r$ coordinates on which the projection still has rank $r$, take $r$ independent projected points as a basis, and for each tail in $\{\pm1\}^{r-1}$ set values $=(1,\text{tail})$, solve $Bh=\text{values}$ exactly over $\mathbb Q$, and accept the form iff $|\langle x,h\rangle|=1$ for EVERY projected point $x$. Returns the accepted value-vectors as the projective full dual in evaluation coordinates. Notes: Normalization to first evaluation $=1$ is exactly the projective quotient by $\pm1$; enumerating tails is complete because a full-dual form is determined by its values on a basis of the fibre. This makes the full dual computable exactly, which is the pivot on which the whole finite programme rests.

[Cor final-scale of arXiv:2605.08052, 'Rapid phase ordering of Ising dynamics on $\mathbb Z^2$'] In the setting of Theorem~(thm:inductive-step of the paper), there exists $c>0$ such that for all $\beta>\beta_0$, if $t_N = e^{ c \beta \bar \kappa N^2}$ and $\delta_N = c e^ { - c^{-1} \bar \kappa N}$, then for all $N$ such that $2^N\ge \beta^2 e^{2\beta}$, the statement $\mathcal A(L_N,t_N,\delta_N)$ holds. 
    
    At the same time, if $L\in [e^{\beta/10}, \beta^2 e^{2\beta}]$, then $\mathcal A(L, t, e^{ - t e^{- c \beta(\log L)^2}})$ holds for all $t$.

[Lemma 3 (Transversal response stability) of arXiv:2608.16701, 'Order-Sensitive Fast-Synapse Limits in Sparse Excitatory--Inhibitory Threshold--Reset Netw'] If $T$ is regular, there is $C_{\rm hit}<\infty$ such that, for every class
$q$ and every continuous current $J$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak d_{q,T}(J,I)
 \le C_{\rm hit}\|J-I\|_{L^1(0,T)}.
 
\end{equation}
For sufficiently small current error, the firing counts agree and matched
firing times differ by at most
$C_{\rm hit}\|J-I\|_{L^1(0,T)}$.

body:
Let Lambda be a compact hyperbolic set for a diffeomorphism f. Then f restricted to Lambda is EXPANSIVE: there is a constant c > 0 (an expansive constant) such that if x and y are in Lambda and d(f^n(x), f^n(y)) <= c for EVERY integer n, then x = y. Equivalently two distinct orbits in a hyperbolic set must separate to distance more than c at some time, forwards or backwards. Consequently the shadowing orbit of a pseudo-orbit is unique, and by Walters' theorem any partition of a generating diameter below the expansive constant is a generator for entropy purposes.
Both directions of time are used - expansiveness here is two-sided, for an invertible f on a hyperbolic set.
For non-invertible maps the corresponding notion is positive expansiveness, which is a genuinely different and more restrictive condition.

[Theorem 11 (Chained relative concentration of LOO) of arXiv:2608.30261, 'Estimating Population-Risk Curves Along Nonconvex Gradient Flows from the Training Sample'] Assume $L_{n-1}^{\rm hyp},\beta_{n-1}^{\rm mix}<\infty$ for the quantities in
\cref{eq:hyper-lipschitz-constant,eq:mixed-stability}, assume
$\mathfrak E(\cH,d_{\cH})<\infty$ for the entropy integral in
\eqref{eq:entropy-integral}, and assume \eqref{eq:loo-joint-measurability}
with $\mathcal U=\cH$ and $u=(t,\lambda)$.  Define the
finite deterministic mixed-increment scale $a_n^{\rm mix}\in[0,\infty)$ by
\begin{equation}
 a_n^{\rm mix}=L_{n-1}^{\rm hyp}+(n-1)\beta_{n-1}^{\rm mix}.
\end{equation}
For a deterministic anchor $(t_0,\lambda_0)\in\cH$, define the
sample-dependent anchored increment process
$D_S^\circ(\mathord\cdot;t_0,\lambda_0):\cH\to\R$ by
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 D_S^\circ(t,\lambda;t_0,\lambda_0)
 &=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[
   L_{n-1,(t,\lambda)}(S_{-i},Z_i)
   -L_{n-1,(t_0,\lambda_0)}(S_{-i},Z_i)\\
 &\qquad
   -P_0\{L_{n-1,(t,\lambda)}(S_{-i},Z)
   -L_{n-1,(t_0,\lambda_0)}(S_{-i},Z)\}\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
There is a universal constant $C_{\rm ch}\in(0,\infty)$ such that, for every
deterministic anchor $(t_0,\lambda_0)$ and every $\delta\in(0,1)$, the finite deterministic chained radius
$s_n^{\rm ch}(\delta)\in[0,\infty)$ is defined in
\eqref{eq:chained-loo-relative-bound}, and, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{(t,\lambda)\in\cH}|D_S^\circ(t,\lambda;t_0,\lambda_0)|
 \leq s_n^{\rm ch}(\delta)
 :=\frac{C_{\rm ch}a_n^{\rm mix}}{\sqrt n}
 \left\{\mathfrak E(\cH,d_{\cH})
       +D_{\cH}\sqrt{\log\frac4\delta}\right\}.
\end{equation}
If the deterministic anchor satisfies \eqref{eq:loo-anchor-integrability},
then $D_S:\cH\to\R$ is real-valued and
\[
 D_S^\circ(t,\lambda;t_0,\lambda_0)
 =D_S(t,\lambda)-D_S(t_0,\lambda_0),
 \qquad (t,\lambda)\in\cH.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For fixed t>0, N=floor(nt), h_(n,k)=D P_((N-k)/n)f, both exact and hybrid ReLU chains satisfy sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E[theta_k h_(n,k)(U_k);alive]=(D_t/a)log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1). Assumptions: Fixed theta0 in (0,pi], iid Gaussian zero-bias ReLU layers; U=1/(n theta) only on alive states; hybrid kernel from C039. Limiting diffusion starts at0. The full modified-operator occupation identity is stated for the hybrid chain with finite reciprocal moments. The angle transition uses n independent row pairs x=max(g,0), y=max(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h,0), g,h iid standard Gaussians, independent across layers, and the angle between the resulting vectors. Kill at zero norm or zero angle. For the hybrid kernel use a fixed small concentration box for (mean(x^2+y^2),mean((x-y)^2)/theta^2,mean(x^2-y^2)/theta) at small theta, and ordinary Gram averages at larger theta, each centered at its expectation; self-loop on failure. Limit: Unaudited proof. Occupation of the correction is identified, but it has not yet been equated to terminal weak error by a globally controlled telescoping argument. P_s g(u)=E[g(V_s^u)] for dV=(2V+a)ds+sqrt(2)VdW,V0=u,a=1/(3pi). The semigroup sensitivity D_t=D P_t f(0)=E[exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t-V_t^0)], f(u)=1-exp(-u).

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:1fb5aaa46c694c612ced14804ff7512208355a610189cd2c4d16f2d008a8d6f7","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/1f/1fb5aaa46c694c612ced14804ff7512208355a610189cd2c4d16f2d008a8d6f7.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:98724c8e7c4c4475db5c666bd81d25ff0417c42dc077cf1ae14f24f3ad7d26fa","bundle_entry_key":"relu-weighted-log-occupation","bundle_id":"population.t244-logarithmic-bounded-weak-rate-015","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_015.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-relu-weighted-log-occupation","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C040-C041: sharp mesoscopic angle and weighted logarithmic occupation

Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target 1, kind moved. Proofs (unaudited).
Use C039's global hybrid normalized/ordinary Gram regularization. Its
reciprocal U=1/(n theta) is finite; no raw exact-chain reciprocal mean is
used. Fix theta0 in (0,pi] and T<infinity. Constants may depend on theta0,T.
Let a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2).

## C040: quantitative mesoscopic angular law

For either the hybrid chain or the exact chain killed at degeneracy,

    E|k theta_k-1/a|
          <= C_(theta0,T)[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)],
                         1<=k<=floor(Tn), n sufficiently large. (1)

The exact angle is defined to be zero after killing. Consequently
k_n theta_(k_n) -> 3pi in L1 whenever k_n -> infinity and k_n/n -> 0.
The constants are not uniform as theta0 decreases to zero.

### Global reciprocal estimates for the hybrid chain

For all theta in (0,pi], with u=1/(n theta), its one-step multiplier
R=U_next/u=theta/theta_next satisfies

    E[R^q] <= 1+C_q(theta+1/n), q=1,2,
    E[(R-1)^2] <= C(theta^2+1/n),                  (2)
    |E(U_next-u)-(a+2u)/n|
                   <= C[theta/n+1/n^2+u/n^(3/2)]. (3)

To check (2), the multiplier and its coordinate derivatives are uniformly
bounded on each hybrid good box, and equal one off it. Sample-average
Taylor expansion gives E R^q=(theta/F(theta))^q+O_q(1/n), while the
Lipschitz estimate gives E|R-theta/F(theta)|^2<=C/n. The deterministic
ratio theta/F(theta)=1+O(theta) uniformly on (0,pi], proving (2).

For small theta the same centered Taylor expansion through order two
has third-absolute-moment remainder O(n^(-3/2)), uniformly in theta.
The covariance-Hessian contraction for R at theta=0 is2 (C032), its
variation is O(theta), and its deterministic term is
theta/F(theta)=1+a theta+O(theta^2). Hence

    E R=1+a theta+2/n
                    +O(theta^2+theta/n+n^(-3/2)).

Multiplication by u and u*theta=1/n proves (3) on that range. On the
remaining compact angle interval, u<=C/n; bounded multipliers imply
an O(1/n) error, which is bounded by C theta/n since theta is bounded
below there. Thus (3) holds globally. None of these estimates takes
the expectation of an unregularized reciprocal.

Let m_q(j)=E U_j^q. From (2),

    m_1(j+1)<=(1+C/n)m_1(j)+C/n,
    m_2(j+1)<=(1+C/n)m_2(j)+(C/n)m_1(j).

Since U0=1/(n theta0), summing these two recurrences in that order gives

    E U_j<=C_(theta0,T)(j+1)/n,
    E U_j^2<=C_(theta0,T)(j+1)^2/n^2,
                                          0<=j<=Tn.            (4)

The second estimate includes the initial square and the sum of the first
estimate divided by n. Equation (2) also gives

    E[(U_(j+1)-U_j)^2 | U_j,theta_j]
                                      <=C(U_j^2/n+1/n^2).      (5)

### Martingale tracking and inversion

Decompose U_k-U0 into its conditional mean increments and the square-
integrable martingale M_k. Orthogonality of martingale increments and
(4)-(5) imply

    ||M_k||_2 <= C[sqrt(k^3/n^3)+sqrt(k)/n].                    (6)

Using (3), (4), and the global p=2 angle bound from C039, Minkowski gives

    ||U_k-U0-a k/n-M_k||_2
       <= (2/n)sum_(j<k)||U_j||_2
          +C/n sum_(j<k)||theta_j||_2+Ck/n^2
          +C/n^(3/2)sum_(j<k)||U_j||_2
       <= C[k(k+1)/n^2+log(k+1)/n+k/n^2
                                      +k(k+1)/n^(5/2)].        (7)

Thus with Z_k=nU_k/k,

    ||Z_k-a||_2<=C[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)], 1<=k<=Tn.              (8)

Here log(k+1)/k<=C/sqrt(k), k/n<=sqrt(T)*sqrt(k/n), and the initial
nU0/k term is O_(theta0)(1/k). These justify the simplification in (8).

Now Y_k=k theta_k=1/Z_k. C039 with p=2 gives a uniform bound E Y_k^2<=C_T.
On {Z_k>=a/2}, |Y_k-1/a|<=2|Z_k-a|/a^2. On the complementary event,
Chebyshev bounds its probability by4||Z_k-a||_2^2/a^2. Cauchy-Schwarz
and the uniform second moment of Y_k bound its contribution to the L1
error by C||Z_k-a||_2 (if this norm is large, the same inequality follows
by increasing C). This proves (1) for the hybrid chain.

Couple the exact chain with it through time k as in C039. The discrepancy
probability is Ck exp(-cn). Both angles lie in [0,pi], so the additional
L1 error in k theta_k is at most Ck^2 exp(-cn). For k<=Tn this is absorbed
by C_(T)/sqrt(k). This proves (1) for the exact chain.

## C041: the network's weighted singular occupation coefficient

Let P_s be the semigroup of dV=(2V+a)ds+sqrt(2)V dW, V0=0, and
f(u)=1-exp(-u). Fix t>0, N=floor(nt), t_n=N/n, and

    h_(n,k)(u)=D P_(t_n-k/n)f(u), 1<=k<N,
    D_t=D P_t f(0)=E[exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t-V_t)].

For both the hybrid chain and the exact chain with the alive indicator,

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E[theta_k h_(n,k)(U_k);alive]
                            =(D_t/a) log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1).   (9)

For the hybrid chain, with C=B-A^2/2 from C033,

    (1/n^2)sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E[(C P_(t_n-k/n)f)(U_k)]
                    =D_t log(n)/(2pi n)+O_(theta0,t)(1/n).     (10)

This is an occupation calculation on actual chain states, not yet a
telescoped weak-error formula for the terminal observable.

Proof. The affine solution V_v^u=V_v^0+uJ_v, J_v=exp(v+sqrt(2)W_v),
gives bounded first and second initial-value derivatives of P_v f,
uniformly for 0<=v<=t and u>=0. The time derivative of D P_v f is bounded
as in C034: (Af)' is bounded and E J_v is finite. Therefore

    |h_(n,k)(u)-D_(t_n)|<=C_t(k/n+u).                         (11)

On alive states theta_k U_k=1/n. C039 gives E theta_k<=C/(k+1), so

    E[theta_k |h_(n,k)(U_k)-D_(t_n)|;alive]<=C_t/n.

Its sum is O_t(1). From (1),

    |E theta_k-1/(ak)|<=C[k^(-3/2)+1/sqrt(nk)],

whose sum from1 toN-1 is bounded by C_(theta0,t). Consequently
sum E theta_k=(1/a)log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1). Combining these facts and
|D_(t_n)-D_t|<=C_t/n proves (9). The killed exact chain has the same
estimates and the identity theta*U=1/n only on alive states, as required.

The singular drift term in C is b/u. In (10) its contribution is b/n
times (9), giving (b/a)D_t log(n)/n. The remaining terms are

    (8u+a/5) D P_v f+(4u^2-3au/5) D^2 P_v f.

Their expected absolute values are uniformly bounded using the bounded
derivatives and (4) through time t_n. Their n^-2 sum is therefore O(1/n).
Finally b/a=1/(2pi), proving (10).

The remaining global weak-rate step is a semigroup telescoping identity
whose accumulated local errors are O(1/n) for this unbounded reciprocal
state space and whose initial-layer contribution is also O(1/n).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:48d5412d05f2566420246d906fe5e2cb5ea63da0a7aee9e2d7460ec5d88ae3f3","revision_digest":"sha256:32b753a4fdf7fd9e737ebbe90b58f470577d6a40e9cfebd36fc13ae67d0ee2b2","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C041:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary cor:qRacah_hexagon_kernel_spectral_description of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] The fixed-slice correlation kernel $K_t(x,y)$
	(equation eq:K_t_x_y_fixed_slice of the paper) of the $q$-Racah
	nonintersecting path ensemble inside the hexagon with
	sides $a,b,c,a,b,c$ (where $T=b+c$, $S=c$, $N=a$) is the
	kernel of the orthogonal spectral projection onto the
	subspace corresponding to the spectral interval
	\begin{equation}
		
		\left[ -q^{-N+1}(1-q^{N-1})(q^{-T-N}-1),0 \right]
	\end{equation}
	of the
	difference operator
	\begin{equation}
		
		\bigl(\mathfrak{D}g\bigr)(x)\coloneqq

[Corollary 17 of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Consider the following classes of wavelet bases:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item A wavelet basis of \(L^2(\mathbb{R})\) associated with an MRA.
    \item A vector-valued wavelet basis of \(L^2(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}^m)\) (\(m \ge 2\)) associated with a VMRA.
    \item An \(m\)-multiwavelet basis of \(L^2(\mathbb{R})\) associated with an MRA.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
  \textup{(1)} \;\implies\; \textup{(2)}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \textup{(2)} \;\iff\; \textup{(3)}.
\]
In particular, any basis in \textup{(1)} yields bases in \textup{(2)} and \textup{(3)}, and the construction preserves regularity, vanishing moments, and compact support.

[Lemma NEW-l:strong-solution-diffusion of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] {lacker2019local}}]

Consider the finite or locally finite, infinite graph $\Psi({\cal X })$ on ${\cal X }$ 
equipped with  initial conditions $\{M(x)\}_{x \in {\cal X }}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$, $d'\in\mathbb{N}$,  and
uniformly  bounded over  ${\cal X }$, i.e.,
 $\sup_{x\in{\cal X }}|M(x)|\le L$. 
Consider i.i.d. standard Brownian motions $\{Z_x(\cdot)\}_{x \in {\cal X }}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ on $[0,t_0]$, for $t_0\in(0,\infty)$ and  
 the Lipschitz drift and diffusion  coefficients $b$, $\sigma$
 as per Definition~(NEW-d:lip_assum of the paper). Then the system~(equation NEW-e:sys_ID_V of the paper), with initial conditions as above, admits a {\em unique solution with the family of processes $\{M[x]\}_{x \in \mathcal{X}}$},  taking values in the space of continuous paths $\mathbb {M} \owns M[x]=(M(x,t); t \in [0, t_0])$. Moreover, the trajectories $M[x]$ are uniformly bounded in $L^2$:
 \begin{equation}
 \sup_{x\in{\cal X }}\mathbb{E}  [\| M[x]\|^2] <C',
 \end{equation}
 where  the constant $C'$ depends only on $t_0$, the Lipschitz constant $K_{t_0}$, as well as on the bound $L$ of  the initial conditions, and {\em not} on the graph structure.

[Proposition 4 (Zvonkin change-of-variables identity) of arXiv:2608.29726, '\LARGE A Priori Estimates for Singular Fractional Stochastic Burgers Equations'] For smooth data, the variable \(m\) from \eqref{eq:m-def} solves
\begin{equation}
  m_t-\partial_y\Dcal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}m
  =\partial_y\bigl(a m^2+2Q_\lambda m+R\bigr),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  a&=(J^2)^\Phi,
  &\qquad Q_0&=(\ell J)^\Phi,\\
  Q_\lambda&=Q_0+\frac\lambda2\psi^\Phi,
  &\qquad R&=(\ell^2)^\Phi.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For a scalar field \(f\), define the transformed flux operator by
\begin{equation}
  \Dcal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}f
  =\bigl[
    \Rcal_\gamma(Jf^\Psi)
    +f^\Psi\Lambda^\gamma\psi
  \bigr]^\Phi.
\end{equation}
Throughout, \(\Dcal_\Psi^\gamma\) and
\(\Acal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}:=-\partial_y\Dcal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}\) are,
respectively, the transformed flux and diffusion operators.
Here \(a=(J^2)^\Phi\) is the coefficient of the quadratic transport
flux; the principal diffusion coefficient is
\((J^\gamma)^\Phi\).

[Theorem Riesz–Markov–Kakutani on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) \cite{rudin1987real} of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Every bounded linear functional 
\[
  L: C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathbb{C}
\]
is of the form
\[
  L(f) \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x)\,d\mu(x),
  \qquad f \in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d),
\]
for a unique complex Radon measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).  Moreover,
\[
  \|L\|_{(C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d))^*} 
  \;=\; \|\mu\|
  \;=\; \lvert \mu\rvert(\mathbb{R}^d),
\]
where \(\|\mu\|\) is the total variation of \(\mu\).  Conversely, each complex Radon measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) of finite total variation defines a bounded linear functional on \(C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d)\) via integration. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Riesz–Markov–Kakutani on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) \cite{rudin1987real}

[Proposition 1 (Pareto law of nearest-neighbor ratios) of arXiv:2608.27634, 'Curvature-Aware Radius Shrinkage for Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Classification'] Suppose the observations in a neighborhood of $x$ are generated by a
	homogeneous Poisson point process of (locally constant) rate $\rho$ on the
	$d$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$, restricted to the scale spanned by
	the first two nearest neighbors of $x$ (local density homogeneity). Then
	$\mu(x) = r_2(x)/r_1(x)$ has cumulative distribution function
	\begin{equation}
		F(\mu) = 1 - \mu^{-d}, \qquad \mu \geq 1,
		
	\end{equation}
	i.e., $\mu(x)$ follows a Pareto distribution with unit scale and shape
	parameter equal to the intrinsic dimension $d$, independently of the local
	density $\rho$.

[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Let $\{X_n\}$ be real valued random variables with probability measures $\{\mu_n\}$. Suppose for every $m=0, 1, \ldots$, 
$\mathbb{E}(X_n^m)$ converges to say $\beta_m$ (finite). Then there is
a probability measure $\mu$ whose moments are $\{\beta_m\}$. If $\{\beta_m\}$ determines a unique probability measure
$\mu$, then $\mu_n$ converges weakly to $\mu$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let G be a finite undirected loopless multigraph on n vertices with positive edge weights w_e, L its weighted Laplacian, and t > 0. A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). Z(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests, and Q_t = (I + tL)^-1. Then det(I + tL) = Z(t) = sum over spanning rooted forests F of t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e. (P. Chebotarev and E. Shamis.)

body: In probability theory, de Finetti's theorem states that exchangeable observations are conditionally independent relative to some latent variable. An epistemic probability distribution could then be assigned to this variable. It is named in honor of Bruno de Finetti, and one of its uses is in providing a pragmatic approach to de Finetti's well-known dictum "Probability does not exist".
title: De Finetti's theorem

body: For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). Consequently the enclosing-ball (quadratic lower) curvature condition excess >= c d^2/r holds at the axis if and only if p <= 2: for p < 2 the excess is of larger order than quadratic (the condition holds with room), at p = 2 it is exactly quadratic with constant 2, and for every p > 2 the contact is quartic or flatter and the enclosing-ball constant is ZERO. The curvature hypothesis consumed by localization arguments is therefore genuinely restrictive - entire familiar norm families fail it at their axis directions - and cannot be discharged by convexity or symmetry alone. Numerically verified: measured excess/predicted ratios 0.9995-1.0000 across p in {1.5, 2, 3, 4} at two offsets, and the quadratic test excess/(d^2/r) converges to a constant for p <= 2 and to zero for p > 2.

[Lemma lem:isometry_Zk of arXiv:2604.10602, 'Fractional Navier-Stokes Equations with Caputo Derivative Driven by Hermite Noise'] Let $\phi : [0,t] \to \mathcal{L}_2(L^2,\dot{H}^\nu)$ be a deterministic function such that
\[
\int_0^t\int_0^t \langle \phi(u), \phi(v) \rangle_{\mathcal{L}_2} |u-v|^{2H-2} du dv < \infty.
\]
Then the stochastic integral $\int_0^t \phi(s) dZ_H^k(s)$ belongs to the $k$-th Wiener chaos and satisfies
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\int_0^t \phi(s) dZ_H^k(s)\right\|_\nu^2\right]
= H(2H-1) \int_0^t\int_0^t \langle \phi(u), \phi(v) \rangle_{\mathcal{L}_2} |u-v|^{2H-2} du dv.
\]

[Theorem 17 of arXiv:2607.04012, 'Hölder regularity for backward stochastic Volterra integral equations and applications to '] Let Assumption \ref{assumption:continuity-nodal-data} hold, and let $(\Psi^\pi,G^\pi)$ be the left-point data defined in \eqref{eq:left-point-data}. Assume also that there exists a constant $L>0$, independent of $\pi$, such that $\max_{0\leq k\leq N-2} \Delta_k/\Delta_{k+1}\leq L$.
Then there exists a constant $C>0$, independent of $\pi$, such that, for $|\pi|$ sufficiently small,
\begin{flalign*}
    \mathcal E^Y(\pi)+\mathcal E^Z(\pi)
    &\leq
    C\bigg(
    \rho(|\pi|)^2
    +
    |\pi|
    +
    \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}
    \Delta_k
    \mathbb E\bigg[
    \int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}
    |Z^\pi(t_k,s)|^2\,ds
    \bigg]
    \\
    &\quad+
    \sum_{k=0}^{N-2}
    \Delta_k
    \sum_{l=k+1}^{N-2}
    \mathbb E\bigg[
    \int_{t_l}^{t_{l+1}}
    \big|
    Z^\pi(t_k,s)-\scalar{Z^\pi}_{k,l+1}
    \big|^2\,ds
    \bigg]
    \bigg).
\end{flalign*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 17 of arXiv:2607.04012

\begin{equation}

    u^\beta(t,x)
    =
    \P(
        \sigma^{\beta}>t,\,
        X_t>x
    ).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
    u^\beta=v^{\beta},
    \qquad
    \sigma^{\beta}\sim\beta.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

  Let $\sF\supseteq\sigma(W)$ be a $\sigma$-algebra, let $\lambda>0$, and define $R_1$ and $R_2$ via~\eqref{eq: Regression Property} and~\eqref{eq: Correlation Property}.

body: In mathematics, the free group $F_{S}$ over a given set $S$ consists of all words that can be built from members of $S$, considering two words to be different unless their equality follows from the group axioms (e.g. $st=suu^{-1}t$ but $s\neq t^{-1}$ for $s,t,u\in S$). The members of $S$ are called generators of $F_{S}$, and the number of generators is the rank of the free group. An arbitrary group $G$ is called free if it is isomorphic to $F_{S}$ for some subset $S$ of $G$, that is, if there is a subset $S$ of $G$ such that every element of $G$ can be written in exactly one way as a product of finitely many elements of $S$ and their inverses (disregarding trivial variations such as $st=suu^{-1}t$).

body: [Defn def:alephcomp of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] The \textbf{$\aleph$-completion} of $\mathcal{Z}(\Phi)$, denoted by $\mathcal{Z}_\aleph(\Phi)$, is the subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ defined as follows. A multislope $\bm{s} = (s_1, \dots, s_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is in $\mathcal{Z}_\aleph(\Phi)$ if and only if there is a generalized multislope $(\widetilde s_1,\dots,\widetilde s_n)$ realized by a $\Phi$-horizontal foliation such that each index $i$ satisfies either $\widetilde{s}_i = s_i$ or $\widetilde{s}_i=\aleph$; in other words, $\aleph$ may be treated as a wildcard.
title: Defn def:alephcomp of arXiv:2608.30031

[Theorem 6 (Anderson's strong Wigner theorem) of arXiv:2608.04824, 'Strong Convergence for a General Class of Random Matrix Models'] For each \(1\leq j\leq m\), let \(W_{j,n}\) be \(n^{-1/2}\) times the
upper-left \(n\times n\) corner of an infinite Hermitian Wigner array
satisfying the hypotheses of
\cite[Theorems~1 and~2 and Corollary~1]{anderson-2013-polynomial}: its
off-diagonal entries are centered with unit second absolute moment and finite
fourth moment, its diagonal entries are centered real variables with finite
fourth moment, and the real and imaginary parts of each off-diagonal entry
are independent.  Assume that the arrays are independent.  Then
\((W_{1,n},\ldots,W_{m,n})\) converges almost surely strongly in
\(*\)-distribution to a free standard semicircular family.  The conclusion
also holds for polynomials with fixed matrix coefficients. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Anderson's strong Wigner theorem

body:
[Lemma 7 (Standard properties of Friedrichs mollifiers,
		see \cite{Li-Liu-Tang-2021-SPA,Taylor-2011-PDEbook3}) of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let $J_n$ be defined by \eqref{Define Jn}. Then the following properties
		hold.
		\begin{enumerate}[label={\bf (\arabic*)},leftmargin=0.79cm]
			\setlength\itemsep{0.2em}
			\item For every $r\in\mathbb R$, $J_n$ is self-adjoint on $H^r$:
			\[
			\langle J_nf,g\rangle_{H^r}
			=
			\langle f,J_ng\rangle_{H^r},
			\quad f,g\in H^r.
			\]
			Moreover, $J_n$ commutes with every Fourier multiplier; in particular,
			it commutes with $\mathcal D^r$, $\partial_x$, and $\mathcal H$ whenever
			the corresponding compositions are defined.
			
			\item For every $r\in\mathbb R$ and $f\in H^r$,
			\[
			\sup_{n\ge1}\|J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^r;H^r)}\le1,
			\quad
			\lim_{n\to\infty}\|J_nf-f\|_{H^r}=0.
			\]
			In addition,
			\[
			\sup_{n\ge1}
			\|J_n\|_{\mathscr L(L^\infty;L^\infty)}<\infty.
			\]
			
			\item For every $a,b\in\mathbb R$ with $a>b$,
			\[
			\|\mathbf I-J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)}
			\lesssim
			n^{-(a-b)},
			\]
			whereas, for $a<b$,
			\[
			\|J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)}
			\lesssim
			n^{b-a}.
			\]
			Consequently, for each fixed $n\ge1$, $J_n$ is a smoothing operator:
			$J_n\in\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title:
Standard properties of Friedrichs mollifiers,
		see \cite{Li-Liu-Tang-2021-SPA,Taylor-2011-PDEbook3}

[Openquestion 29 (Fairness from fixed-length compatibility) of arXiv:2601.16580, 'Coin flipping and waiting times paradoxes \\ Why fair coins are exceptional'] Assume the stochastic-dominance relation \(\prec_{\mathrm{st}}\) is defined as in Section~\ref{sec:stoch-dom}.
We proved that a fair die induces a total pre-order (hence no \(\prec_{\mathrm{st}}\)-cycles) at each fixed length.
Is the converse true? That is, if for every fixed \(k\ge 2\) the relation \(\prec_{\mathrm{st}}\) has no directed cycle on \(\mathcal{A}^k\), must the die be fair? (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

body:
[Lemma 30 (Cutoff tails for the linear and cross-quadratic fields) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $0\le\theta<1/2-\betasum$.  For the difference from the uncut field, let
$p_{a,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}$ and
$q_{\Theta,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}$ be nonnegative majorants of the sum of the
static covariance density and the normalized time-increment density.  For
every $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{align}
 p_{a,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)
 &\lesssim
 \one_{\{|\xi|\ge c_0\Lambda\}}
 \langle\xi\rangle^{-2+2\beta_a+2\theta},
 \\
 q_{\Theta,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)
 &\lesssim_{\varepsilon}
 \max\{\langle\xi\rangle,\Lambda\}^{-1+2\betasum+2\theta+\varepsilon}.
 
\end{align}
The corresponding difference of two non-nested admissible cutoffs is bounded
by the sum of the two right-hand sides.  Moreover, for every
\[
 s<-\frac12-\beta_a
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 r<-1-\betasum,
\]
one can choose $\theta,\varepsilon,\delta>0$ so that
\begin{align}
 \sum_{N\in\Dyd}N^{2s+3+\delta}
 \sup_{|\xi|\sim N}p_{a,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)&\longrightarrow0,
 \\
 \sum_{N\in\Dyd}N^{2r+3+\delta}
 \sup_{|\xi|\sim N}q_{\Theta,>\Lambda}^{(\theta)}(\xi)&\longrightarrow0.
 
\end{align}
Both tails decay polynomially along dyadic $\Lambda$.

body:
[Defn def Holder of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] A function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ on an infinite product space $X = \prod_{n\in \mathbb{N}} X_n$ of metric spaces $(X_n,d_n)$ is H\"older continuous with respect to the standard metric on $X$ given by
\[d(x,y) = \sum_{n\in \mathbb{N}} 2^{-n} \min\{1, d_n(x_n,y_n)\},\]
if there exists $\alpha >0$ such that
\[\abs{f(x)-f(y)}\leq d(x,y)^{\alpha} \quad \text{for all } x,y\in X. 

\]
title: Defn def Holder of arXiv:2411.14350

[Definition 11 of arXiv:2609.04033, 'From configuration spaces to graph complexes via $\mathbf{FA}$-modules'] Let $A$ be an $\mathbf{FS}^{op}$-module. The bar construction of $A$, denoted $\mathsf{B}(A)$, is a sequence of chain complexes $\mathsf{B}(A)(n)$.  The underlying graded vector spaces are defined by:
	$$
	\mathsf{B}(A)(n) = \ds\bigoplus_{\substack{ (\mathsf{t},v)} \in n\text{-Tree}_\ast} A(\mathsf{t},v)\tensor det(\mathsf{t}).
	$$
The differential is the linear extension of the map $d_{(\mathsf{t},v)}:= \sum_{e\in E(\mathsf{t})} d_e$.
title: Definition 11 of arXiv:2609.04033

[Definition 4 of arXiv:2608.27398, 'Strict Stability and Strict Minimality of Regular Area-Minimizing Hypercones: A Quantitati'] The cone $\C$ is \emph{strictly minimizing} if there is $\Theta_\C>0$
such that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf M(\C_1)
    \leq \mathbf M(T)-\Theta_\C\varepsilon^n
\end{equation}
whenever $\varepsilon>0$ and $T$ is an integer-multiplicity
$n$-current satisfying
$$
    \spt T\subset\R^{n+1}\setminus B_\varepsilon,
    \qquad
    \partial T=\partial\C_1.
$$
title: Definition 4 of arXiv:2608.27398

[Theorem 9 (Pressure; the Jensen gap as a chord--tangent inequality) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Under uniform ellipticity and irreducibility:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\varphi$ is convex on $[0,\infty)$ and real-analytic, with $\varphi(0)=\log m_*$ and $\varphi(1)=\log\rho(M)$.
\item $\varphi'(0)=\E_{q\otimes q}[\log p_{d,d'}]$, and for $\nu_h$-a.e.\ ray $\xi$, $n^{-1}\sum_{e\in o\to\xi,\ |e|\le n}\log p_e\to\E_{q\otimes q}[\log p]$; i.e.\ $\varphi(0)+\varphi'(0)=\ell$ is the quenched rate of Theorem~\ref{thm:gap} (with $w\equiv1$).
\item (The gap.) $\varphi(1)\ge\varphi(0)+\varphi'(0)$, i.e.
\[
\rho(M)\ge m_*\,e^{\E_{q\otimes q}[\log p]}=e^{\ell},
\]
with equality if and only if $p_{d,d'}$ is constant on $\supp q\times\supp q$. This is the sharp form of the gap in Theorem~\ref{thm:gap}(3).
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma ues1a of arXiv:2604.11412, 'Stability of invariant measures of the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation with vani'] If (equation 1.1 of the paper)  holds,
then for every
 $\mathbf{u}_0 \in H^1({\mathbb R}^2)$, 
 the solution $\mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta}
(t,  \mathbf{u}_0)$ of (equation 1.3* of the paper)
 satisfies: for all $t\ge 0$,
  $\varepsilon\in [0,1]$ and $\delta\in (0,1]$,  
 $$
\mathrm{E}
\left (
 \|
 \mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta} (t,  \mathbf{u}_0) \|^2_{H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)}
 \right )
 +
  \int_0^t e^{s-t}  \mathrm{E}
\left ( \|
 \mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta} (s,  \mathbf{u}_0) \|^2_{H^2(\mathbb{R}^2)}
 +
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^2}
 |\mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta} (s,  \mathbf{u}_0)|^2
 |\nabla \mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta} (s,  \mathbf{u}_0)|^2  dx
 \right )
 ds$$
 $$
 +\delta\int_0^t e^{s-t}  \mathrm{E}
\left ( \|
 \mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta} (s,  \mathbf{u}_0) \|^2_{H^3(\mathbb{R}^2)}\right)ds
 \le
   M_3 +M_3 e^{-t}\| \mathbf{u}_0 \|^2_{H^1({\mathbb R}^2)},
 $$
 and
 $$
   \int_0^t   \mathrm{E}
\left ( \|
 \mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta} (s,  \mathbf{u}_0) \|^2_{H^2(\mathbb{R}^2)}
 + 
   \delta   
  \|
 \mathbf{u}^{\varepsilon,\delta} (s,  \mathbf{u}_0) \|^2_{H^3(\mathbb{R}^2)}\right)ds
 \le
   M_3 t +M_3 \| \mathbf{u}_0 \|^2_{H^1({\mathbb R}^2)},
  $$

[Thm weak_cv_mean_rev_process of arXiv:2605.29073, 'Volterra clocks and their pure-jump limits: \\hitting times of curved boundaries'] We consider $K \in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb R_+\,, \mathbb R_+)$ a completely monotone kernel, $\lambda\,, \nu\,, T > 0\,$, and $f$ satisfying Assumption (assumption:f of the paper). Let $a\,,b : \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+ \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+\,$, with $a$ non-decreasing and $b$ locally bounded and measurable, and define 
    $$
    G_0^n(t) := \int_0^t\,g_0^n(s)\,ds\,, \quad g_0^{n}(t) := a(t) + n\,\int_0^t\,K(t-s)\,b(s)\,ds\,, \quad t \geq 0\,,
    $$
    i.e.~$g_0^n \in \mathcal G_{nK}\,$. For each $n \geq 0\,$, let $(W^n\,, X^n)$ be a weak solution to (equation eq:Volterra_clock of the paper) on $[0\,,T]$ for the input $(K\,, G_0^n\,, f\,, n \lambda\,, n \nu)\,$, which exists by Theorem (thm:weak_existence_Volterra_clock_DDS of the paper). Then, as $n \to + \infty\,$, $(W^n \,, X^n) \Rightarrow (W^*\,, X^*)$ in $D^{\circ}[0\,, T]\,$, where $W^*$ is a standard Brownian motion, and 
    $$
    X^{*}_t := \inf \{s \geq 0\,:\, \lambda\,s - \nu\,W^*_{f(s)} > \bar b(t) \}\,, \quad t \leq T\,,
    $$
    with $\bar b := \int_0^{\cdot}\,b(s)\,ds\,$.

[Theorem 39 of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] For every integer $n\geq4$, there exists a nondegenerate continuum
$K\subset S^n$ with $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}K=1$ such that, with
$M:=S^n\setminus K$, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $M$ is a contractible smooth open manifold that is not simply connected at infinity.

\item There exists a smooth function $\phi:M\to(0,\infty)$ with
$m_0:=\inf_M\phi>0$ such that, for every $t\in(-m_0,\infty)$,
\[
g^{(t)}:=(\phi+t)^{4/(n-2)}g_{st}|_M
\]
is smooth, complete, and locally conformally flat, with
\[
\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}=n(n-1)t(\phi+t)^{-(n+2)/(n-2)}.
\]
Hence $\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}$ is negative, zero, or positive according as
$t<0$, $t=0$, or $t>0$, and
\[
\lim_{t\to0}\int_M|\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}|^{n/2}\,dV_{g^{(t)}}=0.
\]
For $t>0$, the rescaled metric
\[
\bar g^{(t)}
:=t^{-4/(n-2)}g^{(t)}
=\left(1+\frac{\phi}{t}\right)^{4/(n-2)}g_{st}|_M
\]
satisfies
\[
0<\mathrm{Sc}_{\bar g^{(t)}}<n(n-1),
\]
and its scalar curvature decays uniformly to zero at $K$ in the sense
that
\[
 \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
 \sup_{\substack{x\in M\\ d_{g_{st}}(x,K)<\delta}}
 \mathrm{Sc}_{\bar g^{(t)}}(x)=0.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition prop:F-root of arXiv:2608.19050, 'Online Permutation Embedding: \\ Optimal Stopping and Scaling Laws'] Fix $p,q \ge 0$, let $\phi := \phi_{p,q}$ be defined by (equation eq: phipq definition of the paper), and, for $v\in\RR$, define $I_v:=\{x\in[0,1]\,:\,\phi(x)<v\}$ and
\[
    F(v):=\int_{I_v}(v-\phi(x))\,dx
    =
    \int_0^1 (v-\phi(x))_+\,dx.
\]
Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $v\in\RR$, $I_v$ is a (possibly empty) interval subset of $[0,1]$.
    \item There exists a unique $v_*$ such that $F(v_*)=1$.
    \item Let $a_*:=\inf I_{v_*}$ and $b_*:=\sup I_{v_*}$ denote the endpoints of  $I_{v_*}$. Then $0\le a_*<b_*\le1$, and
    \begin{equation}
        v_*
        =
        G_{p,q}(a_*,b_*)
        =
        \min_{0\le a<b\le1}G_{p,q}(a,b),
    \end{equation}
where $G_{p,q}$ is given by (equation eq: Gpq definition of the paper).
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:node-stability of arXiv:2608.29719, 'Persistence Pairing Graphs: Tracking Changes of Selected Homology Bases'] Let $f,g:\mathcal K\longrightarrow\mathbb R$ be filtration functions on the same finite CW complex, and suppose
\[
\|f-g\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon.
\]
Then the $q$-th persistence diagrams admit a bottleneck matching of cost at most $\varepsilon$.

If an off-diagonal interval $u$ is matched to an off-diagonal interval $M(u)$, then
\[
\widetilde c_{\mathrm{node}}(u,M(u)) \leq \min\left\{\frac{\varepsilon}{s_q}, 1\right\}.
\]
The same bound holds when an essential interval is matched to an essential interval.

body:
[Dfn 217 (stochastic control and achievable measures for symmetrized projection pursuit) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $B, W$ be one-dimensional standard Brownian motions, and let $U,U' \sim \unif([0,1])$ (with $B,W,U,U'$ mutually independent).
Define the filtrations 
\[\begin{aligned}
    \cF_X(t) &= \sigma(U, (B(s) : 0\le s\le t))\,, \\
    \cF_{\Ising}(t) &= \sigma(U', (W(s) : 0\le s\le t))\,.
\end{aligned}\]
Let $\ProgMsrbl(\cF_X)$ denote the space of stochastic processes that are progressively measurable with respect to $\cF_X$, and similarly $\ProgMsrbl(\cF_{\Ising})$ for $\cF_{\Ising}$. For $\sigma\in\ProgMsrbl(\cF_X)$ and $w\in\ProgMsrbl(\cF_{\Ising})$, let  
	\begin{align}
	
	X(t)
	&\equiv\int_0^s \sigma_t\,dB(s)\,,\\
	X^\Ising(t)
	&\equiv\int_0^t w_s\,dW(s)
	
	\end{align}
Let $\cM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ be the set of measures $\mu$ which can be expressed as $\mu=\Law(|X(1)|)$
(i.e., $\mu$ is the law of the real-valued random variable $|X(1)|$)
 for $X$ defined by \eqref{eq:main-process-intro-p=1}, and for controls $(\sigma,w)$ satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item the nonnegativity condition
$\sigma_t\ge0$ for all $t\in[0,1]$,
\item the time parametrization condition
$\E[(w_t)^2]=1$ for all $t\in[0,1]$,
\item the \textbf{budget constraint}
	\beq
	\E\Big[(\sigma_t-1)^2\Big]
	\le \frac{(\E w_t)^2}{\alpha}
	\eeq
for all $t\in[0,1]$, and 
\item the \textbf{endpoint condition}
$|X^{\Ising}(1)|=1$.
\end{itemize}
 Let $\cM^{\sph,\sym}(\alpha)$ be the set of measures $\mu$ which can be expressed as $\mu=\Law(|X(1)|)$ for $X$ defined by \eqref{eq:main-process-intro-p=1}, and for controls $(\sigma,w\equiv1)$ satisfying the same conditions as above, \textbf{except for the endpoint constraint}. We use $\bar{\cM}^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$,
$\bar{\cM}^{\sph,\sym}(\alpha)$ to denote the closures with respect to the $2$-Wasserstein metric $\bbW_2$ (defined by \eqref{def:W2} below).
title: stochastic control and achievable measures for symmetrized projection pursuit

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2607.23791, 'Precise cover times for branching random walks on Hamming graphs: (iterated) logarithmic c'] Fix $\delta,\kappa,C_0>0$ and let $0\leq r_d \le C_0d-\kappa\log d$.  From every particle alive at $r_d$, follow
its descendants for time $\kappa\log d$ and kill each  lineage upon its
$\lfloor\delta d/3\rfloor$th mutation.  For every nonempty, possibly
$\cF_{r_d}$-measurable, $\delta d$-separated set $\cC_d$, the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item each truncated descendant cluster hits at most one point of $\cC_d$;
\item $\Pp(\text{truncation deletes a visit to }\cC_d)=o(1)$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Lemma 9 of arXiv:2607.23791

body: In mathematics, specifically functional analysis, a trace-class operator is a linear operator for which a trace may be defined, such that the trace is a finite number independent of the choice of basis used to compute the trace. This trace of trace-class operators generalizes the trace of matrices studied in linear algebra. All trace-class operators are compact operators.

[Theorem S1T1 of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Suppose that $\mathfrak{L}^N$ is a sequence of random elements in $\mathbb{Y}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ that satisfies Assumptions 1 and 2 above. Define the sequence $\mathcal{L}^N = \{\mathcal{L}_i^N\}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \in C(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R})$ by
$$\mathcal{L}^N_i(t) = \sigma^{-1} d_N^{-1/2} \cdot \left( L_i^N(t d_N) - p td_N - C_N\right), $$
where $L_i^N(s)$ is defined for non-integer $s$ by linear interpolation. Then, $\mathcal{L}^N$ is a tight sequence of random elements in $C(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R})$. Moreover, any subsequential limit satisfies the Brownian Gibbs property from [CorHamA], see also [DM21]. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma Feller of arXiv:2601.15223, 'Large time behaviour for a class of 2D and 3D stochastic non-Newtonian fluids of different'] The family $\{\mathrm{T}_t\}_{t\geq 0}$ is Feller, that is, $\mathrm{T}_tg\in\mathrm{C}_{b}(\mathbb{H})$ if $g\in\mathrm{C}_b(\mathbb{H})$. Moreover, for any $g\in\mathrm{C}_b(\mathbb{H})$, $\mathrm{T}_tg(\boldsymbol{x})\to g(\boldsymbol{x})$ as $t\downarrow 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma Feller of arXiv:2601.15223

Let integer d>=1, p>0, and mu,nu be Borel probability measures on Q=(-1,1]^d. Let P_ell be the half-open dyadic partitions of Q into2^(d ell) cubes of side2^(1-ell), and set D_p(mu,nu)=[(2^p-1)/2]sum_{ell>=1}2^(-p ell)sum_{F in P_ell}|mu(F)-nu(F)|. Define T_p(mu,nu)=inf_{pi in Couplings(mu,nu)} integral_{Q x Q}||x-y||_2^p pi(dx,dy). Then T_p(mu,nu)<=kappa_(p,d)D_p(mu,nu), where kappa_(p,d)=2^(p(1+d/2))(2^p+1)/(2^p-1). This is the compact case in Step1 ofLemma5p6,1312.2128v1. For p>1 it yields W_p(mu,nu)<=[kappa_(p,d)D_p(mu,nu)]^(1/p) under W_p=T_p^(1/p). The transport inequality is deterministic, so it applies to empirical measures with dependent samples as well; their cell-discrepancy estimates require their own probabilistic hypotheses.
integer d>=1 and real p>0
arbitrary Borel probability measures on Q=(-1,1]^d
Euclidean p-transport cost T_p as explicitly defined
the exact normalized dyadic discrepancy stated; sample independence is not required for this deterministic inequality

body:
[Definition Sublinear expectation \cite{pengbook} of arXiv:2606.15203, 'The existence of invariant sublinear expectations for $G\text{-}$SDEs'] A sublinear expectation $\mathbb{E}$ is a functional $\mathbb{E}$: $\mathcal{H} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ satisfying \\
 \rm{(1).} Monotonicity. $\mathbb{E}[X] \leq \mathbb{E}[Y], \ \mathrm{if}\  X \leq Y$.\\
    
     

 \rm{(2)}. Constant preserving. $ \mathbb{E}[c] = c\ \mathrm{for}\ c\in \mathbb{R}$.\\

 
 
\rm{(3)}. Sub-additivity. For each $X,Y \in \mathcal{H}$, $ \mathbb{E}[X+Y] \leq  \mathbb{E}[X]+ \mathbb{E}[Y]$.\\

 
 
 \rm{(4)}. Positive homogeneity. $\mathbb{E}[\lambda X] =  \lambda\mathbb{E}[X]\ \mathrm{for}\ \lambda \geq 0$.\\
title: Sublinear expectation \cite{pengbook}

[Theorem thm:general-diffuse of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Assume that quorum weights are diffuse. Fix $\theta\in(0,1)$ and suppose there exist positive scales $(a_N)_{N\in \mathbb{N}}$ and a continuous, strictly increasing function $F:[0,\infty)\to[0,1)$ with
\[
F(0)=0,
\qquad
\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}F(\alpha)=1,
\]
such that for every $\alpha\ge 0$,
\[
m_N(a_N\alpha)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{} F(\alpha).
\]
Let $\alpha_\theta$ be the unique solution of $F(\alpha_\theta)=\theta$. Then
\[
\frac{\tau_{N,\theta}}{a_N}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{\mathbb{P}}\alpha_\theta.
\]

[Theorem theo:ImbrieNewman of arXiv:2512.12124, 'A discontinuous percolation phase transition on the hierarchical lattice'] Let $\mathcal{J} : \left[0,\infty\right) \times E \to \left[0,\infty \right)$ be a proper family of kernels with $\lambda_c(\mathcal{J})<\infty$. If the limit $\beta = \lim_{|e|\to \infty} L^{-d}\mathcal{J}(\lambda_c,e) |e|^{2d} \left(\log\log|e|\right)^{-1}$
	is well-defined and finite, then
        $\mathbb{P}_{\lambda_c} \left( 0\leftrightarrow  \infty \right)^2 \beta = 1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theo of arXiv:2411.07158, 'Markov chains on trees: almost lower and upper directed cases'] Let $\;{\sf U}$ be an irreducible {\sf AUD}\xspace transition matrix on a finite or infinite tree $T$, and let $\pi:=(\pi_v,v\in T)$ be an invariant measure of $\;{\sf U}$. Set, for all $u,v \in T$,
  \begin{eqnarray} {\sf D}_{v,u}=\pi_u{\sf U}_{u,v}/\pi_v, ~~~u,v\in T.\end{eqnarray}
  \begin{itemize} \topsep0pt   \itemsep=0pt   \partopsep=0pt   \parsep=0pt \setcounter{c}{0}
  \addtocounter{c}{1}\item[($\roman{c}$)] ${\sf D}$ is an {\sf ALD}\xspace irreducible transition matrix, which possesses also $\pi$ as invariant measure
  \addtocounter{c}{1}\item[($\roman{c}$)] ${\sf D}$ is positive recurrent iff ${\sf U}$ is,
  \addtocounter{c}{1}\item[($\roman{c}$)] ${\sf D}$ is recurrent iff ${\sf U}$ is,
  \addtocounter{c}{1}\item[($\roman{c}$)] If ${\sf U}$ has a right eigenvector $R=(R_u,u\in T)$ with positive coordinate (and associated with the eigenvalue 1) then $\begin{pmatrix} \pi_u R_u,u\in T\end{pmatrix}$ is an invariant measure for ${\sf D}$ (so that this property extends to cones). 
  \end{itemize}\vspace{-2em}~ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered theo of arXiv:2411.07158, 'Markov chains on trees: almost lower and upper directed case'

body:
[Problem 24 of arXiv:2512.02538, 'On the spectral geometry of Liouville quantum gravity'] One \emph{can} hear the shape of LQG. In other words,  given a domain $\Sigma$ and the eigenvalue sequence $(\bl_n)_{n\ge 1}$ of LQG, one can measurably recover the underlying Gaussian free field $\ph$. More precisely, there exists a measurable function $\Phi = \Phi_\Sigma: \R^\N \to H^{-1} (\Sigma)$ such that 
$$
\Phi_\Sigma( (\bl_n)_{n\ge 1}) = \ph, \text{ a.s.} 
$$
In fact, we conjecture that it is possible to measurably recover the pair $(\Sigma, \ph)$ up to isometry, i.e., up to equivalence of quantum surfaces, in the sense of \cite{DS}. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Problem 24 of arXiv:2512.02538

[Theorem 2 (Uniform lower mass bound) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] Consider critical nearest-neighbour bond percolation on $\Z^d$ with $d\geq 11$. For every $\delta>0$,
\[
\lim_{\eta\rightarrow 0}\;\limsup_{R\rightarrow\infty}\;
\bP\left(\inf_{x\in \mathcal C}\bigl|\mathcal C\cap Q_{x,\delta R}\bigr|
\leq \eta R^4 \:\Big\vert\:0\leftrightarrow (Q_{0,R})^c\right)=0,
\]
and the same holds when the conditioning event is replaced by
$\{|\mathcal C|\geq R^4\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform lower mass bound

body:
[Thm 2 (Neumann-boundary compactness and stationarity) of arXiv:2609.00739, '2609.00739'] Let $\Omega\subset\R^2$ be a bounded $C^3$ domain, let $V$ satisfy
Assumption~\ref{assum:potential}, and let
$\eps_j\in(0,1]$ satisfy $\eps_j\downarrow0$.  Let
$u_j:=u_{\eps_j}\in H^1(\Omega;\R^k)$ be weak solutions of
\eqref{eq:intro-system}.  Suppose that
\begin{equation}
\cE_{\eps_j}(u_j;\Omega)\leq M_0
\quad\text{for some }M_0<+\infty.
\end{equation}
Then, after passing to a subsequence, there are a closed countably
$1$-rectifiable set $\Sstar\subset\overline\Omega$, a finite-perimeter
partition $(E_\alpha)_{\alpha=1}^q$ of $\Omega$, Radon measures
$\nustar,\zetastar$, and finite signed Radon measures
$\upmu_{\star,ij}$ on $\overline\Omega$ with the
following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[label=$(\theenumi)$]
\item The phase fields satisfy
\[
 u_j\to u_0:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^q\upsigma_\alpha\mathbf1_{E_\alpha}
 \quad\text{in }L^1(\Omega),
\]
with
$\sum_{\alpha=1}^q\Per(E_\alpha;\Omega)\leq C(V)M_0$, and the convergence is uniform on
compact subsets of $\overline\Omega\backslash \Sstar$ to a locally constant
map $\bar u_0:\overline\Omega\backslash \Sstar\to\Sigma$ that agrees almost
everywhere in $\Omega\backslash \Sstar$ with
$\sum_{\alpha=1}^q\upsigma_\alpha\mathbf1_{E_\alpha}$.

\item The concentration set satisfies
\[
 \Sstar=\supp\nustar=\supp\zetastar,
 \quad
 \cH^1(\Sstar)\leq C(V,\Omega)M_0.
\]

\item The measures in \eqref{eq:intro-measures} converge weakly star to
$\nustar$, $\zetastar$, and $\upmu_{\star,ij}$, respectively, and
\begin{equation}
 \nustar=e\,\cH^1\llcorner\Sstar,
 \quad
 \zetastar=\Uptheta\,\cH^1\llcorner\Sstar,
 \quad
 \upmu_{\star,ij}=m_{ij}\,\cH^1\llcorner\Sstar.
\end{equation}
There are constants $c_0=c_0(V,\Omega)>0$ and
$C_0,C_1<\infty$, depending only on $V$, $\Omega$, and $M_0$, such that
\begin{equation}
 c_0\leq\Uptheta\leq e\leq C_0\Uptheta\leq C_1,
 \quad
 \abs{m_{ij}}\leq2e
 \quad\text{for }\cH^1\text{-almost every }x\in \Sstar.
\end{equation}

\item At $\cH^1$-almost every point of $\Sstar$, let $(\tau,n)$ denote the
approximate tangent-normal frame of $\Sstar$.  For
$a,b\in\{\tau,n\}$ set $m_{ab}:=a^Tm b$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 2\Uptheta=m_{nn}-m_{\tau\tau},
 \quad
 m_{n\tau}=0,
 \quad
 e=m_{nn}.
\end{equation}

\item The rectifiable varifold $\Vbold(\Sstar,\Uptheta)$ is stationary with
free boundary:
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\Sstar}\diver_{T_x\Sstar}X\,\dd\zetastar(x)=0
\end{equation}
for every $X\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\R^2)$ satisfying
$X\cdot\nOmega=0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

\item In the interior, the local straight-segment and constant-density
description of \cite[Theorem 1.3]{Bethuel2025} holds away from an
$\cH^1$-null set.  On a boundary-supported regular arc with no incident
interior branch, $\Uptheta$ has a positive constant representative.  At a
finite-type boundary junction $p$ of $(\Sstar,\zetastar)$ in the sense of
Definition~\ref{defn:finite-type-boundary}, each incident punctured branch
carries a positive constant weight $\Uptheta_\ell$, and
\begin{equation}
 P_{T_p\partial\Omega}
 \left(\sum_\ell\Uptheta_\ell\tau_\ell\right)=0.
\end{equation}
In particular, if the decomposition in
Definition~\ref{defn:finite-type-boundary} consists of exactly one
non-boundary half-arc and no boundary-supported or additional branch, then
that half-arc meets $\partial\Omega$ orthogonally.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Neumann-boundary compactness and stationarity

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2606.17452, 'Optional Stopping for Superhedging Supermartingales'] For a given node $(S, j)$ and a general $f \in P$ define
\begin{equation} \nonumber
\overline{I}_j f (S)\equiv  \inf \left\{\sum_{m \geq 1} V^m: ~~f \leq  \sum_{m \geq 1} \liminf_{n\to \infty}~~\Pi_{j, n}^{V^m, H^m}\;\;\;\mbox{on}\;\; \Se_{(S,j)},\; \Pi_{j, n}^{V^m, H^m}\in \mathcal{E}_{(S,j)}^+  ~~\forall ~~n \geq j \right\}.
\end{equation}
We will use the notation $\overline{I}f \equiv \overline{I}_0f$. We also set, for a general $f \in Q$:
\begin{equation} \nonumber
||f||_j(S) \equiv \overline{I}_j|f|(S)~~\mbox{and}~~||f|| \equiv ||f||_0(S).
\end{equation}
